_childDocuments_.review: I've been keeping an eye on this game while it was in development, and was excited for its release. Like many others have said, the art and character design in this game is extremely charming. There definitely was a lot of love and polish put into the visual aspects of AKA. While the attention to the 2d and 3d art is incredibly admirable for a single developer (not 100% sure about this), the game suffers from what I can only imagine a lack of time against a publishing deadline and an amateur's knowledge of the more nuanced parts of game development. The UI, title screen, story, quest lines, writing, and map all suffer from a lack of polish and a handful of bugs and UX design make playing AKA a fun, but bumpy experience. But in my eyes, that can mostly be forgiven considering how monumental of a task making a game of this size with a team of one. My only real issue that can't be chalked up to lack of time, is that I found the story and dialogue to be ham-fisted in trying to make you feel sad/touched. It's blunt messaging about war, inner peace, loss, trauma, and survivor's guilt, backdropped with a pan-oriental world, made the story seem pretty superficial and an inauthentic experience. That being said, you can tell a lot of love was put into this game. It's influences from Ghibli, Animal Crossing, and A Short Hike are clear. AKA does nail down a peaceful environment and gaming experience without lending itself to a colonial and capitalist mindset, which plagues many other games like this. The ability to tangibly help those around you and exploring the islands was really fun, and I played this game a lot longer than I expected it would last. I surprisingly enjoyed the card game minigame a lot and figuring out the mini environmental puzzles. The casts of characters that you are able to interact with are super cute and I look forward to more from this developer in the future.. But hopefully next time with some help from a professional team so the developer can focus on what they do best.

Find inner peace in a top-down, small, open-world game.
Make things better by growing plants, help others, craft and discover a carefully handcrafted island...
but demons from your past might come back to remind you what you want to forget.

***
Explore different biomes, from cloud forests to snowy mountains.
Connect with the island inhabitants.
A farming experience inspired by permaculture.
Gather resources to craft houses, musical instruments, clothes, etc.
Cook and prepare medicines.
Relax and the back of a giant monster, looking at the clouds or in hot springs under a cherry blossom tree.

But your hardest task will be to find a way to talk to these poor souls who are wandering on the island. These war victims are waiting for your help.

detailed_description: SAMURAI WARRIORS 5 Digital Deluxe Edition Features of the 'SAMURAI WARRIORS 5 Deluxe Edition' A valuable set that, in addition to the game, includes the content below. [Deluxe Edition Bonuses] - Special Blade Rift Blade - Special Katana Masterpiece - Special Spear Sharpened Fang Spear - Special Bow Sky Piercer - Special Horse - Special Skill Gem Set - Items [Season Pass] A pass that allows you to obtain a variety of DLC available after the game's release at a discount. - Additional Scenario & BGM Sets (6) - Additional Weapons Sets (5) (each set has 3 weapons) - Additional Horses (6) [Season Pass Bonus] Allows you to obtain items that can be used to upgrade in-game characters, funds that can be used to upgrade or purchase weapons, and more. Note: 'SAMURAI WARRIORS 5' is also available. Please be careful when making your purchase. Note: Details about the DLC released with the Season Pass as well as their release period will be announced later. Please check the official website. Note: The Season Pass and DLC included in the Season Pass are also planned to be available for individual purchase. Please be careful to avoid making a redundant purchase. About the Game A new SAMURAI WARRIORS begins. After a 7-year wait, a new instalment in the tactical action series 'SAMURAI WARRIORS' is finally here! With this title, the historical period depicted in the first title of the 'SAMURAI WARRIORS' series released in 2004 has been revamped. With visuals that have largely evolved since the first 'SAMURAI WARRIORS', additional officers, and evolved actions, an even deeper drama set in the warring states is depicted. Also, with a focus on the lives of officers Nobunaga Oda and Mitsuhide Akechi, in order to more intensely and boldly depict the warring states era spanning from the end of the Ōnin War to the Incident at Honnōji, the title is the beginning of a new series, in which the stories and characters from the traditional 'SAMURAI WARRIORS' have been revamped. Features of 'SAMURAI WARRIORS 5' ■With officers whose designs have been revamped, as well as new officers, a total of 27 Samurai Warriors join the battle Officers such as a young Nobunaga Oda, known as the 'Great Fool', and daimyō Yoshimoto Imagawa, who was called the 'Greatest Archer in all of Kaidō', appear with new designs that match the setting of this title. Also, new officers such as Toshimitsu Saitō, a retainer of Mitsuhide Akechi, as well as Kōga ninja Mitsuki join the battle. A total of 27 Samurai Warriors interweave their fates to create a dramatic warring states era. ■WARRIORS actions are more thrilling and dazzling than ever before In this title, players can once again enjoy the 'thrill of sending enemies flying' that the WARRIORS series is renowned for. And with new actions that have been added with this title, as well as new depictions that give off a Japanese flair, the WARRIORS actions have become even more stunning. Note: The 'SAMURAI WARRIORS 5 Digital Deluxe Edition' is also available. Please be careful when making your purchase. With the Trial version, you can play the earlier portions of the story. Save data from the Trial version can be carried over to the retail version of the game. ※In order to transfer your save file from the Trial version, you will need to ensure your game is up to date with the latest patch. * The images are from an in-development build and may differ from the final version.

_childDocuments_.review: Samurai Warriors 5 has a surprisingly good PC port. I ran it at 4k and 60 FPS with a midline card with very few drops. It's one of the best ports the series has ever had. The new character designs and story sequences are also damn good, although people will miss the zanier characters. If you've never played a Musou game before, this one might seem pretty great. If you have played one, you'll be shocked at how few movesets there are. Sure, there are nearly 40 characters. But only 27 have unique actions. Those unique actions are basically like the EX moves from DW7. Because Omega Force brought weapon switching back! That thing we all hate bitterly! There are only 15 weapons, so 15 movesets. Samurai Warriors 5, as a result, has very little value in comparison to other games in the series. If you haven't played Orochi 4 or, hell, Spirit of Sanada, you should PROBABLY not spend $60 bucks on a game. For real, this game has less than a third of the movesets that vanilla SW4 had SEVEN YEARS AGO. It has a FRACTION OF THE CONTENT of a SEVEN YEAR OLD GAME.  The dual katanas moveset also appears to be directly borrowed from Zoro from Pirate Warriors. As such, the game gets boring fast. Some of the movesets are really cool, though, such as the drum and ninja blade. But then there are the sleep inducing weapons. The katana. The odachi. The spear. The heavy spear. Want to play as Tadakatsu? He plays exactly like Toshiie. What fun! The story's pretty good, at least, but I think this is the most bored I've been by a Musou game since the first Pirate Warriors came out. There's no good excuse for this amount of cloning. The game also has a dearth of new ideas, plus rush attacks don't have charge attacks anymore, so they're worse than before for no good reason. Not a bad game by any means, but a super disappointing one.
_childDocuments_.name: SAMURAI WARRIORS 5

_childDocuments_.review: If you've never played a musou game, this is the one to try.If you haven't played one in a while, this is the one to come back to.If you have musou fatigue, understandable, but you still need to play this.+ Visuals, art style, presentation is brilliant+ The hack/slash is just premium with familiar and new mechanics+ Campaign is pretty good, character depth/perspectives like never done before with a lot of familiar VAs+ Lots and lots of replayability+ Character designs are really one of the best in the entire series+ Music, bgms+ PC port is great+ Valve Regional prices- Only Japanese VA, only a problem when its difficult to read and play at the same time at tight situations, but you can replay the entire conversation in the menu during the mission- Basic movesets are attached to weapon types rather than characters. So 2 characters using a katana would have most of the same moves except for a few that are unique to the character. The musou animations are unique to the characters and with those few unique moves, it barely makes 2 character play and feel differently. So it cuts down the roster in half in terms of unique playstyles. But If you only play with some of the characters that you really like, like myself, rather than every single one of the 50+ characters of the previous games, then it shouldnt be a deal breaker.

_childDocuments_.review: I really didn't want to have to write this review, because I had high hopes for a game that everyone said was a 'return to form.' The reality is, this is half a game, where they fixed the wrong things and doubled down on the wrong things. They learned the wrong lessons from Dynasty Warriors 9 and Samurai Warriors 4, and it shows. First, let's talk roster. The game ends/cuts off after Nobunaga dies, so fan favorites that have been in the game since the first one on the PS2 aren't here. Shimazu? Date? Chosokabe? None of them make an appearance. But wait, I hear you say, the roster in 4 was bloated and needed trimming! And that's right, but they still managed to add characters that barely appear in the story and who don't have much character on their own. Furthermore, with less than 30 characters, they still managed to not have unique weapons for each character! Let me repeat that: with a roster of less than 30 characters, they failed to add more than 12 different weapons into the game. They have done less work than the people who made the first Samurai Warriors did on the PLAYSTATION 2. At the heart of this game is a profound laziness. It have any pride in itself and it doesn't care about you, the consumer. There's a rot in the entire Warriors franchise, and it perpetuates it here. I do not understand what it thinks it's selling point is. The roster is smaller, but that hasn't translated to more care in the individual characters, or their presentation. The story is not well written; if it wants its selling point to be that it's telling a detailed story about Nobunaga and Mitsuhide, then it failed utterly. The story harps on the idea that Nobunaga is ending the chaos, and then he dies, and the story just ends, despite it being clear to everyone that there is still chaos, because even the most cursory knowledge of the period knows that there's a lot more conflict in the future. Is the game fun to play? Mostly, but that's the BARE MINIMUM when it comes to one of these. We are five entries into this series, not counting spinoffs like Empires, and they have yet to surpass the second game on the ps2 in terms of quality or uniqueness. But speaking of the gameplay, one of the real problems is that everything is reliant on events. Now that's not inherently bad, but because you'll often kill things before the events even trigger, you're left waiting for the game to catch up and open doors for you. On most maps, over half the map is closed off to you, because you have to wait for events to trigger on their own. It has never felt more like you are not the one playing a battle, you just happen to be around for one that's going on. Events will often fire, telling you to kill officers you've already killed, or you'll be trapped running around with nothing to do, while people talk about things that are not going on! And let's talk about the audio. There is NO EXCUSE to not have a dub here. I love subs if I'm watching a movie, but this is a game. Half the time I don't even mentally realize that there are people talking, because I don't speak japanese, and it blends into the background with the exultations of the characters you're playing. The game has TONS of dialogue being spouted off, and you probably aren't even aware of it, because you're busy playing an ACTION GAME, and you can't both stop to read things and play an action game. It doesn't work! The game also KNOWS THIS, because frequently it will stop the entire game to show you a screen and make the map huge because it needs you to know what to do, because it knows you entirely tuned out the fact that characters were talking. You want this to be a AAA game? Hire some English voice actors! You did it on the PS2! There's no excuse for not doing it here. Never have I felt that a game was so lacking in any kind of self worth as I have with this one. This is a game that feels like it was squatted out because they needed to keep the franchise alive, not a game made with care or love. There's no passion here, there's no desire to make a good game here. This is half a game with barely passing marks that has less in it than it's ps2 fore-bearers. I would be embarrassed to have my name attached to this game, because at every turn it reveals how lazy and uninspired it is. I have more respect for DW9, a game that tried something new and failed, than I do this, which tried nothing new and failed. It is half a game with half the passion and care you would expect from this. Just absolutely disappointing.

_childDocuments_.review: Buy if you are a fan of Warriors games. The gameplay is still there, and it's an interesting look at a different starting timeline. If you've never played a SW game before, get Spirit of Sanada or SW4. This is a step-back in the franchise.Upon writing this review, I only have around 6 hours in playtime, but having played many Warriors games previously I know it's not going to change much from here. As far as I'm concerned this is actually a step backwards for Samurai Warriors, rather than an improvement on the formula. This is a smaller scale, character focused narrative, like Spirit of Sanada, but it is lacking in a lot of areas. I'll start with the good things first.- The new art style is good. It's not super different from previous installments, but the new cel-shaded look they have added really works. I hope they keep it for future games.- The new setting for the story is fresh. No warriors game has really touched upon the very early parts of Oda's career. It typically starts when Imagawa is killed, from Tokugawa's perspective, but here, it starts long before that, before Oda even meets Tokugawa for the first time. It's great.- Some of the new/rebooted characters are actually great fun to play. The knuckles moveset (Mitsuki/Yasuke) is great. As is Sandayu Momochi, who uses a kusarigama. Hattori Hanzo uses a new weapon, which is a sword and ninja stars, and I found it much more fun than his old kusarigama moveset. Takenaka Hanbei's new drum weapon is so much better and more interesting than his bladed sundial from previous installments.- Hyper attacks are so good in this game because cancelling them into normals is made easier. It makes you very mobile and it's ace at blending up the generic soldier enemies. Ditto on the weapon skills, which are similar to the magic items from Warriors Orochi 4. It adds much more to the combat.Now, the bad:- There is a mysterious lack of some characters that had very close ties to the characters or events happening in-game. Lady Nene, Hideyoshi's wife, does not make an appearance. Neither does Ishida Mitsunari, his most loyal retainer. The whole Sanada family is absent, even though they had close relations with both the Takeda, Tokugawa, and Toyotomi, who are all main players in the plot.  There is no Kanetsugu Naoe, even though the Uesugi appear quite often as side characters. - I am not a fan of some of the new character designs or the weapon changes. Uesugi doesn't have his cool Seven Pronged Sword anymore. Tokugawa uses dual katanas instead of a spear-cannon, and looks like a femboy. He keeps this look all the way until the end, which is weird because Oda and Mitsuhide have a separate aged look in the 5th chapter, so why does he still look like a little boy? Shibata Katsuie uses a generic spear now instead of dual axes. Saika Magoichi uses a handheld cannon instead of a Bayonetted Rifle. Maeda Toshiie uses a spear instead of a Sword and two Halberds. Matsunaga Hisahide loses the spider motif and just uses a hand cannon now. Takeda Shingen uses a spear instead of a war fan. The list is almost endless. Overall, most characters fantastic personality and aesthetics have been reeled in to be more realistic and down to earth, which is an absolutely terrible decision for a franchise that relies on being crazy and exciting.- The homogenization of movesets. Despite only having 39 playable characters, a lot of them share weapons. Some of the playable characters you unlock don't even have their own signature moves or musou attacks. What makes this worse is that most of these people are actually NEWLY PLAYABLE (as in, showed up as generic npcs in other games) characters in SW5, but don't even get their own movesets. Why even bother making them playable? The katana is the worst offender, because both of the main characters use it, and apart from some unique power attacks, the moveset is exactly the same. Oda actually starts with an Odachi (also not a unique weapon as Uesugi Kenshin also uses it), but not long into the game his preferred weapon becomes the Katana. One of the parts that offended me the most was the first mission where you meet Nagamasa Azai. In previous Warriors games, he uses a Jousting Lance, which is a really cool and unique style of weapon. However, in this one, you control him for the first time while playing Mitsuhide's missions (katana user), and he rocks up, looking all cool and ♥♥♥♥ on his horse, then you find out he is ALSO just a regular katana user. Total pisstake. One of the best things about Warriors games is how basically everyone has their own unique weapon OR moveset. I don't know what ♥♥♥♥ Koei Tecmo is on, but the dumbing down of weapons in DW9 and SW5 is one of the worst decisions they've ever made.- If you compare this game to Spirit of Sanada, it is so much worse. Oda is a more boring character (to play as) than Yukimura. You play Yukimura the whole time, but he evolves over the course of the game, and by the end of it, he has a moveset that is as destructive as Lu Bu, as mobile as Xu Shu, and is at least twice as long as any other characters. He becomes so robust, but Oda never gets to that point, and ends up as boring to play.- The story is even more japanese soap opera-y than Spirit of Sanada, but not even as engaging. Bar Oda and Mitsuhide, most characters motivations and ambitions are a complete mystery, and a lot of them we don't even get to see realised because the game ends with Oda's death at Honnoji. Obviously that's a given, because the game is about Oda's journey, but Spirit of Sanada has left a very high bar to leap over.- Mitsuhide gets his own path in addition to Nobunaga, where you get to play battles that he was involved in from his perspective. Unfortunately, he spent most of his adult life as a retainer of Nobunaga, so most of the missions in this path are rehashes of Nobunaga's battles. It's very disappointing. The few unique ones he gets are great. The game just needed more like that.- No castle towns to walk around and interact with characters in. It's replaced by a tower defense mode which unlocks events between characters. For such a story focused game I think this is something that should not have been taken out.- I've found this game to be a terrible port. It will not recognise my controller properly and keeps switching it to player 2. The camera movement when playing with keyboard and mouse is so janky as well. Rather than being able to freely look around, it's more like you're turning to designated points of view on an axis.Overall I think it's still a good game, but would not recommend it to people who aren't already fans of the series. Get on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: When I click the "yes" on "do you recommend this game?", I find myself hesitating. It's really hard to say, for me. Do I recommend this game because it's good, or do I recommend this game because it's new? Fresh? Different? Has a fist weapon moveset that's pretty good?I have numerous problems with Samurai Warriors 5. Most of them stem from being a fan of other Koei games. I will list them below, before I list what's good. You can decide for yourself which matters more.PROBLEMS:-The changes to the characters in personality, design, and writing are almost universally downgrades. Yoshimoto Imagawa is better than he's been in any game besides Nioh 2, and Older!Nobunaga's new design is pretty damned good. That's the list of things that are better. I ESPECIALLY hate what they did with Hideyoshi Toyotomi (all monkey, nothing else to him), Ieyasu Tokugawa (He's just a shota and it's the most cringe awful ♥♥♥♥ ever), and Noh/Kicho (she goes from consistently being one of the coolest characters in any of these games, ANY OF THESE GAMES - including games like Kessen 3 that nobody else bothered to buy! - into being a wishywashy wimp of a waif, and it's a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ tragedy.)-Game runs choppy, but I guess that's par for the course?-Weapon upgrade system still kind of sucks, despite being better than most games in this broader series.-I'm not straight. I feel the need to preface this with that: the way the game completely turns on its axis around Nobunaga Oda and Mitsuhide Akechi having some weird quasi-gay relationship is extremely bizarre as a twist on the usual and I think it exists to the massive detriment of most other things in the game.-I have never been a fan of "every character has access to the same weapons and the same movesets, they just get like 1 or 2 new moves with 1 weapon", I think it's incredibly lame. I miss the hell out of the days when you could count on every character having a different moveset from every other character, even if there were similarities here and there. (Nene and Kunoichi back in the day had very similar movesets but weren't EXACTLY the same.) This game's weapon list feels lacking in breadth of options as a result, and I find that extremely disappointing.-The game could really stand to be longer. There's not enough to do after you beat the main story. If you don't play these games much it might sound weird to say that when I've already logged 24 hours, but I promise you a Musou game is expected to last 60+ minimum to keep up with its contemporaries and there really just isn't that much to this game.All those negatives aside, there ARE upsides!-This game is GORGEOUS, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Whatever they do next, I am begging Omega Force to keep this painting-style art. It's AMAZING. Even with most character redesigns being downgrades, the game is so gorgeous that it almost cancels that out.-Gameplay is a HUGE improvement over its immediate predecessors in the series - not since Spirit of Sanada has Musou been so good in the hands.-What weapons there are are ALMOST all VERY good. Aside from pistol + saber, they're basically all an improvement over their past equivalents. Never has there been a bow moveset this good, never have cannons been so fun, never have fists been this fun in a mainline Musou game (Age of Calamity stomps this game's ♥♥♥♥ as far as gameplay goes but that's not on Steam, now is it?) It's not going to revolutionize the industry, but it's certainly a huge step in the right direction compared to games like Warriors Orochi 4 and Dynasty Warriors 9. And while I don't like how limiting the weapons are per character for the most part, the pivotal exceptions are Nobunaga Oda and Mitsuhide Akechi. Those two feel FANTASTIC to play and if every character were like them, this game would be a 10/10 masterpiece.-While not that great, the weapon upgrade system IS better than basically any other musou game, so I'll give it that.-It's not quite as good as Spirit of Sanada in most of the ways it's good, but it feels like an attempt to bridge the gap between SoS and a more traditional Samurai Warriors. This is a good thing.Overall, for me, the good outweighs the bad. But the bad is certainly there.

_childDocuments_.review: The enemy commander is surrounded, trapped in their castle. Twenty officers surround them and strike them down in a flurry of blows. BUT WAIT!! Haha, the commander decides he wants to retreat and escapes! Damn, if only there were an entire battlefield to stop them...But seriously. 90% of the main campaign is this happening repeatedly; you'd think there would be a training of some kind to teach officers how actually to land a killing blow.    Good fun in short bursts Insane amount of grinding required to 100% Absolutely none existent Probably not Coop mode is available First game in the Samurai Warriors Universe. Please take that into account when reading my review If you love the hack and slash genre and want a sprinkling of story, then yes. Time played as of this review: 18 hoursGame status: Finished Nobunaga's story + a boatload of grindingTLDR at the end ->While there is a story in KOEI's beloved hack and slash genre, it isn't the draw in for most of us. Yet, despite that, I found the main Musou mode (Nobunaga) to be interesting, to say the least. It depicts his descent into becoming a cold-hearted ruler, with a few turns here and there to keep things interesting. As far as depth goes, not a lot, but some interesting interactions with the other officers. There are three stories: Nobunaga's, Mitsuhide's & then a 'hypothetical' story that you can unlock once you meet specific requirements. A fair decent amount of main content to get through.KOEI's games' bread and butter and this iteration feel the most refined out of their game series. Combat feels fluid enough. It's a shame move set is tied to the weapon used, but at least officers keep a unique move or two, including their Musou move and a striking pose for their rage move. Each officer has access to ultimate moves that can be used to clear enemies or buff oneself. You obtain more through levelling the weapon you're using. You only ever get access to a handful at a time, so you'll only be using the same few as you progress through the game. Unless you're playing on the higher difficulties, there's no real reason ever to block. Smash buttons and get pai... KO's. Same formula, done in a great fashion. Finally, switching between your main character and a partner makes traversing the map far easier and saves time. If you put your strategist cap on, you can predict what the game will throw at you and position your partner accordingly for an easy objective defence or officer kill. Okay, let's address the elephant in the room. I don't mind grinding. Roguelites are one of my favourite genres, and they usually require a tonne of grinding. But here, it's like the main attraction. Everyone has their own levels, weapon levels, and relationship levels (citadel mode). As the campaign gets more challenging, so do the enemy officers, yet yours only improve if you allocate your finite resources to levelling them. You can avoid a chunk of this by hard levelling Nobunaga, but when he isn't present in a mission, it can get rather tricky. The Citadel mode is a shoehorned mode that allows you to grind for resources. You can use these resources to level the various buildings to improve how much you can level your characters, level and upgrade equipment, level your horses or buy from the shop at an increased rarity. Some of the requirements here get absurd as you get to the higher building levels, thoroughly validating my thought that both this mode and the progression was purposefully restricted in this way to give a middle finger to all completionists out there. You will be grinding a lot if you want to see everything the game has to offer, and that grind never gets more interesting than spamming the X button until your fingers bleed. A great addition to the well-known formula that we've come to expect from KOEI. While this didn't grip me more than DW8, it did provide a more fruitful combat experience. Unfortunately, I can't overlook the sheer grinding that is required on top of what is already an incredibly repetitive game genre - worth picking up if you love these types of games. Wait for a sale if you're on the fence.

_childDocuments_.review: Let's just say, nostalgia is one hell of a drug, so much so that I snatched SW5 up as soon as there was a sale, and I have to say it was far from a mistake. Of course, there are some things that hold back the game from its fullest potential, but first, the good:One versus thousand combat, what more is there to say? SW5 puts you in the shoes of historical Sengoku era figures, and pits you up against insurmountable odds. There is no greater rush than cutting through hordes of peons, dueling with enemy officers, and charging across the battlefield in what I would consider one of the more streamlined and fluid musou games released to this date. Sometimes it's just fun to let loose and unleash a storm of steel as you steamroll everything in your path with fluid combos, hyper attacks, zipping around the various stages.While that alone may be enough to seal the deal and make a good game, what makes this game exceptional in my eyes is the soundtrack. I can't claim that the soundtrack is indisputably good- look hard enough and there will be detractors, and to each their own- but if you ask me, it's truly a gift, a masterpiece of atmospheric design. Nobunaga's theme and Mitsuhide's theme slaps, to say the least, and the little leitmotifs and melodies really set the mood for each battle as they are, helping to elevate what are already well done gameplay systems into an immersive, enrapturing experience. Even the generic battle themes sound good (minus the Citadel mode theme, but I'm probably just sick of hearing it cut in after 5k points every single battle). Could you find better, more fluid combat? Perhaps. Could you get the same one-versus-thousand experience elsewhere? If you look hard enough, most likely. But could you get the same quality of soaring symphonies, melodic blends of J-rock and traditional instruments and harmonies that elevate stages to truly amazing experiences? I'd say that's a little harder to find.Speaking of atmosphere, the story beats were enough to keep me invested in the story, in this new rendition of the oft-mysterious Sengoku era. In fact, it was SW1 that got me interested enough in this time period of history to send me on a decade long rabbit hole into the Sengoku period. A word of caution for history buffs though; as you can tell, this isn't meant to be historical, more like history-adjacent, but the artistic licence taken is a welcome one in my eyes. I do really appreciate the new ways Koei have tried to tell the story of Nobunaga and Mitsuhide, and I definitely recognize the care in designing a more coherent, more full story experience from start to finish. Evolution becomes a big (though not big enough) part of the story, and as a lover of stories and narratives, I really appreciated the character development Nobunaga and Mitsuhide go through, even if it feels rushed at times. SW5 tells two tales, the growth of a young, ambitious warlord into a ruthless (but albeit not unfeeling) conqueror jaded by loss and hardened by the chaos of the time, and the story of an honorable warrior's struggle to uphold his lifelong principles as they are subverted, and challenged at every turn throughout his life. Side note though, I personally didn't like the Momochi arc as it felt kind of shoehorned in, but at least the plot twist was pretty good the first time around. Is it worth its price? I'm a little more hesitant in that regard. It's exceptional content, but I don't think it's Elden Ring price level worthy, not to mention the exorbitant price for DLC. Pricing is anything but fair here, and it's kind of a bummer because I know it's a pain point for a lot of other fellow musou lovers when they see the hefty price tag offered here for a game that, unfortunately, does not offer the enjoyment per dollar ratio that other games can offer- it's just not as replayable. I'm about 60 hours in now, and I've basically full cleared almost everything in the game already, and I've moved on to other games, because there just isn't that much left to do once you've maxed all the characters, made a broken weapon and cleared every stage on Nightmare. Another bummer of course is the lost potential, and that there are almost half of the characters on the roster that are available as effectively free-play only characters, since they either feature in a small side story (or none), or are unplayable because of the story structure that the game has taken. Some examples: Nobuyuki (features during the revolt, can be played in free mode, but isn't given a chance to shine), Dosan (a lot of lost potential here! I would have loved a further Saito digression during Act 1, that maybe captured what Dosan saw in Nobunaga to make him so sure of his capabilities, as insinuated in the Chronicle of Lord Nobunaga by Ota Gyuichi), Katsuyori (was a side character for a decent period of time, sure, but not much was explored in terms of his dynamic with Shingen, which in itself was a pretty interesting take Koei presented but didn't expand on), even Ieyasu (who remains childlike in appearance throughout the entire period even though Koei tries to present his growth as clan leader of the Tokugawa).As for Citadel mode though, I did not really enjoy it at all. It was like playing through the story missions with all the fun, engaging plot points and special conditions taken out for something that honestly felt like mobile game levels of cheap gameplay. I grinded it out to its end, but let me just say that I didn't have much fun doing it at all. The only thing I really got out of it was learning how to hit insane combo counts under time pressure, which kind of helped for my S rank Nightmare runs I guess.Despite all this though, I heartily recommend this game, for newcomers and veterans alike. SW5's soaring melodies, invigorating gameplay and likeable story captured my heart, and despite its flaws and the lost potential, it remains one of Koei's stronger entries in terms of Musou games. One thing though, do your wallet a favor, get it on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Let's start to say, it is a Koei game, it never almost never changes, besides a few things here and there. Feels like a Fast and Furious movie: you know it is fast, you know its action, but expect some absurd things here.I've been playing the musou series since the early 2000s.Yes, I'd recommend this game, but the game is very flawed there are a few things to consider before playing/buying. Let's begin our review:-The campaign, is the worst of any in the musou series; its 2 main stories, one of Nobunaga Oda, and other is Mitsuhide Akechi (Oda's Right Hand), but here is the catch, on Mitsuhide's side of the campaign, IT IS THE SAME THING, but with a slight change in dialogues "so you can see his point of view"... that is the laziest sheet I've ever seen Koei do.-First time EVER in the musou series that you can't play multiplayer campaign, but only on "some" maps, and many maps, specially on the first chapters you MUST play solo. I've been playing for over 20 years of these games, and this frustrated me the most... I couldn't play it with my friend, and we had to watch and take turns playing, and it was boring and mostly unfun. Fire the sheethead who thought this was a great idea for the game.-The weapon system is something somewhat new, because it is present in the Orochi series and new to Samurai series; i'm not against it, but it is very flawed. Most of the weapons are meh/ok while some are incredibly weak and unplayable, with a very few being strong: The great spear and twin katanas. Hammers, Drums, Naginatas are completely underwhelming weak, almost feel like a joke. I ended up changing weapons with most characters to play with other weapon.-The Castle system is another bad joke. On the samurai series you had to play the campaign to unlock certain items, and play the castle for bonus unlocks like horses, skills, even some characters, but now, it is there for grind only. And grind what? Grind resources...for what? For upgrading the castle...for what? That is it, nothing else. You upgrade the castle for some really slight changes, but not that affects your game play. I finished the game and never really touched anything from the stables, blacksmith or the shops.-Ranking S and objectives: The game isn't clear about them, you have to search for guides on the internet or steam forums to start understanding what they are because the game won't explain anything, nor show afterwards what is missing.If you want to grind the S rank weapons you have to get S rank on every stage, get all objectives done PLUS, play on a very specific character on a specific level to obtain it! To the hell with that. You will grind for hours trying to get the perfect score and never understanding where you failed.-The graphics are very okay/meh too, I think they made, so every potato can run it; it doesn't go beyond 60 fps which is very lame for koei, since fps unlock is not a new thing. If you are targeting consoles I understand the 60 fps lock, but for pcs, come on, unlock it already.My conclusion is that the game could have been better, but it is fun for a while and the end game is just a grind for perfection and I think only the hard core fans will enjoy that. If you are new to the series, consider buying this on a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: While being a decent musou game (albeit very bare bones with how little content it got post release), my biggest complaint is simply that this game is yet another case of a developer pursing a new audience while leaving the old audience to rot.This game forces on Nobunaga's life, which sold me at first. I had assumed Nouhime would have been a large part of this game, but something strange happens: she dies very early on in the game. She dies in the middle of game despite the fact that the historical figure either died alongside Nobunaga or survived honnoji and became a recluse. Why? Because this is a game for fujoshi. The main appeal here is yaoi and a pretty boy being married to a woman is a big no-no in yaoi. So Nouhime was cut out of the picture to focus on Nobunaga and Mitsuhide's bromance.You'll notice that almost every female character from previous SW games got removed, even those who were alive during this period and should have played a roll in this game, such as Naotora Ii. There are only 4 female characters in this game 2 of which die mid way through, one has a minor roll and last is a completely original character who is what I assume is the writer's self insert character. Said self insert character basically takes Nouhime's roll in the story after the real one dies, but is Nobunaga's "daughter" so she doesn't get in the way on any of the Nobunaga/MItsuhide scenes. It's very strange how SW4 was seen as one of the better SW titles, yet this company decided to throw out their time-tested formula on being a stupid fun samurai game with 50+ characters and turn it into a yaoi/otome game with a limited roster.It's competent in what it's trying to do, but it's not the tone I expected from Samurai Warriors and its clear I'm not the target audience for it, so I simply can't recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: Review from a Musou first-timer.Pros:- Fast, satisfying gameplay. Game gives you broken weapons and you feel like a badass. Simple two-button combo system that has enough depth to not bore.- Stable 60fps with zero drops.- Great music, fusion of traditional Japanese instruments with modern genres.- Story is well presented and enjoyable (even if all the cinematics are people standing or sitting cross-legged while talking).- The overall presentation is very sleek.- Characters are cool, a mixture between anime and J-Rock sex gods.Cons:- There really isn't much to the game. There's only Story mode and a Base Defense mode. If you've played one stage you've played them all, so you really have to enjoy this type of gameplay.- There's three difficulties + a harder one that unlocks when you beat both Story modes. You're so overpowered (unless you bring in a character you haven't leveled) that there really isn't much difference between them.- The game feels like it has levels, skill trees, horse stats, all for the sake of having something to do. But there's no reason to do any of this, and it's completely superfluous. Only the craftable weapons give any kind of customization.- There's 15 weapons but 37 characters. Some of the characters use the same weapons as others, and any character can use any weapon. Movesets are shared. So no reason to really play as any of the second-tier characters, unless you're compulsive-obsessive and just want to level everyone to 50 to check off a list.Because of the last points, the game feels kind of... pointless? It's more of a way to decompress and just pass the time mindlessly. Which is both a pro and a con. I just wish it had something more, something to unlock or strive for.Overall, still highly recommended. The gameplay is fun. I'll definitely be purchasing the next Musou game.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay so like, I kinda like this, and I also kinda don't?Hear me out right;Samurai Warriors 5 is a visual masterpiece, with more men on screen than ever where they once bragged about striving for 1,000 kills, you can hit 2.5k easily now! You truly are one anime-esque badass cutting through swathes of warriors to epic guitar riffs and overly exaggerated and inspiring music. Just what every teen needs, to be honest.The Team at Koei have tried to tell much more of the Nobunaga era of the Sengoku Jidai, unlike their Dynasty Warriors series, which is a work of fiction based on a work of fiction loosely based on historical events that people know little about, Samurai Warriors is a work of Fiction based on History. They lean a little more into this, exploring some of the lesser known battles, with cutscenes eluding to some more intrigue and personality than before. By no way am I saying it's historically accurate, because it's most certainly not, but it does do a lot of work to try to build character and develop the Oda, instead of them just appearing like badasses.BUT, I am a long time fan of this series, and as a long time fan... it's weird. Jurota Kosugi's ICONIC Nobunaga Performances is no more, and Nobunaga's appearance would have you thinking he was Miyamoto Musashi or some of the other later-era generic characters.Other Plusses:- The Gameplay is Fun, if not a little samey- The system continues to be reworked to be a little different to titles before it- The new designs ARE interesting, and people probably like them if they are not used to the old onesOther Cons:- I hate the new Nobunaga personally, I much prefer my demon-sword swinging mad man voiced by an absolute legend, but that might just be me- It revives the same, ♥♥♥♥♥♥ weapon system from DW7, taking away a lot of the uniqueness of characters- It forces replayability with hidden objectives, instead of encouraging replayability with fun mechanics or options- There. Is. No. Mori. Ranmaru. :(

_childDocuments_.review: Every "Warriors" title should be rated in two styles. The first style is for newcomers to the series and/or people who aren't major fans. The second style is for Warriors veterans who by a lot of the games despite their similarities to one another.This is one of the rare Warriors titles that I can recommend equally to both. In fact, this is my favorite Samurai Warriors game and it is even better than every Dynasty Warriors game except for 8 and its spin-offs. That is a big compliment from me, a person who has always enjoyed the DW of a given year more than its equivalent SW title.To outsiders, this is a polished and well-executed one-versus-thousands action hack-and-slasher. You play one famous (mostly real-life) leader and help your army defeat the enemy. There is a story that is (again, mostly) based on real history but with the characters exaggerated into larger-than-life superheroes along the lines of Achilles or Hercules. The voice acting has no English option, but there are subtitles and the Japanese voice acting sounds great to me (a person who speaks no Japanese, by the way). There are essentially two methods of fighting that you can switch between and weave into one another with ease. One mode is used for fighting officers and other powerful opponents while the other is used to quickly clear hordes of enemy troops. While you can use them for cross-purposes, they are not especially effective in that role.To Warriors veterans, the biggest point with this game is that it is a sort of reboot of the franchise. That is to say, many important figures are characterized differently and the art is all changed. Rather than focus on one of the typical protagonist-type heroes, the story focuses on a young Oda Nobunaga and sheds a lot of the "demon king" baggage the character has carried in previous versions. That being said, after a series of major upheavals, the story ages Nobunaga up and he essentially becomes the character we remember from previous Samurai Warriors games. As someone who was always a bigger fan of DW and played SW games to tide me over until the next Chinese adventure, the character changes were not an issue for me. In particular, a lot of the silly characters got a more serious treatment and more serious weapons. While some of the high level weapons get odd and there are certainly "mystic" weapons that deal damage with magic (a drum, origami), nothing here is as goofy as the leather balls or umbrellas from previous games.Anyway, after my extreme disappointment in Dynasty Warriors 9, this game was a breath of fresh air. Samurai Warriors 5 is the Warriors formula at its best. If you are not a fan of that formula, this one might just be enough to change your mind, but I wouldn't bet on it. If you like the formula, then this is a kick-ass execution of that idea.
_childDocuments_.name: SAMURAI WARRIORS 5

_childDocuments_.review: Koei has taken a huge risk here, effectively rebooting the Samurai Warriors franchise, and it amazingly works.I've been a fan of the Warriors series for most of my life, starting with DW2, I've seen the highs and lows of this franchise, and the start of the Samurai side series.  I consider DW8XL one of, if not the best of the series, and everything about 9 was a complete failure to reimagine and reinvigorate.  So when news broke of Samurai Warriors 5 and it also attempting to reimagine the series, I like many, dreaded the worst.  Now, 16 hours in, I can confidently say Koei has a massive success in this rebooted franchise.Firstly, if you're new the the series, you wont mind both the reduced roster and scope of the game.  For veterans, it could be a deal breaker.  The game focuses now entirely on the story of Nobunaga's rise to power and sudden fall.  This means many characters have not made a return, including series poster boy Yukimura and personal favorite Masamune.  If your favorite wasnt important to Nobunaga's story, there's a high chance they're gone.  Even a few characters that were close to Oda are gone, namely Ranmaru and Keiji.  As a tradeoff, the characters remaining have been incredibly well characterized, and the singular story fleshed out.  Imagawa is now a presence that lasts several missions, rather than being killed off in the first mission.The other major concern is the case of cloned movesets, which is somewhat helpedd by the vast majority of characters having several unique power moves.  While it means that no moveset is completely unique, most characters have something going for them that might change how you play them.  In addition, each of the weapon types has a unique feature, such as naginata's air combos and knuckles' power installing.  Most weapon movesets feel good to play.  It's not perfect, but it's not DW6.Lastly, the new designs and art styles.  Again, newcomers wont have much issue here, but the changes are dramatic for a veteran.  Some work really well, like Hideyoshi and Lady No, others less so, like eternally young Ieyasu.  Some new characters also have odd choices, namely Shikanosuke's very stupid sun visor.  Strangest, later in the story Nobunaga and Akechi gain aged-up designs while no other characters do.  This is more or less a gripe in that Ieyasu and maybe Hideyoshi should have also gotten aged-up models.All that said, the gameplay is among the best the series has had the offer.  It's fast and energetic, has many options, and can be challenging at times.  On top of that, the story is told incredibly well.  Koei actually tried with this one, and it pays off.

_childDocuments_.review: Really love the soft reboot of the series. Overall gameplay are fun, something you could expect from a Samurai Warriors game (2 characters switching on a stage, Hyper attack, etc). There are 39 new characters (2 of them are mature version of Nobunaga Oda and Mitsuhide Akechi). And there's like 16 weapons in total, which you guessed it, some character have shared weapon with each other (read: cloned movesets). Similiar to Dynasty Warriors 7, some character will have a preferred weapon and it will have a unique charge attack for said character (think of like EX attack from DW7/8). New to this entry is this Ultimate skill which you can use by holding R1 button. And you can mix and match the skill too but they are tied to your current equipped weapon so keep that in mind (exceptions are the unique ultimate skill that each characters has. You can equip it regardless of weapon type you use).Sadly there's only 2 modes in this game. Musou Mode (+Free Mode) and Citadel Mode. To be frank, Citadel Mode gets boring real fast since what you do there is just defending a base while doing some random objective like, defeat certain enemy or beat 100 troops with musou / ultimate skill. Musou mode on the otherhand, focused on the rise of Nobunaga Oda until Battle of Yamazaki time period, so no Siege of Osaka Castle or Battle of Sekigahara here. Kinda wish they make the next game with this style but focused on Hideyoshi and Ieyasu, continuing the story until Siege of Osaka. And unpopular opinion, i think i like this more than SW4-II. Get this instead of that game. And for the love of god Koei please bring base SW4 into Steam. Thank you

_childDocuments_.review: Despite the fact that Samurai Warriors 5 is quite competent representative of the Musou series, I cannot with clear conscience recommend it.To keep it brief, I will start off with what is wrong with this game.- First off, the title of this game is SW 5. However, this is clearly not another main installment in the series. The story focuses almost entirely on Nobunaga and Mitsuhide. Other characters (not everyone) get additional levels only once in a while.- The content here is extremely modest. The game is divided into two "campaigns": one for Nobunaga Oda and the second one for Mitsuhide Akechi. In total, we have over 70 stages. Is it much? I don't think so. Firstly, there is only 19 unique maps, so you will be replaying all of them few times. Secondly, the stages are rather short and majority of them can be finished within 10-15 minutes. And last but not least, significant portion of Mitsuhide's campaign are literally the same levels from Nobunaga's campaign. For example, Akechi's first chapter has 4 stages. Two of them are literally taken from the Nobunaga's campaign. In the third one, instead of attacking (like it was in Oda's mission), we are defending against Oda. Only fourth stage in the first chapter is unique to Akechi.- The number of characters is also rather lacking. We get only 27 main characters and around 10 secondary ones (they do not have any unique attacks). However, there is only 13 weapons/fighting styles, so the number of clones is quite high. Also, many of these weapons are just different variations of spears and swords.- Also, many of the fan-favourite characters are missing from this part. Yukimura Sanada, Sakon Shima, Kotaro Fuma, just to name some of them.- Not counting free mode (replaying main stages with other characters), there is only one additional game mode - citadel mode. This is probably the weakest extra game mode from all musou games that I've played. This mode uses maps from the main campaigns, so there is nothing truly unique here. There is the same goal on every map - protect entrances to specific point from enemy forces. This mode is extremely boring and repetative. Additional scenes of interactions between characters are not worth it at all.+ On the other hand, there are many things that I like about this game. For the beginning, the combat system is quite great, probably my favourite from Musou games (maybe not counting One Piece Pirate Warriors 4). Main characters have their own unique combos and special actions and overall feeling of combat is pretty good.+ New, kinda cel-shading graphics are also looking great.+ Redesigns of classic characters (Nobunaga, Shingen and Kenshin look really good, no h-o-m-o)+ Soundtrack is niceOverall, the price tag for the amount of content here is ridicolous. Dynasty Warriors 8 XL had almost three times more characters (with more weapons) and twice as much stages (plus, pretty fine Ambition Mode on top of it all).

_childDocuments_.review: 20+ year musou boomer here.This game fails at being a reboot regardless of if you're a combo/high-level gameplay junkie like me or not. The Samurai Warriors series has historically only had one clone in its entire run before this game (Kunoichi and Nene), but now over half the cast is cloned. The few movesets that are in the game aren't even created equally, with the ninjato breaking the game to pieces and stuff like the bow and naginata feeling dreadful to use. Officers have ridiculous amounts of super armor and tech out of even canned animations, meaning that there's little depth here besides just using your most powerful move over and over. The grind in this game is insane and the gameplay is devoid of depth, so you'll likely get bored before you do all it expects of you. There's just nothing here indicative of a seven year hiatus, or the claims of this being a reboot when it's clear the developers were rushed to get this out, as evidenced by all the clones.The game does look nice, has great music and I really liked some of the redesigns. I ended up trying some characters I normally didn't touch like Ieyasu because he has a better moveset this time around. Godspeed attacks feel less gimmicky here as they both chain into normal attacks and actually stagger officers this time. Sadly, that's basically all the positive elements of it. Sadly, a video game needs to have good gameplay and a reason to do grinding if the game is designed around it, and the poor combat system and metric asston of clones ruin that at its core.The game gets some points for putting Yasuke, the first brother in a musou game in at least. Hope they put you in a better game, dude.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: A strong narrative and exhilarating combat mechanics are undermined by cut corners and bafflingly awful design decisions. Diehard musou fans will still find a lot to love here, but everyone else might be better served waiting for the developer to inevitably release a more complete and refined version of the game. Starting out with the positives, this game has one of the strongest, most focused narratives I’ve experienced in a mainline musou game. Rather than give equal time to every warring clan in the Sengoku period, Samurai Warriors 5 focuses almost exclusively on the rise and fall of Nobunaga Oda and his friend/rival Mitsuhide Akechi. Oda clan retainers and allies are also given there due to some extent, but the majority of other clans such as the Mori and Takeda are relegated to minor antagonist roles. By following events almost exclusively from the perspectives of Nobunaga and Mitsuhide, the story is able to develop a real emotional core, making the triumphs, tragedies, and compromises these men experience hit all the harder. Unfortunately, the approach does have its downsides. The old ‘win the fight, lose in the cutscene’ trope frequently rears it’s ugly head, as no matter how well you do in some battles, history demands the Oda clan must lose. It is almost blackly comic at times, as you’ll mercilessly batter senior citizens, only to have them scamper off totally unscathed, shouting ‘I’ll get you next time’ over their shoulder like a Saturday morning cartoon villain. The game also shamelessly copy-pastes certain battles wholesale between it’s two parallel campaigns, with both Nobunaga and Mitsuhide experiencing identical scenarios and objectives. In terms of presentation, this is easily the best looking entry in the series yet. The game has adopted a semi-cell shaded style that fits this series so well it’s shocking it was never used before. Character designs are excellent, and the battleground scenery isn’t half bad either. Music is the typical musou fusion of butt rock and traditional instruments, but it’s for the most part unobtrusive and fits the atmosphere. What’s getting harder and harder to forgive with each successive entry of this series however is the lack of an English dub. This is a matter of pragmatism rather than taste, as objectives and battlefield updates are barked at you in such rapid succession it can be almost impossible to follow it all while in the thick of the action. I typically prefer the native Japanese performances and don’t mind subtitles, but having to constantly take my eyes off of combat to read the dialogue becomes extremely aggravating at times. Gameplay for this one is an absolute rollercoaster of exhilarating highs and infuriating lows. To start with the positives, this game’s combat fundamentals are extremely fun and satisfying. Like most musou games you have your typical combo system of weak attacks capped off by strong finishers. What sets the Samurai Warriors series apart though is the addition of the hyper attack, which propels your character rapidly across the battlefield, slicing through dozens of enemies in his wake. Hyper attack almost becomes your primary method of movement in the thick of combat, and it's often so effective your horse seems redundant. Mashing the same button repeatedly to blitz through hundreds of helpless mooks might seem repetitive, but honestly it’s so damn fun I never got tired of it. The fact that you can instantly transition back into a normal combo just makes the whole system feel all the more fluid. This entry also introduces the ‘ultimate skill’ system, which allows you to equip four combat or support skills to your character that operate on a cooldown system. There’s definitely potential to build a character around these skills, but for the most part I found them a bit underwhelming. The only real sour note here is the weapon system, which is now independent of the characters. Any character can now wield any weapon, although they generally have a favorite with a small handful of unique attacks. There are far fewer weapon types than characters, which means a lot of the roster feels redundant at times. Each character does have their own skill tree, but these mostly break down to a few underwhelming stat buffs that are unlikely to make much difference in your performance. It’s strange that given how much fun the core combat can be, the game seems to take every opportunity possible to undermine it. It feels unbelievably awesome to hyper attack your way across the battlefield like a human ninja star, so why are there so many common enemies this attack bounces right off of? Previous entries restricted this buff to officers, which made sense, but now there are barricades all over the place with damage sponge enemies that stop you in your tracks. On top of that, most of these enemies also have extremely annoying attacks that stun or knock you down in a single hit. The aggravation extends to officers as well, who now have hyper armor whenever they feel like it and almost exclusively favor attack combos that stun you. This game at its best is a power fantasy that is all about propulsive momentum, and yet it is constantly doing everything in its power to slow you down. Compounding these frustrations is some of the worst map and mission design I have ever seen in this series. Rather than favoring wide open battlefields that give the combat room to breath, almost every map is structured as a rats nest of corridors that snake around in indirect and arbitrary loops. Getting from point A to point B is always a hassle, and the developers clearly noticed it was bad enough to require breadcrumb trails superimposed on the mini map. What’s worse, the objectives you pursue seem deliberately sequenced to require an extreme amount of backtracking. Objectives will lure you to the far corners of the map, only to have a scripted ambush occur at your home base that drags you all the way back to the start point. This happened in more battles than I could count, and the difficulty of traversing the maze-like maps only made this more aggravating. Rather than battles having a sense of direction, momentum and progress, you are instead constantly ping ponging all over the place putting out fires as fast as you can until the enemy commander finally deigns to come out of his gated off compound and fight. Winning the battle, only to have the following cutscene say you experienced a humiliating defeat, was just more salt in the wound. I wanted to like this game, and in truth I did have a lot of fun with it. However, this was also easily the most aggravating experience I have had with this series. This developer has a proven track record of releasing more complete and refined follow-up versions of their games, so unless you’re a die-hard fan, it may be better to wait and see if these issues are addressed later on. Otherwise, maybe try Warriors Orochi 4 instead, which is a far more complete package and better value at this point.

_childDocuments_.review: Samurai Warriors 5 continues the Musou type legacy while being fresh & fancy. To those unfamiliar with the term , Musou games are the ones on which you fight thousands of small fry enemies in each stage with a couple elite ones & boss types. For what it matters, KOEI was the one that started the genre with the Dynasty Warrior Series and they continue delivering strong titles on that department. So what to expect from this one?  Story & characters are based on real historical events & figures of Edo-Sengoku period.You start off as a young version of the infamous Oda Nobunaga on his vision to unify Japan and as you progress you unlock more renown figures to play as from that time, such as Yoshimoto Imagawa, Hattori Hanzo , Tokugawa Ieyasu & many more. The Cinematics are really note worthy , with really good art direction, camera angles, nice flow and great voice acting that will keep you engaged. Visually , other than you typical 3D shader graphics you'll encounter quite a few of traditional ukyo-e art in either character introductions, descriptions & story videos.  Gameplay is quite straightforward, you have your typical light-heavy combo attacks that'll be your bread & butter, 4 customizable skills which can be either special attack types or provide some passive timed benefit & stylish Ultimate attacks that vary depending on the circumstances. As you progress you unlock more skills & ultimates so you can customize your characters the way that feels or looks better for you. After each stage you return to your "castle"which is more of just a UI with options to upgrade characters & levels, craft, dismantle & equip passive skills on weapons, breed horses (yeap you you cut heads off while riding your horse from 1st stage) and more. While it has a greaty variety of options & categories regarding customization, most of those are unlocked slowly by progressing the game and are explained through tooltips when that's done , so you won't be overwhelmed. Other than Story mode, you also unlock quite early a new mode to the series, Citadel Mode!!A combination of the classical musou gameplay but with tower defence elements, which is a really neat addition and adds a lot to the already good replayability the game offers. And last but not least, the OST which is phenomenal imo, resembles old traditional Japanese instrumental folk, with either soothing flute melodies, groovie shamishen riffs and heavy wardrums, all adding in a magnificent way to the overall experience.  Regarding its performance, i had stable 60fps @1080p with my oldie 980 GTX even when fighting against enormous crowds of enemies and i haven't encountered a single bug, as far as my understanding goes at least.  I really have nothing negative to say about SW5 , i ve read some reviews complaining about online co-op being bad since you re forced to actually beat the stage alone first before being able to co-op with others on it, ofc its a bummer for the people who only want to co-op play this with a friend. Locally though, you can play it 2 players even if it's the first time you play a stage, so you can try remote play for online sessions till KOEI hotfixes this issue. Regardless if you re a musou fan or a newcomer, if you re even slightly interested in this genre this game will do you justice.

Odachi and Greatspears make me feel like more of an utterly unstoppable force of nature than most Musou games, and that's some good stuff and I want another hit.Obviously, you can tell they still haven't gotten used to the new engine yet, considering that there's dupe signature weapons on specific characters, which DID NOT happen often at all before DW9, but all of the weapons themselves feel really nice. _childDocuments_.review: Just in general a fun Musou/Warriors title. You probably know what you're getting into if you buy this.As a little background on my person experience with these games: I started playing these games with Dynasty Warriors 3 on the Xbox. The previous title I played of this series was actually Dragon Quest Heroes 2, and before that it's actually Samurai Warriors 4, and before that it was probably Dynasty Warriors 5 or something like that (it's been a long time). Smaller character roster and lesser number of fighting styles aside, Samurai Warriors 5 feels like large improvement over these games.Having picked up Warriors Orochi 4 Ultimate more recently, Samurai Warriors 5 also seems to be a decent improvement over that, in terms of gameplay and balance (plus  better storytelling), with the caveat that Samurai Warriors 5 has less content by a fair margin.There's not much to say about the combat, if you're familiar with this kind of game. Press buttons and cut down hundreds of men with ease. You know the drill. That said, this game adds Ultimate Skills to the formula, which are just sets of buffs and special attacks that are on cooldown. They're a solid addition, adding a little more depth to the combat, while also giving the officer enemies hard-hitting skills with telegraphs. It doesn't change up the combat a huge amount, so it's still all pretty standard fare, but it's certainly a welcome addition. It's also notable that the combat styles are somewhat "generic". Every character can use every weapon, and the basic attack sets for each weapon will always be the same, so the number of combat styles is extremely limited compared to what you're probably used to. That said, this also means you're free to use whatever character you want and pick a combat style you like. It's also notable that most characters have special charge attack sets with their preferred weapon, like Mitsuki (a purely fictional kunoichi) calling out a clone and firing waves forward from her palms with one of her power attack combos with fists. Aside from your characters themselves, the enemy mobs are actually more varied than you might be used to. Soldiers wielding spears or large shields can effectively brace, blocking hyper attacks and impeding horses, as well as dealing damage and staggering in the case of spears. Squads of riflemen and archers can be organized in firing lines that shoot staggering charged shots at you. Drummers exist that boost morale of units around them in a relatively large area. On occasion, things like mages and cavalry exist, which cast small spells and charge at you, respectively. Again, these don't change the dynamic of the combat a huge amount, but they make the standard enemies something you actually may want to look out for and adapt to, since you can't always just mindlessly hyper attack and murder everything but officers, and they may actually serve as mild impediments when you're facing off against officers (particularly lots of squads of riflemen shooting at you).That said, what surprised me about this game is how well the story is told. I'm used to Musou games sort of being a matter of "and then this happened and there was a battle you'll take part in". Pretty dry stuff, honestly, but the story was never what anyone was probably looking for in the majority of these games (licensed titles like One Piece aside). Samurai Warriors 5, however, tells a solid tale of ambition, obsession, loss, and betrayal. In previous titles I couldn't really say I liked characters beyond their design and combat style, but here, at least with what I've played so far (all of Nobunaga's story and 2/3rds of Mitsuhide's), I can genuinely say I really like a good number of the characters and was invested in what would happen to them (even if I knew beforehand many of them would meet tragic ends, because history). I find the storytelling and characters are a big plus here, which I was certainly not expecting. The only negative I can really see is that I find Citadel mode to be kind of bad. Every single battle is 5-minute defense mission where you've got 2 characters defending one or more gates with a few guards and the ability to summon three squads of units (all the other units on the field are enemies). To make things worse, this is tied to some upgrade progression and building character relationships to see short scenes between them... and I actually care about unlocking the scenes with these characters.This isn't my favorite title in this genre (that still goes to Senran Kagura: Estival Versus, actually), but it's certainly my favorite that's come out of KOEI, with the caveat that I don't play all that many of these that come from them because I find most of them to be so incredibly similar. If these games had an active dodge and more reliable aerial combos, and of course balance tweaks to accommodate the systems (basically if they were a more like Senran Kagura's combat system), I can reasonably see this having a chance to have been my favorite (but since Musou/Warriors games aren't like that, it's not). Still, even if it's not what I find to be the best, it's extremely solid. I just wish I didn't have to grind out relationships in Citadel mode.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: If these games are your drug of choice, you can likely get something out of it. Price point would be a concern, as it feels a bit thin in content with two main lines only.----------------------------------Last main line Warriors game I played was Dynasty Warriors 8. Needed that point of reference.The game looks fantastic, and feels great to play. The weapon loot system is much easier to manage, and isn't a time sink to deal with. The maps are pretty great as well. Lots of distinct set pieces, and they can change during play with more impact than I initially expected. Not sure yet how much content there is in it, as I've only finished one of the two main story lines @35 hours. About half way into the second, and then the "Reverie" stuff after that.To sum up, the game's engine is solid, and I'd like more like this.Okay, now for the reasons to not recommend it. Like all of their games, this one is also a soap opera. In regards to that, the framing is better, but the script doesn't do enough proper work. I don't mind them playing loose with history, if it makes a better game, but changing major history points like when characters die, to try to give a better emotional reasoning for things, doesn't work for me. As a result, I find the "Reverie" missions being described as a "What-if" series, just laughable, as the main line is part fantasy itself.The way the plot is presented is also troublesome. Instead of the player being able to walk with the flow or guess the flow of the events, I find myself playing catch up, trying to reason out things after the fact. This doesn't help the player enjoy the story at all. Motivations aren't clear for anyone, aside Nobunaga and Mitsuhide. "We're attacking who, because they didn't march to where when ordered? When did that happen?" Other characters are just there to hang out in the periphery with inferiority complexes, trying to explain to the player emotional changes in the main cast. That isn't enjoyable. Perhaps things would flow better if, I didn't have to read (and get tired of doing so) mid-fight, trying to keep the combo up. Might explain more, but can't comment, because I stopped reading those in general to get to the next objective.The last Samurai Warriors game I played was 2, so it has been a while, but I remember enjoying the much wider range of paths in the history. There is no Yukimura Sanada in this, which was a disappointment, but that isn't something I'm going to directly hold against this version.I think there are some issues with the subtitles as well. Changes of meaning, and even one scene so far where the auto-play skips to the next line too quickly (spoken line is shorter than the written in this case, so it skips exactly when the last letter is displayed in the subtitle). Can tell how important a scene is based on how well it is lip-sync'd too, which I found funny.The character voices are alright I suppose. I do think there is a bias towards higher pitch voices or those in a constant state of excitement, which I'm not a fan of, but I can live. Just not as fun when a lot of characters sound like hyped up anime voices. Might have my favorite version of Hideyoshi so far, which surprised me. His intro is annoying, but after that, he isn't. I hate monkeys in general, and after that intro, they don't lean into that nickname as much.The Citadel system to upgrade the Blacksmith and such, is easy enough to understand how to use, and use, but the missions feel..... flat. I suppose since I'm comparing it to DW8's system, SW5 doesn't have a lot of variety in those missions, so it is repeating the same ones again and again to rank up Relation between characters, and grind out far too many resources to upgrade the Stables (and others).

_childDocuments_.review: Good game.Main story was enjoyable - two storylines with 6 chapters (23 main + 11 extra for Nobunaga, 23 main + 4 extra for Mitsuhide), 9 extra scenarios in Reverie mode (require S completion for some other story chapters to unlock and have 9 and 10 stars).Extra Citadel mode is not really intersting, you defend 1 to 6 gates from three waves of enemies with just 2 characters and three summons which you can relocate. There is a 5 minute timer which can be increase by 30 seconds by completing one random mission at the beginning of each wave and there is an extra enemy somewhere on the other side of the map to distract you from defending the base.Crafting is not really interesting too. You get random drops with 1-8 slots with gems. You can dismantle those weapons and put gems into another one. After leveling up weapon skills to level S for any character you get tier 2 weapon with 8 empty slots, so you can add those gems that you got from dismantling and level them up using cash. You can't lock a weapon to avoid dismantling it by accident.The story and game flow are great. Having a focus on few characters means that you are able to get involved in their story instead of just breezing through it. Searching for hidden missions during scenarios is also fun. You see an empty room just near your escape route, you explore it just in case and you find enemies hiding waiting to ambush you, you get access to hidden mission to destroy them. It is much easier to find those missions when you play the scenario multiple times because you already know what will happen but finding them on your first playthrough just by being observant feels really nice.There are four difficulties - Easy, Normal, Hard and Nightmare (unlocked after completing both main storylines). The game felt really balanced on Normal with base weapons. First missions felt kinda easy, but I didn't have to farm for better weapons or levels, I could just go into the next mission as soon as I unlocked it. You can use characters that just joined your roster on new missions without much trouble. Only on few 8 and 9 star missions in 5th and 6th chapters I had to use infinite musou attacks when near death to clear them. Before that I could just fight and win normally.Overall I liked the game even though crafting and extra mode parts were disappointing.
