_childDocuments_.review: And obviously, as anyone could accurately expect from my whopping 8 minutes spent in the game, I can't in good faith say much of anything about the game itself.  whether by necessity or otherwise, and with the disclaimer that your experience could be different than mine. And I hope it is! I wanted to leave a review especially because the game is currently ranked as "Playable" under Steam Deck verification. A lot of us are aware that this verification is wayward at best: Some titles are so beautifully optimized for Deck that it makes me forget it's originally a PC game,  while others are marked as "Verified" and run like absolute garbage or have to be played under a microscope after spending 2 hours painstakingly mapping controls. So, often, when I see the verification status, I don't pay it much attention. If I play a game that's "Playable" or "Verified" and it comes off as "Playable If User Is a Masochist" or "Verified To Be a ♥♥♥♥ Time At First And Possibly Forever", then I want to try to spare other Deck users at least some frustration and disappointment.So...while I'd been inspired by the announcement of the new update to finally buy Terra Nil and give it the shot I'd been wanting to give it since before it got fully released, I'm going to have to come back to it later when it's more fully optimized for Deck, which is the only platform on which I can personally play it for now. And in case anyone feels inclined to defend in the direction of "well how can you expect them to [do anything with steam deck to make it more playable and less immersion-breaking]"— regarding Steam Deck optimization, I offer in comparison to Terra Nil the demo of Horticular, which is in the same genre realm, is of a similar overall gamefiles size, and is gorgeously optimized for Decks. And it's not even released yet. I can't accurately offer much on the game itself, but as far as for players who intend to get it for their Decks: hold off for a while. _childDocuments_.review: I first got this game several years ago when it was a prototype on itch.io and even in that early state it felt unique and special. It is a satisfying strategy game, testing your planning and spatial reasoning, but there are many games that could be described that way. Terra Nil is special because of its unique premise and immaculate vibes. There is something so relaxing about making a ruined world lush and beautiful again, and leaving without a trace. I am especially fond of the "Appreciate" button after you complete a level, which shows you slow panning shots of the environment you created, letting you check out the little animals and beautiful greenery. There are "difficulty" options as well, offering different ways to play. If you want to focus on making a beautiful world, you can enable "Zen Mode" which removes the cost for buildings. Since those early days the game has improved in every way, I'm so happy to see it fully released, and I 100% recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: The trailer's lush greens and serene music caught my attention, and I had some very nice moments playing this game. Unfortunately, I think the game is quite overpriced for what it is. There's really not a lot of content. It's an extremely quick play-through, and there's little replayable value for me. _childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: This is a unique game of its kind. A combination of puzzle game and base builder with a theme of restoring nature. In my opinion a very solarpunk game and I really enjoy playing it when I want to relax and have nice visuals of a gray landscape filling up with green.The game is not very challenging and even though some strategy is required, it's not too hard to get a high score or 100% completion after understanding the interplay between the different buildings. It's almost impossible to mess up as the game is very forgiving, but some planning is necessary to actually get to a 100% for each region.There is quite a bit of variety with different biomes, buildings and ecosystems. There's no story, but at least some kind of feeling of progression.The game could be more challenging by adding contradicting needs that actually need to be balanced. There is a little bit with different animals, but since they can migrate they resolve the inbalance by itself as long as you've built enough viable space for everyone. More interesting would be adding the human factor where once would need to balance the ecosystem while working the land for food or how to manage temperature in a concrete jungle of a city. But there is no human factor other than the tech you use and some ruins.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: I don't generally leave game reviews on games that just came out, but honestly, this game scratched an itch I never knew I had.  The whole intro and game play so far have been satisfying to watch things come to life and transform into their better state.  A few small hints for people who are just starting out:  Place your recyclers close to your rivers if at all possible, it's required to complete a mission.   Use excavators near the end of the process, or only where needed - buildings stop the excavator beams.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Genuinely enjoyed this game. A unique approach to resource management that was challenging but not impossible. I've heard a rumor that people are saying this game is "too short." I don't see how anyone can say that. It took me just over 13 hours to complete the initial phase of the game. Beating the initial phase then unlocks four alternate maps. Even if we subtract 4 hours because I'm not the best gamer, that's still 9 hours PLUS additional maps that I haven't yet played.There are multiple levels of difficulty, including a "zen" mode if you just want a sandbox version. The one drawback I had was a bug in the city map that prevented the level from progressing. Once I exited the game and reloaded, the bug cleared and I completed the level without issue.I highly recommend this fresh take on resource management and "city" builders.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: An amazing puzzle and ecological game where you clean and then reclaim the wastes and return them to their former healthy environments. 4 different climate types each with 2 levels each and 4 different biomes each. Each one has different puzzle requirements. Create the necessary biomes and then spawn the wildlife.At the end you recycle all your buildings and leave the new wilderness untouched and self-sustaining.One the last level you build an Ark and then leave to seed life on new alien worlds.A wonderful experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Love the game, super relaxing and cute graphics. _childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game I've been following for a while and played the demo like 2 dozen times. This is my first review and I will write first a review for possible buyers and secondly some improvements for gameplay that may drive people off.The game is fantastically designed and the music is a feelgood chill out beauty, exactly what this game needs. The mix of visuals and music along with the satisfying animation whenever grass or biomes pop up is perfectly mixed and really activates  your neurons. I cannot quite put my finger on it but the game is addicting, that being said it is also relatively short and for a variety of reasons I would recommend the game be played on the easiest difficulty if you are coming in blind.Some of the negatives of the game is some poor optimization in some areas that need fixing. Buildings have an AoE that lag every once in a while. there are animation problems on the map, especially when water or lava touch the edge of the map they create a waterfall beneath the ground. I have seen some remnants of the AoE indicators of certain buildings (like power pylons and conveyor nodes) remain after the building is placed. There are some unkown variables in certain aspects that are not mentioned in the toolkit, like lava creating rock when meeting clear water but not dirty water (not complicated but throws you off the first time you see it) and the effects of ground stability on the last area.What will drive most people away is how often you have to unfairly restart the map. There is nothing more annoying than noticing that you softlocked yourself because of terrain generation issues.Also the best way to play this game is to know everything about it beforehand. Both climate achievements and animals sometimes require vastly different and very specific conditions (e.x. the first map you need to have a forest next to a grassland on the same elevation in order to have wolves, also flowers next to wetlands for frogs). A mix of terrain gen and biome conditions can ♥♥♥♥ you over as well: if you don't have enough free river space in map 1 to have ducks, if there is not enough free space on the ocean or ice did't form close to it for the narwhals in map 3, if you spent too much rainforest to increase temp in map 2.Again, in order to play properly you need to take all aspects of the map into account (biomes, animals, weather and recycling) at the same time before even placing your first building, which I believe is actually intended and is super satisfying when experienced but awkward at best the first time.For the developers, a list of things that could be added for improvements
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: I don't play a lot of strategy games or city builders but I had a great time with this. Mechanically, I'd say it might be a tiny bit underdeveloped, but there was enough depth to keep the game interesting for me. I would recommend switching to the highest difficulty setting once you've got your bearings after the first couple of levels. _childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Somehow I lost 2 hrs playing this game today. It would have been more but work, ya know? But as for the game itself the soundtrack is amazing and relaxing. _childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: This is an easy recommend for me.  It's a chill city de-builder, a casual teraform sim. _childDocuments_.review: A joy to play, and great take on city builders. The basic idea is that you start with a toxic wasteland and slowly build an ecosystem. The game is based on short cycles, each of which focuses on a small map.- Phase 1: start adding buildings to clean toxins, humidify the land, plant "pioneer species"- Phase 2: add more buildings to create the right conditions for specific ecosystems and grow them.- Phase 3: clean up everything y ou have build and leave the ecosystem to function on its own.It's a great idea, and it's just a neat concept that your own buildings are not the "thing" you are building, but rather a means to an end, something you eventually want to get rid of.The game works very nicely but is also quite simple, so there were some systems that I would have loved to have seen a more complex and intricate version of. This is fine: I like a game that gives you some neat ideas without taking up all of yoru time, but this one did make me think: oh, I wish these ideas make it into a bigger game some day.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Makes me sad to leave this review, I so wish there was a "Yes but no" option. _childDocuments_.review: [8/10] If you want to read why I gave this score:Terra Nil is a wonderful, relaxing ‘reverse city builder’, that offers an engaging, calming experience that will get you hooked. The message behind the game, as well as the care put in by its developers is felt throughout the experience!I do wish that there was more to explore in the game beyond what I experienced in the 8.5 hours it took me to 100%, but it still felt like a very worthwhile experience nonetheless. Support indies! [8/10] The game overs a unique spin on city-building/puzzle games where, instead of colonising a new space and building up civilisation, you seek to heal the damage done by humanity.The game’s core flow covers restoring the natural environment to its intended state, fixing the climate and reintroducing wildlife with clever placement of machinery, followed by a satisfying cleanup phase leaves you with an incredibly satisfying feeling of fixing the puzzle laid out conclusively.The game offers a healthy variety of maps and structures to leave it feeling engaging for a reasonable amount of time, but I really wish there was more to sink my teeth into- it ended too soon! [7/10]Simple, but effective. Terra Nil’s art clearly communicates its range of flora and fauna and brings some unique, pretty illustrations to the handbook that functions as your guide throughout. A pretty game, but nothing groundbreaking going on here. Solid nonetheless! [7/10] I’m writing this review a few days after 100% the game, and I actually had to open it up again to remind myself of the audio :P at the very least, it wasn’t too memorable.The game’s music is light, calming, and augments the curious/peaceful atmosphere that the game presents everywhere else. The addition of crunchy sound effects in both the structures and the ambient environment really fill the void very well between music tracks.  [9/10] No major crashes or bugs in my playthrough. My only complaint is that there are some really sticky tooltips that you have to wrestle against to declutter your screen. I’m sure this will get fixed in future.  [-/10] While this game has a somewhat implied story, it doesn’t feel appropriate to judge it on this!  [9/10] Terra Nil comes together to form a really engaging experience that just… hits right. It’s a relaxing, cathartic experience that is really hard to put down once you get started. A game I thoroughly enjoyed and, will most definitely pick up again as soon as more content drops.(There’s something really magical when the rain starts to fall on a new map <3)

_childDocuments_.review: I'm going to preface this: I am very likely bad at this game. _childDocuments_.review: is a gorgeous game with a clever premise. Fanciful as they might be, it gives me hope that perhaps humanity will be able to use technologies like the ones in the game to restore ecosystems after we've destroyed the planet. Unfortunately, though, I didn't find it particularly enjoyable to play, so I don't recommend it.At its core,  is a puzzle game in which the objective is to restore a wasteland to its natural state by placing buildings that modify the terrain, and consequently, the ecosystem. You have a limited budget with which to place the buildings, and while some of them return resources to you if placed correctly, many do not. There are restrictions to which surfaces many buildings can be placed on, as well as environmental requirements that must be met before they can be placed. You have to work within these constraints to find the correct number, combination, and placement of buildings to fully restore all of the target biomes.As I mentioned, it's a clever premise. But the way it's implemented feels too much like trial and error. Some of the buildings and their environmental constraints and interactions are not explained well enough, so the best way to figure out how everything works is by playing through a map, likely failing on the first try, and then starting over. You can undo a single turn at a time, but you can't rewind beyond that, so if your approach fails you will eventually reach a point of now return after which you must restart the stage. It also feels like stages can be much harder or easier depending on how lucky you are with the procedural map generation.Other reviews have mentioned that the game is quite short, with only four maps, each of which has two total variants. This is true, but I don't think I would have minded it so much if the game was more fun. If it really were a "reverse city builder," as the description states, you could probably replay the different maps many times. But as it is, I'm finding the third stage a bit tedious, so I'm unsure if I'll even finish the game.

_childDocuments_.user: the fuzziest moth in the West
_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr: it's way too short and way too easy, but otherwise it's fantasticThings I like:The game is beautiful! The visuals are simple but pleasant to look at. The music is great too, and the way that it expands as you bring life to the wasteland until it swells as you approach completion of a map is one of my favorite audio phenomena in any game I've played.The gameplay is simple but fun. I've never played a game that was this relaxing while remaining engaging. The central conceit is one of hope. No matter how ruined the world is, not all hope is lost. Sometimes that's a message I need to be reminded of, and if you feel the same way, you might benefit from sitting down with this one for a few hours.Things I don't like:It's too short. As other reviews have mentioned, if you blitz through the game just clearing each map, you can beat the whole game in a couple hours. 100%ing it took me six hours.It's too easy. On the easiest difficulty, Gardener, you can essentially completely ignore the game's primary resource. You simply cannot fail a map without intentionally trying. On the normal difficulty, Ecologist, it is still extremely difficult to fail a map. If you've never played a strategy game of any kind in your life, then maaaybe you'll fail a map one time. There isn't much replay value. Once you've completed each of the maps (contrary to the most popular review, there are 8 maps, not 4) once, there isn't much of a reason to replay them for anything other than completionism (100% and achievement hunting) because while the maps are procedurally generated, they're still pretty much identical every time you play them.All told, get it if you want a brief little jaunt into a beautiful world of hopeful restoration, but if you're looking for a game you can play for hours and hours and hours, look elsewhere.

_childDocuments_.review: For the short time that it lasts, Terra Nil is a fun, addictive and relaxing city-sim. It’s a little hard to recommend at its current price of $37 AUD (on Steam) but is certainly worth checking out whenever it goes on sale. The breadth of content brings the overall experience down quite a bit, as once you’ve given the four biomes a go there isn’t a whole lot left to do. That said, if you like the sound of creating beautiful environments, without having to use your brain too much, then you’re likely to have fun with Terra Nil.Full review here:

_childDocuments_.review: I think the value of the game is my biggest issue.  Was expecting something more at 100%, but it's just a tracker.  I feel like I just learned a good set of skills, and now I have nowhere to apply them.The game is fun, it just feels like it needs more.  And with the backbone in place it feels reasonable to expect more maps.  Having completely wrapped up the game I would have liked to see new maps at 4x size and new challenges. From a game play perspective there is a little polish I'd like to see.  I'd really like to see us encouraged to take maps in different directions in each different play through.  Aside from edge cases (need to make tundra before raising humidity, activating snow before cranking temperature) the temp/humidity seem to encourage being cranked as high as they can go.  Also it felt really bad when I couldn't get one of the animals due to what felt like an obvious construction choice in phase 2.  And really bad when rivers needed to be really wide for animals when the terrain only has small rivers.  Just blowing up things in the last phase to try to make rivers.Since the game is very formulaic, I'm not seeing a ton of replayability. Yet anyway.  If the game gets free or 5 dollar DLC I think it could easily change this to a yes.  But due to a lack of replayability, maybe wait until it's on sale right now.

_childDocuments_.review: I tried the Terra Nil demo a while ago & loved it, it went straight onto my wish list. _childDocuments_.review: It's a pretty cool game, interesting idea, and, quite a fun puzzle to achieve the set goal... I wish i could recommend it, but... I've played this game for 2 days with Steam Recording enabled, and have collected enough material to fill the entire thread with documented bugs. The game is completely broken, some systems not function at all or are bugged to all hell.And don't get me started on the performance. What you see on the screenshots above gets ~20fps on a machine that gets stable 60 in modern AAA games on mid-settings. The optimisation is atrocious, and game doesn't have graphics settings, except for LOD that goes from "♥♥♥♥ quality even when you zoom in all the way" to "max resolution textures and highest quality models for every single object, even when you zoom out all the way out", with no settings in-between.The state of this game is dreadful.On top of that, some design decisions in this game are completely arse-backwards. Like needing to have all species of animals present for level to be considered 100%-ed. A species of animals will only appear when it has *correct* conditions present for it. You're not told for which animals you need to create conditions for on each individual level, you just have to luck out into them, then luck out for RNG to spawn that specific animal in that specific place, then you can see. Oh, did i also mention that same animal species will have different conditions in different levels? Can't see which animals can be present on this map until you satisfy their conditions, and you can't see their conditions until they appear, from you satisfying their conditions. Fun!Or terraforming tools being revealed out in two stages. Not "unlocked" - revealed! So when you're doing the first stage of terraforming, which is supposed to serve as a base for the second stage - you are not told which tools you will have in the second stage. Why would you want to know that? That is, on top of not knowing which animals you will need to satisfy until they start spawning late into stage 2, some of which require conditions you could only really set up in stage 1. That is, on top of many terraforming changes being irreversible, and potentially softlocking you half an hour later. Naturally, game has no manual saves, "revert to start of the phase" that partially forgets the progress you made by the start of that phase, often in such way that you are unable to achieve the "forgotten" goals from this point on, and, naturally, "undo" button not working quite often.That is, if you can even finish a level, because, surprise! One of the VERY frequent bugs is game just refusing to let you leave once you've satisfied all of the animals and recycled all of the buildings. The button to do so simply doesn't appear, and you have to screw around to try to unsstuck the game, and pray.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: In a word, this game is RELAXING. It's SATISFYING. It's somewhat educational and I could see it becoming a stable in school computer labs one day. It's also short with not much content. I really hope that the developers add more biomes and scenarios! As is, it's worth playing if it looks like something that's exactly your jam or if it's on sale, but that's not a bad thing! I thoroughly enjoyed this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Terra Nil is a puzzle game about restoring a dead planet using fantasy technology.The game is divided into four environments, each with two separate scenarios. Each scenario provides its own challenges, and the maps are randomly generated each game. This makes every puzzle a unique challenge. Though there are three difficulty settings, they only influence the resources you have and don't fundamentally change how the game is played.Each level has three basic phases:1. Restore the physical environment.2. Create a variety of ecosystems.3. Clean up everything you placed.All in all, it's a satisfying experience to turn a dead environment into one that is full of life. The difficulty overall is on the low end, but some thought is required. Beating every level and fully restoring the planet will take 6-12 hours, making this a fairly short game, though levels can be replayed as they offer a slightly different challenge every time. Achievement seekers as usual will spend a little longer in the game.As an environmental philosopher, I find this game relaxing and even therapeutic despite the fantastic technology involved and its focus on climate engineering. Though true environmental issues cannot be solved technologically as presented in this game, this does allow an experience similar to Power Washing Simulator, House Flipper, and other games where you clean or fix something for the pure enjoyment of making something better. As a result, this gets a solid recommendation from, me for anyone looking for a relaxing experience combined with solid puzzle mechanics.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed Terra Nil! It was a refreshing take on the city building genre. I'm quite slow when I play games and I felt like Terra Nil suited my natural play style. The art is gorgeous, the music is amazing and meditative, and seeing life return to once polluted wastelands was super satisfying. I would happily play this again :)
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: I played several hours of the demo. When the final game was released i figured I could look past the poor graphics and just enjoy the game... I figured, surely they would have a lot of content for the price they were asking for. _childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: More of a puzzle game with cute graphics and a nice theme. But it's about as deep as a puddle, and not very wide either. You play through it once and you are done for. I honestly cannot recommend the game to anyone. Which is not to say I had no fun in it. But not enough to justify the time itself, not to mention the money.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: I thought I would enjoy this game as a casual stress reliever, I was surprised at how engaged I got with the maps. Suddenly I found several hours had passed! I like the enhanced maps after you complete the different continents once. With the way they generate their maps, I am looking forward to some decent replayability
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: A fun, challenging game with the nice objective of restoring nature rather than exploiting it like most games. I did find some of the puzzle elements too much for someone like myself who was placing elements haphazardly so I appreciated having a easier mode so I could just enjoy how the mechanics functioned and could watch the map change. There are more challenging modes which might be more enjoyable for players looking for that which is good.The art is lovely and creates lush environments that are a joy to appreciate. The music is calm and tranquil.The tactile feedback every time you place machines makes each decision feel weighted and when you begin to recycle all the machines you get the same joy of watching and hearing it all be re-collected.Negatives, there are only 8 levels sadly with 4 environments and I think the tutorial could do a better job of introducing the economics of the game mechanics.Overall a relaxing and challenging game which feels lovely to play.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Great for casual gamers. Really enjoying this one. Once you finish the four maps, it gives different, more challenging starting conditions which basically gives you another four maps that require much more planning and understanding of the mechanics. But there's something about this that isn't frustrating when you get stuck. You eventually get is by restarting/re-randomizing the map of one of the four regions until you figure it out.Also nice to have an eco game that doesn't throw in politics, agendas, global warming blame, and all that nonsense. It's simply a nice nature game set on an enjoyable puzzle mechanic.Highly recommend this one if you're looking for a small download and a few hours to kill.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: I really liked the original Terra Nil. This Steam version remake took the original set of mechanics, added different variants of them and then puts a subset of those in each Level. It feels highly arbitrary. Why would I have suddenly a completely different set of buildings in the Area right besides the previous one. It artificially inflates the Puzzle mechanic in illogical ways and throws you off every time you enter a new Level.From a pacing point of view its just not fun. You can no longer rely on what you learnt in previous levels. It's like learning from (near) zero again each level.On the plus side, the premise, graphics and audio are great!
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Terra Nil is a game that attempts to subvert common city builder tropes. With an environmentalist mindset, the aim of the game is to essentially work backwards and turn destroyed, barren wastelands into thriving ecosystems, wiping any trace of your influence, and leaving. It's a great premise for a game. But it lacks the foundational complexity of city builders to really be much more than a painfully linear experience who's entire purpose is nothing other than subversion. As a result, the game plays almost the exact same way every time, and what's being played can more or less rather simply be dumbed down to 'try to maximise the amount of tiles'. It becomes less about planning as a result, and more like a loose jigsaw puzzle that can only really be completed in a few number of ways.  Games are more than the sum of their parts. I can't honestly judge a game by picking it apart and estimating its value through its individual components because that defeats the purpose of examining how I actually *felt* playing it. That being said, I genuinely don't see what the fuss is about with this game. I don't think I would have lost much by just looking it up and watching someone else play it on Youtube.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: This is a beautiful and relaxing strategy game / "anti-city-builder" game. A decent amount of complexity yet not overwhelming. Solarpunk vibes. Cute graphics. Beautiful melodies.Like, at the end of restoring a region on a planet you actually have to recycle all of the buildings you used to build yourself a spaceship and get out, leaving basically no trace you were ever there in the first place. How cute is that!?I loved the concepts here.brb, going to hug a tree
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Fun little game.The challenge comes from figuring out how to use the different tools given to you to solve problems unique to each area. You can solve each area fairly easily, but it takes some planning (or like, 5 restarts - I'm slow) to get 100% for each one.It's also oddly rewarding to see your work complete in a fully restored world, with no trace of you having done anything at all.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Terra Nil is an amazing game, it was pretty much the only thing I played these past few days since release and for good reason. The game is beautifully made in its visual and sound design, every moment whether or not the player is doing something has some sort of spectacle going on. The flowing of the leaves, the bubbling of water, the cascade of leaves and the satisfying noise as your currency goes up in response to cleaning up part of the world or planting trees. The game feel is just phenomenal. As an actual strategy game it offers some actual meat and difficulty, especially on the 4th normal level, and all of the remix levels. You carefully have to prepare and minimize overlap/redundancies to eek on by certain points of the game. I do wish the difficulty curve within each level was more uniform, there comes a point in nearly every level where currency because no longer a problem, but up till that point the game can be extremely hard.I'm extremely excited to see if there is going to be more content, paid or otherwise for this game. I want to see a desert level, an undersea level, or more layouts for current levels.Edit: with the first major content update out, I would like to say besides a few bugs the game has only gotten better. The new revised animal system added that smoothing of the difficulty curve that I was looking for, while the final third of the level is still going to be a lot easier, it is no longer trivial and head empty. There is a lot of strategy in trying to get the balancing act of the new system just right, it's no longer just spam the map until you find the right spot, you now have to care about if an animal could logically travel a distance, and gives you a reason to use water and terrain tools in the end game instead of just at the beginning.I really like the new levels so far, they are interesting enough new designs that feel familiar but different enough to be worth a playthrough.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: I really ended up loving this game so much. What i thought would be a relaxing way to pass time ended up being so much more then that!! Although I wish it was a lot longer (finished in just under 25 hours), im sure they'll add more, as their new 3D map is fully rotatable. Either way, i will be going back to play a second time!

I think a desert biome would've been a neat addition to the game, that and a couple of the animals have incredibly vague requirements to find them (especially the narwhal), but in all I don't regret the $20 I spent on it, though I do think the price was a bit high for the amount of stuff you get.TL;DR - I recommend playing the game... but maybe wait for it to go on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Terra Nil is its gorgeous and serene visuals. The game's art style is inspired by low-poly landscapes, and the colors are bright and vibrant, creating a calming and meditative atmosphere that is perfect for players who want to unwind while playing a game.Gameplay-wise, Terra Nil is a puzzle game where players must strategically place buildings and plants to restore the environment. The goal is to transform a barren wasteland into a thriving ecosystem complete with rivers, forests, and wildlife. The game is split into different levels, and each level presents unique challenges that require careful planning and execution.Another aspect that makes Terra Nil stand out is its soundtrack. The music is soothing and relaxing, and it perfectly complements the game's overall vibe. The sound effects are also well-done, from the gentle sound of flowing water to the chirping of birds.Overall, Terra Nil is a unique and enjoyable game that offers a refreshing take on the city-building genre. Its beautiful visuals, calming soundtrack, and eco-conscious gameplay make it a great choice for players who want a relaxing and meaningful gaming experience. I highly recommend giving Terra Nil a try!

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful game, several moments especially towards the end were absolutely genius. _childDocuments_.review: I originally saw Angory Tom's videos on this game a while back and thought it looked really cool, and now I've played through myself I love it even more.Very cosy and chill but with enough puzzle elements to keep you thinking and I love the way the game looks too. _childDocuments_.review: A calming experience. Each level is its own small puzzle and might need a try or two to get 100% in a level as it requires forward planning that sometimes isn't possible first try. In easier difficulties you snowball your resources fast and cant really loose. I beat the game and estimate another couple hours to 100% everything I missed.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Relaxing game with focus on ecosystem restoration. That's in short what is main goal. Turning hostile, often poisonous wasteland into thriving and blooming nature.Concept brings quite fresh wind into management genre games. Allowing player to control how will land change based on his actions. Every game is different thanks to random map generator. And even identical map can end up with differently based on steps player takes.Four basic "bioms" require versatility in restoration approach. Ever single of them provides different set of tools. By utilizing them nature can be restored into quite breath taking landscapes.After completing campaign , alternated maps are unlocked. These provide altered set of tools and therefore restoration takes different road. Maps are also slightly more challenging.In conclusion I recommend this game since it was not only entertainment but also quite calming experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fairly basic puzzle game.  There's no city building, eco system management, or any of the things I feel like the video suggested there would be.  I found it pretty much the same in each level, which became boring quickly.If you're looking for an eco themed puzzle game then this might be for you, but if you're looking for more depth then probably look elsewhere.  Maybe worth a go on sale.  Definitely not at full price.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Cute game but nowhere near enough content to justify the price tag. There are 4 biomes with 2 variations each, and the entire game can be beaten with all optional side objectives in a single afternoon. Yes, it is procedurally generated, but that generation cannot give enough variation to be worth playing through more than a few times.Not worth it unless deeply discounted.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: This game is gripping. Its increasingly-complex puzzles set up by its very simple premise are supported by some incredibly appealing art, visual effects, and animation. The buildings are easilyA lot of options are missing. There's no way to better-highlight buildings hidden behind trees or other buildings. One of the maps, Polluted Fjord, gives you exactly 4 spots to place a starting tidal generator, one of which never reaches the mainland and includes no associated ocean-building tiles to facilitate its use. There are a lot of good options for gameplay, but no colorblind modes that I could find.The game is a little buggy. More than once I placed down a species call, decided it was the wrong move, pressed the undo button, and found the species stuck around to poke at grass. On other occasions, I reached the precipitation benchmark for a map and then precipitation did not start (which was especially frustrating when I very much needed the burst of resources rain would have provided).The game is fairly poorly tutorialized, making the figuring out of the gameplay portion of the game a puzzle all its own. Some of the text ill-explains itself unless you read each tooltip -thoroughly. The monorail in particular took a few minutes of trial and error.Despite these issues, I want more of this game. I want DLC, paid or otherwise, which I will devour. I want mapmaking tools to enable players to challenge one another to renew particularly challenging stretches of wasteland. New levels would be nice but aren't necessary-- I just want to be able to tackle the same levels with new tools. Or make my own levels, or make my own ecosystems. Whatever the next major content update for this game is, I will be watching closely and with interest.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this game, I found it very peaceful. It has what I would call a 'strategy front' because you cant really fail a level with the amount of resources you start with but that isn't a bad thing. Gives you the feeling of progression and accomplishment without the pressure, there are other strategy based games to play for the challenge. Played it a couple times over because the graphics are gorgeous, did only take me 16 hours to finish the game about 3 times so would suggest waiting for more content or for a sale. Can't wait to see what comes in the future though.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Game-breaking bugs and glitches on launch. Only 4 levels "With randomization!" which adds minimal extra game mechanics.As a core concept, it's a great idea for a game! Restore a wasteland and then clean up and look at your handiwork. But there's too much that doesn't make sense for it to be engaging. Most buildings "fire" once and are done. Your irrigation center sprays water once, and it's ready to be recycled... unless you have a monorail system, in which case you move it 1 foot to the left and presto it can be used again! Everything is paid for with leaves which come from... grass? Is someone paying us? Are we doing this out of the kindness of our hearts? Come to think of it, where is everyone else on planet Earth and how did the humans die, but the pandas survive? There are too many questions and I can safely say the game does not answer them."Well, sometimes realism is sacrificed in the name of good gameplay" Fair point, fair point. But uh, what *is* the gameplay? The closest this can be mapped to is a puzzle game where you optimally overlap building ranges. It is about as challenging as building a sandwich, slicing the cheese and the tomato and the bread to the right sizes. Spatial optimization is nifty, but in most games I've seen it (like Anno) it's a background mechanic. The one change this game brings to the concept is threatening bankruptcy if you misclick and only giving 1 undo at a time. Which seems to run counter to the wholesome, relaxed atmosphere every other component is trying to build.Lastly, let's talk about pricing. This is a low-gear game for either children or adults who want to relax like a kid again. It is very pretty to look at when the visuals aren't glitching. It is well-paced to 1-hour game sessions. It makes me feel wholesome, despite everything in it going against my training as an environmental engineer. I would pay 5, maybe 10 dollars. 20 dollars on release, because I was still hyped from the demo almost a year ago. But $25 is too much. For that price, I could grab one of the older, greener, high-tech-ier Anno games and still be obsessing over building placement for eight hours this weekend... and I could undo my mistakes.Oh, right, last little stinger: the RNG is so broken I spent 4 of my 8 hours on levels that were impossible to win from the start. Thanks for wasting as much of my time as you improved. I hope sunflowers over nuclear waste becomes a meme.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Anti-city builder, chill, reasonably cute game. Pretty short (8 maps) but I loved the theme and art. Played in easy mode and it was relaxing and rewarding enough. Lot of potential if the editor adds more worlds or options to generate maps randomly ;)8/10 would play again occasionally.PS: October's update added native Linux support so gg devs!
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Its a wonderfully relaxing game, with a beautiful solar-punk concept and soundtrack.My recommendation is to buy this game when it is on sale.My reasoning:Games should for a certain price point, provide a certain amount of playtime.A game you pay little for has little expectations for how long it needs to keep you engaged, and a higher cost needs to have higher playtime.This game IS wonderful, but i feel like for the short amount of time it takes before you can fully beat the game, (for me 10.7 hours for both the main campaign and post campaign) its 32.99 CAD price seems a little steep. Now if it were an early access game with more planned on the way, I might understand. But as far as I know, this is it in full release.I'm not trying to discourage you from purchasing, because I quite enjoyed it, but for its short gameplay, it feels like its worth closer to 10-15$ unless more content is later provided.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: In this game, you place units to provide power, change the nature of soil then irrigate it. This part is boringly easy.Once a unit is placed, you cannot move it anymore. At most you can do one undo.I find this annoying.You have limitations about where you can place the units too and it's another little frustration because you can't reach everywhere.Then you need to cater for animals, except that most of your interaction with them will be to see them unhappy and you'll not be able to do anything for them. As stated above you can only add units.In the end I decided to ignore the critters and do my thing.Then, I'm being asked to pack everything and leave.  This is consistent in placing "trash cans" to gather your units, then send a boat to gather everything.I've spent about one hour in this game and I the amount of fun I had is way into in the negative.

_childDocuments_.review: I played the demo for a total of 18 hours. The demo. And this game is exactly what I was hoping for. It's beautiful, peaceful, and juuuuust difficult to have me mess up now and again, but not enough to annoy me (on medium difficulty anyway). I actually found myself smiling and giggling randomly cause it was just so satisfying to watch the grass and trees pop up. Not many games make me feel like a kid again, but damn, this one did.It's not a long game, I'm making my way through the second half (you get to replay regions, but with trickier maps) and taking my time to admire it too. So probably a 8-12 hour game if you take it slow. However the maps are randomized and I expect to replay this constantly.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is marketed as serene and relaxing but what you actually get is a game that is intentionally difficult. I even put zen mode on and this game is still making me cry. The mechanics behind it are forcing you into difficult situations that make it borderline impossible to pass a level.As others reviewing have been saying, I think this game was marketing in the incorrect categories.  It does not play like a reverse city builder where you would be able to highly fine tune your environments, but more like a puzzle game where there is one predetermined combination to win.  I understand others might enjoy this game as it is, but I did not.I had to restart a level 8 times to finally clear it, which is highly frustrating.  There is absolutely no room for error in these levels, once you set a building down its extremely difficult or impossible to move it or pick it back up. The worst part is the recycling aspect. In the level that just caused me to finally give up and quit, the game is forcing you to recycle all your buildings through the waterways. The stupid journal doesn't tell you this ahead of time either, you have to progress far enough to unlock the buildings in the final/3rd wave to see what you get. Waterway recycling requires you to excavate rivers to connect all of the ponds in the map, I would have to put down 20 drills to accomplish this. The most irritating thing about that is the fact that the level allows for monorails, which have a special building you can place on them to signal the recycler to come pick them up, but the level intentionally denies you access to this tool. So I spent over an hour progressing the level only to find out all the work I have been doing was for nothing. This game is so frustrating and hardly rewarding I cannot believe it costs $25. I was so excited for this game and it was not nearly as fun as I had hoped. The mechanics are terrible for no reason other than to make the game more difficult.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Fun little indie game. It's not the best thing I've ever played, but I genuinely enjoyed it. The game play was very relaxed and slower paced, which was a nice break, and it was rewarding to see your little world develop. Only complaint is that it has very little replay value due to only having 8 maps that are always basically the same, and after beating them I basically forgot about the game for like a year. But, for the 8-10 hours it gave me, it was very enjoyable and chill. I give it an 8/10 overall.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: This game is great! It has strong puzzle and resource management systems, a unique interaction between pieces and the world, and very satisfying "AHA!" moments where you figure out what the games wants you to do with some of the advanced variations of maps you've played before once you've finished a first pass. The game is amazingly beautiful and it warrants mentioning that I wish you had the ability to watch a fast-forwarding of the each successful game with matching music because the contrast between the barren beginnings and the lush, vibrant restored world would exemplify everything the game is about.Pros:- The game is satisfying, fun, and poses a challenge- Puzzles are easy enough to understand and the pacing works well enough- Beautiful score that exemplifies the message of the game- Truly well done graphical choices that make the rest of the game feel alive, or in other cases, dead and barren- Price point matches the time you'll get out of the game; I only expected a few hours of fun, but I got over ten and I still have more to enjoyCons:- Once you understand the base loop, the game isn't too much complexThere are definitely more issues I feel the game has, but they are minor gripes and honestly, some of them are intentional. For example, I was annoyed at first the it is possible to rebuild the environment in such a way that you can't reintroduce certain species without significant alterations, but I think that is intentional so that you can have a goal with your restoration as you begin a new game in the same region. All in all, this is a wonderfully calm game with a great message and a fun game play loop. Even if I never play it again I feel like it was worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: I really, really want this game to succeed. It's beautiful, it's hopeful, it supports a good cause and it tries something new with a topic that is difficult and complicated and strangely absent from video games: hope in the time of the climate crisis. I work in the industry and it's my fervent belief that we need more games like this. (Thinking back I think the closest thing to it is 1996 Maxi's Sim Park.)For this reason I'm not going to judge it very harshly on the resource mechanics and strategy aspect. It can be a little hard to understand the resource management at first glance; how things are best placed and how to maximise the numbers (at least for an idiot like me). I finished a level and was about to recycle my constructs, when I accidentally placed a monorail outside of range, was not able to undo and my only option was to restart the level from scratch. It's a bit awkward, but at the same time, the recycling aspect is my favourite feature - I've never seen a game ask you to remove yourself from what you've built in order to let it flourish continuously without your input. It's a really beautiful feature imho.In any case, I really enjoy this game for its calm, beautiful gameplay and philosophy behind it. Would love to see it scaled for DLC, maybe into different species and rewilding tactics for ecosystems? (Though that's probably outside the scope.) Beautiful work!
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Terra Nil is a very relaxed, casual game. Fairly short with 8 maps split across 4 biomes that each take roughly a half hour to 45 minutes each if you take it slow like I did. I think there is some procedural generation in the maps to make each one slightly different but I'm not sure. There is only one resource to manage and the challenges are simple combinations of temperature, humidity, pollution and (for one biome) radiation. Despite completing the "campaign" which is just the maps I find myself drawn back to it to play the settings again and again if only because it is a relaxing and pretty game. if you can grab it on a sale I'd recommend it to someone looking for a quick, simple, pretty puzzle/strategy game.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to love this game, but unfortunately I was disappointed. I love both puzzle games and zen games and this could very well do both, depending on the difficulty, but right now it does neither well. There are lots of little bugs and at least one gamebreaking one. The big one is the game making a mistake when calculating the loss condition, which leads to it forcing you to restart the level when you haven't actually lost yet. It makes the highest difficulty unplayable, which robs the game of the puzzle play mode. It's not an issue in the other game modes as you are rarery short on resources.The little bugs and quality of life issues are not gamebreaking, but distracting. That is not very relaxing, so it's not really an zen game either.Maybe the bugs will be fixed in the future, but I found mentions of at least the big issue from months ago and it is still in the game. So unfortunately I can not recommend this game right now. It's a shame, because I love the idea and the art design and for the first hour or so I was really enjoying myself. If you can get it for less than 10$ it might still be worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a forest ecologist / forest health specialist and I enjoy Terra Nil. I'm also a longtime gamer, so I do see some design issues that could make this puzzle game significantly better, but they have done a great job here in general. Recognize that despite the ecosystem restoration theme of this game, it's basically a puzzle game. The ecology aspect is not terribly strong; nothing like SimLife or Gundan Frontier. But all aspects of the game do have some connection to ecology or ecosystem restoration. The biggest issues of the game, in my opinion are: 1. One of your final goals is to make all the animal populations happy by creating ideal mixes of adjacent environments. HOWEVER, you don't get info on how good these are until after multiple stages of the game, including AFTER you create the habitats. So you are forced to guess at good habitat placement during the stage where it matters most. 2. Fine tuning environments to give ideal conditions after the animals show up can be really frustrating. Many of your methods for manipulating environments AFTER they have been built are destructive and have significant tradeoffs that can ruin other habitats. Again, the time to make these habitat combinations properly is during the habitat building phase, NOT at the end when everything is already on the board. 3.  The encyclopedia gives only vague information on what animals want. Only in game ONCE THEY ARE ALREADY PRESENT do you see the finer details of what they need. The time to have this information available is during the habitat building stage. 4. Replayability isn't very strong, as you create most of the content yourself, so replaying a level doesn't add anything new to the experience. On top of that, there are no technology unlocks so there's no incentive to put additional time into the game. Finally, due to the frustrations above, I just want to call my previous successes good and not re-experience the frustrations. Ok, so that's alot of criticism, and there's more I could get into, but the overall game is good and it's clear the developers care about this game and the subject. A recent update came out that adds some quality of life improvements and some new dynamics that improve the game (plus new content that I haven't unlocked yet). Terra Nil is priced appropriately for the quality of its content, and there isn't much else like it. I highly recommend this game, just be prepared for some frustration as noted above.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: 8,5/10In a not so distant future, humanity reached the level of being able to explore space, allowing it to reach other planets and transform them, to allow its colonization. Unfortunately despite all these advances, certain things unfortunately still seem not to have changed, such as the desire for natural resources, even if that means having to destroy all the fauna and flora of a planet, while at the same time polluting the soil and waters. But one planet in particular could be the beginning of a big change in humanity's relationship with nature. ^^It is here that a great project begins, on a planet that no longer harbors humanity, but where traces of it are found everywhere. Here, the mission will begin, through the use of a wide variety of technologies, to transform this barren soil, with dry riverbeds and polluted seas, into a green paradise again, from tropical islands to cold tundra, cleaning and restoring vegetation, and later the fauna back, thus allowing nature in this world to have a new chance, and who knows if everything works out, in the future the same will happen in other worlds. ^^+ A very relaxing and fun game, where we don't have to build cities, nations or empires, but use technology to restore nature back to its place.+ Four biomes, with their vegetation, animals, characteristics and specific constructions for their restoration.+ Procedurally generated map, so even if the region and biome are the same, the map will always have a unique terrain.+ Simple system that uses points, which are spent when building buildings, and earned as vegetation is restored, from grass to jungles and forests.+ All biomes have at least three different types of vegetation, and six species of animals to restore and appreciate the beauty.+ Beautiful arts, I really liked the artist part and thought it was very beautiful.+ Relaxing music and sound effects.- It's a fun game, but unfortunately it only has four biomes, with a smaller and a larger map for each.- Most of the time is relaxing, but the beginning of all maps can be a little stressful, as it is the part with the highest expenditure of points that are limited and the lowest return.And so begins the player's mission with the objective of restoring the regions of the planet, using a very simple system, with the currency of exchange being points, these points are spent when making constructions to clean the soil, produce energy, change the climate, and is gained by making the flora grow, promoting the growth of vegetation such as grass, forests, coral reefs, mosses among other biomes, thus allowing the player to seek the balance between spending preparing the environment, and the return by making the vegetation flourish. ^^Once I've learned how to balance the points, I need to learn how to balance the environment, as each biome has three or four different types of vegetation, which need to occupy a minimum area, as well as each one has its prerequisites, some can only be done in places of low or high terrain, others need to be built on land and then taken to the sea, some need the place to have grass first, while others even need the region to have suffered a fire beforehand, thus making it equally more challenging and interesting, the mission to restore while adapting to the requirements of each type of vegetation. ^^Produced by the South African studio Free Lives, I was really surprised by the quality of the art, I really liked it and found it to be very beautiful, both during the restoration process and in the final part, where we can see the art and beauty of the restored nature of the various biomes, and the plants and animals that live in them. As for the soundtrack, I was also very satisfied, finding the songs very calm and peaceful, and very pleasant to listen to while playing or even outside the game to relax. ^^Terra Nil was a game I'd had my eye on for some time, having played since the first demo that was made available, and bought it on pre-order. And now after having played and explored it, I can say that I liked what I saw, while restoring the four available biomes, some more challenging than others. For those looking for a large amount of content, maybe this game is not very pleasing, because as said before, it only has four biomes, but for those looking for a different, relaxing and fun experience, while looking to make the places gray and lifeless, again in landscapes full of green and life, this is a game that I recommend. ^^

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR:Like the vibes? - Get it.Like pure gameplay? - Wait for saleLike a mix? - Read below.~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~People keep saying that it's short, but that's not full story. This game falls in to 2 genres: chill and management game. Chill games usually have wild price points, because people who play them seek reeeally unique experiences. These unique experiences are not efficient to develop for the general audience - hard work for a small group of people, that's why prices are sometimes disproportionally big with small play time.On the other hand, management games are complete oposite, they have superb replay value and a lot of content for relatively low price, but when it comes to visual stuff and vibes, they can underdeliver.This game is primarily a chill game priced accordingly, so if eou really enjoy the vibes of this game - get it. If you are interested in pure gameplay - wait for a sale, if you have a mix decide which side of the game you prefer more and if you are like me and love the vibes and management side of this Terra Nil - it is an excellent time.

_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Terra Nil is a ecological restoration game where you are tasked with helping animals and wildlife move into the land. When you begin, you will get a guide to show you what work needs to be done in that area. Every level you go through three phases:                    - Restoring the land                  - Increasing diversity of plants and bushes. Animals will potentially move in at this point,                    - Collecting all your technology before leaving the site. it is a very relaxing and slow game, so it is not the type to be rushed. There is a challenging achievement where ALL groups of animals need to be satisfied in one area, so really it is about patient and balancing what you add to the land. Also very educational about nature and wildlife. I throughly enjoyed as a someone who really connects to animals and nature.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: This was a charming game. Sometimes, one just wants a peaceful happy time- and this is that game. The music is soothing, the gameplay loop doesn't have any dire time pressures upon the player so the strategy/puzzle can be approached at one's own pace. The tutorial/first playthrough has a good curve to introduce you to the game (although once you are experienced, you are much better served being at a higher difficulty so as to have all your tools available sooner).The 'story ending' 4th level was a fantastic idea to cap off the journey of restoring the world. I loved just flipping through the notebook to see all the little doodles of crittersI have very minor complaints about the game- there was not an arid/desert environment. All of the stages (with small exception) are 'increase humidity/temperature'.

_childDocuments_.review: So after about 7 hours in, im down to the last bits to complete. The game is chill. If i want a challenge I can have it, but if I suddenly just wanna go brain dead and relax in the chill of cleaning up the wasteland, i can. I admit that I find myself going back and wanting to play it again (which I can). I do love the different biomes and god that audio on the thunder is enough to put me to sleep from the get go (in a good way). i know this a bit of a scatter brained review but it is 1am and barely awake.in the end, this is my breakdown on it.Story: None (it's a zen reverse city builder, so no story)Music: damn good. 8/10 Sound: while over all, it is fine, there are 2 main complaints for me: one is how some audio with suddenly jump from left ear to right ear, even though you havent move the camera. Not really game breaking but a little disorienting. Two is the sound of ice freezing over rivers and water can be a bit jarring when it starts freezing in bulk.Gameplay: Solid 9/10. The levels are fun, and the coordinates give you replay-ability with friends, the entering thing is pretty straight forward and offers enough variety of ways to handle situations without breaking the zen feelingBugs: there are a few, unfortunately. not many, maybe 1 or 2. i ran into 1 where it wouldnt let me place a animal scanner down and the only option it gave was for me finish recycling and launch. it only happened once and i wasnt able to recreate the issue. another is the audio for water flowing into a empty river bed got stuck in a loop. fixed after i placed a second water pump. 3rd (and it has happened a few times) if you recycle too fast when you reach your flying recycle drown, it can get stuck and SLOWLY move towards the recycle point (like to fly the space of 2 tiles can take up to a full mintue)all in all im giving this game a solid 8.5 out of 10. it is everything i hoped for, and hope to keep playing it (and hope for maybe some dlc with new areas one day)

_childDocuments_.review: While I did enjoy the experience, it was a mild enjoyment that I cannot recommend at full price due to the lack of content and depth. I would suggest you wait for a sale for many reasons. Games like this are why I wish the recommendation system wasn't so strict on forcing you to choose yes or no with no middle-ground options - because I did like it, I just don't think it's worth $25.The game concept is certainly interesting, but the problem is that it lacks depth and falls short. I was able to 100% the whole game, with bonus levels, achieving all optional goals, and 6/6 animals on all maps in just over 5 hours. This itself isn't a huge problem but it lacks replay-ability which I'll get to later. This play time is including time spent troubleshooting the numerous bugs I ran into that required me to reload multiple times.Bugs aren't a huge issue as those should be fixed soon, but as I said the game lacks depth. It was a very easy game start to finish, which might be what you're looking for, but if you want a challenge then skip this one. The animals are a good example, the "harder" levels really should have had different species, at least cosmetically. I was honestly expecting the last 4 levels to do something new but they are just the first 4 again, with a slightly different strategy that stops being different once you get into making biomes.It is a charming game, and it has great visuals. It has a good concept and a good gameplay loop in the levels. There just isn't enough there for me. I don't find it to be an enjoyable replayable experience either because of the fact that the entire game is sort of the same thing on repeat with slight variations, and no real change in strategy along the way aside from different buildings that do the same things as previous ones, only with different placement requirements.Tbh the most strategic depth this game had for me was being required to do things they don't flat-out tell you for some levels, such as:1. Building a  will  immediately.2. You can use a  to  to make them  when you lack .Overall I find myself walking away from this one feeling unimpressed. It was not a memorable experience because it felt so repetitive with not enough distinct content to break the repetition. I certainly think it needed to be longer with more variety of strategies. 4 main levels and 4 bonus levels that are just slightly harder versions of the main levels is not enough to justify a $25 release imo. Maybe $15 - $20,TL;DR: 8 Levels, giving 4-6 Hours of gameplay - for 25 Dollars? Idk about that one chief. I can't say this one is worth it at full price, especially considering the game is essentially the same 4 levels, twice in a row.

_childDocuments_.review: An extremely enjoyable and addictive unique terraforming game that feels a little limited.I love this game. That's the short of it. I've followed it's development and played the demos whenever I could, and now that the end product is out, I love it. You're presented with a campaign of sorts where you work through four separate biomes and restore them from apocalyptic wastelands to vivid and beautifully realised habitats; contending with each biomes relatively unique challenges but fundamentally using the same mechanics in each to achieve the goals. A little buggy occasionally but nothing game breaking and certainly nothing that got in the way of my overall enjoyment. The animals are meant to be the cherry on the cake once the habitat is restored, and while they look great they are frustratingly mismatched and poorly researched; penguins are presented alongside a roster of Arctic animals even though they are from the Antarctic (just use seals...), tortoises don't live on beaches (they're predominant grazers), and hawksbill turtles are marine turtles and not lagoon/freshwater dwelling (there's plenty of actual freshwater turtles that they could be swapped with). At 11 hours playtime I have completed it, secured all bar one of the steam achievements and replayed some of the maps a number of times. It is a short game with limited replayability aside from achievement hunting, perhaps best treated as a kick back and relax puzzle game to fill time or chill.A wishlist:- Bigger maps for that 'great plains' feel and to make the tundra really feel like a tundra, the maps often end up feeling cluttered.- Creative mode? The art style is outstanding and an opportunity to fully utilise and appreciate it in a freeform creative mode would be incredible.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wish there was a mixed option, but the fact of the matter is the game wasn't worth the asking price.Don't get me wrong, the game is visually wonderful, and what's there gameplay-wise was really cool when it comes to its ideas of reclaiming a destroyed ecosystem. My problems are similar to many others reviewing it, I beat this game in two hours on the normal difficulty, and the game only has 4 maps with no real replayability. Visually pretty maps with its own mechanics, but in the end, each map plays out the same with no real puzzle solving that really uses all the tools at your disposal. Are there ways to make it interesting? Yeah, and I feel that might be possible through more environmental challenges that could pop up during the reclamation, but this game doesn't have that factor to it, leading to a no stress one track puzzles with no real deviations.The no stress nature of this is not really a problem, hell, it's pretty relaxing at its core, but I feel that compared to games like Dorf Romantik or Islanders, which fall in that relaxing puzzle solving gameplay loop this game tries to tap into, it falls very short. I think what ties into that is the fact the latter two have fun puzzles to solve that are guided by your own planning, and replay-ability despite the randomness of tiles, buildings, and maps. At the moment, Terra Nil doesn't have enough of that similar design philosophy to really make replaying it any more fun.That said, if they do add stuff and improve it, I'd gladly change my review, but as it stands $25 is pretty steep for something that could be completed in two lunchbreaks.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is less of a strategy game and more of a puzzle game with some simple, but time delayed puzzles. You would think there is little that could go wrong with that formula, alas it is not the case.The first phase of each puzzle, where you always purify the land/water is painfully boring but messing up placements of buildings can (and does) soft lock you in later phases. This is particularly true in any map where you are dealing with lava as it's far less forgiving to adjust where it flows. The second phase of each puzzle you build out the habitats. While this is more interesting there are several habitats that are spawned by single use objects (sky scrapers for example) and activating them at the wrong time can and will softlock you. For example if you get taken off guard by nuclear waste in a few of the puzzles, you might watch your bamboo get deleted and be unable to make more.The third phase of each puzzle is optimizing the environments and... clean up. As far as optimizing goes, the AI that determines how a creature's habitat spreads is not very smart. For example it's entirely possible for you to drop an animal that needs water tiles next to a river or lake and watch it's territory expand entirely away from the water and not satisfy it's water need even if there's plenty of unused tiles. Instead the game expects you to corral territories with sonic devices that disrupt all habitats around them for a short while. This can obviously mess up perfectly happy nearby animals and shouldn't need to be done.Cleanup is a tedious chore on most of the puzzles as it involves guiding a little boat or monorail car around the map recycle all your buildings. For the boat if you don't have nearby water it then becomes a silly game of blasting new channels to make rivers after everything is in place. For the monorails, it's a silly game of shuffling around rocks so that you can build a monorail network. Monorail cars can also get stuck in their animation and requires going back to the main menu and back into the game to free them.

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful, soothing puzzle game. Ever play Slipways? It's a bit like that. You get a randomly generated map and you need to logistics your way to success, which in this game means restoring a polluted wasteland to its beautiful and majestic natural state.It is definitely satisfying to work your way through a map, then look at the overall sum of the happy accidents that resulted from your efforts. You may have been focused on the logistics during the run, but once it's over (within an hour usually), you can step back and see the unique landscape you've more-or-less accidentally crafted, replete with different sub-biomes, flora, and of course, little animals tacked on at the end.Each level comes with cool optional unlocks for meeting certain conditions, like an aurora borealis or salmon spawning or something.The one thing that seems gamey and unsatisfying to me is the idea that once you hit a condition once, that thing sticks around for good. For example, snowfall requires a certain coldness of temperature and moisture level. But once you unlock snowfall, it doesn't seem to matter if you crank up the heat afterwards. It will keep snowing.NOTE: You will get the end credits after about 6 hours as there are only 4 basic regions with unique mechanics. After that, you can replay the map types on randomized maps and increase the difficulty, but they didn't seem to make an effort to randomize elements of the mechanics or bonus rewards that could theoretically lead to an endless gameplay loop. Shame.Also, the in-game resources are incorrect and unreliable at times. Imagine an in-game encyclopedia on game mechanics that tells you something that is wrong, which obscures the solution to an advanced stage. This is bad but patchable.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Play the demo, that is the game. If $25 is a lot for you wait for a sale.I don't review stuff often on steam but I played like 20+ hours of the original prototype of this game so I felt important to review the final version. Part of me wishes there was a mixed option, but I'd still recommend this over not.First off this game is getting a lot of flack for not having enough "content". Yes after 4 hours you will see every biome and every building, I feel like if this is the main criticism of the game maybe people have only been playing games from the last 8 years or something. It's a puzzle game that has procedural levels, that is what the content and replayability is, the gameplay, not what types of biomes there are.To me it's like complaining that you've seen all the content in a game like Tetris or Sim City after 5 minutes, because you technically have. There is no meta progression where you get new pieces in Tetris, there is no alternate biomes or mechanics in Sim City. You just get one thing done well.I do think the price of the game is a little high and it feels like it was because it was picked up by a "larger indie" publisher and they felt they needed to recoup their costs. Which is a little disappointing.It would also be nice if we did get just some basic updates with more achievements, optional larger maps, maybe a custom map maker, and some additional challenge modes or difficulty. In a lot of ways this game feels a bit easier than the hardest maps on the prototype, and as someone who has basically already played it a lot in an earlier for it would have been nice to see something to allow for that without having to add "new content".If $25 for a game is a lot for you then you should probably hold off. Play the demo, that is what the game is + a few more biomes. The replayability is just enjoying the puzzle mechanics of the game, not meta progression or unlocking things. If you NEED that kind of gameplay to be engaged by a game then this probably isn't for you. That doesn't make it a bad game though as there are TONS of games that do one thing simple, and straightforward, without a ton of content and they are fantastic.
