_childDocuments_.review: I don't really care for these types of games, as I'm not into growing civilizations or anything of the sort. But since Terra Nil is about rejuvenating the environment instead of building onto it, I find it very compelling. The premise is simple – you have a wasteland and it's your job to restore it. You generate power, scrub a small area of toxins, and then add greenery. The first phase is always about adding enough of this greenery (or purifying enough of the nearby waters). The game is fairly complex but it does a pretty good job of guiding you forward. The second phase is trickier, as you need to restore four biomes. The last phase is about reintroducing animal life and then removing all of your machines so you can leave the land without a trace of your involvement. It's immensely satisfying.The game has four areas that you unlock sequentially, but each area has a second version that unlocks once you complete all of the initial ones. These mix things up by adding in machines and features from across the initial four levels. They can get pretty difficult, though. In the second version of the second area requires you to build forests by constructing shade pillars. But shade pillars can only be placed on cliffs and need to be in a triangle and you have to dredge up all of the level's land from the ocean. If you don't dredge up the ocean in preparation for this, you'll need to restart the whole level. But things aren't usually THIS demanding. You can zoom in extremely close and the graphics are lovely and detailed. The game isn't massively long but I feel like it's got enough content, especially since the levels are all generated, which makes attempts feel fresher than otherwise. At the end of the last area, you have to build a rocket, which is neat and it does a great job of making you feel like you accomplished something during the last four levels. You can restart any of a level's three phases once you get stuck and you can often undo your last move, which is helpful, but you can't quicksave or undo multiple moves in a row, so the game isn't extremely forgiving of mistakes, so you can sink yourself if you're not careful. But I think Terra Nil is highly enjoyable and recommend it to anyone who wants an anti-city builder that often feels like a puzzle game.

_childDocuments_.review: Here's a list of what's in the full game that's not in the demo:The game in general and the UI are more polished now. There is a weather system where weather buildings must be placed to reach specific humidity and temperature thresholds that must be met for certain buildings to be placed and for events to happen in the world. Most of these are cosmetic and just grant points, but a few aren't such as rain which fills in grass in all the stray tiles you missed. There is an animal system during the recycling phase where you have to find places in the map that are suitable to each species. Some of these are pretty specific and may require you to manipulate the map a bit to create the right conditions. In terms of content, the demo is level 1 of the final game and is mostly the same outside of adding the above features. There are three more levels each with their own unique biomes, buildings, and mechanics that are generally more complex as you progress. There is also a second version of each level where the goals are the same but the terrain generation is different and some of your buildings are replaced with ones from different levels, significantly changing the experience.

It was relaxing and satisfying to watch my biomes come together in a way that felt plausible; an excellent wake up in the morning and drink your coffee game. _childDocuments_.review: instead of the 4X genre (Explore, Expand, Exploit, Exterminate) which normally formes the foundation for ressource management games where you start out exploring your surroundings to find ressources, then expanding with those ressources to build larger and larger industry, which you can then use to further exploit the ressources in your enviornment, before finally exterminating some kind of threat meant to test the efficiency of your industry this game is instead a new genre of its own the 4R (Reclaim, Restore, Rewild, Retreat) firstly to reclaim the irradiated wasteland, completely devoid of nature and exploited to the fullest extend, then you restore bringing back green planes and water ways, however this is still a wasteland so you'll need to rewild it restore ecosystems and inefficiency, and finally, your ultimate goal is to tear down all the infrastructure you have build, to clean up all the little buildings you have littered the region with, and to retreat.and this is very much something that is needed in our current day, because the colonialist conventions of the 4X genre are exatly the same processes which have placed us in the ecological collapse which we are facing in the real world, which is why its in some ways reassuring and nice to see a game that presents an alternative game structure, and grounds itself in real approaches to enviornmental restoration and highlights some enviornmental lessons about how even fire and volcanic erruptions are an important part of a healthy ecosystem, to how sunflowers can even play an important role in restoring enviornments we would otherwise consider dead and gone.

The Vita Nova update this year adds more depth to the game and changes the way that you interact with the animals and environment.  Playing through on the toughest difficulty I'm on the second level and feeling like I'm genuinely challenged to make smart decisions but without it being obstinate.  Stoked to keep going on another playthrough!

_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Aesthetically and thematically pleasing with repetitive and shallow gameplay.GAMEPLAYWhile the game talks a lot about (bio)diversity), the gameplay lacks diversity in any form. It is essentially about zoning and tile hunting, where a badly generated map can lock you out of some aspects of the level or its objectives before you even begin, which I found very annoying.The mechanics are very simple, you'll mostly be concerned with zoning everything perfectly (tedious messing around trying to find the perfect tile) and finding the correct sequence to do the various things (zoning, temperature and humidity adjustment) that the main and optional objectives require.LENGTHThere are four levels in total, and if you know what you are doing, they shouldn't take more than 15 minutes each, but in the beginning they can take longer. Each map has an alternate version, which requires different tools, but the mechanics stay essentially the same. I don't think there is much replay value to be had, as the objectives don't change much and there is a very limited way for you to get to them. LEVEL SPECIFICSAfter taking care of the flora, in the final stage you get to introduce animals, but they are there just eye-candy. You don’t get to interact with them in any way. Except for the fact that this can also be a point where you realise you’ve locked yourself out of a certain species because of improper zoning. The game doesn’t tell you this in advance in any way, which to some might seem organic, but to me its just annoying, as you have to start the level again, just to get that brown bear.At the end of each level, you have to clean up after yourself, that is recycle all your structures. While thematically this is nice, the mechanics make it tedious, boring and convoluted. You can’t help but feel it’s there to stretch out the time, but when you get to recycling, you are basically done with the level anyway.CONTROLS, UIThe controls and the UI are not great either. You can't rotate the map, so a lot of your time will be taken up by tile hunting (trying to find the tile where you can place a specific structure, when most of what you see is blocked by vegetation or elevation).  The maps are also small, so you don’t get the sense of a great natural expanse, instead you’ll feel crowded to get everything packed into such a limited space.PRICEAs a large chunk of sales go towards a good cause I wouldn’t recommend against buying the title if you like it, but in hindsight if the games was half of its original price (25 Euro), I would still have been disappointed.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: You get what you see in the demo, with a couple of small surprises, but that's not a bad thing - this is a lovely little puzzle game with a few strategy elements later,. and as you might expect from the demo, relaxing - mostly. It is possible to screw up later on, but you're probably not going to get any stress earlier.There's not enough of it, is the only thing!
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Earth is destroyed, it’s full of toxins, and all life disappears. You are sent here to return everything back and make Earth green again. First things first, you need electricity to power up a Toxin Scrubber that clears soil and prepares it for an Irrigator that creates grass. The game offers four regions: Temperate, Tropical, Polar and Continental. Each of them has different starting conditions. For example, while in the Temperate region, you can easily build wind turbines on rocks, in the Polar you will have to blow up fissures to create magma, and then you will be able to build a power plant. The game has a nice guide which will teach you everything you need to know.So when you successfully finish the first phase you can move to the second – create biomes. Again, each region is specific and has its own biomes to make a perfect biodiversity. You will be creating forests, tundras, tropical rainforests, beaches, swamps, corals and more. To achieve perfect conditions in a biome, it is a good idea to complete optional tasks that tell you how high or low the air temperature should be, how much humidity you should have, or how many toxins you should remove. Completing them will give you more leaves, which can be used as currency to build more buildings, or you can summon rain or snow, which will clean every tile on a map and give you a huge amount of leaves. I recommend you complete the optional tasks as they will help you complete your restoration mission.Once you have created biomes, you can move on to the final stage - life and recycling. Each biome hides animals that you can discover using the Animal Observatory. Most animals require two or more types of biome to be discovered successfully. So, if you build biomes in the wrong places, you won't be able to find them all in one playthrough. It’s ok, you can replay the region, but keep in mind that it will be a little bit different because each map is randomly generated. It won’t be completely different, but some small changes can appear, like repositioned rocks or river bands. To complete your mission you have to find only three species of animals. After that, you can finally build an airship by recycling buildings. You can achieve it by boat, monorail train or later you will unlock a flying drone as well.After clearing your traces, you can enjoy a nice view of how beautiful the region you created. The game doesn’t have ultra-modern graphics with raytracing, but it has a nice colourful palette and an awesome drawn environment that fits the game perfectly. I call it eye candy visuals. Only one thing can ruin immersion. It's an outline created by Animal Observatory that won’t disappear after closing a popup of a scanned location. It happens only on water, but it’s a little bit distracting when you want to create a nice screenshot or just watch what you have created. I also run into two bugs. First was when I wasn’t able to recycle a building, but returning to main main fixed it and sometimes movement around the map was lagging.

_childDocuments_.review: Relaxing game with an innovative new take on city builders, but a great strategy game in itself, it does not rely only on the novelty concept.The sound track and atmosphere give a really chill vibe.Yes, as some other reviews point out the content is limited, but if you play normally without rushing it should be at least 15 hours of play time without repeating a scenario, which I find acceptable for this price.The demo gives a good impression but the game adds to it with additional mechanics and the other 3 settings.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Visually delightful tessellation based puzzle game with solar punk aesthetic. Really need more games to go for this genre, good soul food.Latest update has been a major overhaul, that has added more content but frustrated the game to the point of disappointment.One major complaint I have is that the game now chugs, on my high end spec gaming PC, this games chug, both the pathing of the little boat, the mono rails and all the animals, feels like a memory leak, it really chugs and needs fixing.  It has somehow both complicated the animals in a very frustrating manner. They spawn without control in inappropriate conditions then trap you in a game phase until you chase them across the map with a ping tool. The update has also revamped the games levels, whilst there are technically more maps, it now uses most of the mechanics less feeling more underutilised than ever. we have so many slight variations of the same puzzles, none of them have been balanced well enough to be satisfying.Some maps have the balance completely broken, buildings that are supposed to be bought and placed down once and then relocated are so cheap they can be spammed.fix the performance, and pick whether the game is about making beautiful landscapes (make it easier and double the map size greater land height variation, give us control of that too) OR a difficult puzzle game (make the buildings much more expensive and the level very failable, let us introduce animals manually as a 4th puzzle phase) as it is, it currently fails at both.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Played the original version on Itch.io and this is a wonderful upgrade. It is so much fun. Don't go in expecting a big puzzle game but rather a joyful exploration of nature and cause and effect.The in game manual is full of lovely illustrations. The animations and visuals are lovely.Just a wholesome biscuit for your inner child.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Very good "Enviroment Builder Sim" The Presentation is good, I had no issues playing it. It takes a minute to wrap your mind around how to use the various tools you are given but it wasn't mind boggling or anything, relaxing music and Interesting concepts. For 18USD, it wasn't a bad evening playing this game. 4 new Alternate areas open up for me to try at the end. EDIT For free DLC Vita Nova: Added 4 new maps and improved how the Animals achieve happiness. New Maps are great and provide new challenges and biomes. Animals are not so picky as they used to be about their areas, They plan to keep rolling out small updates like this, and they are welcome. Adding more animals and ways to renew a area has boosted my score to a solid 7/10( from a 6/10 for how short the game was without this free update) and if this is your cup of tea, possibly 8/10. _childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Prior to the recent update, I used to LOVE this game, I have replayed it twice now (once on a friend's account and once on this one) and I was so excited about the new levels in the new update. Unfortunately, the animal system was also changed completely and now the game is so infuriating. I'm struggling to get through the first tutorial level on medium difficulty (and I've played this game twice already so I understand there is some level of early-game strategy to it). I'm gonna attempt to make this concise but I've never been good at that so here goes:- Adding the animals to the game earlier is distracting and unnecessary, I'm likely going to drastically change the terrain before I'm ready to consider what the animals want so there is no need to have their pop ups and needs jumping up on screen.- The amount of animal groups you need to have is wild, it's so many more than before and it has me scratching my head wondering how on earth the later, more completed levels are gonna go if I only got 9/12 on the first one before it started feeling too crowded to continue.- Once I DID get 9/12 animals happy, the icon that shows the list of animals on the side of the screen just disappeared and I couldn't actually finish the level (probably just a bug but still added to my frustration).- The timers until the animals leave are so short and barely give new (or seasoned!) players time to make significant or complex changes to the terrain to keep the animals- The needs of the animals aren't as clear as they once were and it's really unnecessarily confusing.- I don't understand what the names down the list of animals is for. Why do I have 4 different groups of deer all with randomised names? Is that the name of the herd? Is it meant to be a single deer that has shown up? - I have seen BoonMike mention that this new animal system has soft-locked them from continuing to play the game and I have to say that it's the same for me.Overall, I'm not really going to touch the game again if the animal system is like this. I honestly feel that this could've been the beta version of the animal system and the one before the update was the improved, simplified one. I know lots of work went into this update but unfortunately I just can't recommend it like this. The animal system wasn't broken and seemed to work perfectly fine before, it just seems odd that it's been overhauled like this for no reason.----Edit to respond to dev: Hi Sam, I played on medium difficulty (I've forgotten the terms for it now, apologies). I do understand that it was meant to feel more reactive and I suppose it does in a literal sense of the word but it feels clunky and not nearly as satisfying. Before, with the scanning method, it felt like a satisfying last piece of the puzzle, to get that last tick on the last animal.It takes away some of the control that you have throughout the rest of the game, just to have the animals randomly appear. I liked that I could control where I placed the animals rather than just winging it with the terrain and waiting for them to show up and hope it's enough for them to stay. When you're trying to do that and balance multiple different demanding species (I didn't get far but for example, the wolves in the first level), it can get hectic, especially when the only way to change the terrain for some animals is to destroy a whole area and start again (heck, sometimes you'd have to restart the whole map), thus getting rid of other connecting animal groups that share habitats close by, all of which may not come back if you change the habitat drastically enough to suit that first species that wasn't happy. Maybe a way to make this feel less random is to have the animal needs made easily accessible and clearly stated in the book (at least the needs of the species that arrived but left due to them being unsatisfied) so it's possible to mould the terrain around them as you go.When you don't know what habitats you need at the start, it makes is frustrating when you're doing your best to unlock all the tabs to get to the end of the level only to realise you don't have two particular biomes directly next to each other and you have to (literally) burn a significant part of the map down just to start again. I know a lot of effort and passion has been put into this so I'm sorry the game didn't feel as amazing to me as what I think it was meant to be, it's an awesome and unique concept and I haven't see anything like it but this change has really put me off of it now unfortunately. I don't see many negative reviews to perhaps it's just not working for me or I'm missing something but I hope my response might've also clarified something for you? Thanks for the response Sam!

_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: This game is so satisfying. I was raised to be very conservation minded. For ages, my issue with any city builder or civilisation or even RTS game is how you have to destroy the landscape and build a city over it.This game focuses on restoration and rewilding - which are rewarding by themselves - and turns it into an entertaining, serotonin-boosting game.AND some of the proceeds go to the Endangered Wildlife Trust, so you don't just have the illusion of doing something good for the planet by playing, but you are actually helping support a cause that actively does good things for the planet! Buy it for your friends, save the world ;)

_childDocuments_.review: Hopecore. Fun, casual puzzle/resource management game about cultivating an ecosystem that supports a set of animals. It's certainly not a city builder, and not turn based either. Every other tag is accurate though.  You purify soils, water them, seed clouds, control-burn vegetation so you can grow large forests. Animals start to move in and you satisfy their requirements. It keeps sending different subspecies based on the composition of your ecosystem, so if you want a certain set of animals then yes it becomes complicated. However, the game only requires a certain number, not specific kinds (at least for the first two levels). In my experience it's easy to end each level having pleased enough species. Then you place log bridges for animals to cross streams or climb cliffs, and once you're done it's one last puzzle to use your water-fairing recycle drone to clean up your tech. At the end you sit back and admire your work with a cutscene that showcases your ecosystem. I think it's pretty neatThere's no time limit on each level, but the ecosystem does slowly changed over time. There are time requirements before animal groups are unsatisfied and leave, but they get replaced by another group so no big deal. There's also an option called Zen Mode that gets rid of resource requirements for a super casual mode.For all the reviews there are on this game, only 6.8% of players have completed the second level according to the achievements.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Great ideas and lovely graphics, but this game is so complicated and sometimes incomprehensive that it isn't really relaxing and becomes frustrating in any way.For example, I want to grow a forest in this particular grassland, but there is no tree to place a beehive. A beehive is needed to grow a meadow. After that, I need to burn the meadow and place a foresthouse on this burned soil to let the forest grow.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: The idea behind this game is different than other 'city builder' or management games and that was my appeal to wanting to try out the game.After the basic environmental conditions are met, you have to incorporate separate ecosystems in the same area and then make all the animals happy with where they are. Then after that is done, you have to recycle all the hardware so the animals can live peacefully. Sounds like a lot and some of the maps, I took my time on. Some maps, I ended up having to redo 1-2 times because I didn't plan correctly ahead.One thing is for certain - ALWAYS build the animal relocator building and pay close attention to what makes them happy. You can move an animal as many times as you want but you can't move them within certain amount of space from the same animals, it seems. Basically, different packs of the same animals don't seem to mix in that well together.Also, the music is amazing in the game, very peaceful and destressing.Only issues with the game are:1) I wish you could rotate the map.2) Larger hardware in the way of smaller things (like the monorail pillars) are not selectable because the larger item overlaps it.3) When things like  the sound is choppy Overall, I really loved this game and would recommend it (actually already have) to people.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Terra Nil: A unique reverse city-builder game set in a post-apocalyptic world. Restore the environment by reclaiming barren lands, rewilding nature, and creating a self-sustaining ecosystem. Use strategic planning and renewable resources to revitalize the world. A beautiful and relaxing experience promoting ecological restoration.The gameplay revolves around a simple yet deeply satisfying loop. Players start with a depleted environment and limited resources, requiring strategic planning and decision-making to bring life back to the land. By placing various environmental elements, such as soil tiles, trees, and water sources, players set in motion a delicate ecological balance.The gameplay's appeal lies in its intricacy. Players must carefully manage their resources, optimizing the placement of each element to maximize the ecosystem's revival while ensuring its stability. The game doesn't penalize experimentation, allowing players to learn from mistakes and adapt their strategies as they progress through the levels.Furthermore, it features procedurally generated levels, providing an element of surprise and variety in each playthrough. This design choice enhances replayability, as no two landscapes are ever the same, challenging players to rethink their approach and try out new strategies.A visual strike a perfect balance between simplicity and beauty. The use of vibrant colors brings life to the previously desolate landscapes, while the clean and uncluttered design allows players to focus on the core mechanics of restoration. Each element, from flora to water bodies, is distinct and easily recognizable, adding to the overall sense of accomplishment as the ecosystem flourishes under the player's nurturing.Accompanied by a soothing and atmospheric soundtrack, the audio design complements the gameplay remarkably well. The serene melodies blend seamlessly with the contemplative gameplay, creating an immersive and peaceful environment that encourages players to immerse themselves fully in their ecological endeavors.Beyond its gameplay and aesthetics, it also serves as an environmental allegory, urging players to reflect on real-world ecological challenges. As they witness the rejuvenation of the virtual landscapes, players are encouraged to contemplate the impact of human actions on the environment and the importance of conservation and sustainability.  Terra Nil is an exquisite gem in the city-building and simulation genre. With its visually arresting minimalism, calming soundtrack, and stimulating gameplay, the game crafts a serene and immersive experience that resonates long after the player has put down the controller. Moreover, its poignant environmental message elevates Terra Nil from being just another game to a powerful and relevant artistic statement.For gamers seeking a meditative and environmentally conscious journey, It's an absolute must-play. Embrace the role of an ecological steward and embark on a serene quest to restore nature's balance in this captivating and thought-provoking gem.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: This is such a beautiful, calm puzzle game. You are on a planet that has fallen into ruin and it's your job to help nature recover and thrive again. You do this in 3 phases:1. Clean the toxic wasteland, create fertile soil, water it.2. Grow vegetation, create different biomes until animals return to the area.3. Make sure the animals are happy, recycle your man-made buildings until only nature remains, leave with your space ship.In these 3 phases you also manipulate the climate (temperature, humidity). There are main goals and optional tasks to make sure the area is restored as best as possible.Unlike others, I had little problem satisfying animal needs. The key to make sure that every animal group is happy is to diversify the landscape (for example, don't place one big forest in one corner of the map, but place three or four smaller forests across the map).To me, other mechanics were more frustrating, so I think the following mechanics need some improvement:1. You can undo only the very last step. I wish you could undo the last three or maybe five last steps because sometimes you need to place three or more buildings in order to see if everything works out the way you planned. Undoing only one step and then realizing that my plan wouldn't work out was frustrating because I wasted precious resources.2. I don't like the way the save game works. If you play a session, you have the 3 phases mentioned above. If you pass a phase but fail the next one, you can restart the failed phase. I wish I could save freely, but I guess the developers felt the need to restrict this in order to make the game feel more like a puzzle.3. If you pass a phase, you sometimes unlock new buildings. The problem is, you don't see which buildings you will unlock. This can potentially lead to you making mistakes in the phases before because you don't know how the session will unfold. I wish you could see the upcoming buildings in order to plan everything better.Still, I enjoyed this game a lot and if new maps will come out in a future update, I will definitely pick up the game again. I wish there was more content because I had a lot of fun with this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Super chill and relaxing game that requires some strategic thinking especially in higher difficulties. It's quite fun and the different environments and layouts and changing items keep the game from getting boring. It's also really nice to just appreciate your work once you are done and see all of the animals doing their own things.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Incredibly satisfying ecopunk puzzle game, where you slowly revive nature.There are various steps to be taken and you will have to keep an eye on your eco ressource which you need to place buildings. At least in the higher difficulties. Sadly the game is also horribly short (6 missions, 2 for each biome), clocking only 10 hours for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very relaxing game. as is with Townscaper, Dorfromantik and co. it aims at being visually pleasing while doing some tasks of balancing environments and eco-systems. The play time of the main 4 levels is about 4-8hours depending on difficulty and wether one rushes it or goes for a complete finish. In my opinion it could be a little cheaper as others have also said before, however it still has good potential for further maps and development so I for my part hope there will be new regions to discover in the future.As far as I can see there aren't really any bugs though I had a problem at several points where one loses the game by doing something too early (don't wanna spoiler) and you don't get told, resulting in having to restart the region since you can't reverse some processes (SPOILER: the problem has to do with Lava getting turned into stone). Maybe it's actually wanted to be that way but I found it to be kind of fustrating the first time. But hey it kind of also poses a challenge and maybe I was just too incautious.Other than that it really is fun to play and I can defenitely recommend the game as long as it is on sale or something. Hope this helps, have fun!
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Soothing, peaceful, and therapeutic, Terra Nil is a game about helping heal a world left in disrepair, and then teaching yourself to stand aside and let it flourish. This is basically the game I play to calm myself when Im stressed, and its worked every time.Genuinely fun mechanics, and there is a strategy that has to be considered. I'd best describe it as the inverse of Sim City: You are building a better world for everything besides humans. No spoilers on the ending, but it's incredibly satisfying, and worth playing again and again!If you've been looking for a good solarpunk, gardening, or sim game, Terra Nil has got you.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Absolultely marvelous gameI have more than 8 hours on the demo, and they have improved so many things since thenThe game is beautiful, the environments are so very detailed, the sound design is ON POINTIf you are looking for a cute chill and not too long game to play, I definitely recommend it (given that it has a lot of different gameplays possible, completionist, or just enjoying what you have in front of your eyes; different levels of difficulty, maps randomly generated...)I wouldn't recommend it enough, and I'm usually not a fan of simulation/strategy games (also the devs and publishers are absolute chads)
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: It's a cute game, very satisfying and makes you think strategy and about the state of our world. Let me be clear though, if I could rate it a maybe I would except for just 1 fact. (Outside of the fact that maybe ratings dont exist.) A percentage of the profits are going to charities. This alone kept me from even thinking about a negative review, however from a gameplay standpoint there's some big problems.For starters the undo button only works for your previous move, and there are several buildings that once place also need to be activated, which counts as 2 moves. It makes it very hard to experiment and learn in the early game as even a few mistakes will require an entire reset of the level, and these take ~30 minutes on average. Secondly the recycling feature where you remove your buildings is awesome, except for when the only way to do it is by boat when there's several levels where you can do it by drone or monorail. What's the issue with the boat? Half the time you have to carve new rivers into the landscape, doing so also corrupts the grass so if you aren't planning for the recycle stage before laying grass in phase one you could end up in trouble. That and the straight lines the excavators make can look ugly against the more wild rivers. This both potentially seperates animals, ruins the landscape after you worked so hard to restore it, and just generally fights against the theme of the game.Then there's RNG portions. Some biomes can only be created within certain conditions, such as a small pond. A few of the levels provide you limited tools to create ponds, and depending on terrain generation, you may not be able to at all, at least not enough to satisfy the "x amount of biome required to progress" bar. I've had to reset 6 different levels to get new generation to pass them.But hey, when the game wasn't bending me over it was a calm and relaxing experience. If the devs would just fix these issues this game would be 10/10 on a bad day.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: this is a really cute game, and I wish I could recommend it. however, for some reason the devs didn't include any controller support, and so the game is horribly unplayable on the steam deck. if the devs think that steam deck mouse emulation is sufficient for this game, they need to give their heads a shake. no idea how anyone thought launching a game in the 2020s without controller support is acceptable, but it's real unfortunate.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

_childDocuments_.review: Really enjoyed this game. Paid full price for it, and should'nt have. It's not 25€ worth of content. I'd say 15€ max. It's one of those small gems with simple graphics that manage to convey a very good art design. The game overall is good, even though it is quite short. I liked the challenges offered by the puzzles, and the increasing difficulty is well calibrated. The aspect of cleaning and having to remove all our machinery is well thought. The part where you have to find the animals is good, but I felt a bit cheated when I modulated flooded city in a way that didn't allow me to find one of the species later on. What I'd like to see added in the near future : more maps and a better system for the last map (flooded city) where the rocket is pretty lame to build.
_childDocuments_.name: Terra Nil

Usual playtime will be 5-8 hours and it is very much worth it for everyone who looks to get into a cozy game that has a low difficulty spike.I enjoyed my time very much so far and got to 100% quickly.
