_childDocuments_.review: First off, Tinykin is not like Pikmin. Any review that says it's similar has no idea what makes either game unique. So, if you're thinking about playing Tinykin because of the comparison, stop right there. Let me explain the difference.Pikmin is an RTS about managing and nurturing a growing army of tiny soldiers. You must guide them through battle and away from hazards that will crush, burn, and drown their fragile little bodies. When they die, it will be due to your own incompetence, and you will feel bad because you have failed them as a commander.Tinykin is a 3D platformer with a sort of metroidvania exploration style. Your tinykin cannot die. They do not need to be controlled. They cannot fall off cliffs and get stuck. They do not get lost. You receive an exact and precise number of them and that number never rises or falls until you collect more from preset locations.There are, however, two similarities between this and Pikmin. The first is that you have a swarm of small critters that follow you around. And yet, the gameplay of Tinykin would barely change if that swarm were taken away and replaced with a resource counter. If you did that to Pikmin, the strategy of the entire game would change.The second thing is that it gives you a childlike feeling of being very small in a very large world. In fact, I think Tinykin does that far better than Pikmin. All of the terrain and obstacles are brilliantly constructed out of the things that a child might use to build a world for tiny people.All I can really say is, if you like 3D platformers, buy this game! This is a very fun game. The controls are extremely tight and responsive. The music is fantastic and enjoyable, especially some of the boom box tracks. The level design is very clever and highly polished.I bought this game because it looked like Pikmin and I love Pikmin. I loved this game because of its own strengths.
_childDocuments_.name: Tinykin

_childDocuments_.review: I cannot say enough kind things about Tinykin. I really feel like the trailer did not do this game justice, as this game is way more fun than how it looked in the trailer. If you're a completionist, someone who loves collecting every little thing in a game, and someone who loves cute games—Tinykin is for you. I had so much fun playing this and I definitely plan on going back to try and 100% it. The concept is incredibly cute and the ending was unlike anything that I expected. There were few to no bugs that I experienced in my playthrough, and it seemed to be very polished.The artstyle is gorgeous. I love the 2D character (Milodane) mixed with the 3D, real-life world. It just fit perfectly, and it was so addicting and painfully hard to put this game down. I highly recommend this game if you're on the fence about it or if you're skeptical about paying full price, wait for a sale. I would say that this game is worth the price with the number of hours that you can get in just your first playthrough alone. While there isn't much replay value (that I know of), this game is a great and beautiful experience.All in all, like I said before, I highly recommend this game. I really enjoyed it, and it's super fun and unique!Rating: 9.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: What a delight!Pure exploration and platforming fun! I really love the concept of being tiny in a huge world so this one caught my eye from the get go and more than delivered.The game is a a 3D collectathon platformer with a dose of Pikmin. This is a very dry way to describe it, I would say it's Pikmin but you are very mobile and fast in a extremely well designed world (maps like fromsoftware, everything is beautifully connected). To complete the package, the art, OST, sound effects and writing (if you want) is all great!Each room in the house is it's own little town with it's theme, culture and characters. Also, by the end, the story revels to be more than what it appears...On a side note, the guys from this studio are former Ubisoft Montpellier devs. When I see such a indie gem like this coming from former huge studio devs I can't help but wonder how many cool ideas are trapped behind corporate bottom line focus... or maybe I'm just salty because Ubi doesn't make a new 3D Rayman...

_childDocuments_.review: It's not pikmin at all, in the sense that there is no managing of your tinykin, you don't tend to them and they frankly don't need you at all, they're collectible that you need to find to do puzzles and that's it.Tinykin is a collectathon in interesting setpieces with light platforming elements. I found the story pretty bland and the music, while not being out of place, to be serviceable at best.I enjoyed the environment, the exploration of the levels (with little things hidden everywhere) and its character design (too bad I didn't actually enjoy interacting with said characters)Get it if you want a chill low difficulty platformer about exploring places and collecting things, that's what it's good at.

_childDocuments_.review: So far, probably the best 3D collect-a-thon platformer on Steam.It may look like a Pikmin clone on the surface, but beyond collecting a small army of little helper NPCs to throw at your problems, it's really nothing like that.  The movement around the levels, and general gameplay is much more acrobatic, so it feels more like a 3D Mario or Banjo game, and the Tinykin are really just the tools you collect in order to deal with the various obstacles in your way.The music is nice, the levels are big, and packed densely with stuff to do, and stuff to collect.  The graphics are very pleasant, the controls are responsive and rarely if ever frustrating. You get to skate around on a little piece of soap and that isn't even a feature that's locked off until later.. you'll get it 10 or 15 minutes into the game, and it makes movement a lot of fun.Speaking of the levels again, I've mostly seen the first one so far (the first big one, not the tutorial room), but they seem designed really well.  Big, complex, crammed with stuff, full of little secret nooks and crannies with collectibles in them.  As you move throughout, you'll find ropes and silk lines that you can deploy to create shortcuts and interconnectivity between different parts.The stages are all based on being a tiny-sized person in a normal-sized house, and bugs have been developing a society in the house, so you get to see how they've built and repurposed objects in the house to make their own little homes and businesses.All those various pieces of furniture, books, instruments, toys, and other household objects all make for a big, beautiful world that presents itself in a way that begs you to explore everywhere.  Not even just for the collectibles, but to see all the little areas up-close.  I found a place where an old VHS box was turned into a tall, narrow little house, with an upper balcony and everything.  Very cute.If you've been hankering for a good 3D platformer, and either you're done with stuff like Hat in Time and Yooka Laylee, or never liked them that much to begin with, give this one a try.
_childDocuments_.name: Tinykin

_childDocuments_.review: You can't tell a hero by his size, just a Tinykin little super guy.Ah yes, Bizarro Pikmin.Me: As a cultured, hardcore gamer I just cannot get into those Pikmin Nintendo games!Also Me: Guys, you’ve GOT to check out this cute little leadership game on Steam… Tinykin!This is one of those games I got for my kids, then proceeded to play until 3 in the morning. Very lighthearted, lots of fun, great animation, and puzzles that were challenging but not too challenging. Tinykin is one of the most delightful and charming gaming experiences I've had in a long time.I heard about it from a comments section on a Facebook gaming group a couple of months ago. They described it as Pikmin meets Paper Mario and I thought ‘that sounds like a bloody good time’.After downloading and playing for an hour I knew it was something special. I had to stop for the night because I had work the next morning but the next day all I could think about was getting to play it when I got home, which is a feeling I haven’t had since a certain other game this year (Sex with Hitler 3D).Well now this has easily become one of my favorite games of the past year, if not of all time. It's a 3D platformer that shares a lot of its DNA with collect-a-thons of old. You're an explorer trying to get the pieces to put a spaceship together so you can get back to your home planet, and you're thrown into these massive, intricately-crafted levels to get the various pieces.You're about the size of a beetle, and the whole game takes place in a house, with each of the levels being various rooms, like the kitchen or bathroom or greenhouse. Think the “Honey, I Shrunk The Kids!” environment as you are running around someone’s 1990s house as a 6 inch tall tiny person.So you get that cool perspective of being miniature in these settings that you're familiar with. The house and its different rooms are populated by various bug species, and there's so much charm in seeing how they've terraformed these various human rooms into insect societies. The kitchen is their agricultural sector, so they leave the kitchen faucet flowing and have an assortment of straws leading the water into a waterfall beneath the sink which then becomes a river that flows down the kitchen and provides irrigation for the farmland—which is really just overturned sponges. Each of the rooms have their own purpose and it's so charming exploring them and seeing how they're arranged. The levels are all pretty big, but not overwhelmingly so. It's fun to explore all of the different areas, and there's usually a central area in the level. As you explore around, you reveal these webs that allow you to quickly move between the hub and the outer areas. So you get that satisfaction of unlocking new shortcuts for yourself. As you explore around you find and can talk to various NPCs, who usually have something funny to say. Your goal for the level is to complete whatever task is asked of you in order to get the spaceship part, but there's also two or three sidequests that various NPCs will ask of you. Beyond that, you're also collecting pollen which is scattered about everywhere. That's the "coins" of this game, and it's super enjoyable to collect.Something else you'll be collecting is the game's namesake: the tinikyn. These are little guys you find throughout the levels that follow you around and can be used for different tasks or interactions as you play. You need to find tinykins who follow you around, each with their own abilities such as lifting objects, blowing up road blocks, conducting electricity, building towers or bridges in order to progress through the level. This might make you think of Pikmin, but it’s not like that at all.So the levels consist of exploring around, collecting tinykin and pollen and completing the task that'll get you the spaceship part—which'll be something like baking a giant cake, requiring you to collect the eggs, sugar, flour, etc. scattered around the level and putting them in the mixing bowl. I truly think this game is a masterclass in 3D platformer design. All of the exploration and the signposting feels so organic in that at every moment you have three or four options of where to go next, will choose one, end up looping around on yourself and then find that you’re at the start of another path of pollen to follow and explore.The frame rate and controls are silky smooth and, as a result, it’s always a pleasure to play. The puzzles are super simple but the reward is in going for 100% - which I know isn’t everyone’s bag but finding all of the pollen in a level is an experience that’s always fun and never tiring/arduous.Normally I don’t feel obligated to 100% these collect-a-thon games but I was having so much fun exploring and zipping around that I wanted to make sure I saw all the nooks and crannies of the house and obtained every last collectable in the game. I think maybe Paper Mario meets Pikmin isn’t quite right - I’d say something along the lines of Banjo-Kazooie meets Pikmin meets Chibi-Robo is a more accurate description (big vibes of all three throughout).The movement and gameplay is tight and just feels right. You can run and can do a single jump, but holding the jump button puts you in this bubble that you can use to float around temporarily. As you collect pollen you can increase the duration of this bubble float, which is cool. You also get this soapboard (it's a skateboard, but a bar of soap) that you can use to skate around the level for some extra speed. This thing carries its momentum into jumps and can be really fun to use while zooming around levels. The soapboard and upgraded bubble—along with the tinykin that gives you an instant ladder—allows for some really versatile movement, and you're able to cover a lot of ground with these tools. After you complete a level, you can go back and do one or two races that are available, and I found these to be a ton of fun. You're really able to zip around the map and the races are really well designed. Getting gold medals for them also unlocks new costumes for your characters. So that's basically the long and short of it. I've loved it. It really appeals to a childlike fantasy of being a tiny little guy in a big house and traversing things from that perspective. This game has been nothing but an unbridled joy to play, and it's been so fun to sit back and play what feels like such a classic video game. Just a man and his controller, jumping around a world. It’s one of the best feelings when you play a game you had no idea you needed in that moment in time. Tinykin, you beautiful bastard, you took me back to my childhood of playing Banjo Kazooie. If you enjoy 3D platformers and collect-a-thons this one is a must play. It’s a great “turn your brain off” and just have fun kind of game. I highly recommend it.10/10

_childDocuments_.review: is a rather incredible 3D platformer. I knew it was something special ever since I played the demo... the full game manages to exceed my expectations. It's a fun, relaxing, wholesome, and extremely polished experience.At first glance you may think the game is inspired by Pikmin, but in reality it's more like a mix of Overlord and Super Mario Odyssey gameplay-wise. Sure, you do collect Tinykins that have special abilities, but those only serve the platforming aspect. You don't need to manage your tiny companions or use them in combat like Pikmin. As a 3D platformer Tinykin gets the basics right: your movement throughout the levels is smooth and effortless and the actual platforming is top-notch. The game smartly gives you the majority of the platforming options as early as possible, making it quite enjoyable to explore each level. And the levels themselves are great: you really will feel like a tiny person inside a huge house. Something about that early 90s (specifically, 1991) setting is just so fascinating to me as it also reflects my childhood. You may feel overwhelmed when you're dropped inside such massive levels, but the game quickly allows you to overcome that feeling thanks to the memorable layouts and paths you can take through them. I cannot praise the level design enough, it's downright brilliant how you discover secrets and shortcuts. The way you are guided subtly towards your objectives without any obvious handholding is another nice touch. Collectibles add enough replay value to the levels as it's unlikely you'll get every single one the first time. Some collectibles like the bubble upgrades also enhance the actual gameplay potential as you can practically fly forever once you've fully collected them. Performance is another area where the game impresses. I did not notice any framedrops or stutters. No noticeable bugs either during my playthrough and zero crashes. Loading times are fast enough, it's easy to start the game and immediately jump into a level.I can't find much to criticize here, aside from the fact that the game is a bit on the shorter side (6-8 hours to complete the main story, around 10-12 hours if you want to do ). But I feel like it's the perfect length for the game as it emphasizes quality over quantity. The last two Tinykin types feel a bit underutilized and underwhelming compared to the first four which you'll use a lot. The lack of a dedicated photo mode is a bit of a downside to me as I love taking screenshots while playing. Still, all of these are minor complaints.If you love 3D platformers, you'll enjoy Tinykin.

_childDocuments_.review: is a love letter to collect-a-thon games, very reminiscent of the classic Nintendo 64 games back in the day. Its 3D puzzle platformer also takes inspiration from Pikmin, whereby you acquire  to help you solve puzzles throughout the game. It definitely stands its own ground with being a completely different game from aforementioned Pikmin, spliced together with satisfying, but not overly challenging, platforming. • Intricately designed levels• Addictive collect-a-thon that doesn’t outstay its welcome• Loads of secrets and hidden areas for thoroughly exploring• Huge, sprawling, open levels that make you excited to explore• Adorable and cute art style• Attention to detail in the music and environment• Be a small guy exploring a huge house• Lacks challenge in platforming that you might expectThroughout the game, you’ll be exploring a house as a shrunk person, with each room being a different level. Each is intricately crafted to complement the puzzle platforming you’ll be doing throughout the game. Unlocking shortcuts and destroying obstacles allow you to access previously hard to reach areas in case you need to come back later. The level design is very reminiscent of Nintendo 64 collect-a-thons, huge open sprawling maps that, at first, seem overwhelming, but offer more than just a linear path. You’ll find yourself stumbling across hidden paths, secret areas (oh boy do they love hiding stuff) and shiny collectibles that only side track you more and more away from your primary goal. Just like moths to a flame, as soon as you see something you haven’t collected, you’ll instantly be drawn to it, at least that’s what happens to me often. The puzzle elements come in forms of using your Tinykin to solve and work around problems. Each level starts you out with no Tinykin to command, but by the end of it, you will have amassed an army big enough to go to war with anyone who might look at you funny… *ahem*… Tinykin can come in different forms and variations, using them to move objects around the map, stack and climb up to access new areas, throw at objects to destroy them (they die in this process and seem to enjoy it… I kinda had to question that…) and so on. These are your puzzle pieces, your pawns to do your bidding, throwing them at obstacles you want to move, using them as your own personal bombs to clear a path or to access different areas. Never once was I stumped by a puzzle throughout my playthrough. If I came across something I didn’t know how to overcome yet, I’d simply put it on the back burner, and keep exploring the level.That being said, whilst each level was a joy in itself to explore, along with the constant supply of dopamine by collecting pollen (a collectible), solving puzzles to gain artifacts and accumulating an army of Tinykin to help you solve puzzles and explore previously inaccessible areas, the lack of challenge was apparent, especially in the later levels. Not to say that this took away from the enjoyment this game offers, but I did feel like more could’ve been done with the platforming elements.Your main objective throughout the game is to build a machine from a blueprint found to get back to your home planet, Aegis. Conveniently, all the pieces you need are held in different parts of the house, which are guarded or owned by different insect species. They, obviously, want a favour in exchange for the part you require, which is what’ll keep you busy most of the time. Actually no, what will keep you busy most of the time is your inability to say no to collecting shiny collectibles whilst doing the primary objective. These favours range from resolving conflict between two different species, to solving hunger by baking a cake.The idea of being small and puny whilst exploring a now huge house has always been a fun and interesting environment for me, putting so many things into a new perspective because of your size. The way each level is designed using common household objects as platforms or slopes for that particular room really does something for me, and I can’t explain why or how. The creativity used to build each level is second to none, the cartoonish art style that I couldn’t help but be in awe with for most of the game never ceased to impress me. Yes, the Tinykin were adorable to look at throughout this game, and I now wonder what it would be like to have them as pets… But I digress. Even though the cutscenes were far and few between, I was always pleasantly surprised when they did come up. Though short, they really captured the essence of this adorable game, both in and outside the cutscenes.Whilst I didn't really expect much from this game going into it, I can’t help but praise it for how fun, compelling and adorable it was from start to finish. I couldn’t get enough of collecting things and whilst I didn’t get 100% completion, I can see myself getting back into it to clean up what I missed. This is a must-have for anyone who adores collect-a-thons, it's short, sweet and to the point that doesn’t outstay its welcome, highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: After the main story completed, let me share what my time with Tinykin was like.The art style is beautiful, the mix of 2D for characters and 3D for the environment is seamless, the devs really pulled it off. Very fitting for the tone of the game. As far as level design and controls go, Tinykin is a dream to play. It's a platformer through and through, and not once did it get frustrating in these eight hours. Because even if you do miss a jump, there are cleverly placed shortcuts everywhere to help you get back.The mechanics took Pikmin as a basis and ran with it in its own direction, which is cool. I especially enjoyed how mobile the green (climbing) Tinykins made me feel. When you get the hang of using them, traversing the house becomes an absolute joyride and easily my favorite part of the game. Just scaling the furniture around the rooms and zooming on a soapboard.The sound design is very nice, especially in relation to movement and interactions with the world. However, the soundtrack didn't really stand out.Story-wise, the main premise and goals are very clear, but I can't say I very much cared for all the side objectives and characters. THAT BEING SAID, I can appreciate the love and care given to each insect inhabitant of the house, and all the clever pop culture references inserted. It's obvious the devs had fun with the game, and their dedication shows.Also - I really liked the ending. It was unexpected, to be honest, the twist was really cool.All in all, Tinykins was a wonderful experience, 8 hours long for the main story and all the side quests (I still haven't done some of the post-game challenges and missed a bit of the achievements). I would recommend it if you're a fan of platformers, since Splashteam really delivers on that front. I would also recommend it if you liked the trailer and the visual style, because the game is PACKED with eye-candy. Just don't go in looking for a Pikmin carbon-copy, or something overly complex. The puzzles are easy, and there to just enhance the whole experience. You collect Tinykins, collect pollen nuggets, solve small quests, and platform around. That's it. But it's done JUST RIGHT //chefkissA lot of effort was put into the game, and for that it's well worth the price.

_childDocuments_.review: I’ve always enjoyed the concepts used in Pikmin and games similar to that like Overlord. Games where you’re managing minions and making use of them for some greater goal land somewhere between action games, puzzle games, and real-time strategies. Tinykin takes this seldom used, but often entertaining design and blends it with player-friendly “collect-a-thon” gameplay to create something unique but also so familiar and intuitive that it immediately feels like cozy warm nostalgia.Abbreviated Review: It’s easy to look at Tinykin and say “this is a Pikmin knockoff.” It’s even playing off the name a bit with the title – which is the name also used for the little creatures you make use of as tools within the game. However, despite some overlaps in the gameplay, the feel of the game is quite different from that classic franchise. The biggest change is that there isn’t any sort of failure state in Tinykin. You can die from falling too far or ending up in water or fire – which are both uncommon – but even then you respawn instantly where you were last alive. You also can’t lose any of your tinykin (aside from the ones you use to explode barriers) as there’s no combat and they aren’t affected by any environmental hazards. The gameplay challenge comes entirely from platforming and puzzle solving.Platforming is another big departure from Pikmin’s inspiration. Much of what is necessary to succeed comes from you using your tinykin and abilities to move through the levels. There is a massive amount of verticality within each level and most of the time your goal is to track down enough tinykin and enhance your floating bubble power so you can access it all. You won’t have to fight any of the bug creatures you encounter and usually, the most challenging aspect is figuring out where hidden secrets are and unlocking them. Here, it leans much more toward games like Banjo Kazooie and other games where opening pathways and picking up floating doodads are the focus.The premise of Tinykin does also overlap a bit with that of Pikmin. You venture from your planet of humans to investigate what you believe is the homeworld of humanity and, in the process, lose your ability to travel. You end up a small fish in what appears to be a big pond but is actually just a normal size house. Being about the size of a bug, you soon come face to face with a whole collection of them – though they have evolved into a complex human-like society with structures and jobs. One of them becomes your guide and directs you to the plans to build a transportation ship that would serve as your rescue vessel and thus creates the central theme of the game – finding parts.This splits the game into five(ish) levels that are represented within the unique rooms in a house. The bedroom has been turned into the central capital with a large temple dedicated to the insect world’s teacher and mystical figurehead Ardwin. An atrium-styled workshop is the plant-dominated greenhouse home of the mantises. The bathroom is split between the timid dung beetles and the flashy party squad of silverfish where toilets, vanities, and bathtubs all become catalysts for puzzles and adventure. These themes of turning everyday rooms and objects within them into massive set pieces for your character to climb over, under, and through are common throughout the game. Some of the most appealing aspects of the whole experience are discovering what you can unlock and how you’ll manipulate the world to achieve your goals. It makes the environment as much a part of the allure as anything else you do.When you’re introduced to a new area, you don’t have any tinykin available (they stay within each level), so after a brief introduction to the new map and the discovery of the tasks ahead of you, you’ll need to start exploring. This is made pretty easy with the inclusion of a bar of soap that serves as a speed-enhancing skateboard and your ability to press the jump button in the air to float on a soap bubble. Your bubble ends up being one of the primary non-tinykin tools you need to navigate levels and solve puzzles. However, you’re not going to make it very far without picking up some of those little fuzzy boys.Tinykin come in a select variety – each of which is collected from a color-specific egg on surfaces. The first ones you encounter have the strength to carry objects, weigh down pullies, and just generally knock ♥♥♥♥ around. They’re soon joined by the only expendable group, the bomb tinykin that are used to break open collections of pollen and passageways you need to navigate. Green tinykin can stack up to form a ladder giving you that all-too-important access to the vertically designed worlds and yellow tinykin perform a similar task but with a ramp that can only be used in designated areas. The final type, the blue tinykin, are used in niche situations of chaining together to connect power outlets to exposed cables. This assortment of characters is used seamlessly to help you transition around each level and often are given in an abundance that allows you to get where you need to go even without having all of them. However, the collect-a-thon nature of the game encourages you to find them all regardless.I believe if you avoided the side missions and the somewhat tedious task of finding every tinykin and last speck of popcorn-shaped pollen dotted in the recesses of every map, Tinykin would only be a few hours long at best. Even completing majority of that, I only clocked in less than seven hours. Of course, I put in probably three hours in the demo (over two playthroughs) which carried over to the full game, so it may be at least an hour or two longer. Still, it might not be as appealing of a prospect if you’re racing through it. However, it’s so rewarding to find these items and fully explore the worlds that I can’t imagine playing the game without attempting to get most of it. The little details, bug characters, and magnificent environment design are, on their own, worth every moment invested.If I could find any fault in the game, it's that the insect NPCs and much of the world are very static without your involvement. I think it would have done a great deal for the immersion and brought life to the environment if the bugs were moving around and performing basic tasks. I didn’t mind the 2D character design and it’s one of the most well-integrated examples of 2D sprites in a 3D environment. Yet, the only real problem I have is that I can’t have even more of this game. It was such an engrossing and enjoyable experience that I felt like I could easily play twice as much without any hesitation. I can only hope that the developers are willing to add to this exceptional experience soon.I somehow forgot to mention how great the soundtrack is for this game. Each of the five rooms/zones has its own theme - and all of those are great - but the best part is that they change depending on where you go within the map. For instance, in the first area, you can go into a guitar that serves as a nightclub and the theme takes on the twang of a guitar. The rooms have at least a few of these areas and it makes exploration even more rewarding. Ok now that's all - play this game!

_childDocuments_.review: Tinykin is a delightful 3D platformer that merges elements of classic collect-a-thon gameplay with unique puzzle-solving mechanics. Set in a miniature world within a human household, you’ll explore vibrant, intricately designed levels, all while leading an army of adorable creatures called Tinykin.Why You Should Play:- Charming Visuals: The blend of 2D characters in a 3D environment creates a captivating and nostalgic aesthetic reminiscent of Saturday morning cartoons.- Engaging Puzzles: Each type of Tinykin has distinct abilities, and mastering how to combine them to navigate obstacles and solve puzzles keeps the gameplay fresh and rewarding.- Exploration: The level design encourages exploration and rewards players with collectibles, hidden areas, and clever environmental storytelling.- Smooth Platforming: The controls are tight and responsive, making it a joy to leap, glide, and command your Tinykin army through the game's diverse environments.If you enjoy games like Pikmin, Katamari Damacy, or classic platformers, Tinykin will be a refreshing and charming addition to your library. Perfect for those looking for a light-hearted yet deeply engaging adventure.

_childDocuments_.review: Tinykin is a difficult game to evaluate.Is it fun? Sure, the movement feels good, tight, and responsive. Skating around levels on your soapboard is satisfying and quick. The levels are massive and intuitively designed, possibly some of the best 3D level design I've experienced for that matter; constantly offering multiple options to explore that always seem to loop back in on themselves and branch into other routes. After getting the hang of the game it flows extremely naturally and you wind up completing the entire level without ever losing the wind in your sails until, essentially, the very end when you're just doing cleanup of the last few ambrosia you missed (this game's sort of "coin" collectible, with over a thousand per level).The visuals are incredibly charming as well, transforming everyday objects into not just obstacles but things that are functional for the NPCs as much as they are engaging to interact with. One particular level has an entire sink with a running faucet that overflows into an irrigation system, using sponges for farmland (which happen to be as evergreen as grass). The character designs are similarly cute and visually interesting.And... Surprisingly, the game's writing is pretty good. There's actually somehow relatively interesting politics internally from stage to stage that showcases thoughtful worldbuilding. Similarly I didn't expect the very ending to be so... Strangely melancholic and tragic. Still, it wasn't an unwelcomed tonal shift to close out the ten hour runtime.So what's the hang-up? Why can't I rate it any higher when the game is so expertly and lovingly crafted?The game is just... Too easy. It feels like wasted potential. There isn't a single stretch of difficult platforming to be seen nor is there an engaging puzzle. The highest compliment I can give this game amounts to "the most fun you can have with your brain turned off", which is an unfortunate statement to have to make. There's no fail state, no way to be punished or to make a decision that can lead to any form of punishment. You can't even lose progress in longer stretches of vertical platforming because there are shortcuts to the bottom every layer up.I'm not asking for tedium, but even Mario Odyssey, a game that (at times) just hands you a decent amount of your moons for free in the name of accessibility, still offers entirely optional venues for sometimes extremely challenging platforming. I don't think this is a particularly difficult design choice to at least keep in mind, but what Tinykin offers in the ways of intriguing challenge is entirely zero. I understand that challenge isn't the point of every game, games are made to be fun, but it's the extreme lack of stimulation I felt while engaging with the content that bogged down an otherwise great experience.I still highly recommend the game in spite of this if you have a few hours to burn and find yourself even remotely interested. It's short and I do believe it deserves full support, but I just found it lacking. I hope they continue to make games as they clearly have an incredible vision for this type of thing.

_childDocuments_.review: 13h 3/10 1  made some very nice video's with all the collectibles with time stamps and also mentions the hidden pollen, which are most likely the ones you're missing.  No No, at any point you can go back to each level and find the collectibles No No No No No No difficulty option NoI had such high hopes for this game.... and I'm still BLOWN AWAY!!! I fell in love with tinykin in the first 20 minutes of the game and that feeling got stronger and stronger. What an amazing game, I loved the looks, the feeling, the stories! Each level felt overwhelming at first, but so so amazing and they aren't that big when you understand the layout and open up a lot of shortcuts. And that last level.... that was such an amazing theme... but wait, let me stop here and first tell you more about the game. In Tinykin you control a few different types of "Tinykin", just like in Pikmin/Overlord/The Wild at Heart. You start off with the strong type that can help you push or pull items, in further levels you unlock 4 other Tinykin with their own unique abilities which I will not spoil here. Every time you find a new one you get a short cutscene that introduced the tinykin and their ability to you. When you start the game you'll get a short intro and then land in the hallway of a 1991 home, this year is specifically mentioned in the game because you'll find all kinds of stuff that was so normal in 1991 in this home. This added a layer of nostalgia for me as that was during my childhood. You have a very brief tutorial on how to move and how to find Tinykin and use them, but I almost can't call this a tutorial but just a brief instruction. The game won't waste much of your time on learning the game but just shattered around the levels a robot kinda station with a very brief description of how this new mechanic works. In most of the game, this is enough and you're quickly on your way, I only need a bit of time to understand the blue tinykins, but got it after a few minutes. There is no fighting in Tinykin,  but you won't miss that at all, you'll be busy enough with platforming around, solving puzzles and finding hidden items. The art style is unique but so so cute. Before I played the game I noticed that there is a different art style for your character and the Tinykins compared to the surroundings, but during the game you wouldn't notice this much anymore as it will grip your attention and make you smile while exploring. I love both art styles but I think I have a sweet spot for the art style of the surroundings. Tinykin blew me away, which is impressive because as stated before, I was hyped for this game and most of the time hype leads more easily toward disappointment. If my body didn't need sleep I would have played through this game in one sitting, but now I did it in 2. I just couldn't stop playing. The achievements are very straightforward forward and like 80% of them you'll unlock them without even paying attention to the achievements. The most challenging ones will all come together with finding all the pollen and all the Tinkins. Which are scattered all over the levels, also in very hidden spots. This can become frustrating but for me, the videos from WheatYT on Youtube helped me to just find those few hidden pollen I had missed. UPDATE: They have added information of the tinykin you found in each level on the status screen, which is a very welcome addition and makes this game just easier for achievement hunters, now you know where to search for those last few pesky tinykin. I loved loved loved Tinykin...did I already told you that I love Tinykin? And that ending... it leaves the door open for a second installment and I'm all in! Please "Splashteam" make a second installment <3

_childDocuments_.review: I'm shocked at the small review count for this game, but not even remotely surprised at the 98% positive rating. This game is incredibly good.Tinykin is a 3D Collect-a-Thon with two gimmicks: 1) you're a tiny person in an ordinary household and 2) there's a bunch of little bugs scattered in every level that will do your bidding when you find them. These bugs have abilities depending on their color-- some can climb on top of one another to build a ladder for you, some will group up to carry around objects that are way to heavy for you, etc. This encourages you to explore the first sub-region of a level pretty thoroughly before you move on to the next one (e.g. you might need a 20-bug ladder in order to reach the next area). This keeps you from zooming through levels and rushing to the end. That might sound inconvenient, but it's an idea that perfectly suits this game because you'll find that slowing down is the best way to play. There's tons of insect npcs with really funny dialogue, and the world is really fun to look at and think about. Once you have completed the whole level and are just cleaning up some collectibles, you'll find it much easier to zoom around-- the movement is fluid, and there's even an optional time trial in every level to highlight this. I can comfortably say that Tinykin is one of my favorite 3D Collect-a-Thons of all time. It's also, surprisingly, somewhat obscure-- so please check it out and tell a friend about it.

_childDocuments_.review: Tinykin is one of those games that you start playing and have to force yourself to stop because you're having too much fun and don't want to end it all too quickly. I suggest you stop reading right now and go buy it, but if you're interested in knowing more about it, go on.This is a puzzle 3D platformer collectathon. The game wears its influences on its sleeve. It's clearly patterned after other games, but it doesn't pretend otherwise, and is its expert execution that makes it great. Both of its most obvious influences are Pikmin and Super Mario 64, both Nintendo games that have never seen a PC release, so it's great that we finally have something to compensate for their absence in this platform. That being said, this game isn't content with just aping those titles and comes up with its own formula.The main mechanic borrowed from Pikim is the title characters themselves: the tinykin. These are small creatures that you encounter as you progress through the game, color-coded according to their respective ability, who follow you around and help you achieve your goals. Some of them allow you to push or carry heavy objects, others allow you to create platforms to cross, others can destroy obstacles and so on. Puzzles are generally solved by finding an objective and figuring out how to reach that goal with the use of your available tinykin.From Super Mario 64 this game borrows its level design and sense of exploration. Levels are large and open without feeling overwhelming or labyrinthine. They are expertly designed to let you see just enough without making it obvious at first how you're going to reach all those interesting places and just what you might find in them. As you progress through each level you get to see areas you've visited from different angles and realize you might have missed something, which encourages to revisit those places. I'm a sucker for games that reward exploration, and this one is fantastic in that regard.Each level has a main objective (usually divided in parts) you need to complete to advance and a few sidequests you can discover and do if you choose. There's no combat and character progression is minimal (you only really upgrade one ability), but sidequests allow you to grab collectibles, which gradually help you make sense of the world and its story. They are also fun to do, so there's really no reason to avoid them. There are, of course, a bunch of achievements to do as well, tied to the story, collectibles and a few specific actions you need to do.The best way to describe this game is just pure, undiluted fun. Challenge isn't high, but movement is fast, dialogue is funny and the visuals are beautiful. While I did encounter a few frame dips a couple of times generally the game runs great and it'll take you between 8-9 hours to complete if you do all the sidequests and hunt for achievements, which is a lot of bang for your buck.I wholly recommend this game and I'm looking forward to a potential sequel.

_childDocuments_.review: I just want to start off by saying that I've never in my life, completely fallen in love with a game so fast ever before.I mean, this game is literally perfect to me. I also never really write reviews, BUT this game deserves it dammit! First of all, the art style is original and very cute, not to mention super creative level design using everyday mundane household objects to really make it feel like the creatures of the house have been there for years. I also really love that there was so much to explore, so many nooks and crannies that weren't just empty spaces but actually had some kind of collectible or character to talk with, which is a really nice way to reward the player for exploring the huge worlds.The story building and lore is also very interesting and I was wondering about so many things until nearing the end.Next, the soundtrack... O M G... the soundtrack almost brought tears to my eyes and really gave this game that extra oomph of personality that I feel a lot of games like this just lack. And the sound design *chefs kiss* I swear the sound effects for everything you interact with really makes it feel alive just so much more.Thirdly, the controls are soooo nice and I never once felt like I didn't have control of the character, and the move set was not overly complicated or hard to remember which button does what. The abilities also made it really nice by allowing the player to move freely and explore in a non-linear way, and I often found myself finding different ways to get to the same places. The speed was also fast enough that it wasn't boring just running/sliding/gliding anywhere.One last thing of note, the references! And the comedy! I loved it all as there were always some funny conversations to walk into which always made me giggle tehe.All in all, Tinykin is a game that you can really feel all the love and care that the creators put into it, so I definitely recommend it to anyone that loves cute platformers. I really love the Banjo-Kazooie series and I'm always finding myself with that "I gotta play a fun platformer/collectathon" itch. which honestly is hard the find the right game for, but Tinykin really scratched that itch.

_childDocuments_.review: With these cryptic sentence blocks, the puzzle platformer Tinykin welcomes you and gives the starting signal for an insanely sweet adventure.While narrative has never really been a focus in a platformer, Tinykin has a premise that is interesting enough to get players invested right away. When they take on the role of Milodane, an explorer who comes to earth in search of discoveries, things take a eerie turn when there are no humans left and time hasn't passed since 1991, but the feeling that someone or something is watching his every move remains.To get home, with the help of the funny creatures known as Tinykin and other colorful characters, you'll have to build a special machine in a sprawling ant-sized metropolis full of bugs and other insects to make things even more fun.As if this wasn't strange enough, the friendly Ridmi – a strange, white-bearded creature that appears out of nowhere – offers you his help and explains the simple of the game in a short tutorial. Thus, you'll jump over gigantic records, float through the air for a short time thanks to your bubble backpack, and get to know your first little helpers – the droll Tinykin.These lively henchmen all have special abilities that you can take advantage of during your adventure. For example, purple Tinykins are extremely strong and can combine forces to move heavy objects or transport them around to open up new paths, while green Tinykins can stack on top of each other and serve as useful ladders. Blue gnomes are excellent conductors of electricity, red bombers blow up obstacles, and yellow acrobats quickly build a staircase out of nothing to reach unimagined heights with ease.Of course, not all types of Tinykins are available to you at the beginning. However, in the course of your adventure, you'll gradually meet new ones, so your gaming experience will always be motivating, and each new level will bring a breath of fresh air into the game. The music also underlines the whole experience. The melodies in every part of the house never become an annoyance, and the various tunes fit the ambience of the area Milo is currently in.Nevertheless, the game takes you firmly by the hand at all times and literally "asks" you to use the required Tinykins in explicit places. In addition, all objects that can be interacted with flash in the respective color of the needed Tinykins, so you don't have to experiment wildly to finally make progress. However, even though the objects literally jump out at you, you still need the required number of Tinykins to solve the task or puzzle. For example, a door will only open when enough purple helpers join forces.If you are still lacking energetic support, you may have to take a different path first. This makes the levels a bit more complex and extensive, but with a bit of patience and perseverance you will inevitably reach your goal. This also forces you to remember the exact path you took because if you can't solve a puzzle, you should know later on where you left off. Furthermore, collected Tinykins are only available in the level in which you collected them – simply taking a whole motley crew with you to the next doesn't work.Your main task will be to restore your aircraft, which has been damaged, so that you can leave this strange place. For this, however, you'll need some objects that are hidden in the different rooms of the house. You'll travel through the fragrant kitchen, the untidy children's room or the foaming bathroom and complete various tasks and solve one or the other puzzle.The Chrysal workshop is your base, from which all future operations start. Here you return the found objects from the levels and start new missions to other rooms. Unfortunately, there is no quick travel function in Tinykin, so if you want to restart a level, to find all the pollen or to finish optional missions, you'll have to take the sometimes tedious path that often leads you back to the workshop – fortunately, a smooth soap board is already at your disposal at the beginning, with which you can slide through the levels quite quickly.In the varied levels, you'll find countless details and lovely cuteness that will undoubtedly enhance your entertaining adventure. The creative level design is really impressive and offers plenty of space for extensive explorations through the insects' cities inside the house. Everywhere you can uncover exciting secrets, discover hidden passages and solve puzzling tasks.You'll also encounter chatty cockroaches, buzzing dragonflies and other creepy-crawlies everywhere, which will not only make you smile with humorous pop culture references, but also have optional missions up their sleeves.For example, in each level, you can find a certain amount of golden pollen, which your friend Sikaru will use to brew delicious concoctions and also reward you with an extra bubble to float in. Thus, meticulous treasure hunters – in this case, eager pollen hunters – will sooner or later have advantages in fun exploring the exciting environments, as each new bubble will allow you to travel longer distances and thus reach new areas.With the help of a striking overview via spyglass you can see new and undiscovered missions at any time. If you want to collect every pollen, successfully complete all the main missions and finish all the side quests, you'll certainly be busy for around ten hours plus.Especially the concise 2D representations of the protagonists, who otherwise cavort in a three-dimensional world, are a nice eye-catcher. In addition, the positively playful melodies will surely animate you to sway along happily once in a while, and thus ensure a good mood.At first glance, Tinykin may seem overwhelming with its various mechanics and collectibles to find, but somehow the game keeps you moving at a steady, yet entertaining pace. As a bare minimum, you'll still have at least six hours of fun trying to get Milo home. However, opt. to complete in full, and you'll be able to extend the total game time by a few hours, or more, of satisfaction by solving increasingly difficult puzzles. And although it doesn't necessarily have that strategic component of Pikmin, Tinykin makes the most of its interpretation of the genre, while adding its own adorable mascots for one of the best 3D platformers of recent years, especially on Gamepass. This is hands down my personal GOTY 2022 and childhood dream wrapped in a superb collect-a-thon platforming experience.

_childDocuments_.review: The core loop is you go to a room, collect some Tinykin to help you solve a number of puzzles (move a thing, collect a thing, retrieve a thing, etc.) and eventually you collect a object that goes towards the game's primary goal and return to the centre of operations.  Each room is a platforming puzzle that as you go through it you'll unlock shortcuts to make it easier to move around, as well as having to take advantage of each kind of Tinykin.  As far as I got, each room introduced a new kind of Tinykin that would help you in a unique way: the first Tinykin and pick up or push heavy objects, the second can be thrown to destroy breakable objects, and the third stack to create an impromptu ladder, etc. It is quite like Pikmin, but it's been a long time since I played that so I can't get into the details.  If you liked Pikmin you'll enjoy Tinykin.It's got a very Cartoon Network feel with flat characters drawn in 3D spaces and a has nostalgic quality to it because of this.  The cutscenes are very cute as well.  This also goes for the sounds, it's very late 90s cartoony.Controls are intuitive, you get a double jump/glide right away, and a soap-based hoverboard equivalent plus things to climb up and slide down, but most of the movement is just running and jumping.While I think it's fun enough to finish I don't really see any replay value except for if you want to 100% it.

_childDocuments_.review: A Hat in Time gained a reputation for being a great alternative to 3D Mario. It certainly had solid writing, characters, and unique scenarios, but it wasn’t a good platformer. With its extremely restrictive moveset, basic platforming challenges, and collectables that quickly lost their purpose, it was more akin to an amateur’s first stab at the genre.Tinykin is essentially a weaker version of that title. Somehow, it’s more rudimentary while also lacking most of A Hat in Time’s redeeming qualities.Every single mechanic in Tinykin can be traced back to a better title. The game’s namesake are the most obvious example, functioning as Pikmin that don’t require babysitting. This is fine for a platformer, but of the five types of Tinykin, only the green variety enhances the platforming in any way. The rest are used for puzzles that essentially solve themselves.The core moveset is a lot shallower than an open-zone 3D platformer has any right to be. Take the jumping. Milodane barely has any hang time, so he drops like a rock after peak jump height. It really doesn’t pair well with his ability to glide around like Bunny Mario. The soapbar is decent, but there’s so little to master outside of the time trials. At the time of writing this, I haven’t played Tony Hawk’s Pro Skater or Jet Set Radio, the clearest inspirations for the soapbar’s physics, but it doesn’t take a pro to see how much more effort those older classics put into their movement systems.The more I played Tinykin, the more I wondered what the point of it all was. The hub and spoke level design is neat at first glance, but the theming is just for show. Take away the wallpaper and each level plays exactly the same, even down to the number of side quests available in each one. The numerous collectables do an adequate job making the player feel like they accomplished something, but why bother collecting everything when there’s no system to help players find those last few collectibles you’re missing? The least it could do is be more friendly to completionists than Super Mario Sunshine.Between all of that is the most uninspired platforming I’ve seen in a long time. Incredibly simple jumps and sparse use of hazards that barely punish the player to begin with. Calling it a B-grade platformer would be an insult to non-Mario platformers that actually bothered to engage the player like Banjo-Kazooie, Sonic Adventure, or Pac-Man World 2. Even A Hat in Time’s weakest challenges were more involved than this.The story is whatever. I think it would have been more interesting if there were only a few characters that needed to learn the house’s inner workings rather than dozens of NPCs spelling out everything or telling bad jokes. Not much else to say really.I’m willing to bet everyone reading this grew up playing at least one 3D platformer that delivered an unparalleled feeling of wonder. Given all the advancements in technology and game design, I think it’s fair to expect modern representatives of the genre to recapture that excitement. If Tinykin accomplished that for you, then please ignore my whining and be happy! I’m not here to upset readers. However, I’m not going to apologize for being honest with myself. In a world where 3D platformers are unpopular among indie and AAA studios, I cannot help but be disappointed with Tinykin’s mundanity.

_childDocuments_.review: Update: Comments were made on my review by a certain developer who shall remain unnamed that were rather rude and chlidish sounding. They either clearly agreed with this sentiment or where told off by a fellow dev on the project as the comments are now deleted. I'll take the deletes as an admission of guilt, or at least being somewhat self aware of the negative look and let bygones be bygones, but I'm leaving my comments below and this here for context regardless. I'm not one to endorse any bullying or witch hunting but that wasn't cool.Not a No that I enjoy handing out, but I think this game is getting too much praise for what it is. It's a cute fun romp through some neat levels, but the entire experience is shallow as a water drop on pavement. Most of the challenges and problems presented are simply resolved by walking around and finding more tinykin, or just walking from one end of the room to another. Problems solve themselves as there is only ever one solution, with no room for player creativity, ingenuity, or expression, short of the ladder tinykin. It's a shame that the ladder tinykin rear their head, because it shows that the game is NEARLY able to let the player do something creative, but never steps further than that. If you're looking for something akin to a walking simulator, then you might find fun here, but the game seems almost like a prank on anyone who wanted to actually play a game, rubbing the scent of Pikmin in our face and then ripping it away once you know what's happening. Add on laughable 100% achievements that are built on random useless tinykin being hidden around every corner, and the game just feels like a slap to the face.This really just feels like someone played Pikmin and Chibi-Robo and completely missed the point beyond a surface level """charm""". Pikmin was enjoyable and slightly challenging due to a (rather generous) time limit, on top of very alien creatures that kept you guessing how things worked, despite the familiar earth setting. You needed to protect your Pikmin and grow more of them, mistakes causing you possible days, making you care much more about the carrot things. The lack of any real danger, threat, or failure state means I often didn't even keep track of how many tinykin I had. Additionally, the roles of the pikmin make an infinite amount more sense and are much more interesting. Why can only the pink tinykin pick things up? There's a reason Pikmin didn't do that, because the three colors had multiple roles, thus reducing an amount of bloat that would otherwise be caused by needing a new Pikmin for every role, like tinykin does. As such, the tinykin end up feeling much more like a set of tools that have limited uses. I don't know how you expect me to care about them when I'm throwing them at the wall to blow them to gibs, but they're not willing to carry a bit of mail.Similarly, Chibi-Robo thrived off the battery limitation being a natural gate keeper, encouraging you to play the role of a cleaning robot to earn money and upgrades, pushing you towards more enjoyable platforming that opens up with new tools and your actions causing changes in the house and with other characters. The actions you were forced to take put you in the mindset of Chibi, building a personal bond with the house and all inside. Tinykin feels more like I'm just playing a GMod map, noclipping around only sometimes being stopped by needing to press E on a nearby object. Not only am I not being challenged in any capacity, but I feel that my input is meaningless as both a player and as the character. Nothing I do couldn't be done by a bug if it weren't for an arbitrary usage of tinykin.The story is the last strike against the game. You've filled the game with so many individual bugs that all have their own dialogue, stories that continue between rooms and quest that build on each other, and instead of making the story about them you decide to suddenly pull some horribly convoluted BS about time travel, multi-world stuff, and whatever the hell was up with the ending cutscene. I liked the bugs, I don't give a damn about the one other human character or his plight.I'll suggest this game if everything I've said doesn't bother you that much and you just want to walk around a cute world with little bug things that make funny faces, but even then not at 25 dollars. That's theft for the amount and quality of content on offer. Get it at least 50% off.

_childDocuments_.review: Some say Tinykin is like It Takes Two - I can't agree. The only common might be characters are all shrank, making regular items incredibly big and troublesome. Similarly, in TinyKin, minions are to be found around the map to join you to solve puzzles (open doors, cross a gap etc.), either carry stuff, build a ladder or a bridge, the main difference is you are to not solve puzzles rather than conquer lands in Overlord. I'm lazy not doing any research but I won't be surprised if devs get ideas from Overlord.It's amusing most of the time - to go around the corner, gather minions, interact with a magnified world, climb high and glide or slide on strings, funny characters... The favorite goes to the apologizing dung beetles, who are sorry for messing with dulls because they are dung beetles. _childDocuments_.review: An exploration-focused 3D platformer with the core gameplay of , the level design of , and the mission structure of old-school collectathons; all tweaked to streamline and optimize the fun factor. Its launch day version needs a few minor bug fixes (namely bugged achievements), and it would benefit greatly from a post-game collectible tracker to avoid the tedium of finding those last few collectibles; but both are hopefully resolved in due time. With about an 8-hour playtime if you're a completionist--and just a bit less if you're not--it just might be the easiest recommendation I'll make this year.  is a 3D platformer about a human on the distant planet of Aegis named Milodane, who deduces that humanity actually originated on another planet and sets out to explore it. When his teleporter sends him to a suburban house on what we know as Earth, things aren't as they should be: his navigation equipment has been damaged, he's  smaller than he should be, the house is technologically stuck in 1991, there are no humans in sight, and the environment is populated by an array of intelligent insects. Among these is a species of hivemind-like creatures called tinykin that inexplicably see Milodane as their leader and respond to his every command, and he'll need to enlist their help to find a way home--and uncover what happened to humanity in the process. . Each of the game's six locations (corresponding to rooms in the house) hold a certain number of tinykin that you need to find and hatch from their eggs, and doing so will have them follow you around so you can throw them at things they can interact with. You can't take them with you into other rooms, but they will wait for you where you left them; so unlike the  strategy of grinding to build up an all-purpose army, you have to rely on the tinykin you're given in that room to accomplish your goals there. There are five types of tinykin total, each with their own special abilities: some are used to solve puzzles, others open new shortcuts or make it easier to traverse the environment, but all of them are valuable in the long run., focusing purely on "play at your own pace" exploration and platforming, and not on things like combat or sequences demanding fast reflexes. There are no enemies or boss battles to be found, but there are a handful of environmental hazards you'll need to watch out for, like water, fire, or simple gravity since fall damage does exist here. The challenge factor comes from the puzzle-platforming involved in main and side missions, though I wouldn't describe any of it as "hard". The only potential source of frustration might be in its "collectathon" side, namely in the hundreds of the collectible "pollen" to be found in every nook and cranny of the house. Collecting around 75% of the pollen in a room lets you buy a movement upgrade, but getting 100% of the pollen is just for unlocking achievements--though you could argue that going for 100% is the point of collectathons. If you choose to do this, know that you'll run into a problem that plagues many games in this genre: the frustration and monotony of running around to try and find those last few collectibles you somehow missed. , maybe as a post-game upgrade or a reward for finishing all the side missions so this issue can be avoided. They already have a function to switch to first-person view for a better look at your surroundings--complete with markers that highlight the location of mission ojectives--so hopefully it'll be expanded in a future update to also highlight missing pollen, and perhaps unhatched tinykin since there's an achievement for finding all of them as well.That's really the only frustration I had while playing, because . These are just a few examples I found while playing of little design decisions that went a surprisingly long way towards maintaining my enjoyment throughout:, but players who choose to avoid that last, tedious hunt for their final missing collectibles can still finish satisfied in a bit less time. The list of my favorite games growing up includes the likes of , , and several N64/Gamecube-era collectathons; and playing something that seamlessly combines elements from all three, while taking steps to remove most of the tedium from each one, makes for a game that does more than just feel nostalgic: it makes for a game that feels almost tailor-made for me. P.S. , showing missing progress even if you've done what's required. If this happens, revisit old locations so it re-checks your progress there and it should update properly.

_childDocuments_.review: Finally, someone brings a Nintendo formula to the PC.Tinykin is Pikmin.  I’ve seen people call it everything from Chibi Robo to Mario but this is absolutely a Pikmin clone. I’m always amazed at how few PC games are based on Nintendo Franchises, but Tinykin does this right and it’s fantastic. You explore a large house and meet various creatures that can accomplish different goals. At the same time, Tinykin is a bit short with only 6 levels. There are collectibles, and small challenges after the game, but it may only last about 10 hours. There’s not a lot of challenge either but it’s still quite fun. The gameplay is really solid, and the style is brilliant, every level is a different piece of the house, and the experience here is fantastic. Pick this up if you like Pikmin, or if you just want an interesting game where you explore a house. This should get a lot of attention and it’s the perfect game to play with your kids or just by yourself. I enjoyed this game so much that I bought a copy on Steam because I want more games like this. A small note, there does appear to be a problem with AMD graphics cards and this game. Not everyone is having it, but a friend of mine’s game is unplayable at this point, which is a shame because he also enjoyed the first level. Hopefully, they can fix that.

_childDocuments_.review: Tinykin is the game you get when somebody asks "What if somebody made a faster-paced Pikmin where you can explore in three dimensions?"The player is Milodane, a human space explorer who crash lands on a deserted human planet where he's insect-sized, in a house where the insects worship a long-vanished human named Ardwin. For no apparent reason, even tinier creatures called Tinykin have an irresistible urge to follow Milodane around and help him do stuff.All of this is a thinly-veiled plot device to allow the player to explore the different areas of the house, climbing onto and into the furniture, using the different Tinykins' abilities to manipulate the environment and incidentally help the insects while unlocking more areas of the house.Each area introduces a new type of Tinykin and coincidentally contains some obstacles that require their special ability to overcome.Tinykin streamlines the classic Pikmin gameplay in a number of ways:The different rooms are gorgeous and fun to explore, and each one has a cohesive theme. Additionally, there's plenty of optional stuff to find, collect, and achieve.I had a lot of fun, and the game ended before it had a chance to get old.If you like Pikmin, or if you like the  of Pikmin but the games themselves are too slow-paced for you, give Tinykin a try!

_childDocuments_.review: What. A. Game!I honestly can't remember when I spent so much contiguous time* on a single game and was utterly delighted by every** single moment. One of those games you really want to get through so you can see everything, while at the same time wish would never end.* Ignore my playtime; I didn't bother shutting the game down when busy with annoying but somewhat important distractions like work and sleep and eating.** As always, the bane of 3D platformers on a 2D screen is judging depth and the exact positions of things, and some jumpy bits got a bit frustrating at times.The level design and mechanics start off interesting, clever, and well thought out. And just keep getting get more interesting, extra cleverer, and better thoughter outerer.There aren't very many levels, but they are (especially the last few) exquisitely designed. The intro flyovers on the last few main levels took my breath away. And I was also immediately thinking "O.M.G. Where the **** am I even going to start with this one?!?". But in every case once you look about about a bit, gradually everything becomes clear, and shortcuts open up to make repeating things you've already done unnecessary to follow different paths.The dialogue of the characters is well written and sometimes pretty amusing. But there is a heck of a lot of it, to the point it becomes a bit distracting from the game's pace and mechanics. Fortunately, almost all of it is optional if you find it a bit weary-some. I did about half way through, but next play through I'll probably take my time a bit more and read it all.For maximum story effect, I recommend the approach I accidentally took. Don't look at any of the museum items until you have them all. And then look at them before getting into the ship at the end. Basically; I can't recommend highly enough.
