_childDocuments_.review: I have to be honest, when I played through the Story Mode I liked the game, but it did not grab me enough to return due to the scripted events similar to Frostpunk 1. Sure, maybe I try one or two more runs and that is it. Then I tried out the Utopia Builder and my opinion of the game has drastically changed since then. The story in this one is more like a tutorial, yet the real main attraction of the game and I would say the game in itself, is the Utopia Mode. It has much more content than the first game including the Story Mode and I would say it is an evolution with more complexity on a macro level scale. I come back to it thinking stuff like: "Hey how about we now just produce robots out of oil and keep the population to a minimum, while thinking about how I can maximise the food output and turn coal into oil with the help of the materials I got from a sewer treating facility, so we can survive the next -110 Celsius storm which will disable much of the output of my food colony on the other side of the map, as I do not like to turn dead people into food because understandably it will lead a faction to go haywire on me."Think of Anno mixed with a society simulator where you battle internal conflict in combination with the harsh elements, including your moral standards together with the population of your city.My only real issue I have with the game is the performance. The game looks really freaking cool, however I would say it needs polish. This could be because 11-Bit has yet to learn how to optimise a city builder made with Unreal. To me It seems like Frostpunk 1 used a house-made engine and thus had the better "Polish" on its side.Lastly, If you a want a more micro approach similar to Frostpunk 1, this ain't it and it might be not your cup of tea and that is ok. If you like going big and enjoy more complexity in a survival city builder and want some replay value, this is your kinda game.

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of Frostpunk 1, I was prepared to throw my wallet at anything with the Frostpunk title. Unfortunately it took me 5 hours, which is over Steam's refund policy, to realize that this game has very little to do with Frostpunk. The focus on the game is on politics. It's not a survival game, it's a politics simulator. If you are into that stuff, this game is probably your GOTY.I'll briefly sum up some things that bothered me:- Due to the large scale, the game feels soulless. A death is meaningless, there is no day and night, you can't even see your people going to work and going home. You are only looking at numbers, week after week of the same. You are not building houses, you are assigning districts.- Oil/coal and heat are almost irrelevant. It's the backdrop to what is basically a game about navigating several political parties who disagree with each other. In FP 1 the main problem was that people are freezing in the night and the hospitals get overcrowded. The biggest problem in FP 2 is that political party A is crying that political party B passed their vote. Yawn.- The UI is absolutely terrible. I hear they released some patches to fix some stuff so who knows, maybe it'll get better.- The game doesn't explain anything. Many mechanics aren't intuitive, and you will end up on google quite a lot. This isn't a showstopper but it was responsible for me rolling my eyes a couple of times. They could have handled this a lot better.Overall, it's brave of the creators to do something completely different, but it's not for me. I was very disappointed. It gives me the feeling that it shouldn't have been named "Frostpunk 2". It should have been its own name. I might give the game another go a bit later, after some patch cycles, and hopefully I'll get some enjoyment out of my money.

_childDocuments_.review: For all fans of the first Frostpunk, this second chapter will be a big disappointment. Not only does it lose all its charm, but you feel so distant from the people that it doesn't matter how many die. You no longer have to create a city in detail but build entire districts that appear from nowhere as if by magic.The addition of the parliament is interesting if it weren't so annoying to have to manage the factions that are never satisfied and prevent you from doing what you need to survive.Frostpunk 2 is a city builder with the Frostpunk skin, but it feels more like a puzzle game.I rush to do all the things before it's late and it's not fun, I don't have time to enjoy the experience.it's a cold mechanical system that has no heart or soul, the first game from 11bits studio that disappointed me.. the day has come.

_childDocuments_.review: I truly recommend the game. I was a big fan of the first game (played it like 200h in a pirated version). But the first time when I heard the second game was being made I truly didn't give a ♥♥♥♥, yes I enjoyed the first one but I thought the second game will be frostpunk but with petrol, the same thing but a little different.When I saw the first trailer, my jaw dropped. I couldn't of imagined that they had the balls to do something this drastically different from the first one, while still truly fallowing the vision and narrative path of the first.The game is amazing in most that it is trying to do, and shows that it learned from the 'mishaps' of the first. The first game was centered around the main scenario, and for many the main scenario was the peak of the game, and for many the rest even if the rest of the scenarios were good, it didn't scratch the same itch, also the first game took a while to release the endless mode that also ended up being underwhelming, since after a while there would be nothing to do in such a scenario. The second game focused on the sandbox and endless mode, since unlike the first it isn't about the cost of survival but the cost of ambition. The main campaign is more like a tutorial for the player to understand all the components of the game and to go experiment and test themselves in the utopia builder mode. All the mechanics are also focused on the prolonging game, the laws can be signed, unsigned and changed unlike the rigid one in the first game, all resources are limited(with few and negligible exceptions) and the population increases to a staggering amount and all this people form under ideological believes and enter in conflicts among themselves.The first game was about surviving the end of the world, a great challenge which after beaten left nothing to do in that game. The second game is about continuing and prospering in the storm that never ends, with the problems that don't have a permanent solution.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to love this game but i dont and I am kinda surprised it got so many good reviews. The resource management part is kinda basic. There are very few goods to manage and only one currency thats restricting all your actions for most of the time. While that doesnt have to be something bad, if thats not the main part of the game there need to be something else and for Frostpunk 2 thats the politics system. And honestly thats great, at first. But it comes with some major issues:-  E.g. if dialogs force you to make decisions without being able to look up the consequences/alternative laws for the category. It also happens that even tho a fraction is supporting a change of law, they start raging because its breaking a promise you made before so you gotta keep track on your promises as the game wont necessarily tell you. - There are straight up  in the system. In my latest play through when i enforced captains law it froze the state of guided voting impact with all groups at extremely bad which caused tons of trouble for like the next 5h in the game. Than the whole politics system became stable (i still had worst relations with all groups, despite guided voting was the only negative impact for some of the groups) and stopped giving me problems to solve, so that i was left with a rly basic and boring although great looking resource management city builder.There are a couple  which can often lead to confusion and frustrations.Another thing i wanna mention is that in "endless", once you made it past week 400 (~5-6h) with a decent strategy, stacking effects starts kicking in and the week 400 - 2000 becomes easy/boring even on highest difficult level. Also the game runs into some serious performance issues in endgame where auto save and even build menu lag the game for multiple seconds. The whole endless mode feels more like BETA state. So in the end its not a bad game, but it lacks depth and at its current state it doenst feel worth the full price. Lets see what kind of bugfixes and DLC content we might get in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: I would love to say that I recommend this game. I was a huge fan of the first one and this second installment has a lot of potential!It's a lot more of a "society balancer" or "political game" than it is a City Building/Resource management in my opinion but that's not what it suffers from. The smaller issue is that there's a tutorial and guide that explains some of how things work, but not everything. I frequently found myself trying to understand why "this thing is red". However, you can work around that, google, reddit, whathave you.The bigger issue for me is performance.While the step towards a bigger broader scope seemed like the right thing to do for the sequal, the bigger and broader scope seems to have been too much for the team to promise at launch.The game has crashed on me 5 times in my 10 hours of play. It has stuttered, halted, and struggled many times within that 10 hours as well. The farther you get with more districts and outposts, the worse it is.And forget the autosave. That stopped working for me about 5 hours in. With some time and bug fixes, optimizations, and some work to not overtax the computer, I think this game has potential, even if it has faults in the game play.

_childDocuments_.review: Meh.... The scale is definitely larger than Frostpunk 1, but that's not necessarily a good thing. In Frostpunk 1, you saw and dealt with individuals. Your decisions meant that this individual person might live or die. In this game, you're dealing with a city entire districts at a time. The people are nameless, faceless numbers on a screen. Like a darker atmosphere SimCity. Additionally, there's just so much information and new systems presented that the UI doesn't do a great job of presenting. There's an Index, which is helpful, but that's also really tedious. There has to be a better way of introducing new systems to the player without them having to resort to reading volumes over and over.Seems like it has potential and could be fun, but I just couldn't get into it.

_childDocuments_.review: It is okay I guess. This game takes much more broad and distant perspective compared to the Frostpunk 1. There are still humanizing elements and fates of people in the game but you definitely feel more like head of a council rather than captain of a ship. Story wise I think it makes sense. The city is trough the bottleneck and now it is time to expand. Still I do prefer the first games feel.The game play is much more complex but also more forgiving. I played on officer difficulty and most of the time I was not planning that much ahead and still got trough the game while swimming in resources most of the time. I did not even figure out how some of the mechanics work. But the game did throw some challenging  curveballs and can't say I was not enthralled most of the game.The game looks pretty but it also feels bit janky/stuttery at times. Hopefully some patches will fix that.

_childDocuments_.review: After playing on standard difficulty for about 15 hours and getting one of the endings I will say wow, despite never being able to get into 4X games in the past, this one felt very accessible and focused. I had a lot of fun. Lots to micromanage but it never felt like it was too much. The factions were different enough to provide some cool variety and I'm excited to see what other factions offer in different playthroughs. The game has some performance issues, particularly around the endgame, but I'm not sure if that's poor optimization or just the natural result of a game trying to manage tens of thousands of units doing their own little bits of math per second. I do also wish there was some QOL, like being able to queue up buildings or districts while another is in the process of being demolished. At one point in the game I had to replace half my old infrastructure for newer, more efficient infrastructure and it was a total nightmare. Other than those problems, definitely recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: In my opinion, fans of the first game (like myself) will enjoy this one. Let's break it down point by point (I played on the highest difficulty):  The game’s visuals are stunning. The event illustrations, the locations in the frozen wastelands, the research screens—all are amazing. The interface is a joy to use. I zoomed in a couple of times to check out individual districts and buildings, but my favorite view is zooming out one or two scrolls above the colony to admire the frozen landscape.The soundtrack retains its unique style, which is a relief. It adds just as much emotion as the visuals do while you're playing. There are 7 different maps in the utopia builder mode to suit any preference. And that's just at launch! Playing these is actually much harder than the story campaign. I do have a few minor issues, but I'm sure the devs will fix them soon: As for optimization, I can’t complain—I had no problems. My 4070ti handled ultra settings without a hitch. I definitely recommend the game. The devs delivered on all fronts!P.S. Some players claim that the new game kills off the mechanics and principles of the first one, but I think that’s nonsense. If you’re looking for a high-quality, natural progression of the series that keeps the best elements from its predecessor, Frostpunk 2 is a perfect example. But if you want the new game to just be a copy of the old one with a few tweaks, then go play Civilization.

_childDocuments_.review: As it turns out, scaling up Frostpunk makes it not Frostpunk....if you loved the unique story telling of Frostpunk 1, this game is not for you.if you loved the way Frostpunk 1 made you care about your citizens, this game is not for you.if you loved the way you got immersed into the world of New London, shouting "The City Must Survive!" as you and your citizens take on the storm...this game is not for you---who this game is for.People who love the constant stress of decision making and 'sliding to the finish line'Where Frostpunk 1 focused on the story of New London as it comes to represent the human condition, the sequel takes out the soul and just gives you a steady drip of BS for the whiniest NPCs I've ever seen in a city builder.I never felt like I could breathe and admire the city, or sigh and think to myself “I need to find a way to solve this problem”. I am constantly trying to find food/materials/housing - and the moment I had everything balanced, some brat shank'd someone causing my citizens to demand a new policy, after which I had to do some research as a quid pro quo for the policy (that they wanted!),  After that I had to rebalance my food/materials/housing again. Then the funeral for the guy the kid stabbed caused some controversy because some people think funerals are a waste of resources and want the body donated to science causing another demand for policy - and then quid pro quo research, repeat.Where Frostpunk 1 was a nice introspective of "how far will you go to ensure humanity survives", and "how will we overcome this situation". This game is "how well can you juggle and multitask while people yell at you: the game".I leave feeling "why am I even doing all this? just to say I beat the game?". All that said, I encourage everyone who dropped it at the Prologue to power through Ch1. The Prologue is not a good showcase of the gameplay, it gets a bit better - but in the end, it's still not why I liked Frostpunk. Without those, it's kind of just a mediocre city builder....It's not a bad game, I'm not mad, I enjoyed some parts, but I am disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: tldr; Good base of a game, wait for some patches to come out and fix the QoL issues. If there was a neutral rating I would give it. There is a good core of the game here, keeping much of the spirit of the first game.There is a good core of the game here, keeping much of the spirit of the first game.Pros 1 - Game looks great. Good atmosphere and art on the menus. Colors and well done to lean into the overall dystopia steam punk vibe. 2 - More of a natural society progression. You don't just get to choose what society you'll be with a simple choice. Your laws, the factions you favor and your choices in events grow your society. This leads to tech and law unlocks. Makes for a fun RP experience and something refreshing to see in a city builder.3 - Most of the core mechanics of the first game are intact, so resources and heat management especially are still very much the priority.  4 - Game still has a great soundtrack and atmosphere all around.Neutral 1 -  It's on a larger scale than the first game so you don't build individual buildings, you just build districts. Your ascetic control of your colony is basically non-existent. For me this is irksome, but this really comes down to a personal preference. I miss being able to craft my colony to look a certain way. But this is purely an ascetic issue and I can't knock the game for it. Cons 1 - This game should have an early access tag. It has several small bugs that can really just kill your run. You'll spend some amount of time online trying to figure out what happened until you realize it's a bug.                - Example - First scenario in new london, you establish a colony for oil. My progress just stopped even with ample frost teams. I paused all other outpots to get more frost teams, that did not restart progress. When I sent people to establish the colony, it reduce the number of works in all my buildings in new london. This caused me to have less frost teams. Even after increasing worker count, my colony would not progress in building. Had to reload. Seems like a minor bug, but annoying because if you don't catch it right away it can kill your run.2 - QoL is poor. Resource management is an integral part of this game. Everything is a slider when it comes to resources, being workers or raw materials. Some you can get precise numbers on because the slider also has small button allowing 1 quantity changes. Others do not have this option, because reasons. So you sometimes have exact control over how many workers are somewhere, or how many resources you send/receive. Other times you just get to throw a handful of workers at a new colony and hope it's close enough to the number you want. Also you can't scroll with arrow key, or middle mouse with the sliders either. Just click and hold. You also can't cancel buildings in progress, and if you lay a building down wrong have to just deal with it later. You also while planning to build, can only cancel in sequential order. Can't click on a tile to cancel just one and build somewhere else. Minor issue but again, just more lifting for the user for seemingly no reason. 3 - UI is bad, like all form over function bad. You can hotkey to most important things, which is fine. You can also hover over your resources and most of the numbers up top to see a better breakdown. But the idea to have the 5 categories hang below your top UI not really be intractable at all is baffling to me. The worse they get, the longer the tail they get, which can end up cluttering the top of your screen. You also get zero information about them. Some are derived stats, some are all ready covered in your resource needs. They feel redundant and don't serve much purpose beyond the look. You also cannot short cut most actions in a district. It has an empty building slot? Well can't click on the building slot to do anything. Have to exit looking at the district, go to your buildings build menu which is different from your district build menu, find the right sub category for the building you want, then select it. Seems like a minor gripe but like...you can't build any of the buildings outside of their specific district type besides heat ones. Why do they need their own menu, why can they not be done from the district menu? They're upgrades, not independent items. Game becomes more dependent on pause with small things like this. 4 - Game is gonna chug after you set up some colonies and managing more than one city. Needs some performance optimization.

_childDocuments_.review: 11 Bit Studios has taken a massive risk and it’s paid off. I can strongly recommend Frostpunk 2. For those on the fence, the developers have increased the scope and responsibility massively. This makes perfect sense given how the story of the first game ended. The Frost has been overcome. You survived. Now it’s time to chart a course forward for humanity beyond just survival. In practical terms, this means that the game is no longer a colony simulator but a strategy akin to Civilization. Gameplay: Probably the most controversial point for people. Given the big changes to promote the story, you are virtually playing a new game. Consequently some of the game loops have changed dramatically with you being in charge of multiple cities and settlements with thousands upon thousands of people. I don’t think this is bad in any way, shape, or form. If you want a strategy, you can play Frostpunk 2. If you want a colony simulator, you can play the first part. While the basic management in the sequel is simplified, other mechanics have expanded dramatically. Ideology and managing multiple factions has never been more fun. Ideas, the council, the tech tree - all work together to provide the vision you are aiming for. This schism of thoughts has branched out massively compared to the first game. You can promote merit or equality, tradition or progress, adaptation or technology, and more. Or a mixed approach. This is executed through actual buildings, laws, tech with massive variation. You can build the cities you want with significantly more depth, control, and choice. The population reacts and you will often feel the weight of your decisions through social commentary. No decision is universally good or bad just as the first game. The citizens will react with snippets. An example - I picked ''Merit'' to allow only useful outsiders into the city. A child was allowed to enter my city but her mother was not because she's lost her arm due to frost-bite. The child will never see her mother as a result of my choices something reflected in the commentary they provided. This definitely made me consider repealing my law into something more equal despite the obvious benefits. There is moral weight to decisions. The atmosphere: Visual art and music are top notch. If you liked the first game, you will love everything here. The graphics: Obvious improvement from the first game in every way. As the above, if you enjoyed the previous installment, you will like all the improvements. Time to play: It took me about 15 hours to complete the story mode which has 1 scenario currently with 5 chapters. I managed to achieve one of possible multiple endings or variations. The Utopia mode at the moment has 7 different scenarios which provide a lot of variety and replayability. There’s multiple factions in each scenario from what I can see unique to the other. Overall ability to replay and experiment is great. I can definitely see myself sinking another 100-150 hours with what I’ve currently got at least. Overall: Resource management and building is slightly simpler in terms of Micro. In terms of Macro, significant depth has been added towards exploration, ideology, tech, laws, faction management. You are playing a proper strategy, rather than a single colony simulator. This can be off-putting to some people but I think 11 Bit Studios have stayed faithful to the Frostpunk vision. Rather than deliver the same thing, they’ve continued the story in a natural way that makes sense. It’s an original and new game and I can’t wait to see the extra content that they come up with. Strong recommendation. 11 Bit Studios continue to experiment and push the boundary rather than playing it safe. In 2024, that’s rare.

_childDocuments_.review: Frostpunk 2 takes the chilling survival mechanics of its predecessor and elevates them to a grander scale, immersing players in its unforgiving frozen wasteland. Cities are at a larger scale, and you will have to plan districts, buildings, and hubs to achieve an ever fleeting balance of production, heat, food, housing and more.The addition of communities and factions introduces intriguing moral dilemmas, forcing players to balance survival with ethical choices that impact population dynamics. The visuals are stunning, capturing the bleak beauty of the ice-covered landscape and the desperation of human endurance. Managing colonies and balancing goods between them adds an interesting strategic layer to the game. While the gameplay retains the punishing difficulty of its predecessor, the expanded mechanics and depth provide a refreshing and rewarding challenge. I highly recommend trying it out!

_childDocuments_.review: This game lacks soul. Or something in-between.Frostpunk made us relate to, and care about our citizens. Every single one mattered. Every single cold wave made us fight for the survival of all of our fellow citizens. Deciding if we should lower heating in the hospital, or maybe in the food farm. Decisions, hard decisions.Frostpunk 2 is more like... excel balancing simulator. I do understand that time has passed and the city building is a bit on the bigger scale, but having tens of thousands people? I'm completely detached from them. They are just a number in a sheet. Hell, I can't even see them - the game just adds some Tron-like light-lazers traveling around the city. Also, what the hell is going on with the roads connections (the automatically generated ones)?I wish it was more like Frostpunk 1, just with maybe hundreds-to-thousands instead of tens of thousands of people? The politics aren't too bad, but they are a bit annoying and with the detachement from our citizens... Meh.Also, heatstamps. That's a hard pass. "We are staaarving! We have the resources to build food producing buildings, but we rather die than build it without getting those sweet, sweet heatstamps!" -_-...Performance also seems to be an issue.I have radeon 7900 XTX (24GB vram), Ryzen 7900, 64 GB RAM and 12000mb/s SSD.I'd expect this game to have a bit more than just 25-30 FPS on 4k resolution having everything on ultra. 90% of display is literally snow, doesn't seem to be super complicated to compute. There's no ray-tracing. Turning on FSR to Quality mode and turning on frame generation makes it better, 80-100 FPS, but dear lord, those options should be an addition for lower end computers, not a must-have on a non-raytracing game.

_childDocuments_.review: Let's get one thing of the way real quick: Is this a bad game? Not at all, there's a very good amount of work and passion put into it. Now, is this a good sequel to Frostpunk? Well, you can see the negative on top of the review, so let me break this down:First of all, the game has been streamlined substantially (And that goes past the logical consequences of having a game with a larger scale, mind you).Automatons and their unique playstyle? Now they are just additional workforce, if you happen to find them.Day-night cycle, with the corresponding differences in gameplay? GoneGranular system of healing, sickness and amputees? GoneManaging heat zones and individual temperatures? All has been combined under just "Heat". If you have positive heat, you're good, and if you don't, turning off individual districts is even more busywork than turning heaters off was in FP1.The city building portion is kind of a missed opportunity. They play around with the idea of tiles interacting with each other, but it doesn't go past "Huddle districts together for heat" and "Houses next to industries increase Squalor". There are some "valuable" tiles (Like crevasses that provide a Shelter and Heat bonus), but overall this system, while cool, is way underutilized. The buildings are interesting, but rather than developing unique buildings for different alignments like there was in FP1, the buildings are basically either “Regular building” or “Regular building+X bonus/penalizer”, which makes them feel pretty samey. Sure, there are alignment-specific buildings, but they are the exception rather than the rule.For all the comments about how much grander the scale of this game is compared to the first one, this game can be seriously micro-intensive. For the FP1 veterans who are reading this: Remember The Refugees, and how one of the challenges was having to deal with a constantly increasing population for the first half of the game? The whole game is like this. The population keeps expanding at a fairly ridiculous pace, both from births and from “people migrating to the city” (Fairly surprising, considering that we were supposedly the last city on Earth, but there we go). Losing due to a population boom is a very real risk, and you have to be constantly building new housing districts and infrastructure to support your ever-increasing population. It gets to the point that one of the most coveted late game abilities is one that can decrease your population growth.The first (and so far, only) scenario gives me mixed feelings. On one hand, it’s really nice to revisit the Frostlands and see all references to the previous game, but on the other, the scenario looks more like a beefed-up tutorial than an actual campaign, and the finale absolutely pales in comparison to the one in A New Home. Besides, the game absolutely railroads you into the events of the finale, and they can come off as really contrived depending on your actions throughout the game.Also, for all the big talk about the transition to oil, it is basically coal by another name. It doesn’t require any special infrastructure to store or process compared to coal, and other than focusing exclusively on oil for fuel (Which is optional), not much changes when you discover it.However, there are some actual improvements here too. Some laws can synergize with other laws or buildings to improve their function, and you can amend some laws to make them less extreme after passing them. The announcer, as well as the vignettes you get in response to certain laws and events are nicely written and help you connect a bit with the regular lives of your citizens. Also, while the game pretty much forces you to play with more than one settlement (At least in the campaign), having to babysit more than one instance is fairly nicely done and it did not make me want to punch my monitor like other similar games did, so kudos for that.As it stands, besides the bugs and poor performance (Which will probably get patched soon), the game is pretty deficient in content at the moment. Sure, FP1 did not have Endless at launch and only had 3 scenarios, but there is only so much you can do in Utopia before it starts to get stale (And this game is 50% more expensive than FP1, mind you).Unless they pull all the stops with their DLCs (Or bank on the modding community to pick up the slack for them), as it stands, I am not sure if this can be a decent follow up to Frostpunk 1. Keep your expectations seriously in check.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is a good follow up to FP1 and I applaud the devs for making something entirely new on an existing IP, and for frostpunk fans I think it's a decent follow up, before I played FP2 I got the DLC for FP1 and played some of that, which got me even more excited but all I could think about for a bit playing FP2 was "I should play FP1" and after finishing the campaign I wasn't engaged anymore and the game has sat untouched for a few days now.I think most of this comes down the the game being mostly a spreadsheet simulator, it's too much zoomed out now. Instead of a housing district having x number of living spaces it has x of "shelter", shelter being a requirement to keep cold down for people, more people more shelter you need. Districts themselves are also really simplistic, there's some modifiers in certain areas, districts next to another contribute heat to each other and some areas provide extra shelter / heat to a district placed in them. However if you want to build a district on the edge of your city nothing is stopping you, roads are just cosmetic and they get placed automatically. I think this especially shows with automatons, they can still be found in frostland and dismantled, but sending them back just gives you bonus manpower.Another part is the UI, it's really nicely themed and really brings the point across what society is now but it's readability suffers as a result, not a massive problem when you know how the game works but really confusing when you're just starting out.There's a lot that comes to mind but a lot of it comes back to that the game is just too oversimplified, while there are a lot of visual effects that try to tell a story the gameplay just doesn't back it up

_childDocuments_.review: In fact, I have some ideas about new game.As it turned out, my expectations differed from the developers' plans. I don't know how much the changes spoil the new game, it's up to you to decide.The new game was created with an emphasis on politics, not building. Now there is no possibility to build a single building, as it was in the first game. In the new game, building is possible in entire districts or settlements. That’s I don’t like. Of course, it greatly expands the city, but in my opinion, manual building of single houses with a separate possibility of building districts would be more interesting.The interface has changed a lot, it has become less clear and convenient. The first half hour of the game I had to figure out the interface. The light background is somehow not very suitable for this game.Unlike the first game, the new game does not have such ultimate tasks as in the first one. For example, such as: "the end justifies the means" or "sacrifice everything for the sake of survival and the building of reactors." Now, instead of building a reactor as quickly as possible, you have to spend more time searching for resources and politics.I don't know if it worth making a new game with such differences. Personally, I expected a continuation of the first game, with approximately the same mechanics, but on a larger scale, variability and content.If the scale was possible to make in the new game, then the rest is questionable. Was it worth sacrificing the ability to manually build one-offs for the sake of scale? And the content  in the form of individual buildings, such as medical centers, taverns, etc., will not increase using district construction methods. Thanks to the advent of politics with variability, everything is now fine, but the realistic ultimatum from the first part is gone.The graphics in the game look good, but I did not notice any serious improvements compared to the first game.It is upset that the zoom only works on significant buildings that are built after research. That is, the developers did not work out the details of most of the buildings that occupy a vast area of ​​the map, so you won't be able to see them up close. By the way, the optimization at the start of the game can be called "normal" compared to many other new products in recent years :)Overall, I think it turned out to be a good continuation of the series with new features and a larger scale. Someone will definitely like the new product, someone, like me, will not like it because of the innovations listed. The quality of the game does not get worse from this, and the desire for something new creates new impressions and encourages interest. Therefore, I give it a positive rating.

_childDocuments_.review: The decisions made for improvements from Frostpunk 1 to Frostpunk 2 are a downgrade what made the first unique. Bigger does not always mean beter and this is the case in Frostpunk situation, where it was a turn off for the majority of Frostpunk fans including myself. In Frostpunk 1 the deaths of people had meaningfull impact for the story and your gameplay, as in Frostpunk 2 its just like "yeah we will just allow some randoms in our City to compensate for the loses". What was cool at start were the different buffs and nerfs you can combine and role the dice if it will apply through the voting system. However it becomes boring fast and I mean really fast as it just RNG system similar as with slotmachines but you can influence or manipulate the votes in your favor. You are so busy learning and playing with these complex systems that you forget that you playing a survival sim instead of another sim city clone.I miss the tense situation I had with the last mission in Frostpunk1, where my small city was almost burning through the last  coals during a snowstorm with possible revolts could happen any time. My people still had hope and put all their trust in me as their leader. With tensions rising I made the decisions to become a dictator, where i made some unethical decisions, that resulted in unhappiness and revolts everywhere. On the brink of losing everything, and I had no options to turn the situation around anymore. The snowstorm ended and a notification came that we survived. I am still surprised that I finished the mission as I replayed the last mission many times and failed. Never knew the dictator route got me through this hard mission.If they ever make a Frostpunk 3, they should go back to smaller cities or towns, where the immersion and the impact of decisions is more visable and meaningful. Now your materials are running out... You increased materials? _childDocuments_.review: Frostpunk 2 is the future of Frostpunk 1, meaning the base and the core is the same but it's bigger, larger and deeper. Before one scenario was one city, now on one scenario you can have multiple cities and outpost to manage on the same region. Before it was Religion or Security but people of this game have learned as they would do IRL. They have learnt new things, they learned from the errors of the past so higher technologies comes in, diplomacy is coming back, multiple factions are created in response of your actions and the environment. Now you have to manage a MUCH bigger amount of people, so you will rarely build one building and than the other, no, you will now instruct to others to build entire zones (residence, industry, extraction, logistic, etc). Game looks amazing, optimization needs to be better for sure, my PC is taking hard on this game and is overheating with all on ultra + 4K (RTX 3090, 32GO RAM DDR4, AMD Ryzen 3700X 8-Core). They had the same issue on the first one. Level design is awesome, much more verticality added, building adapting to a chasm and mountains really well. To finish, i completely recommend it, it's not the first one but it is also the same core, which many fails to do (Call of Duty, Battlefield, FIFA, i dont play those games but all of these are clones, next to zero evolution each games). It's a logic evolution of the first, logic evolution of Frostpunk 1 is what resume this game the best. IT MAKES SENSE. And i'm happy that i can still come back on the first one for a more micromanagement, buildings by buildings on a smaller scale, i love it. This one being more macro don't mean you have less things to do, no, cause more things are added and it feels more hard and punitive than the first one. Frostpunk is a hard licence with a steep learning curve, it's a real survival game on a base of  a city builder. I recommend this game as the first one so much. They revolutionized the city building genre at the time that most of the city builders that came after took one or more ideas from Frostpunk if not even completely clone it in another universe. Frostpunk is a reference. The number 2 is too.---------------------------------------------- 17/20 : Evolution of the first one, bigger, larger, deeper, much more macro than micro. I like the 1st one for what it is and i like playing the 2 for a new experience, in the end, nice gameplay, balanced, unique, punitive, and as much more option into success than others like to pretend, no there is not just one way to succeed, in the 1st scenarios that shows you step by step the game and that is more scripted yes, but not later on and clearly not in sandbox mode. Great ideas, love it.  17/20 : It's clearly a 2024 game, it's on of the best looking city builder for sure. 18/20 : I mean it's speak for itself, it evolves on the base of the first one that was a slap in the face at the time, it keeps this unique identity, steampunk, blizzard, post-apo.  10/20 : This is where the game needs a tone of work, like the first one i would say, maybe worst. On sandbox, on a 5 hour save (main town space fully completed + 2 more outpost) , its barely playable (PC Specs : RTX 3090, AMD Ryzen 7 3700x, 32 GO RAM DDR4). I'm sure it will get a lot better soon but for the moment, honesty being the guide for my reviews, it's kind of bad.  14/20 : Really nice OST but less effective than the first one in my opinion, less remindable but still great quality and it pushes the tension in moments of blizzards higher. 16/20 : Really nice work, clear, unique, works well. But too much popups in my opinion for useless things like "your town as gone for equality" and 2 minutes after "town as gone for adaptation", useless.  15/20PS : 15/20 is really a great note, don't take as reference the press critics on Ubisoft games. The worst note i gave was 5/20, so 15 is excellent to me.

_childDocuments_.review: With less than two hours in, I am sorely disappointed with the crashing in this game. I want to call for a meeting to do it immediately.I press the button, the game crashes. I restart it a while later, play for a bit, and press the same button. The game crashes again.I am impressed by the presentation so far but I cannot honestly recommend a game that crashes in the first map, on a button press. I will keep playing it if I can see past the crashing but I hope I don't regret refunding it while I had the chance.EDIT:After beating the story and enduring fps drops and game hangs, I have to say the crashes stopped but were replaced by 30-second long pauses where nothing happens (this is not the game autosaving), which made me stop and try to save and reload the game. Positives:The themes explored all the way until the end are perfect; I chose the authoritarian route and stepped over all the politics by the end, the useful idiots (hopeful technofascists themselves) did not see me coming! The music, the frost hiding everything slowly and then suddenly, the sad stories, everything fits together so well and the plot lines in the story mode wrap up nicely. My ending even came with a personal threat from people I oppressed (for good reasons, of course).It's a shame the game is not stable, as this would be an easy recommendation. _childDocuments_.review: Such a shame i was really looking forward to this game having clocked 100's of hours on the original but it seems the developers have lost sight of what made the 1st game so addictive.My issues with the game are as follows.* No longer a city builder - The starting generator now looks like a city in and of itself with the individual buildings of the first game now replaced with "districts". All the districts looks largely the same but for a small colour difference.* Graphics - In the original i loved being able to zoom in at any point in your city and see individual people going about their work. _childDocuments_.review: I just finished my first playthrough with the Reconciliation ending. Once again, I got chills from the final scene, which quoted the iconic line you hear when launching Frostpunk 1: “The trail of peace is narrow, but it stretches as long as we roam the steel-cold world.”The two games tackle fundamentally different concepts. In the first game, you play as the Captain, who knows every citizen by face, earning their unconditional trust. The sequel, however, shifts the focus to macroeconomics and politics, where the Steward views people as mere numbers on a spreadsheet, so insignificant that they aren't tracked in real time.The mini-events have also evolved, moving beyond questions of morality to explore political radicalization. The narrative highlights how people lose compassion even for their own families, placing political allegiance above personal bonds.Finally, the game would not be the same without Piotr Musiał's soundtrack—a true masterpiece that elevates the entire experience.

_childDocuments_.review: I have to disagree with many of the negative reviews. For me, moving away from managing individual people to focusing on a larger scale feels like a positive change. The district placement puzzle may be a familiar mechanic, but it still works well, and I have no complaints there. In the previous game, I didn’t enjoy placing everything around the generator because of the autoscale feature, which felt clunky. The unpredictable heat zones from the extra towers were also not fun to manage. That said, the shift to the new model overall feels like a good direction for me. I definitely don’t miss the hassle of micromanaging individual sick workers based on their location.That being said, just like the original game, the developers still haven’t provided the necessary tools to plan effectively. In a game all about planning, where are the tools? There are none. You’d probably have to print out a map and plan everything on paper.There’s no way to keep hexes visible, no way to view the map without height interference, no way to force district borders to show, no way to pre-place or mark something. How are you supposed to PLAN your city? In a game where the core gameplay loop revolves around city planning, this lack of tools is a serious issue. It turns into an exercise in frustration.Maybe the developers expect you to plan hundreds of tiles in your head, or offline, or think it’s fun to play suboptimally because "planning is tough" - but none of that is enjoyable. I need the ability to mark the map, plan districts, and predict how things will turn out. The challenge should come from meaningful choices, not from a cumbersome UI. A bad interface is not a fun challenge. The first game could get away with a suboptimal UI because it was innovative. This game, however, has an even worse UI, yet relies more heavily on it for its core puzzle, and that’s just unacceptable.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: The story, the artwork, the thought put into decisions... 10/10Unfortunately, this is not a city builder. You just plop a single district over a resource, and the gameplay is mostly switching around the map clicking more or less workforceI wanted Anno Frostpunk, I got Democracy 3 Frostpunk.Perhaps this will change with some ambitious modding, but I got 3 nights of fun out of it and there is no replayability, All it did was make me want to go play Frostpunk 1 again.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Frostpunk 2 is in a quite tough spot, some will say that it is like the first one, which may be a positive or a negative depending on what they expected, some would say that it isn't like the first one, and again this may be a positive or a negative....Frostpunk 1 offer a very tight and simple story from the first minutes of the introduction: You have to survive and do whatever it takes to have that generator running. From that all the aspect of the game is derived, the story, the intensity feels tighter and more dense. In Frostpunk 2 while the generator importance is still here, the narrative and the intensity are more diluted and less centered around the generator and its need for survival. Quite the opposite, the take here is that it is not about survival, it is about to live again, what kind of life is there for the ones who survived....and so the frostpunk 1 appeal and fantasy is no longer part of this game.Yet the game build on its predecessor, and it isn't nor a frostpunk 1.5 nor another city builder with the frostpunk name on it. You have to accept that frostpunk 2 aim towards something else than the first one. To really judge if the game does a great job at that, I should done mutlitples playthroughs to see how the game respond to different situations...though I may not done that now, But as a early recommendation after finishing the game, I think the game is worth playing.The drawback is certainly the UI, and how informations is presented to the player, I miss the graphs from the first one. It is in the same time very messy (specially the production of heat) yet sometimes it is very well done...considering how much there is to manadge. And there are some very annoying part, like when I don't understand why I couldn't use automatons to safely break ice, or how the game is not clear about how to do some basic stuff. Another anoying thing is the the move from one chapter to another...once the criteria is met, you go automatically onto the next chapter which will interrupt some moves/plan you were doing at the same time, meaning, if you were doing good, and able to take advantage of some situation, then it will kill that when the next chapter appears.The music still is expertly craft and very feeting in every moment of the game, nor to quiet, nor to loud, it enhance the mood and the experience overall.The council system is interesting to say the least.Overall I very much liked my time with the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: I only have a few hours so take my review for what it's worth, but this, to me, feels undeniably like Frostpunk. The choices, the balance, the line walked between safety and barbarism, are all Frostpunk at their core. I don't understand the people comparing this to Civ(???). It's bigger, it's less intimate, but it feels bang on for what I would expect "Frostpunk but 30 years later" to feel like. I recommend it for Frostpunk 1 players who weren't just expecting more of the same, and consider it a worthwhile successor.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: I like how the game has changed.  This game doesn't feel as polished as FP1, but maybe that's viewing FP1 through the lense of it getting years of support first.  People say its lifeless and lacks the tension of decision.  Nah, that's still there.  If you aren't feeling feels when 200-500 citizens are dying because of toxic gas.  Then you got issues.  But it doesn't surprise me with the culture of gamers...per-say...being focus'd on Trump era individualism over the collective as a whole.  Its slower paced.  Seems easier, though I've only played on Normal.  But the feeling of FP is still there.  And that's what's important I think.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: I have finally finished playing the game on the hardest playthrough for my first run. idk why i did this, but i have to say frostpunk 2 is so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ interesting and fun to play, i probably wouldve had so much more fun on easier difficulties but it just helped cement how hopeless it can be sometimes and how you can easily make the wrong choice and piss just enough people off to kick you out.This game builds on the Relations system of frostpunk 1 for the most part and it has a lot of building and planning but its not the same as the first game. Frankly if your fine with something new and instead of the same thing as before youd love it, Although i just could not get over how you have a political system it was the coolest thing for me (although i still went authoritarian as hell to secure my place)but i do have to say Its a Great Game.Love what these devs did and they absolutely made me love the series more
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: the FP 1 essence is still there, there is just less emphasis in how you build the city as the generator is not the main focus. definitely a bit frustrating to learn if you jump in with all the know how of FP1, I actually liked that you have to re-learn many things as it makes it feel more of a sequel and less "more of the same".I didnt enjoy my first few hours as it was quite hard to know what was going on at all times. I replayed parts that I felt I was doing okay looking to improve them even further and it took me 25hrs to break my first complete playthrough.MY ONLY BIG COMPLAIN IS THE UX, there are times that you try to click a district, a building or a settlement and it wont register the click, you have to be at an ideal zoom level for it to access what you intend to click, this made it quite frustrating when wanting to do things quick. I cant wait for the other scenarios.I also wish that once you pass a law the ramifications of such law spiral even further, then having other factions suggest the opposite of such law and be able to go back and forth makes them a bit nonsense imo.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR; This is a very different game than Frostpunk. IMO none of what made Frostpunk great made it into the sequel.Frostpunk 2 seems like a misnomer. The game has very little in common with the original. City construction is overly simplistic: clear land, build on a hex, wait for resources to dry up. Outposts and frostland gathering are even more basic, making it feel like a grind to search for and import resources. There are constant distractions from events that slow down what already feels like a slog waiting for construction to finish, waiting on resources for the next project, waiting for a search party to find something, waiting for votes to be counted... The factions don't seem to have any meaningful game play, only adding to the feeling of the grind. Top it all off with a naked old man in a wheelchair freezing to death and citizens whispering "Steward" in the creepiest way possible every time you interact with them and you have a bizarre game that isn't sure what it wants to be, least of all an actual follow-up to Frostpunk.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: This game is definitely different from the first Frostpunk, but it is ENTIRELY worth it. I'll admit, I haven't played the original in awhile at this point- but I remember it because it was a game that surprisingly drew me in. Not the traditional type I typically like to play, but it really sucked me in.For me, Frostpunk felt like establishing the game- but Frostpunk 2 takes -off- with the game. There are so many components, so many interests, so many things to juggle. The story is fantastic as well, and what really engages the player is just how far the ripples of your decisions go. Some actions will have very far-reaching consequences which makes the game all that more exciting.In closing, I really think Frostpunk 2 is worth it. This game brings to the table various mechanics that really make you feel like you're fighting to establish humanity's last foothold in this frozen climate.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Looks like good economy survival. Yet it is only in world of frostpunk, there is no such binding with your survivalists, no responsibility feeling, building zones is strange and boring, animations of citizens or machines arent really representing what's they actually do.So if you want economy survival game in frostpunk world - not bad choice. If you want Frostpunk 2 it is not the game. It is not what you had from Frostpunk game, its different, a lot.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: The good: You can tell how much the devs care about the game which is something that's missing from a lot of the gaming industry right now. The art and music are awesome.The bad: A big part of the enjoyment for me from the first game was the immersion. For example, you could watch individual citizens and their struggles which flushed out the world and made it more intimate. Despite the focus on city politics, FP2 is more about the buildings than the people. The city building looks bigger but is actually oversimplified. Buildings are now just a part of click-to-build districts. You have to press a button to zoom in and observe the people in them and once you do you see repeat animations quickly.Glad some people are enjoying the game but I can't recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Goty strategy and still one of the best.Whining about how it not alike FP1 is so stupid cuz that's a different game man.Lack of atmosphere during to bigger scale? _childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Never had I played a game where I got chills watching consequences, good and bad happened while New London's orchestra plays out epicly at the background. This is all complemented by beautiful visuals, human stories and hauntingly top tier music. TLDR: You'll love it
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful sequel to the first one. Keeps the intensity of the first game, but makes it feel new and different. It takes a little bit to get used to the differences between the games, but is a ton of fun once you figure it out. The increased number of factions adds a layer of intensity to the game as well. _childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: I like that the devs improved upon the first games law mechanics by showing outcomes of each of the different factions. _childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Yes, it's quite different than the first. Less tedious building overall. _childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: If you're looking for a game that plays like Frostpunk 1, with more too do and new challenges and environments, Frostpunk 2 is not that game. I think a lot of people, like myself, were expecting a game with the same feel and gameplay as Frostpunk 1. Frostpunk 2 pulls the camera way back and scales up the city management is a way that makes your choices feel less important. Sometimes bigger isnt always better. Frostpunk 2 is a good city management simulator that loses all the charm of the first game. If you're looking for an experience close to Frostpunk 1, this is not that game.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Like many Frostpunk 1 players, I did not enjoy this game at first. I would go as far as to say that I resented or even hated it, because this sequel took away many features from the original that I enjoyed (e.g. actual city planning/building, not this district thing) and it was difficult to understand what I was doing at first.However, after a certain amount of time spent trying and failing, everything will eventually click for you (it took me about 5 hours before I really understood what I'm supposed to do). After that it was pretty much smooth sailing, and I did end up enjoying the story mode overall, even if endgame feels a bit underwhelming. The dev team's commitment to expanding the "lore" of Frostpunk with this sequel's story mode is definitely one of the game's strongest positives in my opinion, and the various decisions or paths you could go down were equally compelling. The Parliament feature and vote-based technology is also a fresh addition to this type of game.My advice is to not give up on the game too soon; maybe it still won't be your cup of tea in the end, but you should at least come to understand the mechanics/strategy before determining whether you like it or not. For me, I'm invested, and I am excited to try out endless mode as well as whatever DLC content comes out in the future.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: I wish there was a "Mostly recommend" button. This game is very different from the first, but in a way that makes sense for the Frostpunk universe.  It is engaging and fun for those of us that enjoyed Frostpunk and Civilization type games. However, if you don't like macro management type games, then I'd recommend you just go replay the original Frostpunk. The difficulty curve needs work though. Chapter 1 is the most challenging and it just gets easier and easier from there.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely loved the first game, and this game does not disappoint as a sequel. The same nail biting, on a knifes edge, survival at all costs vibe is still here, wrapped up in the same beautiful diesel punk, post-apocalypse paint job. This go around, the city is much, much bigger, and you are not controlling each individual building. Instead, you are managing districts. While some of the natural, ever growing organism-ness of the cities in the first game is gone, I would say it feels like a natural evolution of the franchise. The biggest new thing is the addition of factions in your city. There are a lot, all with competing world views. They are what is going to produce the most amount of headache for you, learning to manage them is probably the hardest part of making sure your city doesnt fall. The way the factions develop and become more and more extreme, in different ways, is extremely interesting. It is truly impressive all the ways the game lets you deal with them. Lock them up, exile them, build them a new city to live in or purge them in a violent civil war. The choice is yours and it is going to matter. Frostpunk 2 is a worthy successor to the first game, and this franchise is beyond a doubt one of the best city builders out there. 8.5/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Personally, I don't like it. It's too far off from the original in terms of personal connections, and everything feels too automated with these "Districts." I feel they’re a bit too restrictive, and the voting system is a bit lacking. The appeal of the first game, for me at least, was the way you could personally build up your city from the ground up. You felt more connected with individual citizens, so when one of them died, you’d go, "Oh, f*ck!" But here, if "300 people froze to death," I just go, "k."So, if you're a fan of the original and were looking for a good sequel, this isn't it. In a vacuum, the game is good enough to stand on its own merits, but as a sequel to the original? Nope, I can't say that.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: More of the same, but in a very different package. what I loved about the first frostpunk was the feeling that no decision i made felt like a truly correct decision. more like trading one unfortunate event from another maybe less terrible but still horrible event. I loved the anxiety i had with each building i put down, trying to balances what limited resources i had. Frostpunk 2 is a very different game from a mechanics standpoint, do not expect the same game. But i was very glad to see that when i loaded up this game it was giving that exact same feeling again from very different problems. I know some people are not going to like how different the gameplay itself is, but in my opinion it does exactly what a sequel should do. it keeps the core messaging and reasons to love it, while growing, adapting, and experimenting with new levels not attainable in its previous title. i am more than happy this is not just a copy of the first game. it feels evolved while still hitting the core of what it was in the first place.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, a good game, about 7.0/10. The climate doesn't feel as impactful, as the first one, maybe intended but it makes the game not immersive.Summary: A good survival city building game, not a good Frostpunk game.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Frostpunk 2 is an incredible followup to the first game. The gameplay mechanics, graphics, story, and overall sense of scale are just a couple factors that make it not just a fantastic game; but a fantastic sequel.Now it does have its fair share of bugs and glitches to be sure, just as Frostpunk 1 did on release. There are also some issues with graphical fidelity and performance but the devs are already working on it.My biggest gripe at this moment in time is actually in Utopia mode: There is a little button to abandon your colony adjacent to the button you use all the time to transfer resources. This wouldn't be an issue if pressing the "abandon" button prompted a "yes" or "no" button but as of right now: The colony just instantly removes itself. Other than that I haven't run into any serious moments of ick.Anyways, if you enjoyed the original Frostpunk or are just looking for something in the hardcore colony builder genre Frostpunk 2 is an excellent choice. All that being said: This game is NOT Frostpunk 1. If you're looking for *exactly* the same gameplay loop: This isn't that. The devs were pretty clear about how different Frostpunk 2 was going to be.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: The game is solid, its currently at time of review got a instability issue, I've had the game crash more often than I've closed it.Secondly the UI could have important things jump out at you better, too often will you miss that you can pass a law or start a research becasue all you get is a tiny little diamond that pops up, if your focused on something else you can easily overlook even the banner that pops up to inform you a research is complete, I think going the way FP1 went with a large satisfying CRUNCHY ice sound when law o clock as arrived. Demand my attention becasue so many other things in the game already do i know my researchers deserve more attention than the Lords do.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Just completed the campaign and overall enjoyed the game. I think it's slightly overpriced based on the length of the campaign, but that didn't take away from the experience. Definitely worth picking up if it ever goes on sale.Pros:- Even on easy mode, there are still tough decisions to make and the game throws enough at you where you're always juggling resources, trying to keep conflicting promises to different factions, etc.- The general game systems are well designed. There's nothing that stood out as frustrating, cumbersome, or difficult for the sake of being difficult.  - The story does a good job teaching the core mechanics without holding your hand too much. - The UX for managing multiple settlements is excellent. It's easy to quickly bounce between your settlements to check on statuses and they made it easy to share resources.- The menus/UI are really well design. There's a tooltip for just about everything in every menu, so you're never at a shortage for information or bouncing back and forth between menus to try to make the right decisions.- Generally fun and engaging. Each "chapter' of the story introduces a new mechanic/challenge that complicates things in an interesting way.- The decisions you make throughout the game influence how much each faction supports you, which does impact the story and ending.Cons:- Campaign gave me a solid ~12ish hours of enjoyable game play. Those 12 hours were great, but I have to admit I expected a bit of a longer experience in the main mode for a $45 title. They do have some DLCs planned, but unless you bought the $75 deluxe edition, they will certainly be at an extra cost.- No option to continue working on your city at the end of the campaign. Reloading the save brings you back to your most recent save right before the ending. If you want to keep playing, you have to start a completely new settlement in the utopia mode, which does offer endless play and has some variations (maps, resources, factions) but from what I can tell after a couple hours is very similar to the campaign mode, just lacks the narrative.Overall worth the buy if you know you'll play the campaign a couple times OR the campaign and the utopia mode afterward, but if you're a one-and-done player who just plays the campaign and moves on to the next thing...could be a skip for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: For everyone who expected another version of Frostpunk 1, nope, this is a completely new game and I must say it is great. They have done a nice job, completely new "game design", you no longer follow individual people but a whole civilisation with different factions, groups and a much more complex world.Only downside - it took me rougly 12 hours to finish the whole campaign... and no I did not rush it, almost had everything developed (on Officer difficulty, the lowest difficulty is too easy).Looking forward for new content maybe a new campaign though.And the "endless mode" Utopia is also an option, will proceed with that now.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Frostpunk was probably the most tense survival game I have ever reviewed under time constraints. It was for a small website, and we had to hit embargo. I needed all the cold blood I could muster to make it through to the ending, even on the easiest difficulty. It was no different with my review of Frostpunk 2, which I started playing just four days ago. I completed the main storyline in about 18 hours, and I am now deep into the Utopia Builder mode while planning a harder run of the Story mode.I’m usually skeptical of sequels for strategy games; they tend to only vaguely improve on the game mechanics, or to make them virtually the same game with maybe better graphics and a few more bells and whistles. Frostpunk 2 feels instead like a complete remake of the game mechanics and an expansion of its worldbuilding, though not without some rough spots in terms of user experience and a cluttered UI scheme.The symmetrical circular design of Frostpunk has been retired for a sprawling, dynamic, free-form hex city-builder. This will be a welcome innovation to those who, like me, tend to get hung up on symmetrical buildings and schemes, even when it gets in the way of more effective gameplay. Frostpunk 2 embraces the disorderly, the sprawling and spreading of settlements, ideologies, and the clashes of factions.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: I started playing the game on a Saturday - 11 pm, and before i knew it its was 7 in the morning the next day. there are significant changes and additions to the game compared to FP1 and all of these changes work together to make the experience more complex and rich. the socio-political aspect and the consequences of passing a law or researching a technology has been vastly expanded upon. the scale of city building and the economic aspects in the game has shifted to a more macro level which to be honest at first i thought i wouldn't like it but as i played through the first few minutes, I instantly appreciated the scale and understood the reasoning behind it. Overall it is still a very rich and challenging game and the studio has done more than expected in setting itself apart as well as maintaining and expanding elements of the first game that made it a dark, thrilling and gritty experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Good game. It's different than the first one and some people didn't like it but that was kind of the point of changing, expanding on and adding mechanics rather than just reusing them. Now instead of micro it's more macro management. Only feedback maybe is that I feel like the last act could have been more on point, I get that you probably didn't want to do another "big blizzard" but I don't feel it landed with the same punch. Still worked just not at the max standard that you set.Can't wait for the DLC's which are always top tier.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is great! The themes from FP1 are all still there just expanded to a much larger scale.Gameplay is more like 4dx than the original but still leaves room for that intimate feeling.My only constructive criticism is that I wish population updated more frequently. It currently updates around once per year or so and is explained that it is from taking a census. This would make sense if you had a city with population over 250k but we still don't come close to those numbers. 15k-50k people would probably want a weekly update, at least I know I would. It would definitely make gampelay more fluid. There's always enough material to build but the pop comes in waves of 2k-3k, so I build a bunch and then wait for the next pop influx. Population issue aside, I'll be playing this game for the next couple years for sure. Buy it!

_childDocuments_.review: Frostpunk 2 is mixed for me. So I settled on positive with the assumption that the game would fix a lot of technical problems I'm going to complain about and that part of the problem is just me as a player.If you played Frostpunk 1(you don't have too to understand/play this game by the way) your skill is transferable. The scope here is much broader, you don't see individuals in the snow or machinery/automatons truck out to an area to clear it. The individualism banding together to survive the frost fades away into people having gotten a foothold and talking about politics and ways of life. People die but there are swaths in the Frostland to recruit making it numbers to refill over personal worry. Instead of four different types of workers(Worker, Engineer, Automaton, child) they are now one conglomerate workforce. The game wants to have 'gotcha' moments about peoples personal lives and health, much like the first game had 'did you cross the line' moments, but for players returning that can feel off. They'll probably notice that individual, close-knit intimacy with the cities survivors was gone. The game is run on bigger time scales, bigger cities, bigger and lofty ideas. It's a grand way to go for a sequel but I missed the intimacy of the first. Truly though, that's a me problem I just think others might have. It's good game with some:Technical problems. That would include bad UI placement. I'm trying to research something and click it but the game decides I actually clicked on the nearby but not overlapping map icon, bad. Or I interact with someone but the buttons available to do anything don't register unless I click on the far left side specifically. Researching grinds my gear a little, requiring Heatstamps(currency here) but not letting you see what you have without exiting and re-entering the screen. It also doesn't show what you're researching. You have to find it. For infinite resources you can place a Deep Drill onto a 'infinite' tile but it doesn't say that anywhere. Replacing a law doesn't tell you what effects are lost/changing, or if there's a law in place at all. The game stutters hard when autosaving and stutters some when going to the map via scroll out. Adaptation is laughably overpowered compared to anything else, the easy modes easy mode.The music is beautiful and the visuals, especially people and how it's stylized in pop ups, are gorgeous. The game oozes 'ends meet the means' in game form.Good game but if you're a Frostpunk 1 fan be ready for the changes. I personally would've been happier at $30. I 100% it, but I'm not sure if I'll be back beyond base game.Generic tricks and tips for the interested:-Build Housing Districts next to each other to lower heat requirement, and keep in mind Districts can be expanded so there's no need to go all out building like 5 housing Districts off the bat-Get prefabs. They are different from Material-Get a Logistics Center relatively early to explore the land around you-Research Hospitals and medical hubs. On hubs, leave a empty tile or a few when building another district to plan for it being filled by a hub-Heatstamps will define your early game-If you're playing Adaptation specifically. When you get to a city to, well, adapt to it, it'll have problems you need to solve by placing something on the tiles with skulls(not air fumes)

_childDocuments_.review: Let's get one thing straight before we begin: Frostpunk 2 is NOT Frostpunk 1. If you're buying it expecting the radial city builder the first one was, then you'll be disappointed.With that out of the way, let's talk about what Frostpunk 2 really is and its similarities with 1:11 bit studios decided to leave the city building part as secondary and go straight forward for the political game. You'll be taking a lot of hard decision about the city and how it should be managed. Some will be angry, some will die, favor will be lost and gained and the city will respond accordingly. In this aspect, Frostpunk 2 makes you feel like the city is truly alive. Your residents will comment on your actions, both positive and negatively. New groups looking for change will arise, and if not pleased will revolt and disrupt the city. Political mechanics takes a hold on every single part of the decision taking, and you'll have the play around it constantly.And the game is beautiful as ever. The thematic is still the same beautiful bright colors on the pure white snow, with highly detailed buildings for your districts. The narrative tools used to push the story forward fitted perfectly, adding more details to the game's lore.Now, let's talk about where Frostpunk 2 falls short:The interface can be very confusing at first. When you learn how to use your tools, it becomes pretty easy. But the problem is: when you are having your first experience, the tutorial pages don't give you enough mechanical information about how to use these tools to begin with, and you are let to discover it by yourself.Not only that, but there will be countless times you'll have to take blind decisions because the game won't allow you to minimize the decision screen. Let's say you want to make a promise about a rule for a certain group: the screen will show you which law they want, but won't tell you if it will substitute another passed law or what this new law will do.About performance, the game struggles to run even on more powerful computers. If you're expecting to play it on the best graphics settings, you better be ready to have a very powerful rig to support those beautiful graphics.Another problem is about the progression. The game is separated in chapters, which you progress based on some milestones you complete on each one. Your city carries on from one chapter to another, and if you just barely made it to the next one, maybe you just bricked your save and will have to start over or reload several weeks back. Frostpunk 1 had a lot of restarts, that's true. But the difference lies on the fact that you had different scenarios and, although you would need to replay these scenarios a number of times to finish it perfectly, they are short and restart wasn't much of a pain.If you're an experienced player, this won't bother you too much in lower difficulties, but if you're new to the series, you might find it frustrating. Overall, I've been enjoying my experience through the game. you can see that, although 11 bit studios fell short on some technical aspects, the game was made with love and it's a worth sequel to the Frostpunk universe.
