_childDocuments_.review: this is a true successor. i know a lot of people have been complaining about it, but in my opinion this is how you do a AAA sequal to a game.. not just copy pasting and upgrading graphics but creating something new while keeping true to the original game feel. they managed to do all that.the game is new, it has fresh mechanics, some that have never existed in a tycoon ever before, and they all feel nice together. all while keeping the Frostpunk vibe alive. However, as other people are saying, the UI sucks. After finishing the story mode, i was still in constant "fights" with it. From screens that do not have an obvious close button, to tabs that do not really act like tabs, to hidden buildings behind factions. Whoever designed it, focused too much on the visual design of the UI and too little on the actual UX part, and this breaks immersion sometimes. I hope they will fix it a bit, or at least someone from the modding community will (game is now open to mods, unlike FP1). All in all, for a FP1 fan that enjoyed the story and the universe, and wants a new game with the same feel, this game is worth the full price.

_childDocuments_.review: It's good - if you liked the original, you'll probably enjoy this! It's much bigger than the original (which loses a lot of detail, as all the critiques outline) but because you're managing multiple locations with 20,000-40,000 people, it's not feasible to design the city street-by-street, or manage your economy building-by-building. The original is better, but to be fair they did try and be ambitious, rather than just re-doing the same, and then with added bells/whistles. The original's intimacy is what made it, it's your people, your city, managing the generator during the final hours of the whiteout, with the epic music playing... by going up in scale, Frostpunk 2 (inevitably?) loses that intimacy (but does give you a substantially different product with that greater scale).The campaign is thorough, it took me ~14 hours playing slowly and methodically, and then there are ~7 maps to free roam.7.2/10

_childDocuments_.review: Let's start with I enjoy this game.  I have always been a big fan of city builders and the original Frostpunk drew me in HARD.  Played that game for hours running through the mechanics and for sure the game played like a traditional city builder.  DLCs building on the original game were also worth it.  I liked how Frostpunk 2 brought in some of the story line from the original series.  Certainly appreciate the fan service and adds the feel of integration from its predecessor.If you haven't played the original Frostpunk and enjoy city builders, it's worth a $20 price tag.With that said, this game is not in line with the original frost punk, it's something different.  I compare it to when I played Dinosaur Island.  Game was (and still is) epic and has lots of replay value.  Needless to say when Pandasaurus came out with Dinosaur World, I was pretty excited but it didn't have the same magic as the original.  It was a decent game to play, but it wasn't what one would call a true successor to Dinosaur Island.  I will agree with the folks posting here that the decisions you have to make feel less dire when you make them.  I always feel that I have a decent counter or a workaround to problems that arise.  Original Frostpunk felt like I was killing everyone or ruining the world when I made a series of bad calls.It's how I feel with Frostpunk 2.  I'm 80 hours in and enjoy the game, but it's not a true successor to Frostpunk.  There's plenty of reviews and videos to look at in order to get a feel for the game.  Do your research and go in with the expectation that this is a completely different game, along the same theme as Frostpunk.

_childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer: if what you are looking for is just a review of the game, look elsewhere. I want to share my story, and this is where it will happen.It all started with me watching Frostpunk playthroughs on youtube. And I don't mean playthrough as a series, multiple episodes and such - the ones that do well on YT. I watched, what were essentially, stream vods. Many hours, 6 to more than 9 depending on what was exactly happening. I fell in love with the game. It's design, lore, gameplay. But I wasn't able to play it. Then, a few years later I managed to score a discount on Epic (or was it free? Don't remember, sorry). I sat down and, even though I had school on the next day, played through the opening scenario in one sitting - still have the recording from that one.I never was a big fan of trying to 100% a game, playing endless modes or rouge-like titles. I love watching people play them, but I'm not really into playing them. The same stood for Frostpunk.I picked up the game again when the sequel was announced, got all the DLCs and played through the whole game. I'm not a very hardcore gamer so I played through the scenarios only, and on the normal difficulty. After that, I got the pre-order for this game and waited. Once it released I sat at it again, and didn't leave until I finished the story. Granted, it took me more than just 5 hours to finish it this time.And now the review part of this "review".I, personally, love the game.To me, it kept the spirit of a Survival-City builder while changing things up. It's not a direct sequel. By that I mean it's not like a direct continuation - think the Dark Souls series (these have tiny story/location/equipment changes, but the games are essentialy the same). This game is placed in the same universe, and it's similar enough that I would call it a spiritual-sequel. A similar example to what happend between FP1 and FP2 would be Darkest Dungeon - the games are set in the same universe, same background lore, but the gameplay and style is different (also, I know that many people say they like DD1 more than DD2 [same as here] but I actually like the 2nd one more).To me I like that, since the scope of the cities/colonies is different, 11 bit made the decision to make this a different game, rather than an overblown DLC to the first one.A lot of people are complaining/moaning/are upset that this game is so much different from FP1. What I have to say to them is: Instead of spreading hate and negative energy because you don't like the 2nd game. Just play the 1st one. And if you're bored of replaying the same maps on endless for the past 800h, maybe just look for something different?To conclude,I like both games, so far I have played more of the first one - simply because there's only one story/campaign/scenario mission in the 2nd one. I have played a Utopia Builder run, but, as mentioned before, endless isn't for me.Thank you for coming to my TedTalkBye(I turned comments on so I'd welcome any input any of you have c: )

_childDocuments_.review: "Oh, so Mother Nature needs a favor?! Well, maybe she should have thought of that when she was besetting us with droughts and floods and poison monkeys. Nature started the fight for survival, and now she wants to quit because she's losing. Well, I say hard cheese." - Mr BurnsFrostpunk was about the desperate fight for survival. In a world that turned to humanity and swung on them with a violent frosty fury. While the exact cause of the Frost still isn't known; a combination of volcanic eruptions, the possible dimming of the sun and the potential of the growing industrial age all, at least, had some hand in it. Knocked to the ground, humanity survived by sheer force of will. Ripping and tearing into the far north to drag what resources it could into craters, caves and pretty much anywhere that was out of the wind. Whether saving every life one could or sacrificing for the greater good... Humanity survived, YOU survived.Frostpunk 2 is NOT about survival, it's about thriving. It's about standing up from harsh winds and blinding snows of the Whiteout and saying "My turn!". It's about building a society that can one day reclaim the world that was taken from us. Do you adapt to the cold? Do you build a city on the merit of the individual? Does true equality fit your world view? Or maybe continuing the traditions of old? Humanity, as always, is divided; It's up to you to give them guidance and purpose. What ever world you build, it will be one step forward on the path towards taking it back.

_childDocuments_.review: The sequel is quite a different experience from the first one. Whereas the first game required you to build around the generator for efficient heating, this one does not. Instead, the city layout is based on the location of your resources and careful planning of your districts adjacency bonuses. Overall, I like the gameplay and I don't mind the attempt to innovate the core gameplay of the first game, but the game is lacking a couple of things: some QOL changes for city management, the main story feels very short and some problems in the city become too easy to solve, mainly by having way too much fuel and the ability to stockpile it makes the heating problem trivial by the midpoint of the story. More importantly, the story is missing a key ingredient; the first game from the start sets a very harsh tone; it throws a lot of curveballs at you and just when you thought you had one problem under control, you'd get another (or multiple) pressing emergency on your hand which made a lot of impact on the overall tone of bleakness and hopelessness of the game. That tone made your success all the more satisfying which I think the sequel lacks. Still a decent sequel.

_childDocuments_.review: Frostpunk 2 is a tough and unforgiving experience, but its greatest strength lies in forcing you to explore the frostland. The key to survival doesn’t just rest on managing your city—it’s about venturing out into the frozen wilderness. Critical discoveries, resources, and even potential allies are all waiting to be found, making exploration an absolute necessity.While the game involves balancing politics and deciding which research paths to pursue, the real breakthroughs happen outside the city. On Citizen (easy) difficulty, the game is more forgiving, allowing you to focus on building up your city, but the importance of exploration never fades. Every venture into the frostland carries risk, but it's where the major turning points happen, shaping your city's future.The pressure to choose what to research and when to act is constant, but the frostland’s secrets often hold the key to your survival or downfall. Frostpunk 2 makes sure you never forget that there’s always something out there waiting to be discovered.

_childDocuments_.review: A large shift in scale from the previous game. Sadly to say, I don't like it. It is, however, a very interesting twist. It just doesn't have the same heart to it that FP1 had. It is much more focused on the macro-scale economy and to me starts to feel a little soulless. Deaths in the first game *mattered* due to how few people you had to work with. Now its just like "Oh 1000 people died? just bury them in the snow, I don't care".The UI is also honestly terrible. White on White background? C'mon guys. Did anyone even LOOK at this UI before release?Also, the difficulty is vastly unforgiving, even when compared to the first game, which is my main problem currently. Very little room for error (even on "normal") and it requires very meticulous planning of more complex mechanics and more of those mechanics. Expect to sink many, many hours into the game playing and re-playing and re-playing and re-playing the same scenarios over and over again. This last part might be a bit unfair, but I felt like FP1 had more variation in scenarios, and it has kept me going back to it time and time again. FP2 is just one longer "grand campaign", which just starts to bore the hell out of me after awhile.I think this is an avoid until there is more content, especially considering it is more expensive than the first game.

_childDocuments_.review: BLUF: If you like FP1's world, and don't mind a broader scope at the cost of micromanagement-focused gameplay, this is a solid title.As a big fan of the first game, I enjoy the return to the frozen wastes.  This game is absolutely not "More of the first game", but is instead a cousin of the first game.  While it takes place in the same setting, it focuses more on macro-management of your society to include multiple outposts and exploration/exploitation of the wastes as opposed to micromanagement of a single city.  Some may find this "wide and shallow" as opposed to "narrow and deep" but I'm enjoying the change of scope -- If I want to micromanage, I'll fire FP1 up again.Looking to the fit and finish of the world, I'm enjoying the look of the game in general.  The graphics are compelling and fit nicely with the world narrative and lend an appropriate atmosphere.  The soundscape is similarly well crafted and helps add legitimacy to the atmosphere the game is portraying.  The aggregate of these accurately conveys a grim world where survival is a struggle.I find the story to be compelling, and the political management to be entertaining and interesting.  I enjoy that many of the decisions you'll have to make effectively amount to a "trolley problem" sort of situation where there is no perfect option that satisfies everyone; It's all shades of grey.  The game does well to point out both sides of the outcome of your decisions, and similarly to the first, doesn't shy away from some horrifying moral choices, such as sending the kids into the mines to increase efficiency.The UI/UX integrates nicely with the bleak narrative, for those who don't want to go snowblind with white UI elements there is a dark mode that is in beta within the options, however it does have a disclaimer regarding not all menus looking appropriate -- I have not dug into this and can't comment on how well it actually works or doesn't.  The only UX gripe I have is that clicking a district will move the camera to show the district's information card, which can be annoying when you're just trying to toggle/adjust something on that card and wish to do it quickly.Performance is adequate, although it could use some polish/optimization.  In my experience many Unreal Engine games generally optimize well in the post-launch world as successive patches are brought forward, I'm not terribly concerned about this aspect going forward.  I have encountered some small bugs with buildings and resource generation math not adding up correctly, but I feel these will be fixed in time.I feel satisfied with this purchase, for those who enjoy the world of Frost Punk and don't mind having a higher-level view of the society to manage, I'd say this game is a solid purchase.

_childDocuments_.review: Rating: ★★★★☆ (4/5)Ah, , the game that takes the phrase “chilling experience” a little too literally. If you’ve ever thought, "Hey, I love city builders, but I also want to question my morality while freezing to death constantly," then this is the game for you. It’s the post-apocalypse again, and instead of the usual zombies or radioactive wastelands, you’ve got something much worse: endless snow. You’re tasked with keeping your city alive, even though the only warmth you'll feel is the fleeting satisfaction of a tough decision made—before your citizens immediately hate you for it. Spoiler:  It’s a balancing act between keeping your city alive and keeping your humanity intact—or, more likely, sacrificing your humanity for just a bit more coal. Sure, you could invest in sustainable energy and have everyone sing kumbaya, or you could push your workers to the point where they literally start a rebellion. The moral dilemmas make the occasional blizzard feel like a day at the beach.New in : instead of simply watching your people freeze to death, now you can watch them  freeze to death while mining oil. Oil: because nothing screams survival like trading environmental collapse for temporary warmth! It’s like we never learned. It’s bleak, it’s cold, and it’s beautiful in the most depressing way possible. The art direction is so good you’ll start to shiver in real life, or maybe that’s just the guilt creeping in from sending children to work. Again. Sweeping, epic, and occasionally terrifying. The soundtrack will remind you that, yes, you are the villain here. Those haunting violins aren’t there to help; they’re just playing the background music of your moral downfall. If you’re looking for a game that will make you question your leadership skills, your ethics, and possibly your life choices, then  is perfect. Just don’t expect a happy ending. Or warmth. Or sleep.P.S.: If you think you’ll  keep your people happy this time, you’re wrong. They’ll still banish you in a snowstorm when things go south... or rather, further north.

_childDocuments_.review: The most unenjoyable "city builder" I have played in years, even considering its a 3 day early access. It is a travesty to even consider this is related to Frostpunk. It is a spin off. The only similarity this has with the original game is that they're in the same universe.The entire time I played this, I was comparing it to the original, and even reinstalled Frostpunk just to make sure I wasn't wrong. I put 3x the amount of time into Frostpunk over the past 2 days than I did playing this 3 day early access.Lets start with the graphics. There is nothing notably better than Frostpunk 1 (FP1). The only thing I noticed is that FP2 is horribly optimized, leading to regular lag spikes and average frame rate below 60 fps on medium graphics.Update: I wrote this in google docs yesterday and just to prove a point before posting, just for this game I decided to repair my computer that has a 4090 and i9-14900KF. With V-Sync enabled, constant lag, sub 60 fps. With DLSS and Frame Gen on, V-Sync off, I got a little above 60. I don't know how they managed to do this. Almost top of the line PC and still struggles.Next is the buildings. In FP1 you built buildings but in FP2 you draw districts. After placing these districts you can place a single building on it to increase output at the expense of using more workers, but its the only way to actually get large amounts of resources. You can expand a district to house ONE additional building. The housing district needs to be expanded to have a building, and can only support one. The game encourages you to plan your cities by having different districts give proximity debuffs. It is awful.If the city building was rather just placing buildings on hexagonal grids with proximity debuffs, or free form district drawing, I would probably have no issues, but this system is simply ghoulish to play with and not enjoyable to me.Next is the scouts. Unlike FP1, FP2 requires you to "frostbreak" (excavate) to the border of the map to build a logistics district. This will give you 15 "Frostland Teams". These are your scouts. Rather than have singular scout teams that can go everywhere, FP2 has turned it into a resource meaning some undiscovered areas will require more Frostland Teams than others to go to. There is also a new danger system for exploring that is useless as you can just research to decrease the danger. This system is flawed, but not really bad. Just needs some numbers tweaked to balance it out.Similar to FP1 Settlements, FP2 has outposts, settlements, and colonies. Outposts are found with your Frostland Teams, and can have a trade route established using some resources and your Frostland Teams. Outposts can be upgraded into Settlements for more Frostland Teams and resources. It will also take some population to construct it. The downside to Outposts and Settlements is that they have very limited amount of resources before they run out.Colonies are mini cities that you can actually build in and trade resources with. They're used for getting more resources from other locations after you run out in your main city. They are essentially resource depots. You can also shuttle your populations between them if you need more workers in the colony vs city. I don't like or hate the Outposts and Settlements, but I COMPLETELY adore Colonies. They are the most enjoyable aspect of the game by far.I'm not even going to bother explaining resources because I'm simply too dumb to. I don't hate the new system but I hate the resource balance and how buildings are required if you want to not immediately fall apart. I will say this though. Heatstamps are required for every building and district in the game. You gain them passively from people living in the city, and this number can be increased by producing ample amounts of goods. It is the worst "addition" as it literally is just there to impede progress. It is similar to the hospital death spiral in FP1. If you go into a deficit while not having enough goods and you can't get heatstamps quick enough, its game over. I found that 230 weeks in.That is all I can remember of what I would personally like to completely forget. I would add more but I've largely forgotten and will not be relaunching until at least the first patch. I don't hate this because it's different or new. I did like the outposts, but thats it. The best game I can compare this to in recent memory is Sins of a Solar Empire II. The planetary buildings and poor resource collection is very similar to Frostpunk II in my opinion.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played around 50 hours now and almost every minute was a lot of immersive fun to me! I've played the first part as well and loved it too. And I really don't understand the negative ratings for the second part here.The game is definitely not just a Frostpunk 1,5 and thats a really really good thing in my opinion (i hate that Ubisoft-change setting-always the same gameplay-games). It keeps the unique and immersive setting but changes the gameplay in mayor ways. So it forces you to learn a new way of playing. And the gameplay is amazing! I have to add that you have to play the game at least on Stuart difficulty. Everything below is way to easy and will make the stress of survival dissappear which you dont wanne miss cause that's what the game is about!The game takes place 30 years after the first part. It's not just surviving of a small community anymore. It's more about getting started building society again under the new circumstances. Important is resource management, the way you place the districts and the political and scientific decisions you make. Sometimes you are forced to make certain decisions and that fits perfectly to the role you play here; you are a Stuart, not a captain (yet). So I paid around 44 € for this game and already had 50 h of amazing gameplay and going to have a lot more. I'm hoping for some more late game elements in the future and in some areas a little more handiness but in general this game is an easy buy for everybody who likes strategy with strong survival elements in an interesting and immersive setting.

_childDocuments_.review: Frost punk 2 is not frost punk 1, People saying frost punk lost its souls  are justified because its not the same soul. They wanted a city builder like frost punk 1 where the cold is your greatest enemy.   In frost punk 2 its the people that are your greatest enemy.  You survived now you deal with politics. Frost punk 2 plays like a story generator like stellaris where the political and economic developments all play together to tell a story. This is why i enjoy frost punk 2 more than frost punk 1. I'll leave you with this story: in a utopia play thru, a group forms known as the overseers, a combination of machinists and lords that backed me fully as i had made the lords and machinists happy while keeping foragers neutral. I funded them as a little pet project keeping them happy and directing them to benefit  the city. Good had been a struggle to produce in decent quantities. i finally was able to get in the black for them with a mechanical factory within my main industrial district. There had been some rumbling of people not happy with some laws( like only allowing productive outsiders.) and a more radical group known as the bohemians  formed. They formed a protest shutting down the whole industrial district by lying down on mats. When trying to negotiate they demand to much within the time frame to appease them. An attempt for more direct intervention was vetoed by the council. I asked the overseers to counter the protest instead. This lead to a brawl with some overseers leaving the faction due to facing such radicalization from the bohemans but the overseers forming a rally to radicalize themselves in support of the steward and to rival the bohemans. Now the city is a powerkeg with a white out in 20 weeks,  Instead of caring about each individual within the city you are caring more about the story of the city and what it will become. What will happen and how will its story be shaped.

_childDocuments_.review: Frostpunk 2 does justice to the original while bringing some interesting new game play. I do miss the small scale of Frostpunk 1 at times. Starting off with a handful of settlers and watching them trudge throw snow and ice, some freezing to death, in a desperate effort to collect enough coal and other resources to survive. Frostpunk 2s larger scale results in not experiencing or witnessing your citizens in the same way, but overall there can be no doubt Frostpunk 2 will be a successful sequel.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Games goodthe shift of scope compared to first game is fine IMOCould do with more flavour, unique events, and multiple choice events.Great art music and thematicGame-play is more engaging with more moving parts IMO but parts can be finicky (district adjacency and hub placement)If you liked the first one, and the shift away from interpersonal relations and individual's problems to communities needs and wants isn't a deal breaker, you'll like this one as well.Long review:-My take on the shift of scopeGreat game, I really appreciate the shift from individual people to the problems and wants of *peoples* while still reflecting some of the challenges they entail for the individuals on the ground, i do however wish for more flavour text that reflects the reality you're creating for the people on the ground group OR individual. While i get that some fans miss the more interpersonal problems in the first game, i don't think the shift to the new grander scale is bad, I'd much rather have a new take on the formula instead of just an expensive DLC which some people seemingly wanted.-My take on game-play mechanicsThe one game-play complaint i have is the district adjacency bonus mechanic, having 3 segments touching the other one while the rest can stick out into the frozen landscape doesn't feel intuitive, and makes placing districts optimally more of a puzzle game than a strategy survival city builder.my suggested fix: Is to have each district segment have its own heat modifiers, make each section of the district be able to be warmer or colder than the other ones. It makes no sense for the segment that's wrapped up in other segments and has a heating hub to be as warm as the other ones sticking into the cold. And micro managing as many 3 point connections as possible is obnoxious, I want to manage resources and make strategic choices, not play candy crush with my districts and hubs.-Flavour textAnother somewhat lacking thing, which can easily be fixed post release, is the lack of multiple-choice pop-ups compared to the first one, there are a few like when the pilgrims ask for supplies ahead of a frost out to search for supplies, or when the wanderers ask for oil ahead of a whiteout and you can chose to give them a large lump of oil to survive, or make guards to fight them, or when the laws clash and you are asked how to handle the miss-match of doctrine etc. that's great stuff i want more of. More multiple choice events in general would be great, more random events that make each play through more unique would be fantastic as well as having to handle different hardships. -Differences in runscredit where credit is due, the random map and random interest groups add some diversity on the utopia builder mode. In my run for a long time i had certain good laws straight up locked out, because none of my interest groups wanted it which gave my utopia run some unique challenges which was fun, and the politics do have lots of moving parts which can alter which groups are stronger, and can influence your strategy in regards to them. -Things game does greatJust to quickly give credit where credit is due, the narrative is great, the storytelling is great even if it lacks some closer looks at the society you're building, visuals and music is phenomenal, in a way the game feels a lot more human than the first one, as it tackles the human condition a lot more which i enjoy, people want money, they have their own visions they work towards. They're not just machines that run on a vague notion of trust like they kind of were in the first game. While the general make like you a group may feel woefully disrespected and feel like they live in the tyranny of the majority. You have to guide society between the fine lines of survival and efficiency, compliance, thriving, and loyalty of all the different groups. However as stated i'd like to see the effects of these laws and choices reflected more on the city, groups, and people. Be it pop ups, changes in architecture, events, there are speaker broadcasts which reflect these though which is great, but i want more.-ConclusionGames great, but has lots of unrealised potential, and can at times be a bit finicky

_childDocuments_.review: This is a tough one, it's very middle of the road and for the first some hours I liked it. I head to restart a bunch because I went straight for high difficulty but eventually beat it and looking back while it did have some high moments, overall I'm more disappointed than pleased.Frostpunk 1 is one of my favorite games of all times and this just doesn't live up to it. First off, I don't feel like playing it again after beating the story mode, that's a major red flag for a city builder/strategy game. And that's because underneath all the shiny graphics and story lines... the game has very little strategic depth. There are a lot of buildings that do the same thing and pretty look the same too and the political system heavily discourages combining technologies/ideologies. So you can play it a couple of times to try focusing on equality vs merit/adaptation vs progress tradition vs reason.... but then that's really it, you've seen it all in two play throughs. For the most part there is just one way to play the game. Kind of a joke to even put a strategy tag on it. It's really a pretty linear, and very short, RPG with a veneer  of strategy/city building on it. On the technical side... the interface is terrible and slow and honestly just an absolute nightmare, and the game is not very responsive to input even on high end systems, but that's been said many times already.Now the story is pretty good, and was the main thing that kept me interested BUT, but it had a pretty major issue with it too... it's way too zoomed out. There are no characters, the people are more concepts than anything else. The storytelling could really use more real faces of people to ground the story more, it's "interesting" but it's hard to care and get invested the way the story in Frostpunk 1 did.Overall my feeling about it was "meh, it was ok" and that's kind of a let down for the sequel to one of my favorite games : / To be constructive here is how i would fix it:- Story mode needs be longer and feel more like a real campaign rather than an extended tutorial, add the chance to expand new London into some giant metropolis than survive a brutal white out or something that feels like a truly epic final challenge that story line.- Make the political system and faction pleasing less overwhelming it limits how technologies must be researched and what you we can build to avoid tension, add more technologies to research building options that aren't political in nature and add actual strategic depth and city building mechanics to the game.- Weave in more individual characters and their storylines told on a more personal level within the larger story to make it more gripping and emotional and pull the player in more.- Please keep improving performance.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: FP2 is one level closer to a grand strategy game as compared to the original that had you assigning and moving individual citizens from job to job. For some, this is less engaging because it lacks either the narrative or roleplaying elements that made Frostpunk so enthralling. For me, the old Frostpunk was fully realized and didn't have much room left to grow. I like Frostpunk 2 a lot, I think it'll take some time and additional content for it to really settle it along side its predecessor as a best-of-genre example, but it's already a complete game experience. It also retains the outstanding art direction and transcendent soundtrack.Some things about the main story could be better - the final chapters weren't as interesting as I hoped, and it was the only moment where I really thought, man, the original was just better at the drama and constantly ramping up the stakes (what can match the "Should we send the children into the mines, knowing they will surely die, but it might save the city?" type decisions during the Great Storm?) - but overall it's pretty good and definitely has multiple paths for expansion. Not everyone's going to love the faction system and I would like more options to reach Captain's Authority, or start my own faction or something, but this is one area the game is unquestionably better than the original. Do you want factions demanding you do something, or do you want to be given the unwinnable "keep all homes warm" quest for the tenth time?Lastly, one criticism is that I haven't really felt like I was ever at risk during my two playthroughs. I think I was exiled to die in the frost at least a dozen times on some of the old scenarios, even before getting to Survivor playthroughs, but Stuart has basically never faced anything other than a brief 'lower tension or else' moment at the beginning of Chapter 5. Frostpunk is at its best when the stakes are do or die, and sometimes I just didn't care what happened to the opposing faction. Keeping my colonies happy was just a game of sliders. Certain tech paths seem mandatory and others seem like they probably don't have any purpose other than a very specific Captain/Survivor level strategy. That's all fine, but there could be more to *care* about each of these elements. Colonists should get angrier faster and threaten to secede, like in On the Edge. I worked the Dreadnaught colony to the bone for years - basically no consequences. Just...amp it up. Have the dissident faction take the generator hostage. Flood Central with oil and light it on fire. Did you decide to blast Winterhome? Uh oh, frostquakes are damaging your nearby outposts! Did you settle Winterhome? Uh oh, it's cursed and people are getting dismembered in the housing districts! You mandated communal parenthood? No thanks, 3,000 citizens, including the baby that was born when you reactivated the generator, have stolen your prefabs and left. (Maybe some of these are possible - I've only played it through twice).In any case, I still love it. Great game.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: This game kicks ass.We've gone from crying about individual people dying or the tragedy of a few dozen in the first game, to nation building and the statistical "costs" associated with it. The age of coal is over, now is the time of oil and diesel punk in the frozen wastes. Everything is bigger and grander, at times at the cost of some of that personal connection. Over is the struggle to build another automaton to support a few hundred more lives, now we are dealing with tens of thousands with multiple simultaneous colonies and supply lines.How one decides to structure their society has also evolved. We get commentary about workers rights versus profiteering, that existed in the late 19 and early 20th century; eugenics and questionable utilitarian policies; technocrats, survivalists, and traditionalists; and the glory of having to wrangle them all in a Senate. For any history buff that is familiar with strife and the competing zeitgeists of the Edwardian era and subsequent jazz age, you'll love it.For people that expected a re-skinned copy of the first game, this is not that. This plays a bit more like a hybrid between a 4x and city builder. Not too dissimilar from the pure management aspects of the district system found in Endless Legend and Civilization 6. Think multiple simulated settlements with their own sub-districts managed via a hex tile system.  All of this is then wired together with trade systems that are constantly under threat from the harsh environment and internal strife.The music is just as bombastic as the first and the art is stellar. Every area one builds a settlement is ripe with handcrafted detail, while city districts expand procedurally with custom art for specialty buildings.  Flavour and lore from citizens is still here, though the impact it has is more akin to a CEO or leader reading a review for their company or a letter from one of their constituents. The days of being the floor manager down in the pits of the first game are gone with the ability to click on individual citizens being absent. Instead, the city pulses, appears alive, and reacts to the mood of the people. Traffic and activity is now represented via a constant stream and flicker of light, reminiscent of timelapse and tiltshift photography. It holds up well but may be a disappointment for those expecting the visceral and personal connection of the first game.If I had a few gripes, the game does need some more love with performance patches, as I did encounter a pretty nasty memory leak late game and saving can occasionally look like the game is frozen. I do expect these to come and it could be sorted out. In terms of replay-ability, the utopia/endless mode doesn't repopulate resources like the first game, and it is possible to cap out, making it hard to scratch that perfectionist itch.I eagerly await the DLC and a potential followup.I'd give it a solid 8/10Pros- You are no longer the Amazon warehouse manager during an ice age, you are now Steward Jeff Bezos.- This is not a re-skin of the first game, it is a game with different mechanics in the same universe.- Attention to detail, art, and the music is just as incredible as the first.Cons- A few performance hiccups and minor bugs. Far more polished than the stuff put out by major studios nowadays.- The grander scale does lose some of the charm and personal connection of the first game.

_childDocuments_.review: People complain about how this game is not a true continuation to the first one - but i think this is fine in itself, i can deal with the changes developers have introduced.Instead of beating that horse, i want to talk about something that has greatly disappointed me - the political system. In pre-release notes it was hyped up as a main feature of the game, an expansive system that would represent a diverse landscape of political thoughts in your population. And what do we get in the end? A bland, static parody of what could have been a pure gem in the gaming industry.You have 4 factions in the campaign and 5 in free-play mode. There are also Colonists, but they don't take part in politics and exist only in your secondary cities so you can safely ignore them. Existing factions are divided into 2 camps - pro-progress and pro-tradition. That's the whole political complexity, the end. No, seriously, there is no intermingling of ideas between them, no situations where 1 group wants something and 3(4) others are strongly against it. You don't even get your own gang of loyalists once you become a Captain. Those groups exist only as statistics, equally spread among your living districts.  They don't try to push for any agenda on their own unless you really piss them off - and they won't fight with one another (with the exception of the campaign ending, but that's spoilers).Overall, the political system is a major disappointment. It could have created a layer of gameplay of its own, but ends up being just a distraction from city management - which was not as captivating as I hoped. It starts great but falls off closer to the endgame, where the difficulty goes out of the window. You have so much resources that building colonies feels pointless - your main city + resource depots on the map have enough of everything to win you the game. You don't even need oil if you manage coal properly - and steam is not even available properly in the campaign!I also must admit that swapping between colonies does not feel great. It is too tedious once you get to 3 or 4, and i ended up just making every single one into a self-sufficient hub just so i don't have to manage resources there. At least in free-play, you can name them (but not the permanent outposts for some reason). Also, as I mentioned before, there are no factions in your colonies, only nameless colonists that would be fine with you proclaiming to be god-emperor and stealing their kneecaps. Lots of wasted potential over here, something like dynamics between colonies-capital city based on your approach towards local resources, or perhaps population that was forced out of comfortable capital and now forced to live in a frozen hellhole once again.Overall I enjoyed some parts of the game, it was a pleasant experience. But Frostpunk one felt much more memorable when compared to this. If there was a neutral score I would give it, but for now, it is a negative one. Maybe updates and DLCs would make the situation better, Frostpunk 2 is very close to being a good game.

_childDocuments_.review: After putting some hours into the game i am quite satisfied with it.Its not frostpunk 1. Thematically its the very same but it takes a long leap into district management and community building. Basically now you you try to stack perks from adjacent buildings and districts instead of trying to hammer in as many buildings as you can inside influence radius of nearest fighting pit, church or soup stop. In addition you spend a lot more time on world map and try to develop lesser colonies to keep main city flourishing. This was a thing in the earlier game but now its more emphasized.Community management side took a huge change where you reach towards your own goals while also trying to serve several existing factions which each having their aligning or opposite goals. The "legacy faction" is either the military or the church. Then there are new londoners, frostlanders etc. Everyone want something, some want the same thing. This reaches to the tech-tree as well where you can satisfy one or all factions by researching their supported buildings or upgrades. If something you want is unpopular, you can negotiate with factions to gain support for your decision, but what they demand in return might not be something you want.. or maybe it is and its win-win.Interestingly there are some hidden buffs aswell. Some researches unlock a building, some stance you have taken cause a reaction where you get extra benefit.Once you get past the initial learning curve, get some basics of efficient city planning under your belt and know to leave some space for efficiency boosting additional structures the game starts to feel really entertaining. I absolutely love how the game shows FP1:s initial crater where you built your core city was just a minor smudge on the map and now you set out to claim the frozen desert.

_childDocuments_.review: This review is just my personal opinion, not intended to convince anyone of anything. Right off the bat, before I dive into the details, I want to say that I liked Frostpunk 2. I don’t think the game is a failure in terms of design, although I recognize that many players may not agree with me. That said, before we get into the main points, I should mention that I bought the game with my own money, and on top of that, I own the Deluxe Edition. I’d been eagerly waiting for the release, especially since I loved the first game in the series. Sure, the delayed release was a bit of a letdown, but not a huge deal — at this point, that’s all in the past.So, Frostpunk 2.I got the chance to play it three days before the official release (thanks to the Deluxe Edition, as mentioned earlier), but the pre-release didn’t go off without a hitch. The game wasn’t available for download on Steam for about half an hour. In this case, though, I’m more inclined to blame Steam itself. The release of another game, The Casting of Frank Stone, by a completely different studio, had similar issues. From what I’ve heard, this isn’t uncommon, and users often run into these kinds of problems. Interestingly, I’ve heard that players on other platforms, like EGS, didn’t experience any delays with the pre-release. Of course, I might be wrong, but for now, I can’t fault 11 bit studios for something out of their control.Now, let’s break things down.**Single-Player Campaign and Story Mode**The story mode opens with beautifully stylized cinematics that capture the essence of the Frostpunk universe. These cinematics accompany every chapter of the campaign, and they’re just a pleasure to watch. As a fan of the franchise, I couldn’t help but appreciate the visual and audio design. Is it stunning? That’s subjective. But the visuals perfectly convey the atmosphere of the world — total despair in frozen wastelands where all that awaits is frostbite and death. It’s pretty impactful, especially considering the leap between the first and second games in this regard. The campaign is divided into chapters, starting, of course, with the Prologue, which does a great job of fleshing out the game’s lore. I have no complaints about the storytelling; the delivery of information is smooth and engaging.**Graphics**While graphics aren’t the main focus in a game like this, I have to say the visuals in Frostpunk 2 are solid. It’s not groundbreaking or hyper-realistic, but within the context of the genre, the game’s graphics hold up well and leave a positive impression.**Optimization and Bugs**This is a big topic for many modern games, and I’ve even heard people say that Frostpunk 2 suffers from poor optimization. Personally, I didn’t run into any issues, either in the pre-release or afterward. The game runs smoothly for me, with stable FPS, no stuttering, and it all works like clockwork. As for bugs, I didn’t encounter any, and while I can’t claim they don’t exist, they didn’t affect my experience. From my perspective, the studio did a good job here.**Gameplay**The heart of any city-building strategy game is the gameplay. It’s the core of the experience, and Frostpunk 2 delivers. I’m not going to do a direct comparison between Frostpunk and Frostpunk 2, because gameplay-wise, they’re quite different games, even if they share similar mechanics and ideas. The first game feels more intimate, almost cozy in a way, while the second one is more complex and global in scope. I’ve described Frostpunk 2 as a mix of Frostpunk and Cities: Skylines, with some added faction management and political elements. And I like that. I can’t say whether the second game is better than the first — it’s hard to compare because they offer such different experiences. But the new mechanics and their blend with the old ones definitely gave me a lot of enjoyment, and that’s a win in my book. Speaking of politics — relationships with factions are a bit simplistic. I’d have liked a deeper system for more hardcore gameplay, but for a broader audience, this simplicity is probably a plus. And despite that, the game still retains its brutal, frostbitten challenge, making progression much tougher.In conclusion, I honestly don’t get the negativity toward Frostpunk 2. The game has evolved, becoming bigger, more ambitious, and more global, without losing its hardcore edge. At the same time, it’s added elements that make it accessible to a wider audience, so both casual players and hardcore fans can enjoy it. Thank you, 11 bit studios — I loved the first game in the series, and now I’m really happy with the second. I hope the market situation improves soon, and your company continues to thrive, bringing us new projects, including future installments in this franchise.

_childDocuments_.review: This is an excellent game! And you can tell this not just by giving it a fair chance and playing it yourself past the prologue-tutorial (which is when this game really shows what it's about) but also by looking at the negative reviews. To the last one, they are written by hardcore fans of Frostpunk 1 who just cannot accept that 11 Bit had had the courage to release a new installment with original content instead of giving them another DLC under the guise of a new game. Which means that only those stuck in their FP1 ways do not like the new game. Everyone else (including some of those more open-minded hardcore fans too) enjoys it a lot. So if you’re fresh to the genre, you have high chances of loving this game too. Bare in mind though, the game is hard. The difficulty is in the design. The entire point is to struggle against opposition and through clever city-planning, resource-management, decision-making and, yes, back-stabbing too come out successful the other end. So if you’re looking for a cozy game, this isn’t for you. However, if you do enjoy a challenge and love this feeling of success that follows a struggle (sometimes requiring a restart so that you get things done better this time) then this game is most certainly for you. Now to say a few things to those hard-core, stuck in their ways fans who just wanted more of the same (even though they already have it in the first game):Frostpunk 2 is a natural progression from the first. It makes sense not just story-wise but also systems-wise. You have survived the storm, now you have to rebuild. You no longer manage a tiny, desolate town but an actual city and some of its off-shots (that grew over the course of the last thirty years) while your worst enemy is no longer the cold (not as much as before, anyway) but the people who all have different ideas of what this new world should be. How much more realistic can this get than a bunch of people surviving a calamity as a unified front under the leadership of a dictator only to, once the worst has passed, suddenly remember that they have a voice too and want to have a say in what is done to their precious heaven that has protected them thus far?I see a lot of comments from hardcore fans that the game lacks heart or soul because they have to build entire neighborhoods now (even though you can still build buildings) or because they can’t zoom in enough and see individual people walking the streets (you can but you have to find the button) or that the population numbers go in thousands instead of just tens and it is simply “too hard to care” about them. First of all, the game does give you little snippets: brief insights into the minds of individual people that tell you how your laws have affected them which, for some, is enough to “care” or feel bad about their choices. And second of all, have any of you ever thought that managing an entire country as its prime minister or president is exactly that? Being presented with those enormous numbers and still trying to see the individual behind and pushing yourself to care? Doesn’t just the scale of this game already say something very meaningful and thought-provoking about ruling a nation? How much easier it is in such circumstances to condemn people to the cold or starvation or smog when all you see is numbers? Does that “ease” make the game worse or rather say something about humanity and the burdens of decision-making? This alone is enough for me to elevate this game above others. In times of remakes, short-cuts, risk-averse solutions and feel-good entertainment, very few have the courage to tell us uncomfortable truths. We no longer see originality in anything. Our opinions are no longer confronted. We are no longer asked to think for ourselves. Well, this game is different. It does not treat you like an idiot. It does not take the easy way. It does challenge your views; makes you doubt what you have taken for granted so far. It doesn’t necessarily have to change your mind but it makes you rethink your opinions in ways you rarely have before. It asks uncomfortable questions that help you understand the wider spectrum of consequences for your most absolute truths. Most of all, however, what this game does best is make you realize how there is no solution that suits all. How every decision can be right for someone and wrong for another. How every idea has a cost. And that is worth a lot in a polarized world of absolutes.

_childDocuments_.review: Welcome to the frost fields, Pilgrim. Now get to work for the Steward needs another colony.Games alright, I guess, enjoyed it during my first play-through of the story (Order route) however upon playing again knowing how to play efficiently allowing me to focus on details I realised the game has a lot of flaws and not the type you simply iron out with a bug patch.As other people have said the story is extremely short (only 5 chapters and took me less than 4 hours) but also the story doesn't have much depth depth.Game play is quite dull when you look at it, no heat zones (upgrading gen only makes it more fuel efficient rather than increasing its output and AOE) so there's no real reason to build housing as close to the generator as possible (on some maps there's no reason at all).You can't micro manage buildings (or districts in FP2's case) nor is there different types of workers such as workers, Engineers, amputees, children, automatons instead we just have "workforce" which is very dull and as such you don't suffer any consequences from say, having a bunch of kids working in the research buildings instead you get squaller if too many people are unemployed due to efficiency.The tech tree is awful, most of the tech unlocks buildings and policy's which is ok if it weren't for how useless most of them are, hub buildings are useless 90% of the time (except for storage hubs) as you can just build a district building and get better results. District buildings are dull and don't change depending on the faction with the most people or your actions (used to love seeing the banners fly on the propaganda building and the watch towers in the order route in FP1).Choices, choices, choices, I loved the fact that once you had picked something on the adaptation tree in FP1 you had to stick with it no matter what making them important with the possibility of making it slightly better or worse depending on events later on. FP2 has none of that, in the tech tree and don't know whether to research the Stalwarts version or the pilgrims version? No problem, just research them both! Can't decide if you should implement strict immigration restrictions or allow everyone in? No problem, you can vote one in and then swap it 10 weeks later with almost zero consequences.Hex and districts building system is quite ass, would much prefer if districts were just upscalled versions of buildings with fixed sizes and shapes along with having more districts such as entertainment or communal districts and that at the very least we could build major roads. I also wished the building looked the same as it was in the game play trailer*Factions and politics*The politics were a cool idea, a good way to add new flavour into the mix however its dry and bland, factions grow seemingly randomly, no clue how the Pilgrims take up 25% of the population despite being portrayed as monsters for the past 10 years yet the Stalwarts only have 14% despite existing since the founding of new London, being in control of new London and me as the player constantly funding and supporting them.Factions can hold protests and rally's, they don't do much apart from show a symbol above the district they're in and provide small buffs or shut down a districts production. They don't fly up banners or flags to Identify themselves, they don't form community's inside districts (so no Stalwart gated community's with less crime due to everyone conforming to order through unity or Pilgrim Ghettos.I know FP2 only just came out and still needs time but the fact that the only reason this review is as short as it is is because I was too lazy to add more complaints should show that this game needed more time to bake before being released.
