_childDocuments_.review: Everyone is saying that if you liked Frostpunk for its intimacy and smaller scale, you may not like Frostpunk 2's grander design/strategy as much. This has been gone over a lot already, but I will say that this is true. I love the direction they took the game. Everything from the resource planning, district planning, managing research and the council, the differing factions -- they are all things you have to think about and balance at once, which makes coming through the tough times that much more rewarding. However, this game is not perfect. Firstly, I feel that while the faction origins are different from each other, they generally fall in the camp of "far left group, moderate left group, moderate right group, far right group" in terms of social spectrum. while there isn't anything wrong with this, I had a hard time telling apart some of the factions because while they had different ideals, they wound up supporting the same ideas all the same meaning they didn't feel different. But by far the biggest issue with the game is the stability. Quite frankly, releasing a game this unstable is just unacceptable. There are way too many crashes, and they can honestly happen at any time but it usually happens when navigating the map. I've lost a lot of playtime due to having to either re-trace my steps from my last step, or having to save consistently because i don't want to lose a lot of progress. While I trust they will get this fixed, in the meantime i would recommend saving after every important action you take, even if it feels monotonous and isn't something we should have to do, it will save you for now. Overall, great game. the campaign does a good job introducing the core mechanics for endless mode, and im excited to see what story elements they introduce next as DLC. 8/10, will be bumped up to a 9/10 once stability is fixed.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Why so coldhearted? Oh wait!?Positive: + Game is taken to a new level! Gives you the best of the survival colony genre with all the new mind boggling game play mechanics to figure out. It is what you would expect a good sequel to be!+ Deep dive into Frostpunk universe! The story is only the tip of the iceberg really, the thrill of the music is giving shivers, the loading of the last save to do things better is givvng the chillz!+ Right now spending hours trying to figure out best plan for my districts, so captivating! 'Negative- My computer is trash, for a game that mostly resembles a board game it could run better on lowest setting. My computer struggles by chapter 3. Enjoy Stewards!P.S. Considering FS1 nostalgia prevailing in the comments I'd love to see devs encouraged to produce another DLC to FS1. Seems more than fitting!
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: With all support to 11 bit studios.Frostpunk 2 has delivered more mechanics, new lore and more space for movement and growing. The next game is much bigger and based on the previous one.Well done, lads. Thanks for your job.When winter is coming, there is a good change to play FP2. And remember — THE CITY MUST NOT FALL.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: A fantastic sequel to the original Frostpunk. All of the best features and ideas from the original game (including The Last Autumn) expanded and grown in a very natural way, with interesting mechanics and new ideas blended seamlessly. Solid recommend for any fan of the original, and a recommendation in general as well.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, I quite like Frostpunk 2. Would I say it was as enthralling or as atmospheric as the first game? No. It really wasn't, and I see where a lot of people are coming from in their criticisms towards feeling "disconnected" from their citizens. The political system was pretty neat, though you definitely end up being hemmed in by trying to please everyone only to end up pleasing no one and stuck with a civil war regardless. It's something that could definitely do with a bit of work, and I hope we will see that in future DLCs. For a city (state) builder however, I quite enjoyed it, I felt the placement of city districts was quite simplistic at times but the number crunching involved especially as you get outposts and colonies set up helped satisfy that part of my brain anyhow. The OST was nothing short of phenomenal, and they were very much on point with their whole dieselpunk/post-apocalyptic aesthetic. I liked the little lore tidbits you come across in the frostland here and there, and you can tell the sort of directions they're hoping to go with as far as DLC is concerned, so I will be looking forward to that also.Overall, it's a good game, just not a fantastic game. But with a bit of long term support from the devs and a fledgling modding community gearing up, I can see it being around for a long time yet.I'll give it a solid 7/10, good but definitely has room to improve.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: An interesting city builder on the onset, but quickly turns into a very complex game of Tetris where one spends their time solving the problem of optimal placement of districts such as to maximize benefits and minimize cost. The map doesn’t offer much in terms of feedback, the graphics aren’t immersive because we don’t really see anyone doing anything. Rather, we get generic animations that don’t really mean anything and spend most of the time on pause trying to think where to place the next district. tl;dr it’s boring, but also cerebrally complex in a way that makes it hard to relax while playing. It’s not like Frostpunk 1 where you can get lost in watching the city get built with amazing visuals. Here, the visuals are essentially static so there’s no real beauty to get lost into.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: A tedious politics simulator trying to disguise itself as a city builder.You stare at a handful of numbers going up or down, engage with an arcade-y, watered down version of city management to change them, and then are seemingly meant to spend the majority of your time dealing with factions and laws.And the politics gameplay loop is rough. A barrage of requests from each faction and then dealing with the fallout of your decisions is how you should expect to spend the majority of your time playing this. Very little player agency allowed here.Not much of what made the first Frostpunk good has been translated into this game sadly.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: It's not a bad game or anything, but it's so much more complex than Frostpunk 1 and personally I feel like it's not a benefit.It's harder to get an overview of anything, the faction system is a pain after the first couple of hours and I personally hate the multiple settlements thing.If you haven't played Frostpunk 1, I'd reccomend it, if you have then throw away all your expectations first, because if you don't then you're going to be disappointed. It feels like you're constantly spammed with "Steward" to the point where it just becomes background noise rather than the notification it's supposed to be.Each individual sound is cool but combined it just becomes too much. It feels like you barely notice the weather until you look at it or suddenly run out of fuel, the sound cues and atmosphere of Frostpunk 1 just aren't there.When people die here, it's just a number popping up, it feels annoying while it's much harder to tell exactly what to do to improve.The reason the faction system becomes annoying is quite simple, it reverses your progress. At the beginning where you don't have a lot of laws implemented, it's fine because every law is progress but maybe around 150-200 weeks in, they just constantly try to change the laws you already implemented and like. And if you negotiate and vote you're forced through the same short voting cutscene over and over, it's just tedious with no benefit after that amount of time.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: The game is okay, at best. I cannot recommend it for now as there a lot of performance issues and sound glitches. On another note, the game lacks a soul compared to FP1. Although choice have impacts, they feel meaningless since you have little to no influence on most of the events coming at you. Whatever way you push, the other side push back. It's essentially a game of seesaw. At a certain point it's as if the game plays itself and you're just there to watch and place little districts here and there. Plus ... performance issues and sound glitches on a game like that, who's core attractive aspect is it's immersion? Come on ... You can do better than that.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: A pretty solid sequel to Frostpunk 1. The balance is very wonky, with the early game being somewhat hard even on the lower difficulties and the late game being easy to the point of almost being boring, however apart from that i can't complain much about it. It follows the ideal sequel model in that it diverges enough to be unique and interesting yet still keeps several concepts from Frostpunk 1 and expands the story. The new political system is very fun and rewarding especially once you fully understand how it works. I do also like the idea of radicalism not inherently being a bad thing, as though it causes strife it isn't portrayed as morally evil, just controversial. I also like how each ideology has some truly bad ideas on how to run things that are almost objectively worse, so you have to weigh practicality and controversy.Overall, a pretty solid game which does a lot good albeit with some bad 8/10
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Brilliant game! The politics, factions, and economy are incredibly well-developed. The graphics, as always, are stunning and atmospheric. The music is the cherry on top, with Piotr Musiał in top form. The atmosphere is different from the first game, as we move from managing a single unit to managing the society that emerged from the events of the first game, which makes complete sense as a logical progression. I completely don’t understand the negative opinions complaining that it’s not like the first game. I also strongly disagree with comments about a lack of atmosphere in the game. On the contrary, the game forces many tough decisions, constantly balancing on the edge of collapse. It quickly reveals whether we are cynics, sensitive to justice and human suffering, or simply fanatics. Yes, the game is challenging, but isn’t that a good thing? The developers are doing their best to ensure the game doesn’t get boring after just two hours of playing, right? The only illogical decision from the developers that I can critique is why, after expanding the settlement in the prologue, it isn’t as developed in later parts of the game based on how we guided it in the prologue. For me, it's a 9/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Disappointing for me.I lost immersion with the new, bigger scale of the city (suddenly appearing/disappearing frostbreaking machines).What’s the difference between frozen ground and frost-breaking it? I can’t see any change.Where is the melting snow when I start the generator?I don’t feel the cold from the game anymore.Sorry, 11 bit studios, I usually praise your games, but this one is not for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Its a little different from first frostpunk, but that's what makes it special and good. creators not just coping first game and changing it a little is a fact that makes it good, not better than first part , but it has potential as game is developing now. It is one of the reason i say polish companies know how to make games (after cyberpunk and Vedmak)
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Would I recommend it? Yes. Have I played it enough to give a well rounded and full review? No. Am I gonna review it anyways? Yes.In the simplest of terms, the game is a solid city builder, with common resource management supply lines. The environment of the game is more unique than the core gameplay loop, as the snow and interesting post-apocalyptic steampunk look offers an interesting design and look. Compared to many other city builders it offers more on the story side of things. Gameplay loop and multitude of difficulty settings seems to offer good replayability value and challenge.How does it compare to Frostpunk 1? Would I recommend it to people who liked the first game?I would say the first game offers more variance and story with all the different scenarios. The first game was more focused on the individuals and the closer camera angle to your city and citizens made you feel more close to the people and their suffering. I personally also felt that the first game had more options in progression, with population based workforce compared to automatons. Frostpunk 2 has quite a good amount of research, map exploration, secondary colonies, etc. that are interesting changes compared to the first game.In my honest opinion, if you liked the story and personal connection of the first game more than the city building aspects, you might not like Frostpunk 2 as much. Overall it is a solid sequel that evolved in most aspects and stepped back in others.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: After playing Frostpunk 2, I feel like Frostpunk 1 was just a trailer of 2. Dont get me wrong, 1 was pretty good too. But 2 is on another level. Unlike other games, (e.g. call of duty etc.), developers didnt just change few things and add new maps. They changed the gameplay in a more meaningful way.  You do less micro management on buildings, but do more management on the policy part. Personally, I loved it. It is kinda confusing in the beginning, but still so much fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer: I purchased the Deluxe EditionFP2 is a wonderful evolution of the Frostpunk IP. Expanding the scope of the game play and pushing the story into a post-post-apocalyptic setting. The game remains as challenging as its predecessor while staying engaging to play. Without sounding like a corporate game reviewer, this is truely the Dark Souls of city builders combining a high skill ceiling with gripping story and visuals. I'd recommend this game to anyone who loved the original game and to any new players looking for a challenge.THE CITY MUST SURVIVE
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: I held 30min before asking a refund. What a disaster.It's easily one of the worst UI I've ever seen since Hunt Showndown new UI. It's cryptic. The Hexagonal map is a betrayal to the original, circular map. The icebreaking is a completely useless mechanic. You're forced to place districts in several cases. Need only 3 cases? ♥♥♥♥ you, you need to put 6 or cancel it.Time goes too fast too. I barely started work that 60 people died?! Give me a break. I don't know how to manage heat, it's just created when distrinct are near each other, I suppose people just carry around bags of heat to give to their neighbours. No people walking in the street. No managing of the shift (tho you can order emergency shift I suppose...). In term of sound design, the game is several orders of magnetude behind the previous one. I can still hear the sound that stop the game speed when a grave event happens. It appears on your screen, and you know something is going on. Here it is invisible, no sound, black yellow on black is invisible, ughJust play the first one...
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: I think it's good! I really do! Play on Captain difficulty and you'll be struggling and thinking about what you'll be doing right until the end. A first playthrough of the story mode on it is especially stressful as you balance problems cropping up until you finally hit the stability you long for.Just don't look for the same experience as frostpunk 1. It's different! It's different in a good way, but it still retains the base that made frostpunk 1 awesome, too. You still gotta survive, you still gotta collect resources and explore, you know how it is. Balancing the politics is fun, making sure everyone gets a piece of the pie and is ultimately happy with you is really hard and a good challenge.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: I'm glad they devs keep working on this game and I'm really glad that mod support was a planned aspect of it. I still think I'll wait a bit longer for more released content and more changes before I really delve further into the game. It's a good game, it just lacks the impact of Frostpunk in terms of gameplay, emotion, music, and so on.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Game is good. Like, really good! It doesn't try to be like Frostpunk 1 and I'm all for it. Different mechanics give it a fresh take, but at its core it stays true to the Frostpunk vibe. If you enjoy thinking 5 steps ahead like in Frostpunk 1 you will definitely enjoy Frostpunk 2. Bought it on release day, worked flawlessly. Game is really polished. Highly recommend, 10/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Mixed emotions of the game.First of all, this isn’t FP1, except for the recurring themes of ruinous cold and the stupid morality tied to your decisions.When it comes to gameplay, I’m disappointed by the so-called "infinite" resources. Massive numbers aren’t infinite, and I realized this in my last playthrough—my oil ran dry, and my city collapsed because I’d invested in oil-only generator techs. While some resources like food and materials might feel virtually infinite if they would last for 170,000 weeks, oil is definitely not one of them; it runs out very fast. After about six hours of gameplay, my oil colony became dry.Then there’s the annoyingly bleak interface with many shortcomings. For instance, how can I figure out how many anti-squalor buildings I need? What buildings produce squalor? How do I highlight districts to quickly see what I already have? There are so many little things missing here. And else, and else. In comparison to FP1, the interface sucks. Buildings. Why are we limited to building only within districts? It’s absurd that I can’t place anything outside a district, and if I need an extra prison, I have to build a whole new housing district just for it.Factions conflict seems pretty but feels underdeveloped. There’s so much potential here, but it’s hard to say exactly what would make it better.The game is nice, but it needs a lot of patches and polish. Better to wait for DLCs, maybe?
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Turns out i'm switching my review to a negative one.I liked the first game, in the first one, actions actually mattered, laws would have greater impact, frost would be hard to handle, hope and trust aswell.In this game is almost completely different. It took me a little while to get used to the UI and how the game works.Now, the game centers around politicis, passing laws and managing your population's anger, because you decided to make them pay to get access to food. None of the laws you pass will affect your gameplay in a sense that will block you later on. At most you will eventually get people slightly angry, and you can just decide to change the law applied.You will generally pass laws like a true capitalist most of the time, since early on you want to survive and subsist the needs of the city ( Heat, food etc.).The research tree is also somewhat weird, as a lot of the researchs don't make any sense since there are usually a better alternative.The cities are so big now and the population too and if some of them die nothing will change, you may have lost 600 civilians but it's whatever, in a few more weeks i'll get 1500 back. And now that the cities are bigger you can't build per building but per districts.And on top of that your population will grow unless you can pass a law that prevent that which is also an event that may or may not occur, i hope you're ready to spend your time building houses because you keep getting around 1000-2000 people every months.Unlike the first one this game can borderline be played in autoplay, i didn't play in easy nor in hardest difficulty.Summary :- Constructions are in a district format, each constructions will cost you prefabs / heatstamps /  workforce and eventually steam cores no iron or wood - laws that are passed don't matter except for simplifying your game and if your population isn't happy about it you can just keep playing they'll cope with it- Inexistant impact in the game related to laws passed or buildings beside the typical "we're unhappy about it"- you can have ten thousand dead it's whatever- storms aren't as scary as in the first one since you can afford to let half your city die- game is once again fairly short outside of endless mode- UI is horrendous- Where are the super stress inducing soundtracks ?If you're willing to give a try to this game, you have to play it thinking you're not playing the first one at all or you have no idea what frostpunk is and you started with this one
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Frostpunk 2 is amazing. The only issues I have is the insane stuttering a bit into the story mode. Might be due to everything going on in the background at other settlements. Also, the audio gets messed up with static sounds when commentary plays or music.. Other then those things, I have had a blast playing. Highly recommend if you are a fan of the first iteration.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: So, I didn't initially like this game, specifically due to the change in management scope, but I decided to at least give it a few hours to form a better impression. This game needs some significant balancing. The game is built around societal interactions and all of your research and policies are reflected in the disposition of these disparate groups. Unfortunately, the mechanic is underdeveloped, and not fun to engage with. It's an obstacle more often than naught, to actually enjoying the game. There are some aspects that have started growing on me, but overall my initial impression remains accurate, and my position is predominantly negative.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Ultimately the game is a really good city builder but it kinda lost a lot of its impact from the first game. somehow there are 6 factions but none of them feel like they have any impact at all. I felt no need to really interact with them or their special techs until the game artificially forces you to by forcing something that wouldn't happen if you had good relations with all factions and placated them all throughout.The district building is interesting but I liked the first game for the small scale of desperate small hold outs of humanity. not thousands and thousands of people which creates a sense that the people dont even matter anymore, previously every death meant something now it kind just becomes a pop up which hardly has impact at all.the law system by the end removed any sense of impact when things are voted on by people who can change it constantly. the first while it felt interesting but eventually with so many laws constantly changing I forgot what all of them did and began ignoring it other than when I needed influence with a specific groupresources feel really dumbed down, just found myself placing a new district whenever the last one ran out, no sense of urgency to get resources since almost everything resource wise is a mundane upkeep with only 1 actual "resource" being used for building.Sense of the heat was completely lost, maybe I just minmaxed without realising it but literally all my fuel that kept me going for the whole game was secured within the first year. I went back to the location to upgrade it maybe once.The big story event that is meant to create tension is a new whiteout similar to the first game, is a complete joke, no sense of impending doom, didnt even touch my resource count, I was literally still producing excess food and fuel throughout the whiteout which in the end was only annoying because it stopped me from scouting. I still seen everything and could interact my colony which was completely unaffected and still somehow was shipping fuel in what was apparently so bad a storm it is meant to bring everything to a stop.The other big story plot factor of either taming the cold or adapting to it was dull at best. I didnt feel at the end I had tamed the cold, I felt like that after maybe the first chapter? and in a "I have unlimited fuel" way not a "we are saving the world" way. The other route, adaptation really doesnt feel like adapting at all, sure the laws and research are stuff like foraging etc but I didnt at all feel like I was becoming nomads or really taking advantage of the wasteland.a huge amount of the story leans on locations from the first game too and not in a good way, there are locations like the prison ship which could be extremely interesting are literally just a little bit of text and a choice with 0 impact, you can find teslas experiments and even find a strange formation caused by it where you can "drill in to investigate" I got really exicted and interested but there was no flavour after that just a small amount of resources. Let me colonise these locations, continue the experiments, theres even mention of nuclear power from a group and then it isnt touched. Old locations return only for it to be tied to a choice and that you might just lose access to it after maybe 5 weeks at it which is such a short amount of time in the game time.Again even after bashing all these things its a good city builder and it does everything well for a city builder that is meant to be about making political bargains whilst also balancing resources but I dont feel like im surviving and hardly hanging on like in one, I dont feel like I am making deep choices that have huge impacts on my people like in one and I feel like thats what the heart of the first game was, it was a city builder yeah but it was a dark gritty survival game forcing YOU not some council to make the hard choices for your people. I mustve played all the scenarios of FP1 into the double digits over the years, I imagine I will only come back to this to play DLC which I have already paid for since I punished myself by avoiding any early access gameplay. The game scaled too much too fast and as I keep saying lost its character as the cost which for a game which people got for the character and environment is kinda sadI recommend this game but do not expect anywhere as much grit and atmosphere as the first one, its less frostpunk and more a city builder in a snowy wasteland now.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: 7.5/10Frostpunk 2 continues the story from 1 but has a vastly extended scope. Not only will you be managing thousands of people, but also have to deal with politics and a vast wilderness. 7/10Good, though I can understand how some people are a bit tired of the constant “steward” sounds. Overall though, I think the sound effects are great, the music is really good, and even the “steward” isn’t as repetitive as some claim. 8/10Big improvement, enjoy the changes they’ve made to the game in this regard. Perhaps the only downside is the colored lines that spread through your city and change depending on the tension, they look too artificial and forced. 7.5/10It’s similar enough to Frostpunk 1 that you won’t miss a beat, though it has some significant changes. Politics are added where certain ideas you research must be voted, plus rules for the city and its citizens. That is a cool factor, though I have had only a few opportunities where I wasn’t able to move the votes in my favor.On the other hand, districts and the expansions and how they work are interesting. I think this was a much-needed upgrade to the game. I only wished they created more of a visual impact in the game; I feel like in this sense Frostpunk 1’s buildings actually changed the environment.Now, what is a bit lackluster is the campaign. Because of the way it is divided by chapters, you slowly get all the tools necessary to succeed and, though I felt out of control sometimes, I was always pulling through.One last negative aspect though is that there are no different views of the city. In 1 you could see heat zones for example, here you can’t, and you need to individually click every building to see how much material and heat they require. Why isn’t there an option to change the city view and instantly understand the issues your city has.  7.5/10I liked the story for the most part, and the fact that you have to change or find new energy sources, but I feel that it ends a bit too soon and that there could have been more to be done. The biggest decision is in Chapter 4, and that felt like it could be a monumental one, but in the end feels a bit rushed.Same with the ending credits, I feel like 1’s had more power in letting you know the decisions you took and the impact it had. While politics are an important part of the gameplay, regarding the story they didn’t feel like they had as much power or stake as they could have.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished the main campaign. As someone who has played frostpunk over and over and over and over, this is definitely NOT like the original frostpunk. As the city grows, you, the player, now has a very macro view of the city. You no longer build houses or cookhouses, you build housing districts and industrial districts. This sets a very different tone from the original because you do not feel like you're in the trenches with the common people. People are now numbers on the screen. In the original frostpunk, every death hurt and the chiming bell made your heart sink. Here, 500 people die and you don't even flinch. This game is a move towards a typical sim game. I don't believe the creators were inviting comparisons to the original. They have tried to create a middle ground between the original and city skylines.The graphics aren't as detailed as they were in the original. The city looks and feels cartoonish. Frostland is breathtaking though. Laws and research systems are very complex and will take a few tries to learn.The game introduces politics and complexity like never before. The challenges are meaningful and very well executed. The overhaul of scouts, settlements, expansion etc all of it is phenomenal. The game lives up to its reputation in terms of gameplay and mechanics. Definitely recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: It's good, try it. They did not made a reskin of frostpunk 1 but one-upped scope to nearly proper 4x. More politics, colonies, everlasting need to expand due to limited resources.Performance is very much ehhhhh tho, even on high in 1080p, stutters and fps drops are there. 3090+5800X3D+32GBRAM - should be enough, but evidently it's not.

I didn't play the original, but this is a great game to relax to, yet still provides challenging tasks.  The political system in this game makes it a lot of fun to propose deals with factions and all of the little details in the game allow for endless replays.

_childDocuments_.review: If you loved frost punk frost punk two is more of the same taken to the next step, where frost punk 1 was about building the city and living through the coming winter, frost punk 2 is far more about what to do now that you have made it through, building distracts, thousands of people versus a few hundred the city must not fall, will you make it as the steward or is the captain the only one who can see us through yet again?

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game they've done a great job with it. It's important to note this is not frostpunk 1 they tried something different which I ended up enjoying a lot. I do hope they add more buildings and variety but maybe thats going to come out with the dlc's later on, looking forward to replaying this every few months for the next few years!

_childDocuments_.review: Great mood. The DLC will come with additional story content, but there's actually lot of depth in learning how to politically manage your city and govern correctly. Replayability is high if you're an achievement hunter. My recommendation for a full experience is to play utopia mode and finish a game with each set of communities and one game on each available map. Don't forget to name your settlements.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent successor to Frostpunk 1, bigger and better in almost every way. Thirty years after the Great Storm, you are the new Steward of New London. The now-dead Captain of FP1 was a classic player dictator. You have to consider the wants of the city's people beyond mere survival as you try to manage the city's many issues as it expands beyond its crater furnace. The core gameplay loop is still familiar: build districts and expand them with buildings, extract resources, explore the wastes, and make choices. Many more choices. Each choice garnering feedback in the form of small popups, little stories, follow-up choices, and announcements via loudspeaker about ongoing events (CITIZENS, DO NOT FEED THE CHILDREN!). Reading comprehension is important: what I thought was a law establishing government-run daycare was actually a law collectivizing children.  The graphics and music are gorgeous. There are a tiny number of questionable UX choices: the inability to fully zoom out in the overworld map; some difficulty clicking on tiles in one of the settlement maps are the only two that come immediately to mind. The campaign is a good introduction to the game, but clearly the focus is on the free-form Utopia Builder. The forced choice at the end of the campaign is jarring, but if you know what is coming it's fairly trivial to wrap everything up in maybe 15 minutes from that point and move on.On the whole, this is an excellent city-society builder with a plentitude of interesting choices.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: I was initially disappointed by Frostpunk 2. The original was such a great game and one I sunk a lot of time into—and Frostpunk 2 is, as others have noted, very different. Its much more of a management game than a city builder, and that initially struck me as an awful shame because first, I love city builders and, second, the original Frostpunk was such an innovative and fun city builder. But once I put all of that aside and treated Frostpunk 2 as its own game, judging it on its own merits and not by my preconceived notions of what a Frostpunk game should be like, I had a lot of fun. There are a few things that I don't like as much--including people being reduced to a number instead of a living breathing person whom you would grow attached to, but none of them are dealbreakers for me. Frostpunk 2 is a great game set in the Frostpunk universe, and while it is a literal narrative sequel to the original Frostpunk, it is not a sequel in the gameplay sense. The closest comparison I can make is the original Star Wars (aka A New Hope) and Rogue One. Rogue One is a literal narrative prequel to A New Hope, but they are vastly different films made in different eras and with different technologies. I enjoyed both films a lot, but trying to compare them from a filmmaking perspective would be hopeless, and pointless, and trying to judge Rogue One through my nostalgia for A New Hope is equally pointless. They're both great films ... full stop. Frostpunk and Frostpunk 2 are both great games, full stop. And as long as I put my nostalgia for Frostpunk aside and just enjoyed Frostpunk 2, I had a good time playing it. My only material reservation is replayability as there appear to be less opportunities for replayability in Frostpunk 2 than in the original Frostpunk due to the move from city builder to city manager. But I don't have enough time in the game to make that judgement one way or another, so I'll put a pin in that issue and come back to it once I've played more hours. In conclusion, if you liked the original Frostpunk beyond it just scratching your city builder itch, then I think you will like Frostpunk 2. If you're looking for a gameplay and mechanics sequel, then you may be disappointed. And you may be disappointed initially anyway—as I was—but if you give it a chance I think Frostpunk 2 will quickly grow on you. But if it doesn't, I think that's perfectly fair—its a very different game. That said, I hope you do enjoy it :-)

_childDocuments_.review: I was apprehensive during the limited access beta, Now that the game's come out and I finished my first play through, I am ecstatic to say it is an excellent sequel to the beloved first Frostpunk.The game explores the growing societal and ideological struggles that arise when basic necessities are no longer the sole focus of every citizen. Survival is by no means guaranteed however, and you are thrust into a position of managing a growingly restless city while guaranteeing the survival of its very own citizens who are starting to take it for granted. The first game's no-brainer practical research trees or societal laws that align with an effective strategy are no longer obvious choices, as a bias towards a specific survival philosophy will alienate citizen factions who envision a different way of life with lasting consequences. Laws, buildings, and policies can have unforeseen second and third order effects that can spiral the city out of control. Diligent planning and politicking are key to forging the future that is now not only yours to decide.The game overall expands on the storytelling and mechanics that made the first one great. With the larger scale you lose some of the personal touch the first game had with every citizen. On the other hand however, this choice of scale helps the focus of the game, which serves as a perfect sequel to the first game's question of 'how will we survive', by asking: 'who will we become?' 11 Bit Studio offers another excellent introspective game that will see you fighting and adapting an environment where humans become just as dangerous as the cold.

_childDocuments_.review: It’s a  game, but I wouldn’t say necessarily better than original. Still very much worth buying.Gameplay loop is less about defeating frost and more about dealing with political factions, map exploration and multiple colonies. Yes all that district building and resource gathering and tech tree stuff is here, BUT the meat of the game is political system, buying people off, promising them stuff, stealing their money by force, slowly radicalising yourself untill you convince yourself prisons, propaganda and martial law are a necessity. This replaced the old law system and is very engaging, It’s perfect, though in many ways more flexible, which makes problem solving somewhat easier at times, but game can still humble you. Frostpunk 2 is set 30 years after the original and it delivers amazing experience in gameplay, audiovisually and in endless mode. It’s remarkably stable even before release date with only minor hiccups. With 3 major dlcs to come, the game will only get substantially better. _childDocuments_.review: This game scratches an itch I've had for over a decade at this point. Of doing proper city management (or in this case, cities), while also doing genuinely engaging and challenging political maneuvering that is inherent to a representative democracy. Is this nerdy as ♥♥♥♥? Absolutely. But it makes literal politics, not boring. Ideas on how to solve problems is a political affair. And there's consequences to taking less productive options, just to ensure a faction stays on your good side. Let alone the ever present allure of being able to centralize power in your own hands, chip away at the fragile democracy you've been chosen to safeguard... until there's only a hollow shell of it left, and you've created a dictatorship in all but name. And once you've done so... there's no going back. Its deliciously bleak, while also remaining oddly hopeful, in a way these talented ♥♥♥♥♥ over at 11bit knows how to nail. Because you will find endless pointless suffering. Remnants of the long dead on the frozen dying earth, but also endless resistance to giving up. Countless examples of people wanting to fight on, in spite of it. For a future. For principle. Or hell, just for their own damn happiness once in a while... and that's where the conflict comes in, since not everyone agrees on what they fight for, even looks like. If you like feeling the tension of fending off frost, famine, and filibusterers... This is a game for you. And I know its a game for me, specifically. No seriously, they bored holes in my brain, and checked off every damned box they could find. Its incredible. I will buy ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ every damn DLC for this game, the nanosecond they come out, because I'll be eating good for sure. Best roasted rat in all of New London I hear!

_childDocuments_.review: I still remember the first time I send the people to gather coal in Frostpunk, the emotions I felt when I saw them walking through that thick snow, it immediately made me think "these guys (the devs) nailed it". That sensation is missing from Frostpunk 2. The social/moral choices don't really matter. For example if you follow the merit path and try to keep your people focused on their individual strenghts, you'll end up creating a servant faction! How does that even make sense? Are the devs trying to tell us something? The game feels pointless, there is no urgency, no impending doom no real sacrifise.At the end of Frostpunk you felt that there was hope, even if you made hard choises (like sending children to fix the generator moments before everything collapsed). _childDocuments_.review: Building upon the first games survival style city builder, with a dash (a lot) of politics, in my opinion this is one the best sequels ever made for a game. At times, it feels like I am struggling to fend off the cold and other times I feel like I am playing Roman Senator simulator and sometimes both of these things clash at the same time. Makes for some real tense moments that don't fade away after one play through. Just realize, you are no longer the captain. You are not in total control like before. Instead of hundreds, you have tens of thousands, and instead of single buildings, you have entire districts. Its FP1, scaled up in a massive way with new buildings, tech, and politics. I don't know what else to say. It is an amazing game, and for fans of the first game, this is a MUST have.

_childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately, Frostpunk 2 has to be a 'not recommended' from me. I really liked the first game even though I was never competent or patient enough to do the harder difficulties or challenges - just getting through the base game was fun enough for me. Where Frostpunk was more comparable to classic city builders where you have individual control over the placement of buildings and can interact with the individual citizens, Frostpunk 2 is closer to games like Cities Skylines - you clear ground, place Districts, and then largely just sit back and wait while those things happen. The events that cropped up in Frostpunk still happen, but of the 5 or 6 that happened I only got to make a choice on one of them (the rest were essentially just warnings about supply levels, all of which I was just waiting on construction to compensate for already) and even that was a 'this decision will affect future decisions but not affect anything you're actually running into right now' decisions.It's entirely possible there's more direct involvement in everything available past the prologue and that it becomes more fun then, but if a game's prologue couldn't hold my interest then I'm not going to sit through it and risk outrunning Steam's refund window 'just in case it gets more fun.' _childDocuments_.review: I finished Frostpunk 2's story mode. I didn't like it quite as much as the first one, but it's very good. The game still manages to capture the feeling of "I am *not* secure and I need to scramble to survive" most of the time, while doing it in a slightly different mode than the first one. The scale is much larger and takes place over months/years instead of days. On top of the usual problems of Don't Freeze or Starve you now get to deal with balancing factions in the populace. My biggest problems had to do with unclear mechanics for actions in the game but fortunately the tips section in-game and the internet had me covered. 8/10 a good time.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is excellent - do not listen to the 2-hours-on-record reviewers who expected the same game as last time, with a new skin. This is how you make a sequel - you push the concept in a new and exciting direction while maintaining the spirit and feel of the old game! This is an excellent and deep city buidling, reminding me of the early days of the genre in the 90's. Yes, there is a deep political system to understand, but once you do, the system does a great work at puting the different factions in your city at odds with each other, with you trying to minimize the damage....or just taking outright control. Some people have complained about that the placement of buildings doesnt matter, that the game is simple to beat without spending time with careful placement. There is a solution to that, obviously...increase the difficulty. I have tried the highest difficulty, and trust me, at that point every single decision and buidling has to be very thought through. 11/10, would incarcerate, sterilize and exile the opposition again.

_childDocuments_.review: 30 years... after the captain's death, everyone thought it was time for change... LOL, no)) Who will work the mines for you!? GET TO WORK NOW!We built a parliament. Just like in the 'good old days' my parents told me about. People now feel they have more control over the city, to the point that instead of debates, we had a bear fight in the center of the hall, thanks to the icebloods. On one hand, it's democracy! On the other hand, where’s my law banning bears?Little Timmy complained about harsh working conditions. I gave him a teddy bear, and miracle of miracles – now he's ready to work even harder! Maybe we need to invest more in teddy bears or reform the pay system. Teddy bears for every home!We're running low on coal. We need to send people to explore new lands. There are some particularly dangerous areas... and that's great! We can send a few protesters – if we're lucky, we'll get resources; if not, at least there will be fewer problems! Maybe we should include this in management textbooks?You know that moment when you think your city is the only one to survive the Great Storm, and then you find a group of people saying: 'Hello! We've been here for 30 years and everything is great!' They live in their futuristic cities, everything runs on renewable energy, and instead of sawdust soup, they have hot chocolate... Our people were shocked. They even had a dinosaur! Though it turned out to be a set for some trailer filming... but I said: 'No, we stick to our traditions: freezing, fighting for every piece of coal, and building generators!' How could we betray the old ways where every day is a new challenge? So, we erased that settlement from the map.The situation is critical. A new storm is approaching. Everyone gathered to vote on an emergency survival plan. The life-and-death question turned into a circus: half the council argued about whether to vote now or wait until the temperature dropped to -200 degrees for scientific experiments. One council member’s flashlight broke and they weren’t allowed to vote. And someone just went for lunch because they found the vote too stressful. 50 votes 'for', 48 'against', one absent and one undecided because they still couldn't decide if the storm is real. The law rejected. And now we're waiting for the storm, discussing whether those teddy bears will save us...

_childDocuments_.review: After finishing the Campaign and nearly completing one of the Utopia modes with under 14 hours since launch, I can definitely recommend this game in its current state.A lot of people are complaining about two main things:- FP1 vs FP2- the politicsLet's get it straight, FP2 is the sequel to FP1; it is not a rendition or an overhaul of it. It's not as simple as comparing Cities Skylines 1 vs Cities Skylines 2, where you can lazily compare the introduction of new mechanics, assets, graphics, optimization, etc. It is a different game within the same backdrop, lore, and world-building of FP1.With that said, it is still a survival game, but survival is heavily predicated on the politics/Factions component of it. How you survive is up to the choices you make based on the RNG Policies you enforce, the Laws you enact, and the Research you unlock and decide to employ - which are all based on the Trust of your community and the gravitas you hold with the multiple Factions.Factions are split up into two sides, with subfactions aligned closely to the two main "head" Factions. I'll admit, my first playthrough it was excruciatingly annoying and challenging to deal with. I did have to save scum the campaign. However, once I figured out how to play within the faction system through the Campaign and some failed playthrough in Utopia, it became an engaging and fun game to play. I think people get intimidated by the Factions with how demanding and polarizing they are, a lot of times it feels like you'll have to undo everything you've done to ephemerally please one side, but I promise you, if you stick it out long enough, survive the Whitefrost a few times, you'll be able to make it through... either with one main faction, both main factions, or unity under your rule. The game can be very punishing, but it can similarly also be very rewarding. You really need to understand the technology tree and what is unlocks for you. Your resources will run out eventually, the weather will get harsher, and the politics will get more demanding; you will need to expand, set up Settlement Outposts (not to be confused with Cities - and is something you research), and you will need to drop the mix/max mentality. Dedicating resources to exploring the massive and unlockable map will provide you with more lore, a sustainable (unlimited and permanent) amount of resources in some cases, the potential to expand, and a plethora of decisions for short-term or long-term sustenance. My only suggestion to the Devs for user retention at this moment would be to dial down the negative effects of Factions in the early game. I think people playing this game are just giving up the moment a few series of Faction decisions hinder them from playing the way they think things should go. And to be frank, I was so ready to leave a negative review, but I stuck with it, and actually find it as a game I can positively recommend.Edit: will review again after significant patches :)

_childDocuments_.review: Having played through the story twice (there is enough mechanical difference to make it interesting I think) I would say it is a good game and a worthy successor to the first frostpunk. However, that comes with two caveats. First, this is NOT just another frostpunk. The mechanics are quite different (hexagonal building area in a wider zone vs the cramped circular system around the generator), how you arrange things is quite different, and so are some of your goals. It is also more zoomed out, less of the personal touch to citizens.  Second, this game lacks a moment similar to the climax of the first game. I feel like the end conflict is a bit too obvious (both from the game itself and the advertising), yet you can do nothing to avoid your city erupting into civil war. The storm from the first game was sort of a blindsiding threat, combined with the fact you were constantly having both predictions and the storm itself get worse. It was a genuine test of your skills, and I feel like this is less of one. And a bonus note; I only just realized you can select individual council members and get story about them.

_childDocuments_.review: Frostpunk 2 is not a perfect game. However, it is far, far better than the people complaining about it being "too different" say it is. Its story is rich and the city building mechanics are fun. That said, it is not as deep as Frostpunk 1 was, with city building being simplified to make room for a political system. I personally like the political system, I think it is possibly one of the deepest political systems in a city building game. A lot of the "radical ideas" don't seem to have a massive impact on gameplay, despite having a big ethical impact, and I think that's a huge missed opportunity. The presence of radical ideas also limits how much research you can really do, since there is not as much non-radical research to make up for it imo. The distribution of radical ideas is also super strange- why are there so few radical ideas for equality? It might just be that I haven't used utopia builder too much, but considering that The Last Autumn was a fantastic portrayal of actual ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ communism, it's weird that equality in this game can't go further than stopping resource hoarding. All of that pales in comparison to the biggest problem I have with this game: It's not hard enough. I beat the story mode on officer difficulty second try, and beat it on captain after three. That's just not hard enough. And yes, a lot of that difficulty comes not just from trying to survive, but to keep as many people alive as possible. Even still, when you know your city will be okay, it doesn't feel as worrying. I think people should be more angry about deaths, and votes of confidence should be more common. All of this can be fixed with updates. I still think the game is worth it full price, but at the moment it's an 8/10 sequel to a 10/10 game. Frostpunk 2 is a very, very good game, but know that just because you liked Frostpunk 1 doesn't mean you will like Fp2.

_childDocuments_.review: Frostpunk 2 is a step back from the first one. It's greatly lacking in a tutorial at the beginning and expects players to understand what to click and where to place districts. What's sad about this is that they have a prologue city that they could have expanded the tutorial for, but they decided to skip any instruction or guidance. The cities have set resources, and it lacks any customization that the first Frostpunk had. When you build, you're building on hexagon tiles to create districts, and placing these tiles will automatically create all buildings and roads. There is no real management of each disctrict. Within the first Frostpunk, you would need to employ citizens, manage heat levels, there was a real intimacy within the city's success. With this one, you have a higher level of population, and you're really just setting districts down and forgetting them. There's no need to manage or even come back to them. You'll see hundreds of people die off at a time...and not care. Where as the first Frostpunk, it was a HUGE deal anytime someone died and it really effected everything in the city. The exploration is so frustrating. It's a massive space that you can explore and find resources, and is really incredible! But you can't zoom out to see the whole thing. So once you have started really moving out, it's such a hassle to track where you have been, what locations you've already settled. A zoom would fix a lot here. They also added a system to ship resources from locations and settlements to your cities, which again, very cool. But when starting there is no instruction on how to do this. They just expect players to know how to use these little pitons, know how far it can go, to know what already has connections and what doesn't (there is no clear indication of already established routes, and it lets you build right over them, wasting resources). Adding new settlements REALLY bogs down play. The more settlements you manage, the more laggy the game gets. Especially during these whiteouts. I was playing through Utopia with one settlement and a whiteout occurred, the game froze for about 10 minutes before it could continue, and after that it was laggy the rest of the way through the whiteout. That's when I just gave up on the game. All in all, it's a completely different game from the first Frostpunk, so some people will love the changes, and some will not. I personally feel like they tried to add too many new things into one game, and the stress and tension I felt playing the first frostpunk is non-existent with this second one. There is just not enough intimate management for me to care about any of the people, or the cities. I set districts down, I leave them, I find a new settlement, I set districts down in the new settlement, rinse and repeat.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, the story has several great improvements, like a parliament, a new major resource, and a more complicated system of laws. A whole new political game takes place within your game, where you have to balance the relationship between factions, and make deals to pass your laws. If you are looking for a unique city-state builder, this game has got it.Why a negative review? Minor nitpicks concern the game's UI, or design of the buildings: this just doesn't feel as gritty as the first game. Instead of planning individual buildings, we are placing a whole district in tiles of an arbitrary number. Sure, that's fine, but I can't plan my city as closely. On a larger scale, the greatest negative departure from the first game is the lack of connection with your citizens. Unfortunately, this game doesn't feel as personal as the first Frostpunk, which I loved. The fact that I can't see individual settlers, name individual automatons, or customize them in any way - is a major downgrade. The game is stressful, but it could be worth it if you could connect with your citizens on some level. I used to name citizens after my friends, or I made up fictional characters with background stories about them, which gave me extra purpose to keep them alive. In Frostpunk 2, some council members have generated backgrounds, but you have no control over it. They just felt like faceless, nameless numbers, a statistic and nothing more. Death of 60 people due to frost shouldn't feel like an annoying notification in the early game that you just brush away with annoyance.

_childDocuments_.review: Freezing to Death has never been so fun!A fantastic game with a few issues. One thing to be aware of is that this is a very different game from the first game. You play on a much larger scale than the first. Despite the differences, I gave it a chance and after a few hours of tinkering and experimenting I fell in love. I think the overall presentation and the story are a major improvement and are top notch! The basic gameplay systems could perhaps use a little tweaking. If you aren't sure about this one you might want to look up some gameplay first to see if it is something you would like, particularly because it is so different from the first. One big struggle for me was the tutorial system, Even after going through the prologue and reading the tutorial pages I still found myself googling things often to figure out things that should have been simple like using the scroll wheel to look through new improvements since they aren't all shown to you. Building in general can be a little more tedious since you have to research not just buildings and improvements, but ideas which you then have to pass into law. It feels like a step or two has been added to what was sometimes already a tedious process. Some resources are not explained very well particularly in what they do or how to obtain them. The only thing that I consider a failure is the optimization for mac. I have a PC (Ryzen 7, 64GB Ram) at home and a MAC laptop (M1, 16 Gb Ram) I take on the go for work. On my PC I had a few little technical glitches like slowdowns but nothing crazy. I played about 60% of the game and ruined my situation so royally I decided to start a new playthrough on mac. On my mac I experienced several crashes in the later section of the game to the point I had to start saving every 2-5 minutes whenever I made any progress or it would all be lost. If you're playing on mac you may want to wait a little longer until the bugs are sorted out with this one. All that said, I'm looking forward to future updates! I can't wait to see what comes next.

_childDocuments_.review: The negative reviews are just dumbasses who can't understand parts of the game, always make sure to check their playtime before believing anything like "resources don't matter" or claiming that the political factions do nothing, because I can assure you they DO matter and they can ♥♥♥♥ you over if you don't manage them. The original frostpunk was the survival of a city, it's flat out ignorant and stupid to expect the 2nd to be the exact same when that goal was already accomplished. People that look at the game are whine that the immersion is different cannot see the bigger picture of the game and rather choose to complain about it being different from the 1st, it's incredibly frustrating to see an amazing addition to the first game be criticized over half assed ideals and opinions.Resources are a long term problem because they're supplying a society now, not just a city. Now there is a flaw with the game, it can feel very repetitive when starting out or in a long running game. The first frostpunk had this same issue don't get me wrong, but it seems pretty noticeable in this one. Not to say it's ruining the game in the slightest, it actually gives you some breathing room to figure out your gameplan. But I can understand people's problem with thisHappy steam awards everybody!

_childDocuments_.review: A very cool game( haha) with interesting features. The game is a direct sequel, 30 years passed since we saved the people from the cold. But things were not easy, people managed to build more and expand but ultimatly are stuck in the same position as before. The game also switches from steampunk to dieselpunk.I played and showed the game modes here I also started a lets play on the hardest difficulty after experimenting about 5 hours Pros: great atmosphere, great story, interesting building mechanics, hard to manage the city but it becomes easier once you unite the people wich is the main goal, game looks nice and it really feels and looks cold, definetly created it's own genre: the polar city building survival wich is a great thing!Cons: mostly depends on what you expect but the game has too much down time,  you are mostly waiting for a few extra heatstamps(money from stamps) to build something or for the council to vote for a new law to help us.Not having enough survival or building made me give the game an 8/10 instead of an 9/10, the gameplay is just too static. Voting is RNG so sometimes you need to promise another technology to get a vote through wich will delay the game even more so  a lot of time is spent passing time.Another problem is that the game performance is pretty bad so you have to enable scaling and frame generation wich makes the game look blury.Neutral: Exploration of the map could have been better as well, you have a chance to find many things but then you can also make outposts to send back resources. The problem is that this becomes extremly slow and clunky with building connecting points between them and the city.Game is hex grind based now, you frostbreak and build on grids whole sectors now between 3-6 slots. While not necesarly bad, it tends to dumb down the game a lot in the begining and later you can build special buildings in these hexes.Overall the game is great and its worth playing but i am not sure it's worth the full price. The base game has 5 chapters in the campaign and 7 scenarios but they are not as fun or unique as frostpunk 1. Playing the game for long periods of time can be pretty boring. Campaign lenght is mostly dependant on difficulty but it's around 10 hours.I like it but i feel like they could have done more with the game, introduced more active mechanics and more things to do to advance the game faster. Sadly, it's not a big bang of a sequel, it's more or less the same quality as frostpunk 1 wich is great but could have been more.It used all it's goodwill with me, if they make another game i probably won't play it if it's in this style but this is a personal opinion.The game is not a strategy game, it's more like a sim or a civ game

_childDocuments_.review: I loved the first game, it was a gem, something unique, something intimate. Struggling to save your small group of people against all the odds. I didn't want FP2 to be exactly the same, that would be dull, but expected the sequel to evolve and keep the essence which made the first game a success, as most developers do, but...11 Bit thought it would be a great idea to strip away pretty much everything that made the first game so special and turn Frostpunk 2 into some sort of numbers game, a visual spreadsheet if you will. I don't care about the people any more, why should I, they are just a number in the top left of the screen.Politics takes a front seat and so now the citizens are just cannon fodder while factions fight for power. Most of your time is spent fulfilling objectives and then just waiting for something to happen, some text will pop up, you read it and you don't care. Nothing really seems to have any impact.Disappointed is an understatement.

_childDocuments_.review: I was done in 8 hours,I am confusion. I am disappointment.(Spoilers for Frostpunk 2 campaign and game mechanics ahead, read it with that in mind)The following review is about the story mode of Frostpunk 2. (and nothing else)- - -A lot of the mechanics from the first game are removed. There is no "building automatons" now, you will occasionally hear people talking about them and they just exist but never really adressed. They tried framing it as "automated workforce" but it beats the purpose of having robots if both them and the people are going to be counted under the same category. There is a certain law that occasionally reduces population, meaning those "automated workforces" (whatever they are, as they are never explained) will go down as well just like usual workers.Progression is very linear and doesn't take long whatsoever. As I have stated in my opening, it took me 8 hours to play through the story. There are 5 chapters and 1 prologue (which is basically a tutorial area). Construction elements are heavily simplified into districts, now you are not allowed to build individual buildings and need to specify districts in a hexagonal grid-like map area. There are building elements which are forced to be built onto specific districts, each district can accomodate a single building and this goes up to 2 when upgraded. (Residential ones often can have a maximum of 1). This severely limits building usage as players will be forced to create new districts (which takes away workforce) just to place down a building.They also introduced Frostbreaking which just feels like is there to make the game feel longer than it actually is. They don't contribute to anything, and feels like they were added just for the Winterhold section as the devs needed some way to stall the players.UI elements are unclear, as resource symbols are very similar to one another. They for some reason introduced new materials instead of just using what they had. Which causes issues with the words used to describe them.There is a significant problem with audio rendering. Which seems to occur during or after autosaves which will ruin your entire experience until it decides to stop. It basically creates this white-noise like popping sounds as a part of the ambient or environmental sounds.You can construct paths for scouts and they even added "airways?" but you can't even see them in the game. Kinda feels pointless if they are to be hyped that much.Research tree is also disappointing. With less of everything, you have the tree narrowed down into several choices now. As an example, single research node for house insulation compared to 3 or more in the first game.There is a council mechanic now, which is supposed to give people a sway on the decisions of the city. But you can get around this by supporting one faction continuously. Last chapter features a "civil war" scenario (which was one of the side stories in the first game).Music tracks are also meh, not sure if they tried getting Piotr Musial again and the guy said no. So they resorted to "Piotr Musial at home" probably. Tracks try to mimic the feel of the first game, but none of them really have unique or identifiable features. They all sound the same basically.Performance is not ideal either. Game can ramdomly froze if an autosave happens to align with you trying to click an icon. This locks the UI and you can't click on anything. But the autosave also struggles to save properly, taking even longer than usual. (Because 200 years of game development experience imaright lads)They tried the good old appeal to emotion fallacy with a baby who is born during the start of your rule and grows up until the end of the story to around teen ages. Game tries to trauma dump you with your choices but you really couldn't care less of a character who is so randomly placed into the game, never interacted with you or has been affected by your choices.Remember how in the first game sending a kid into the engine to fix the core and prevent overheat failures were one of the most heartbreaking things? Ah yeah, about that... uhm... how should I put it.... well, this game, has... NONE OF THAT. I can't stand how the core part of frostpunks gameplay can be removed just like that. If there are no hard decisions, if there are no tradeoffs, if there are no human lives being at risk then what makes this game Frostpunk? It is just in the name and nowhere else. It is a soulless piece of .... you get the point.Resources feel somewhat limiting at the start, but once you find exploration areas with the said resource, the scarcity becomes obsolete. Once you also obtain oil and finish Winterhold to upgrade the engine, the sense of struggle fades away. Long story short, the resource needs are there for show in the early stages of the game.The "Faith vs Order" mechanic from the previous game is also narrowed down (ikr can they stop with this downgrading ffs).The city also has these "energy lines?" (thats the best we can describe it) that are around the central city area and extended towards the outer segment automatically during expansion. What are these? Why are they there? Do they transfer heat? If so, why are they built automatically, shouldn't they cost something?Connected to the previous point, there is no longer a cold-factor for work places. Which makes worker heat requirements non-existent. I'm not sure if this has something to do with the previous point. But the fact is that, the need to heat up workplaces  and ensure efficient production areas was a significant part of the gameplay in the first game. Removing this meant that there is no downside to placing these district wherever you want. (Excluding the "near district" heat buff and "contamination" debuffs for production districts)They were also talking about a train before the release? I'm really wondering how hard they were coping at the time. With such a lame gameplay, a train is just what we need to save the day.There is no trust and discontent anymore, only trust. Which simplifies the problems you face as now you only need to watch a single resource. With the new law system, there is no building cemeteries or building more sickbeds for the ill; you just pass laws and problems disappear magically. So the trust meter doesn't really get affected by the actual problems, it instead goes down if you don't let people pass the laws they want. It is not the solution that satisfies the public, but the idea of a solution. (Which doesn't make sense in the logic of Frostpunk, as it is supposed to be taking a realistic approach.)They also hyped this "Steward" term a lot, as if it has some form of deeper meaning. But no it was just to raise artifical hype for the release.(I really feel like I'm missing more negatives here)Exploration is limited like the first game. People were asking for the ability to add different colonies and expand upon the world, instead of that, the devs added 2 areas mandatory for the main quest and forced locked the areas with limited reasources so that the most these places can become are outposts dependant on the main city. (Which defeats the pur... I think you get it with how many times this happened by now)-District mechanics, as well as the narrowing of the tech tree seems to have diminished the gameplay value greatly. Game is relatively shorter and has less depth. People just wanted more Frostpunk, and it feels like they made a Chinese knock-off or something.If you are enjoying the game, then go ahead.I just couldn't see my money's worth in this. It doesn't feel like a finished game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game isn't bad, and if you like the world of Frostpunk you will probably like this game. However if you wanted more of FP1, you will be disappointed. _childDocuments_.review: Original Frostpunk is a masterpiece, and this sequel is just ok.A few new mechanics are interesting, but some are just boring chores and anything but fun. _childDocuments_.review: I would like to give this a 'Neutral' rating. I've completed the main story on the Captain difficulty (Hardest) and have some thoughts, there will be some spoilers ahead. Straight up, it's not a bad game, and I can tell a lot of thought has gone into the new systems, specifically with the council mechanics; however, the phrase "as wide as an ocean, as deep as a puddle" comes to mind.Starting with the bad, the story feels weaker than it does in its predecessor. There were a few moments in the main story where events didn't quite make sense and felt forced for the sake of causing an artificial sense of trouble in your city. The weakest part of the game for me was the start of Winterhome. There is little lead-up to this point in the story, and the reasoning for going there is that it somewhat aligns with the reformist faction and their idea of expanding into the wasteland. This would be alright if it weren't for the fact this is never mentioned previously in the game, and when it is mentioned, there is no build-up; simply 'go there and colonise it'.They have this excellent council system in the game, and winterhome would have been a good opportunity to utilise this. Depending on your standing with the factions up to this point, you would put these choices to a vote, and you would have to promise to do certain things in winterhome when you got there as a consequence of getting people to vote to colonise it.Other than the story, the move away from traditional micro city builder to macro is an interesting choice that could have worked well if a bit more fleshed out. Currently, the district system feels bland, and the expansion mechanics to allow buildings to be placed in them seem strange. The trade-off appears to be that tile space and heat are the limiting factors, yet space is not an issue in the game. I reached the end with 1/4 of the map used, and the heat mechanics, even on the hardest difficulty, can be mitigated by sniping a few key techs. Instead of having to expand districts to get the buildings inside of them, the buildings themselves should have their own tiles that provide an aura effect like the hubs do; this would give you a reason to plan your housing districts instead of house next to house for heat.The UI is one of the weakest areas of the game. For systems such as law, research and frost teams, which are critical to your survival, there is no notification or indication that any of these things are available. The amount of times I missed these because there's simply no noise or visual indicator and had to reload because I missed valuable weeks' worth of time is just poor. I don't know how this got past the QA because these systems are so critical to progressing in the game. For reference, Frostpunk 1 had a loud noise and big indicator to show when frost teams or research were available.Moving onto the good, the graphics and general ascetic are perfect for the setting. Snow howls across your screen, and during whiteouts, you can see the snow rolling in the harsh winds; the addition of being able to physically see the frostland map when zoomed in is a nice touch. I can tell this is where a lot of the focus went.The council mechanics are cool, and I like the voting for and against minigame with promises, as this does affect your build sequence through the game. I often had to decide between researching key techs or the ones I had promised to a faction, which is a nice little tradeoff. Sometimes, it was hard to discern why a specific faction liked/disliked a law, but I think the information is buried in the UI.In conclusion, I have seen others say this doesn't feel like Frostpunk, and I have to agree. One of the things that made the first game so appealing was the feeling of being on the brink of survival, which you don't get in Frostpunk 2. There's no 'soul', as I see people describe it, just a reduced-down version where one death was a tragedy in the first game; now in this game, it's just a statistic amongst thousands.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Much more abstract than the first game by necessity, given the scale is much broader. A lot of reviews are thumbing down because of this, but what else could they have done? For a sequel they either would have needed to go much more micro in scale, or macro. Macro was the most natural evolution for the series.So far it's a bit easier as a result. It's completely possible that some wrench will get thrown into the campaign later on that upends everything, as often happens in FP1. But I'm kinda enjoying the fact that trial and error isn't so necessary here. In FP1, you absolutely had to know how and when certain disasters are triggered, not so much to ensure a win but rather to simply avoid losing. In FP2 intuitive planning is rewarded, and I'm enjoying this approach rather than simply failing a run and memorizing event triggers for the next attempt.

_childDocuments_.review: These games are just great.  I really appreciate the detail that goes into the theme and story of both FP1 and FP2. I think if you allow that it isn't the same game as FP1, you can really enjoy FP2.  This game is great if you enjoy resource management, research, and diplomacy games.
