_childDocuments_.review: I want to love it because the first one was so special but I can't recommend it due to UI/UX issues, stability/lag, poor scenario design, and overall lack of replayability. Honestly pretty disappointing. UI/UXLack of information and poor wayfinding are a consistent problem. I won't list them all but here's one small but very annoying example: the game will often show an icon above a district indicating a problem, but the icon isn't clickable and is actually positioned such that attempting to click it selects a different district, forcing you to click around a whole bunch, reading each info panel, in an attempt to select the correct one. Also, it's very hard to know what buildings are where... it would have been so easy to make them a little more visibly obvious but often to find something you have to click in to every similar district and look at its info panel to find a specific building. In a game that depends entirely on finding a precarious balancing point on a lot of different metrics at once, there is virtually zero visual feedback when placing buildings, adjusting sliders, etc.INSTABILITYEvery time the game auto-saves, everything totally freezes and it's a 3-5 second lag. Frequent audio bugs, everything from distortion to certain sounds continuing to play forever even after their context has ended. The most annoying of these is the chorus of voices shouting "SteWard, sTewArD, stEwaRD!!!" over and over. Most of these audio bugs require a full exit/relaunch.SCENARIO DESIGNWithout giving away too many spoilers, the sets up a final "crisis" for you that can be completely nonsensical given the state of your game. You can have a population that completely loves you and is completely happy, and they will start to riot anyway because of sCenAriO and even if you get them to completely happy again, the process will repeat forever  until you do one of a few specific actions. It's pretty dumb and immersion-breaking and feels very on rails in a bad way.CHOICESWhile there are a few major choices that affect how the overarching story-line plays out, everything else just feels like splitting hairs. The split/factional research tree and buildings really feel like the only reason to choose one thing or another is to placate whichever group you currently need favor with. There are a small number technologies where one choice or the other is more situationally helpful but most just have small differences in their numeric bonus.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Recommend, great game but not FP1. Game is a resource and city/city state management game instead of more of a survival game (Still is in some ways). Think FP1 but on a much larger scale where the end of the game in FP1 is just a regular thing now.I played the first one quite a bit, and pretty much got winning down to a T. This game is much more a politics simulator and hub management than the previous style of city building. With that being said, I find this game significantly harder. There are tons of long term cascading affects that will happen by ignoring a small thing like goods. Now you have less money, now people are arguing, now there are protests and you have less workers to meet the tasks at hand and it may become a death spiral if you aren't careful. Needless to say I love it but it is a quite bit different from the first game so keep that in mind. I believe it is so much different there should be a demo if I am being honest.*SMALL SPOILERS BELOW*With all that being said, I took the "American route" if you will. I went religious route for the city and just as in real life the religious people are easily manipulated as long as you let them do their prayers publically and do small things for them you can lie say you support them and pass laws completely opposed to their views and they won't be mad at all and they will continue supporting you as a goddess on the Earth. I love how realistic this. Great job devs! The radical non scientific faction in the game are also the complete opposite and will get mad about every little thing you do that they don't like and will actively try to protest against you. You can make everyone happy but it is VERY hard and requires really good resource management.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played Frostpunk 1 for over 500+ hours on both Steam and Non-Steam versions, and Frostpunk 2 is what I've been waiting for. The game features much better graphics, a larger city scale, and deeper legal, social, and technological systems. Your decisions continuously impact society.It's a very difficult game—you have to stay mindful. The scale is much larger than FP1. Instead of managing a small city with a population of 300-500+ people, you are now overseeing a state with a population of 1,000-10,000++. The population is divided into factions, and any laws you draft or actions you take must pass through the council by a majority vote.The deeper systems depict a society truly in the middle of a disaster. No one is entirely an enemy or a friend. The real enemies are hunger and cold, as it was in FP1, and the weapons to combat them are resource management, politics, and your decisions.The city-building system looks different, but the basics remain the same as in FP1. You don't build a city to look beautiful. There is no beauty in the main story—survival is your only goal. Proper management, not aesthetics, will make the city thrive and beautiful itself. YOU MUST BE MINDFUL! MUST GITGUD!I really enjoy the whole game, but my only complaint is that the camera movement feels slippery. When I press and release the movement key, the view doesn’t stop immediately, and the sliding effect is quite annoying.I'm a little sad that there's no thermal camera view anymore. Or am I just not finding it?

_childDocuments_.review: If you played Frostpunk before then it might be easier for you. I could never play the first game because of endless crashes. Luckily this iteration ran mostly smoothly.Pros1. Graphics/animations of the city are amazing and really hit home on what situation everyone's in2. Good story that drives you forward but also warns you when to proceed and if you might be ready or not3. Research tree actually carries progression and has a lot of customization to how you want to play4. Plenty of other small things that make gameplay great and immersion deeperCons1. The tutorial throws a few pictures at you and a LOT of words but nothing solid to help understand some systems in the game(law's, research, connecting nodes). I had to watch videos on youtube that explained it better in 30 seconds.2. There a lot of useless scouting spots around the map when you start exploring. I maybe only did 20% of them and started ignoring it because my economy was fine by itself.3. The storyline is great, but its a bit broad and you go from like -200% to literally 1000% chaos. I got lucky and had just randomly placed some district addons before i even knew what would happen. _childDocuments_.review: The game is really good, but how they force the story down your throat isn't.First things first, some actions that are NECESSARY to be successful can only be taken if you have already played, not because it is a mechanic u must learn, etc, it is simply because some events are completely unpredictable and can't be fixed if u didn't prepare for them. If u have kept crime low and haven't built any prisons, when the civil war starts u can't stop battles because u don't have any prisons. -u also can't predict this-Secondly, if u have managed to keep good balance between all factions during the story, the civil war starts anyway and u will get extreme tension penalties so that it can happen. But story mode ends up being frustrating if you try to keep balance between factions, because u end up with the same endgame situation and with ur position weakened, since no faction completely rallies behind u...

_childDocuments_.review: Nah! Very disappointed me and I wish I could refund it . Very generic,  no freedom to build , I hate tiles! Why did you add the tiles ? You made a great game Very miserable.  Why would they take all the good out of feostpunk and replace it with very common and similar mechanisms like other boring RTS ? Because it's about money , they have rushed this one to make quick money.  It's all generic , you don't control anything.  I hate tiles!!! Don't buy it , buy the first one which is on sale . Feels like original company was sold to some money hungry , untalented developers who used the credit of first frost Punk love and care that was given in to it and made Frost Punk 2 very quickly.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: The game is different from the 1st one. The scale being far greater makes it lose a bit of the "organic" feeling you had when seeing the black smoke escaping the generator, or the coal stacks accumulating in the snow, in the 1st one.But honestly it's the only negative thing I can find about this game. They renewed themselves, and it worked wonders. I still didn't finish the main campaign but the story is great (the end of the world is far from finished). The new building system with the districts works well. The council mechanic to enact laws is good and interacts really well with the factions mechanic. You can also colonize outposts and develop them at the same time as your main city, and I love that.Also it's still beautiful, and there's still this satisfying feeling of knowing you have enough resources, at least for now.10/10 would freeze again.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a lot different from the first game in a lot of ways, but that's not necessarily a bad thingYes, you don't have to take care of every single person in New London or build hospitals when the number of sick people grows. You don't have to build new hunting houses when food is low.Fine, but you have other problems to deal with. There's politics involved. You're balancing on the edge between the different views of the political parties. If you try to get along well with one, the others don't like it, and complain unbelievably and give you a hard time. And riots in your city are the last thing you wantOverall, I think Frostpunk 2 is a game that deserves attention. While some people are bothered that it's not more like the first game, I think if it was going to be like the first game, they wouldn't need to make a new game, but rather DLC. New game, new mechanics, new story. I give this game a solid 9/10
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely love the game to bits. It is a gorgeous game. They are still updating the UI and it is getting better with each patch. In some ways I think the campaign should be a bit longer. It has a nice build up from the prologue through to maybe chapter 3? But once you hit a certain point you have to rush then you solve that situation but its basically caused tensions to rise and it makes me think I should have just focused on exploring more. I admit to playing on easy but there are a fair amount of mechanics and I wanted to see as much as I could in the first run. It is a little disappointing how zoomed out you are in comparison to New London from the past, but I still felt very involved. I kind of wish there were more factions to be honest, unless I did something wrong I ended up with 5 and the majority of the game I had 3. I expected at least 1 or two more.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: There are already dozens upon dozens of reviews writing about the exact same thing I have problems with, so I'll keep this very brief by saying just this one thing: way too many features crammed into way too small a room causes balance problems and makes the game feel quite unfair in the utopia builder
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Love the new direction 11bit took this game and the courage to make it something different. Awesome visuals, super engaging game play, and the faction and council system is a really interesting take on power that serves as an excellent reflection of modern politics without being preachy or ham-fisted.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not sure what the direction this game is going in but it feels like it doesn't understand what made its predecessor so successful. The old constructing building function was swapped for some zone system and i constantly feel that i don't have enough manpower to do ANYTHING in the game. I'm just watching a city i have no control over for most of the gameplay. Hopefully i am an isolated incident here and everyone else gets the mechanics and enjoys the game but i do not.... at all.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Everything in this game is OK/mhe the only thing that pulls it up form a 5/10 to a 7/10 Is the aesthetic. But it lacks the soul and immersion witch the first game had. Its not City-builder, Its not a "decision game".... The closes it gets to a genre is resource management, But it all lacks complexity to be a strategy game. Therefore it all feels like bissy work most of the time and you start to wonder " Who was the game designer to make this micromanage mess?". I forgot to add that nothing feels connected, One reason is the lack off complexity in management  and the lack off systems that supports ethoter. I whould ask "how can i make the game less tidius but still keep the same feel?" and "what change in some aspect to make it just a bit more deep?". Got 4 answers to it. 1 make the district more manageable with POP% (factions), Heat and buildings/inporvment. 2 I whould have Classes (Rich,poor ECT) like the first game and also factions. 3 let the exploration be passive but you chose how menny goes to supplying and maping. 4 make the smaller cityies shere the same stockpile as the main city, But you can manage the "reserve stockpile" when supplychain is getting cut. Its mostly to take away the constant attention you need for the samller city´s... or ateast some other chancesBut overal its a 7/10 good but the only thing special is the aesthetic
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: First off, lets get this out of the way.If you are coming from the first expecting the exact same game, you're going to be a bit if not completely disappointed. This game has a whole different scope and is a whole different game focusing heavily on the politics and whole city rather than caring about individual people in the city and the buildings like the first.While yes you are able to build within in a district, you can get through the game completely if not very far, building next to no buildings within districts, even on the higher difficulties.Unfortunately i am unable to lose myself in this game and lose track of the time like the first game, finding myself bored after playing only for a few hours at a time and needing to take a break.Recommend this solely because we can't just a mixed rating, and while it is vastly different than the first and a bit of a disappointment with the direction they took, it still is enjoyable to a certain point. I recommend giving it a try, but wait for a sale unless you have no doubt you will enjoy what you see.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Frostpunk 2 is a strange beast. On one hand it's a good game about large scale city management, social problems, and politics. On the other hand, its story, worldbuilding, and art design is much worse than the original and lacks the incredible vibes from the last game. The soundtrack, graphics, general sound design, UI, and polish (despite a good amount of late game chugging) are mostly pretty darn good. I've heard Frostpunk 1 described as "lightning in a bottle" and I'd have to agree with that, a perfect combination of story, worldbuilding, gameplay, difficulty, sound design, music, art style, everything. If you're looking for a near perfect post apocalyptic city builder play Frostpunk 1 but if you're looking for a better than average city builder with politics go for the second game,
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: I have 75 hours of play time on Frostpunk 1 and I could only give Frostpunk 2 about 3 hours before I realized it wasn't made for me. I'm sure the 2nd one has some excellent choices if you are a bit more numbers and systems oriented, but the whole game seemed like homework to me rather than a game. The onboarding experience was very flat and I wondered if that's what they ended up creating in order to get people adjusted to the UI? It felt rushed and didn't really cover information I felt like was deeply necessary to cover. In addition to that, a good portion of their onboarding was throwing walls of text at me in book form - that's fine, I guess you could argue it's like a board game at that point, and Im glad I am at least getting all the info I might need that way but it was off-putting for me in video game form, and really not selling me on a world I cared to keep playing.  The game got way too deep into macro mechanics and politics which is probably fun for some, but it felt like all the most boring parts of Star Wars was going to be thrown at me. Just not my thing personally. It's like the designers that got all the input in how the game played were the types who only stared at spreadsheets and forgot games are supposed to be fun? And one of the weirdest details that was removed were all the excellent audio cues and touches the first one had that really helped tie the environment and mood of the atmosphere together. Like, why? It ended up being part one of the many reasons this game felt soulless and lacking the vibe of the previous game. I perhaps need to give it more of a chance, but I pre-ordered this thing with high hopes excited to play in July, but also happy they were willing to push out the date to September to improve it. Great, make it better. But I'm playing it now in September and this is just not the game I wanted... I think it was meant for a different type of gamer. I will maybe give it another shot if there is a price drop but I knew within 3 hours I was going to hate a slog of breaking ice only to then be able to place buildings in very specific spots while being interrupted by a full council of 4 different factions that I needed to pay off to be quiet. I was more interested in maximizing saving tons of people from the previous game and enjoying how my black and white choices really impacted them and the city overall, not the minutia of the politics and number crunching.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: I spent a lot of time playing the first Frostpunk. It was one of the first games I bought after swearing off AAA studios and developers about 10 years ago. At the time, I was pleasantly surprised at the genuine love and care with which the original was designed and executed.I'm only about 12 hours into the sequel; but that 12 hours went by in a sitting before I realized it; if that tells you anything.The campaign is divided into chapters, and the chapters begin progressively throwing more and more complex problems at you. Your research and development aren't artificially gated; there's just never enough time to knock out one problem before the next rears its ugly head. The game forces players to make choices and sacrifices just due to the nature of the environment. Once you throw in political infighting; things get very complex very quickly.The music and sound design are pretty amazing, and never become sandpaper on the ears. All in all this is so far a fantastic game from developers that seem to take pride in the quality of their work.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Frostpunk 2 is a worthy successor to the original, with a slightly different but still captivating atmosphere.I completed the campaign on the hardest difficulty, and it was incredibly satisfying. Careful planning is essential—where and when to build can make or break your city's survival. Once you understand the game's mechanics, it becomes really fun to figure out clever ways to get through the political dilemmas.The campaign consists of five chapters, and each allows you to choose different paths for expansion. Even though it's a single main storyline, I noticed at least a dozen different ways it could end, which really changes the gameplay experience. I can't wait to try new ways of developing my city!The atmosphere is a bit less intense compared to the first game, but I still really enjoyed it. The music in Frostpunk 2 is still beautiful and enhances the experience, though the soundtrack from the first Frostpunk remains a true masterpiece that's hard to surpass.Overall, Frostpunk 2 delivers a solid experience, and I was happy to save some money with the deluxe edition!
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: It absolutely is not Frostpunk 1, and that is good. Frostpunk 1 was an amazing game and easily one of my all time favorites, but there was not much more to explore mechanically. Frostpunk 2 diverges by creating a fantastic strategic city builder that still captures the hopelessness while also being incredibly fun and different. I love the game, and if you enjoy Grand Strategy or games that focus heavily on strategy, then you will probably enjoy this game a lot.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: A fantastic follow up to Frostpunk, but keep in mind this is not a traditional city builder. It's much more of a strategy/4X/grand strategy style of game. There's a deep layer of politics, and the scale is way bigger than the original game. Expect a constantly shifting power dynamic while you struggle to expand New London and thrive!
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: This is not a city builder. This is a political simulator. Unfortunately, most of the time your decisions don't really matter that much either. The game feels empty and lifeless, and the frostbreaking mechanic needs to go away. It's such a waste of time. One positive? The graphics look okay. I'm definitely disappointed in this game. Especially since the first one was such a success.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: The worst aspects of this game can hopefully be fixed with patches, but right now it runs absolutely abysmally. It started out pretty good, but as the city expands, the issues mount. I have a good gaming PC but the game is struggling to run even on the lowest settings. The framerate is constantly dropping and the audio is constantly crackling and breaking up and these issues get worse and worse as the game progresses.Unfortunately, gameplay wise, this game is a mess. Overly complicated and bloated with far too many new mechanics that aren't explained properly. I can't stress how bad the game is at explaining the new mechanics and how fast I was overwhelmed even on the easiest difficulty (for anyone who thinks it's a skill issue, I regularly played multiple modes of the first Frostpunk on hard). The tutorial section of the game is also too short, poorly explained, and ends up completely disjointed from the main campaign. It has also lost a lot of the heart of the first game, with things now feeling more like Civ or Cities Skylines, with decisions having very little emotional impact due to the scale.The UI also needs a lot of work as it's very unclear what is happening most of the time. Important things are blocked from view at inopportune times and the camera is constantly moving around when trying to open information screens on various aspects of your city, you end up awkwardly chasing things around trying to re-manoeuvre the camera so that everything is in view. It needed more work before release, and the fact that this is what was released after a fairly long delay makes me wonder what sort of state it was in originally if this is what they have deemed publishable.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Democracy sucks. Everybody hates me. We die. Achievement earned: Have negative relations with all factions.I do enjoy it, but it's a completely different game: impersonal, politics, voting, more politics, more voting, civ-like strategy and not the good civ, but the one with districts, I hate the district idea in both games. Great graphics, beautiful interface, good UX, hey, give me back control over my city, what do you mean everyone's voting on the laws??I promised a faction that I would research some kind of crops. Could not for the life of me find that research option in the tree. They hate me now, I need a search bar in that idea tree.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Long due review.I enjoyed the game to a degree, and at the same time, I still feel Frostpunk 1 is the better game.Personally, I enjoy city building, and thinking of strategies of how my city should operate.So when I got this tech tree, and all the options, I get excited - what do I want the theme of my city to be?For instance - one such idea was to build a city that focused on reducing required resources. I found this idea fitting with a wasteland that has limited such resources.I like this about the game very much.But then, you get your factions. And the factions, well they have other plans. I personally get annoyed by the factions. I don't find it a fun game mechanic. I normally just end up building prisons and jailing them, so I can build the base I'd like to build.This is where I think Frostpunk 2 is not as fun as it's predecessor. I don't feel like I'm in control of my city - I feel like the factions are and their constant nagging for what it is they want - and their ability to completely lock down your city if you don't listen to them, especially on higher difficulties. This is why personally I enjoy the story mode a lot more than I do captains mode.So in such, Frostpunk 2 (especially in captains mode) is not so much a building sim, as it is a political sim, where I found myself constantly trying to appease factions, and finding a middle road, instead of, trying to build the city I myself envision.But then, the building is fun. It's not like 1, it's a bit different, but the puzzle aspect of building your districts and optimizing hubs, is a fun addition. I think the cracks in the landscape where you can build districts for an added heat bonus is fantastic. I think it's great that hubs stack. If you do it well you can put 3 heating hubs that affect 4 districts, and reduce their heat requirements by 120. Then you can micromanage these buildings towards your current heat requirement, to save it's materials cost. And this in turn reduces your coal/oil/steam requirements. I also really enjoy the addition of new fuel sources, although I do feel that there's not enough control as to which fuel resources are prioritized over others. (You can pick main resource, but that's about it, and often I find that it will use coal or oil, and completely neglect my steam output which then goes to waste.)I'm also personally not a big fan of outposts. (You have settlements, which are automatic, and outposts which you have to expand like you do your main city by building districts and creating an equilibrium, by either creating the necessary districts or sending available resources.).I think this mainly stems from a lack of visibility. There seem to be too little tools to really keep track of your colonies and their needs and demands, which makes keeping an eye on them a bit of a hassle.All in all, I can say I enjoyed the game. So it get's a positive from me, and personally, I hope, that someone will release a mod that removed factions from a play through, and perhaps adds UI elements to better track outposts.I also expect the DLCs the flesh things out a bit further, and that some bugs and nuisances that are currently still in the game will eventually get patched.That said - I do enjoy how the factions grow and evolve over the story - there's a theme and a personality.I just wish they where a bit less whiny.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: While the setting is cool, the game feels a bit underbaked. While the scale is cool and all, I feel more disconnected from the inhabitants of the town than something unimmersive like civ6. Camera controls are also a bit weird. You cannot zoom neither close in nor far out. Some gameplay mechanics seems buggy. Perhaps after a few patches it will be worth a revisit.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Great game. Game is super engaging and makes you feel like you're on the brink of failure with little moments of relief. The replay-ability is lacking after the campaign though, and the end of the campaign felt very abrupt. I was sad to stop playing my save without any continuation after the final milestone.There is a utopia mode, but it lacks a lot of what made the campaign great. The challenge is definitely there on captain difficulty, but it requires an almost perfect formulaic play through unlike the campaign. Campaign had some give for mistakes, tons of interesting POI's in the frost land (Some are even related to the factions in your settlement), an  I would love to see an option to continue after the campaign, and I think the utopia mode should reflect more of what made the campaign great (not including major story elements). I also would love to see some sort of major white-out events after the campaign and late into utopia mode. These could potentially destroy parts of your settlement, destroy settlements in the frost-lands and their connections. This would give you a refresh of POI's, things to fix or build, could potentially erode ideas you have unlocked and would be a great way to scale back someones progress after in the late game.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: I think my experience of Frostpunk 1 has lead to a disappointing playthrough of the 2nd. The game feels underwhelming & a few steps back in a few ways, especially when considering it took 3 years for them to design an entirely new game & mechanics that lack the soul the first game had.Bigger doesn't always mean better unfortunately, I miss being able to see your citizens actually trudging through the snow, slowly making a permanent path, the automatians from the first game seem to have vanished, buildings are all generic and all look the same only being identifiable by the 1 of 4 colours they will be, the new buildings hex system is a step backwards, it also seems that now ai operates the generator in the frost punk future as it's very limited in it's management settings & heating districts/ areas hardly even feels like a part of the game now with how the new heat & generator system work. I do not however hate the game, I did enjoy some aspects of it that made it feel more complex & fleshed out, like the council system, building new settlements & trade routes through the frost land however my biggest gripe with the game is that the last expansions of Fp1 introduced new mechanics & ideas that made the game feel more personal, complex & enjoyable & I think myself and a large part of the community wanted those aspects of the game to me further explored & expanded on but this was not the case.I think you'll enjoy Fp2 if you  haven't played the first however with that being said currently the first game is more fun so go buy and play that instead while it's on sale for dirt cheap and maybe one day after a lot of updates this game will meet expectations fans have for what the game should / could have been.

_childDocuments_.review: This is NOT like Frostpunk 1. Feels like a Civ game but with the social management of Frostpunk. Less micro than FP1, but still plenty of opportunity to adjust workforce and outputs with branching tech tree options... very much a successor to FP1 and I can't wait to play the DLC eventually (once I beat the game a few times and explore the endings).
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: So far, with what little the beta has available, this is a really solid city builder and resource management game. Gameplay is pretty different to the first with how construction and how policies are enacted. Rather than utilizing a direct resource to building model it uses something similar to Cities Skylines districts where you lay out district areas that have an initial currency cost. Yes currency. I've not gotten to iron yet but wood is used for maintaining districts and for making goods which is needed to keep your people happy and crime low. I've not played enough to give a full solid review, but so far this is starkly different with how the game was before. I'm not sure if it's all good, but so far I've enjoyed it.The other aspect, the laws and social aspect has also been overhauled where instead of going strictly religious or industrial, you now have multiple sub-factions in your settlement who all have their own views on what they want and what they are against. This is where the council aspect comes into play, where you have laws that are voted on by these factions and depending on how prominent they are in the settlement will determine how many seats they will have at the council. The council is made up of 100 seats which are divided between each faction, and you can directly influence how prominent each faction is and isn't with favors, promising the faction they can say what the next law to be voted in is, promoting the faction, or just straight up paying them project funding. Each faction has their own benefits and drawbacks, and they each have their own demands and acts they stand against. It's not easy to keep everyone happy, but it seems like it's possible. I'm not sure yet what happens if you completely neglect or try to push a faction out.Overall, it's a major difference in the prior game in how it's played, I am interested in how the faction system works and the fact that laws are now based on chance that you can influence based on your actions. Having things directly cost one resource I'm a bit iffy on, the introduction of currency vs the prior method of having each building have a material cost of iron and wood, as well as having limited upgrade slots for districts dependent on how much you expand them is a little bit of a drawback for me.Space is now a premium and you can carve out space around you. The area around your generator is buildable on a hex grid, but if you want to expand you'll have do dig through frost hardened snow and free up the land for use. This is a change I'm not against, but I'm still on the fence about since I need to plan my builds a bit more. But it's an interesting change none the less that I'm going to be playing with more.As for exploration and what not, it's a bit harder to best gauge how well this is done since you have a time limit to play. You got a limited number of weeks in game to build, explore, and make your choices, which exploration does cut a large chunk of time out of. Exploration seems mostly unchanged with the exception of instead of having one place to make your expeditionary forces, you now have logistic districts over old exploration hubs which grants you expedition resources. Gone are dedicated expedition teams, as now each expedition is based on difficulty of the location and how many expedition resources are required to send a team there. One change that I find interesting is when you find and make resource outposts you can now draw paths from these outposts to one of your logistics outposts which I assume makes travel to and from more efficient. Also yes, the expedition map is not just a bunch of dots on a map to send people to, you can see the layout of your settlement from the world map and its connections to the world map.The other part that I am impressed with is the higher quality graphics and the fact god cam is now no longer as limited as it was in the first game. You can freely move around your settlement, rotate the camera around a point, zoom in and out, and rotate the view up and down. You can go full top-down view or bring the camera down to the ground and get some scenery views since the settlement and world map are both cohesive. This game is gorgeous and you can get some amazing views now that you're more free to move around.Music I didn't get to experience much of since it's just the one gamemode, but what I hear so far is very reminiscent of the first game music. That is to say that I did enjoy what I heard. Most of what I heard was background music, meaning it wasn't noticed very often but that's good. I did notice that nothing felt missing when it came to the atmosphere this game made, as I felt more dedicated to ensuring the well being of my people and hearing out what each faction has to say. It felt very in place.Overall, I can say with certainty that this is a good addition to the Frostpunk name, it's a bit of a radical turn in how you build and make changes, but it's not a bad thing in my opinion. I'm looking forward to the full release and I can say that I do recommend any FP1 fans give this game a try.----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------With all that said, I'll be playing the release version of the game soon and add to this review as needed.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Slightly above average, but a significant downgrade compared to the first game.They removed interesting and well working gameplay elements and added rather boring or annoying mechanics that do not really enrich the gameplay experience.Compared to the first game, this one feels impersonal and managerial compared to the direct and personal survival struggle of the predecessor.I was determined to give this game a chance, but the only word that comes to mind is "dull."
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Frostpunk 1 Humanity vs Mother NatureFrostpunk 2 Humanity vs Human NatureFrostpunk 2 got me into the frostpunk games most of the complaints i see about this game is that it not Frostpunk 1. This is a great game if you remove the rose tinted glasses that is viewing it through the lens of its predecessor. Survival city builder about balancing resources while maintaining faction trust and passing laws. 8.5 out of 10 very happy with my purchase.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: The first run through is very fun but the game is too repetitive to be fun after that. Once you have learnt the mechanics, there is very little to be excited about. I am hoping the DLCs add more mechanics. At the moment, this game combines an economy game and political sim, while not implementing either well. I imagine the devs did this to try and appeal to the largest player base possible, but all this has done has made a game that is fun for everyone for a few hours, and boring afterwards.On a separate note, the OST is very good, and the way the UI changes as the tension in the city changes is very cool.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Inferior to frostpunk 1.The scale is too big. In frostpunk 1 you managed individuals. In this you manage people by the 100s if not thousands.This trivializes the aspects that were making frostpunk 1 shine, namely the heavy atmosphere.You knew that when you send 10 children into a coal mine in frostpunk 1 that a few would die. This is absent here. All that is left is a maybe 6, maybe 7/10 city builder with some survival aspects. So far i couldnt see any of the grimness that set fp 1 apart from other such game.I do not think this can be patched or fixed and therefore I will not be recommending this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: The game lacks much of what made Frostpunk 1 compelling. While it’s a decent city management game it isn't worth its current price—maybe for €15, but certainly not the steep €45.I completed the campaign once (about 20 hours, playing at a very slow pace) and have no desire to replay it. The game felt monotonous from start to finish. In the early game, I struggled to connect with the world. By chapter two, my city was running like a utopia, with no resource struggles until the end.- A "tick" of time is now one full day, and city management happens on a weekly basis. The day/night shift is gone.- No quantitative effect descriptions (e.g., "reduce pollution by a little", "Increase disease by a substantial amount").- No time-lapse of the city’s construction upon game completion!- UI is very clunky (overlaps, camera is moved, can't clic notifications, etc)- There’s no sense of battling the cold.- Deaths have little to no impact.- The city feels soulless—you don’t see its inhabitants.- The final recap storytelling tries to guilt trip me for things that the game decided for me. And at the same time it doesn't strike at all. I am not a dictator commander rulling in a desperate situation. There was a council vote for everything, I had the Peacemaker ending, and everything went fine.I won't comment on districts, others have done it already. And IMO, it doesn’t matter. Because I finished the game using ONLY 1/3 of the available space!!! Optimizing the layout feels irrelevant since heated space is no longer a critical resource! Land used to be so valuable that new technologies that would free-up some precious m² really mathered.Now you can just expand across the entire map—who cares? You don't need to pack things around the generator.I ended up breaking the permafrost over the whole map, but didn't use the space.And the roads? They’re gone. I used to enjoy designing roads; they shaped the city and were satisfying to build.Initially interesting, the council system quickly became repetitive. You’re given 2-3 law choice per topic, but I didn’t care which one I picked. As long as you choose 1 law per topic, you get a bonus. The factions just flip-flop between choices, but it doesn’t impact the city at all.For example: "Require fewer materials" vs. "Produce more materials." The result is essentially the same, and since I wasn’t facing resource issues, I couldn’t care less. This pattern persists for every decision.And again, no numbers. Only "fewer", "more" etcThe research tree is largely pointless. As I mentioned, I didn’t struggle with resources after the first few upgrades. Subsequent research merely offered marginal improvements—around 10% more efficiency—while costing a steam core. Nothing I unlocked changed my city’s economy or layout.The area-of-effect buildings were underwhelming. I spammed them to increase storage capacity, not for the benefits they supposedly provided. If they affected 2 districts, they were worth it, but the new buildings you can unlock are, frankly, unnecessary.In the end, I felt nothing playing this game—it was a dull experience throughout.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Frostpunk 2 Delivers!You can start a new game multiple times and recreate numerous experiences as you plan your future utopia against the cold. There is serious replay value in starting a new campaign and choosing a new intro and unique groups/factions which make up your colony. Beta tested: It was worth the extra wait for launch. _childDocuments_.review: Frostpunk 2 is, and definitely feels like, a sequel to the original game.The micro-base building from the original game is gone, now in order to survive we build the base on a more macro size; no longer we need to place individual buildings, but instead we need to manage various districts around the city that provide services and resources.The game still has the tough choices, sacrifices and decisions as we have witnessed in the original game - now, as the city grows in size, a council is created and various factions of the city need to be pleased, otherwise they will protest against you and ultimately overthrow you as the leader.Difficulty level is still as high as it has ever been.. after 4 restarts, I have finally made it to chapter 3! But, at any point I could've just gone back and played on lower difficulty.Graphics are beautiful, but as some have already pointed out, I wish we saw more of the people moving around the city and not just the orange/red lines.Finally, can the heatmaps be removed? Most of the time they just slow down progression for no apparent reason.With all that said, I definitely recommend this sequel.

_childDocuments_.review: It is fundamentally a very different game from the first one. The survival challenges aren't as tough, the moral choices of the game don't make you question things as much and it is much more distant then the first one. I heard the criticism that it is more linear aswel, I myself did not feel that way. I think this game pretty much went in the only possible direction it could, and since it had to raise the scales since making a copy-pasted game from the first one wasn't an option they chose a different approach but at the core the game remained much the same. It is more distant because that's the point, it feels less heavy on the choices because it is much more about politics where you have to look at the bigger picture than the individual, but it doesn't forget the individuals either. You just have to go into the experience with a fresh mindset and learn all this game has to offer. It's worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: Truly an awesome game from start to finish, Frostpunk 2 took everything I loved from the first game and made it even greater. Although the game has a bit of difficult learning curve for new players to the series and returning, I found myself in complete control over my entire city once I got around mastering all its resources. With challenging elements of bickering factions, getting the needed delegates to pass laws through negotiations and promises, and the dangerous elements of the frozen wasteland, FP2 is addictive to pick up and much harder to put down!PROS- Diverse and branching visions you can decide/vote on for the city. Whether you want to embrace the life of the frost or conquer it, the game challenges you with so many different events like protests, civil wars, and surviving the whiteouts. There is always something happening, and sometimes would have to make on the fly decisions or face dire consequences. You have to work to earn victory!- A rich and expansive building mechanic. There are so many buildings/districts I can use to build my frozen utopia but they come with their own issues like disease/squalor, and you can never learn to heavily on one side of the city's adaption or progress path early on or you'll risk failing the run. It makes you think of real time strategies!- Massive Frozen Wasteland to explore! Settlement/outpost building in FP2 has to be one of my most favorite additions to the series. I recall seeing this slightly implemented in the On the Edge DLC from the first game or at least through story, and FP2 makes use of that to grow your city even larger! Colonizing the Old Dreadnought and Winterhome held their own challenges, yet with a vast amount of resources to extract in the wastes, there are many ways to survival!CONS- Convoluted guide on how to use certain buildings/districts. Wished there was clearer guidance on how to use everything instead of beginning given an index.- Use of City Abilities should be on the main player's UI, not located at the generator itself. This is confusing and I couldn't figure out how to use it until the very end of the game.- At the time of this writing, the game has a ton of moving assets and isn't properly optimized to handle end-game amounts of buildings and districts. I currently have a RTX 4080 Super TI with 64GB of RAM, and noticed the game beginning to struggle. Lags got really bad and had two CTEs.

_childDocuments_.review: I fell in love with the first Frostpunk, the original trailer still gives me goosebumps to this day, the atmosphere and the attention to detail, the masterfully crafted gameplay and the grand narrative all served to leave a lasting impression. I have replayed Frostpunk many times over.I have now completed frostpunk 2. What a colossal disappointment. The detail is gone, the complexity is gone, the performance is spotty, the campaign is short and does not hold up to the standard of the first. This has all the complexity of a mobile game. The detail that entrapped me so much in the first game, the people going about their lives in the city, the machines working back and forth, the building that linked to one another, all that is gone replaced with glowing lines... that’s it. Occasionally you can see characters like ghost’s popping in and fading away if you look really hard. The fact that you do not make paths or anything really and the AI dose that all for you using a district system makes for a very stupid looking city. The fact that you only have a limited set of maps and the buildings are not designed for them, clipping, resizing when you zoom the camera, 3 tunnel entrances in a row… That last one probably dose not make sense to people that have not seen it and I could go on but now I am to depressed.Frostpunk 1 struck such an astonishing vista. Frostpunk 2 makes me wonder if it was made by the same people. Did they fire the entire dev team and hire a new one under the same name? Seems like it, as this seems like a cheap imitation cash grab.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall I like it. It's larger in scope than Frostpunk 2, so you don't do the day-to-day decisions like "which child do I send down which mine?" and more like "how do my citizens live in general?" I like the different factions and ideologies, I don't like some very annoying UI aspects. For example: I hate the fact, that you don't get notified when you can pass a new law, do new research, or when frostland expedition teams are available. How can you go from Frostpunk 1's awesome UI and sound design to this? How did no playtester say "I really would like the crunchy noise back to tell me when a law can be passed." ? Or the fact, that we have no way of seeing the cooldowns of faction interactions without laboriously clicking on each faction and each tab individually. The hubs should also be highlighted when building, so I can see, at a glance where I want to build.But those are details, all in all I like this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Frostpunk 2's user interface feels overly complicated and cluttered compared to the streamlined design of the first game. The shift away from the neatness of the original makes it difficult to understand what’s happening at times, with too much filler content. Some research options appear across multiple tabs, causing confusion, and there’s a noticeable lack of quality-of-life features like the ability to cancel construction. Additionally, heat continues to be consumed even when a district is turned off, which feels counterintuitive. The six-slot district system seems like a questionable design choice, though it’s not my main issue. While I love the direction the game has taken, the execution feels lacking, with clutter and disorganisation detracting from the experience.

_childDocuments_.review: A Masterpiece of Strategy and SurvivalAt first, I found myself a bit confused by the tutorial and was missing some of the older animations from the original game, but now, after completing the game, I fully understand the scale and depth this game offers. It’s an absolute 15/10 experience.The game is a fantastic continuation of the first, with a gripping tone that expertly blends emotions, stress, and careful planning, especially on the maximum difficulty level. The management and micro-management systems are nothing short of brilliant—every decision feels meaningful, and the level of control you have over your city’s fate is both exhilarating and terrifying.The graphics and atmosphere are stunning, pulling you into the cold, desolate world in a way that few games can. There’s also plenty of lore from the first game, which enriches the story and makes it even more engaging for returning players. The seamless integration of lore ties Frostpunk 2 to its predecessor beautifully.With around 11 hours of gameplay (at least for me), it offers a deep, satisfying experience that's well worth the money. If you loved the first game, or if you're new to the series but enjoy challenging strategy and survival games, Frostpunk 2 is a must-play. It’s a shining example of how a sequel can build upon and elevate an already incredible game.

_childDocuments_.review: I waited for this game with some anticipation, because Frostpunk was one of my most-played favourites. I wasn't disappointed with the successor.They managed to pull off the trick of keeping the same atmosphere and sense of dread/threat as the first, but with enough new features to ensure you weren't just replaying the same game but with the names changed.The key difference is there is much more focus on managing competing factions, even as you also have to maintain and grow your city in the face of the environmental threats and resource limits. You need to use the complex system of researching and passing laws, as well as researching and building buildings, to influence the factions positively or negatively, and a balance is very hard to find. At one point, I had good relations with all four, and felt a real achievement. But by the end I was in civil war. I guess when the pie isn't big enough, people will fight over slices!Exploration is also a much more developed element, with a large hinterland which provides various surprises. There was a welcome return of the colonization/outpost element we saw in Frostpunk 1's expansion - again with more development, so that each colony felt like a mini-city of its own.At various points in the game, I felt like I was trying to juggle so many balls at once, that some were inevitably going to crash on my head, and so it proved. But that's what makes Frostpunk so enjoyable: there's a genuine challenge which many city builders aspire to, but few achieve.A worthy successor to the first game, and I recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: Frostpunk 2 is a great pretender. A pretender of depth where there is none. The game is shallow, perhaps even shallower than frostpunk 1 was. The art:10/10Music and graphics and effects are all top-tier, nothing to complain about. I did notice a lack of diveristy in the music not seen in 1. Weird.The story: 1/10 Worst part IMO - Sometimes feels nonsensical. I could be a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ steward making ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ decisions, or literally build a utopia - The outcome is the same - always two radically opposing factions form, that never support you. Along the way one of those parties tries to gain power, which you of course grant, because a democracy in a survival situation makes no sense, and then you watch as the other party becomes straight up terrorists that bomb your buildings, protest all the time, etc.The story is completely unconclusive and doesn't feel as good as frostpunk 1's ending did - ESPECIALLY the storm. The storm in 1 was that "one-final-effort" push and after, a promised redemption.Here? You just press some buttons the game tells you to press, it gives you a title screen and essentially tells you the game is over. Nothing after. No environmental danger, just societal collapse as the danger, which of course doesn't happen because you can just kill/jail the opposing guys.  The story rewrites the ending of FP1 (still turbo winter, even after the storm) as well - which is cringe.Difficulty design: 3/10 There is no point in Trying to feed, heal, heat your people. You ALWAYS have a surplus of workers (and you're always looking for a way to kill them off), you ALWAYS have enough of everything (played on the second hardest difficulty for my first playthrough, was surprised at how easy and autopilot it was).Worst part about this is how they designed the coal/oil resource - At the beginning it's good - you're scrambling for scraps of coal - But later on they switch 100% to Oil you essentially ship in back to your main city, from an outpost city-like you build. That "city" is always the same oil dreadnaught, with 3 nodes of oil containing 4 million oil that never runs out. Compare this to FP1's system of coal nodes, as well as having to use thumpers and gathering stations, and you have something that is literally a downgrade in depth.Dumbed down the gameplay for no reason.All the research and civics are mostly just stat boosts - Enormous ones at that - Which means no real "improvement" you see with your own two eyes - You just have to "pretend" that something happened and suspend your disbelief a little.The gameplay: 4/10Like I said i difficulty, the gameplay is severely dumbed down compared to Fp1. Not being able to build buildings yourself, but districts in hextiles really "disconnects" you from your infrastructure. You cannot build roads, the buildings are all random, and looking very similar. Buildings are essentially "district plug-ins" that serve as stat boosts or abilities for the district, which IMO is a strict downgrade to what was before.Example:In frostpunk1, I could build a propaganda center. That propaganda center had a nice mesh, it had flags, it had speakers, it had a dedicated ability on it's building click, it had a strong effect and was quite expensive.In frostpunk 2, you "research" the propaganda center, and then your city just kinda "has it". People start talking about it, but you cannot see it, you cannot see any of it's abilities, you cannot really know what it does.I also despise not using numbers - Who came up with "Severely affects" and "Minor addition" instead of a simple +50 / -12 to something? You know this is what people want to see, right? So many times I saw "Severely reduces crime" only to see it basically do nothing because my population was 30k+.The district system is a boring borefest that disconnects you from your citybuilder hard enough that you start to disassociate with it - not a good thing.Exploration took a hit too - Most of the options seem completely... pointless? I don't think I used a single outpost the entire game except for the starter coal node, and they dedicated like an entire tree of research and civics for this. Why? Did they not play their own game?The balance: 6/10Balance was good on steward difficulty - none of the things felt too punishing, but some things felt way too good. This is what made the game really easy for me, and way easier than frostpunk 1. The game also retains the problem from 1 - IF you know how to beat it once, you will never have another problem ever again. It's a memory puzzle instead of a colony builder game.The biggest problem is the currency system - Everything in the game is bound to "Heatstamps" (gold) which essentially means that if you don't prioritize gold income early, you lose because you cannot outpace the cold.The cold is also basically not a problem - in the campaign, there is only one "proto-storm" that goes down to -110 celsius, but of course this doesn't mean anything - They made heat only relevant to the consumption of fuel for some reason - No more upgrades for the generator, no more area upgrades, just "every building uses X amount of heat per level of cold".Remember how in Frostpunk 1 you had to balance taking in refugees with how much heat you could output, so they wouldn't all die? Yeah. Not a thing here, everybody just strolling around when it's -110 deg outside if you have fuel in abundance (and you will).The feel: 3/10Overall the game is quite buggy, choppy framerate even with DLSS and frame gen: ON, on an RTX4080.It seems unpolished in many places and gives off a kinda "early access" feel.Additionally, please god make the "STEWARD, STEWARD WE CALL YOU" voices stop for god's sake - After 5h of constant STEWARD screaming i was exhausted.Overall: 4/10.Very sad to say this because I was a big enjoyer of FP1, despite it's flaws. Frostpunk 2 ultimately dumbs down the core gameplay while pretending it's deep - especially around the council mechanic.

_childDocuments_.review: My initial impressions with the game, having played the original Frostpunk for 130+ hours, has not been great. The game itself is... fine. Not great. But it's not some buggy mess, it just struggles to be fun. There is some part of me that wonders if we're going to see a mobile release follow shortly, because a lot of the structure of the gameplay could be akin to a mobile game. But outside of the setting, the vast majority of core mechanics have changed. It seems as if the team wanted to fix how late game Frostpunk 1 required quite a bit of building micro-management at times, but they've responded by throwing the entire gameplay style of the original out the window. Not only is there upsettingly little control over the actual resource harvesting itself, but furthermore there really isn't the opportunity to do much truly of value town customization wise. There is essentially zero opportunity to create your wasteland town as there was in the original game, all you truly do is pick which tiles are used for a very generic production pattern. Everything is tile locked, and it feels more like some sort of modded version of Civ V than it does the original Frostpunk game. If this wasn't being published by the original studio, I'd have sworn the Frostpunk IP had been sold off to another developer, because there is really nothing in common with the original gameplay loop. To make the changes easier to grasp, here's a list of what I've noted so far:- Time flows has been changed, with there no longer being a day/night cycle. Weeks fly by rather meaninglessly, rather than spending the day optimizing your town for what resources you need next.- Resources are stockpiled now. To what end, outside of occasional gameplay objectives, is pretty valueless. All it does is prevent debuffs from things like starving, or lack of goods, or lack of housing - and those debuffs generally aren't noticeable. Starving as a whole is pretty meaningless, as is your citizens dying, as they'll generally repopulate at a faster rate than whatever they're dying at. It's a minor inconvenience.- Research is entirely unclear as to what needs to be focused, as research generally doesn't unlock buildings, but rather bonuses. Personally, I think that lacks the punch of being able to then place the newly researched building afterwards, so it feels lackluster.- Heat is just this abstract thing that you have to make by getting fuel, but there's really no need to research to upgrade the generator in this gameplay loop. You just feed it more oil/coal, and you get more heat. No need for heat zones anymore. It feels pretty unrewarding generally, and while there's some small bonuses for planning your town to optimize heat, the bonuses are lackluster and almost not worth pursuing.- Breaking through the frostpack to build more buildings is pretty much just a bloat function to slow down the gameplay. It costs you resources, and I believe it's there to make you have to plan your settlement. But it fails at that, because you break through the frostpack in whatever section you choose pretty quickly. So it essentially just ends up being a credit drain, which isn't a fun or challenging dynamic, it just means you frequently find yourself unable to do anything as you wait for resources to build up.- The colony system, while somewhat novel, really just makes this game a resource balancing game between settlements. It does not seem to be intended to be a resource balancing game, so it's a pretty poor resource balancing game.- When you create a colony, it takes workforce equally from all your buildings. While it's nice that it doesn't do it randomly, thus ruining your economy, it does mean now every building you have is understaffed, and you will have to manually fix that for each and every one.- Frostland exploration feels like a checklist. There has yet to be any big decisions, or excitement from finding steam cores, or excitement from finding anything. Outposts you establish can give you a trickle of resources, but not a meaningful amount that does any more than replace one building in your city, and you already have to make one building to get the frost scouts to establish the outposts. I'm not excited when my frost scouts are going somewhere new. It's just another task that apparently has to be done.- Crime ends up being a factor, but it's just another debuff, rather than something where you're worried about your precious citizens being killed in the night. (Although again, night doesn't exist anymore) You might get a heartbreaking message about a missing child, but that child will be replaced within the next day by ordinary population growth.- The "roads" are just flavor on the screen, and appear to generate almost randomly. Zero regard is made for "would you actually make a road this way", and I want to compare it to slime mold paths, but slime mold paths actually try to be efficient.- You can't even zoom in far enough to truly enjoy the hustle and bustle of your city you're making. Gone are the days of seeing church processions in the night, your citizens are just gold streaks on a path.- Automatons, in all ways but flavor text and non-interactive objects on your road, appear to have been completely removed from the game.- Temperature changes happen. They're generally meaningless outside of suddenly you require more coal/oil. They're also far less frequent, so they tend to sneak up on you, at which point you are met with a generally uncompelling alert telling you things got colder. You tend to forget that occurred within about 15 seconds, because you really don't have to do anything.At time of writing, I've gone through the prologue and part of chapter 1. There has yet to be any compelling story, just "you're running out of coal, establish an outpost to get oil!" There's still plenty of content to follow, and I won't be refunding the game. Thus I'm hopeful I'll change this review down the line. But so far, I've been horrendously disappointed considering I was hoping this would be the original game, with expanded content and mechanics. Instead, this has been a kneecapped homage to the original. The changes that have been made to the original gameplay loop have been at best, different, and more frequently just downright worse. I want to give the game a chance to get fun, but so far it just hasn't been.One positive has been the town council meetings. It's a cool dynamic to add so far, and having the need to sway votes with other political votes has been interesting to have to factor into the gameplay. But even this aspect requires some criticism, as interactions with factions generally has felt like interacting with monoliths of different names. Each faction is really only being distinguished by what they may ask for, or how much they have to offer voting support wise.I could see how some people could find the game to be a 6/10. Maybe even a 7/10 if you like mobile games. But the insane amount of 9/10 reviews Frostpunk 2 is touting in it's advertising is just baffling to me. The vast majority of Metacritic reviews all seem to have one thing in common - very few of them mention any actual gameplay, and rather focus on the setting itself. Which would be fine if this was a visual novel, but it's a game being sold at AAA prices. On top of that, the setting is notably far less compelling than the first iteration of the franchise. Somehow, the studio that made This War of Mine, one of the most emotionally compelling games I have ever played in my life, has managed to make the emotional attachment you have to your citizens colder than the frostland itself.In conclusion, if you're looking at buying this because you loved the original, I do not think you'll enjoy how the gameplay loop has changed. If you're looking at buying this because you loved the setting, you may be able to trick yourself into enjoying it.

_childDocuments_.review: ---MINOR SPOILERS FOR SOME PARTS OF FROSTPUNK 2--I was an avid fan of the first Frostpunk, and let me just say, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. This blew my expectations out of the water. 11Bit took what the original game did well and expanded on it, while also introducing enough new concepts to keep gameplay fresh and interesting. I have only recently finished the game's main story, but I don't think I am anywhere near done with Frostpunk 2 just yet. Now if you're going through and reading more reviews as I have, you may notice that quite a few of the negative reviews have been pointing out and criticizing things that, at least for me, don't really do the game justice. There are some valid criticisms being made, like some design choices made for some of the ingame UI, specifically with how you interact with the generator.Now if you played FP1 you'll notice right away there being big differences from then to now, but from my experience it feels like a natural progression in the world of FP. It's been thirty years since this great storm and New London has evolved from the hole in the ground it was when The Captain established it. Which is another thing I absolutely loved about this game. The Captain is dead, there is a new leader (The Steward), and there are new ideas and new groups that are vying for power in the city, and the game makes sure to let you know it. Dealing with the factions, at least for me, was one of the most enjoyable aspects.I'm gonna cut this off here to avoid drawing the review out to long, but as a parting word, if youre undecided on Frostpunk 2, whether as a newcomer to the world of Frostpunk or as one of the already initiated, I think the game is well worth the price tag.

It also throws multiple bases at you almost immediately, which makes all the management feel extremely impersonal, when half your city might die off just because you were watching a different one.While the huge amount of choices might help with replayability, and some might like the hectic pace of gameplay, having to manage multiple bases at the same time is just too much effort for me

_childDocuments_.review: Is it good?  Yes, quite.Is it Frostpunk?  Yes, but with a caveat.Frostpunk 2 takes a more macro approach to managing New London and the surrounding frost-lands. Focusing more on district-level production and building, rather than micro-managing every single building in the settlement.It DOES lose a bit of the intimacy that the original brought to the table because of this. Given the deliberate nature of the story and general experience i have to assume that this, too, was deliberate. It still delivers a well thought out story and visceral experience fraught with no-win scenarios and bleak choices. But, those choices don't really carry the same emotional weight as Frostpunk 1. Despite this lack of intimate emotional exchange between you and the hopeless survivors of the frosty apocalypse, this seems a natural progression in the franchise and one that broadens the scope of the world. Now that basic survival has been taken care of in the first game, of course the people of New London would focus on other, more political matters. Makes perfect sense. The amount of choices and paths you can guide your society down are ample and perhaps to some, at first, a bit overwhelming.All in all its bigger, ostensibly better, well refined, and well narrated. Yet another great game from 11 Bit Studios.

_childDocuments_.review: A true sequel to Frostpunk.Not only does this sequel expand on the story of Frostpunk, but the game mechanics too. If you're familiar with Frostpunk you'll enjoy the familiar aspects like exploration of the frostland and meeting the needs of the citizens, but FP2 offers also new mechanics to better manage a society and a city, rather than a group of survivors huddled around the generator.FP2 is fundamentally different from the original, enough that both games are enjoyable and i still find myself playing the first game, however there are still new things to try in the sequel. FP2 truly shines in story mode, which has a surprising amount of replayablility with the different starting factions or siding with the opposition, you can get 4 completely different playthroughs, and that's not including the different choices you make through the game. After these 4 playthroughs though, story mode feels quite repetitive and you shift to utopia (endless) mode. While this mode isn't as interesting as story mode, if you pick a map that doesn't reuse the story mode frostland you can still get a unique and fun experience. While this game "technically" has infinite replayability, theirs only so many vastly different choices to make that majorly change the game. You can probably get a dozen fun, interesting, and varied enough playthroughs to enjoy the game (one focused on each faction in story/utopia mode), but after that you'll probably find yourself waiting for DLCs, pursuing achievements, or following wacky self imposed rules to make your own interesting playthough (which is fun in it's own right)TL:DR: Good game different enough from the original Frostpunk to have fun with both, you can probably get 4 story mode playthroughs and 8 Endless runs that are enjoyably different. Worth getting at even a 10-20% discount if you can snag it.

_childDocuments_.review: Frostpunk 2 is a worthy successor to the original, building on its core mechanics while introducing new layers of complexity and decision-making. The shift from managing a struggling outpost to running a sprawling city with political factions and competing interests adds depth to the experience, making every choice feel  .The game captures the bleak beauty of its setting, and the Council Hall dynamics create a constant sense of tension. While some of the raw emotional weight of the first game’s survival stories feels a bit diluted with the scale-up, the broader societal challenges make up for it by offering a richer, more nuanced experience.Yes, certain mechanics can feel unintuitive at first, but Frostpunk isn’t about hand-holding. It’s about   and challenging your strategies. If you’re looking for an immersive, thought-provoking city-building game with a survival twist, Frostpunk 2 delivers. A must-play for fans of the series and anyone who enjoys morally complex gameplay.10/10 – Prepare to lead, adapt, and .

_childDocuments_.review: I really liked the story mode.I found it significantly better then Frostpunk 1: not as formulaic in its builder-gameplay, way more intense storytelling and setting, more expansive in terms of content, way more re -playable, and of course updated graphics and a great soundtrack. Beware that at the time of this review, the game is very demanding on your hardware, and even if it runs at a high frame-rate on a powerful rig, it unfortunately suffers from some annoying stutter while panning the camera, so if that's a deal-breaker to you (it nearly was for me, then a patch improved it a bit) avoid it for now.My take in regards to the big controversy:this is another case like Darkest Dungeon 2: a sequel which is substantially different from its predecessor, and precisely like in that other case, your reaction to this will largely depend on your opinion of the first game: if all you wanted was more of the same, and though that it was perfect as it was, be ready for disappointment because this is not it. If you instead thought the original was awesome in some ways, but the gameplay loop/formula had major issues or was at least vastly perfectible in other ways, and you're ready to approach this not as a pure "sequel" but as a significantly different game based on the same setting and theme, than chances are you will love it.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: I wanted to like it but didn't. Turned from survival city-builder to city-builder survival. Due to increased scale the game feels nowhere near as immersive and people's deaths are no longer a true problem, just a minor setback that has no real weight.I'm going to be honest, I don't like Frostpunk 2. I know that for someone it'll be GOTY, and that's fine by me. I do not want a sequel to be a direct clone of the previous game, and I know they spent forever working on this to make it interesting. It has amazingly fleshed out political mechanics, a robust research tree, and a sprawling overworld to explore. This is also where it falls short for me.To me, this isn't Frostpunk 2. This is at best a spinoff in a similar genre in terms of gameplay. Whereas before it was just you and your small city versus the terrible expanse of a frozen world where you do only what is necessary to survive while trying not to lose yourself and the few people left in the process. Now, with society progressing again, people become a number. Deaths can easily count in the 100s and make no real long-term difference in your run. This is no longer a survival city-builder, but a city-builder survival. The priorities feel flipped, and now it's closer to Cities than it is to Frostpunk 1 in terms of scale.I really wanted to like this game. I really, really did. I just can't bring myself to. It isn't a game for me and not what I feel like it should have been so I can't recommend it, but I know that there will be people who will love it. While each mechanic is amazingly fleshed out and interesting, even as someone who loves his color matching Grand Strategy games I feel like there is simply too much going on at one time and when combined doesn't feel natural and homogeneous but instead a jumbled mess.

I found myself constantly struggling to find what I needed, which killed the immersion and made the experience frustrating.On top of that, the game isn’t well optimized. This makes it hard to enjoy the game's atmospheric visuals and adds to the feeling that this sequel lacks the polish and finesse of its predecessor.I really wanted to love this game, but right now, it just feels like a missed opportunity.
