_childDocuments_.review: I might be slightly biased when i say this, but this game is incredible. (spoiler warning further down, rest is safe to read. :D )You remember the first game? Pretty much all the faults of that game went out the window here (Except optimisation on release, but that'll get fixed eventually) Due to how the storyline mechanics work, there are many, many endings to the story scenario, both good and bad, so you get plenty of replayability value (both with self-imposed rules, difficulty, and political choices)Great stuff from the first game:-Tough moral choices (also improved upon) It's quite scary if you get self conscious enough to see that you're going mad with power of your own volition..... Like trying to push a radical law even though it isn't necessary.... To see yourself become a monster like all those 'evil politicians in the news'....Yeah, that's good game design, thank you 11bit; I have anxiety about politics now.-Rewarding the player for strategizing (much more recognizable in this game's building mechanics)-Good skill floor for new players with plenty of room for error-Godlike music (Listen to the main theme please, it even has the violin solo from the first game's climax music track, it's amazing)-Exploring the frostland (much more complex here, but the game doesn't tell you to RUSH LOGISTICS DISTRICTS ASAP... a free tip from me :P )-British humor in a citizen's speech is so good to see.-Plenty, plenty more amazing stuff that I don't really have the energy rn to write. I havent eaten lunch yet. :>There are cameos of places from the first game's DLC's! Yayyyy!Now, for some of my gripes, but more like suggestions for balance changes or ranting about small issues that could use some polish (pun intended) -Optimization..... My Pc was almost burning for the 7,5 hours I played this on medium-high settings. (A little over exaggerating here, it's not as bad as with cyberpunk, but y'know...) Working on optimizing the game wouldn't hurt.... even though i think it's already pretty well optimized on lower settings, and ppl playing on ultra are coping their 2006 laptop can't run it smoothly.  :P-Tutorials ain't exactly accurate, or more accurately: they're incomplete. Like with heat surplus. How does it benefit the city??? Also, on a more personal note, please tell people to not sleep on Logistics districts or something, it's a huge lifeline that can provide very efficient supplies with minimal workforce commitment. It'd do this game much good if it became common sense in the community..... and save a game journalist a couple braincells :P-UI is a little bit clunky at times, and you end up clicking research instead of a hub building you want, or deadlines being very imprecise (it shows how many full weeks you get to do something, but not days, so it might get confusing)(Scary wall of text ahead  D:  ) (A tip included)-Balance change proposal: The Fervour  and faction relationship is... very weird. It has no cap, so if you keep antagonizing one of the radical factions for a long time, it is almost impossible to know how many points of fervour a faction has accumulated (and the biggest consequences are at fervor 3...... i got to something like +10 i think) -(Tip for beginners, use at your own risk) You can easily cheese the political system by repeatedly denouncing and antagonizing one of the radical factions to reduce their size and support, thus weakening them..... Yes, you can turn a political party into a harmless chiuaua this way; and make a 'powerful fanatical guard dog that'll follow you through hell and back' out of the other one. If you manage your city well, you can try out one of the laws under 'Rule' category that requires like 2/3 or 3/4 majority to pass... and having a unflinchingly loyal faction helps a bit. And if you succeed... the council is a cakewalk from then on (not really, you still gotta keep the normies happy enough, so they'll let you get away with everything). TLDR: Suppressing a faction from the beginning of the game makes it much easier to play, but limits your choices later on. Recommended if you start your first game of frostpunk on officer difficulty. -Suggested fix: Change the fervor mechanic into something similar to the favorability mechanic, or give larger punishment for maxing out the fervor. Add caps to the favorability and fervor mechanics, so that it doesn't go past the max... give it a bigger bad event, or some other penalty except tension (Fightclub or two can fix that easily.) (on the other hand, favorability is fine as it is, because you can keep raising funds from your loyal fanatics..... yeah keep it cuz heatstamps are very difficult to get in a pinch. :>  )  SPOILER AREA AHEAD:-SPOILER (Stalwarts): it's kinda sad that you don't get to keep using the second colony after the civil war hits if you go with dismantling it for cores and build the last upgrade too early. (ngl, if you can afford that thing, something went very right, and there isn't much left ahead.) -Also, some of the cores are very hard to access due to elevation or ravines, and sometimes it's simply too late to realize that you can't access that deposit because of elevation shenanigans, even though the district you just built is directly bordering those sweet steam cores. I might add more stuff as I play through the other endings.(SPOILERS OVER)Not much else, this is fun as all hell, politics included! _childDocuments_.review: I played Frostpunk 1 and I love it.I played Frostpunk 2 and I love it.The user interface needs quite a bit of polish, but otherwise this is a brilliant game that nails the Frostpunk vibe while significantly expanding the gameplay mechanics, and shares with the original the same sense of tension and dread when there is a major decision or things don't go to plan. _childDocuments_.review: A worthy successor and a fun game over all. I like the new larger scope and the sector puzzling mechanic is fun. The senate system with you always trying to get majorities on your side is a well designed mechanic.However, after now playing through both FP2 and the FP1 scenarios again - FP2 does not quite reach the level of FP1 for me.As the game is easier and most decisions you take are reversible, they are much less meaningfull than in FP1. _childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: The first Frostpunk looks so tiny in comparision. I remember when it came out, it was already a slap in the face. Want to build a nice city around a reactor? Good luck, we'll make you run out of everything constantly and give you choices along the way that'll make as miserable as we can! Oh you managed better this time? Let's have a blizzard that kills half your population, how about that? In the end I managed to tame Frostpunk. I play it for fun now from time to time. I know exactly what I have to do and I found a path to manouver through everything quite nicely. Now Frostpunk 2 came out and it's just another slap in the face. Oh so now you learned how to handle 600 people in Frostpunk 1, let's see how you do with 50.000. Not just do they hate you, they hate each other as well. No trickery with the ressources either this time, you will run out of everything, it's just a matter of time. While it starts out pretty reasonable s*** is hitting the fan pretty quickly and pretty hard. And if you thought measures in the first installment were severe, you have no idea how ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ crazy people get this time around. But hey, there's "sensible" things you can do against this: Dictatorship, Apartheit, heavily mechanize your population or even make them evovlve into freaks. Simple as that. Now, most people just wanted to have another Frostpunk 1 and are disappointed that they didn't get one and thats reasonable. But you have to know that 11bit studios is not here to provide comfort, they're here to push the envelope. And they did. This is not a settlement builder anymore, it's a city builder now. Everything has been upped by a level. You're not building single buildings, you're building districts. Your research won't just have two options, but more. Your laws will have greater impact. Your people are more volatile. The frostland is more complicated and more important than before. It's a completely different game, with only two things in common with the first one: The cold setting and that the game actively tries to make you miserable. And that's it. It's a very ballsy sequel and it looks absolutely beautiful. Well done.

_childDocuments_.review: It's an evolution of the previous game, as everything is in larger scales. Plus, sometimes I get CTD, though it is quite rare.

_childDocuments_.review: I keep forgetting to eat. In that sense its very much like the first game. Will provide full review after full completion, or death from malnutrition. Some more general things, a pop up for when research/when you can enact laws/when you explored areas would be nice too, it's hard to focus on every little thing sometimes. There's probably some other stuff.Anyway this game's atmosphere, story telling, and mechanics are incredible. 10/10 would recomend.

_childDocuments_.review: I guess I just wanted a larger, more complex version of FP1. This isn't it.It's not a city-builder anymore, instead it's just a zoning game with a politics system. You just zone. This also has the sad consequence of making the game just, well, unimmersive. You don't care about that city, you can't zoom on to see the citizens, there are no customizations option, even that god-awful zoning looks terrible as you must leave holes in your city to account for future buildings so even that contributes to ruining the immersion.Finally, the absolute worse in my opinion, the rework of the heating system completely killed the survival aspect of the game for me. That was the heart of the first game. "Heat" is just a resource now. Ok. Boring.

_childDocuments_.review: It's the resource management gameplay of Frostpunk 1 abstracted one level higher than before.  You don't manage individual people and buildings, but instead districts and factions.  There's a trade-off here, and depending on what you valued in the first game, you may find the change an improvement, or off-putting.City design lost a lot of granularity. Painting down districts on the hex-based maps lacks that cozy feeling of sculpting and optimising layouts just right and the limited positioning of special buildings definitely feels less impactful. You will also likely miss that feeling of getting your tents and coal thumper snugly inside the heat radius in the first game, instead getting abstracted adjacency bonuses from tiling certain districts together or building area of effect hubs and awkwardly positioning  your city around them.The game gained a lot of such granularity back in its law system however.  No longer a selection of black and whites, laws and research have been opened wide up, with different ways of tackling problems which can be researched and proposed by different interest groups.  Not only are the options widened, but your motivations for choosing accordingly are made more complex.  Perhaps you want to extract oil and quickly as possible with fracking because the storm is approaching and coal is almost depleted, but your faction of damn hippies want to pursue a less destructive method and are too close to protesting your rule for you to slight them further.Music and visuals remain good, although in both cases are not quite matching up against Frostpunk 1 which had a more focused, immersive and useful UI along with a more impressive sound track.The frostland exploration is on a much larger scale than in the first game, with more considerations about how to explore, budget your time and safety concerns for scouts. Additionally there are colonies, including buildable colonies you can establish out there.  If the lack of additional colonies bothered you in the prequel, this could be for you, although personally I found that management of multiple colonies a clumsy situation, not aided by the lack of useful information on the interface. Overall, it's a different playing experience from Frostpunk 1, but hits the same notes of fighting for survival in a grim, resource-starved information.  While I don't think it will make quite the splash that Frostpunk 1 did, it's an enjoyable game in its own right.It took quite some resolve to write an actual review instead of just putting "Get back to work!" here.  I trust it will be appreciated.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: The game is good. A lot of people are complaining that it feels different from Frostpunk 1, which it does, but I'd like to point out that Frostpunk 1 still exists and is playable. This game works on a larger scale, with a narrative advancement from the first game that I think is incredibly interesting for a city builder. It starts from the assumption that you won the first game, and that the society you're starting with is larger and more successful as a baseline because of that. It hasn't lost the "soul" of Frostpunk, it respects the first game's narrative and builds on it, which in my opinion is much, much better than just re-doing Frost Punk 1 in a new engine.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: This is the true successor title I wish so many other games could take notes from. This isn't just Frostpunk 1: Part Two, this is what you get from a talented team rethinking systems from the ground up. You still have the same survival mechanics from FP1, but now the context is different. It's no longer a game where your every whim is obeyed, you must negotiate with the various factions at play in your city. Your actions affect how those factions grow and that changes how you negotiate going forward.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: As much as I wish I could recommend it, I can't;- horribly optimized, especially in the late game, where you regularly have pretty bad stuttering and freezes (heh)- the political fight is somewhat arbitrarily instigated; If people are doing well, even if they don't like the direction of where their nation is heading, they're unlikely to rebel. Civil wars don't really happen over ideology, but usually because an ideology offers betterment to absolutely horrid conditions. I was doing VERY WELL by the midgame and the crisis just didn't make sense to me.- Someone scuffed the resource balancing. By the time I had the political situation under control and got close to passing the final resolution... I ran out of food. From the entire map.On the 2nd lowest difficulty.The two endless sources fully upgraded simply could not keep up with my demand, leading to a constant trust-lowering death spiral. Did nobody get over 50k population in beta-testing?Overall, there's a good bit of meat to this, I'm just disappointed there's bone shards and rocks in it, too.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: What a fantastic game, cant recommend it enough, same with the first Frostpunk. The gameplay is so fun, having to balance recourses for your people survival, while also juggling politics and how people feel is a unique challenge. In the first game you had to pass laws in order to advance your city, this is also true in the second game, but you have a counsil hall now. Each faction in your city will have a certain number of seats in the counsil representing the population percentage of that faction. You have to let your people vote on the laws you propose. And most of the time because of how divided the ideologies of everyone are, you will have to make promises to people in exchange for them voting the way you want them too on what laws pass or not. Super cool. But I guess people will hate eachother even in the most dire of situations. And the atmousphere is great too and works to enhance the gameplay. And maaaaaaaan the soundtrack is so gooooooooooood. Like if the rest of the game is a 10/10, the soundtrack is an 11. Lastly, I think one of the games best charms is that all the super crazy ideas, the martial law, child workers, rigging the voting on laws, you only pass them out of necessity because your city is in bad shape. You only become a dictator because of your own inadequacies. With better preperation and forethought, everyone CAN be happy, and I think that is really cool. 11 Bit Studios should be really proud of what they have created, and I look forward to what they make next.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very different take on Frostpunk. Its one that at first I did not enjoy nothing compared to the original Frostpunk but the more I played it. The more I began to enjoy the new mechanics added the politics added is very interesting as is the tension that builds until dealt with. Would I say this is Frostpunk 2? Yes and no its Frostpunk 2 in it is a bigger scale and direction its not what I would have expected but I am happy with the direction that 11-bit went and took a chance! You do loose the personal aspect when people are lost but on a scale like this it makes sense why it went this way. I am happy that 11-bit is very receptive to feedback and takes it to consideration all that was provided in the April open beta. Pushing the game back not many devs do that anymore to fine tune out details and feedback instead of lets launch fix it in a patch. If you want a game that is a society survival political simulator this fits that criteria very well! For those who were expecting something like Frostpunk 1, give it time I was bummed out but you can't stay small scale 30 years have passed its time for a future and that future requires big picture planning and thinking. Something that Frostpunk 1, would not be able to do very well with the different time keeping in hours and days not days weeks and years in Frostpunk 2. I look forward to what the future of the game will be and the additional content brought and the fact that 11-bit is still receptive to feedback even after release the fact they gave us unlimited deep deposits in Utopia!
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: The game is great, however, those looking for a remake of Frostpunk will be disappointed. This is a completely different game, with wholly new mechanics, new goals and challenges. It took 13 hours to understand the game mechanics well enough to finish the first two chapters of the story. What's good: Laws and Research interact with one another. Be careful which laws you choose because it can pigeonhole your lawmaking ability since delegates can "steal" the floor. Start with laws that everyone agrees with and check before passing any laws whether you can promise that law to any group.Frostbreaking and district placement are a tough but rewarding challenge. Understanding how to place districts and hubs to get all the adjacency bonuses. One thing to keep in mind is build more than you need. Two adjacent extraction districts staffed half-full are warmer than one district fully-staffed, with the added bonus that as people come in, you can fill those districts instead of scrambling to give them something to do.I like how they implemented the built in resource stockpiles. It's easy to tell how much longer a district has before it runs out, allowing you to juggle workforce to meet all your requirements.What's bad:Glitches/Incomplete UI. There is no Expedition indicator within the City to let me know when the Old Dreadnought is setup. You must click out to the Frostland map to see progress. I see the progress indicator line, so I think they just forgot to implement it. This alone has ruined two or three runs since it got setup but I didn't notice it and wasted a bunch of time not developing it.Along the same lines, event notifications are easily the worst implemented feature of the game. They made the gong sound quieter than last game, and also made the sound the same for every event. It needs to be louder with a distiction between LAW, RESEARCH, EXPEDITION and STORYLINE EVENT. There is SO MUCH going on -- more than FP1 -- and missing ANY event can mean disaster. Please fix this, 11bit.To compound this issue, 11bit removed the autosave feature, so if you miss an event, there's no restarting at the beginning of the day like FP1. You have to start at the beginning of the Chapter. Frustrating, but now that I know I make sure to save more frequently than I would otherwise.All in all, a great game. Difficult to pull off, very engaging. It has some bugs and a couple of bad design decisions, but overall, like with all 11bit games, you can tell they care about their games. This one is no different.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: This is still a builder - but the theme is this universe's priority. In other words...how could you continue just adding buildings in the thematic follow up of the lore of the first game?11 Bits thought of a very bold yet complete alternative new vision. Age of Wonders+civ. You build districts, buildings, special buildings/upgrades, logistic lines.One thing that the first game was lacking was meaningful and crucial political/survival elements. This time, politics not only matters, but it has incredible depth - even the tech tree influence said political sphere. While i get that fans of the first one may feel at odd here - they're mistaken and backward when it comes to how to approach this game. 11 bits outdid themselves here in almost everyway. The game is more complex, more meaningful, at a bigger scale (as it was the only true option to go about it here)
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: I cannot begin to describe the replayability of this game. Every choice, law, building, district, faction request matters. Everything you do or don't do matters, and WILL be reflected at the end of the game. Trial and error is the goal here. Losing is how you learn. I don't want to spoil anything or say too much but this experience was well worth the money for pre-order, with more content to come. I've only played through twice and each experience was significantly different. 100/100 HIGHLY recommend this game. If you were a fan of the first Frostpunk, this is a huge improvement and 11bit really reached for the stars here
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: A great evolution from the first game, the scale of the city has naturally evolved into tens of thousands of people, with you placing down districts instead of just individual buildings. This doesn't diminish the human element of the first game, as with every decision you make, there are comments by the population on how it impacts them. The council mechanic isn't as tedious as some describe, and giving out promises is a skill that you can hone to help elevate the city in the direction you want while placating the different factions. For those that feel it is too easy, they probably need to turn up the difficulty which makes the factions more easily angry. Some of the reviews here are flat out wrong, like the one that mentions the announcer not being as prominent. The announcer doesn't just speak when a law is passed, theres voicelines for when a rally is happening, protests and just general day to day activities. Overall, you might not like the changes from one, but I love that there is an evolution in the series instead of rehashing what has already been done. People should look out for who has put in little hours before giving a negative review.

_childDocuments_.review: There is the same Darkest Dungeon 2 feeling, like the artistic vision and general design were somewhere lost along the way and replaced with in-cohesive flurry of stuff someone thought would be cool to implement. And they are, by themselves on paper. In realty, you are constantly annoyed be the endless stream of stuff you are not sure even worth your attention. If they were at least introduced in a reasonable fashion, it at the very least wouldn't be so apparent, but right now i have a feeling like i am loading in someone else's save mid game. The only actual responses the game managed to evoke in me so far are either irritation from being constantly bombarded by stuff and general confusion about what does it do and what is expected of me. Sadly i am well past refund date, but i dont think i will ever boot the game again simply because i had around 8 hours behind my back and i have no clue why would i.

_childDocuments_.review: Took me about 13 hours to beat the campaign and I have to say that this was a very intriguing story as you climb through the stories. Once you understand all the different elements of the game it starts to click. I'd say you kind of just go with the flow and and read some of the tutorial tool tips and you'll be good to go. I like how the game doesn't give away everything you need to do and makes you figure it out. All in all i'd give it a solid 9/10. If they made it a bit longer maybe another 5-10 chapters it would get me 10/10. Either way super satisfied with this game and will probably play it again at some point.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely fabulous! It takes bravery to take a sequel in a radically new direction, and I think it pays off massively here. The gameplay takes a step back from the scope of Frostpunk 1, because as the city grows it only makes sense to work at a larger scale. There is an even larger amount of events than the first game, and the way they weave into the political system adds a ton of replayability to the game.As always, the soundtrack is out of this world and beautifully composed for the new type of game. The graphic design is just stellar as well.All in all, Frostpunk 2 is a beautiful game that innovates on its genre yet again. I highly recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: negative reviews seem to consist solely of people who just wanted to play the first game again. frostpunk 2 tells you from the first 5 minutes it is a different game, with a bigger scale and different challenges and systems. if you dont want that, don't buy it. that said, the game has plenty of challenge, dread, and hope, and is worth the purchase if you want another good survival city sim. _childDocuments_.review: Had an issue initially when I first installed the game. Upon start an error message would appear explaining that DirectX 12 is not supported. But when I checked I had the latest installations and everything was up to date. It took me approximately 1.30 hrs to troubleshoot the issue and after uninstalling and reinstalling the latest version of the driver it worked. Unfortunately, the games graphics are poor and lagging making the game unplayable. Do not buy this game unless you have a brand new high spec computer, it will only disappoint.
_childDocuments_.name: Frostpunk 2

_childDocuments_.review: Frostpunk 2 is bigger in scope than its predesessor, Frostounk 1. The transition from New london into the new game is portrayed nicely by starting with a view of your former feat of survival like a small piece of your larger citymap. You still juggle resources, try to maximize and prioritieze your choices. The micromanagement in buildings from FP1 have been replaces by smart placing in the hexsystem to recieve bonuses. That is a good change. I like almost all changes in this game, even though  really loved the citybuilder that was Frostpunk 1The new factions and laws are neat and feels implemented nicely. The factions could be more active though, they should be more of a problem atleast on more difficult levels. The laws become redunant late game, and that is a shame. The book of laws could be vastly expanded on, the more research you do. Also the factions wills and wishes follow a quite predictable patern. Early game could be more challanging if my factions varied their goals and agendas. I woulnd't mind if they also put demands on me as a steward spontanously. They are to easily manipulated as it stands now.Graphics are great. Sound is somewhat distant, even if it is good. Music is very good, but the howling winds gets to sing more in this game. And that is also nice. You face more threats in the frostland. I would like more active threats to your scouts and settlements. Like raiders or scouts from other parties. Frostpunk 2 will be successful. It will suffer from a very vocal and loving frostpunk 1 community that wanted to keep eating the same cake. I call it the Kylix999 syndrome. Its pathological and nothing to bother about.  When modding, patches and DLCs have done this game over. It will be a classic. I for one like the bigger scope. I recommend anyone that like resource juggling and survival to get this gem.

_childDocuments_.review: Very different from the first game but in my personal view, this makes sense. Let me explain..In the first game things start small. Clusters of people eking out an existence. Localised industry if you were lucky to find the things necessary. On a small scale one person or group could keep control. Now things have grown to a massive scale! More people means more industry. which in turn means more fuel...In addition one persons dream is no longer enough. More people means more ideas, more systems of thought. More factions. Hence the need for a Parliament like system of government. The need for oil and less reliance on coal makes sense when you realise your little community has/is heading for the next industrial revolution. With this context in mind...The new way Frostpunk plays makes sense on so many levels. Yes the first game felt more personal. You knew people and their names. Each person felt important, and you felt each and every loss deeply. But now, the city has grown so large, its not possible to have that close connection. Your only connection is through the representatives of these different groups who give you a rough idea of what is best for your city. The control of your citizens is more detailed as now the emphasis is not just survival but developing a new civilisation. In conclusion....If you are expecting the same game as the first frostpunk, you will be disappointed. But for the reasons i have given (in line with the lore) if you change your perspective and see why the changes have been made....you will LOVE this game. Its more in depth, more complicated, more detailed, more demanding to control your city. Before the Generator was everything, but now it has become the beating heart of this living, breathing, multi-headed beast...the city!

_childDocuments_.review: The city must not fall. You start as Stewart in a stable and growing city, your borders must expand for the city to keep thriving. Thus you're set out to explore the frostland once more to find resources and a way to keep the generator running. As Stewart you have lost your captains rights and are forced to take part in a political society with democracy at it's core. The advantage with being Stewart is that you can make promises to the fractions of the city and thus create relationships which grant you abilities and buffs, were the biggest drawback is that the Stewart is blamed for all the consequences that arise from what the council decides.The fractions are different sized groups of the populations with a changeable precentage of supporters depending on how they get treated by the Stewart in regards to heeding advice and/or promotion for said fraction. Many of the fractions have their own world views which gives different options in the research tree. The research tree allows you to bring forward ideas on new laws and technology for the city. The supporters clearly favour different world views such as equality or merit, giving you the possibility to create your own city's values. Similar to Frostpunk 1 you can set the course for what your city will adopt, though there are more than just two ways to choose from in Frostpunk 2.The storymode comes in six different chapters where in the first chapter you learn how to use and place the district, in the first game you were handeling the city on a more micro managing level moving a few workers here and there, placing medical tents for every five people and so on. Where in the first game the placement of your housings were mostly only dependent on the access to heat and roads. Now in the second game you handle housing district which will be affected negatively by being close to any industrial district spewing out dust from the sawmills and such, also food districts will be affected negatively by being close to housing, industrial or other districts.You manage districts and the buildings within after what buffs you want them to give your city, lower disease or crime rate etc. And as you progress through out the game you get to face more challenging endeavours to test your management abilities. As always I can put my trust to 11 bit studios to do something challenging, miserable and absolutely enjoyable. Thank you for this addition to the franchise. I am roughly 25 hours into the game and am ready to go for a different trial or maybe the utopia mode. Baught the game pre-release, definitely worth it.It gladens me to see that the scouts were quite similar to the first game, and there were none of that nonsense from the DLC the Last Autumn.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a proper sequel to Frostpunk, and it deserves every praise I can give it.It's not easy. Like the first game, the game really doesn't hold your hand when getting the hand of the game systems. I found myself restarting the game twice before I finally finished the story on my third run, having already realized some things about the core mechanics. This time, it's not about each building - you have to build an entire city, and placing every district counts both for the health of your citizens (try living next to the smog-vomiting industrial district, to see whether you like it) and their warmth (because now, placing districts neatly together and cramped can block wind and they'll insulate each other - something absent from the first game).The resource needs are different - people can cook for themselves, so now you only have to make sure you have food. Wood and metal? No. This time, you need raw materials, whichever they are - and now, you need those materials raw for maintenance, or processed into building supplies and consumer goods - it's not about surviving, it's about thriving despite all odds. Coal is still there, but Oil is much more valuable, efficient, the lifeblood of the generator. And then, there are the people, and the factions. Where they were mostly silent in the first game, the factions are loud, vocal, and they don't want to survive - they want to be heard, to matter, to feel important. It's a game about hubris, about vision, about fearmongers, riot rousers and political devotion. You can have a faction protesting your rule, and another rallying for support at the same time, and you can even direct them one against the other. As the captain, you were absolute until people get fed up with you. Now, the Steward suffer the same risk, but with less control than the captain had. People here are often unable to think past their own wants, to look up to their best interests, some will be angry if you're planning for the future, some will be enraged if you think on short-term unsustainable goals, and someone will be mad at anything you do. Damned if you do, damned if you don't.After all, the game has expanded. 30 years have passed since the great storm. Population has grown to the thousands (at the start of the game), of course the city would grow. It's not about a handful of survivors anymore, but about their children and their grandchildren - people who have been born in the frozen wastes, who aren't afraid of merely surviving anymore. First, we built the city, and had it survive. Now, we have a state, and need it to grow. And for growth, and survival, we need people. Now, the consequences of every law you pass, of every tech you research are shown via popup stories - someone who sabotaged something out of jealousy, someone who destroyed their own life because you trusted them with too much freedom, someone who turned to stealing because you don't produce enough for them to live... It feels raw, visceral, and no deed shall go unpunished.Yes, there are compatibility problems. The game gets so heavy nearing the end chapters that stutterings and straight up freezes became common for me (not a high-end computer, but not a bad one, though). At one point, I couldn't even load a savegame, since it'd freeze the game and force me to shut it down via task manager, so I had to revert to a previous save. Using the maximum speed was not an option anymore, as it'd again freeze everything, and it was awful, but i'm positive that can be fixed in future patches, especially since so many people are having the same problems. Who am I to complain about bugs? I love Bethesda games and have played Cyberpunk at launch - this game was (pardon the pun) chill about it - playing on regular and medium speed, I managed to finish an entire story run, and plan to do many more.I've become a fan of 11 bit studios with This War of Mine. At Frostpunk 1, I loved the core game and every single DLC. And now, I loved this game too and am excited for the future DLC I already purchased with the Deluxe edition. For my tastes this game is a solid 8.5/10, with the potential to reach 9/10 once the lategame stutters are fixed.

_childDocuments_.review: Reviewed after aprox. 15h of playtime, via the code provided by publisher.Verdict:Frostpunk 2, inherits the path to greatness from its predecessor. While maintaining Frostpunk 1's perfectly balanced, yet difficult survival elements, it manages to change their perspective in order to deliver a fresh, yet similar experience. The Story takes place exactly where the previous title left off and it’s as cruel, dark and ruthless as ever. In Frostpunk 2, every decision counts, one wrong move may lead to defeat. And every move, every decision, has its consequences. One may destroy one person’s life, while it fulfils another’s dreams. But in the end, it makes the player think: “Was it worth it?”All in all, Frostpunk 2 is an addictive, immersive and entertaining title, which both Frostpunk veterans and newcomers will enjoy.+ Entertaining campaign mode with variety of different scenarios+ Addictive gameplay, with balanced yet challenging survival elements+ Incredible freedom of action in quest completion+ mesmerizing graphics- complexity of some elements might be frustrating for some players, specially newcomers to Frostpunk series- some minor performance issues such as fps dips and stuttering8.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately, Frostpunk 2 falls short of expectations. It has deviated significantly from the original game, which could have been a positive change had the developers focused more on testing and refining the gameplay. The choice between settling colonies and drilling into deep ice deposits feels superficial.We either settle colonies in the frozen world, or stubbornly drill ice to reach deep deposits. The question is, what are deep fertile soil deposits? Why, having such advanced food production technologies, do they even need fertile soil? Spoiler – whatever you do, you'll know that your city will die of starvation, as by week 600 you realize that all the food on the map is not enough to feed the growing population because the soil is finite, and you must finish the game earlier. So why is this a bad game design decision? Because it prevents us from being able to unlock technologies to drill deep deposits or settle colonies. If you're playing as the technocrats, you still have to connect outposts to the main city until the resources are exhausted! This is purely artificial limitation that contradicts COMMON SENSE, which you're supposed to embrace if you choose the technocrats. Meanwhile, creating an oil settlement isn't against their "religion," but creating one or two more is taboo (because it's a dumb script)! Don't you understand how artificial and cheap this looks!? I played on Captain twice. And you know what? The colony route is much easier! You have colonies on the map that bring infinite resources, and you absolutely don't worry about their housing, morale, etc., just sending them crumbs of food and oil. And even founding a colony is cheaper resource-wise than building a district with a deep mining upgrade! These colonies steadily provide you with resources despite all the riots in the main city, just like the two other cities you personally control, but if the district with deep mining riots, you risk losing the upgrade and have to rebuild it! Now to the factions – the funniest part is you can easily maintain good relations with both opposing factions (even on the highest difficulty)... IF IT WEREN'T FOR THE DAMN SCRIPTS! The game is heavily scripted, and the first part suffered from this too, but in this one, it's just insane. In the last chapter, all factions go off the rails regardless of your previous relations. And even with this, the game is very easy! I got the 0.3% achievement "Checks and Balance" (not passing any captain's laws) on my second playthrough as soon as I found out about its existence! There was no survival challenge, just idiotic political squabbles over which I had even less control due to the achievement run. I passed most of the scenarios from the first game on Survivor, and that took effort, knowledge of the game, but here it's not required. And yeah, developers, where are the achievements for Survivor difficulty? Why should I play it if the highest achievements are only for Captain difficulty, and there are no others! As a buyer of the premium edition, I am extremely disappointed. I saw the game's problems back in early access, and unfortunately, they were not fixed but left as the game’s concept. I'll check the DLCs they release later (I've already paid for them... the cactus hurts, but I keep eating it...), but I don't have much hope for improvements.

_childDocuments_.review: Having played and thoroughly enjoyed the first Frostpunk, this game actually lives up to the standard set by its predecessor and even surpasses it in many ways. The story is about on par with the first game, so if you enjoyed the story of the first you will probably enjoy the story mode this time. I expect it will be expanded in the future with DLCs just like FP1 was. There are several different endings you can get, and several different paths to take throughout the story, giving it a good amount of replayability.The mechanics relating to actually constructing the city and placing districts and buildings is much easier and more robust than in the original Frostpunk. You no longer have to worry about placing roads in strange ways, fighting the annoying snap system, just to fit more buildings inside a ring. Frostpunk 2 uses a non-uniform hexagonal-ish grid system instead which eliminates this issue entirely while still allowing you to maintain a circle city aesthetic if you wish.The scope of the game is also much larger. In the first game, the time scale was measured in days, with scenarios not lasting longer than about 2 months. In Frostpunk 2, the time scale is measured in WEEKS, with days passing by in mere seconds. I had always thought it was a little bit unbelievable how in the first game you could go from basically a small village of survivors cooperating and helping each other to a totalitarian dictatorship or an extremist cult in a matter of 48 days. In Frostpunk 2, the time it takes for a societal shift of that magnitude is years, which is far more realistic.The research and law systems have much greater depth than in FP1. In this game, laws are actually voted on by a council comprised of members made up of different factions and communities within your city. You can make deals with the delegates in order to sway the vote in your favor, but you will be punished if you do not follow through on your end of the bargain. Research is also dependent on factions and tech can have a variation applied to it that favors the values of whatever faction is assigned to research it. It's a very cool system and there are hidden synergies that you can discover with the various laws and techs. Additionally, if you enjoyed the idea of being able to build and control outposts like in the "On the Edge" DLC from the first game, you can do that in Frostpunk 2 as part of the main story and in Utopia Builder (sandbox/endless mode) and switch back and forth between the main city and your outposts.There are a few bugs and performance issues that will likely get worked out in hotfixes in the coming weeks, but the important thing is that the game is feature-complete and is completely playable from start to finish of the main story in its current state.I could go on, but the overall message I'm trying to send is that if you enjoyed the first game, you'll really enjoy this one too. And if you haven't tried either one, I highly recommend them both. That being said, you won't necessarily need to have played the first to understand the events of the second, so if you can only afford one of them, give it a try!

_childDocuments_.review: 11bit's highly anticipated sequel to their smash hit Frostpunk is finally here. This game is a far more ambitious title than its predecessor, and it does not disappoint. Instead of building only individual houses and industrial buildings, you are now responsible for planning entire districts, with specialized buildings within them. Creating your city requires even more careful planning, as there are bonuses for having symbiotic districts next to each other, such as housing/food, and extraction/industry. The Frostland exploration is now done through Logistics districts, with specialized buildings providing bonuses to safety and exploration time. The law system has been entirely reworked, where before you could simply sign a law and it would take effect, now a council of 100 will vote on every proposal you put forward, which may require some careful negotiation should you not have the votes outright. New laws also have to be researched, but they don't require any resources to do so, aside from time. Your citizens now belong to factions, and those factions will influence how your city develops. If you ignore one faction for too long, tension develops, which can boil over into a full blow riot. The research tree has also be reworked, with buildings requiring heatstamps to research. Each faction will have specialized buildings, each with their own bonuses and costs associated.The economy system has also be reworked, requiring not just materials, but currency as well, in the form of heatstamps. Your citizens provide heatstamps, but if their needs are left unmet, the amount you receive becomes lower and lower, which can cause further issues when attempting to expand. This new, more complex gameplay system is incredible. 11bit swung for the fences, and delivered on almost every point. However, the only drawback is you have lost the individualism from the first game, as you used to be able to click on each individual citizen, and they had a name, and a family. You have the ability to zoom in on districts, and see your citizens working, but you no longer have that connection with them. Overall, 11bit took a massive risk with this title, and it payed off. I can see myself playing this game for hundreds of hours like the previous one. I can't wait to see how they develop this world further.

_childDocuments_.review: WAIT FOR THEM TO BUGPATCH. There's a lot to like in this new vision for Frostpunk. Whether you like this new flavour (or not) will come down to your preferences, but I gave it a proper shake as I'd love to write well of it. However, I've ultimately come away frustrated, drained and with a bad taste in my mouth. I can't recommend anyone buy it until they patch it some. Among the things to wait to be fixed are:-  PATCHED AND FIXED (26/09)- Absence of really commonplace city-builder QoL features e.g. 'cancel construction'. - Abominable performance in the later stages - the game wants to hold onto its fore-bearer's prettiness, but it's utterly unoptimised for the 'scale' of city that the narrative demands. What is 'pretty' in your first hour will become irrelevant clutter by your fifth hour, FPS-destroying obnoxious noise by your 8th... and then it'll get worse from there. - Outposts are a key part of this version, which makes the Dev's choices about what information to provide, and what to hide, utterly bewildering. Have you got infrastructure that'll handle 600 units, but it won't handle more than 4 if those units are materials? Any idea why? Might as well guess - the game won't tell you anywhere. Been waiting so long and patiently for this - I'm really disappointed. All the worst because I spent my playthrough stumbling over these QOL shortcomings going "oh, okay, that's an early release bug" only to fight my way to the climax and have to give up due to a bug that makes it impossible to finish (or maybe it's just a catastrophic failure of UI design? Frostpunk 2 is the sequel to the highly acclaimed, BAFTA-nominated society survival game that blended city building, strategy and management gameplay, creating a brand new genre. Its successor takes place 30 years after the apocalyptic blizzard storm, and Earth is still overwhelmed by the icy climate of neverending frost and harsh weather.

Demands and expectations of various factions will raise tensions and evoke conflicts, but will a cold-blooded rule and a Machiavellian approach to politics be necessary? _childDocuments_.review: As a big Atlus/Persona fan, I never thought I'd refund a Persona game ever. It was a painful and difficult decision.I cannot recommend the game as it is right now. The PC Port is really bad to the point that it ruins the game experience.If you take a look closely at the Steam reviews, almost all positive reviews are just people simping for Adachi. Most of the real reviews of this game are negative due to the terrible port.P4AU itself is an incredible game, very fun to play with excellent characters and a very colorful, flashy and vibrant visuals.My PS3 broke due to a power surge that came from the network cable in a stormy day about a month after P4AU got released 9 years ago so I could never play it since then. I was really excited to finally be able play it now in current-gen hardware, especially on PC, but unfortunately the awful port ruined my experience of this great game.There are several random crashing issues in different modes, very inconsistent audio volumes that are either inaudibly quiet or freaking loud, plus video playback issues (init render and separate "active movie window" pop-up).The developers didn't even bother to upscale the game graphical assets from 720p to a higher resolution.Online matching crashes when searching for rooms with more than 2 slots and when it finds any rooms there are like only 3 people available. Ranked works but I can only find like 4 people with a 0 bar connection. I understand that this game is not popular in my region but I was expecting to find more than 7 people online at launch day.Lobbies have been removed in this version for no real reason.Atlus completely trolled us all at launch by unlocking the game 5 hours after the Steam page release time.The game is expensive for a bad 9 year old "remaster" and doesn't have regional pricing. I decided to buy it anyway because I'm a big Persona fan and I was really excited to play this game that I could never play for 9 years. The game itself is excellent, but the terrible PC Port and the big number of issues alongside a bad delay based netcode completely ruined the enjoyment of the game.Maybe I'll reconsider buying it again once rollback is implemented and the issues are fixed, but for now I can't recommend P4AU in it's current state. The negatives are greater than the positives and I felt a big disrespect from Atlus this time. I wasted too much time waiting the game troll release time, trying to fix the port issues, and trying to find people with acceptable connection online.It was a difficult decision, but I had to refund it unfortunately.

_childDocuments_.review: As I’m only okay-ish at fighting games like this one, this review will focus on the story modes of  instead. However, I don’t want to stick to just reviewing this time and instead also share some information on how to correctly approach the story modes – so you won’t make the same mistakes I did.The most important thing to know about the story of  is that it’s a canon continuation of ,  (+ FES) and  (+ Golden). And I do mean “continuation”, because  will spoil the events of both games for you - if you aren’t already familiar with them. I can’t emphasize this enough: If you’re even remotely interested in the story of , make sure to experience them before engaging with the story modes of . In fact, stop reading this review, other reviews and leave the store page and make sure you’re prepared before coming back.Still here?Already know what happens in  (or just don’t care)?Good. Here’s what else you need to know about the story modes of .If you’re opening the “story mode” part of the main menu for the first time, the game conveniently selects “Episode P4” for you to play. . What you instead want to check out is the bottom option, “P4A: Story MODE”. This is where the story really begins, set between the ending of  and the epilogue of . But why this confusing mix-up?To keep things simple, here’s the short version: Initially, this game only released as  in 2012 – and it only contained the story mode that’s now called “P4A: Story Mode” in the main menu. Two years later (at least in the West),  released as an updated version of the game, containing more content and other refinements. And yes, this includes new story modes, which serve as a direct continuation of the original  storyline. However, for some reason, the main menu put these new story episodes on top the menu – quite confusing. Anyway, tldr;  .Alright, let’s talk about the story of  then. In short, you’ll have to play through a few character stories in order to unlock the whole story. Here’s the problem though: Considering you’re exploring (mostly) the same events only with a different character, you’ll quickly get tired of seeing the same events over and over again. So here’s the shortest way to unlock the actual ending of :1. Play through the story of Yu, Yosuke, Chie or Yukiko until you reach a “to be continued” state. This unlocks the story of  or .2. Play through the story of another character until you again reach a “to be continued” state – it doesn’t matter if which story you pick as long as you got two stories in a “two be continued” state. This unlocks the stories of  as well as .3. Now, reach the “to be continued” state with one of the  characters. This unlocks the story of .4. Clearing the story of  finally allows you to continue past the “to be continued” state of all . Get to the real end of one of these character’s stories and you are now able continue past the “to be continued” state with the remaining characters.5. You guessed it, reach the real end of one of the  as well and you’ll unlock the last character story: .You can still reach the ending of the remaining character stories if you wish to do, but again, that’s going to be one hell of a repetitive task. I’d suggest going for the bare minimum instead and then continuing with the story mode the game initially wanted you to play: “Episode P4”.This story is, thankfully, not asking you to experience the same things over and over again. It’s actually pretty straightforward and getting to the end should be no problem: you can even let the AI fight for you if you don’t want to battle yourself (although this doesn’t always work well. I let the AI play against the final boss a few times to see how it fares and it actually lost quite often).After clearing “Episode P4”, you’ll unlock two more story episodes:  and .However, in true  fashion, there’s also a true ending to the story of . This unfortunately isn’t just unlocked by beating the story modes of . Instead, .That’s it, you beat the story of  in the correct way!No, for the review part: Should you even bother doing so? That’s mostly depending on how much you enjoy spending more time with the characters of .  really is mostly fanservice and while I enjoyed one of the new additions to the cast (), the story really only works if you’re invested in both  games to the point you’d even play a fighting game to see how the story continues (again, this is canon). did a better job at serving as a connection between  than I thought (longer as well, took me about 11h to see the endings of ). However, the game really likes to keep you busy with the same events, which can make it a real slog to play/read through at times. I feel like going for a linear campaign would’ve been a way better choice here, even if it meant having less content to play through. But well, fighting games and story modes …Anyway, you want more ? Check out the story modes here, even if they are longer than they need to be. If not or if you simply dislike unnecessarily long or repetitive fighting game stories, maybe just read through a Wiki summary. _childDocuments_.review: Just know that this review is only negative because of the quality of the port, and not the game itselfI'll open with this, P4 Arena quickly became one of my favorite fighting games when I first played it because it has all the things I look for in a fighting game. It's fast paced, frantic, technical, has a large and diverse character roster, and is just plain fun. This is on top of being a love letter to personas 4 and 3, with a fairly decent, and canon, story mode to play through as well. With all of that being said I was very disappointed in this port having the issues it does have, because I wanted to see this game get a second chance in the spotlight. While I haven't ran into nearly as many issues as others have, there are still some very OBVIOUS issues that ANY PLAY-TESTING would've revealed instantly. Very bad audio mixing making the FMVs and random sound effects incredibly loud compared to the rest of the game, and generally poor online performance. From my experience it was mostly fine during matches although due to not having rollback yet, random stuttering will happen, and that is not ideal at all for a technical fighting game of this nature. If that wasn't bad enough, simply trying to get into a match and find players who you haven't played against before can be a real hassle. Also the game ran perfect from my experience, but I have friends who had the game run unplayably slow, despite having great PCs. This sucks because not only is it a gamble on the game FUNCTIONING for you, but for whoever you may want to play with as well. I just straight up can't play this game with some of my friends until they fix the optimization or whatever is causing this. All of this being said, it makes me very upset that this game wasn't handled with the respect it deserved, and was clearly rushed to meet a deadline. The player base is already pretty small, and I can very well see these issues making people drop the game or not want to pick it up entirely. TLDR, fantastic game, but buy with caution

_childDocuments_.review: Serving as a direct sequel to both Persona 3 and Persona 4, Persona 4 Arena Ultimax is a  2D anime fighting game with its own canonical story mode following the events of the two games mentioned. Taking place 2 months after the end of Persona 4. The story itself is mostly told through a visual novel style presentation split between fighting segments. If you're picking this up for story you're gonna need to be ready for a lot of reading as there's a lot of dialouge between fights, for better or worse that's what they went for. The game meshes casts from both Persona 3 and Persona 4 into a unified story and fans of both games will be delighted to see the interactions they form, lots of fanservice to go around in that department. The game includes the original Arena story and its subsequent sequel Ultimax. As for the plot, the new character Labrys is a fantastic introduction and her origin story was delightfully tragic. The callbacks to Persona 3 feel very nostalgic. Sho Minazuki not so much.  The story is very dependant on you knowing/having played their one of/both of the respective entries for you to understand it so that's best done before getting into this if you plan on playing through the story. Story mode also features an 'Automatic' mode for you to toggle if you just wanna experience the story but don't want to do any of the fighting and just let the CPU do it for you. Gameplay wise it's a very fluid and enjoyable experience as far as 2D fighters go. There's a lot to work with here in terms of the skill ceiling while also being incredibly easy to get into even if you never played a fighting game in your life. The character roster is distinct and comes in many flavors that you can bet at least one of them will be to your liking. As far as offline content goes it features a serviceable arcade mode that does its job but nothing on the level of Tekken regarding quality. The multiplayer is mostly dead last I checked unfortunately. In my experience you can easily enough invite a friend to play a few rounds with and the connection is fantastic, results vary depending on connection quality of course. Lots of fun to be had if you can make it work! A solid 8 if you like fighting games and enjoy Persona. Probably less if not so much.

_childDocuments_.review: Ultimax is an excellent fighting game, and I couldn't be happier that it's finally received a PC port. However, I cannot possibly recommend picking up this version.Crashing is constant. I literally could not enter training mode without the game crashing completely. Changing graphics settings would sometimes do the same. I couldn't even enter an online match in a private lobby without a crash, and eventually a BSOD.Borderless window mode is broken as well, which wouldn't be as big of a deal if alt-tabbing the game didn't mess with the game & cause freezes/lag for others in a lobby.With some investigating with friends, it seems the most issues will plague you if you have an AMD GPU. _childDocuments_.review: In keeping with tradition, ATLUS has decided to skip over Persona 5, 3, or any other mainline entry and give us the fighting game instead. Having played it now though, I can’t say I’m complaining.Persona is usually a JRPG series, but this is a fighting game and it’s one developed between ATLUS and the prestigious Arc System Works - who brought us classics like BlazBlue and Guilty Gear. This game plays a lot like those two, but does so while incorporating a ton of elements from Persona and honestly, it’s a bit brilliant how it all works out.Each character has moves of their own, but also has their persona with unique moves on top of that and the game basically revolves around combining these two to build up some nasty combos. It is a very cool mechanic and, while complex on paper, I managed to pick it up pretty quickly.The base combat is some incredibly polished stuff too - before you even get to the extras like personas or super moves. It’s fast, fluid, responsive, and way more fun than I thought it was going to be if I am being honest. Maybe it’s because I am just coming off of playing Phantom Breaker, but this one just feels good to play. It has that perfect blend of move variety, gameplay mechanics, and audiovisual feedback to give the combat that unique Arc System touch and it makes for some very satisfying gameplay.You’ve got arcade mode, score attack, lessons, training, challenges, and this RPG-like endless mode called Golden Arena. In that one, you basically fight to earn XP to level up a certain character’s stats and even unlock abilities for them. It’s nothing too complex, but it’s a nice touch over the “endless mode” that we usually get.The story is also notable - both for its length (around 18 hours of VN scenes and fighting) and its insane entry barrier. Not only is this game a direct sequel to Persona 4, but Persona 3 as well and you will get spoiled on major plot points for both if you just jump in right here. I would speak on the quality of that story - but I am going to be honest, I have not completed either Persona 3 or 4 and don’t want to be spoiled myself, so I did not play through Arena’s storyline.At launch, the game is not going to have rollback netcode, but the devs have announced that it will be implemented in an update sometime this summer. A bit odd that they didn’t just do that right off the bat, but at least there is official confirmation. I was unable to test the netcode as it is because I played before release, so hopefully it’s at least decent enough to hold out until summer.PRAU is a solid fighting game all around, bunch of stuff to learn and master, yet still not this massive wall to get into. It looks great with that flashy Persona aesthetic, has that similarly great music, and also runs just fine and I had no technical issues whatsoever. I will note that while I did play at 1440p, the game is actually locked to 1080 internally and only scales up from there - disappointing to see.Persona 4 Arena Ultimax is a fairly easy recommendation to make. If you are a fan of any of Arc System Works’ previous fighting games, then you’ll likely have a lot of fun here. Persona fans too or even just fighting game fans in general. The story might be lost on that latter group, but the gameplay, the characters, the mechanics, all of that is incredibly polished and this is definitely one that will be on my fighting game rotation for a while. Now please just give us Persona 3 and 5.Follow my  for more reviews + videos!

_childDocuments_.review: Summary: Persona 4 Arena Ultimax is a very fun fighting game with lots of style, but the game being dead with no one playing online ruins it. If you are a Persona fan, buy it, if not, don't.     Persona 4 Arena Ultimax is a very fun but flawed game. Positives of this game include having the story mode from the original Persona 4 Arena, having great music, stages, and characters, and being a very fun fighting game. The fighting mechanics are kind of complicated at first, but if you have played a traditional fighting game before, then they are very familiar, once you learn the mechanics, it is surprisingly fun and in depth. Games such as Dragonball FighterZ and Street Fighter are very similar control wise as well.      But once you actually get more into the game, the cracks start to show. Minor issues such as load times, difficulty, and overall how confusing the game is for newcomers. Load times can get upwards to a minute (for me at least), the game also has major difficulty spikes in the arcade and story mode and to change the difficulty, it's hidden away in the options, and lastly the game does not give you a proper tutorial, you have to go and find lessons, which is over 70 and took almost an hour, not to mention over half of them just give you button combos.     Those may seem like minor nitpicks, but the major issue of the game is the lack of support. Other successful fighting games continue to have support in ways like adding new characters, stages, or even having a battle pass (which i'm not saying battle passes are good, they just help the game stay alive). These are mainly excusable considering this was a PS3 game from 10 years ago, but the fact that the online for this game is dead just ruins it. There is absolutely no one online, i'm not even exaggerating, I waited an hour for someone to join my match, no one ever did. Online matches are a huge factor in keeping a game alive, just look at Super Smash Bros for example. When the game came out there was not Rollback Netcode, which pretty much every fighting game has. This lack of Rollback Netcode let to the game being dead on arrival. The game being dead is the most major issue that plagues this game.      So, should you buy this game? I would say if you are a Persona fan, like myself, just buy it, the game has interactions between much of the Persona 3 and Persona 4 cast, making it very fun for fans of the series. But if you are a fan of fighting games or haven't heard of persona, don't buy it unless it's on sale for less than $10. And lastly, if you want to get into persona and choose this game, first of all don't, second this game is very "fan-servicy", third, you should buy Persona 4 Golden instead because it's $10 cheaper, and will provide much more playtime, and is a proper introduction to the series.But it has Adachi 100/10

_childDocuments_.review: Persona 4 Arena Ultimax vastly improves on the gameplay from the original - which was already rather fantastic. That being said, there are a few unbalanced moves and the shadow characters tend to be overpowered.I spent most of my time playing the Switch port, as this PC port has audio issues; fails to start up for some; etc.The lack of rollback netcode at launch is also something that I cannot support, especially when it was in the original. However, I have had a rather fun time playing this game with friends.For the most part, the ranked online was extremely entertaining: being able to combat skilled players from all over the world was rather invigorating. Although, this does not come without its flaws: there are a vast number of "troll players". Troll players constantly spam moves merely to rank themselves up, it truly makes the experience irritating for most - and almost made me give up entirely before I learned how to overcome them. Regrettably, no fighting game comes without these, but Persona 4 Arena Ultimax's lack of cooldowns, ability to spam, etc makes it far more annoying.The story drags on quite a bit, and the lack of a Persona 3 port/remaster on any console is rather bizarre - considering that this is a spiritual successor to both that and Persona 4, but ATLUS will be ATLUS. Overall, though, having all of the DLC stories and mainline ones included is a fairly nice surprise - and the writing is what you'd expect from a Persona game. Seeing the SEES crew grown-up was a lovely shock as well, to be sure.The AI in Ultimax, in comparison to the original, is vastly improved upon. You can alter the difficulty of these AIs for a nice challenge, and the single-player modes will keep you entertained.I love having the DLC characters like: Adachi, Marie and Margaret - the only thing missing is the Persona Q music, plus some other DLC songs, but I suppose those aren't necessary.In conclusion, I would highly recommend this game - but only once the patches for the PC release have been put out. If you do not wish to wait, then the Switch or PS4 version is an excellent substitute.

_childDocuments_.review: My short time with Persona 4 Arena has left me with one primary takeaway: A plausible Persona 5 Arena can't possibly be worse.Looking at this from the perspective of someone who enjoyed a good amount of the writing in Persona 4 (save some characters I think were handled poorly), and has had a good time with Guilty Gear Strive and Xrd (newer fighting games from Arc System Works), I couldn't be more disappointed. I'm not really certain what people enjoy about this from a fighting game perspective or a story perspective, at least from where I'm standing.As a fighting game, I popped it open on a Saturday night to play with my buddy, as I have with many fighting games in the past year. We generally get a good time out of some of them, playing them for a couple night or sometimes much longer.  Injustice/Mortal Kombat weren't really our style, but it's clear there's something there that just doesn't gel with us. Tekken 7 and Guilty Gear Strive/Xrd have stuck around much longer. P4AU took maybe two or three matches before we were absolutely confounded at the thought that this game was developed by the same company that made several games we've been actively enjoying for several months. Most combos are either mashing the same button over and over again, or insanely varied and frame-perfect inputs, there's no in-between. The entire experience feels like it's stuck in some weird mode that focuses on making the game "accessible" and, in turn, makes learning and executing moves extremely difficult to compensate. I know I'm relatively new to the genre, but it seems like this lack of control goes solidly against why folks would play it. Either way, we tried it a couple times and could only bring ourselves to play maybe 30-40 total matches before we decided it just wasn't fun.So gameplay is out, but this is a Persona game. Even the weird spin-offs tend to still bring back our cast of memorable characters and still deliver an engaging story, even if the main gameplay loop of day-to-day life is no longer the focus. Strikers was a beautiful example of how they can shift into a different genre and bring our old pals from the main game along for an enjoyable adventure. The question is: Does P4AU do this well? I'd say, unfortunately, no. From the onset, there were a couple things that were a bit off-putting but not dealbreakers. For instance, the main character from Persona 4 is now fully voiced, rather than just having a few callouts in the game. An improvement if I'm being honest, just a little weird from someone who's spent hours playing as the guy, only to finally hear him have emotions and a personality. Another addition is voices are "lip-synced" to characters, meaning as they speak, it toggles between a "mouth open" and "mouth closed" portrait. This...was not a good change. More work for a lesser outcome unfortunately. But hey, it's a little goofy, but that's not all. It wasn't for a bit that we realized the main downfall of this game: narration. Whoever wrote for this game had dreams of writing novels and expressed that overwhelmingly here. For most scenes in this game, there are maybe a couple of voiced lines of dialogue interspersed with absolutely massive paragraphs of silent narration that absolutely obliterate the flow of the story. The story itself is already pretty mediocre (from what we've played of it) and this aspect drops it down to the floor. You'll hear a character say something to another, and you'll hear the worry in their voice about what's going on. This will be immediately followed by three paragraphs of "I was worried for her, I really did attack her with all I had, but I had no choice! It's like she wasn't hearing the words I was saying and beating the crap out of her was the only way to get my point across! I really wish there was another way. Seriously, what is going on right now?". It's like it's written for people to casually leave it play while they walk in and out of the room washing dishes, doing laundry, etc.I would love nothing more than to recommend you buy this game and prove to Atlus that these fighting games are a profitable avenue to keep going down, as the concept of getting a Persona 5 Arena is a dream. Unfortunately, I can't endorse this game as being worth your money, either for fans of these characters and series, or as a fighting game. I was genuinely excited for announcement of this coming to steam and, despite my mediocre expectations given its age, I can't help but be disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: Having played Persona 4 Arena and Arena Ultimax's stories a few months ago (Emulated Arena using rpcs3, and purcahsed Ultimax for the 360) its 10 years in the waiting PC port is a welcome move from Sega, allowing Atlus's masterpiece Persona series to become more accessible for the general audience.That being said, this port does every thing you would want it to. HOWEVER, it isn't great, there are some glaring issues that I have heard of and also experienced such as the issue with border less window, audio issues and the fact that they didn't bother up scaling the visuals, leading to the conclusion that this was not a move for accessibility, instead, it was a cash-grab from Sega, following the brilliant performance of Persona 4 Golden on PC.If you have beaten Persona 4 Golden, this is a must, as it creates a canon relationship between the P4 and P3 cast, which is fan-service galore, something that I love. I am not impressed with this port, I did pre-order it because I am a Persona simp, but I hope that this means we get more, future Persona and Megami Tensei titles on PC, I am personally looking forward to a possible SMT V port and the upcoming Soul Hackers 2.

_childDocuments_.review: My favorite fighting game series of all time is finally on PC! I wish they had included the original P4A and not just Ultimax, or at least have ability to play as the original characters (like how you can pic GG and GGX mode in Guilty Gear Accent Core + R) or have the original yellow UI (health bars and meters) as a customization option. The lack of rollback netcode on release was a completely ignorant decision, and after a huge backlash the devs announced they will be providing rollback netcode in a later patch. Aside from that, the game does not currently function well as a PC game because if you alt+tab, it freezes the game for both players, and this can disconnect you from matches. So far, I have not seen players abusing this to cheat (aka lagswitching) but it should be patched out immediately as no other fighting game has this issue. Connecting to matches often fails, and sometimes the same player names appear on the ranked list twice. As people have mentioned, remote play has been disabled, which is a shame because that probably provides a better online multiplayer experience than the delay-based netcode the game currently has. There is almost nothing to spend the points you earn by playing matches on. You can buy a profile icon, and that's it. Other games let you buy colors for characters, but this game comes with every color unlocked. I enjoy unlocking colors in Under Night In-Birth and outfit pieces in Soul Calibur, so I wish it was the same here. Once you're in a match, the gameplay is a lot of fun, but I hope the devs improve the other aspects of the game to be the same level of quality.
