_childDocuments_.review: It's a unique game which feels like 70% social deduction, 20% RPG and 10% visual novel.It has a low story-to-gameplay ratio and is quite grindy to unlock the various story and lore bits.I repeat: do NOT play this game assuming it will be a visual novel with some gameplay. You should approach it as a roguelite RPG with (fairly repetitive) "encounters" with backstory, special events and dialogs sprinkled here and there.The social deduction mechanics, despite playing against AI, is quite fun as the AI characters have behaviors that fit their personality and game rules have enough randomness and quirks to keep it interesting through many runs.Art is fine, music is great. My main gripe is that character lines get repetitive very fast during normal gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: This'll be a different review than what most people would expect to find in a negative review.First things first: I like the characters and the story, let me make that clear.The OST is, although very experimental, quite nice. It definitely creates an unique atmosphere, especially when combined with the art of the game.I would give this game a 7/10. However, I would never recommend it to anyone.What the game gives to me, in exchange of the effort I put on it... Is absolutely not worth it.This game's constructed nature easily rejects smooth pacing, script writing, dialouge depth and realism; by sacrificing these elements in exchange of making the interactive gameplay work. And how that happens? Due to the fact that these elements are evolving around the interactive gameplay.You're definitely "playing" a story and its characters, for sure. But in this case, it's a torture. Spoilers are ahead!I hope I could clarify my frustration enough. Basically, the game won't reward you enough, not at all, for all of the effort and time you put into its gameplay. And some of its problems could be fixed so easily too...For example, if I fail, let me press a button that'll reset things. Another example, let us save the game at times. What about more examples? Let me have a skip button. (Maybe there's one and I'm dumb. But CTRL not working says a lot in itself.)According to steam, I've spent 24 hours for this game(probably longer since I played it offline too), and a lot of it came from the gameplay.Please, listen to me. There are richly written stories that are like this one, but way more relaxing to go through. Way more focused, paced way better, given way more depth to its dialouge and etc.These types of VN's reward the player for simply experiencing their stories. I could recommend them to you, and you would have a much better time than having to endure what gnosia makes you do.It's... Just not worth it for your time and effort.Gnosia's gameplay is flawed; It doesn't think of the player's comfort at all. It asks way too much, even though there are alternatives to its type of story that are way more comfortable to go through.

_childDocuments_.review: I did not expect to enjoy this as much as I did, I fully expected to get tired of the loops as many reviews before had stated. Instead I was hooked and for the two or so weeks that it took for me to complete this game, I was well and truly hooked. When I didn't play at the time, I wish I was. When I couldn't be playing at the time, I thought of ways to get to it. What makes it great? The way the social deduction type of gameplay has been integrated into the story. Inbetween gameplay segments you're able to experience character events. I think this is a wonderful way to combine gameplay and story and in the end, combined with the stats page of each character, the backstory and the way everyone acted in gameplay, the characetrs truly came to life in a way that no other game has really done for me. It lets you connect the dots to an extent, as you slowly understand each character's way of acting, who you can and can not trust. The events were frequent enough that I never felt as if I was grinding for it, apart from the very end, where it was still fortunately a brief stint.The dev team seems to be so small, but I loved every aspect of the game so much, the art, the music, the gameplay.. it managed to throw in scenes that were outright horror in their nature as well as a few laughs here and there. I highly, highly suggest this game. Thank you, Petit Depotto and Playism <3  One of my favourite games of all time. I really appreciated the nonbinary representation of this game as well.

_childDocuments_.review: Originally released on PS Vita and Nintendo Switch, Gnosia is a social deduction game in the form of visual novel. Inspired by ,  and , this is a compeletely single player experience that proves how social deduction games can be played alone. Gnos, an unknown alien parasite, has infected the crew members of a drifting spaceship. Stuck in a never ending time loop, they are now forced to re-live every moment trying to find who the Gnosia is. Each day the crew will meet, discuss and vote the most suspicious person who will be put into cold sleep, while every night the Gnosia will kill one member of their choice. It’s up to you to discover why all of this is happening and how to stop this alien lifeform from taking control of the ship.The Gnosia is not the only threat though. There is another dangerous enemy known as the Bug, which apparently can destroy the entire universe. If the Bug manages to survive until a winner has been decided among the humans and Gnosia, the victory goes to the Bug. Apart from this, there are a few other roles that are crucial to the gameplay. The Engineer can scan a player each round to detect any sign of infection, while the Doctor can discover the role of those who have been put into sleep. A Guardian Angel is able to protect a single crew member (but not themselves) from Gnosia attack, while an AC follower is a devoted person who would do anything to make the Gnosia win.At the start of the game you can choose your name, select your gender (male, female, non-binary), pick an avatar and tweak your initial stats. From there, each loop will gradually introduce you to the gameplay mechanics and I can fairly say that everything up to the 20th loop can be considered part of the tutorial. After these introductory loops, you can finally setup your own game, choosing the number of crew members, the number of Gnosia infected and if you want to allow any other role in your game. You can also choose your own, of course, and it’s best advised to play them all to unlock different scenes.Each meeting is made of five rounds where the crew members can suspect others while defending from accusations. You can also stay silent, which is a good strategy if you don’t want to raise any suspicion on yourself. At the end of the fifth round, a vote is held and the most suspected member is put into cold sleep. After the vote, you can visit one location of your choice, speaking to others, getting closer to them and adapting to their unique traits. During the night, someone will die and the next day you will have a new meeting, until either the Gnosia or humans win. From the main menu you can always check discussion logs, voting results, crew data, engineer and doctor reports, which will help you to better understand your crewmates’ behaviour.The game follows a roguelite structure, with fragments of the story being unlocked progressively by knowing more about the characters and filling the “special items” section in the crew member tab. To unlock these special items you need to succed at certain events, which only appear when some conditions are met (like playing with different roles, having a high level of affection for another character etc.). It certainly takes many loops and a bit of luck to progress further with the plot, but once you get to know your crewmates you will be deeply absorbed by their stories. You can even team up with another crew member to collaborate and find the Gnosia. This is also one of the fastest way to trigger events that can improve your relationship with that character. It’s recommended to collaborate even when you know your teammate is lying, as this will still unlock special scenes you don’t want to miss.There are some stats that you can increase by gaining experience after each loop: Charisma, Intuition, Logic, Charm, Performance and Stealth. They all can be improved when leveling up, with new skills being unlocked after reaching a certain threshold. This way you can become more convincing with your actions and detect liars more easily. Each gameplay loop offers interesting situations and while it’s hard to survive at the beginning, due to the low level and lack of abilities, it will become much easier to debate and prove your point when you have increased your stats enough.The AI does a good job at creating difficult situations, but it’s not immune to failures. One time the remaining crew started accusing me of being Gnosia and one character jumped to my defense, but soon after he voted against me and I ended up being frozen (too bad; I was indeed the Gnosia).I must confess that the game is far more enjoyable when played in short sessions. Each loop can take from 5 to 15 minutes, depending on the events. The game was meant for mobile devices after all and it should be perfect for Steam Deck. This doesn’t mean that it’s not enjoyable on PC, but after playing for a few hours it obviously shows its repetitiveness due to dialogues that rarely change during the voting phase.Graphically, the game includes detailed backgrounds and art. Characters look fancy and the camera zooming in and out helps give a decent sense of animation. Unfortunately, there are no voice overs and the recurrent soundtrack is nothing memorable.I’m personally not a fan of visual novels, but Gnosia trapped me with its social deduction mechanics, making me way more interested about my crewmates than I first thought. Its addicting roguelite formula offers a good sense of progression and makes each playthrough different. While the setting is not new, the story becomes more gripping as you connect with the other characters and unlock new scenes after each loop.
_childDocuments_.name: GNOSIA

_childDocuments_.review: There's aspects of this that are alright, and the concept is neat, but there are two major problems:1. The game itself, the social deduction aspect, is just... bad. It's not really based so much on logic and reasoning as it is a stat grind, and even then, there's no real... logic arguments made, you just point fingers and hope your pointed finger is more convincing than the other pointed fingers. Answers could be blatantly obvious - a detective who got two gnosia voted off catches the third gnosia but because it's someone the AI "likes" they will vote the detective instead. The entire game operates off vague feelings and only once in a blue moon do you get to make a logical deduction. And for the longest time, the game will punish you for even trying to play, because "talking too much" gets people to tell you to shut up and then almost always voted off for it. This can be the first time you talk in a round, until you raise your stats high enough to diminish this, anyways. You're basically not playing the game at all until like two-thirds of the way through when you actually start to gain influence and the gnosia are often so transparent that finding them isn't especially satisfying.2. This is the worst progression system I've ever seen in a VN, hell, in a game ever. Do you like waiting for randomly triggered events to show up? What if it took over an hour? What if you're convinced the game doesn't work right unless you do a fresh boot literally every time you start a new round? Or how about the more convoluted ones, like getting two specific people to counterclaim, or covering a person whose always barely a part of the conversation and not really worth even considering most of the time? Or two specific characters both being a specific role? Progression has absolutely /nothing/ to do with the game itself most of the time, there's a few events related to winning games but most of them are just luck and convoluted nonsense and the pacing is abysmal because you'll be seeing new story once every half hour at best, meanwhile playing the same mediocre social deduction game over and over and over.The story itself is... fine. The music is pretty good, some of the characters are likeable (and some of them are complete voids of personality - hello chipie) but actually playing the game is excruciating and once the initial charm of the first hour or two fades you're left with another 20ish hours of tedium and frustration and I have to ask myself why I even bothered playing all the way through this one. And I don't have a great answer. You can do better, skip this.

_childDocuments_.review: Short version: I absolutely love GNOSIA and can't recommend it enough. I gushed over it so much when I had a Switch that my sis gifted it to me so I could play it again and I couldn't be more thankful. This game is an amazing ride and truly feels like it was crafted by people who wanted to tell you a story, wanted you engrossed and caring for everything that is going on in it. I am just gonna tell you to get it. Buy it. Enjoy it. If you want more details, see below.In GNOSIA, you find yourself playing a game of find-the-impostor/detective where every time you succeed (and fail, though to a lesser extent) you get XP to tailor your characters to what you think is your strongest point, or more useful, in helping you survive the day. It blends rogue and RPG elements into a visual novel format, which makes it strangely compelling to play.Every character in this game is unique in their own way, and tend to be deeper than what you see on the surface (you know, actual good writing?) and it is up to you to discover all of their personalities. I have my favourites, but I think everyone except Sha-Ming is pretty cool. No, seriously, ♥♥♥♥ you Sha-Ming. They are the sauce that makes the meat of the game work. One complaint? More varied dialogues I guess? But when you're making something like this, in what I assume was a low budget, absolutely nothing wrong with repeating some lines because of the entire setting of the game.The music is also top-tier and I wish the soundtrack was on sale here on Steam so I could get that legally too (I'm an old man, I like to own my music) and the aesthetic is also unique enough to make it stand out in a "generic anime" world of visual novels.All in all, this game is a strong 9/10 and everyone should play it. It should be legally required to play it, or even done in school. So now you know. GO. DO IT.

_childDocuments_.review: A very strange visual novel with the format of a round-based hidden deduction game, where you try to figure out who the secret aliens are (or try to kill all the humans) much like Among Us or Werewolves except.... in a singleplayer, visual novel format in an interesting setting with relatively interesting characters. By playing to unlock more of the meta-narrative as well as earn XP you can spend to improve your abilities (like lying, deduction or logic) and learn secrets about other characters. Really fascinating and different. Worth playing if any of the above sounds interesting.

_childDocuments_.review: GNOSIA is an intriguing detective-visual novel style game set in a sci-fi universe, with a very charming and unique art style. After escaping in a ship from a GNOSIA infested planet, you must deduce the crew members who have also been infected that managed to get onto the ship. The main game play is a lot of fun, as you learn the various personalities of the characters and their mannerisms when the debate is going on. Each character has their own stats, which will affect how they will act during a debate. This is further expanded upon as more roles open up and more characters join with each debate. Though, as the game goes on, the mechanic will start to get stale, and with the abilities you gain as you level up, the deduction will become a lot easier. By this time, the main thing carrying GNOSIA is its story. Each character has their own background, which is revealed little by little through the game play loop itself. These backgrounds contribute to GNOSIA's overarching narrative, which does a good job of slowly revealing the surface of a deep, interesting, and well expanded universe.Unlocking the character events can become tedious and annoying due to some RNG, but there's a way to get around this by maxing out your stats, which lets you easily manipulate the characters into the outcomes you need.When the game play does become stale, I recommend either farming exp, or manipulating the exp values with something like cheat engine, to level up all your stats to max. This will stop the game from becoming stale and save you time. This, along with a walk-through, will make it easier to get all the events for all the characters, which you will eventually need for the true ending.While GNOSIA has a pacing issue due to story events being locked behind a somewhat annoying RNG game-play loop, I wholeheartedly can recommend this unique game because of its great art, story and characters.Also that soundtrack hit pretty hard :^)
_childDocuments_.name: GNOSIA

_childDocuments_.review: GNOSIA is a visual novel styled type of game that plays like the communication games of "Werewolf" or "Mafia". I'm only familiar with the former, and it felt like a similar game but with an altered scenario to it. These games usually require a group of people to play, so GNOSIA manages to turn it into a single player experience by having a skill system that allows the player to strengthen their skills with experience they gain from playing, and additionally by having a cast of characters with set personalities and behavioral patterns. The key to victory alongside understanding the rules of the game is to master playing around the different characters, knowing when to trust or doubt them.The gameplay loop asks the player to continue to experience "actual loops" of the situation they find themselves in, trapped in a spaceship where a contamination from Gnosia has been confirmed. There is a main plot which revolves around finding out new information about the participants and the loop itself, progression is presented with special events that trigger at the beginning, throughout or at the end of loops. I found the story to be really engaging even if it isn't incredibly strong. The whole suspense that's caused by the continuous loops was really captivating.A little bit of luck on your side is required for the progression, as certain events require specific situations to trigger, which involve certain events to happen during discussion and specific characters to be around. This COULD be annoying but the game provides a feature that will make it more likely to discover something you lack. Once you're in the right track, even if you fail to meet some situation through the end, you'll be left with a clue on what to replicate to get it again. I personally didn't really struggle finding the events and I did enjoy the discussion game, so that kept me entertained even if I wasn't finding something new every loop. Recommended for fans of discussion games of this type.

_childDocuments_.review: This is an unfortunately buggy port of an otherwise fantastic VN. The game mechanics are extremely fun, varied, and inventive.... when they work.The game avoids trial an error as you work through infinite loops of a "Werewolf/Mafia" style deduction game with an incredibly well done and varied crew of space faring misfits by using clever character progression and a built in system that points you in the direction of new content so loops are wasted. At least, it's supposed to.Gnosia on steam suffers from a plethora of progression related issues in it's current state. The game's event system and the RPG elements tied to NPCs completely fail to progress if you play for extended sessions, requiring you to restart loops and reload your save over and over until the game "snaps out of it". Given the trial and error nature of some late game mechanics it can be hard to tell if you are having bad luck or if the game is broken. Chances are, it's actually broken.I did manage to get past the bugs with about an hours worth of time wasted exiting to menu and reloading my save and the story is so unbelievably rewarding that I'm still giving it the thumbs up but if you don't want to deal with bugs I'd give it a few weeks.Couple side notes:is it horny? Kinda, not really, no lewds.Is it scary? No? There's some creepy but no real jump scares or the sortIs it "woke"? If you are the sad kind of person who cares if a game is "woke" then ya, its probably too "woke" ya baby

_childDocuments_.review: I knew this was going to be a great game after booting it up for the first time and hearing "do you think humans deserve to be destroyed?" from the very first character you meet Setsu as one of the first sentences you hear in the game.But on a more serious note it was a great experience, the combination of a single player Mafia/Werewolf inspired social deduction game mixed with a futuristic "loop" themed visual novel filled with many different colorful characters worked surprisingly well.One of the game's biggest strengths to me were the art style, the futurstic colorful and also some strange character designs and of course the story with the main gameplay loop falling a little flat deep into the loops due to it feeling a little grindy at that point with me trying to get the last of the character notesThe music was unpleasant at times, but overall it was still not badIf you're not into story based games I'd pass on this game, but if you want to take part in an unique story that you wish you could forget to experience it anew I'd highly recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: Take a concept and refine it to perfection and that´s Gnosia and that concept is NOT a strategy game. I love strategy games and I had to let go of that side of myself in order to really enjoy this. There´s a LOT to like here. The atmosphere and tone are brilliantly set up, the story has been really interesting so far, I love the characters and I´m really starting to like the different play styles that are available and how elements of deception and strategy are introduced and integrated into the gameplay, the gameplay being a coin toss.You know how people say you should "spice things up"? This game is all spice. It´s consistently interesting. But what are we spicing up? We´re spicing up a dice roll. By god, its the most interesting dice roll I´ve ever played. I really really recommend this game. It´s a remarkably interesting experience and it´s FUN and it has a lot of strategy but its NOT a strategy game.

_childDocuments_.review: Not only do i not normally edit reviews i definitely dont edit them a SECOND time, but it must be said that throughout my casual returns and playing the game i finished it by accident, and it has by far one of the worst, most shoe-horned "noble sacrifice" endings ive seen in a game in a LONG time. horrendous execution and nonsensical explanation.I don't normally edit reviews, but after going back and playing a bit more ive a few things to say, i still dont recomend this game whatsoever really, but something must be said about the sheer impressiveness of the character design and programming thats put into this, each character having their own stats and tendencies make the loops feel a bit less up to RNG and like a mystery you can genuinely solve. i will probably keep coming back to this  game now and again just for that alone but i have NO plans to properly finish it as its just not worth the slog.OP Review: TL:DR getting exactly what you want for Christmas, but it's wrapped with metal.Gnosia is, what i believe to be, the first of its kind, A Story-packed Social deduction game, but also a rougelite? An astonishingly innovate and interesting idea, and the sole reason i bought it in the hopes ofBut as soon as i started it my immense interest turned into ramping disappointment. *EVERYTHING* in this game looked ready to work in its favor, the characters, the setting, the story, All of it is appealing and packed with a cool layer of mystery. BUT the one thing that brings this down, is the game-play itself. Its immensely repetitive even after just an hour of playing. It's almost painful how fast this game boiled down into a patter of hitting the same dialogue options until you finish the loop. Its rough. What started with the idea of a story that changes around me instead turned into a pseudo branching path system from the Zero Escape series...But unlike in Z.E where i can pop back in the timeline to where the story branches off to see the new stuff, you are instead wading around through dialogue options to watch events that put characters backstory together bit by bit, yet somehow ending up at the same dead end because a character died when they weren't supposed to or you didn't use a skill at a certain time. Which grows frustrating very fast with how convoluted some of these events can be to trigger. Turning this game from a Story driven social mystery into a very repetitive VN with tacked on RPG stats making it a grind to see the story to its end. All this frustration in only 52 minutes of gameplay.An incredibly original concept, but painfully boring to experience. Watch a let's play of this one.

_childDocuments_.review: I played this game back on Switch and rebought it for steam because I loved it so much.For those interested in this game, it is a single player werewolf sim, where you need to find and seek out the Gnosia. The Gnosia seek to destroy humanity. However you and a character named Setsu are looping through time over and over. Each gameplay session has you loop to a new scenario with different crew assigned to different roles. The crew must vote out one person per night and the Gnosia can eliminate one person per night. There are other unique roles such as Engineer that can identify the Gnosia etc. You also get exp to put into stats that alter how characters perceive you and what skills you can use during discussions.The game focuses on looping over and over and finding discrepancies among the crew while trying to figure out why you are stuck in a time loop. Even when you lose, you still gain exp and may even get story content that you couldn't get otherwise which is nice because at the beginning you will lose a lot as you learn how to play the game and each individual character's behavior.  If you have any interest in sci-fi, time travel, visual novels or werewolf/among us type of games, I highly recommend trying this game.
_childDocuments_.name: GNOSIA

_childDocuments_.review: A social deduction visual novel where you have to figure out which character is the enemy and put them into cold sleep. The game takes place within a time loop with the overarching story revolving around gathering information in order to escape the loop. In each loop characters are randomly assigned various roles granting them different abilities to help them detect the enemy, but whether or not those who claim to have taken on those roles are genuine is up to the player to deduce. An impressive game with quite a few moving parts going on behind the scenes. As a social deduction game, it's not simply about being right, it's about convincing others that you are right too. This can be quite difficult to do at first, and it may seem like characters are throwing out accusations at random, but the key to success lies not only in your ability to deduce the logic but also your ability to understand and interact amicably with the characters as well. Some characters operate purely on logic, while others can be more emotional. Knowing how to treat these characters and pull information from them as well as understanding their individual strategies and how they operate will massively influence your chances of winning. The randomly assigned roles can sometimes lead to some fairly chaotic situations, but more often than not they lead to incredible moments of emergent game play which produces some genuinely entertaining logic puzzles. Using the collectively available information to figure out and prove definitively to all the other characters that someone is lying is incredibly satisfying. While other mystery-style games are usually designed so that you will always eventually win through trial and error, that isn't possible here. The possibility of making bad choices and failing to interpret the information correctly makes figuring things out so much more rewarding and provides an experience not found in many other games.

_childDocuments_.review: Oh this game is SOO good, so f*cking amazing! I felt skeptical at first because I thought it was gonna be just singleplayer among us and nothing else, but oh was I wrong. The story kicks ass, the art style is stunning and the discussions can get so intense, it got me glued to the screen for a whole week. It's difficult to compare it with another game specifically, it combines social deduction with RPG elements which make progression feel great, you'll have to start out hiding behind other characters and supporting their statements without having much repercussion, but as you get more EXP and unlock more abilities you can create your own build and specialize in several fronts. Other characters also level up their stats and unlock new abilities each time you advance their stories, so this prevents you from steamrolling everyone late game and keeps discussions fresh.The events that advance the story are great, I have to admit more than one made me say "What the f*ck was that?!" out loud. The only negative I found is that 2 or 3 events can be pretty difficult to obtain, you're either gonna get them by pure luck while playing or you'll have to look up the wiki, and the game can get monotonous if you're just playing aimlessly and trying to win every single round instead of interacting with unusual situations, that's why it's important to read the "How to play" section in the pause menu, which explains everything in extreme detail and it's a 10 min read at most. So yeah, definitely give this game a try, probably my favorite of 2022.

_childDocuments_.review: I am gonna be absolutely honest if you are looking for mysterious murder story... Gnosia is not a story game. It sounds weird for a game with VN tag. It's a philosophic game with plenty of questions and not enough answers.Enigmatic mood,Enigmatic characters, Enigmatic one of a kind results.This game contains bunch of events that may trigger or not. Depending who will stay alive, who will be in certain role. Results will be diversed, just like in classic wolf game theme. Find the wolf before you die, but sometimes maybe it's not the case. There is a system that points you what set up may trigger event and characters bio. Each event gives you more info on game participants and thats it. Just a small crumbles of story here and there, hiden behind a wall of good gameplay. You see what my problem is?Story and the lack of intergrity.Nothing is explained enough. They just straight up leaving you on space ship. It's well crafted game with satisfying deductions but not a book. Someone should take it a step further, creating magnificent story out of this idea and this gameplay. If someone came back to it and prepared branched story. _childDocuments_.review: On one hand, Gnosia is a mix of two genres I don’t particularly care about – a social deduction game and a visual novel. On another – it’s so shockingly fascinating and well put together, that I was engaged until the final ending of the game.You read that right – this is a mix of two genres that don’t seem compatible. Social deduction games (like Mafia or Werewolf) tend to be multiplayer titles with little to no story, like its popular video game adaptations – Town of Salem or Among Us. While Visual Novels are almost exclusively singleplayer games about telling a linear (but often full of divergent paths and choices) story. So how can this work?The main gameplay is all based around the Mafia-like process, except all of the characters involved (apart from the player) are NPCs. To make it interesting, all of these NPCs have lots of special traits and skills to them, meaning that whenever they are an enemy (titular Gnosia) or a human of any supporting role, they have certain “patterns” to them. A lot of this isn’t extremely obvious, to not make the game boring, yet a patient and attentive player will start noticing the specific choices and elements of behavior between the loops.Oh and yes – the loops. The overall structure of the game is based around a time loop of several days, after the presence of Gnosia-infected humans is discovered until the victory of one of the sides, after which the loop resets. The properties of each loop change, so people usually change roles and you yourself will get to play all roles as well. The game will explain all of this (and much more) via the story driven interludes between the arguments about who suspects whom, which play as a Visual Novel.And eventually you will be given a lot of freedom in how you want to play the game, while also searching for special events that can trigger with different properties. Some of which tell more about the characters and the overall story. And some might unlock the NPC skills for you. Because you get a set of skills and attributes of your own to affect the gameplay, since you’re dealing with the NPCs and not real players. It’s a very simple, but a very engaging concept and if you like the social deduction type games, you will probably love this.If you don’t… Well, I have to say that the game does take a bit too long to go through the story, if you care about it first and foremost and I do wish that some of the story events weren’t so hard to trigger. It does get easier with leveling up and your own experience, and it does seem like the game gets progressively more lenient on letting you achieve the goal, although maybe I was imagining things. But if you don’t like the main gameplay loop, you might start getting a bit bored at a certain point. I’m very glad I went through it to the end. But I won’t keep on searching for non-vital events and unlocking the last skills.Gnosia is a shockingly good game with really awesome soundtrack, simple but engaging gameplay and story and memorable characters. It falters from time to time. And I wish it didn’t do the typical “everyone is horny about the player” visual novel thing at several points. But it wasn’t enough to detract from my enjoyment and I definitely recommend checking Gnosia out.

_childDocuments_.review: A very engaging and surprisingly deep story in what could be summarized as a 'single player Among Us' visual novel, featuring a time looping story of mystery and social deduction mechanics. How does this work? Well, be prepared to likely either get killed or be voted for cold sleep a lot early on, while you work on stats and slowly get an idea how everyone thinks. Events trigger randomly, depending on who's alive, their roles, and how they react to you, but slowly gives you clues to help you find answers as you navigate through the loops and the mystery behind it all. As long as you use the 'search for event' feature, you should be able to keep subtly making progress in case you're lost, or at least give you an idea. Story driven loops also happen, where you may need to do something with unique conditions like winning but a certain person needing to survive alongside you.Despite the gameplay taking up the majority of your time, the characters have a lot of depth and backstory to them with limited dialogue, although some can get weird as heck. It's mostly in a good way. Setsu's story though, being the most important character beside you, can hit pretty hard. Some characters's stories can get heavy with some events in their life.They are a few iffy designs or eye-rolling moments (mainly Comet I think, but the general art and other character designs are great), some bad endings that are brief and subtle but maybe uncomfortable. As you get closer to the end, getting the last events may be harder to figure out without a guide, or if you're being a completionist, although I still enjoyed going after them. Enjoyed it to the point where I actually got every achievement and even did the optional pure gameplay challenges it mentions. Ended up being one of the most memorable stories I ended experiencing, with its very unique take on gameplay. Took me a while to get to this because it barely ever goes on sale, but well worth it at any price.

_childDocuments_.review: This review is spoiler-free.For those who still don't know what Im talking about, here are the basics:You and up to 14 other people are trapped in a spacecraft. Unfortunately for you, some fellow crew members were infected with Gnosia and they want to kill everyone on thatship. You can't really distinguish them from others by looks, the only way to do so is through social deduction. Each day, everyone shares their opinion on who they think the Gnosias are and, at the end, all of you will vote on whom to put into a cold freeze. Each night, however, Gnosias act as well, as they will decide who should disappear without a trace. There are multiple roles characters can have that give them some sort of special ability or purpose (for example: the Engineer can check each night, whether or not the selected person is human). Once all impostors are frozen or half of the crew are Gnosias, the game ends. But when one game (or loop as this game calls it) ends, another begins, with different role assignments and different situations. Not only that, but you can also choose to play as those malicious Gnosias, completely changing your approach to the game.That's the general idea, but these types of games are always played with real people, so how does this singleplayer system work? Well, each day has 5 rounds, and each round you have numerous actions to perform. For example, you can doubt someone, everyone then can defend the person or agree with you. You can also do nothing (which you will be doing the most, since talking too much or not talking enough makes you suspicious), allowing someone else to state their opinion, letting you react with different skills.These actions are called skills. They can range from simply defending a fellow crewmate, through starting a collaboration with someone, all the way to making small talk, tricking Gnosias into thinking you are either useless or not a threat. There are around 40 of these skills, and each does something unique, even if it doesn't appear so at first.Each loop, you gain experience points and you can spend them on developing your 6 stats which will drastically change how you play. For example, you can level up your Performance, making your lies hard to spot, or you can opt into Charisma, making it easier to convince others into believing you. These taught and visible mechanics alone aren't really worth the term “complex”, but there is a ton of stuff going on behind the scenes. Take the friendship meter for example, everyone likes others more or less and it drastically changes how they interact. To this day, after 30 hours in the game, I still discover completely new mechanics and special situations that can occur thanks to them.Each crewmember has their own stats and skill set. I have played around 150 loops, and, thanks to the characters, I remained fully immersed in all of them. Not only are the characters really interesting, but each and every one of them has a unique personality. The best part is that a character's personality is not only aesthetic but also plays a huge part in how they act. For example, we have Jonas, who has a very high overall statline but due to years of loneliness cruising through the galaxy, is very chaotic and eccentric. So he rarely puts those good stats and skills to use. On the other hand, we have Raqio, who has absurdly high logic stat, making them a fearful enemy, or a powerful ally in the late game, where there is a lot of information from previous days. That is if they can get into the late game, since they tend to be put into a cold sleep early, due to their playful nature and unlikeability. Throughout the game characters also improve alongside you, unlocking new skills and improving their stats. So you never truly know what to expect from them. However, the best part is, in those 150 loops, I could not ever figure out or cheese the AI. It always feels real and absolutely never acts against one’s personality. Even occasional logic flaws are delivered to you by people on the more foolish side (yes I'm talking mostly about Shigemichi), you can still pinpoint these flaws and correct them, making you feel like you are playing with actual human beings that can make mistakes. Especially when they are more or less connected to the ongoing…While most of the players pick this game up out of curiosity and interest in its mechanics, I can still confidently say almost everyone stays for the story. The developers actually acknowledged this - at the beginning there is little focus on world building and character development, letting you familiarize yourself with the main mechanics. Only later, after several dozen loops, do you slowly begin to uncover the story. Which, without getting into spoilers, is one of the most interesting and memorable tales I was able to experience in my life (I truly mean it).Each character has several events giving you some information about them. By collecting this data, you can progress through the story, but you also get a lot of information about this universe. Where the game can get a bit frustrating, at times, is how you come across these events. For each one, in addition to requiring a specific situation to take place, there is also an aspect of randomness. You can not encounter a specific event, despite having all the right conditions repeatedly. This is not a problem for most of the playthrough, since the sheer amount of events ensures if a specific event doesn't happen, another will. Still, towards the end, getting the last few pieces of information you need to get the ending, can be a bit time consuming.While not particularly groundbreaking, character sprites and special scenes with them are very well drawn. Getting a random event almost always means a new special image, and, trust me, there are a lot of these in the game. The UI is also really fitting and somewhat minimalistic, not overwhelming the player that, at first, already has a lot to take in.In terms of music, there are only around 5-6 tracks, but each and every one of them is not only special, but high-quality as well. Once again, nothing outstanding, but always fitting the mood, which  is very important for the soundtrack - and this game never fails to do that.Gnosia is not a game for everyone. That said, I think it is simply a masterpiece. Very rarely am I able to play games that I actively want to forget, just so I could experience them once more.This visual novel is just on another level when it comes to interesting and unique characters, exciting and emotional narrative, as well as absurdly fun and complex game mechanics. This is not only one of the better stories I read, but also one of the most fun I've had in a while. Gnosia is an amazing game, completely worth your attention and money.

_childDocuments_.review: Playing through Gnosia was a roller-coaster for me in more ways than one. Plot-wise, it threw me for loops that I thought were only possible in games by Kotaro Uchikoshi, who worked on the Nonary Games and AI: The Somnium Files. My enjoyment of the game also felt like a roller-coaster, as well. When I had first heard about the game during a Nintendo Indie World, I was already enticed and had decided on buying the game once it had come to Steam. When I actually played the game though, I was a bit disappointed. The gameplay mechanics were different than I had imagined, and the writing style was awkward and prevented me from forming bonds with these characters. Yet, once I had got into the meat of the game -- once I had all members of the crew available and had a heartwarming event with one -- I was enticed to keep playing. I wanted to find out all the info on these characters and figure out how I could manipulate the roles to favor me learning about specific characters. I think that's what the game does best. By allowing the player to experiment with the game to create paths that favor learning about specific characters, the game gives the player enough control so that when they do find information, the player feels rewarded. This is especially shown with more intimate events that are more tricky to get, as they feel like a better reward. The game also makes it easier on players who may have trouble setting up these paths or do not want to bother with it by having the "event search" option, which has the game lay out the paths for you. There are special events, however that can not be gotten as easily, which personally makes me feel like they're a reward to clever players. All in all, I think the premise of Gnosia is an interesting one: a visual novel with rogue-like gameplay, with the details you learn about characters being rewards for each successful attempt, and I think this premise is well delivered. However, the writing still leaves a lot to be desired in terms of letting me create a full and complete bond with each of these characters. Do yourself a favor and try it out! (8/10)Also obligatory comment on who's my fave: WOOOOOOOOO SETSU

_childDocuments_.review: I get tired of rogue style games quickly, I have a like-hate relationship with Visual Novels, and I'm not fond of social deduction games like Secret Werewolf and Among Us.  Despite those, I still wanted to give Gnosia a try because it sounded so unique and hoped it would hold my attention.  And for a bit, it did.  Unfortunately, I began to get tired of it and started getting annoyed at it's random design.  Since its a single player social deduction game without voice acting, you're more reliant on your stats than any deductive capabilities to survive each loop.  Which means you will at some point have to start grinding up EXP so you can appropriately level up stats.  You only get EXP at the end of a loop, and you get significantly more if you "win" in the end.  So grinding in this game is very tedious.  As far as the story is concerned, the overarching plot is not the real focus.  Instead, its about the learning about all 15 of the characters.  Literally,  you have to learn more about each character in order to progress in the plot.  In order to do so, you have to meet certain criteria in a loop in order to trigger an event (like certain characters get voted off, you have to play as Gnosia and keep someone who isn't Gnosia alive until the end, etc.).  However, because this is a roguelike, there's several things that are just random and you have no control over.  You are able to customize SOME aspects about a loop, but unfortunately, you can't customize everything, which means you could start a loop where you don't have all the criteria you need to trigger the specific event you're after.  There's other random elements as well that could completely screw you over.  Like if you need to keep a specific character alive until the end, that character could just get randomly killed while progressing the loop.  There's also the fact that several of these characters I just didn't find interesting enough to actually want to know more about.  Yet in order to progress in the game, I had to put up with random BS in order to try to learn more about this character I don't like.  Another thing, and admittedly this may just be me, but I never liked being the Gnosia in this game.  That could stem from me just not liking being the antagonist in social deduction games, but I also just in general don't want to be the evil character killing off these characters because I don't have any grudge or reason to want to kill them off.  Again, that's probably just me, but since you have to play as the Gnosia (or play as non-Gnosia and help the Gnosia win a loop) to learn more about certain characters, I was at an impasse.  The game is also in general bad at explaining things.  There's a lot of tips and things to know about how to play this game in which it just doesn't properly explain in the game and you're forced to either look it up online or read through the many pages of explanations in the game's pause menu.  You should always properly explain the mechanics of your game in the actual game itself and not relegate it to a menu or an outside resource that someone else made.  And if your game is too complex/complicated to do that, then just make your game simpler for cripes sake.  Plus, there's some criteria for advancing the plot that I don't believe ANYONE could ever figure out.I think the game has some lovely artwork, I appreciate the ambitious attempt, and there are some character I did genuinely like and wanted to know more about.  Unfortunately, I was only on like Loop 16, and many people were saying you'll need to do like 150+ loops to beat the game, and I just couldn't bring myself to keep playing with all of my grievances I was having.

You can choose yours or let it be random.-There is a lot of parameter customization available; you can change the number of characters in a loop, the number of Gnosia (werewolves), and toggle the different special roles. There is an Event Search button that will automatically spit out a random configuration that has the chance to trigger an event, so you don't have to worry about missing something just because you didn't think to have this or that role on. -There are two nonbinary characters and the player character can be nonbinary as well.-You slowly unravel various mysteries as you go.-Setsu is Bestsu. A+ nonbinary video game spouse, Absolute treasure.Cons:-There are gender-locked romantic scenes for male and female characters, but nonbinary characters do not have any unique scenes. The gender-locked scenes are also all m/f. Setsu is in love with the player character regardless of gender, though.-It has unwarned-for themes of sexual assault. _childDocuments_.review: Gnosia is a visual novel where a large chunk of it is playing social deduction. This genre should be familiar, as it's appeared in board-games like Werewolf, and video-games like Among Us.The main gameplay can be boiled down to finding the Gnosia(s) of the given round. But what makes Gnosia so interesting, is that the mechanics behind each character is very well thought-out. People are complicated, and in Gnosia the mechanics overlap perfectly with the character being presented. If it feels like someone is a bit naive, you'll see it in the rounds for finding the bad guys. The only thing missing from playing Werewolf IRL, is that you can’t try and guess whether a person is lying or not based on their body language. However here, there’s a mechanic for that – and even if you’re “perfect” at it, you’re not going to identify people lying all the time.There’re multiple layers of mechanics behind everything, which means that you pointing out that someone might be a Gnosia, has consequences in the short- and long term in the given round. In addition, other character’ abilities and personalities bounce off each other. All of this mixing together, means that it’s never easy. I’ve tried multiple games of noticing 1-2 people lying early, only to have a really hard time getting them voted out because it’s only me that knows about it. And if I do get them voted out, I rarely survive the night. Your goal isn’t just winning a given round, it’s surviving to the end as well.If all of that sounds interesting, the next order of business is the story behind all of this. Personally, I feel it’s very well thought-out and makes perfect use of all kinds of people trapped in very unfortunate circumstances. The vast majority of the characters are unique and has both strengths and weaknesses that’s all in display both while playing and while experiencing the story. The main story becomes complicated and is meant to be interpreted to fully comprehend. So, I wouldn’t recommend the game to someone below the age of ~18~, or you’d probably be more frustrated and confused than thinking and brooding. At least I would in that age. The story is fun, scary, wholesome, depressing and thoughtful.Finally, there’s the aesthetics. I very much enjoy the art and visual style – it’s manga-based, but far from manga-like. You’re not going to find manga tropes or clichés: This is very much its own thing. Something that’s not immediately obvious, is that the soundtrack is amazing. It doesn’t distract you when it doesn’t need to, but helps elevate the mystique/confusion/drama. But, when it needs to, it knocks it out of the park: The main theme, different themes of certain recurring plot elements and credits are all absolutely amazing.My playtime as of writing this review is the time it took me to get 100%.I severely recommend this game to anyone who likes social deduction. But if you’re not, and more of a visual novel fan, I can’t recommend it: The vast, vast majority of the game is about social deduction.

_childDocuments_.review: I certainly did not expect to enjoy an indie game made by literally four people in their basement this much. Look at this playtime. I spent 73 hours on it and it felt like 5. Of course, there are other factors at play, but overall the game is absolutely solid and just for that I should give a thumbs up. The story revolves around a space-time loop. The core of the game sees the player, a customizable character (through stats and some story-related choices) facing off an unknown alien enemy called Gnosia who can infect individual humans and desires either physical violence or control over the human race. Why is Gnosia a thing, who created it and how is set in the background, as the player needs to determine who among fifteen other members of a spaceship have been infected and eliminate them one by one through daily debates and subsequent voting to put the suspects into cryo sleep.The Gnosia infected of course wont stand back and watch, and will actively try to murder the player and his allies during the night where everyone is forced in their own quarters due to the spaceship warping.The player is able to gradually increase their stats inside their own quarters, gaining experience every time they complete a loop (either after eliminating all the Gnosia infected crew members, being murdered, or destroying the current universe - yes that's a thing). The story progresses by acquiring certain notes from the other crew members, and these require you watch specific events unlocked throughout the adventure by setting up the composition of the crew, how many enemies will be present and other parameters. The game generously guides you towards your goals via a convenient button called Event Search so you're not blindly looking for random events (mostly). It's still hard to find the patience for completing each task though, because failing a loop, being murdered in the middle of acquiring a note or having your quest givers killed can halt your progress until the next loop, which is also random, adding exponentially  to the time requirement on the player's part. Simply put, while it does work both in-context and as a game mechanic, it is just not that fun and a bit tedious.This "should" be a 10 hours game, but instead it ends up becoming a 30-40 hours game because of its randomness factor and a series of events that you HAVE to watch and there is no way for you to comprehend how to achieve them unless the player reads a guide.That is the single most frustrating thing about the game as a whole. Everything else simply just works. The entirety of the gameplay revolves around conversations and how the different personalities of the other crew members operate, it feels very rewarding and fun to play around with conversational tropes and try to stir the debate, shift the blame onto others, collaborate to put someone else into the freezer, conspire to eliminate someone or protect potential targets. It feels a bit like Danganronpa but the atmosphere and danger is more immediate, perhaps more tangible, and way less cheesy.I have no doubt in my mind that if this title had any budget whatsover, it would have become a masterpiece in its own right. As it stands, it is "just" a good game. CGs are well drawn, sprites and backgrounds are pretty good, sounds and music are serviceable (they loop too often, pun not intended, it really is apparent where the budget cuts were applied) and the storyline has a satisfying beginning, middle and ending although I would argue they REALLY pushed for all the possible sentimental buttons a bit too far. It's hard to pull at your heartstrings with a story like this, I'll admit. Perhaps if there was more meat in key aspects such as characters' backgrounds, which were often way too vague to justify that kind of attachment. Of the 15 participants, perhaps 5 or 6 were relevant, everyone else was there to fill in for diary entries and worldbuilding.Still, I did not feel disappointed and I will keep playing the postgame for a while longer. Hopefully it gets remastered with proper voice acting, a graphics overhaul and an expanded story.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not usually one to leave reviews on games... but I'm going to make an exception in this case, because Gnosia absolutely deserves a shout-out. It's a fascinating game that is far more than just "Among Us, but as a single-player visual novel with roguelike and RPG elements". Like yes, that's the basic idea, but it's not what makes this game shine.The thing that REALLY makes Gnosia great is the writing. It's hard to say too much about the plot without spoilers, but let's just say that it tackles a notoriously tricky subject to get right and does a great job with it. (Are there some unanswered questions? Yeah, there are. But the plot is pretty solid on the whole, and I cared enough about finding out how the game ends to keep playing through over 34 hours and nearly 200 runs, which says a LOT for this gamer with ADHD and access to a bunch of other shiny things to distract me.)Like a lot of VN-type games, the characters are the core of the experience -- if you get sucked into their stories, then you're going to love the game (even if you HATE some of the characters themselves). And for me at least, Gnosia nailed it on that score. Everybody has a backstory (some more complex than others), and you slowly unravel more information about everybody's deal as you play. NPCs have different habits, personalities, and ideologies -- there are multiple characters who are non-binary and the game handles that really well, making it a part of who they are but not the ONLY thing that those characters are about. They feel very "real". The art and sound design are really good, as well. There are a lot of subtle touches like changes in facial expression that are really well done, and really help bring the characters to life. And the music is inoffensive enough that you won't mind it while you hear it over and over again, even if it's not super-catchy.Is the game perfect? Nope, it has a few minor flaws. As play through repeated runs some of the dialogue does get a bit repetitive, although admittedly there's a lot of variety to it so the experience still feels fresh even if some lines do get old after a while. And because some NPCs have better stats than others, trying to take down certain characters who are infected is WAY more difficult than others, which can be frustrating earlier on before you build up the stats and abilities to crush them. (And when you do get that power, BTW, crushing those NPCs is incredibly satisfying!) Also, at times it can be very hard to figure out how to advance the game's metaplot (I confess I did end up checking a spoiler-free walkthrough at one point for hints about how to trigger the next step forward). And as noted above, some things just never get fully explained, either .But despite those issues, this is the most I've been sucked into a game in a good while, and I can't recommend it enough even to folks who aren't into VNs. At the end of the day, the way that I judge whether a game is truly great is this: does it stick with me even when I'm not playing it? In Gnosia's case, the answer is definitely yes.

_childDocuments_.review: I played a ton of Gnosia on its switch release and this port seems solid on my machine, some UI polish issues aside.This game is incredible. An innovative take on visual novels and interactive storytelling structure that I consider a must-play for any game designer. The basic premise is as follows: They took Werewolf/Mafia and made it a single-player skirmish against AI opponents. You play multiple matches and over time you're unlocking narrative scenes that advance a meta-plot that runs across each match.The details in the execution of this premise are what make it so compelling. Each match, there's a chance for some cast members to be human, some to be Gnosia (the mafia or werewolf equivalent), some to have special roles, etc. However, each member of the cast plays each role differently, and they each have an associated stat block (as do you) that determines how well they play said role. As you play, part of the mastery of the game is learning the quirks of each character and how to play around them. Some characters seem to lie constantly and competently, making them dangerous as a Gnosia but even more difficult to trust as a human. Some characters fold immediately when they're Gnosia, and others go for big lies to cause chaos. Clear archetypes start to emerge that will feel familiar to anyone who's played social deduction games with a consistent social group will recognize.The key here though, is because of how the game has carefully structured both its perfect and imperfect information, you never really "solve" a given character. You know if this one guy is Gnosia he's always going to go for broke and claim the Engineer role to sway the game. If he's saying he's the Engineer, he's probably lying... but what about the times where he isn't? You can't trust that behavior completely, because if you do there'll be games that you throw completely by doing so. It becomes one tidbit in an ocean of information when you're making high-stakes decisions, and there are *15* completely unique characters with gorgeous designs and their own quirks and patterns.Characters will share information with you, with each other, cast doubt and accusations, defend others, catch liars (including you), and they will be doing this with hidden motivations based on their role and what information they have. It's remarkable how "human" they feel as you play this game with them, to the point where I've gone on mutli-page tirades about how angry some characters make me. (♥♥♥♥ you Raqio, you beautiful piece of ♥♥♥♥.) That's kind of the most fascinating thing about this game to me--the characters don't feel like NPCs, they feel like fully realized people when I'm in the middle of a match, people I'm actively trying to persuade, outsmart, and outplay. When a match is going bad in Gnosia, a computer isn't ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ me over. It's a leap forward for video games as a medium and everyone should experience it.

_childDocuments_.review: Please PLAY Gnosia at least once. Don't be misled by the common saying of ''it's singleplayer among us'', because I can reassure you, it's more than that! It has a promising plot, character ability customization, a lot of unexpected twists, and the experience throughout the matches is always different. I ''finished'' the main story twice and I wish I could forget everything I went through just to experience it again - the tears, the joy, everything. Sci-fi world that is written in such a captive way!My only advice for players that feel unsure whether buying his game or not - It IS a visual novel. It's conversation based, but it doesn't feel like one at all because of all the gameplay mechanics. Therefore, it is progressive gameplay, and in order to obtain certain features, you must be dedicated - which means you'll get to think carefully in order to lead each loop in the direction you want to. The characters are very interesting and distinguishable, and engaging with the cast got me immersed further into the story. Just give it a chance if you are looking from something fresh and you can handle the stressful situations that could get you either voted out or make you win a loop.

_childDocuments_.review: This had a great idea and concept but certain things feel way too tedious and repetitive. While at the beginning it seemed kinda fun, by the end I really felt like this needed to end as quickly as possible.I genuinely feel like this would have been a much better told story if this was a linear or flow chart based game. Instead of having to go over and over the same dialogues and basic logic lines in the discussions.It's hard to recommend this game to a VN enthusiast because the amount of story given at the midway point too lacklustre and it's hard to recommend it to anyone wanting VN but with gameplay elements because again they start to feel boring and uninteresting. You just start going through the motions and turn your brain off.

_childDocuments_.review: Its a good attempt at simulating something akin to Werewolf or Mafia, but the mechanics are too lacking for the gameplay to stand up on its own. _childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game, but I honestly can't recommend it. It has many cool ideas and the story seems interesting. But the pacing is awful: you advance through the main story by playing "werewolf" style loops and getting two-sentence bits of backstory from the characters on each loop. What info you get (or if you get any at all) is completely random, and depends on what characters are playing on a given loop, what their roles are, etc. You can signifantly improve your chances through an "Event Search" function, but even so you have to play the Werewolf game (at best) around 120 times. It's fun for a while, but the novelty wears off way before the 100 loops. It gets a lot more frustrating when you have "event chains", in which you need to keep certain character(s) alive through the whole loops to get the info you need. It's so easy to screw those up, since voting and who the "Werewolf" decide to eliminate can feel really random. Currently, I'm on what seems to be the last event chain, and  All in all, it's a shame. Because the game gets so boring that I just stopped caring about the characters. I liked them at the beginning, but right now I couldn't care less about them (even more when they keep actively impeding my progress thorugh the main story). They feel like cardboard cutouts who say the same stuff loop after loop.  Never before has a game made me feel in my own flesh the tedium of being trapped in a time loop like this one has.

_childDocuments_.review: Ehhhh.... So this feels like an Among Us fangame trying to capture that in a single player setting. So I guess if that's what you're looking for, go ahead. It *does* manage to capture the idea of a single-player mafia game to some extent.However, the main story is almost completely absent and drip-fed to you extremely slowly. It's there I guess, but I don't feel like playing for 40 hours to see it. Almost all the time you spend in this will be doing the same thing over and over.There's essentially only one or two characters who have any personality at all. The main character who is your friend and remembers the time loops is Setia (everyone else has their memory reset), who's extremely uninteresting and you're supposed to like it because it's "non-binary". There's also a kind of a glimmer of personality from a few others (alien bro Sakaguchi is funny, Ming is just an arse to everyone and somehow gets away with it), but basically they're just there to be pieces of artwork to look at while selecting a response. Even if you're curious about a character you never really have a chance to interact with them outside of one or two canned scenes on repeat and some out-of-nowhere scenes where a character shows up and is like "I love you let's have sex".Maybe something interesting will happen if you grind through 100 games or something, but at the pace it's going it feels like a massive waste of time. You have to really enjoy the core gameplay loop to push through with it. And... well... I don't. I can see why some people might like this because there's nothing else out there quite like it, but it's neither Danganronpa nor is it Among Us, it's just a waste of time. At least the art is nice.

_childDocuments_.review: This game originally appeared to me as I was looking for visual novels that fit the niche of death games that I have become completely obsessed with. And, considering this basically is just Among Us in a visual novel format, I expected that I would be refunding this game on the premise of trying it and finding it not original or story-driven enough. But, once I started playing it, I didn't slow down until I'd beaten a majority of the main story because I found it a pleasant surprise how addictive the game really is.So, the plot is still really similar to Among Us/Mafia, in which you wake on a ship where there are Gnosia (this game's version of Impostors/Mafia. You've gotta figure out who the Gnosia are by holding a meeting and voting on it before you all split off for the night, allowing a murder to happen. If you're looking for a completely original premise, then this doesn't present a completely unheard of plot. But it's the way that this game tackles the whole idea of playing Mafia that appeals more than these party games. Whilst in any other of these, if you wanted to play another game, you'd simply set up the cards/start another game, in Gnosia, you encounter a time loop that ends every time you die/have won. Whilst this may make the game seem repetitive, unlike how you may expect time loops to work in which everyone loses their memory bar the player, another character, Setsu, who acts as the supporting character, is able to recall some of these loops, giving you an ally in this game. The reason that this game gains much of its points in my books is that it really does well at fleshing out its characters. Setsu's mindset is explored in detail, about how she wants the loops to end but has no clue how to end them and all characters have much to learn about them which unveils why they act the way they do, which adds replayability as a player seeks to find out everything they can about their favourite characters. Plus, there is an element of skill retention in which a player can continuously increase their skills, leading to a greater ease in retaining skills such as gaining influence in the meetings, allowing them to best the strongest players such as Yuriko. To add to this, there is no issue with getting frustrated at being provided a certain role, as before a player begins a game, they can choose their role and which roles are at play, which makes the game much more replayable. As well as fleshing its characters out, the game manages to insert some strong comedic relief characters such as Jonas and Shigemichi, who in one scene somehow end up announcing that they are Gnosia in a certain loop despite this meaning their 'death'. The story can be lackluster in some runs due to you not finding the key to activating the advancement of the plot but the ending of the game and the way in which the story is captivating to the extent that I'm glad I beat the game in its entirety and unravelled the mystery behind the time loops. However, one issue that I feel is only fair to bring up with the game links to an issue caused by its premise. By having a social deduction game in which none of the characters are played by actual humans, there are bound to be limitations as to the mind games that can be played and the range of dialogue. Whilst there are many unlockable special events, some of the meetings can feel dry after a certain point, as characters repeat preset dialogue to express their opinions, an issue which becomes especially prominent when you become so overpowered that when you make a suggestion of who is Gnosia, you are likely to gain the votes needed without much strife.Whilst this can take away from the game somewhat, I still feel that the game is worth playing on the whole, as it offers a fun game of whodunnit where you get to learn the ways in which people act and to discern who is innocent and who is not through mind games, getting close to the members of the diverse cast you want to in each loop.

_childDocuments_.review: Honest truth here: This game was hard to get in to be honest, I found this game frustrating especially with some of the game mechanics. Gnosia was annoying to me... but ever since I actually figured out I needed to do and the strategies to win, GOD DO I LOVE IT!!! Gnosia is very talented game, a couple flaws there and there but other than that... It's perfect! The story is amazing, I love the Sci-fi direction they went for and I love social deduction games and it being single player really made it a lot better from someone with social anxiety! The characters are very likable, of course some more than others. The only character you would hate is Shigemichi and who doesn't hate Shigemichi? Hell, even some characters I used to hate (Sha-Ming, Otome, Raqio) became lovable if you just got to know them well! Now, I understand the problem with some of the social deduction aspects of this game. I hated being Gnosia and went out of my way to not BE Gnosia but honestly you just need to find statergies which I love in this game, instead just lying your way and killing someone random. I took my time and killed people I felt like needed to be killed. Also with the stats, I felt like I was actually thinking about what I needed to level up instead of randomly clicking one. For Crew stats, I went for Stealth, Charm, and Intuition but when I play as the Gnosia, I went for Charisma and Performance and for Skills, Logic! I felt like I actually needed to think and what I needed to play as next!I do have to point out I felt like there was some plot holes there, how repetitive the gameplay and dialogue were, how much the first/normal ending tipped me off... and there and some of the characters wasn't doing it for me... uuugh Shigemichi... but if you can not notice that or accept the fact it kind of becomes the perfect game.And always... Play for Setsu..And maybe for Yuriko, SQ, Gina, Stella, Sha-Ming, and Raqio.

_childDocuments_.review: A gorgeously illustrated series of games of Mafia with a slowly unfolding mystery behind them.Social deduction gameplay is the bulk of the game, so if you're looking for a relaxed, dialogue driven visual novel, this isn't it. The gameplay can also be a little frustrating early on, before you get the hang of it and while your main character's stats are low. But if you give it time to get into full swing, I found the core gameplay pretty fun, and the way the story slowly plays out over many iterations is interesting. The characters are lively and the illustration is top notch. Probably the best character sprites I've ever seen in a visual novel. The vapourwave beats are also pretty good, and help flush out the aesthetic.

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed my time with it, but it had some notable flaws.I had fun exploring the games systems/interacting with the characters/ and experiencing the overall story.-Unique idea of mixing Werewolf-like social deduction gameplay with visual novel storytelling and -You can build your characters stats to focus on your priorities during gameplay (stealth, manipulation, logic, lying etc.)-Unique characters that are fun to interact with, you spend enough time with them that you feel like you get to know them.-Knowing the characters and understanding them is also useful in gameplay, as knowing each characters behaviour and skills/weaknesses is really useful during the debates,  and makes you deal with each character somewhat differently. -It plays with some fun sci-fi tropes, which are just fun (and which I'm not gonna spoil) .-It has a pretty unique identity with its visuals and soundtrack.-Your options to interact during the debates are very limited at the start, you might feel ineffective while your stats are low und you don't have the active skills as additional options.- The games structure/themes/plot results in a lot of repetition, it makes sense in context, but it can get a bit tiring.- Sometimes randomness can be frustrating, especially when you need to rely on it to unlock story scenes. The game later adds an option to pretty much ''rig'' the requirements for new events to spawn, but even then the requirements for the event can seem opaque or counterintuitive.(To the games credit, I only had to look up the requirements for one character event..That felt frustrating, but at least the rest occured somewhat naturally over the ''rig'' option).- Some of the sci-fi stuff felt a bit too incredible to feel believable in the setting. At least for me. I think it's a pretty cool game that hasn't gotten much attention,I only found this game over a throwaway comment in a video that was talking about another game.I don't think the game is something everyone is going to like, checking out the first few minutes on Youtube might be somewhat advisable. ''Menu Gameplay'' and some of the characters weirdness, might not be something that clicks with everyone.The game isn't exhaustingly long, or annoyingly short. I clocked in around 15 hours before I completly finished game.It's probably worth it if you buy it on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: GNOSIA

_childDocuments_.review: It's a social deduction game of similar vein to Town of Salem and Among Us, but in visual novel form. (Actually, this game predates Among Us, but I digress.) Despite the limitations of being styled in a visual novel format, logic and observation are your tools to succeed. There is an RPG element in that you gain XP to level up stats, which help your chances of success and survival.That does make the game grindy at points. I found some of it frustrating at times, but the game offers good laughs and intriguing plot-lines along the way. It's a well written game.7/10 for me, get it when it's on sale.
