_childDocuments_.review: First off, I want to get something clear. I generally dislike roguelites or roguelikes or roguevanias or any other permutation of the rogue-slop. My major exception is Necrodancer, and I haven't tried Hades yet but it looks cool. It's always the exception rather than the rule with this cursed genre. That being said- this game has been frequently described as a roguelite, and I simply don't think that's true. This game has some structural similarities to the genre- it's based around singular runs where a victory state is a start-to-finish deathless completion; rather than a predefined set of levels, you enter randomly chosen layouts and gain randomly chosen boons that power you up as you progress in hopes of being able to sustain progress; and it has some elements of making permanent progress in the form of persistent upgrades.That's where the similarity ends. Map layouts are not randomly generated, rather, there is a pool of premade and quite nicely designed maps for each tileset, and they all flow fantastically with nice, consistently designed encounters that remain challenging even as you learn what to expect. You don't get loot within the levels, but rather, there is a regular and guaranteed structure for boons, so you're not running the risk of being snubbed by RNG that just doesn't produce enough chests or whatever. Instead, you gain a steady flow of money from completing the levels, increased by maintaining the combo meter, and after a set amount of cleared levels, you enter a bar where you can buy drinks with the money you're guaranteed to have that confer passive and active boons. It ensures that you will generally always be able to get SOMETHING.If I had to compare this game to anything other than the obvious, it would be Smash TV for the NES. This game feels like a hyper-advanced take on that game, as a top-down shooter structured around clearing rooms.This game is, honestly, quite amazing and I think its quality should be upheld in its own regard rather than in comparison to anything else. The shooting is fun, and the guns are nice and well represented. It's a rare game that really does respect the danger a gun represents while also being able to make some guns feel more powerful. A pistol can typically down an enemy in two shots, but it will still feel comparatively weak next to other guns because of its ammo capacity and other traits. It's really smartly designed.The drinks system has a lot of fun flavor and is really tightly balanced, and it allows for a lot of build flexibility. There's great mixing and matching to be had. I love doing shotgun runs with El Cycle and High Roller in particular. If I had any criticism of the system, it's just that I wish rerolling the drinks was a bit cheaper, or increased in value slower.The art style is amazing. I can't really even go into detail other than to say it just looks nice and I don't mind that it rotates objects out of line with the pixel grid.The story and lore are vague, but not at all bad. The forefront is definitely the characters, they're all great.Highly recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I have five or so hours in this game as of right now, so might as well write this. OXTO is good. It's really good. It's basically a modern refinement of Hotline Miami as a roguelike, and I love every second of it. Although here's a hot take you might not be prepared for. I don't like Hotline Miami. It has nothing to deal with the violence of the game, because I've played much worse. Miami is about the violent nature of man and it captures it wonderfully, but playing the game itself is not great. Enemies with guns kill you at point blank, it's hard to see what's coming off screen, some encounters you have to cheese, and sometimes you get killed by stray bullets. Some of which are from off screen. Not very fun and the sequel is more frustrating. OTXO looks at this and makes Miami fun for people like me. You have a health bar now, but to compensate enemies come in bigger numbers and rooms are larger. However, you get more room to move around and it's much easier to tell where things are since enemies always have a distinct look and color. Guns come in a variety of flavors, can be picked up easily, and used easily. High accuracy, understandable quirks, and gorey damage. You have a focus ability to slow time down to a crawl and lay down bullets like Max Payne. Making stressful scenarios much easier and allowing for more strategical play. Your health refills when you get the score multiplier up and this encourages you to play fast and violent as possible. The game has a fantastic combat loop overall and I keep coming back to it for more. There are some flaws though. The bosses aren't very great and often find you pumping bullets away at a weak spot. The drinks, otherwise perks, you get during runs range from being really useful to "When would I ever waste coins on this?" The game has a really strange difficulty curve midway through each run, so sometimes you're doing really well and you get killed instantly. Yet, this is the fun of roguelikes. Going back in and doing better, so not much complaint. Oh yeah, I don't know if this game benefits from being a roguelike. On one hand it's really fun like I said. On the other tredging through that first area over and over again gets annoying especially when you mastered it, and I don't know if there's enough variety to give it endless hours of replay value. I haven't beaten the final boss yet, the furthest I've gotten is floor 20, and I wish the game would end soon. I do recommend OTXO, strongly. It's a modernized Hotline Miami and it even contains accessibility options for those who have visual disabilities and such. It's hard, but it is fun and rewarding. One of the hidden gems of 2023.

_childDocuments_.review: Very Very Good for what it is. Is it the next hotline miami? No. Is it worth the $15? In my opinion, yes. If you like the action of hotline miami and the game design of roguelites this is PERFECT.There are a lot of things to break down about the game design but overall I'd say many of the choices the designers made are clearly well-thoughtout and manage to take Hotline Miami's frantic combat while still making it playable as a Roguelite. The player has a proper healthbar, and its pretty generous, too. You can't really have a roguelite if you had Hotline Miami's "dying every 5 seconds" mechanic. It still manages to be extremely frantic as the Combo Meter directly increases the coins you get, which then helps the Roguelite aspect. Honestly it's impressive how the designer has broken fundamental staples of Hotline Miami and Roguelites and still managed to get the best of both worlds.Pro-tip: I don't know if the tutorial explained this, but you can Kick with both the Left Mouse Button AND the Middle Mouse Button. You can even middle click while holding a gun and you can kick without having to drop the weapon.

_childDocuments_.review: it was a super fun game. similar to hotline Miami in a lot of ways but it stands out as its own thing very well in my opinion. the story is simple but very cool also, the main focus is the game play and i love it for that. hotline Miami could only give the player so much violence before the scene ends and the next starts, and then the game is over. but this game has so much more playtime than hotline Miami, Otxo lets the player buy power ups with in game money earned by killing enemies and getting the highest combo you can to earn the most. Otxo lets the player get so powerful that if you're good enough at the game play then you can just absolutely plow through enemy after enemy like butter. and the game play doesn't get old, as the power ups you get are randomized by the bar tender. so it gives a lot of chance to experiment with different combos of power ups and finding out which ones you like the best. it has a play style for everyone, and by everyone i mean EVERYONE. i am not kidding, this game has a lot of power ups to buy. and once you buy them all, it feels so rewarding knowing you have all the power accessible to you its just up to the player as to weather they can get that power or not. i wasn't alive to see the birth of hotline Miami but i was alive to see Otxo's birth, and i can say they are both amazing games and each get a 10/10 from me!

_childDocuments_.review: "OXTO" is an intense, adrenaline-fueled, twin-stick-shooter-roguelike with similar graphics and gameplay as "Hotline Miami", but with its own gorgeous style and the addition of bullet-time, dodgeroll and (a much needed) health bar.The visuals are viscerally noir, the soundtrack slaps you in the face just right, the story and lore of the mysterious entity manifesting as the mansion and the Sisyphus-like task at hand (which is a meta-comment for the genre) is told well and with a grain of existential dread.Unfortunately, the first area of the game can get old when you already did various runs and then it is very hard to die to the first boss, which seems a bit of a chore. Also some of the drinks (skills) seem superior to others, but these two complaints are just a minor setback.I still wholeheartedly recommend this for any fan of these genres or stylish games in general!

_childDocuments_.review: Rougelite Hotline Miami with some small yet smart changes from the admittedly very easy comparison. When only a few enemies remain, they are highlighted in the room to make finding the last stragglers far easier, making the search for those few guys you missed a lot less painful. All of the guns (I've seen so far) can be reloaded, allowing you to hold on to a favorite gun a bit longer at the cost of slowing your momentum by having to wait for the reload animation.The dodge roll can be used to traverse small pieces of furniture, making awkward room structure less of a hassle to traverse while allowing you to still avoid damage.You have a health bar, but the game feels like it's balanced around it accordingly. Enemies are more alert and can also take more than one shot before dying.If you're a HM purist then this all probably sounds like blasphemy, but for everyone else this is loads of fun. Oh, and the soundtrack absolutely slaps.

_childDocuments_.review: Ignore the hours, I pirated this before I bought it to see if I'd like it.The game is super awesome. I love the art style, the music, the characters, even the drinking mechanic. I'd completely recommend the game, but I do want to point out some flaws. The enemies being able to shoot you from just around the corner is usually surprising and leaves the feels of unfairness. That's a big point- the enemies often feel unfair. Due to the closeness, I'll be comparing this to Hotline Miami, so bare with me. In Hotline Miami, getting hit is usually able to be avoided easily, due to being able to understand what and how an enemy will move and do, but in OTXO is can often feel like they can hit you when they shouldn't. The main issue is corners. I feel like enemies can often attack from wall edges and corners and it doesn't feel super consistent. To be honest, this is probably just a skill issue moment and I deserve that, but I think it would be a lot more enjoyable if the enemies moved more like they do in Hotline Miami.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay so its basically Roguelite Hotline Miami. If you enjoyed Hotline you will very much enjoy this game.However keep the following in mind:This game is much more lenient. Where as Hotline Miami is one hit deaths where you need to have quick reaction time this is basically its adrenaline doping cousin. You can take hits. You can spray 'n pray your way through rooms. You can outright customize every weapon that can appear in runs which includes what enemies have (outside of a heavy sniper rifle which can always appear on certain enemies and you always start with a Garand)However this isn't exactly a copy. I'd say its more like... Lies of P compared to Bloodborne. Both are very very similar but have their own clear identity.Best way to describe it is both OTXO and Hotline Miami are games based on being quick, being efficient, and being ruthless. However Hotline is more reaction based while OTXO is more instinctual based. Honestly thats the best I can describe the differences between them.Hotline you can think out your strategy and use what is available to you. You ran the level before. You know the threats. You know the patrols. You pick your mask and go but be careful because death is always right there.OTXO is pick what you want going in then just... GO. Screw strategy outside of the drinks you pick. You can take hits and have slow motion powers. BARGE IN THAT ROOM WITH NO THOUGHTS AND JUST PULL THE TRIGGER ON YOUR GUN.To actually understand this gibberish from my weird mind you have to have played both.Also this games sound track, while not having as many tracks, goes just as hard at Hotline Miami.

_childDocuments_.review: Otxo is a Hotline Miami-esque roguelike that takes the original formula and improves on it tremendously. _childDocuments_.review: I don't leave many reviews at all - As this is my first ever on a game like this. However, OTXO's OST caught my attention and I loved it. Any other OST from any other game is as good as OTXO's, but OTXO's OST, combined with the gameplay, blends in perfectly. Perhaps I read too much into it, but if I do then that's usually the case that the game is very good and does exactly what it needs to, by making a player highly invested into it.For those who are unsure about buying it; I highly recommend it. Especially if you like the OST. If you played Hotline Miami then it's a must-buy. In my view, negative reviews that are mostly literal cope about the enemies from OTXO (Unless they're of course meant as a joke-review, then it's something different) usually indicate the lack of actual interest in improving their skills in the game. I struggle as such, but realise that to just whine about X enemy type is futile when not pondering over my strategy and what my issue was - Not the game. Sure, perhaps it's partially that case: But there's the other end where I could've avoided death. It's amusing how people blame the game but do not admit their fault and wouldn't want to try again adjust their strategy, and adapt by using the drinks (Or liquors) from the game.Overall this game is a damn 11/10, I love it, the OST, and bought as well the OST with it in respect to Lateralis making such an awesome game, something I've been searching for quite a while.Hope this chaotic mess of a review and trying not to spoil anything was somewhat helpful for those wondering if they wanted to buy OTXO.And now if you excuse me, I have to go back to the mansion as The Cycle Repeats.

_childDocuments_.review: To be clear, this is NOT Hotline Miami 3. It has the same aesthetic and shares some features, but health bar, focus (slow motion mechanic) and liquors (gameplay modifiers) make HLM and OTXO feel completely different. But if you like both HLM and rouge-likes this is no brainer. Try this game. The music is great, tonn of guns, the gameplay changes slightly depending on what liqours you have purchased with your hard-earned money. Keeping your combo meter high is the key to fun and more gameplay possibilities and gimmicks. Each new stage features a new type of enemy, which is added to the general pool of enemies and gives your foes a new difficulty modifier. Mid and late bosses hit like a truck. Of the downsides, I would mention the poor visibility and the swarm of enemies out in the open at the later stages.

_childDocuments_.review: I wish I like this more, but there's some fundamental issues that hold it back.First the positive: - The combat feels great, the guns are punchy and when things are flowing nicely it's easy to fall into the zone and cause chaos, and at the end you're left with the blood-splattered evidence of the carnage you created with a sense of pride. - The music is a perfect compliment to the chaos. While it might not have the same identity, variety and personality of the Hotline Miami OST, it does a great service to the mood of world and gameplay.However, I have a lot of problems that keep me from thinking this game lives up to it's potential.- While the  monochromatic aesthetic showcases the viscera perfectly, it also makes the enviroments very difficult to read, especially when you're in the moment and trying to keep up the momentum. I would frequently bump into furniture during tense firefights, particularly large rectangular objects that aren't immediately recognisable as a rug or a floor pattern, which breaks the flow and got me killed multiple times.- While the rogue-like structure might make the gameplay seemingly "infinite", it often makes levels feel carelessly structured and occasionally unfair. You will absolutely still find situations where the rooms and hallways are so large that you'll be shot by enemies you can't see even when you're looking in their direction. It also means that unlike Hotline Miami, there's no way to learn the levels through repeat attempts, so a bad seed and unfair level layouts will probably result in your death with nothing to learn from the experience.- While some liquors are interesting, many of them aren't impactful enough to make repeat runs feel interesting and distinct from each other, so if the base loop isn't enough to keep you interested, you'll be bored after a few runs and the slow progression of importing more liquors makes it feel like you need to grind your way out of the problem.- The bosses are uninspired, and can largely be defeated by just firing in their general direction while circling around the room.6/10. If Steam let me give a more middling recommendation I would, but I don't think my feelings on it are positive enough to give it a full endorsement.
_childDocuments_.name: OTXO

_childDocuments_.review: I came to this game as a Hotline Miami enjoyer looking for a longer, more gameplay focused experience. Ultimately, I don't think that's what this game is. It is something better.At first I thought the departure from HM's one hit kill system was to the game's detriment, but I have come to find it creates a completely unique gameplay loop that allows you to be a complete and utter maniac. Where in HM (especially in 2) every move needed to be carefully calculated because every misstep meant death, in OTXO you can sprint into a hail of bullets, send your own back in return and come out covered in blood, feeling like God's gift to the firearms industry.The best advice I can give someone who isn't immediately hooked by this game is: learn to play like a maniac. There should be no downtime. You should never be stopping. You should always be shooting.My only complaint is the boss fights. They are bullet spongey and are more reliant on knowing attack tells and safe strategies as opposed to the normal combat loop which is 100% off the cuff improv. Luckily they only show up every 6 rooms or so.This game is fantastic. You should play it.

AND THE MUSIC, the music speaks for itself even if you don't play the game the soundtrack is worth it on its own. _childDocuments_.review: If you want Hotline Miami experience, you probably won't get it here in the way you expect it.Pros:+ The gameplay is fun.+ The soundtrack is good.Cons:- The fun from the gameplay is completely overshadowed by the amount of repetition you're expected to do. You will die a lot, but this is not the issue - the problem is that you'll have to look at the same 2-3 rooms again, again and again. It got stale after the first 4 hours.- The repetition of the soundtrack due to you dying again, again and again will make you resent the music very fast.- The story is complete and utter garbage. I'd say that it's mediocre, but compared to similar games it's a beat up corpse.- The difficulty is absurd. This, by itself, would not be a problem if the game would respect player's time - but it doesn't. You don't get any checkpoints, and late game sections are difficult enough to where it's reasonable to assert that average casual player would not be able to complete them. Unlike some games of this type, OTXO does not provide you any difficulty-reducing accessibility options, aside from the "show enemy markers when X enemies are left" setting.OTXO aims to provide you "roguelike"/"roguelite" experience, while completely missing the point of Rogue and roguelikes in general. Roguelikes are popular, because they provide you a gigantic toolset to solve problems, and each run is often incomparable to the previous one due to their VAST amount of parts for procedural content generation. This, paired with the toolset the game provides, makes each run very distinct. This does not exist in OTXO, where, by the game's nature you have only two major mechanics - shooting and Focus ability. The drinks (enhancers) provide nowhere near enough replayability, because the game still feels almost completely the same, which is antithetical to the core of what a roguelike is. This leads to gaming experience, that does not feel rewarding in the slightest. if you fail in a roguelike then chances are that you failed to utilize the entirety of the toolset provided to you. You also don't need to be an expert in all mechanics of a roguelike to beat it. On the other hand, if you fail a run in OTXO, this is very likely because you haven't mastered the very limited toolset you've been provided, and you are expected to master it to actually beat the game.I wish I could recommend this game, I really do - I liked the gameplay a lot - but I just can't. It's not worth your time and effort if you actually intend to beat it.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game, if you like fast-paced actions do yourself a favor and try it. The Hotline Miami influence is obvious but it also reminds me of Enter the Gungeon. _childDocuments_.review: Getting the comparison out of the way, I've held Hotline Miami (and Wrong Number) as some of my favorite indie games of all time for years. Naturally, with the retro-pixel top view gun-switching ultraviolent fast paced shooter action going here, this game had enormous shoes to fill. So my first few runs made me think "this is just fresh enough. Some good ideas, nice visuals... Yeah, this is good".And then I got into a boss battle with a giant mecha snake with machineguns. In my 4th run. And that was awesome. "Hotline Miami, this is not".So yeah, for anyone like me that might have been worried that this is "just bringing some decade old game with more modern considerations", I'm pleased to see that it differentiates itself positively and extremely early. With "bullet time" to slow down the massive amount of bullets on the screen, a fresh variety of enemies and bosses early on, and a generous healthbar that will likely deplete after strings of poor decisions and bad planning, each floor has a lot of adrenaline that doesn't reward "trial and error", but instead, planning how to approach each room.Yeah, planning is rewarded... but so is keeping a high combo multiplier to get more money to make your run better. So there's a lot of high-risk high-reward decisions at every moment. Play too safe and you won't be able to afford upgrades, yet play too reckless and you'll end up surrounded with no "bullet time" to even the odds.It's very good action, extremely fast paced, and while it can feel a bit clunky early on due to the unusual controls, waltzing in and painting this black and white mansion red is very gratifying.So yeah, recommended if you like fast paced action, punishing but fair gameplay, are okay with its violent themes, and if you like roguelikes in general.

_childDocuments_.review: It's Notline Miami.Perfect to get that fix of fast-paced, top-down ultraviolence if you've been itching for it, but without the narrative breaks or trippy story. What OTXO offers is a roguelike experience that boils the Hotline Miami formula down to its essence and packages it in distilled, short bursts of nonstop action. You get a combo meter that rewards you for killing enemies fast, pressuring you to keep pushing pushing pushing. Taking a breather means losing out on cash, which means less upgrades at your next pit stop. A thumping soundtrack that keeps urging you to move fast and be rough. It's amazing.The only thing I really consider a downside is the almost-greyscale artstyle. I understand it's a stylistic choice, but it does at times make things hard to distinguish from one another, allowing enemies or weapons to blend in with the environment, corpses or debris. Fairly minor complaint, though. This ♥♥♥♥ rules.

_childDocuments_.review: Huge fan of the gameplay, music and atmosphere. Definitely not a fan of the roguelike nature of the game, but this is very much a personal preference, not an issue of the game itself. To me, getting to a new boss only to get annihilated by an unexpected attack pattern in seconds and as a result not being able to learn his attacks simply sucks.However, the drink mechanics is amazing and you can keep up the combos, at the later stages you become satisfyingly overpowered with so many buffs stacked and I was pleasantly surprised by how I managed to breeze through a lot of the later encounters even though I've never got that far before. A small tip for new players, there's a firing range where you can test the DPS of different weapons. Significantly helped my experience.In conclusion, if you crave more of the Hotline Miami top-down shooter formula, OTXO's great as it not only recreates it, but actually pushes it further with interesting new mechanics. If you're a fan of roguelikes on top of that, even better. If you despise them, I'd still recommend it because the core gameplay loop is enjoyable enough to keep you going. At least that was the case for me.I think it's also worth mentioning that this was all made by one man, including the music, which is insane. Great job, Nate!

_childDocuments_.review: A part of me kinda feels that reviewing through comparison - in a way - does a disservice to the thing being compared. It's that anxiety that instead of judging something on its own merits, I "taint" my review of it by leaving a reference point in the reader's head......but what should I do when the game does not shy away from its influences at all?Indeed, if you've scrolled down to the review section, you probably will have seen that OTXO's store page mentions positive opinions comparing it to Hotline Miami. Hell, knowing the impact that HM had on the gaming industry, you probably didn't even need anyone to tell you that this is a similar game. But simply drawing the comparison doesn't really describe what makes OTXO stand out from its inspiration. And oh boy, there is  of stuff to go over – and unfortunately I myself will have to fall for that trap and talk for a bit about the other game as I discuss this one.Suffice to say, we are never getting another Hotline Miami game from its creators. Though Dennaton have struck gold with the gameplay formula of being a glass cannon and having your reflexes tested alongside your ability to strategize on the fly, the plot of the games never glorified that violence. Instead, the developers had made a point of portraying most of the main cast as pathetic creatures unleashing death and misery on the world for various selfish reasons, with violence itself leading only to a pitiful end for those who choose to take part in it.And even though the core message chastised the bloodshed, the series took the gaming world by storm because its rendition of violence in gameplay and presentation was . Divorced from the plot and the setting, Hotline Miami offered a  solid experience and a great challenge, with just about the only downside being its linear structure.And so it didn't take long for OTXO to figure out what the good parts were and how to iterate upon them.On a mechanical level, we're talking about another fast-paced top-down shooter which requires good reflexes from the player. However, the first immediate difference is the toolset available to the player. One of the major elements in OTXO's gameplay are the drinks. Every few floors you will run into a bar, whose bartender will sell you liquors which carry different effects. What sets them apart from HM's masks is the fact that you can (and likely will) take various different drinks during a run in order to stack their benefits. A liquor which makes killing enemies with SMGs yield more coins? Neat, let's mix that with a drink which makes you dual-wield one-handed guns – which, conveniently, includes SMGs. Add a few more just for variety and you'll build up a truly formidable otxo.Some of those drinks even interact with your Focus – another major mechanic. Much like Max Payne, you get the ability to slow down time. This allows you to correct positioning mistakes, react faster than your enemies, or even just get the buzz from seeing bullets cut through the air.Another tool is the dodge-roll, which was also present in Hotline Miami for some characters, but OTXO escalates it to a regular gameplay mechanic. Rather predictably, this lets you reposition and dodge some of the projectiles flying your way, but also vault over furniture such as tables and chairs, unlike HM's static props cutting off movement but letting damage through.All of this may sound like it's easy to become really powerful in this game. Make no mistake though, OTXO is no cakewalk. These tools are given to you because the enemies  do not forgive. As you proceed further through the Mansion, its guardian demons will have their own attributes augmented, perhaps most notoriously through shortening their already quick reaction times. Though the game gives you a health meter, letting yourself get caught off-guard and not checking your surroundings will probably cause the meter to deplete completely from an SMG-wielding enemy unloading an entire magazine into your back. And once you die – because you highly likely will, even with prior experience with the genre – you will wake up back at the Beach in front of the Mansion again, with a reminder that the only way to get out and break the cycle is to destroy the Heart of the building. On your way you'll be able to talk to the Nun, who will let you select which weapons will appear during the run as part of the enemy arsenal, or the Girl inside the bar, who handles liquor imports and expands the inventory of drinks that the Bartender may offer.In recent times I've discovered that I'm really fond of roguelite games – and here I found something that managed to scratch that exact itch that's been missing for all those years. Hotline Miami was already an excellent game, but OTXO looked at what worked, and decided to try to do it in its own style. The end result is a remarkable experience, lined by a distinct "red-accented monochrome" artstyle and a truly vicious soundtrack (composed by the one-man studio behind the game! Yes, all of this was made by one person!). HM made me aware of many different artists and introduced me to some really energetic tracks that I still enjoy and listen to even outside of the game – but the soundtrack to OTXO, by the virtue of having one composer for all of its soundtrack instead of licensing different tracks not originally made for the game, feels a lot more cohesive, collected, and concise. And . ( is easily the most violent and vicious track I've heard in , perfectly fitting the high octane bloodbath – and it's not even a boss theme or anything, Despite all of these comparisons to Hotline Miami and the amount of times it's been mentioned in this review, I feel like out of respect for both of these IPs I cannot say that one is flat out better than the other. What I  say, though, is that OTXO – despite being iterative upon concepts we've already seen – manages to stand for itself and carve out its own identity. My very first session in the game, despite me having gotten my butt handed back to me multiple times, had me feeling like I, too, was becoming a prisoner of the Mansion. There was that urge to go for one more run, be the star of another action movie shootout sequence, push onward and conquer the Mansion.And if a game manages to make me crave more  from , I feel like it more than deserves a positive review from me.

_childDocuments_.review: The nature of hotline miami is that it's interesting puzzles/setpieces that are set up in a progression that is satisfying.  I have found games like Hong Kong Massacre to be enjoyable in the same vein, and the addition of things like bullet time are nice in those various games.  I seem to recall Katana Zero did the same, but in a sidescroller format, and I also liked My Friend Pedro, but not quite as much as the ones noted above.I get what this game is trying to do, but it doesn't really use space in interesting ways early on, and given the roguelike nature of it, I wouldn't expect that to change.  It's a good chance that if you just absolutely want more Hotline Miami combat, and you're cool with enemies and  yourself tanking damage more, then this is for you.  It's possible I will come back to this at some point in the future, but in the short term it was asking me do master some controls that felt a bit awkward at first, and not really giving me the same "sense of place" or theme that the other games above have.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, this is really fun for a small sized little Hotline Miami-esque shooter. The gunplay is very fun and engaging and keeps you on your toes. Soundtrack is fantastic, and the sound design is meaty and each gun has a unique feeling of oomph to it. The arsenal in this game has a fine mix of both classic and modern weaponry, ranging from a G36C to an ANM2 Stinger machine gun, and to a damn Blunderbuss. You start off with a small handful of weapons that you can toy with before discovering ways to unlock more as you go. You also have a companion in the game who alters what weapons both you and the enemy can use, which you can use to your advantage. The AI is very smart and differ from Hotline Miami greatly, as you need to either make enough noise to hear them or simply be in front of them, allowing for perfect stealth opportunities. The enemies also get a different and completely random "attribute" for every major area of the Mansion you progress through (think stuff like faster movement, faster reaction time, faster fire rate, etc). The art style of this game is also quite unique although a bit dull on the eyes since its all black, white, and red. This game might be up your alley if you liked Hotline Miami. It isn't a 1:1 clone, but it certainly replicates some aspects well while giving a unique twist to the original formula.

_childDocuments_.review: Lobotomized Hotline Miami.OTXO feels like a game that overcomplicates itself from its source material and misses the points that made the Hotline Miami games enjoyable while not committing fully to its roguelike design, resulting in a confused game that lacks cohesion.The music is great and the game has some nice fancy visual effects. The particles, the environmental debris, the lighting, the shadows, and the ragdoll physics all add a lot to the game's feel and visual feedback. Unfortunately, I can't say the same for the overall presentation. The monochrome visuals resulted in a very dull and samey-looking environment, which was a lot of the appeal I felt with Hotline Miami where each level had a distinct color palette that made them immediately recognizable even beyond the level design. Not to mention visual clarity is also lessened as the white bullets just blend in more with the monochrome backgrounds.The problem also extends beyond the presentation, as the procedural generation of the levels despite the handcrafted rooms just results in everything feeling uniform and derivative. It's usually just a bunch of rooms on the left side and right side of the map, and a big open hallway in the middle. This also doesn't flow very well and clashes with some of the more enjoyable aspects of Hotline Miami, which is to try and fully combo the entire level as you figure out the best pathway in getting through the enemies in succession. The whole scoring aspect is pretty much gimped too. You do still want to keep up high combos for the coins so you can get more abilities, but with the way things work, it's more reliant on having a lucky seed of RNG rather than mastery of the levels and mechanics. Outside this, it's a lot less exciting and inconsistent to score, which again is a shame since I felt this is one of Hotline Miami's main sources of fun.Then we get to one of the biggest offenders which is the whole health system. I feel a lot of the flow and intensity of Hotline Miami came from the almost-always-one-hit-kill system. OXTO opting for varying damage and health makes sense for a roguelike, but it still clashes a lot with the overall feeling of the combat which undeniably does still take a lot from Hotline Miami. All the guns sound fantastic and punchy, but it's such a disconnect when they take 2 to 3 hits to kill someone, and there's a lot less feeling of danger when your character also can tank bullets for the most part. Some weapons can one-hit kill, which extends to the fact that the game ultimately even contradicts itself with the mechanic that allows you to remove weapons from rotation, and only select the ones you want. Thus you have the option of keeping only the weapons that can one-hit kill and negating the whole damage system in the first place.The roguelike design overall just doesn't work with Hotline Miami's style, since another large part of what made Hotline Miami work is the quick inconsequential punishment of death where you can just instantly restart, and learn the level like a time-based puzzle where memorization and then execution comes into play. In OTXO, when you die you start from the beginning, and you're more reliant on getting good RNG with abilities that can help you or layouts that aren't too much of a mess. I did finish this game thrice, with a run that didn't involve using abilities, but most of it devolved into abusing mechanics like the bullet time and dodge rolls. Especially as you get further into a run where all the enemies have different modifiers and they all get stacked haphazardly with no real design in mind how they placed.This then extends to the other poorly thought-out element, which is the boss fights. They're neat on paper, but poor in execution. Except for one samurai-themed boss, most of it comes down to spamming the dodge roll and waiting for your bullet time to cool down, while avoiding the same three or four attack patterns over and over again because the bosses are bullet sponges.There's an unlockable 'Impossible Mode' that makes it feel closer to the original Hotline Miami games, with damage raised across the board, which translates to all guns pretty much being one-hit kills and survivable by two to three through lucky shaves. I wish the game was designed with this mode in mind as it resolves the bullet sponge problem with the bosses and retains the fast exciting pace of Hotline Miami. The rest of the problems are still here, but this is where I had most of my enjoyment. I feel like this game would have been better overall if it's just a linear campaign with a dozen levels or so with an upgrade system slapped onto it. There are some neat elements with the systems here, but they just don't work well together. As a Hotline Miami clone, it lacks a lot of the original game's flow and intensity. As a roguelike, it lacks a lot of the extra systems and mechanics most roguelike games have, including permanent upgrades. Outside some modifiers and the ability to unlock guns and select which of them spawn during a run, there's little progression within the systems themselves.If you're itching for a top-down shooter with some roguelike elements and a Hotline Miami flavoring, and you're willing to look past the shortcomings, this game is mostly fine. But if you just want more Hotline Miami in general, there's a whole bunch of well-made and creative campaigns, levels, and mods out there in the modding scene, even in HM2's Workshop alone. Not to mention the massive overhaul packs and standalone projects. And if you want a roguelike in general, there is a whole sea of them nowadays that also pretty much does a lot of its dedicated systems better.Also, OTXO's a stoopid name.

There is no option to set your mouse sensitivity in game and most likely when you will first start the game it will be super fast for you, the only way to fix this is to change your sensitivity in your PC which again was frustrating.These two things were the deal breaker for me and I ended up refunding the game, however I must add that the soundtrack of the game along with the noir graphics was really cool, shame that it's only capped to 60hz and there's no way that it can go higher than that (I believe that someone from the dev team confirmed that it's not possible because the program that they used to build the game won't allow them to extend that).

_childDocuments_.review: This is a decently fun game but I can't recommend it. It is locked to 60FPS, so moving the camera around feels a little juddery if you are used to playing games at high refresh rates. The enemy AI is very primitive. If they see you, they start blasting or navigating around the level geometry like Pac-Man ghosts. I fundamentally don't like how your weapon inventory is handled, either. Basically you pick up dead enemies' weapons and they come with 1 extra mag. Kill more enemies, take their weapons. You can't just go in with your favorite gun and keep it the whole level. What this means is that you'll often be using guns you don't want. Later in the game, you can meet a nun character to limit the weapons the enemies spawn in with, which effectively limits the weapons you can use, but having it be two-sided like this is not fun. For example, on a recent playthrough I limited the weapons to JUST the 9MM pistol. I got very far in my run because the enemies also use the pistol and it does bad damage compared to other weapons and isn't as accurate long range. Let's say you want to use an LMG or a shotgun on your playthrough... all the enemies will spawn in with these weapons and they will mow you down very quickly.You can get upgrades from a bartender but they only last as long as your given session - I would have much preferred some sort of system where once you bought a perk it was always in your inventory and you could just roll with a set of like 3-5 of them. Also, many of the bartender upgrades aren't really upgrades. They're more like sidegrades or weird game modifiers.And then of course, there's the artstyle. It's black and white and very basic. Finding fallen weapons can sometimes be a bit difficult because of the lack of color contrast. And while the game's style works for what it is, I quickly found it boring.Conceptually, the game is good. And for the most part shooting feels alright. But I feel like the developer fumbled the ball with some obtuse design decisions. And the caveman-level AI ultimately makes the game feel sort of cheap as opposed to intelligently challenging.As far as top down shooters on Steam go, you could do worse. But it is annoying knowing how good this game could be with a few different tweaks - uncapped framerate, more color in the art style, more interesting long-term progression, smarter AI, etc. As it stands I can't give OTXO more than a 6/10.

_childDocuments_.review: I beat this game start to finish in about 6 hours, and I've seen basically everything the game has to offer. 6 hours is an abysmal amount of gameplay for a roguelike. I've dumped dozens of hours into Hades, Slay the Spire, The Binding of Isaac, Wizard of Legend, etc from just their extreme replayability. I have roughly 8 hours of playtime in Enter the Gungeon and I haven't even gotten half way to beating it once, let alone feeling like I've seen it all.It's about the same length as the Hotline Miami games, but without any of the handcrafted level design or creative storytelling.  Most of the upgrades (drinks) feel underwhelming, some are simply useless- it doesn't feel like there is even remotely as much synergy as I wish there would be, most upgrades are boring and only directly or indirectly buff your DPS, Durability, Speed, Focus, etc.  It has some rogueLITE mechanics where you can progress in between runs, but it requires you to spend the currency you need to buy upgrades during the run- so you're essentially forced to hinder your current run or ignore long term progression.Honestly, it's worth your time if you've already played and gotten bored of all the other Roguelikes, Hotline Miamis, Katana Zero, and all the good games like them. Otherwise, go play (or replay) those instead.

_childDocuments_.review: OTXO has two sides to it, the first is the actual gameplay, where you go around shooting enemies and cycle your guns to always have ammo, which i must say is fun, altough is very much lacking depth, the game plays the same 1 minutes in as it does 30 minutes into a run, no matter the unlocks you have. There is also a insentive to play agressivly and stylishly with the combo meeter that duplicates all the coin enemies drop, unfortunetly the way to stylishly kill enemies is limited both in variance, and in opertunities. I think kicking down a door to kill someone may increase your combo more than shooting them, but if it is, the amount of extra combo opertunities is enterely up to enemies choosing to stand close to doors, and the reward for doing so is miniscule (which is why i am unsure style is even a factor, cause i haven't noticed much of a reward). Instead the combo meter is best used by chaining togheter kill, this in combination to semi random layouts means that the skill of keeping the combo is not to play agressivly, but to not miss enemies to keep the combo going, and that hide and seek like minigame does not really play into the power fantasy the game is trying to sell.The other side to the game is the economy, you collect coins by killing enemies and keeping your combo up, the rate at which you get coin can also be affected by perks you buy with said coin, however perks are random so it is all up to luck of wether you can stack enough economy boosting perks early in the game to have a significant advantage late in the game (over those runs where all your perks are combat focused).Furthermore coins are also used to unlock things, so the player has to choose between runs they intend to win, and grinding unlocks while falling behind in power due to the lack of perks. Even worse, the system where you unlock perks functions as a bank, where coin you put into it saves between runs, and once you fill up the investment you get that perk for "free". This encurages a strategy where you invest into these new perks untill you get 99% there, stopping just before you unlock it. Then next run you can get the perk for a pittance by paying for the last 1%, functionally giving you up to 3 almost free perks, this strategy works untill you have bought all of the unlockable perks, making them the most usefull as almost unlocked.If anything i can see why other rouglikes often choose conditional unlocks (do A, unlock B), and/or have a separete currency to actually unlock things, that only can be spent between runs (so no freebies). Since nither of those solutions undermine the actual goal of winning. The solution of some perks boosting your economy is often in a lot of rouglikes offset by giving you free stuff (item rooms in isaac), or just making it so that more damage = more kills = more coins (think risk of rain 2), instead of hard limiting the amount of enemes, and thus coins, in run progression.Soundtrack is a banger tho.

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game, but I figured out how to cheese the game early on, and it's not fun anymore. The other problem is even if I don't do the cheese, the shooting mechanics just aren't that fun to me. The main problem is with the slow motion ability, and how the rooms are sectioned off pretty distinctly. So basically I hit slow-mo, then immediately kick the door in, kill everyone in the room, deactivate slow-mo, wait for it to recharge, rinse and repeat. Some rooms are shaped in ways that make this a little more interesting, but almost every situation seems to be pretty much the same, just taking everyone out as soon as possible. In larger rooms this mechanic still plays out, but you are instead just using obstacles to get your slow-mo meter back to do a quick trigger of the slow-mo as you or the enemy comes around a corner and comes into view, kill them real fast, then disable the slow-mo before it eats too much of the meter up, rinse and repeat until the room is fully cleared. Sure you don't have to play this way, but with how fast the enemy responds it really does feel the game is designed to be played this way, at least to some extent. I feel like if enemies next to the doors leading to nearby rooms were alerted, that might make this game a lot more interesting.As far as every other aspect, like the story, the awesome roguelike type upgrade systems, and overall feel of the game is excellent. But unfortunately I just can't remain interested, even with the cool bosses they throw at you.

_childDocuments_.review: A less melee and tactics focused Hotline Miami with some roguelike elements that gives you a quick to recharge slow motion toggle and dodge move to fight quick reacting enemies.Your characters puts on a mask and suddenly finds themself washed up on a beach near a mansion where he is told he can't leave or die and that he needs to fight his way to the deeper part of the mansion to destroy the heart. You will fight through rooms where you will need to kill all enemies to proceed. To do that you pick up, shoot, reload, and throw guns at enemies, kick enemies and doors with doors near enemies being able to kill them, toggle on slow motion, and perform a dive move that can avoid bullets. The base mechanics are fine but I don't enjoy the enemies that take multiple hits to kill and your own large health bar. Mostly all your trying to avoid doing is destroy too many doors or glass windows that can lead to larger groups of enemies engaging you or sneaking up on you, as long as you don't break open a door or window enemies are unable to get through them.Every three areas and in the first area of a new run is a bar where you can spend coins (first one of the run is free) that you get from killing enemies and maintaining a high combo for higher rewards on different types of alcohol that give you passive bonuses. The abilities you can gain from the bars might do something like allowing you to do more damage when stationary, reload faster, recharge your slow motion ability faster or they can give more targeted buffs to certain types of weapons or give you abilities that allow for unique playstyles like allowing you to block bullets, gain a kunai if you roll while holding no weapon, transform kunai into a throwing axe that you can summon back to you, etc. As the bars are limited to only three kinds of drinks unless you spend even more to restock you could easily thing that your likely to be stuck with completely useless or contradictory things for your runs most of the time but one of the only positives I can give the game is that if you get to a bar and choose to save and go back to the main menu and then reload it will change the drink menu, actually allowing you to pick up skills that might make the game more fun or interesting for you, if you don't mind rerolling drinks as many times as needed.The available weapons can also be changed up by toggling what guns are available or not in your next run which also means it effects what weapons enemies will use. Trying to do an all pistol or sniper rifle run might be fun but you do have to keep in mind that doing so might make boss fights much more difficult. Once you get through six stages you will fight a boss before moving to another area with six stages and a boss, the new area might introduce a new enemy or give enemies a bonus like having extra armor. Every boss is a tedious bullet sponge with a small number of attacks that become easy to predict over time, while the main enemies aren't as much fun as they lack the more visceral nature of the kills of your opponents in something like Hotline Miami or even other slow motion using top down games like The Hong Kong Massacre, these bosses have no reaction to being shot at all and are some of the worst bosses I've seen in a genre like this.Fighting the main enemies is ok but not as much fun as similar games I've played in this style. The bosses are terrible. I personally hate the music. A lot of the guns and abilities just aren't that fun to use. You can, in an inefficient way, tailor a run to work more in a way you find interesting which seems more like an unintentional feature or engine issue (like not being able to use the mouse on menus, not being able to save Steam screenshots, not being able to change the mouse sensitivity that are related to the game engine) as it certainly isn't something the game tells you. If you don't reload for abilities you end up with frequent terrible choices that can have either nothing to do with your playstyle or you might want to play in a certain way but it requires having multiple abilities together that can take too long to find otherwise. There also just isn't that much content and what there is it pretty much wants you to do all of in one run, by the time I was done I didn't even have anything practical left to buy as an upgrade and the logical endpoint of the run should have come around three sets of stages prior.Screenshots:

_childDocuments_.review: Loving it so far.  Sound design, music, weapon feedback, everything feels great.  It's quick to get back into a run when you die and it's satisfying to tear through an area and build that combo multiplier once you hit your stride.The health system is a cool idea in a game like this.  It makes it feel like your successes and failures are the result of your cumulative performance rather than Hotline's system where you can perfectly clear a room only to get instakilled by an offscreen straggler that you missed.My only real criticism is that the bosses kind of hurt the pacing.  None of the bosses I've encountered so far have been too difficult, but they're pretty slow and spongey enemies that feel like they'd be more at home in a title like Enter the Gungeon.  They grind things to a halt in a game where most of your playtime is spent clearing rooms as quickly and efficiently as possible.

_childDocuments_.review: There's a good game hiding here, but you wont find it at the time of this review.--- 3/5OTXO is a game of high potential and with beautiful presentation, hamstrung by misguided design decisions. Fans of Hotline Miami and other fast-paced top-down shooters will find some entertainment here, but OTXO is no memorable experience and unlike its stronger companions, playing it again and again requires the willpower to do so, rather than its systems seducing you into "just one more run".--- 5/5OTXO has a very strong stylized black-and-white-and-red presentation, chunky gun sounds and excellent music. I have nothing bad to say about how great the game presents itself, and it's wonderful to see the effects of your gunshots blow up every imaginable debris possible within the mansion.--- 2/5OTXO suffers from a story which wants to be interesting and mysterious but fails to be neither by overexplaining concepts, characters that are flat and bad dialogue. Intentional obscurity, and characters that push that fact in your face doesn't serve to create interest in the player - rather it feels snobbish and I care little for the story.The background story serves its purpose, and I must admit that I was initially intrigued, until the first character emitted a waterfall of cliché dialogue. There is mystery to be evoked from the beach and the mansion, but the characters must support this mystery and must speak more like real entities living here, instead of strange pseudo gameplay devices too eager to tell the player how lost and mystified they should be.While I wasn't very entertained by the narrative, I do admit that it is wholly unimportant to the experience, and a good narrative would only be sprinkles on top.--- 2/5Giving the gameplay of OTXO a bad score hurts a lot. It is so obvious that the developers have spend tremendous effort to make the gameplay loop as smooth and entertaining as possible, and indeed it is, but the problem lies in the 'meta' roguelike aspects of the game.Upgrades are so abysmally tiny that they feel absolutely horrendous to pick up. 20% extra coins if I kill an enemy while standing still? Slightly increased chance to deal damage to nearby enemies when a foe is dropped? These upgrades are so incredibly boring I started skipping the bar entirely towards my later runs. It's a roguelike! Give the player something fun every time they play, something that lets them change the way they play and actually feel powerful! It's okay, they'll lose it all as soon as they die, and if it makes the game too easy simply put in more enemies!Examples for drinks that would actually be interesting could be "Standing still gives double damage" or "First bullet can penetrate doors", "Killing an enemy gives 50% increased movement speed for 3 seconds", "Holding the trigger down ramps up damage", "Rolling into enemies knocks them down"The combo meter is also good, but falls just short of excellent. Racking up a large combo is awesome, it was awesome in Hotline Miami and it's only better in OTXO since you are rewarded coins for it. But why limit it arbitrarily then? Let it freeze when you complete level instead of resetting your combo between each level. Let skilled players rack up gigantic combos if they are able, racking up 7x, 8x, 9x as they smash through levels keeping up their combos.My last great point of contention is the fact that every boss is the same. It seems you must fight the snake guy first every single time, and the same enemies up until that point. A player will go through that boss every single time they play the game - variety is badly warranted, and it becomes daunting to start a new run, knowing that you'll be treading the exact same steps as before,  considering how your upgrades are going to be as useless again.I would like to say that I appreciated the gun nun, and choosing how you wanted to form your opponents/weapons through this mechanic is excellent.

_childDocuments_.review: It's decent, but feels very light on content and thus replayability. You can unlock some new guns and some new drinks, but the design space is very constrained and nothing feels like it really transforms your run. The weapon variation basically boils down to clip size, spread, ROF, and whether or not it's silenced. The drink effects are all minor to moderate passives, none of which really change the way you play besides maybe favoring one type of gun, or using the slow-mo more or less. The biggest shake-ups come from the kunai and grenade throwables, which are rare, but I could see a run focusing on those being fun. But overall, I can only see doing maybe a dozen runs of OTXO total before it starts getting boring.Basically, if Hotline Miami is your favorite game ever and you want a roguelike version of it, this is that... but IMO it ends up feeling like a shallow retread. Both HM games have way more style and substance, and feel very intentional. This game just makes me want to play better roguelikes.

_childDocuments_.review: Hard pass on this one.This game has a lot of good things going for it but, in my opinion, lacks crucial elements for a roguelite or like or whatever you wanna call it, to be fun.First thing is the perks are "sold" to you. You can imagine this like having access only to the shop in The Binding of Isaac. And I have yet to run into a perk that adds interesting elements to the gameplay. There is this other "relic" room that spawns randomly so you need to save for that too if you want those, but again you can think about The Binding of Isaac where you only run into an expensive trinket slot machine in a secret room where you don't get anything interesting.But wait it gets even better; you need to pay to unlock new perks, so that means you're not getting anything at all until you unlock the actual perks. So that is deadzone for the game from the start, where you just grind and die to the bosses.If you enjoy the gameplay of Hotline Miami with mediocre roguelite elements, bosses and bullet time, you might enjoy this game but I highly doubt it.

_childDocuments_.review: Ok, I tried to find some fun in this, but the game is punishing for no reward. It advertises itself as a Rougelike Hotline Miami, but doesn't really hold up to that.My key gripes are:1. the lack of any melee weapons beyond kicking2. the over-reliance on the Focus mechanic to make it possible to fight any enemy with any sort of chance of not getting overwhelmed. Leading to either rushing ahead and dying to enemies that are always too fast for you or waiting for Focus to recharge, which breaks the flow of the game.3. the fact you're forced to use guns on the bosses. This is a big one for me, cause I went out of my way to build up Kunai, the only non-gun weapon in the game, so I could use it on the bosses and feel like a badass. Only to find that the game won't let you go into the boss room without a gun and if you use an ability to generate Kunai, they just fly through the bosses and do no damage. Which really, really, *really* punishes creativity and is a massive disappointment.If this game were to update to make it so the player is less reliant on the Focus mechanic, added actual melee weapons and doesn't shoehorn you into using guns for the bosses, I might change my review.But for now, no.

_childDocuments_.review: OTXO : By Triple FOTXO," developed by Lateralis Heavy Industries, is a rogue-like, top-down shooter that throws players into an intense and stylish world of fast-paced action, minimalistic storytelling, and surreal visuals. With a blend of unforgiving mechanics and gritty noir aesthetics, "OTXO" seeks to challenge players while immersing them in a dark, mysterious atmosphere reminiscent of films like "John Wick" and "Drive." Set within a sprawling mansion that is as unpredictable as it is dangerous, "OTXO" quickly establishes itself as a unique experience in the rogue-like genre, blending precision-based combat with randomly generated levels and an enigmatic storyline.The game's core strength lies in its visceral and responsive combat system, which puts a high emphasis on skill, speed, and adaptability. Players take control of a lone gunman navigating various procedurally generated rooms filled with enemies, traps, and environmental hazards. The mechanics encourage a fluid, aggressive approach to combat, with fast reloads, slick dodge rolls, and a varied arsenal that invites experimentation. "OTXO" is challenging from the start, with enemies that move and react quickly, forcing players to constantly strategize on the fly. Each weapon has a distinct feel, with tight controls that make each shot and movement matter, a must for a game that prides itself on skillful execution.Complementing the gameplay is "OTXO's" powerful visual and audio design, which works together to create an intense, immersive experience. The game’s monochromatic art style, punctuated by strategic splashes of red, enhances the noir vibe, lending a haunting and memorable look to the chaotic gunfights. This is further amplified by the soundtrack, which pulses with an electronic beat that escalates during combat, adding to the frenetic energy of each room. The atmospheric design is reminiscent of other successful indie titles, yet "OTXO" manages to carve out its own space, using its aesthetic choices to heighten the tension and mystery within each procedurally generated corridor and chamber."OTXO" distinguishes itself within the rogue-like genre by placing a significant focus on risk and reward. Every encounter in the game encourages players to weigh their aggression against the need for survival, as health pickups are sparse and each mistake can be costly. Death, a familiar companion in rogue-likes, forces players to restart their journey through the mansion. However, they are given the option to acquire randomized perks and upgrades that diversify each run, allowing for different tactical approaches. This procedural generation and perk variety help keep each playthrough fresh and engaging, with no two runs feeling exactly the same, a hallmark of well-designed rogue-likes.One of the most interesting aspects of "OTXO" is its minimalist approach to storytelling. Rather than delivering a traditional narrative, it leaves much to interpretation, relying on the player’s exploration and encounters with cryptic NPCs to piece together the plot. The player’s journey is shrouded in mystery, with only subtle hints and eerie interactions guiding them forward. This abstract storytelling style adds to the game's noir atmosphere, allowing the mansion to feel like both a physical and psychological labyrinth. It's an approach that may frustrate players looking for a clear storyline but will captivate those who enjoy piecing together a narrative through atmosphere and context clues.The roguelike design of "OTXO" benefits from its tightly crafted level structure, with each floor of the mansion introducing new enemy types and challenges to keep players on their toes. As players progress, they encounter a variety of boss fights that provide a mix of intense action and unique mechanics. These bosses serve as both a test of skill and an opportunity for players to demonstrate mastery over the game’s mechanics. The pacing feels balanced, with adrenaline-fueled gunfights punctuated by quieter moments that build suspense before diving back into the action.Despite its strengths, "OTXO" can feel repetitive at times, especially during longer runs where the procedural elements might not vary enough to stave off fatigue. The difficulty level is unforgiving, which will appeal to hardcore players but may alienate those looking for a more accessible experience. However, for players who appreciate challenging gameplay with a rich, immersive atmosphere, "OTXO" delivers a solid experience that rewards patience and perseverance. The game’s rogue-like nature means that each loss carries a lesson, and progression feels meaningful as players learn from each encounter and make use of the perks that fit their style.In conclusion, "OTXO" is a bold and stylish rogue-like that combines fast-paced, skill-based combat with a haunting noir aesthetic. The challenging gameplay, combined with its abstract storytelling and atmospheric design, makes it a compelling choice for fans of rogue-likes and top-down shooters. While the high difficulty and minimalistic narrative approach may not appeal to everyone, "OTXO" stands out as a carefully crafted experience that is both visually striking and mechanically rewarding. For those willing to brave its relentless challenge, "OTXO" offers a thrilling and immersive descent into a surreal, gun-smoke-laden underworld.

_childDocuments_.review: ## The ReviewHonestly, after playing virtually every action-roguelite in existence, the release of Hades marked an end-point in the genre for me. Of course there are so many other flavors and varieties of gameplay loops, but Hades really set the bar for what is possible using the action-roguelite formula, and ever since then, I've found it difficult to get that same addictive dopamine burst that the genre is built around. I got a better graphics card, started playing more expansive games that combine RPG elements with shooters and action games and started to appreciate really sinking my teeth into a deep and intricate world that requires patience and pacing to unfold a beautiful narrative. Then a few days ago I downloaded OTXO. **Oh god, the addiction is back**Yeah, it was fun playing Lies of P and the new Cyberpunk expansion. Sure my graphics card can render every single pore of Kratos' skin and show every line of expression in his face during an exceptionally written showdown. But I havent played Lies of P, Cyberpunk 2077, God of War Ragnarok, or any of the hundreds of other AAA and AAAA games in my library. Why? Because **OTXO HAS MADE ME RELAPSE**. OTXO is an experience that is somewhat similar to Hotline Miami in its gameplay, and thats where the similarities end. It is savagely difficult and my first three runs I died in the first ROOM. But like a good action-roguelite does, quickly things started to click and I was getting further and further. The *amazing* soundtrack overlaying a symphony of absolute chaos and death mixed with the high contrast black, white, and blood red palette consumed my senses and for hours upon hours, there was no world except for that of OTXO. The gameplay is excellent; fast, aggressive, and brutal with 1000s of split-second decisions being forced in order to stay alive. Yet at the same time, there is a tactical nature to it all, akin to Hotline Miami except that the enemies are not going to be in the same places every time and you have to learn to study your surroundings while also micromanaging slow-mo, dodge rolls, reloads, health, and which gun you will pick up next when yours runs dry. Its all there. It is essentially digital cocaine; a feeling that I have not experienced since I first played Synthetik or Ultrakill. But alas, although everything I have mentioned makes OTXO such a fantastic game, I was not planning on writing a full review like this until my second day playing when I realized this game's greatest feature. **DEDICATED KICK BUTTON**. **INSTANT KILLS FROM KICKS**. **SORRY HADES, BUT I DONT REMEMBER SEEING YOUR INSTA-KILL KICK BUTTON**. ## In SummaryI am not exaggerating when I say that OTXO has completely reignited my love for action-roguelite games that has been waning ever since Hades appeared on the scene and snapped its fingers with the infinity gauntlet. It is a wild thrill ride on every run and while it will curbstomp your ego, the difficulty is pretty perfectly balanced after an hour of rewiring your brain. I do really want to give a shoutout to the music director as the soundtrack is absolutely *phenomenal*. OTXO could have easily been released with a standard electro-synth soundtrack and been an excellent experience, but the extra effort into the audio presentation makes it stand out among a wildly over-saturated genre. It is a rare day that I can say the best part of a Hotline-Miami-roguelite-spinoff-mutation is the soundtrack.BUT SORRY MUSIC DIRECTOR I WAS LYING THE BEST PART IS **DEDICATED INSTA-KILL KICK BUTTON** ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ I LOVE VIDEO GAMES

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: High 6/10 for me, was not worth full price but maybe on sale. (At the time of posting this review it is on sale).+Music is Great, Fits the action very well.+Slow motion is fun to use+Cool black and white style outside of blood.+Weapons feel different enough (Pistol, Sniper, Shotguns, Smg's,Rifles All deal different damage and spread per bullet).+Story seems interesting enough for a fast paced game like this.+You can Toggle which weapons are available to both you and the enemies in runs-Weapon Unlocks are seemingly RNG based, I DESPISE this kind of mechanic in triple A games let alone indie. You can unlock everything if you wish to grind at least. I know i wont.- "Collectibles" Unnecessarily inflate the grind to unlock weapons first.-The only melee option (Kicking) feels EXTREMELY clunky, a punch while unarmed would probably have been way better.-Other than that, Melee as a whole seems completely absent from the game outside of some bosses.-A lot of the drinks (The Roguelite Feature) really dont feel that impactful at all outside of a few. The best it gets is faster bullets and dual-wielding.-I know hotline miami bosses were not exactly good "bosses" and i like that this game tried to change it up with patterns and such, but it does not feel a WHOLE lot better if im being honest. Many are just sponge bosses that spew projectiles in an unpredictable manner. -Enemy variety is lacking, almost all of them can all be killed in pretty much the exact same way. (Invisible enemies should NOT be a thing in a game like this though!)-This game suffers from the same issue Hotline Miami 2 had, You can be shot by completely off-screen enemies in longer corridors.-You can get stuck on furniture and objects that blend in with the environment (Why is this a thing?!)-I know this was probably a intentional development decision, but thrown guns not harming enemies while a relatively small kunai does, Doesn't feel right.Overrall an interesting roguelite top down shooter with some hotline Miami inspiration. It does plenty to stand out as its own thing, but unfortunately the way they went about it sort of highlights why Hotline Miami was so remembered imo. that games combination of melee and ranged weapons along with all characters taking 1 hit to kill kept things thrilling, even if a bit frustrating at times. Here, giving enemies and the player their own health bar kinda ends up slowing and dragging everything else down and is especially noticeable during the boss fights. 6/10 Can be fun in short bursts but i just dont feel the urge to continue with this one.

_childDocuments_.review: Although I only did two runs, both of which ended relatively quickly as can be seen by how little I've played, the game didn't really succeed in making me want to play more of it as the pace of the gameplay just feels a  I suppose?Calling it fast-paced just feels like a complete and utter underestimate of how fast things really are considering that the game's core even revolves around managing a focus meter to slow the game down and make it more manageable. You're rewarded for going fast and killing enemies in "interesting ways" to get more coins, which are then used on buying drinks at the bar, this games perk/item system, or unlocking new drinks for it to offer you.As focus has to regenerate, you only have so much to play with if you want to go fast. Due to that you'll want to mostly toggle it on and off quickly, just enough to get the drop on the enemies. This constant fast-slow-fast-slow made me feel more disoriented than anything else and after I failed my 2nd run, I moved to refund it as the game wants me to play faster than I find enjoyable while also just making me feel borderline nauseous.Another issue is that there were no options to change the resolution or to swap between fullscreen and windowed. Furthermore, when I tried to change the keyboard bindings for the focus button, shift is uncomfortable for me to use as my pinky is somewhat numb, most of my alternate binds came up as "undefined". Alt, Ctrl and all of the numpad keys weren't being accepted.On a plus side, the soundtrack, what I heard of it, sounded great and the guns themselves also felt satisfying to use.I'm sure the game is plenty enjoyable if you enjoy games that move at the pace of an enthusiastic tourist during their first time on a German Autobahn, but if you're like me, the one who'd be in the passenger seat clawing at the upholstery, legs straight and pushing against the two break pedals they wish were there with all the might they can muster in a vain attempt to stop the madness they're being subjected to, I'd say give this one a pass.

The color paletter is beautiful, but it does not change between the levels in ANY way. For a roguelike, I would say having distinguished levels is pretty important, especially considering lack of enemy variety3. The progression within the run is boring. It looks like it doesn't.

_childDocuments_.review: I got this because I heard it was a Hotline Miami roguelike. It was a really interesting idea but the execution is rather poor. The game play is solid for what you'd expect, it very much feels like Hotline Miami at face value and has great music too!However, there's a lot that takes away from the game. The black & white aesthetic makes it difficult to read a room and with how fast paced it can be, it will often lead you to failure. There is a "focus" power which allows you to slow down time and calculate your room entries but it takes so long to charge up if you really want to use it often, you'll find yourself standing around before breaking a door.As far as the "roguelike" aspect goes, it doesn't really feel like one at all. I only played for about an hour but not only do I feel like I saw the same rooms multiple times, I felt like I saw the same whole levels multiple times in that short time span. It doesn't feel so much like a roguelike as it feels a base game where they maybe randomize the order of levels per world or something to that affect. In addition to that, the rooms are so big you'll often get shot at from off screen.The powers you unlock are through drinks from a bartender between floors. None of them looked very appealing. Every single power up just seemed like "I guess I'll buy that because I have so much money" instead of "Woa, that looks super fun!"Overall, it's an interesting idea but not the best execution. If the roguelike aspects were worked on more and the levels didn't have such big rooms that you'd get killed off screen, it could have some potential. OTXO isn't necessarily a bad game, but I don't think it's a good one either.

_childDocuments_.review: You remember Hotline Miami? Yes? Then play that game.I see no reason to delve deeper into this. The first 10 minutes are filled with pointless pseudo-babbling, followed by uninspired monochrome levels that all look and feel the same.I imagine the game will throw more varied enemies at you, since it seems to be a "rogue-lite", and I use that term very loosely. At least the game hasn't shown anything to warrant that monicker, apart from some basic character upgrades.They claim that every room is hand-crafted, and I'm like "well, an AI would have crafted them just the same". If your game only has 1 colour palette and only 1 art style and you move from rectangled square to rectangled square then I don't see the point.So, is the shooting any good? Honestly, it's "okay", but what made HM for instance so enticing was that everything died in 1 hit. In OTXO you have a health bar and can take like 100 bullets, and even the beginner enemies take about 2 to 3 hits. Every time you get hit the screen starts shaking violently, and you're forced to just keep going, instead of analyzing each room you want to tackle... again, like you did in HM.This feels soulless, even the music is just ... mid, but probably the best part.I could be playing more and see where this is going, but why would I? I have better things to do, and all I see is a badly made HL clone. Also, can't bash people's heads in with doors, so that's a big minus...

_childDocuments_.review: Fun for the first few levels but if you die to a boss you have to restart the whole run and you don't even keep any of your buffs, so good luck trying to learn boss fights. You'll spend most of the game quitting and reloading at the bar so you can get the drinks you actually want. The drinks you invest in to unlock, at least my selection so far, seem so useless that they would just pollute the already half useless pool there is, and I have no intention of putting any points into any of them. And you're stuck with them, because you can only have one save.Also locked to 60fps and the monochrome artstyle makes it hard to tell what's going on.
