_childDocuments_.review: is one of those games where I wish that there was a sideways-thumb on Steam reviews.  It's a one-man game by solo developer Nathan Haddock, and within that context I think that something with this much style and weight is a huge triumph.  However, it also can feel at its worst moments like an incest baby of some of the most tired conventions of the contemporary indie scene, and for a lot of gamers, indie games are where we go when we're looking for innovation, not well-executed convention.The elevator pitch for  is easy: it's  an extremely popular indie darling that changed the face of the indie scene, recontextualized as a roguelike, an extremely popular genre that's gained immense cachet in indie spaces because a semirandom content generator can inexpensively add depth and replayability on a shoestring budget.This has necessitated some changes to the  formula.  The roguelike genre requires a player to ford through many randomized levels in a row and survive all of them in sequence (with failure resetting the entire game), where  presents the player with bespoke, episodic levels that must be individually mastered to progress.  Thus,  cannot adhere to 's extremely tight "one hit and you die" game loop, because the consequences of failure are so much larger in a roguelike.  Instead, both the player and enemies have health bars: time-to-kill is extremely low compared to similar roguelikes like , but it does feel  sluggish and spongy to play compared to the blisteringly-minimalist , especially when using 's slow-mo feature.That -esque slow-mo "Focus Mode" is the game's second adaptation to make a " Roguelike" something that's actually feasible.  Because enemy acquisition times are so high and time-to-kill is so low in keeping with 's gameplay style, the player is provided with the option to slow down the game in limited bursts to pick targets and dispatch them efficiently.  Mastering this ability is all-but-necessary to getting to the game's later levels, once enemy movement and projectile travel speed start becoming so fast that the average player can't reasonably dodge within the limits of human perception time.The random, modular levels are interspersed with simple  or -style bosses who roam around a square arena alternating from a moveset of three to five attacks in different telegraphed patterns.  These boss fights are the weakest part of the game: unable to stick to the  convention of exhausting and discarding weapons without also making the boss health pools so anemic as to end the fight prematurely, they grant the player unlimited ammo and are largely resolved by simply circle-strafing and holding down left-click until the player either dies or exhausts the boss' massive health pool.To be frank, if I were recommending  on gameplay alone, this might be a thumbs-down.  I am in disagreement with the other reviews posted here that  feels like a deserving sequel to , because its adaptation to the roguelike formula has required it to diminish all of the gameplay features that made  so slick.  To me, it's a stellar example that adding roguelike replayability can make a game loop more muddled and samey, rather than novel and exciting.Luckily for , however, its presentation is out-of-this-world.If I believe that the gameplay of  is a failed experiment, then the look is anything but.  Beginning as a top-down, pixelated  riff, the game's starkest departure is its red, white, and black color palette, which is striking and surprisingly readable in the moment-to-moment gameplay.  The pounding, thrumming soundtrack easily matches some of 's most iconic tracks -- albeit with a slightly grimier, more bass-heavy approach reminiscent of the  films -- which is extremely impressive given the fact that the game is a one-man show.Where the game really sold itself to me, though, is in the way it renders the destruction you mete out, which is surprisingly systematized for a game aping a pixel aesthetic.  Enemies are actually semi-3D objects with 'paper doll' joints, and their bodies have heft: unlike the canned death animations of , their falling bodies have interactivity with objects like doors windows, and tables, which themselves have physics actors that go splintering and flying off before finding a resting position to merge back into the background.  Blood spray is simulated based on hit direction and caliber, and it's not unusual to send one enemy pirouetting into another to coat them both in gore.  It makes the gameplay subtly messier than , but in a way that I appreciated rather than, say, those health bars that I don't like.  An enemy keeling over with a bullet in his heart might fling his arms outwards, tossing the gun in his hands that you were hoping to pick up wildly askance from his body, forcing you to refactor your plans.I found myself surprisingly nostalgic about the way that the game renders violence: as much as , it feels like a grown up version of the physics-based 'stick death'-adjacent flash games I grew up with on , like  and   The game's general presentation really landed for me, in a way that the game loop didn't. is a passable way to get your money's worth when scaling for playtime-versus-price, although like most roguelikes it's hard to say how much of that is intentional sculpting versus incidental, randomizer-generated synergies that help bump playtime up.  It's got stiff competition within the "indie roguelike" field and I'm sad to say that I don't count  among my favorites.  However, it remains an extremely impressive feat given the limitations of the developer's operation, and I think that the soundtrack is world-class and will likely survive past the game's lifespan of relevancy.A good "Steam Sale" title.

_childDocuments_.review: I believe the comparisons between this game and Hotline Miami are obvious so I'm not going to cover them. Yes it's an incredible spiritual successor to those games, building on a lot of the visceral gameplay and raw pedal to the metal action. I'll try to keep this review brief, so I'll break it down in a list of pros and cons.Pros:- It's Hotline Miami but better. If you go back and try to play those games, they don't hold up very well. There's a lot of glaring flaws and just general gripes that the gaming industry has evolved out of since they came out.- Healthbar, slowmo, and a usable dodgeroll! These are some of the upgrades to the HM formula which definitely help a great deal. Also they're just fun mechanics to use. - Better aiming controls, better enemy AI, doors aren't an issue. This game took a serious look at a lot of the issues in HM and either iterated them away (in the case of the doors, they're just static now and you kick to shatter them open) or improved upon them greatly.- The gun variety is great!- The gun feel is great!- The enemy variety is great! - The presentation overall is incredible, one of my favorite games as far as visual sound design is concerned. Every gun sounds different, the juice is flowing through this game's presentation. - Style meterCons:- Game hard (maybe that's a plus idk). Even with the healthbar, slowmo and dodgeroll, I still find myself dying a great deal. Don't get me wrong, that death comes out of several minutes of some of the most fun gameplay, I just wish I was better so those minutes could last a lot longer. - The soundtrack has only a handful of songs and they get repetitive quickly. The songs which are there are incredible and definitely fit the vibe of the game, but I'd have liked to hear more tracks. - The buffs you can purchase in a run (drinks) for the most part don't do a whole lot. There's some which can dramatically change up a run but those are mixed in with a lot of marginal (or objectively terrible) upgrades. Would have liked to see a tiered/rarity system or perhaps a secondary set of upgrades which were more wild/extreme. - The method to unlock guns is a literal gatcha machine and it feels bad to use. It would have been nicer to have guns unlock via completion of challenges or you could buy them in a similar fashion to the drink import mechanic. - While I think the sprite work and visual design of this game are amazing, it can be difficult to read which guns enemies have at a glance. I've found myself incorrectly assessing an upcoming encounter multiple times because I thought an enemy had a rifle instead of a shotgun. - It's hard to understand what makes the style meter go up. The game tells you in the intro it's speed and varying kills but I watched a speedrun and it's definitely mostly time. I really would have liked for technique and creativity to be more important but it is what it is. I was most disappointed when I pulled off a kill by kicking a gun into an enemy to kill them and my style didn't go up at all.

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoy fast-paced, difficult, intense games, this is a phenomenal choice. The combat mechanics are satisfying, the art direction is beautiful yet readable, the AI is tough to fight (mostly), and the soundtrack is absolutely phenomenal. For a 15$ game, made by one person, this is an absolute steal.While the game's concept is simple (top-down ultra-violence to save your loved one) it holds far more interesting mechanics beneath the surface. Each room in the game is separated by an impassable door, which allows you to space out, flank, or just absolutely annihilate the enemies within. You can see what's inside the room, allowing you to predict potential threats (tough/more dangerous enemies, difficult cover/layouts) before you have to fight your way through. However, as soon as you open the door (via a swift kick or deluge of bullets) there is no way to close it, so if you open too many doors at once you will get swarmed. Large, open areas are your enemy, since as soon as you can see the enemy, they can see you.On a less boring note, you have the drinks system. The bar is a great way to handle power-ups in the game, and the vast majority of the 100+ are useful barring a few exceptions (Knock Knock is the worst). Not every drink is useful for every run, but that results in an interesting "build" system. If you want to focus on using certain weapons, you take the drinks that fit them. SMGs get drinks that give a massive fire-rate increase and the ability to dual wield, shotguns get more pellets and a tighter spread to nuke enemies, LMGs get an infinite magazine and terrifying amounts of dakka, etc.However this is where one of my biggest problems with the game comes up. The drinks system becomes infuriating after your first couple of runs. To flush out certain builds, you need certain drinks. But you get a rotating selection of three different ones. This makes the chance of getting drinks you want incredibly slim. Which would be fine... if you couldn't reset the drinks by quitting and resuming your run. This entirely removes the cost of rotating the drinks, but takes a long time to do. So you spend minutes just cycling through saving and quitting until eventually you get a drink you want to show up in the shop, so you can continue the game. While you could just, not do this, it is an incredibly easy and useful tool in such a difficult game. And honestly, if it was patched out, I think it would make dealing with the game's intense difficulty far more frustrating.Speaking of this difficulty, it is... conflicting. Like many a roguelike, you have incredible highs and miserable lows. Fights you get through by the skin of your teeth, and fights you lose by one point of health. Sometimes you breeze through a run, getting all the drinks you need, annihilating everything in your path with a hail of rounds. But sometimes you're stuck at 2 health, stumbling through fight after fight, camping at doors to wait for enemies to come your way, until eventually the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that launch acid get a lucky shot and rip away the sliver you had left. These deaths are massively infuriating. However, it pisses you off to try again. I don't want to break my desk after a run going to ♥♥♥♥ like that. I quit the game, take a break, and then come back with a renewed zeal to kick ass.And that is the feeling this game gives you. Even when you get destroyed by it, time after time, you feel like an absolute badass. A major part of this is the sound design. All the weapons have a wonderful mechanical click and a glorious boom (or soft tick, for the silenced weapons). At the bar, the drinks thump onto the counter, are downed quickly by our character, and then are smashed against the ground with a sharp tsk. And the music. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ the music. If you are a fan of fast "video game music" (synthwave, mostly), you will absolutely love OTXO's sound track. "Silent Scream", "Haunting Eternal", & "The Cycle Repeats" are some of the standout tracks. Even if you don't end up getting this game, check out the music.While the criticism around this game is mostly valid (the AI can be a bit dumb at times, deaths can feel unfair, and the bar can be a frustration more than anything else), don't let it discourage you from trying out this wonderful work. There are so many things I didn't bring up here, please experience them for yourself. I can't wait to see what Lateralis Heavy Industries makes next!

_childDocuments_.review: Otxo has a very tight viscerally enjoyable core gameplay loop. Your aim is to clear stages or rooms as quickly as possible and move on to the next one. The guns sound absolutely amazing, which helps portray the power behind a lot of these weapons and makes them more impactful. You will see a lot of comparisons between this game and Hotline Miami and rightfully so but Otxo contains a few key changes which drastically change the gameplay. For one, you have more than one HP, which is more forgiving than a one-shot-kill and encourages the player to take more risks. Secondly, the bullet time mechanic helps in dealing with faster and more numerous enemies more easily, which you will have plenty to deal with as the stages progress. As a rouguelike, there are some aspects which this game does a fine job with, like the upgrades and interactions between them and weapon unlocks. Also, after you beat the game once you also unlock optional modifiers which can drastically alter the game. The pitfalls of Otxo are primarily the boss fights, the randomized room layouts and the relatively minimal shallow upgrade system for a roguelike. Now, I'm not saying that the boss fights are easy by any measure but they do get boring once you figure out the attack patterns. There's no way to modify the boss fights specifically either. The randomized room layouts are frustrating because in order to earn money to buy upgrades you need to clear a room as quickly as possible and the layout can sometimes screw you over with its enemy placement. Additionally, some layouts are just unfair as compared to others. Lastly, if you are looking for a roguelike with the a deep and intricate system of ability and weapon upgrades some of which can change the trajectory of a run, Otxo isn't for you. The upgrades are all passivel ones and there is no stacking individual ones. This means that there are no power spikes during the course of a run, more like a linear increase in strength. To summarize, if you are hooked to the core gameplay loop of Otxo just by playing it once, you will definitely have a good time. I didn't even beat the game until I was 20 hours (skill issue I know) in but honestly I didn't care because the gameplay is just so much fun.

The visuals and music are amazing, the gameplay is masterful, the sound design is better than most AAA games, and the amount of love and passion put into this game bleeds through every single decision the developer made in creating this. Almost every single thing in this game is perfect, subject to zero lapses in quality. But the fishing minigame is ridiculously simple. You wait for a fish to bite the line, and when you see a large splash instead of a small one you press E to reel it in. You then take the fish to a campfire and eat it for money. There are several types of fish, but they offer no consistent differences other than aesthetic. They are not named, and there is nothing behind them. There is no agency in anything to do with the fishing besides whether you will fish. You don't choose a pole, a weight, a line, or bait. You cast, and you wait. Any angler would and should scoff at this. It's really just poor game design, dragging down an otherwise thrilling and exceptional experience. If you're in it for thrilling gunplay and action, music that will stick with you after you stop playing, and an ultra-violent quest to kill your inner demons, this is for you. If you're in it for all that and a sick ass fishing minigame, look somewhere else.

_childDocuments_.review: Though I leave a negative review, I am still going to try and beat the game. Partially to not feel like I wasted my money, partially for hotline miami nostalgia, partially out of spite. I believe this game fails on two fronts; trying to being a hotline miami successor that fixes its problems, and on its own merit as a rouge like. On the whole I believe it to be more frustrating or dull than entertaining. As a hotline miami successor, it keeps a lot of the most frustrating problems from the series. Long sight-lines you get sniped from, buggy enemy AI that is inconsistent, getting close to anything is a death sentence because the enemies run literal circles around you. It lacks any interesting characters, and while the mystery of the mansion may be enticing to some I feel like there is no draw to it. The soundtrack is also more barren and monotone. As it's own rougelike game, it is not fun and fails to deliver a satisfying experience. Unlock and upgrades are few and far between, meaning each run is just beating your head against a brick wall unless you get lucky. Most of the fun or effective upgrades are either buggy or are too uncommon to really enjoy. The rest of the time you have random, often ineffective garbage. I managed to unlock one odd upgrade that is accessible outside the mansion... which requires you to take more time in-between runs if you want to actually use the thing you unlocked. The environment and level design are insane. A game designed with a combo meter and levels (and dumb AI) made to break that combo by forcing you to double back. This on top of the huge readability problem the game has by being in monochrome. In a firefight you can't tell that the grey blob you were trying to move past was a decoration, preventing you from getting around a corner and thus getting you killed. Rooms are full of little things to prevent your movement, the lamps on the walls do it for crying out loud. There isn't enough to make each run feel unique. There feels like a total of 5 soundtracks you will listen too over and over, along with fixed boss music. Each room you enter is only one of a handful of set layouts. Combined with slow unlocks and stingy handouts of unique perks, it feels like the same thing over and over. Avoid this game, there's nothing here that hotline miami didn't really have.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR at bottom:FLOWSTATE is how I'd best describe OTXO. Once everything clicks and you're running through at MACH 2, leaving splatters behind you.... it's addicting. After playing Hotline Miami I wished there was either more, or a version with endless replayability. This is a SOLO DEV project and Nate NAILED IT. That's actually an understatement. Much like how Bloodborne took the souls-like 'playstyle' and made it its own, so did OTXO to Hotline Miami.How the perks (liquor) work, genuinely make every run feel different (plus good variety of fun perks, not just +2 DMG). Weapon variety is great. There are different enemies, though for the most part it'll be the different weapons that make them play in a unique manner. It's interesting HOW the enemies/areas get more difficult as you get further. The AI can be SMART too. Getting aggresive, hiding when supressed, scoping out an area where they heard a noise, just to list a few examples.My biggest gripe going into it was the ART STYLE. I've never been able to looks at Greyscale color pallette games longer than 15 min. Yet it works SO GOOD here. Reason why, is because the enemy ragdoll and blood splatter physics while you're trying to break the sound barrier keeping your combo up is SOOOO satisfying. You're 'coloring' the map as you progress.With a color pallete, maybe the rooms wouldn't look like they've changed much? After 12 hours however, I've seen some of the same areas, BUT they aren't boring. I think due in part to the speed you play and good AI. The background looks fantastic, and he did an amazing job at making the action the forefront and having enough variation (ex: windows & special weapon drops such as grenades) that it doesn't feel too same-y. AND THE SOUNDTRACK. This may be the first gaming playlist I add to my personal queue. CERTIFIED BANGERS.I don't think I need to talk about the combat. Extremely satisfying. 'Nuff said.Customization options are great. Can turn up or down screenshake, and even turn off flashes. Thumbs up for that!If ever DLC comes out down the line with more bosses, rooms, enemies, weapons, etc. That's a DAY 1 purchase. If you enjoyed Hotline Miami or Synthetik Legion Rising, 100% pick this up without a doubt. When it clicks, it clicks. Best Indie in a while. Totally worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: An incredible roguelite that takes many features from Hotline Miami but uses and reinterprets them the way that it really feels like different game. It's the same gameplay idea of "hurting other people" while the agressive electronic music plays on the background, but now game sets main focus on shooting and blends in many abilities that can make your every run unique. It's not Hotline Miami 3... and that's good. This game is good in it's own way-----TLDR Line-----So what you should expect from this game?This game takes agressive gameplay from HM, but adds many own things like turning game into roguelike, making noire visual, adding cool OST in dark techno genre (and all OST was maded by developer himself) and setting main focus only on shooting. Many different guns that shoot and act differently, slo-mo ability, really cool movement system that allows you to dodge bullets by doing rolls or jumping over some obsticles, and destuctible props - all of this make shootouts look more like the one you see in Max Payne and F.E.A.R. games or John Woo films. There's no melee weapon here, you can only kick enemies. And I've read some complaints like "Why there is only firearms and no melee weaponry?". And yeah, it also was an issue for me at first. But the more I played, the better I realised that if you add melee weapons to this game, it can break the feel of tense action movie this game makes. And by that I mean the bullet hell that happens really often, when a crowd of enemies run and shoot at you and you have barely second to think what you should do. If enemies had more melee weapon, it maked those bullet hell situations more rare and less dangerous. Since it is a roguelite, your goal is to pass 8 randomly generated zones. Each zone has 5 levels + boss encounter. Every zone has unique enemies and environment. Death here doesn't make you restart the level or zone, you're gonna restart whole game. Luckly you have a health bar, so you woundn't die of one shot.Every run is unique, and this is achieved by procedural generation of levels, random enemy positioning and types of guns they get in this level. More so, before you start your run you can choose what guns you and enemies will be having at this run. Want only pistol fight? Or you want shootout with shotguns? Or maybe you want go full dakka dakka with machineguns only? Or you want a one specific gun run? Choise is yours. During your run you can (if you want) buy drinks at the bar that will give you different abilities which also changes the way you play. Some of them change your movement, some add damage or rate of fire, some add features like "dual wielding pistols" and etc. You can get your first drink for free before you start your run, for the next ones you should pay with money that you get for killing enemies. Amount of money you get depends on your combo meter. The more kills in a row you make, the more money you will get. That's good because game gives the player reason to play more aggressively. Besides booze you can spend your money on ordering new drinks for the bar, or (if you get lucky and find "special encounters") spend them in special gachapon vending machine and open new weapons or collectibles.Update: now developer added 6 gameplay modifiers, so you can make your walkthrough easier or harder. And if you beat this game with modifier, you'll get 1 new drink for bar and 1 new gun. +1 to replayabilityAll of it makes really action concentrated game loop that somehow hooked me up. And even after I've beat this game, I still want to return and try new ways of playing.  So, if everything I've tried to describe here is somehow interesting to you, you can try to play. I am sure that the game will not disappoint youPS:The only issues I have now is that there is not much graphical settings. Like you can't change resolution or turn on/off some visual effects. I feel like some of the effects that game using affect on perfomance really hard, so processing some of ingame stuff slowdowns the game itself. This wouldn't be a problem on medium or powerful machines, but on weak devices, because of this, the originally conceived fast pace of the game may be disrupted.(Also the weird thing is that somehow turning Vsync setting ON fixed framerate drops in some locations. Magic, but it works...) Also I think it would be cool if there was something like a library here that would have stored all notes that you found in Misplaced Chambers. I know that plot here is not much important, but for me it really sets some mood and atmosphere. And since those notes appear in random order, sometimes you don't understand what is happening. So probably you may want to read some notes again.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the most immediately captivating and extraordinarily slick roguelites I've encountered in some time. The premise is simple: kick down door, mow down enemies, rinse and repeat. And really, what more do you need?The core gameplay feel is much like Hotline Miami: equal parts tactical planning and twitchy clutch maneuver, plus the occasional spray-and-pray. A time-slowing mechanic present in the game makes pulling off those hairpin strategies a bit easier, but you can pretty much ignore it if you'd rather rely solely on your guns to do the talking. And, speaking of guns, they all feel absolutely FANTASTIC, which great haptic feedback from vibration (I've been playing with a controller). Also notable is that they SOUND incredibly satisfying (no puny Enter the Gungeon pea shooters here), with meaty sound design to enhance the sense of power. This is all backed up by a pulse-pounding soundtrack. Seriously, the music is sick -- you'll get absolutely amped as the beat pulses beneath the hail of gunfire and occasional explosion.Of course, the roguelite structure means some key changes from the Hotline Miami base. For one, you don't die in a single hit; you have a much more forgiving health bar that refills after clearing each room (more akin to a floor), and you can boost your health and get some sustain through items as well. It's a necessary change to support the run-based (rather than mission-based) formula. And, of course, there are those aforementioned items (called liquors in-game): you start each run with a free item from a randomized choice of three, and every two or so rooms, you'll encounter the shop, where you can buy pretty much as many as you can afford. Needless to say, you can rack up quite a handful of items relatively quickly, and fast, stylish gameplay rewards you with more money via a combo multiplier. It's worth noting that the items themselves are well-designed, too: exploding corpses, reflecting bullets, health leeching attacks, get-out-of-death-free iframes, and more good stuff like that. Roguelite fans who love to accrue a ton of cool passive upgrades (myself included) will be very happy with this dynamic, and, to sweeten the pot, there are plenty of unlockable liquors as well.In short: you simply must check out this game. Even in my short playtime, I can tell this is something special. Blazing-fast pacing, incredible gunplay, stellar sound design, and meaningful progression make this an incredibly easy game to recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: I REALLY want to write this game a positive review, but I just don't feel like I can in its current state.  Soundfall's main gameplay loop is a lot of fun and I had a blast in the first world, but unfortunately it was mostly downhill from there.  -Soundtrack is generally great and I would say most of the music tracks feel right at home.-Combat mechanics are simple, fun, and satisfying.-Boss fights are very cool.-Environments, characters, and effects look great.  Game runs smoothly.-Weapons and their effects are varied and feel fantastic to wield.-While most tracks feel at home, some genres and songs just do not work in this game at all.  The volcano area (Bolero Hotlands) featured several songs that had me pulling my hair out because the beat was extremely difficult to discern.  Some songs even changed beat in the middle of the song!  Looking at the Steam stats almost 1/3 of players that cleared the previous world did not make it through the Hotlands and I can completely understand why.-Remember those cool boss fights I mentioned?  Yeah, I think there were 2 of them in the whole game.  11 worlds with around 150+ levels (including optional tracks) and only 2 levels feature boss fights.  -New enemies stop appearing after the first worlds and only slight variants of them show up from then on, making most of the game feel like a samey slog.  10 levels also feels like too many for a single area.  They didn't do enough different in the later worlds to justify their existence with only minor environmental effects differentiating gameplay.  I think you should have a choice between 2 areas for where to go next and you can progress the game via either path.  That nearly halves the length of a bloated campaign and you could always choose to go back to the other path and play it later if you like.-Having the metronome at the bottom of the UI is awkward.  I cannot find any option to move it but I'd like it to be in the middle of the screen like I've seen other rhythm games do (the upcoming Metal Hellsinger is a great example).  This problem is exacerbated by the fact that many songs do not properly loop and some of them have a strange amount of silence/dead air at the beginning or end.-Levels are mostly different enough, but certain sections are repeated weirdly often.  You'll stop and say "wait, have I played this level already?" more than a few times during the 10ish hour campaign.  Not a big deal but it is noticeable.-The game sometimes tries to increase the difficulty level despite your character not being an appropriate level for it.  It will automatically increase difficulty and say "recommended level 30" when you're sitting at level 24 because you've been playing most of the game 1 difficulty level lower.  At one point I thought I was stuck because I couldn't beat the next song which recommended a much higher level than I was and I couldn't equip several of my better items because they also required a higher level.  I hated the song and couldn't figure out the beat so that was not ideal either.  I finally realized that instead of grinding previous songs for experience (why would I want to play the same songs repeatedly during a campaign?) I could instead simply turn down the difficulty and continue.  I overlooked this option for a long time because I didn't even realize the difficulty was not-so-gradually increasing with each new world.-Inventory management is tedious and is not sufficiently explained.  I didn't realize I had to break down ♥♥♥♥♥♥ loot as I obtained it and I was extremely disappointed to see my first purple chest armor didn't make it to my inventory because it was apparently full.  Inventory is shared across all characters but 2 of the 5 equipment slots are character-specific which makes it awkward to decide what items to break down if you've neglected to play other characters that use those items.-Luckily you can skip the dialogue but HOLY COW they went overboard on it.  The characters have a new conversion between every level and after a few worlds I was pretty fed up with it.  I appreciated the first few music puns but they well overstayed their welcome.-Reward system is abysmal.  This is my single biggest issue with Soundfall and this section will not be short.  There are the standard RPG/MMO rarity levels on gear of white (common - worst), green (somewhat common), blue (rare), purple (epic), and orange (legendary - best). The problem is in the way you earn these items.  In each stage you are given better chances for high-level gear (blue/purple/orange) if, and ONLY if, you essentially play PERFECTLY.   The first tier/luck increase is reached if you finish a song before it loops.  This makes absolutely no sense since the game also encourages you to explore and find hidden chests, but if you do so you risk not finishing the song in time and being eligible for decent rewards.  You might be eligible for the next reward tier if you either hit 100% of your actions on beat OR had no combo breaks, which I think just means you don't get hit a single time.  The final tier is reached if you do BOTH of those things (100% of actions on beat and don't break any combo).  This is extremely difficult and if you play at an appropriate difficulty for your skill level you will probably never see this happen.  If you hit 99% of your actions on beat and get hit a single time in a level for example, you are only eligible for the bottom reward tier. 100% of actions on beat and no combo breaks also mean nothing if you fail to finish a level before the song loops.  I can understand providing a bonus for perfection, but expecting the player to be perfect to receive anything above green items is insane.That means you are being "rewarded" with green items a large majority of the time - I usually received green items as a reward even if I reached the second reward tier, so as far as I can tell the system is either completely broken or incredibly stingy.  If you want decent loot you have to MASTER whatever song you're playing and there are a LOT of them.  It doesn't feel good to complete a really tough song on a high difficulty only to be greeted with garbage loot at the end. The small amount of purple loot I received came from random chests I found off the beaten path.  I didn't feel as though I had earned it at all but the game doesn't reward anything but perfection at the end of each stage so I took what I could get.  You can also obtain specific loot for characters you're not playing, so it feels bad if you finally get a great drop that you can't even equip on your current character.  There is a rock/paper/scissors style damage bonus depending on the type of enemies you are fighting and the weapons/armor you have equipped, but honestly I was just taking whatever loot I could get - you can't even take advantage of that system without a ton of grinding or luck.  The shop only contains a few items at a time and even at the point of completion the shop is still selling white and green items which is kind of silly at this point.  I don't think I've ever spent a single gold that I collected during the entirety of the campaign.Overall Soundfall is an interesting game that I will likely come back to from time to time, but I simply cannot give it a positive review.  I can tell the developers cared about this title a lot and its main gameplay loop is exactly what I was looking for, so hopefully they can take these problems and address some of the bigger ones that are preventing me from grinding the game like I was hoping to.  Only 2.3% of Soundfall owners have even finished the main story as of right now and these are many of the reasons why.  I can only recommend it on a massive sale or if you are primarily playing co-op.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Its fun for a few hours before it becomes mind numbingly dull. A mismash of fantastic ideas that are glued together with poor execution. Also the demon chick is hot.Pros:-The music is great. Issues you may have with following the beat can largely be attenuated with the metronome option.-The art is great, if a little inconsistent in style.-The levels look incredible. Parts of the level geometry dance in time to the music which is very nice.-The melee combat feels good and weighty.Cons:-While Soundfall wants to be a music game, it falls into the common trap of not actually being about rhythm. You just tap out quarter notes at whatever bpm the song asks for. The game proceeds to then punish you for doing so by placing enemy shots or obstacles that don't line up with the beat. The game's main scoring system hardly even cares about your rhythm, your only indicator being a percentage accuracy at the end of each level which does not at all reflect on your score. This leads to the guns you can hold down for a measure being incredibly powerful as they allow you to ignore the rhythm system the most. It doesn't help that these guns have the best dps either.-While Soundfall wants to be a loot based dungeon crawler, it has the stingiest ranking system I've ever seen. If you finish the level after the song ends, you are locked into the absolute worst loot tier. This is practically guaranteed to happen if you play on the harder difficulties while slightly undergeared which turns enemies into obnoxious bullet sponges or you dare to explore the maps for hidden treasure. The actually good loot is locked either behind grinding and rng with the shop or playing the levels perfectly. If you play without getting hit or without failing a single beat (!) you get a gold rank and finishing with both of these conditions nets you a platinum. Yes, anything worse than perfection is nearly worthless. The map design also suffers from element reuse. It feels like they had a list of songs they wanted to use and not enough time to build levels around them. This along with the dull rhythm gameplay makes the later levels drag like mad.-While Soundfall wants to be a class based coop game, only some of the classes are even slightly viable. The game is simultaneously incredibly easy and incredibly difficult. On most difficulties, you are barely punished for playing like an idiot. Tanking shots matters little as enemies drop insane amounts of healing and playing off the beat just makes the gaem take longer. As mentioned previously however, playing even slightly off from perfect is worth just as much reward as playing awfully. This ties into the characters as 3 of the 5 cast encourage you to play in melee range and stay still and vulnerable for extended periods of time, almost guaranteeing you to get hit. While you can clear the game perfectly fine with these characters, good luck trying to get good scores.Ideas on what could be done:-The rhythm part: I'd add a proper rhythm game ranking system that scores you on a scale based on your performance that hopefully combines how on beat you are as well as how many hits you take. This itself I feel would go a huge way on improving how the game feels instead of the current system where it feels like I just slog through levels silver rank after silver rank with 99% accuracy and the lowest rarity loot to show for it.-The looter shooter part: Could you balance the guns better? The extreme imbalance in guns, effects, characters, etc is made so much worse by the snails pace you obtain loot at. Especially when you can go several levels in a row finding gear that only fits other characters. More loot spewing out of chests please.

_childDocuments_.review: It really breaks my heart to give this game a thumbs down. It's got a great style and a lot of really cool ideas that I would love to see become more common. But there are just a few design decisions the developers made that really ruin the experience for me, and frankly I find them sorta baffling. The biggest one is music choice - some of these songs are just *not* good choices for a rhythm game. Many of them will have quiet periods where the beat is pretty much indistinguishable, or they'll have vocals that drown out the bass to the point where you really don't have a good sense of when to shoot. And coupled with this is the even weirder decision to make many weapons fire multiple rounds or make sound effects that don't match with the beat. It's *infuriating* - it feels like Rhythm Game 101 that your attacks should make a single identifiable sound that acts as a way of reinforcing the beat. But here, it's the opposite, with gun sounds clashing directly with the music in a way that makes it extremely easy to get thrown off. I honestly found myself skipping all but the sniper weapon because it was the only one that didn't do this. Absolutely bizarre choice that actively makes the game much, much worse for no noticeable benefit.It's really frustrating, because as I said there's a lot to like about this game. But right now, it's close to unplayable for me in a lot of spots because of the odd music choices and extremely frustrating weapon design. I'm no expert in these sorts of games, but I could comfortably progress in Crypt of the Necrodancer, Thumper, etc - here, I just feel like I'm constantly being thrown off by my own act of firing, which sucks. Maybe I'm the only one with this problem, but for me it was a dealbreaker, unfortunately.

_childDocuments_.review: An insanely frustrating experience where there are so, so many fun and creative ideas on display but the execution is so poorly executed that I can't justify purchasing this game unless you get it as a gift or at a REALLY steep discount.The game operates on a rhythm based system with copy and pasted assets for each level throughout each world and at most like what, ten enemies? If even that?? There are multiple characters that can be selected as you progress through the story of Soundfall but the vast majority of them aren't worth it if you're trying to get higher ranks on levels.Speaking of that, the largest disgrace the game pulls is its ranking system. For a game with such a light-hearted tone and is encouraged to be played by both casual gamers and rhythm vets, it seems baffling to me that the game's ranking system is as strict as it is for every player involved. Miss one beat on the rhythm? Oops that platinum ranking just went to gold. Get hit a single time by an enemy that ignores the rhythm of the level and you can't dodge to avoid in time because you'll get deducted because you're not dodging on the beat? Oops now you're at a silver medal. The reason I bring up why specific characters aren't worth it is many of them have alternate abilities/melee abilities that put them in place. There's no damage absorption, there's no mechanic that lets them shrug off a hit. You get hit? Oops! Ranking down. It literally discourages you from playing a majority of the characters because if you're just gonna get punished for getting hit, then why consider options that are risky, especially when the ranged weaponry is safer and does comparable damage?It's made even worse when if you don't complete a level within the first loop of a song, it'll immediately lock you to the lowest rating possible. Worse still is that the developers made no attempt to try and seamlessly loop the song within itself and each track will fade out, then back in. How do you make a rhythm game with a continuous track where the song cuts out awkwardly for a few seconds, you couldn't edit the audio or was it out of laziness?? There's even a few songs that completely shift BPM without warning so were you doing well and then suddenly you've lost the beat because oops tempo shift? Ranking down!Rankings ARE important as well as they determine just how decent the loot you get is. If you're actually trying to get decent gear to have some fun and smash through the limited bestiary of enemies, you HAVE to get platinum. Even gold loot feels weak in comparison to playing the level at an AI level of play. Perfect play should reward you with better loot sure, but it shouldn't be the be all end all of getting anything worthwhile. Music always contains some degree of human error and not factoring that in to your ranking system is not only bad design, it's outright disincentivizes the player to continue playing through a song if they make even a single mistake.Imagine if you played a game like Guitar Hero, right? A game that goes off of a 5-star ranking system. Now imagine if when you missed a SINGLE note, it immediately locks you to a 3 star rating. Imagine if you played a game like Hi-Fi RUSH and you were locked immediately to a D rank for a battle if you got hit a single time by an enemy. Nobody would want to play that.

_childDocuments_.review: So I just beat the game.  The gameplay is great!  Each character has a unique feel and when you're dashing through bullets, cleaving through enemies, all while keeping to the beat - it's honestly top tier.So what's the hold-up?  Repetition.  Out of 142 missions in the entire game, 130 of them are the same type: run through the stage, clear the enemies in a room, and go.  While you can explore to get more items from chests, it's oddly discouraged by the game's medal system (in which you get a higher rank by clearing the stage faster).  Traps in each area are mostly unique, which is good, but the enemies don't change.  Even if this game had an endless mode, you'd endlessly be doing the same exact thing.  Frankly, mission types and enemy design needed more time in the oven to cook before they made the rest of the game.The bosses are really fun, with a catch - there's only two of them.  In that sea of 142 missions, only 2 of them are boss fights.  Each area ends with an enemy arena (which I'm generously counting as a separate mission type), taking up the 10 other missions in the game.  Had they took the time to make a boss fight for each area, each step of the way would've been more memorable.The art and set design for each area/characters is great.  The game looks nice and I never had any performance issues or glitches on my end.  In the sandy areas, there's a major issue with the bullets and enemy attack indicators being hard to see, but visually that's the only issue I had.  I think playing with the metronome on constantly is mandatory since some songs will be calibrated slightly off beat in specific sections, or have quiet moments where it's hard to follow the song.Enemy choice (not counting the traps) remain the same within each area.  They do get augmented with different elemental buffs depending on area, but they're all on-hit effects.  It's barely effects the gameplay since regardless of if an enemy was an elemental or not, they felt like they did the same amount of damage on hit.  The bosses also never seem to utilize elements.  The game's story is serviceable, but far from gripping.  It's very Saturday morning cartoon-esque, with the characters being written in that style.  Some of the music jokes were fine, and maybe one or two moments were nice, but otherwise I wouldn't look forward to the story in the game.I really wanted to like this game, and if it gets any updates addressing these issues (which it probably won't, since most of these are core design issues), then I'll change my review.  I hate giving negative reviews because I know what it does to the steam algorithm and this is a small indie team - but I can't give a positive review either.A lot of effort clearly went into it, but it feels unfinished.  The team should think about making a smaller game with a larger emphasis on varying the gameplay through mission types, enemies, and bosses.  If the game had five worlds with banger content rather than ten worlds with mostly recycled content, I think people would've been more receptive to the game.  If you play the demo, you've played 95% of the game.  It was almost really good, and I hope Drastic Games takes the feedback they get and knock it out of the park next time.

_childDocuments_.review: Let's start with the positives since there's plenty to love about this game in the first few hours.Soundfall breathes originality and charm, from its colorful designs to its attempt at a concept I haven't seen utilized much.On paper, this game should have me personally hooked for hours on end. I've played rhythm games all my childhood, was capable of playing every instrument on Expert on Rock Band especially. I'm a composer/producer and obviously a lover of music. I even listen to a lot of different genres varying from EDM, Jazz, Indie, RnB, Hip Hop, Classical and so many more. All of which, this game actually has!But this is where I have to go through an extensive list of things that makes me wish I could get refunded.Alright here we go.Remember when I said that this game had a huge variety of genres? This wasn't a lie. There is however a really big issue that arises where that variety is sectioned by zones. So, you have the volcano zone where it's JUST metal and power metal. There is nothing else and if you're like me and you don't really  for that, then you spend a while playing songs you just do not have any interest in.There is a solution and I am going to segue into a topic that is heavily linked! Yes, you read that right and I'm not even going to mince my words: If you genuinely just want to go through a song because of an issue you have with it, muting it actually gives you a clear advantage. This goes for songs you might even enjoy!You see, Soundfall is at its core, such a basic game that the music matters way less than its name implies.Before I continue, here's how the game works:Music is composed on a BPM (Beats per minute), it's the tempo and a fundamental aspect of music if you want it to be coherent to begin with. Tempo is the foundation on which we can inherently calculate where notes are but luckily, we all have an internal clock which allows us to  the rhythm so that we don't have to count continuously while playing or listening. This is important to this game because the entire gameplay is related to it.In most rhythm games like Guitar Hero or OSU, you're playing a map. The map represents dots on the screen which you have to click/press/play in time with the music. What makes these games a lot of fun is that you're following  rather than simply following the bpm. When the guitar plays a note, there's a visual representation of that note on the screen and it comes to you so that you can react to it and press the correct button, with the goal of being accurate in your timing.This is where Soundfall becomes a chore. All songs play the exact same way, just at different speeds.Okay but what about the rest of the gameplay right? This wouldn't be fair for me to simply stop there so I have to talk about the enemies you have to fight. There are roughly 10 enemy types off the top of my head. That's it. That's the game.You don't get progressively more enemies past the third or fourth zone. I just finished the 6th zone (only 2.8% of people actually bothered doing it too which is impressively low) and I have yet to find new enemies. This is even worse when you consider that the last level in a zone isn't a boss. You just fight the same stuff you've been fighting for hours, just... a lot more of them. You get to fight a single boss after finishing the 5th zone and I imagine a second when you finish the 10th zone. That's about it.Weapons are even worse. To boot, the drop rate for quality is absurdly low. You'll only get uncommon and sometimes rare but epic and legendary is rare as hell. This would be fine if the legendary you get at item level, let's say 35 wasn't outclasses by an uncommon weapon of item level 43.There are a few different "types" of guns but they all play relatively the same way. There's some prefixes and suffixes that changes some attributes. Like lightning makes it so your attacks create a chain of lightning which hurts other mobs, you have fire that burns for 4 beats, blue slows enemies down, purple applies a sticky bomb, green heals you, you get the gist of it.My favorite aspects to complain about is the affixes "Rhythmic" and "Arrhythmic" because they are so funny to me. A blaster with the rhythmic attribute makes your bullets hurt 25% more if they're  while arrhythmic makes it so you're penalized 25% less for shooting . Which... okay.In my honest opinion, since you're shoving the max possible difficulty IN MY FACE constantly despite me wanting to play on moderate because your loot system is absolutely dreadful, it feels to me like you wanted to make a difficult game where the goal is to play perfectly, I respect that. After all, this is the core philosophy of every rhythm game ever made; You press the button ON THE BEAT. So then why would you design things in this game to either reward slightly for being accurate and having half the guns be less punishing instead? It's frustrating when you don't bother checking past the affix to know if the gun is even worth looking at.Then there's just generally speaking the bugs I've encountered where the metronome was off by almost a half beat on some songs from time to time or when the system itself is entirely off and even the metronome can't help you. It's so weird that you would use your automated system to map your songs instead of just setting up the bpm manually. You even have a guide on how to do it if we want to import our own songs which I haven't even bothered with because the game doesn't even really care about the song that's playing, it's all about the tempo.I can tell you've poured a lot of love and sweat into making this game. I really wish I could enjoy it but I simply can't bring myself to play more than 2 songs a day now. This review isn't to dunk on you or make you feel bad but simply frustration at a 30$ I won't get back.Fix the internal metronome bugs on some of the songs where the issue is present. This is the least you can do if you don't wish to make the game more tailored to the character, you're playing i.e.: the drummer playing drum notes. (This was something I wanted to experience, especially Drum & Bass patterns where your weapon is the kick and your melee is the snare!)The difficulty option needs to stop defaulting to the max. Make it so if I picked moderate on a song, the next one will also be set to moderate difficulty.For gods’ sake ADD THE OPTION TO RETRY WHEN PAUSING. This is rhythm game 101.This one is high effort but you really need more variety. Explore more options with what guns and their bullets can do. Hell, even the melee weapons which are pretty fun generally, need it.Especially add more types of enemies. I'm sorry but this is just not enough.I wanted to love this game and I'm sad I didn't. I respect the people who worked on this and again, this review is not written as a hate letter. I simply lost 30$ and I think it's appropriate I explain why I'm unhappy with this. I've paid for games in the past that I've played for too long and couldn't refund anymore but in most cases, it feels like it's mostly my fault for not paying attention. I promise it wasn't the case here, I even hyped the game up to friends and on twitter. I just kept playing because I was convinced that there had to be  I had yet to reach. In any case, good luck with your game!

_childDocuments_.review: This recommendation comes with some massive quotation marks. The game is okay, but is mired with a number of problems and a few fundamental design flaws. The gunplay is fine, but overly punishing. You really feel like you have to stick to the beat if you wanna do anything and I think the game holds that rule a little too tight. The guns are also not explained at all, and you have to depend on loading screen hints to know you can hold the button down on some weapons. Speaking of explanations, there is little to no tutorials about the guns, traps, difficulty selection or what the difficulty means, and at times even character abilities are poorly explained. Can the bow pierce natively? I don't know, I only think it can because of an achievement but I've never figured out if it was true or not. Speaking of, I feel like there's some fundamental flaws that really hold the game back, and one of them is, in fact, the idea of giving a bow as a special weapon to one character when your guns are much more effective and customizable than the bow. But that is a small one compared to the leveling system. Yes, you do gain experience by beating levels (and the game doesn't tell you outside loading screen hints on what this means either). More levels means more damage and better loot. Which means the game becomes very easy very quickly unless you switch difficulty, which the game barely tells you when you unlock them and then barely tells you what those mean either. Why is this all a problem? Because it's a rythm game. And a co-op shooter. And these RPG elements feel unnecessary, especially when, at high levels, the difference between the lowest difficulty and the second lowest is just the number of enemies. You still defeat most things in one beat.In the end the most damning problem this game has is that Hi-Fi Rush exists, and does what this game does a lot better. If you like rythm games, definitely give Soundfall a try! Just know that it's not the best in the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Overall, it's a solid premise with just a few too many frustrating bits for me to recommend it, but I'm glad I tried it.This is really hard to make a call on one way or the other. If I had to break it all down I'd say 40% fun, 20% meh, 20% frustrating and boring songs, and 20% the best flow I've ever been in in a game. My issues mostly arise from the song choice and the reward system. So many songs along the main story path are dull and difficult to find the rhythm in, making the whole premise of the game difficult to interact with. The reward structure is based around finishing he level quickly and never missing a single note, which means never getting hit, which means that close range, aggressive and melee playstyles are inherently punished over longer range and more reactive ones. And timing makes exploration way more risk than reward since the loot is... okay?A lot a low bpm songs feel like you're at the mercy of your rng loot's damage per beat to even have a chance to finish on time. High bpm levels are so short I always finish with half the song remaining which is a massive letdown since those were by far the most fun levels for me.The whole last two areas just kinda drag their butt across the finish line since all the fun was in the earlier areas. And the cherry on top was that I can't finish the last level since the game keeps crashing behind the loading screen. It's a game that feels five steps from greatness but its walking in the wrong direction.An option to have queued actions that come out on the beat would likely go a long way in helping the game's ease of use and wider accessibility as well.

_childDocuments_.review: Soundfall is a rhythm looter-shooter where you are rewarded for slaying enemies while on beat. It combines a fair few different game mechanics to varying levels of success and is fun to play, and while the sound track is good the stage design is heavily reused and gameplay can become very repetitive. I’d recommend it (especially if you can get it on sale), though more for casual play.The world of Symphonia, a place where music is born before it enters the universe is under siege from the forces of discord. 5 guardians of harmony are summoned to help restore the beat. The story is very family friendly, and does a good job of showing character growth across all the guardians by the games end. It’s a fairly wholesome message and usually presented in a humorous manner. Loving puns, I have to applaud the writers. There is a lot of music puns, more than should legally be allowed, and I thought a lot of them were quite clever and caused a few chuckles.Gameplay is nuanced, but also fairly repetitive which is where I think a lot of the criticisms will be levelled. There’s a lot of different systems at play, many of which aren’t really explored in the lower difficulties and should at least had a showing, and at higher difficulties require careful equipment planning to have a chance of making it through a stage within the time limit.At a basic level, all your actions (from shooting, melee, and evading) are meant to be timed to the beat of the song. For someone like me who couldn’t work out the beat if it slapped them in the face, there are plenty of visual cues, along with a bar at the bottom and an audio option as well if required. If you are on beat, your attacks are stronger, have visual effects, apply weapon effects to enemies (like setting them on fire, arcing electricity to other enemies ect), generate ultimate power notes and increase your chain limit and resets the counter which increases your score. Getting hit resets the chain, and missing the beat enough times will cause the chain counter to reset and stops you from attacking while the weapon resets. Timing your attacks is important, as you are vulnerable even when using ultimate attacks, only dashing on beat gives invulnerability. One criticism would be most of the songs don’t change their beat, its steady throughout the entire song (which is its own blessing and curse), though there are a few songs where it varies in places. The game doesn’t support being streamed very well, playing it via a steam link was enough to throw out the beat timer making it impossible to stay on time.When you finish a stage your score becomes your XP, and the loot reward is based on if you stayed on beat 100%, dropped the beat at all, finished in time, or died with the reward system being tiered- if you die you will get the lowest marking, not dying and finishing in time gets you a silver rating ect. The loot rewards are also locked behind character levels and what difficulty you ae playing on, the system won’t really reward you correctly on the lower settings (you can get a perfect score and still get basic loot), though this improved slightly for the few stages at a higher difficulty I didn’t completely suck at. The guns come in a good variety, and can have different stats like shortened range but spreading bullets or being able to be repeated by holding the button down. The real differences come from the weapons effects, which have a rock, scissors, paper relationship against each other. This isn’t explored in the easiest difficulty (other than being bonus effects vs every enemy), but becomes progressively more important the harder the difficulty. With 5 different “elements” to manage having the right weapon and effects applied makes all the difference at higher. This includes the armour you equipped as well, as you could give yourself a 35% increase in damage received. The melee attacks and ultimates are unique to each hero, and but still run off the above principle in addition to their own unique effects. Additional treasures can be found during each stage if you explore or are randomly dropped from enemies, as well as being awarded at the end of each map. The game doesn’t mention that all treasures share a inventory pool of 150 and being awarded them after this is full rejects them, though does advise to sell them for gold which you can use to purchase weapons & equipment. All loot is randomised (think how diablo 3 was initially on launch), though the stage will generally influence the effects (metal songs will generally favour fire based loot and enemies).The game is broken up into different maps, each which focuses on a type of music (could be string, bass, drums, chiptune, ect), which in effect influences which type of enemy are found, as well as the effects of the loot. Each biome generally has set of environmental hazards as well to dodge, though most of the stages seem very repetitive, and usually consist of 3-4 solid areas of waves of enemies, a few side areas where they might be more traps or a treasure, and a final area where there are waves of enemies. Each map has a final stage, but this is usually only more waves of enemies. There are a few exceptions to this where you fight an actual boss, and I wish there was more of these spread throughout the game to break up the constant waves of enemies.While the stages gameplay might be repetitive, they are well drawn and animated. Everything (trees, houses, pots, coffins) bops along to the music, and the things that don’t are the only objects that can’t be destroyed. There are plenty of affects you can applies to enemies, and attacks look flashy when on beat. Enemies attacks are telegraphed, so you can didge if you see them. The menu and UI layout is good and simple to follow, though character screens are squished in co-op. There are enough short animated scenes throughout the game, and these are really well done.The music is what this game is all about. The in game soundtrack is great and has a mix of everything, and the tracks suit the stages they are picked for. You can free play the music anytime you want (there are additional tracks in there that aren’t from the game), and this is where you can also import your own songs. The few I attempted all went to the same game biome No DLC, and I’m disappointed I can’t play the music in the steam music player. Seems like a missed opportunity.The game is more fun co-op, though you are all stuck on the same screen and need to work together. It does become a competition on who gets the best score, and would be the recommended way to lvl up characters quickly via local co-op as the XP rewards are joined for everyone.100% Achievements- OMG no. Platinum’s on every stage on the hardest difficulty, as well as killing 100,000 enemies. That’s some serious grinding.Note: I backed Soundfall on the Fig campaign.For more reviews please visit

_childDocuments_.review: I like this game a lot. I've seen a lot of negative reviews saying the gameplay is repetitive to a fault- there's some truth to that. In terms of pure gameplay, once you've played a couple levels you'll get the gist of it. There's new enemy types and variations later on, and there's new obstacles/environmental hazards, but the gameplay is pretty much the same. There's also truth to the complaints that the loot feels a bit too generic/random. I have a hard time sometimes telling items apart from each other and just go with the bigger number.That sounds pretty negative, so why a positive review? Well, frankly, the music. In a game like this, the music is everything, and the music in this game is fantastic. It's absolutely astounding the number of tracks they have in this game, and while not all of them are my cup of tea, they're all high quality and a very large number of them are great. Playing this game is listening to music with some gameplay layered on top.The story is simplistic but fun, and the art is also really good. But frankly, if you like good music and pressing keys in time to good music, you'll like this game. If you're looking for deep gameplay and the music aspect is secondary, you probably won't find enough here. For me, just jamming out to the tracks while shooting monsters is plenty fun enough.I just beat Requiem Depths (area 7) and I see only 5.6% of players have the achievement for doing so. That's a shame if only because people are missing out on some great tracks.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll update this review once importing issues are fixed. The engine they use is awful at detecting bpm and that leads to a lot of mis-inputs when solely following the music and frustration when following the metronome. I understand that allowing us to set BPM/Zone for a song would take away some of the magic but it really should at least be an option.The worst part is that its frustratingly close to working, but the game decides the bpm is 151 instead of 150, you are going to drift *hard*. Or putting an EDM 180bpm song as a Rock 119.Yes, I understand that there is a custom way to set beatmaps, but it requires third-party software and modification of your sound files, which is already a pain at even small library sizes. This *really* needs to be handled in-game.The base game is fine, actually. The curated songs all play well and the gameplay loop is engaging enough to continue, and I do want the game to succeed.

_childDocuments_.review: Soundfall seems like a game that has a lot of good ideas but never really work due to how procedurally generated the game is. So let's go it one by one.1. Lots of song variety Rock, Classical, Arabic, almost everything you can think off. The problem is, they are not designed for rhythm game, why? Because their rhythm volume is so small. Rock and Arabic are the biggest offender, requiring me and my mate to pay attention on visual metronome instead of following the beat. They never told the composer they are making a rhythm game, they just like to put songs they think are cool.2. Custom Import SongInfinite replayability is there, though their bpm software sucks. I just put in a very slow classical song and the beat for that song was too fast that you can't actually enjoy the game. This extend to the main campaign song, where the beat just doesn't match with the song it is playing. More tweak should be done on the software.3. Looter Shooter AspectThis issue will be apparent especially if you go in with higher diff, weapon drops started to scale down. Currently around lvl 27ish (max 50) and all the weapons I got from the drops are the same level, but is very weak compared to the one you buy from shop. But you can't buy from the shop all the time because the drop in this game is very stingy and weapon sold can barely feed a family with one children. This also means that weapon elemental are sold randomly, meaning you may not get the element you want.Even then the store ♥♥♥♥♥ up and sell item even lower than the one you currently have! 4. HitboxesThe hitboxes in this game is probably the wonkiest aspect. Enemies have too big attack hitbox, with certain enemies still damaging you even if you are behind them. The traps hitboxes are also too big, especially levels like the desert where there is a laser eyes that just circle too fast.I can go on more, but damn does this game quality goes down as you play. The music become this generic "theme" music. The only good music are pop, edm, or chiptune because why? THEY ARE BUILT FOR RHYTHM GAME!

_childDocuments_.review: I would really like to give a positive review on this game but it's not ready for it, yet. I'll explain my point of view.The concept of the rhythm based battle is good and very fun. It kinda reminds me of crypt of the necrodancer but it has more freedom in it, which is not better or worse, just different. I also like how doing things on beat gives great advantages and, even though it's not mandatory in theory, it progressively is the more you advance in the game.Being a rhythm game, it's normal and expected that you have to stay on beat to reap all the advantages, extra exp and loot the game has to offer. The big problem starts when there are songs (from the third to fifth world) that are very hard to follow and not for the right reasons. Some will stay silent for some seconds, others have solos that don't give the smallest hint of the rhythm, and some other will just change their pace and rhythm without any kind of warning, which makes them impossible to perfect the first time and very hard to follow if you decide to replay them. I shouldn't be relying on memory in a rhythm based game like this and I find very annoying that I have to turn on the metronome for such levels.Smaller details that aren't enough on their own but add up to show how this game has a good concept but it's still very unpolished (and not worth the price):Gameplay issues-Weapon variety: 5 weapon types, the rest of the game is just finding higher level versions.-Map variety: when you've done 3 stages of a world, you'll just find the same maps used over and over until you go to the next one.-Enemy variety: if you've started the third world, you've probably already seen all the enemies and what you'll meet later are just a bigger quantity and maybe an elemental variation in higher difficulties.-Heroes are not balanced between them and their only unique trait is their extra personal weapon. Same stats, no passive perks.Secondary issues-With no voice but the same pose and even expression whatever reaction the character has, the conversations and game lore fail to engage me.-Apart from being "boring", dialogues are annoying as hell, as they pop up every time you start or finish a level already completed. They can be skipped, but it's still annoying to having to do that every single time.-With the same logic as the repeating dialogues, If you replay and finish the last level of a world, you'll automatically go back to the world select because it expects you to go on; some of us just want to grind or perfect the levels before advancing, though.-No restart button in the level menu. You have to quit and select the level, skip the dialogues and load the stage all over again.-I've read bad experiences about multiplayer but I can't say anything about those; haven't tried at all.I'm ready to change my mind if some of the things are fixed/changed/added. Right now this games gives me raw, unpolished vibes and it's DEFINITELY NOT worth its price.

_childDocuments_.review: I feel like we need to stop falling for the trick of "import your own music into our rhythm game" kind of games. While it is a tempting proposal, it should ultimately serve as a red flag to warn that the game will be generic and repetitive. Indeed, how could one make a theoretically infinite amount of levels without resorting to some kind of template system. This game is no exception. Even when you are playing the levels within the campaign, nothing feels intentionally designed. I kept seeing the same couple of area formats for each world over and over. The enemy variety is quickly exhausted, leaving you internally begging by the halfway mark to see something new, which of course never happens. The game play is mixed, with the rhythmic combat sometimes offering satisfaction, but equal parts will leave you frustrated. Everything you do is timed to the downbeat of a song, but some enemies and most stage hazards aren't (special shout out to the spiky balls). The song selection is decent, but there are way too many of them where the beat drops out entirely for a significant portion of the song, or has a tempo change in the song. Isn't that a cool decision to make in a game about performing actions in time with the music, and if you screw up even once you are penalized. Anyways, I don't recommend this game. I appreciate it's ambition, I always am interested in seeing how different people work with rhythmic timed game play, but this ultimately falls into the same pitfalls that many of this type of game do.

_childDocuments_.review: It is a real shame that I have to give the game a thumbs down, but it is almost unplayable in some areas in its current state. There are some real issues with the game design from annoying to game breaking that need to be addressed. I've gotten to the cityscape biome so far and here is my feedback: 1. Some of the tracks, especially the forest level, are nigh on impossible to really play in terms of hitting the beat. There are long pauses or no counts, or sudden tempo changes that unless you care about repeating the same song, are just not possible to know and makes it unsatisfying to play2. Playing online multiplayer at the moment is unstable. I've had several freezes lasting from either a couple of seconds to a full minute where I'm frozen.3. If you make a mistake or if the game bugs out, you can't just replay the song. Instead you have to quit the team, rejoin then replay which is clunky.4. Sometimes enemies or players get bugged behind walls when you get locked into a zone making it impossible to complete the area. I really hope these issues are addressed as this game can really shine - the beach biome is a really good example of this as it had a good selection of tracks and honestly the most enjoyable levels.

_childDocuments_.review: I dont write reviews for games often, but this game seems to have great potential and sells itself as something it isnt. It has everything a good rhythm game needs, fun aesthetic, solid modeling and animations, and a cool/unique core gameplay loop. Then downsides of this game heavily outweigh those things though because they arent utilized at all. The music just isnt good for a rhythm game, too many lulls in the songs making it hard to see where the tempo even is, songs ending before you finish a level making it that much harder to continue to the beat when there isnt even music playing. On top of that the whole looter shooter aspect of this game is completely trivialized because it seems to have an illusion of choice when it comes to weapons/gear. There aren't that many variations of gear and instead you just get more powerful versions of the same gear, pretty boring. And when it comes to the world, there isnt one, its just extremely linear stages. Hardly any room for exploration and when there is a slight detour on a map for a bonus chest, then you will surely miss the timer and get a bad rank for the level on top of making the end of the level frustrating because there is no music playing in a RHYTHM game. On top of all that the writing for what seems to be an unnecessary and irrelevant story is just cringe. TLDR: Great aesthetic and design to the game, but for a rhythm game its mechanics are poorly executed and just doesnt have very good music or story.
