_childDocuments_.review: TLDR at the end.First of I'd like to praise the developers for the amazing experience this game presented to me back when it originally released, ignoring some minor crashes/bugs, the game gave me its money's worth and more than I could ask for.When I saw the announcement for the Duty Eternal update/DLC, I was more than excited to have a reason to revisit this awesome game with even more to experience. Unfortunately this was far from the case as I took a deep dive into the game recently.When I originally played trough the game, I played on the second hardest difficulty and because of being more experienced this time, I chose the highest difficulty and I dont think this choice is to be blamed here, but I just want to point it out for the context here. The game started out just fine and just as I was expecting it to be in terms of challenge/difficulty while facing of against the first enemies (poxwalkers/Cultists/Plague bearers/Basic Plague marines) but the moment I started facing these new weaponry added to the enemy's arsenal, the problems of this free update started showing up. The enemy having access to armor ignoring weapons and cover ignoring grenades made the game impossible to play in a way where you could avoid your precious space marines from taking damage in engagements, which results in your space marines being lightly wounded or even wounded no matter how well you play. Another major issue this update (or maybe the DLC, not sure) introduced was enemy reinforcements, which could act on the turn they appeared on the map, which makes it near impossible for the player to prevent himself from getting out numbered and also from getting flanked or pincered which results yet again in taking unavoidable damage, resulting in wounded space marines, no matter what you do as a player.One more thing to mention is that the missions/maps feel packed tight now. Whenever you are fighting a patrol, it is near impossible to go into melee range of the enemy units without risking the line of sight to aggro another patrol/pack of enemies. This completely removes the tactical aspect/option of melee based approach to most missions because at least on the hardest difficulty, its a suicide to fight two patrols/packs of enemies at the same time.These kind of game play mechanics completely ruin the fun for me, because as a player, I seek perfection in my plays and I dont feel rewarded one bit when even while making the best possible moves available, I end up punished instead of rewarded. I cannot personally recommend this game in its current state and I hope the developers will change the game back to the way it used to be, where smart decisions felt rewarding to do.-Review edit after playing 2 campaigns on hardest and 2nd hardest difficulty:The DLC adds new mission types which have a new resource reward called 'Archeotech'. These missions are vastly more difficult than regular missions because you are expected to clear them by having a 5th playable unit in your squad, called Dreadnaught. While the game does give a small warning about the increased difficulty of these missions, there is no way for the player to know at the point of the appearance of these missions, that you will unlock this Dreadnaught unit for yourself way later on, and only then to be expected to actually start clearing these missions. I have no idea why the devs thought it to be a good idea, to make one of the three spawning missions to be this type when you dont have Dreadnaught yet, because all it really does is limit the player's realistic options down to two from three. There is literally no point in doing these missions before you unlock your Dreadnaught and they only serve the purpose of being a "noob trap", which in my opinion is just simply bad game design.-TLDR; Bad additions/changes to the game from recent patch/DLC, which makes it not recommendable: -Armor piercing enemy weapons -Cover ignoring grenades -Reinforcements which gain a turn immediately -Missions/Maps having patrols/packs of enemies too close to each other -Archeotech missions appear before having access to Dreadnaught

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game for those with a love of turn based combat. Leans towards the aggressive, forward pushing side of the genre similar to the equally great Gears Tactics. You are hardly going to be cowering behind cover and the game works all the better once you get your head around this.Not your not vulnerable to overextending - your enemies are also equally dangerous but the synergies that you unlock allow for some AMAZING damage output particularly the interceptor once levelled up on a melee, teleport pathway and with the right buffing characters.Cant wait for DLC or a second game.

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: While the below is still true and I still enjoy and recommend this game, there's a really big need to fix some of the early game balancing. Your guys are too weak and take forever to heal and the enemies are too plentiful to avoid damage. TL;DR 40K-Com which suffers slightly from not being as high budget as X-COM 2 or Gears Tactics but is still well worth playing if you like Turn based tactics games.I love X-COM and I love 40k, so this game is tailor made for me. The standard Games Workshop games issues are obvious though, and that's lack of budget. The core of the gameplay is really solid - which is the most important part. It plays well and features a good range of enemies and load out options, even only 2 hours in. It's not quite as hardcore as X-COM but in a lot of ways that just helps make it less frustrating. The presentation leaves a little to be desired though, the graphics are quite heavily stylised and cartoon-y. I don't mind this, but Grim Dark this isn't. The animations are passable and the sound design is eh (which is a big let down after the glory that was everything audio in Mechanicus). The UI is also pretty weak. I currently recommend this game, it somehow manages to remind me of the original Chaos Gate despite having little to do with it. The important part of the game is great - that being the tactical layer and the characters are fun too, it just needs some tweaks which hopefully will come in patches down the line.

_childDocuments_.review: While very similar to "a certain other game", Chaos Gate really comes into its own after a few hours. I do recommend buying it, provided the following issues don't bother you that much: Gameplay:The game really favors a very aggressive style,  which does mean that it may be a bit too bland and limiting for hardcore strategists. The enemy variety is lackluster for now, and it does take a while before new enemy types are introduced. Also, sending wounded marines to combat leads to a trivial debuff which means that you can just pick 4 favorites and not change them at all (with some exceptions).  The mission variety is not great either, and some missions do feel a bit like a grind, but there are a few very fun surprises thrown here and there which do make it worth it in my opinion. Another annoyance is that you can't re-spec your marines, so if you make a wrong choice or recruit a new high level guy, you are stuck with whatever they have.Story:Theme-wise, this game feels a bit too cheery and goofy for the "grim darkness" of 40k (and not in an Orky way).  The characters are made to be relatable and too "human" for my liking.  One of the worst offenders here is the Mechanicus tech priest which has metal eyebrows and a vox box mouthpiece mimicking a human mouth to achieve what I can only describe as "cuteness" (a similar thing can be said for all other characters).The crew's (and Inquisitor's) behavior is far too childish for the grizzled veterans the story suggests they are and you will feel like a babysitter at times.Power fantasy wise, this game also misses the mark, with some silly situations like a non-mutated human guardsman punching a power-armored space marine and dealing damage, or a terminator armor clad knight walking through some pitiful bit of burning oil and setting himself on fire (yikes).And finally, although it breaks my heart to say this, this game is another one in the long line of media misrepresenting the bolter. The poor bolter is once again little more than a glorified assault rifle instead of the stupid and awesome auto-cannon/rocket-launcher hybrid that it is in the lore.Performance:The game is decently optimized, but it has some significant frame rate drops in certain menus or certain combat arenas. Even though my rig is relatively good, I did end up lowering the graphics quality on certain missions or while interacting with certain ship menus (the second bit was especially annoying and odd). Overall, I still think the game is a lot of fun, and would recommend it to anyone but the most hardcore 40k purists (so that your eyes don't roll away from your sockets). But even for the purists, it may be fun to have a look at this game simply to see an outsider's interpretation of the franchise (just don't take it too seriously, you nerds).I am currently still progressing through the game, and will update this review if anything new or interesting comes up.

_childDocuments_.review: Some remarks beforehand:* Game needs a bit of polish. * The models and animations look like they are from an older era (which has its charms, for sure. But its nothing like Total Warhammer 3 for example). * The weapons and balancing of the armor might need a revision. But all in all, a title i'm already quite enjoying. And while not 'as' in depth as an Xcom 2 game 'yet' (so far for me at least), I'm enjoying it. Solid mechanics idea's so far that really seem to work.I LOVE the fact that i can change minute details about my Knights, down to the voices, armour details, last names ( which are spoken aloud as well as be displayed on the knight on certain places). It really makes me care more about them, instead of 'generic marine nr 5'.I have played several 40K games who have all tried their own spin on this genre of Xcom like gameplay, from mobile to PC games. And this is the first one where i'm actually enjoying myself.Each class of knight has their own feel to them and has a varied roster of traits they can unlock in a tree.(so far, no idea if one Knight can have all of them, but hey.)It feels like Xcom married Dawn of War 2 in terms of loadout mechanics but expanded heavily on them. Such as the ability to unlock upgrades for your gear. I would love to see this kind of game (with perhaps a bigger budget), with other chapters. Could be the same setting for all, with minimal narrative changes or references, so long as the chapters have their own styles or changed options/gameplay. Such as Black Templars (Templar visuals with correct colours, no psykers, themed weapons and traits, stratagems etc) compared to Blood angels or even Imperial Fists and so forth (just some founding chapters would be enough in this case, or possibly to create your own generic second founding one). Just roam about the galaxy, doing missions, trying to beat back a warp event/invasion or other xeno races. Leveling up your Marines, building up your base/fleet in a freeplay scenario. Expending resources or requisitioning more from your chapter/the imperium. Collect gear and personalise all of it like in this game. Heck, a system/game like this with an expanded roster choice to also play as a strike force of Imperial Guard, Sisters of Battle, etc. I would be amazing to have the choice to play as a different faction for another playthrough. Would happily buy the next game in this series if that were the case.

_childDocuments_.review: Chaos Gate is an excellent Xcom like game with some exciting new mechanics and twists that give it it's own identity. Combat feels great, the effects and sounds are satisfyingly chunky. There's a huge amount of cool skills for your knights, and maps also feature a lot of environmental options like knocking statues down on enemies, ledges and gaps that can be jumped, etcs. The game rewards aggression, you can get extra actions from repeatedly hitting enemies to stun and then execute them. Generally foes outrange you so you always want to be charging in, which is a nice change from X-com. Taking too long can give the enemy "warp surges" that do various nasty things to your squad, so efficiently taking out enemies each turn is a great little puzzle at the core of the game.The strategic layer isn't super deep but is a nice break in between missions. Basically you are choosing which missions to take to prevent the plague from spreading too far, it's very reminiscent of the boardgame Pandemic. Your ship starts out heavily damaged so you need to balance repairing your shields and ship guns with facilities that help your knights. There's a separate research tree that has most of the story missions locked behind it, as well as powerful Strategems you can deploy once per mission.Some complaints I do have would be the lack of mission variety. Other than story missions there are only about 4 mission types I believe, with two of them being quite similar. However I did find that switching out my squad composition helped keep things fresh. The game does also suffer from an inverse difficulty curve. I failed several missions early but by the endgame my knights were so strong I could kill bosses in 1 turn without much trouble. This is pretty common in this type of game so didn't bother me too much.Overall if you like tactical games or 40k at all I would highly recommend this one.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fun game.  At first it seems like a shameless X-com 2 knockoff which feels super cheesy, so my expectations were low to start-out.  However it surprised me how fun it got especially towards mid-game where resources are tight and every battle matters.  Another surprise is that gameplay is actually VERY different from XCom in that the gameplay pushes you towards uber aggressive-style play vs extra strategic, stealth or ambush-style set-up type of play.  The aggressive in-battle gameplay has a lot of similarities to Gears Tactics, but the out-of-battle strategy is FAR superior to Gears Tactics (i.e. striving to attain key resources of your choice from successful battles to support and enable your overall campaign style and choices) and this is totally what makes the game a blast.  I would highly recommend it to all fans of the turn-based tactical strategy genre!

_childDocuments_.review: After a few hours of play, I think it is time to review Chaos Gate - Daemonhunters.For the record, I am a big 40K fanboy, and I loved the original Chaos Gate (OG Chaos Gate from now on).Chaos Gate - Daemonhunters mixes the tactical gameplay of Gears of war tactics with a strategic layer like in XCOM.If you have read a few other reviews, you'd probably have come to the conclusion that the game is unforgiving.Except in theme, the game has very little in common with the original Chaos Gate from SSI. It is further apart than the newer XCOM were from their inspiration. Combat is closer from the new XCOM formula, with enemies "pods" that get triggered when you are in visual range of them.The game also relies a lot on special abilities (as in XCOM, the performances of your knights are night and day between a fresh one who just graduated from supplicant school.The immersion is good. I miss the old choir of the original chaos gate, and Nurgle lore is really weirder than Khorne lore, but the game makes a good job of conveying the fact that we are in the 40th Millenium.However, your Grey Knights will suffer from gameplay/lore mismatch: Their survivability is much lower than you would expect, even when faced with mere cultists, and it is one of the areas where OG Chaos Gate got it right:A dozen cultists will be a major threat to your squad of 4 knights, to the point you'd rather face 5 Chaos Space Marines, because their standard power armor offers no damage reduction. I was initially annoyed a lot by this fact, but I learnt to live with it. after all, in the original Chaos Gate, you could just ignore every cultist, and every Chaos Space Marine that didn't wield a heavy or special weapon.I would have preferred a better compromise (like CSM being equipped with anti armor rounds, and a few cultists with special weapons).This result in the early game being quite brutal. The difficulty has been one of the major complains about the game. But it is actually one of the parts I liked the best. Many complained that it was more unfair than XCOM.But it took me a lot of campaign retries to survive the early game in both XCOM 1 & 2 at the highest difficulty level(60 or so for XCOM 1, and around 30 for XCOM 2), before cruising to the end game.Unlike in XCOM 1, I never felt like I had to memorize the maps in Chaos Gate in order to survive in ironman mode. The game difficulty is also front loaded, but not as much as in XCOM.Overall, I agree that the game is difficult, but I don't think it is unfair at all (I completed it on the highest difficulty level in grandmaster mode), and is comparable to XCOM.You have a higher chance to love someone in mission, but the game gives you tool to recover from it (your knights can usually survive getting to 0 HP a few times in their career, and if they don't, their spirit can give boons to their brothers later on).Another issue with difficulty is that the game features a lot of random events whose outcome can be very negative. Unfortunately, it is sometimes pretty hard to make an informed decision without refering to the Steam event guide (or reloading if not playing ironman), which is pretty annoying.The game also likes hiding information that would be really helpful.It won't tell you that you need 8 geared and leveled knights to handle the final battle, but it really should for instance.Surprisingly, there is also quite a lot of randomness for a game that boasts to not have hit chances : the gear you get access to is random, the warp events that give boons to the opponent vary a lot, and there still are many rolls in the game to trigger some abilities, or critical hits, which make a huge difference. It seems rather negative so far, but I really had a blast with this game. It is actually my game of the year on Steam for 2022, because the combat is really satisfying.- You know the location of enemy pods, so you have less surprise triggers (even though it is not as true with the DLC, as some maps get pretty cramped).- The ability can be really fun to combine, and there are many ways to build your squad, depending on the gear you get.- As I wrote earlier, having ways to mitigate your losses really helps compared to XCOM- it focuses a lot more on melee combat, which makes it much more satisfying to use than in XCOM2.To me, the main weakness of Chaos Gate is the lack of variety, both in maps and enemies. The maps in XCOM felt much more impactful, but here, you end up charging in melee most of the time anyway, so the maps don't make a huge difference.The game also lacks mission variety: I liked the set battles, even though I usually don't like boss battles in tactical games, but you only have 3 versions of the repeatable missions, which is an issue the game shares with its main inspiration, Gears of Wars: Tactics (but GoW:T had more hand crafted missions).It departs so much from the original game that it is very hard to compare both. It still has a great atmosphere, but it feels much less faithful to the Codex Astartes (not that Grey Knights follow it), and the character count is much lower (4 instead of 15). It is a downgrade, but on the other hand, a good part of your squads were basically cheerleaders, because there was little more they could do with a bolter against CSM armor.I also preferred fighting over the whole map, than having mini skirmishes with individual pods, like in XCOM 2012.But the choice of equipment, strategic layer, and customization of each knights really adds a lot for me.OG Chaos Gate also had a memorable soudntrack, while the one in CG:Daemonhunter is just serviceable. I still remember some themes from the original, but I would be unable to do so with the new game, despite having freshly spent 200 hours on it.But the choice of equipment, strategic layer, and customization of each knights really adds a lot for me. I like Chaos Gate: Daemonhunters, but I loved his predecessor, so it is similar to the X-COM vs nuXCOM situation for me.So overall, I can only recommend this game, but we warned it is pretty unforgiving, and the first playthrough might seem unfair, especially if played ironman without spoilers.It is my preferred of the tactical or strategic 40K games that have come out in the last 10 years.

_childDocuments_.review: At this point I think I've played almost every 40k game, at least since 2000, and imo this is one of the best ones. Get it on sale though. If you're a 40k fan I think this is a must play, especially if your a fan of space marines or the grey knights. The main gameplay loop during missions is something similar to X-Com, but with less chance. But combat is punishing, and you'll need to learn positioning for encounters. But its rewarding, there is a lot of loot to collect to customize your knights, and their progression is fairly deep. It can take a little while to get access to some of the higher level mechanics and units, but its worth the wait. The narrative is fairly up-front which is nice, with quite a number of 1-2 minute cutscene's, especially in the first 5-6 hours. Then there's smaller narrative moments that you can interact with at your convenience on your ship, adding to ships immersion. I also really like the way they handled their voice acting, seems like a logistics choice but it insured every piece of text has at least some of it voice acted. The story isn't anything overly compelling, but for fans it has a lot of cool moments and characters I was stoked to see. The random events slot in really well with the campaign, adding to my role-playing experience and giving you the opportunity to further personalize your units with event rewards. I'm not a fan of the DLC's integration, when those missions start they are just integrate into the normal campaign, and probably WAY to early for the enemies you come up against. And a few bad defeats in a campaign early on can really derail the whole playthrough.I'm a bit bias as a 40k fan, a fan of the Grey Knights, and a fan of XCom. But, I think this game is the closest anything has come to letting you feel like you're controlling your own chapter of space marines. Also, the maps are pretty awesome. I didn't think they'd be this varied.EDIT: I've since completed the campaign and all my original feelings remain, except I'd give a few extra points to the story because near the end it really picks up again with a lot cutscenes and cool moments and characters appearings. My only gripe to add is that after completing the main story the game is done, with no open ended mode or anything to continue playing any mission you may have left unfininished (I had a few Mechanicus quests still to do). So take your time unless your going for the 500 day achievement. Fingers crossed we get a sequel

_childDocuments_.review: This review comes after a complete playthrough, start to end. You play a Warhammer 40,000 faction, the Grey Knights, battling a Nurgle threat.The good: + The grim-dark Warhammer 40,000 setting for an X-COM-like game is a fresh take on the genre. Unlike X-COM, it does away with much of the random throws (although there are plenty of other random elements).+ The core of the game is solid, turn-based gameplay that rewards tactical planning and smart, considered but aggressive play styles. + The turn-based game play takes place over six or seven varied mission types, not including the unique campaign missions, and it is important and fun to pay attention to the different objectives. + The simple campaign mechanic of time passing while you try to quell a growing existential threat is well handled.+ Most of the mechanics in the overarching campaign (the various currencies and rewards) mesh together well. Managing them requires the type of trade-offs that reward a thinking playstyle. + The Nurgle enemy units are varied and full of character, especially the bosses. + The narrative, plot and characters are engaging and well voiced, although the dialogue is clunky. + The art style and sound are excellent, balancing immersion and distraction well. + For the most part, the difficulty levels are well balanced. + You start with a basic squad of Grey Knights who can be upgraded into super-powered, elite psychic warriors as the game progresses. + The different classes are satisfyingly different from one another and can be combined in interesting ways, meaning that in theory you could try different class combinations in different playthroughs. + Similarly to other games in this genre, your Grey Knights' appearance can be customised, as can their load-outs. + There's around 50 - 80 hours of satisfying gameplay for a single run through of the campaign, depending on how you play it. + At the time of writing, the game has been well-supported by the developer and is refreshingly free of bugs. But: - In the base game you can only play one faction - the Grey Knights - and not as the single enemy faction, Nurgle (which, to be fair, is usual in the genre). - The random events on the campaign map feel like a weak point, interrupting the narrative with opaque, irritating consequences that usually prove very limiting. - Random factors feel arbitrary, meaning you can suddenly find yourself without the currency needed for essential research or upgrades.- The limited numbers of mission types can become repetitive towards the end of the game. - I feel the narrative-driven campaign and repetitive missions limit the game's replay value, a general problem in all the X-COM-alikes. - Most of the scripted plot-related missions spike the difficulty considerably. For example, the final boss mission is a lengthy repetitive grind with no prior information given to help pick squads. It requires careful preparation and thought, which the game does not warn you about. - Other games in the genre have innovated the core formula in more advanced ways, such as turn ordering (e.g. in the excellent X-COM 2 War of the Chosen DLC) , squad bonds and allowing more units in a squad. - No sandbox skirmish mode. A mode allowing you to craft a squad to test which abilities are best combined, so you don't have to play an entire campaign over again, would be a boon. - No multiplayer mode.- No mods or workshop.This is not a casual game. Overall, it's a satisfying way for a gamer who wants a demanding mental workout to scratch the tactical turn-based itch, even if the setting isn't your thing, and it's worth the money.

_childDocuments_.review: Apart from the fact that it's just a cheap knock-off of XCom2 and just plays like an XCom2 mod rather than an independently developed game, it's also one of the most unbalanced games I've ever played.You might think as the game progresses it will get easier (you know from XCom2) as you have higher level characters and better equipment. But all of that just doesn't cut it, as the game not only consistently works to nullify any success or hinder progress. Also, the game conditions just get harder and harder.Level 6+ chars, level 3 equipment and weapons...it all does nothing, as the game simply increases the frequency of triggering positive traits for the enemies or negative traits for your own troops. In addition, opponents also become stronger and stronger. More HP, more armor, or simply more and more enemies that you just can't fight all because of their sheer number.In addition, it does me no good that my knights can be knocked out once per round. Not only do they come back with much less HP, they also lose a "life" and at some point I can't use them at all. The leveling of chars is thus almost completely undermined, since there is always the danger that a highly leveled character simply goes down and all the efforts were in vain. And XP to level the characters is not a dime a dozen. From level 5 to 6 it is 300Xp and from level 6 to 7 it is 350XP. And the average mob only gives 5XP. It can also be that you fight with all your knights on a mob to get 2XP at the end. It's just a joke.In addition, you have a completely unpredictable supervisor who acts as if he has a serious personality disorder, who ♥♥♥♥♥ on you and then rewards you. Or praises you and then punishes you. And we're not talking about punishments that might make the game a little harder. We're talking about punishments that completely disable research for a long period of time or completely prevent access to new equipment. And you never know what the consequences are of the answers you give. Even when you think you've made a sensible decision, you're simply destroying resources that you've been short of all along anyway.Servitors, the mechanics of the spaceship, are constantly in short supply. The ship is constantly being damaged. If you have just repaired a component, it will break again. So you don't even have the chance to build up a certain resource stock, e.g. to build more cost-intensive upgrades for the ship.What happens, for example, when I fly through a warp storm? Ah, another component broken. How do the progosticars work? No idea, just try it out. You just have to spend resources you don't have anyway.I understand that the game is to show that you are in a difficult situation. But you don't play just any soldiers. We're talking about the best super-elite soldiers in the galaxy, selected from the best super-elite soldiers in the galaxy, equipped with weapons and armor that even the other super-duper soldiers wouldn't dream of. And what happens? Some half-dead guy in short pants comes around the corner, slaps the knight in the face, and the knight is in the infirmary for the next 60 days.It's just sad when the biggest success isn't a level 7 char or a successfully completed mission, but that there aren't almost only badly wounded or wounded fighters in the infirmary and that you can actually choose between the individual knights for a mission.In addition, there is a completely consumer-unfriendly advertising policy, from which the devs have at least already retreated once, because they have noticed how much they cut their own flesh with it. Instead of earning more money, they earn less.Nevertheless, exactly this advertising policy shows how completely distant from the player community the developers and publishers of this game are.The price of 45 euros and more is completely excessive for the fact that this is really just a simple XCom clone that is completely unbalanced and not developed to the end.I can't even move the camera when any action is performed. When the ship flies from planet to planet, the camera remains fixed. When the chars are running or fighting in the mission, the camera stays fixed. And that's just one example of many things that go wrong.The game has potential, no question. And just like XCom, many other DLCs can be built on top of it. The only question is whether the devs and publisher will stick around long enough and continue to develop the game or if it will just be another stillborn from the Warhammer 40K universe like many before.At the moment (and probably for the foreseeable future) I cannot recommend the game in its current condition and for the current price under any circumstances. Don´t buy, don´t touch it unless you can get it for a really big discount, are really capable of suffering and frustration resistant or best of all you can wait many more months.Update 28.08.2022: Although getting started on medium difficulty (like hell I'm going to try the harder difficulty levels in this dumpster fire) is really much more enjoyable now, and at least at first you feel like you're commanding a group of elite warriors, the game falls back into old habits as the campaign progresses.Say, unarmored simple humans with the simplest guns still do 1-3 points of damage to the elite warriors with superhuman abilities, in elite armor, while said elite warriors with their ranged weapons need at least two (TWO!!!) shots to eliminate the simplest of the simple enemy combat units. Not to mention later heavier combat units of the opponent.I really have no idea who was responsible for the development of the game. What is certain is that those people never even had a hint of involvement with the Warhammer40K universe, let alone the Grey Knights in particular.You should be ashamed of yourselves. Ashamed to the core and for heaven's sake never be allowed anywhere near a computer game again.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game, strong recommend for 40k fans or fans of tactical turn-based strategy games. I wouldn't bother picking up any DLC, but the core game is solid. It also has a good story with great voice acting that fans of ADB's writing, 40k fans and newcomers alike will appreciate. While CG draws obvious inspiration from XCOM, it innovates enough to stand on its own and improves some of XCOM's core systems, in particular the base (ship) management. Ship management is a constant balancing act of resources, opportunity costs, catch 22s, kiss-curse effects, time sensitivity and escalating pressures. All this makes the campaign feel like a real war of attrition - both narrative and mechanically -  that fits perfectly in the 40k setting. You never outgrow or outpace any of these systems, either - everything matters. What seem like minor oversights at the time could mean the slow, atrophied death of a campaign, so save often. The combat is fun and strategic. Each class of Grey Knight is useful and excels in a particular area, and I recommend using a variety of them for missions suited to their strengths. Overly relying on one squad or combat strategy to carry you through the game is a death sentence.Chaos Gate does a great job at what it sets out to do, but something I would like to see improved in the future is . While there are quite a few enemy types, they're all Nurgle flavored, and you're mostly doing the same 3-4 missions types (not including boss or story missions) with Grey Knights who function more or less similar to each other. While this all makes sense in the context of the story and setting, it would have been awesome to see things like Dreadnoughts (not how they did them in the DLC), Dreadknights, and higher level caps with more build variety. Complex Games has built an amazing foundation for what could be future 40k turn-based strategy games (I would murder for a Deathwatch themed flavor of Chaos Gate). I hope you enjoy it as much as I did!

If you're coming from either series you'll likely find plenty to pick at. For those that slept through hard mode Xcom2, you'll likely struggle in regular mode here. Many of the mechanics echo but they don't rhyme and a semi complicated UI can fuddle the learning curve even further. If you're someone that already struggles with Xcom, you'll be happy to learn that there's a "Restart Mission" button and like ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ in the shower, only the bravest among us are willing to admit to resorting to such extreme measures.Gameplay wise, you'll recognize the core gameplay. ♥♥♥♥♥ ♥♥♥♥♥♥, you're trying to un♥♥♥♥ the ♥♥♥♥ and your success will be based entirely on how well you respond to new ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ♥♥♥♥ through tech building and research. Then you'll use three Justicars and a Purgator until one of them coughs with a little too much enthusiasm and has to spend the next two months learning to walk again.The UI has some real fantastic design if you went to school in Japan and you enjoy reading in whatever ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ direction the wind happens to be blowing that day. It has this weird Borderlands ♥♥♥♥♥♥ World of Warcraft vibe without actually over utilizing either of their art styles. The game likes to randomly run like ♥♥♥♥ for literally no reason at all but like my previous relationships, it doesn't stick around very long. _childDocuments_.review: This is a fairly good tactical turn-based strategy game with a relatively engaging story based on a very interesting background universe.Perhaps what the game does best is presenting an interesting experience in the Warhammer 40K world by putting you in the shoes of one of its most interesting denizens: the Grey Knights, a caste of genetically modified super soldiers, of even more prowess than the 'normal' genetically modified super soldiers.You control a cruiser from the Order of Grey Knights, going from one disaster zone of the Imperium to another fielding your team of Grey Knights to deal with threats that nobody else in all human kind could deal with.Your schedule as a Grey Knight is basically 'Why look at the time, it's time to purge, like always, until I die'.Of course, in terms of game-play, it is inevitable to compare it to XCOM, but instead of forcing careful tactical approach, this game really preaches the best defense is a good offense idiom by rewarding extremely aggressive tactical approach allowing you to feel like true armor-clad super human exterminators as you plow through legions of heretics and demons (As long as you know what you are doing).Randomness is minimized in actual combat. If you point a gun or raise a sword, you are told the exact damage you would do, but factors such cover, angle of fire, statuses, etc. influence the final exact damage number. This design makes it so that the core mechanic of combat is about chaining coordinate attacks to keep the momentum going and not risk breaking the chain due to someone missing a 99% chance to hit a target. This turns the game into series of impromptu puzzles as you try to figure out what series of actions in what order would allow you to wipe out all oppositions on the map while incurring minimal damage.Team building is also a fun exercise, as you try to optimize your team of 4 exterminators to be able to deal with any situations. The variety of enemies, battlefields, and battle modifiers makes it a need to balance your team or build it with specific tactics in mind. There is a surprising depth to the combat system, as every team member must be well designed with each other in mind to ensure you can beat everything.Overall, this is an excellent 40k game that brings a solid take on the tactical turn-based strategy game genre.

_childDocuments_.review: First part of the game is brilliant, a tight must think must strategise game with the bonuses and equipment making many games much harder or easier depending on what you get. Then MID-GAME starts... massive enemy gains on many planets makes any mission in those areas taxing...but doable...And then just after that mid-game starts...where you have wasted many bonuses because there was zero advice on what was happening, like, yeah ill get this mark 1 weapon or that mark 1 equipment or armor coz i dont really know whats going on, and surely this is fine because u get offered this equipement after EVERY mission.... AND BOOM...you get to the DEFEND 3 massive area missions...thats three as in after 2, with 4 men... and you fight juggernaughts and dreadnaughts...SURE u get 3x men in these three areas...do they kill or help? NOPE.So you have an impossible mission and again and again to defend 3 battle-map areas with an awesome great kitted out squad...but soon realise its impossible when the 3x areas u have to defend with enemy dreadnaughts ALSO means you have to kill each unit, not survive, but kill each enemy unit. There are many unfair pc games throughout history, but this really takes the pizzz.  Its IMPOSSIBLE to kill 30+ enemies at 3 OR even 4 different places in the battle map and dont die.I really cannot fathom how other players win, unless they knew how to hoard there bonus points to get the best equipment thats never ever level 1 and make sure they spend it when they get the chance to get level 2 and 3.Its insane anyone can complete these defend 3 key areas THEN kill EVERY enemy when u have only 4 troops and a dozen non armorued non high attack helpers. Even if u kill and defend everything, u still get another 20 deploying bad guys to have to deal with!Really unfair bad crack. And i really did think about all the bonus weapons n gear i could have had rather than taking every piece i could have at the previous mission wins.

_childDocuments_.review: I came into this game, thinking it'd just be a Warhammer 40k skin of an XCOM title. I mean, I play a lot of XCOM games, and the mods available the XCOM 2 allow me to play Warhammer 40k XCOM well enough...But this game, is everything I want and more. Although Grey Knights wouldn't have been my first choice, and I would have loved commanding a squad of say... Blood Angels or Dark Angels, but it's a dynamic I have come to love.This game, is challenging. I started on the Standard Difficulty, as I had zero idea as to what to expect from this game. This game absolutely punishes you if you are sloppy and/or careless. If you make mistakes, the game will make sure to point them out... by slaughtering your squad. If you adopt a lone-wolf style, the game punishes you. If you charge in with teleporting assault marines, the game punishes you... unless you support them. That said, when you get the rythm down pat, the game just runs so smoothly, and the animations, combo-kills and amazing eye-candy just makes this game stand out.

These are all PRO's. The only CON's - I wish boss fights were more challenging and bosses weren't just stationary (except the final boss) and weren't half size of the map. And why soldiers cap off at level 9? I want all their abilities, not half!

_childDocuments_.review: I've been a longtime fan of Warhammer 40k, both for the games on the PC as well as on the tabletop (I've even had the opportunity to play in a weekend tournament at Warhammer World in Nottingham, UK), and currently I have spent 275 hours playing this game at the point this review is being written. So, to save some time for those who would reply "TL;DR", here's my summary: - Very aesthetically pleasing- Great game mechanics- Superb variety of classes- 2 out of 3 of the DLC (Duty Eternal and Execution Force) are worthwhile getting unless everything is in a saleIn more detail:- The graphics of this game are stunning, and my 4080 runs at around 68*C with all settings on max and on 4k resolution. The only downside is that there is no native DLSS option, which would significantly improve temps and FPS. But as it is winter right now, having my PC act as a heater for my office is quite handy! Sorry, I'm digressing. In all honesty, having painted tabletop miniatures for years, I can appreciate the time spent on the level of detail on the models used in game, and not just the knights, but those from Chaos as well. All in all, a solid 9/10. - The game mechanics are very similar to the tabletop. As I have very little free time, the tabletop games can run from 3-6 hours each, depending on the size of the army, so being able to just jump straight in and play a virtual tabletop version of the game with excellently rendered scenery is a godsend. As for those who have moaned about "Urgh, Dawn of War is faster, this game is too slow!" the DoW series of games were enjoyable, but this is much closer to the tabletop version and makes you think about your choices a lot more than DoW ever will. Every choice you make, every move taken, has an impact on your progress, and one miscalculation can end it all, necessitating a reload from an earlier save point. - The variety of classes available to you is vast in the vanilla edition, with different roles available to each class, allowing you the opportunity to decide how you wish to use your knights. IMHO the best combination is the Justicar, Interceptor and Apothecary. Apaart from acting as the tank for the squad, the Justicar can gift your Interceptor 3 move points and an extra willpower point.  The Apothecary can boost the Interceptor's critical chance percentage as well as keep your knights healed. With these two bonuses applied, the Interceptor can then teleport close to a group of enemies, then use a second skill called Teleport Strike to whizz through the warp, hitting a string of enemies close to each other, and sometimes take out an entire group before they can even fire on your knights once! The fourth spot in your squad can be then filled by whatever knight takes your fancy, or, not a knight at all, which leads me to.......- The DLC. Having read about the Castellan Champion, I couldn't see it being worth the full price cost, and err'ed on the side of caution and saved my money. So I can't comment on that. However, the other two DLC (Duty Eternal and Execution Force) are very much a worthwhile purchase. Execution Force gives you access to four types of assassin, my favourite being the Culexus due its absolutely game breaking abilities (closing enemy reinforcement warp rifts before they open!!!) and outright brutal attacks. Duty Eternal provides you with access to a Dreadnought on specific missions, a techmarine for use on any mission, and a very, very welcome second ship in the form of a Gladius frigate that you can use to send another squad to complete a mission when 'The Bloom' spawns. There are multiple negative comments and reviews out there about the lack of availability for deploying the Dreadnought except on certain missions. To be fair, I understand why; if you could take the dreadnought on every mission, the game would be too easy, even on harder difficulties! Keeping it for use on Technophage missions provides a challenge, but without making the game too easy. The techmarine is also a handy tool in the right situations, with their ability to take along a servitor that can be armed with various different ranged (and melee) weapons.All in all, a solidly built game, one you REALLY need to learn to save regularly and often to avoid any game issues, it really is worthwhile buying the base game and the two DLC noted above, eschewing the Castellan Champion unless it is on sale; at £13 it really isn't worth the cost based on the description of how it works in game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game does a fantastic job of capturing the true essence of what it means to be a Grey Knight in the grim darkness of the 41st millenium and introduce a new audience to tactical games in the vein of XCOM, which I have seen this game compared to in many reviews online. In this game, you take control of a strike force of Grey Knights, a secretive chapter of Space Marines dedicated to fighting the Forces of Chaos. What sets these warriors apart from other Space Marine Chapters is that every Grey Knight is a psyker, capable of using the Warp for various kinds of arcane and esoteric effects. Although anyone with psyker abilities has the potential to become corrupted by their power and become a daemonhost, the Grey Knights are singular in that not one has fallen to Chaos in the history of their Chapter. The Grey Knights make their base on the moon of Titan in the Sol System, where they enjoy the best equipment, technology, and requisitions straight from Mars itself. The game itself is very interesting to play. I don't have much experience playing these kinds of games, but I found the combat mechanics easy to understand and implement for success. It is easy to see that the devs have a true love of the lore that permeates everything from the atmosphere, the sound design, the different abilities your Knights can wield, to the overall story which is very fascinating and something out of the Grey Knights Omnibus. Finally, the voice acting is also very good and you feel the weight of the words these characters say, some of whom are many centuries old. Overall, if you love 40k, you will love this game. 9/10

_childDocuments_.review: Went into this game not expecting much, just another Warhammer IP cashgrab but i was pleasantly surprised at how fun the game was, beated first playthrough in Ruthless difficulty with Grandmaster (Ironman) mode on and i think it archived a perfect balance between challenging missions while not feeling impossible without cheese, The story was really good and to be honest was surprised by the final encounter, I expected it to be some kind of Avatar of Nurgle but I was pleasantly surprised. My only complain was that even though they were interesting the Boss encounters were really easy,  each one has some kind of interesting mechanic you are supposed to deal with but even in the ''hard'' difficulty you are fine just ignoring it every single time and focus the boss down and you will win easily( this might not be the case in legendary but i doubt it as i won by a large margin anyways).     TLDR: Good Gameplay, Really Good Warhammer story, Some questionable cut scene animations for certain characters, mediocre boss fights, Fun and challenging difficulty(Don't play normal play Ruthless or Legendary). All in all a great game 3/5

_childDocuments_.review: This game scratches that XCOM itch, while also throwing some new ideas into the mix. Additional action points and fewer restrictions allows for much more freedom in combat. Dropping statues on enemies, pushing an enemy off the map with a hammer or killing five daemons with a teleport doesn't really get old. _childDocuments_.review: There's a good game here buried under mounds of optimization issues. A 3080 and 10600K - far surpassing the recommended spec - will struggle to hit a consistent framerate, with hitches galore, microstutter and in engine cutscenes dropping to the mid 20's in places. There's no raytracing or exceptional graphic fidelity here, so there doesn't seem to be any real excuse for it.It's a shame because the fundamentals of the game, while a bit questionable in places, are pretty good. Right now I can't recommend this - I'll change the review if they actually address it. They were pretty quick patching people getting DLC content for free, so we'll see where their priorities lie.Update: after the dev response below they have released a news update on steam just over 2 hours ago saying they are aware of the issues and are currently investigating. Fingers crossed. Out of interest I did turn debug mode on in the Nvidia Control panel and found it did alleviate stutter slightly but the overall performance is still very uneven and the drastic framedrops were still present in exactly the same scenarios. It's  better, but the major drops are still a big issue.Update 2: Fair play to the devs, they seem receptive of feedback and are addressing things like the issue with items locked behind Twitch pretty quickly. Hopefully this keeps up and I won't have an issue changing this to a positive review.

_childDocuments_.review: This one is honestly one of the better warhammer games. Still I have extremely mixed feelings about recommending it, here's why.Pros:- First half of the playthrough is fun, challenging, interesting. XCom with a few new twists - Aggressive playstyle is much more rewarded than overwatch fiesta.- Some classes are super fun and its interesting to figure out the strengths, weaknesses and synergies between them- The story and the characters are not too bad. Nothing too special either but seeing how it will end was my only reason for torturing myself with the boring endgame, so there's that. - The last mission is epic and gives you this feeling of last stand against an overwhelming force that I love the Warhammer universe for.- Voice acting is okay.- Knight customisation is pretty cool, especially with the sigils. But faces are all looking the same, basically you can decide for "helmet or no helmet" and that's it. More faces please!- The way that your armor changes optically through the game is pretty cool too. Starting out quite plain, it feels as if in the end your knights can barely walk from all the battle-earned medals and adornments. Neat!Cons:- Second half of the playthrough was tedious, repetitive and because of that surprisingly boring. I actually had to take breaks because I was too bored. By that time, you will probably have maxed out your main squad because the max level is only 9. With the right classes, you simply destroy everything while rushing through the levels, and since there is only 2,5 standard mission types (carriers, bloomspawn and spreader which is basically like bloomspawn with a time limit) there is no challenge. Still even if you do everything right, you can't skip standard missions and until the very end you have to keep torturing yourself with them (unless you decide to not give a damn and let the sector rot away while you wait for your research to finish). - Some classes are quite useless. A better balance would have kept it interesting for longer, experimenting with different class combinations. - Character facial and body animations in the cutscenes are quite ugly. It is 2022, right? Come on, a bit more effort wouldnt have hurt anybody :/ I will not touch the game anymore now that I have played it through. Yeah I played 53 hours, but the last 30 felt like a real ordeal that I need to recover from. Some suggestions to make the endgame better:- Give options to skip standard missions or make them less present in the endgame. Prognosticars alone don't really cut it.- Add different mission types, for example something like a point defense where you dont have to run around through a level.- Rebalance some of the weaker classes (apothecary, for example)- Raise max level of knights or give other means to improve your characters in the endgame except for randomized gear rewards after missions- More facesIf what I wrote doesn't scare you off, feel free to buy the game. You will at least have a few hours of very cool gameplay. If you want a game that keeps getting more fun until the very end, maybe keep looking or wait for changes.

_childDocuments_.review: This game fits the vibe of the warhammer universe, in addition its basically an x-com game. This game is difficult, even on the lower difficulties, though i will preface this review with not playing a lot of x-com like games before heading into this. This game has a few flaws and a steep learning curve as well as several opportunities for death spirals that caused me to have to restart my first playthrough. The problem is that you cant point at a specific point and say "heres where i made my mistake" instead its just a slow spiral of increasing difficulty until every mission is a do or die challenge and the only un-injured knights you have are too low level to complete the mission. The game almost demands you play to a failure before making an earnest attempt to complete it.Since i had to restart my first playthrough lets talk about what i did in my second playthrough. i took what i learned from that failure and stayed ahead of the curve and found the game much easier. While trying to stay ahead of the curve I ended up rushing towards story missions and completing bloom missions along the way. This strategy worked for me, however it left me a bit unprepared for the final mission, which once unlocked gives you a certain number of days to undertake or receive a game over (would hate to be on hardcore mode for that). Since i had been rushing i was locked into a do or die situation with only one max level squad with less than stellar gear into the final mission as it requires two squads and no way to level them up or gear them up before the final mission. I hadn't had much trouble with any missions or bosses before that last mission, but upon undertaking the last series of missions you lose access to stratagems which had been the backbone of my success throughout the entirety of the game. What ensued was a very long, difficult, battle of attrition very worthy of a final battle. That said, the combat was enjoyable, every class had its place, and being able to specialize each class was worthwhile. However this isnt without its flaws, as i found some classes to be powerhouses capable of eliminating entire groups by themselves. In addition tier 3 upgraded gear was insanely good compared to lower tier gear without upgrades, resulting in large jumps in power based on chance at the end of missions when i do wish i could use requisition to buy high tier gear as well. I also had a constant shortage of servitors that held back my ship construction which was just based on which missions had the reward of servitors and which missions had a bloom level i needed to deal with as i tried to complete as many missions as possible each cycle in between story missions. This felt a little hectic and made me play a bit rushed as trying to prevent the bloom from overtaking a planet, while trying to do the story, while trying to get my knights leveled and geared left little room for farming.Overall i enjoyed this game, though the steep learning curve and death spiral of my first playthrough soured my experience a bit. The story itself was fairly interesting, but nothing to write home about. I would suggest that anyone that wants to play this game look into tips for the game as well as going in with an understanding that you might run into an unwinnable death spiral that will end your run which is very warhammer 40k. When played with that knowledge the game is very enjoyable, and i prefer this over x-com as they changed some mechanics such as instead of having a percent chance to hit to being based on cover and distance, leading to a more consistent and enjoyable experience. I would give this game a 8 out of 10, its what you would expect from a x-com game in a 40k theme, but its got a few rough edges that might rub people the wrong way.

_childDocuments_.review: According to previews the game seemed to be really good and up my alley as a fan of UFO/XCOM style games. I also have very fond memories of the original Chaosgate from the 90s and this seems to be a commendable approach to re-imagine it with enough new ideas inserted. Here are some of my brief impressions:- Graphics are outdated, but not ugly (only the faces are hidious). Considering this the performance is disappointing, a RTX3080 won’t get you a locked 4k60.- Readability of the maps and characters is not good, the art design itself is OK- The UI looks very soft. It seems like it is designed for FHD and does not scale to 4k. It is also clearly designed for controllers and has quite a few unneccessary clicks required.- Tactical combat and character skills seems closest to Gears Tactics. Does not bring anything significant new to the table.However, because of some BS the publisher is pulling it gets a thumbs down & refund from me.1. The Castellan Champion Edition upcharge comes at 33% of the price of the full game and gets you just one additional character (not class!) and 2, most likely, OP items. This is a very steep price for very little content. (I don’t care about the soundtrack)2. On top of that additional (only cosmetic) content is gated behind streamer drops. Paying the extra money for the Champion Edition is not enough, you need to create accounts at the publisher and the streaming platform and waste apparently 11x 30-45mins with watching streams; aka you need to pay with your personal data and time for earing the privilege to access all available content. Just deplorable.3. Denuvo. I personally think this is only a minor issue, but the money would have been better spend investing it in the game itself rather than in making it worse for your paying customers (multiple pirated games have proven that Denuo can have a significant negative impact on game performance).I am genuinely sorry for the developers, but I will not support these business tactics with a full-price deluxe edition purchase and will refund my preorder after posting this. I can wait until it comes in a bundle or at a steep discount, happy holidays 2023 :-).@Devs: good luck finding a better publisher for your next game, there seems to be plenty of good talent in your team!

Had to restart missions over and over because the game mechanics would be so inconsistent that you couldn't make any real strategic choices. One round it would renew your action points when you encounter a new group of enemies, another it wouldn't. Sometimes you would just bug out and not be able to move and get annihilated. Just a lot of randomness that didn't make sense. In an FPS, whatever. Just then the warp surges, reinforcements. Bugger. Okay new plan, we whack the last guy. This triggers the reinforcing parties for the hold out. 2 groups of space marines to add to the horde of pox walkers. Crap crap crap. I realise the map is quite long, maybe we could... you know run away? So my terminators break towards my purgators who manage to keep the enemies just far enough away to do any major damage. The minute, and I mean the minute, I turn the corner at the top my terminators come face to face with another bloody patrol... They carve into the enemy but one terminator goes down severely injured. He smashed aside some pox walkers and dashes into heavy cover with enough ap to cast aegis shield (fun fact I had actually forgotten about this ability but I digress). _childDocuments_.review: This is a fantastic game, but one for a relatively narrow audience. For one thing, it's unapologetically made for Warhammer 40K fans. The story is a delightful focus on a single, relatively small conflict within this massive universe, but it does very little to introduce said universe and explain important concepts like the Warp. People who aren't familiar with W40K are probably just going to feel lost, the theme will seem bombastic and silly, while the Knights and environments will probably look samey.As well, the game is for players experienced with games a la X-Com. While complaints about the game's difficulty are exaggerated (I started playing on Ruthless and found the level of challenge just right), it does require you to use a pretty wide set of strategies, and make coordinated use of pre-battle planning, varied weaponry, terrain and special abilities. Players who grew up on standard RPG turn-based combat will have a rough time here, as the game demands tactical sagacity from the very first missions.Assuming you fit the intended target audience, the game is absolutely stellar. Long, fun, complex, challenging, full of interesting decisions, replayable, and by a distance the best, most convincing rendition of the Warhammer 40K universe in a game I have seen to date. Literally my only complaint is the character customisation screen, which in a game like this should offer all sort of options but instead turned out to be very limited and boring. Otherwise, A+.

_childDocuments_.review: sees the light on Steam as a sequel to the blockbuster , nearly 6.5 years after the original was released. Having played both games back to back, I can confidently affirm that  is a big step-up from the previous installment. Not only does it bring some brand new mechanics into play and upgraded visuals, but it also manages to re-capture the charm of exploring a half-sunken city similar to the one in the first game, while also building upon the slow-paced, almost meditative-like experience that is now a staple aspect of the series.In both  titles, you take the role of Miku - a young girl who arrives by boat together with her brother Taku in a ruined city, whose remnants have been partially inundated by water. Designed as open-world exploration games, you will have the freedom to explore the small, cozy map at your own pace and gather various collectibles by rowing your boat to navigate the deep waters or by climbing to the top of the buildings. In that regard, the two installments share the same set of core mechanics: Miku will use all sorts of ledges, ladders and drain pipes for her ascension, similarly to a Tomb Raider / Assassin’s Creed action sequence, but without any time pressure or other stress factors. Her movements feel almost effortless, and you won’t even need to time the jumps - the game will automatically do that for you as long as you keep your controller button (or the movement key) pressed. Additionally, in  Miku will also be able to use ropes in order to jump over an obstacle or pull down gates with her boat, activate elevators or slide down zip lines, and also carry stone spheres needed for certain puzzles.In regards to the story, the two games can be played independently of each other, but experiencing the original  first will provide some insight into the siblings’ story and a glimpse into how the cities came to be inundated. While in the previous game Miku’s goal was to gather supply crates that contained the necessary items to tend to her wounded brother, in  the focus is shifted on Miku’s gift of cleansing the corrupted vegetation and restoring the balance of nature in their small world. With Taku being fully healed, the players can now enjoy exploring some of the locations with him instead of Miku, however which of the two characters one controls is fully scripted - the player cannot deliberately choose. The story is still revealed in snippets of 4 symbolic drawings but they are now accompanied by a descriptive text whose scope is to unravel the story, one paragraph at a time.If you played  and thought that there were a lot of collectibles to gather, then brace yourself, since  offers more than twice the amount, totalling to around 250 individual items or pieces. Aside from diaries and boat upgrades, you can now collect ancient relics from the depths and special types of flowers from the main locations. These can then be displayed inside your home, in designated areas - a very nice-to-have feature, one that I enjoyed a lot. Miku can still use her telescope to scout the surroundings for these collectibles, but she can now also climb to the top of lookout towers, which will automatically mark all nearby collectibles on the map, making it easier to hunt down all the secret locations. Also, each of the major areas has a set of 9 pieces of style that you can gather, and which will unlock different boat cosmetics, outfits and hair types for Miku when combined. Overall, I really loved ’s approach to collectibles: they finally stop being a meaningless pixel hunt; instead they're used to provide more customization for the main character or personalize her home.The environments of both  titles are masterfully crafted, depicting a thick vegetation woven into the ruins of the city. But the visual detail in  is absolutely astonishing: the water is so clear that it allows you to see glowing fish swimming beneath your boat or the reef covering the floor of the sea. The whole scenery blooms with colorful flowers when you carry a certain artifact, the walls of the buildings are covered in rose vines or soft moss. It’s an idyllic and wholesome picture, one of mesmerizing beauty. is a must-play for those that enjoyed the first game even in the slightest. It’s longer (7-10h), better, richer in collectibles and surprisingly more gorgeous in terms of aesthetics. For those that didn’t play the original, I warmly recommend giving any of the two titles a try, if you’re that kind of a person who appreciates a completely relaxed experience, devoid of any violence or time pressure.Feel free to also check  of Submerged.

_childDocuments_.review: This game should have been right in my wheelhouse but by the end I genuinely loathed playing it and just ground it out for the finish, there are a few reasons for that but ultimately it comes down to one thing, the boat. Oh my god, that f**king boat.This is a zero risk exploration game, which means that the exploration is a large part of the game and the fun of the game. As I say, I love this sort of thing, Alba, Summer at Mara and Grow are some of my favourite games. But the main way of travelling around and exploring the map here, the boat, just sucks the absolute life out of you such that rather than looking forward to exploring the large and interesting map I was desperately calculating which fast travel location would result in the simplest route possible. You have very little control over the boat most of the time, its like having to ride everywhere on a drunken bear, wearing roller skates, on an ice rink, whilst blindfolded, its just tiresome when every corner and turn has the chance of being a minute of reversing and "steering". Aside from that, the boat feels like a cork in a flushing toilet, it has no sense of weight or placement in the world, constantly bobbing and almost upending, totally destroying any immersion in the game as it almost upends and your characters don't even blink or when it nearly flips while running into a wall and then always just sits perfectly right down where it started.That's indicative of another of the problems here. All these games have zero actual threat or risk, which I'm fine with, that's what I play them for, to chill out. But other games let you have moments where you at least think "whoops", a missed jump meaning you have to go back around a little or something. Here, to complete a series of jumps or swing across poles is exactly the same action and difficulty of walking down a corridor, everything is taken care of for you. In this game nothing you do really matters, you can't miss a jump since you're not in control of them, you can't go the wrong way since there are safety rails around all the wrong routes, thankfully the boat never actually flips or the game would be unplayable, but when it should flip nothing happens. The final sense is one of disengagement and boredom.I will say, for a chilled out exploration game, if you have any kind of problem with liminal spaces or statues, this game is creepy as hell. The thing is that at heart the game is just a bit joyless and po-faced, its not having fun and it doesn't intend that you will. But of my god, that boat, that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ boat.

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? How much beauty can you endure? This game is simply gorgous, at least for an indie production. The first Submerged game was already beautiful, but Hidden Depths looks even better.In the game, you play sister and brother trying to save a dying world, covered by a Black Plant. Ugly black tentacles coming from the sea cover most things on land. Didn't I play something similar recently in Glow: Song of the Evertree? Anyway, that's where the similarities between those two games already end. So what is Hidden Depth? It is an action-adventure (but many games can be called that), I would compare Hidden Depths to a Ubisoft-formula game... without the fights. So, it is like Assassin's Creed, but with only the collectables remaining. The whole map is full of things to explore, things to find and collect, buildings to climb and puzzles to solve.The game was made by a designer who hates violence, so there are no enemies to fight. It takes place in a large city mostly covered by the sea, so you don't see too much of it. There are only some buildings still protruding from the water. You have a small boat and can visit these little islands to discover seeds, creatures, plants, relics, boat upgrades, landmarks, parts of the city history or some things more. Exploring the map with your boat, finding your way through little mazes of walls standing out of the water, and exploring the buildings by foot is the core game mechanic. Find places where you can enter the ruins, climb the old buildings using ladders, ropes, plants or parts of the building, climb lookouts (or use the elevator for going up and down). While you climb like Enzio (from Assassins Creed), it is far easier in this game. You cannot fall down, you don't even have to press a button to jump. The challenge lies in not getting lost, finding collectibles everywhere, finding seeds and bringing them to a place to heal the sourroundings. You see images of dead people while doing so, not because you have a 6th sense but because the Black Plant creates them. On your boat, you can use your telescope to look around and add new locations to the (quite large) map. LOTS of things to find and explore. Above water and... below. Controller works fine.Peaceful game of exploration and discovery. Very good looking. No fights, just many things to find and a story to uncover.
_childDocuments_.name: Submerged: Hidden Depths

_childDocuments_.review: I really love the Submerged series as it has a bit of everything; exploration, nature and its creatures, mystery, lore and collectables.  This one is much easier than the first game as everything you need to use has your chosen colour to show the way. Children can watch you play until the mood changes mid game.Miku and Taku have a new city to explore.  Miku has a gift of restoring life and growth and is able to banish the corruption that has enfolded many of the buildings.  Taku, her brother, is worried about the effect this 'gift' has on her.  Together they explore the city and discover the story via diaries littered around the place.  They also collect boat parts and new styles for their boat, clothing and hair and relics from the past.  Also to be found are the creatures of the sea and land plus the landmarks and lookouts of the city.  So lots to do!One of the great joys of this game is the exploration by boat.  The controls are a bit wonky, but as the game progresses, these become better.  I found that by pressing the space bar...the boat speeds along.  You sail on the ocean with stingrays, dolphins, pelicans, whales and swordfish accompanying you.  A real sense of freedom hits you as you speed across the water.  The day/night cycle is very short, so the scenery is changing all the time and it was just gorgeous!  You even get blasted by tropical storms!The graphics are stunning...quite a markup from the previous game.  It did take its toll on my gaming laptop and heated it up like crazy, but reducing the graphics from ultra to medium helped. You can't die in this game and you can't fall from anything.  You often have to swing across things but just pressing W carries you across, so there isn't much challenge at all.  But it was deliberately designed this way to make this game  accessible to those with less quick reflexes, so I applaud the devs on this decision.Accompanying the gorgeous graphics was soaring orchestral music which made travelling along the boat quite a cinematic experience.  I loved it!  An interesting feature was that every collectable has it's own 'song'....meaning they all had their individual sound.  So if you're close to something and can't see it, you follow the sound.The downside is that Miku sometimes couldn't step onto something....you always have to go via steps.  The movement made me a little nauseous, so I reduced the camera sensitivity which helped massively.In the end, it was a little grindy to get all the collectables and achievements, but once you finish the game you can go back in to mop up the missing pieces.  There is a good map for reference in the game and some excellent walkthroughs for the missing collectables.I reluctantly had to drag myself away from the game as I was having far too much fun in the boat with all the sea creatures.  Ironically, in real life, I get very seasick!!  I can imagine more experienced gamers speedrunning this game, but this is like a good wine; to be savoured slowly and enjoy the view.So put on your suntan lotion and bucket hat and sail into the sunset.  8.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: Coming Home…Isn´t it always a good feeling?To come Home.Yes it is. And thats what i´m feeling.A few Years ago i was looking through Games on Sale.I found Submerged. The Screenshots of a Civilisation taken back by the Nature fascinated me. And the Idea of climbing them got me fast. So i bought it and got an amazing and fantastic Gaming Experience.After completing the Game i have had just one Wish: To continue the Journey.And this whish finally come true.Welcome to SUBMERGED – HIDDEN DEPTHS.In times like this with War and Pandemic it is not easy to think mostly positiv. But a few seconds after starting the Game i have had a smile on my Face and i was diving into another World.  The Story continues, where the first Game ends. Miku and Taku, Sister and Brother, from the first SUBMERGED are returning. A few Years since the first Game had gone by and both arrive again at a half sunken City. You don´t need to play the first Part to understand the new One, but i highly recommend playing both Games because of this really unique Atmosphere. In the Beginning is a short introduction what happened in the first Game.IMPORTANT!!! Like the first part SUBMERGED-HIDDEN DEPTHS has NO fighting Sequences. This is a pure Exploring and relaxing Game with little Puzzle elements.So Miku and Taku arrived and found out something is wrong. Bigger Parts oft he Plants that took over the once proud City were black and vicious. It is up to you to find out with Miku and Taku what happened to this place and to the People who lived there after the cataclysm.Reveal the Story, Piece by Piece , Picture by picture.SUBMERGED-HIDDEN DEPTHS has all the Elements from the first SUBMERGED. You are exploring the Ruins with your Boat, climb on Buildings to continue the Story and find also usefull things for your Boat. Also find Diarys to unfold the whole Story.What is new? You have a Main Place that you can decorate with Relics or Flowers. Both must be find.Also new, you are not playing only with Miku, no, this time you play also with Taku.But don´t get me wrong, you can´t choose between them, when you reach a place where you left the Boat one oft hem Jumps o fit and you get control. While Miku is especially for the 9 Main Buildings because of her special Story driven Ability, Taku takes on Side Ruins. The Animations of both are really detailled and if you take your Time to watch them a little, you will see nice little animations, like Miku taking her Hand through the Water from time to time, while they are travelling on the Boat.By the Way, if you want to impress someone with your Gaming Abilities, this is the Perfect Game. But it is important that you don´t let the other Person know, that you can´t fell to death and that all the amazing climbing, jumping and swinging scenes are done by the Game itself.  Yes, it looks really great to see them doing this things, while you only have to move them tot hat special Points and the just do it. No nerving and no raging Action Scenes. Your Gamepad can gasp of relief.Again the Artwork and Construction of the  Buildings is amazing. There is so much to explore, to see and to find. The Devs put their first Game on a new higher Level and alone the Details everywhere are really breathtaking for me. Again in Combination with a really outstanding Soundtrack, you get an atmosphere that easily lets you dive into it and forget everything around you.This is not a Game, this is an Experience.But it is not for all. This is no fast action Game. This is a relaxing kind of Walking Simulator with light puzzle Elements that focused completly on exploring the Ruins and the Story .Highly recommend.While i played SUBMERGED-HIDDEN DEPTHS it felt so good to be back again. Yes, i got a little happy Tear in my Eye, but i tell you what, i´m not ashamed of it. When a Game creates Emotions like this, then the Devs has done everything right.That is not only Gaming…….. that is passion.Thanks to the Devs for a wish came true, the amazing Experience and Thank YOU for Reading.
