_childDocuments_.review: This game is unimaginably SHALLOW and REPETITIVE, everything becomes a chore after 20 hours of gameplay when the novelty value has gone. The major problem is the broken combat mechanic and shallow alchemy mechanic, I beat very hard mode using the same simple tactic, don't even care what bosses do.Pros:- Voice actingCons:- Repetitive gathering. Even though you know most of what you're gathering are useless, you still need to gather a lot materials. How to gather? Just press 'Q' or press with timing.- Shallow crafting (alchemy) mechanic. It's all about accumulating traits to get better number, you can get +20%, +30%, +100% critical hit rates, or +20%, +50%, etc item damage, or +1 +2 +3 DEF buff. In early game, I crafted one item to get +2 DEF +2 ATT +1 SPD -2 DEBUFF +100 HP to team members, and everyone can use it. Using this item throughout the game makes very hard mode pretty easy. You can craft much more powerful items like bombs, but it's just about accumulating traits together, becomes boring quickly. I don't have any end game weapon because the I'm tired of crafting and I know they just have better number, nothing special.- Repetitive crafting (alchemy) gameplay. It was fun during early game, you can think of it as a little puzzle game, but playing it throughout the game for 100 hours is boring, I literally don't wanna craft anything in late game, but the game force you to upgrade your alchemy level to progress.- Shallow combat mechanic. There are many elements in the combat like passive skills, switching party members, breaking shield, etc. Looks complex, but all you need to do is to keep buff on your team members and keep debuff on boss, and to follow some simple instructions like using fire if boss is weak to fire, not using magic if magic triggers counter-attack.- Similar team members. Everyone is tank with block pose, everyone is dps, healer, etc. Buff/debuff is the only thing you need to consider in combat, and everyone can use crafted items to buff/debuff. Anyone died in combat? Don't panic and no hurry to rescue them, because everyone else can do the same thing.- Shallow upgrading mechanic. There is NO skill choice, you spend upgrading points (TP) on something like +5 attack or +10 speed or +2% critical hit chance, etc. Yes you feel you grow each time, but it's not fun.- Repetitive map and puzzle. Throughout the game, you solve puzzles by using the same skill called changing weather, it works like this, go to place A to change sunny to rainy, now you can access place B, change it to thunder, then the door in front of you will open. Repetitive and boring.- Repetitive boss. There are 4 or 5 elite mobs and 4 or 5 bosses throughout the game, very few, huh? And their skills are quite similar. And they REPEAT. You fight the boar boss 3 times, the dragon boss 3 times, the goddess boss 3 times. How lazy are the game designers?- Cliched story. It's ok if it's a bed time fairy-tale for 12 years old, but it's way too shallow for a 100 hours game.- Tons of meaningless small talk cutscene. The game uses the slow paced small talks to pad game time, even the positive reviewers skip those cutscenes.Maybe there are some more cons I forget to list.After beating nice RPG games like Final Fantasy X, Dragon Quest XI, I feel sad because it's over.After beating RPG games with deep combat mechanics like Octopath Traveler, Divinity II, I wanna play it again to try different strategies.After beating this game? I feel good because the repetition and boredom is over, I deleted it immediately and will definitely not try any atelier game.

_childDocuments_.review: The best Atelier title so far imo. The combat system is great, no longer does half of your party slack in the background while you are fighting.Alchemy 'tetris' system is an improvement over the other "Mysterious" titles, but ends up being overcomplicated. _childDocuments_.review: Atelier Sophie 2 The Alchemist of the Mysterious Dream is the latest installment in the Mysterious games despite it being a sequel only for the first game, which is Atelier Sophie. My thoughts are: This game felt more of a side story arc compared to being part of the main games' timeline, which makes sense because of the events in the game. The plot wasn't bad at all but it was kind of lacking, could have been better. Either way, I enjoyed every bit of the story and its characters, both the "old" and the new ones. As for the gameplay, The battle went back to being the classic turn-based type, so nothing changed much compared to its other Mysterious games. But for the alchemy, in my opinion became harder but funner. I would not be surprised if people dislike Sophie 2's alchemy gameplay even thought the Mysterious games' alchemy has been quite disliked in general.Overall, I give Atelier Sophie 2: The Alchemist of the Mysterious Dream a 6/10 for its decent story but the gameplay made it enjoyable for the most part.~

_childDocuments_.review: So if you're familiar with the atelier series you already know most of what to expect. Relevant points for people who play these games, there are significant quality improvements in this game in terms of graphics, the fast travel is unlocked early and is fairly designed, the port is great and runs well. In terms of combat mechanics, its about as good as turn based gets with a mixture of mechanics from Firis and Sophie along with some of the things Ryza did well. One drawback is that you cannot do charged swings against trees like Ryza but otherwise the gathering is arguably easier and even comes with fun mini games.Besides this we get to beat up a cute butterfly goddess so thats a huge bonus point.

_childDocuments_.review: To me, Atelier Sophie 2 has shown an all round improvement in terms of combat flow, synthesizing, and a new form of exploration system that brings simple puzzle experiences that does not hinder one's progression . Similar to older titles of Atelier games such as Lydie & Suelle and the beginning of Sophie, it heavily focuses on the aspect of gathering and synthesizing, unlocking recipes or making key/items to progress through the story, and utilizing different materials to bring out the best of your equipment for your party. As combat (turn-based) and exploration/story still plays a big role, it acts as a secondary toppings to the core of this game, of being an alchemist synthesizing and mixing whatever great traits/quality materials you have gathered from your adventure. It was enjoyable and engaging when every item or equipment I decide to make brings me to think and formulate ways of putting down tetris-like patterns on the board and min-maxing their ability traits, and it gets even challenging as catalysts are introduced and the board expands. I'm not exaggerating when on average I could last mins to an hour synthesizing one item, and I definitely enjoyed it.I'm a fan of Atelier games and I've played a lot of its series, and there are moments I would love if the combat could have been more engaging, the monsters could be more unique, especially against bosses. If you are looking for that, Atelier Ryza 1 or 2 could be a better option in terms of that aspect. However, if you love to experience the world of being an alchemist, overpowering items and equipment, apart from this title, older titles as mentioned are also some that I would recommend as well!All in All, a 8/10 for a great sequel experience of Sophie's unexpected adventure into the Land of Dreams.

_childDocuments_.review: I can't recommend this. 80% of the "game" is spent watching cutscenes. There are seriously places where it's 30 seconds or less between cutscenes. You enter a building, and get a cutscene. You walk through a door and get another cutscene. Which might have been ok, except that the story has some of the worst writing I've ever seen in any medium, ever, game or otherwise. It's one contrivance and coincidence after another. Flashbacks to things that happened mere minutes ago, people suddenly remembering that they run an alchemy store after you, the alchemist, have been adventuring with them for days, people randomly walking up the moment they're needed, etc.Even the problems to be solved tend to be monumentally stupid. For example, there's a huge quest chain where you're looking for somebody and get blocked by a waist-deep river with some boxes by it. Neither you nor the other alchemist in the party have any idea what the boxes are, but action-girl remembers that she saw the person your'e after use those boxes that one time to stop the rain. You go back to the guild, and everybody knows all about these alchemy-rain-stopping boxes except for the alchemists, and they explain that you need some super rare recharging tool to recharge the boxes, and nobody knows where to find them. A guy who is also not an alchemist walks in right that second and mentions that he has the item you need and gives it to you...but oops, the recharging item needs to be recharged with some rocks that only an alchemist can do that. Suddenly you remember that you know how to make the rock you need to recharge the boxes you had no clue what they were for. You make the rocks and recharge the item and use it to recharge the boxes...which makes the rain stop. Instantly the river dries up and you can cross. Oh, and now you can make rocks to recharge boxes whenever you want, no special item needed anymore, and these boxes suddenly exist all over the place whenever you need to raise or lower a river.This is immediately followed by a mountain pass that you can't get through because a dragon attacked a caravan travelling through it. Does the dragon stop you? Do you have to level up and fight it later? No, of course not. The dragon's already gone, but during the battle he knocked some bags off the caravan, and the bags are blocking your path. So you can't simply help move them, so you'll just have to come back later, never mind the fact that the bags are also waist-high and have huge visible gaps between them.That was about when I gave up on the game.I'll grant that the alchemy minigame is mildly interesting, Drop shapes on a field and try to line up special symbols, score better to make better equipment. But it seems kind of useless, because combat is easy and mostly optional. You can walk around most monsters in the game, and boss fights are easy enough that after 7 hours of play I've yet to lose a battle even though it took me four hours to figure out how to equip anything and I haven't bothered leveling because I can walk around everything that isn't a boss.As a plus, none of the characters are unlikable. This is basically a "cute girls doing cute things" slice-of-life anime, with little bits of running around and easy battles in between. If that's what you want, you might like it. But don't buy this expecting much of a game. Or much of a story.

_childDocuments_.review: My only previous knowledge of Atelier was Ryza 1 and 2 which I loved, so I thought I’d jump into the Sophie games when Sophie 2 was released. I played through 1 first as 2 was a direct continuation of it, but unfortunately, I wasn't a fan of Sophie 1. It was extremely dull and boring, and about 16 hours in I decided enough was enough (a certain red enemy that autoheals for 200HP) and ploughed through the rest of the game to complete it. I was debating whether I should even play Sophie 2, if it was going to be much of the same I wouldn’t. But I gave it a shot and ♥♥♥♥ it’s so much better, the world is beautiful and feels more alive, characters are so expressive and the cutscenes are well made in general. I finished Sophie 1 in 20 hours, and I’m only 20 hours into Sophie 2 and I feel like I’m barely halfway in! Definitely didn’t need to play 1 to enjoy this game, there’s a intro on the main menu which covers the first game, though I do appreciate the few mentions to the characters and world from the first game thanks to playing it firstThe devs must have jumped into Erde Wiege to find a PC from the future to test this on though because performance is all over the place – on an RX 6700xt I can easily reach 120+ inside, and about 70-90 in the main open areas on all high, but there are occasional stutters and framerate dips seemingly out of nowhere. Don’t even think about running this on a Deck: with a 30FPS cap, lower resolution and everything on low it still manages to go lower than 30 sometimes, stutters like crazy, and draws a lot of power. (Edit: actually after further testing it runs okish and looks decent with FSR, but def would rather play on my actual PC) Also, the antialiasing in the game settings is complete garbage, no AA looks a lot better imoAll in all blew my expectations away coming from Sophie 1 and Pirka is adorableEdit: Just finished the game, honestly it was great, glad I played it. The ending felt a bit iffy to me, not sure where to pinpoint it, but overall I liked it!

_childDocuments_.review: The management of crafting and combat is very nice intuitive and pleasant and offers many spaces for replayability.The only weak points that I noticed are the management of the recipe: the unlocking of many of which (especially in the late game) are linked to items that are dropped by unique monsters (and up to here I'm also fine) but that appear in random missions, and the inability to automatically unlock old recipes if you know an already advanced one e.g. the old recipe remain locked until you perform the certain Synthesis/Gather some material you already have to unlock them. _childDocuments_.review: This review is PoV: 18 hours into the game and done but will probably finish it in the future once I'm bored enough.I played this after Ryza 1 & 2 because many were saying it's better than both, only to find that such people were all shills. Everything in the game is worse than Ryza 1.Ryza 1 alchemy was a simple loop with a lot of depth. You could eventually break the system entirely which was half the fun. Sophie's alchemy feels far more on rails; you have to play Tetris with your elemental values instead of just dropping items into loops which while fun at first becomes just annoying later where you need to have X amount of lightning and you want the shapes to match so you can fill your whole Tetris  board. Even then, doing optimal alchemy in Sophie is nearly irrelevant.The best item you can make in Sophie is the items base stats + the stats from 2 ingots + (some) stats from elemental value + some stats from traits - that's 90 damage. It's very easy to make the optimal weapon. Meanwhile in Ryza you could eventually break the alchemy system entirely and make +500 all stat weapons through Loop Morph and optimizing the materials.Ryza alchemy was simple in idea but complex in the sense that you had to gather specific materials, craft specific alchemy ingredients (eg. Effect Spread) to optimize recipes to optimize other recipes. By playing it smart, you could break the system progressively more throughout the game which was half the enjoyment for me.Sophie's is really just "gather random ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that kind of fits the criteria of this item". Eg. You want to get grass with lightning, but you can't directly control how the lightning is spread out on the Tetris board so you just kind of get a bunch of grass and hope it works out. It feels bad, the Tetris board is okay at first but just limiting later, and the limits of Sophie alchemy are unbreakable. You will make the 90 damage item and that's it.Learning new recipes in Sophie is also just "pick up random ingredient and fight specific monster." Ryza's Recipe Morph made way more sense overall, and Ryza's skill tree was  actually mattered tbh.Progressing through Ryza's alchemy made sense. You make a Crystal Element with (Gemstones) and Effect Spread +2. It's useful in every recipe that has (Gemstones). Meanwhile Sophie's is like, you make a (Poisons) item with 5 Wind element in an U-shape. It's now useful in... Recipes that need (Poisons) and Wind and other materials that fit the Tetris board with the U-shape. It never really felt like you got a significant item, just kind of "side-grades that kind of work in the right situation".Combat feels bad mainly because it's just item spam. Playing Ryza on Very Hard, you'd run up against a boss, go craft the best gear you can right now and some utility items like Ice Bombs to slow the boss and you'd just barely beat it. It felt like everything matters.Meanwhile in Sophie, you have no CC limit on your items meaning you can just zerg them. You run up against a boss, go back to craft the best gear only to realize it doesn't matter because the boss has an aura. The only optimal way to break the aura is to make 6x () and spam them every single turn. No CC limit means no punishment for just spamming your bombs, and once the boss's aura breaks, how do you punish the boss while stunned? By spamming more bombs. Gear is only to keep you alive and farm low level enemies.Auras are a boring cancer mechanic that forces you to spam the opposite element of the aura or deal 0 damage, then once the enemy is stunned it takes super damage so you just burst it with bombs. Seeing an aura ruins every single fight, and you guessed it, every single fight has an aura!I remember thinking Ryza should've been turn-based as that would've made the game more strategic. Sophie 2 is turn-based but the combat is so trash it's actually 3 letter grades worse than Ryza's system.The world feels far more hollow in Sophie. It's a random isekai land with no NPC's of note. The main characters are fun, sure, but surrounded by nothing but props. Ryza had a lot of irrelevant NPC's as well, but it didn't feel hollow the same way Sophie does. The other issue is the world is too large and you progress through it too fast, which makes memorizing materials and specific monsters also irrelevant. You just wing it through all areas and gather what you happen to get while running through. Years after playing Ryza 1 I still remember many of the mini-bosses and items found in areas because you actually had to learn those things.Story is okay, it's far too "♥♥♥♥ it we ball" for me though. You go to Isekai World only for everyone to group up with you instantly and breeze through situations with bizarre reactions. eg. A jellyfish monster slowly floating away from you? Let's go back to alchemize Monster Bait to keep it in place. "Oh Sophie, can you go and alchemize an item to break down dimensional barriers real quick?" The story is probably the main reason people recommend this game, and it's okay, just okay.The important characters are okay but just kind of fall flat overall compared to Ryza 1. There's also less of them, eg. there's 3 non-playable characters you actually care about. Ryza 1 & 2 had far more.No one has human dialogue in this game. It's painfully apparent in some cutscenes, but more or less on par for the course for these games. Still, Ryza characters felt far more human and reacted to whatever is going on somewhat understandably.It also feels even lazier than Ryza did in animations and that kind of stuff. Sophie ate some food, they CBA to make the food or even an artwork of the supposed food in the game.The new mechanics in Sophie 2 are all kind of just annoying, like the weather system just forces you to stock up on weather change items and go through every map multiple times with multiple weathers at multiple spots. Oh there's a treasure chest under water here, you now have to run back halfway through the map to turn the weather to sunny to clear the water, then run back. It's unnecessary complexity that just makes it harder to keep track of the few things that actually matter.I especially hate how nothing in the game is retroactive. You're constantly learning recipes by going back somewhere to re-discover an ingredient you already found before, or crafting a recipe you already crafted before. You can't do multiple character talent quests like "Use X ability 10 times" at once either, but slowly one at a time. If you enjoyed Ryza 1 for the systems and alchemy, play Ryza 2. If you only cared for the story and vibe, I guess Sophie 2 is okay for you. For me personally, this really feels like it was released 5 years before Ryza 1, not after it. It can't even compare overall to Ryza 1 as a whole package, and I thought Ryza 2 was boring but it was still much better than Sophie 2.There's clearly a psyop of people shilling for this game. I know not their long-term plan for such action. Anyone who actually enjoyed the alchemy and combat in Ryza 1 & 2 can't possibly enjoy Sophie 2.

_childDocuments_.review: I played 21 hours in two days, yes I recommend it.Edit: Although since making this review, I think Sophie 2 is not good for beginners because of the high variability of grinding for materials; if you want something more consistent I would recommend a different game like Ryza or Ayesha.Jokes aside, it's very addictive and the crafting music is great. _childDocuments_.review: I am writing this review as a first-time Atelier player. To be honest I didn't really know what to expect, but unfortunately the first half hour of the game was enough to tell me this just isn't for me. I just really dislike how slow-paced the game is. Firstly your character is as slow as molasses relative to how large the environments are. I suspected something was off when I saw they were actually selling running speed as DLC (no joke, look at the Digital Deluxe version features), and as it turns out your base speed being obscenely slow is simply due to malevolence rather than incompetence. But that's not all. Characters will talk endlessly and say so little--60% of every conversation can be safely ignored. I'm fine with slice of life but that should come with interesting characters with interesting things to say--this game rides so hard on its moe aesthetic that I guess it's just supposed to make up for the bland dialogue and characters. Yeah the girls are cute but how long can I be expected to endure their one-note innocent kawaii 10-year-old shtick and not get a little tired of it? And would it kill them to include honorifics in the translations? If you're not going to have an English dub, just go all the way and keep the translations literal. The more dissonance between what the characters say vs. what the translations say, the less immersed I am and the less I can transpose the character's Japanese voice to the English words on the screen in my head.Ok now moving on to the graphics--they're not very good. The game looks like a PS3 game. I wasn't expecting a masterpiece but if you're selling the game for $60, it should look nice right? It's actually really jarring because, while the lighting system looks fairly modern, the geometry and textures are easily from 10 years ago if not more. Anyways I'm half an hour in and experienced no gameplay, and I figure I won't even really be in the gameplay loop until 5-6 hours into the game, at which point it's too late to refund. Sorry but I'm not taking that chance. This one is probably best left for the fans. Any newcomers who are interested in buying this game--even if the gameplay seems appealing, you will have to deal with an RPG that is slow in pacing and generally uninteresting. If you're ok trading substance for saccharine character interactions, i.e. you just want to turn your brain off, this might be worth checking out. So what's the takeaway? Am I stamping my feet, demanding the next entry in this series to cater more to me? No. Who am I to come into a niche series with an existing fanbase and say it should change? It shouldn't. It's just not for me, and I'm happy for Atelier fans who get to celebrate another entry in their franchise. I just think it's good for prospective buyers to get an opinion from someone who was new to the series who did not like it. I think most should steer clear, maybe steer clear of Koei Tecmo as a whole as they seem more than content to fleece their customer base (seriously--there's the Atlus tax, then there's these guys).

_childDocuments_.review: 5.1 out of 10, yeah it was a close call between a positive and a negative review.There's so much to like in this game. It has great characters. A very enjoyable story filled with positive messages. Beautiful music and artwork. A challenging battle system that you can use synthesis to overcome the challenges of.The game and the community that supports it have their challenges though. Most of my frustration involves the random elements surrounding synthesis. I could not find any guides (let alone good guides) on strategy for placing components on the synthesis grid. I was eventually able to piece together bits of several posts to understand how to leverage assist skills and the restricted panel to be able to perfect many of the recipes, but when it came to a few end game items I couldn't find any way around the major gathering mini games. I'm old and I am incapable of any amount of success in those mini games. The only way I could see to achieve items with the number of the correct elements with enough link stars on them was by playing the mini games.  I had perfect seeds with perfect quality, and utilized element lv +3 and element lv Max +3 every chance I could but there were still some recipes that I wasn't able to perfect because I didn't have enough link stars. The random chance of rare items dropping from seeds caused me also considerable frustration. I would find myself needing a high quality rare item to complete a recipe and when I'd try and get it from seeds it sometimes took over 100 attempts to get the item (I noticed that the same rare items never seemed to be in short supply after I no longer needed one, I felt like the game knew what I needed and was withholding it). Super Success, what a pain. There's a super success gauge that's supposed to represent the probability of getting a super success at the end of synthesis, but even though I regularly had the gauge above 90% my success rate was about 6 out of 10. I found myself save scumming my synthesis so I didn't waste components when the RNG was mean to me.Synthesis and gathering should have been the stress free safe haven that could be retreated too if the stress of battle became too much and I needed a break. Instead they were in their own way even more of a frustration than the challenges of battle (not that that was much of a challenge once I used seeds to defeat traits and built decent equipment).If random number generation was more accurate and if there was some path to synthesise around the mini games, This game would have been a 9 or 10 out of 10.It's a nice game, probably worth a play for most people, but not as enjoyable for me as the Ryza series (all three of those are an 11 out of 10 for me). Good luck, and I hope you enjoy the game if you decide to play.

_childDocuments_.review: Yes I recommend this, it's the best crafting system in the Mysterious series. However it doesn't get over the central problem that series had, namely the total lack of plot and uneven combat.Pros:- Crafting system. I'm not sure if I prefer Ryza's loop system or this one, but for what it's worth this is the best the mysterious system has.- Gameplay tweaks. I might be imagining it but I think they have taken some gameplay ideas from Ryza and applied them here. They work well and help exploration.- Fast Travel. You get it early and it's everywhere.- Sophie/Plachta. This dynamic makes up for a ton of story and character flaws. It's so strong, especially when the 'plot' get's going.Cons:- Story. Yeah I was never going to like this prequel business but even considering that it's not got the plot or worldbuilding the Ryza series had, nor does it have the small, central goal and lack of plot the mysterious series had. What you're left with is some loose nonsense and a ton of small cut scenes which break flow.- Side characters. The mysterious series never really cared about its side characters, this isn't any different. They're fun and ok, but this is no Ryza.- Combat. The turn based system works, but basic enemies are easy and bosses are a real challenge, so I'm already in this weird position where I rarely bother with combat unless I have to because it's boring. It's uneven, though as I say the powerful enemies/bosses are where it shines. It's shame 90% of the combat is against boring peons.Overall this is recommended for fans of the series, but I still prefer Ryza by miles. The crafting system is what saves it.

_childDocuments_.review: I also have specific complaints about the design of certain core elements, which have a significant effect on the gameplay during your first playthrough. The issues I have in mind are the invisible walls on the maps, the alchemy system/gameplay during the early stages of the game, and the amount of backtracking required to progress. These are just some of the issues I will address in this review.The alchemy part of the game itself feels very good once you’ve reached the later stages of the story, but it is too restrictive during the early stages. In the early parts of the game, you do not have access to the catalysts, which I consider the core component of AS2’s alchemy system, holding AS2 together with all the other content the game has to offer. It's acceptable not to have access to them until the later stages, but missing out on the core part of alchemy until around 50% into the game’s story is quite disappointing.Another issue I've noticed in AS2 is the amount of backtracking required to progress in the story. This is primarily due to the introduction of the weather devices as a core mechanic. The amount of moving back and forth needed to solve the weather device puzzles becomes tiresome when you don't have access to a set warp location yet.Combat is another crucial aspect when playing a JRPG. If I have to summarize how AS2 handles it, unfortunately, I have to say that Koei missed the mark on this one. To put it simply, it sucks. I would even recommend playing on easy mode just to minimize interaction with it. The game’s aura combat mechanic feels stale and slow, which becomes very boring throughout your playthrough. The aura numbers themselves are not bad, but the sheer amount you have to go through during your first playthrough is the main problem. After a certain point in the story, every fight encounter will have such an enemy, which significantly reduces the game’s combat pace, making it unenjoyable. Personally, I would prefer fewer enemies with set combat mechanics, but with higher aura numbers, to make this mechanic feel more special.Firstly, the game’s atmosphere is amazing. I had such a great vibe while playing it. The atmosphere of the various areas you explore to progress the story is phenomenal! The music and the overall buildup of each area are amazing to experience. Additionally, the music in each area is really good! While I wouldn’t consider it the best Atelier OST out there, it is solid overall.The story and side stories are what you would expect from playing an Atelier game. Slice of life, comedy, soft shoujo ai vibes, and a main plot with a secondary b-plot caused by the main story plot. This is what you could consider a certified Atelier classic. Because of this, there isn't much to say about it. The game contains what the franchise has always offered, and I'm completely fine with that.Another improvement I noticed in AS2 is the reduced number of cutscenes that can occur at once compared to the previous Atelier games cough cough Atelier Lydie & Suelle cough cough Atelier Firis. This is overall really pleasant to witness. It's nice that we don't have to endure four cutscenes in a row during your first playthrough, but only one or two occasionally. However, this also has a slight downside, as it makes you feel slightly less connected with the characters in the story, aside from the ones the story is centered around. But to be fair, one can't have it all, and it is what it is.One thing I particularly enjoyed while playing AS2, aside from the alchemy post-story, was the different character designs showcased throughout the story. As expected from a game involving time travel, it is awesome to see characters with distinct aesthetics. Each main character looks great and unique, adding another layer to the game's atmosphere, which is truly enjoyable.

_childDocuments_.review: I have to say I really enjoyed this.The locations were pretty, and the music was awesome. I particularly liked the theme for Thunderbolt Palace.This is the 3rd Atelier game I've played, the first two being Sophie 1, and Ryza 1. As expected of a sequel, it plays much more like Sophie 1 than Ryza 1. Sophie was 16 at the start of Sophie 1, and is 19 for this game, so timeline-wise, it takes place not long before the "original sequel" Firis.Every item, piece of equip, and monster, all have commentary from the characters for them in the in-game listing, which can be pretty entertaining to read. It was actually pretty disappointing to realize when I'd all but filled that listing, since it meant the end of the game was near.I had two very minor complaints. One was that while every other place in the game had a menu detail on the world map, listing which enemies and items were present, in what rarity, in each available weather type, the Heartscapes did not get such a listing, so it was much harder to keep track of what could be obtained there. Even the bonus area from the Atelier Plachta DLC had its own listing, but not the 2 Heartscapes. Pretty annoying.The other minor complaint was that several of the achieves were pretty grindy for me, such as planting enough seeds to get all the greenhouses, and then waiting out the time needed to harvest every type of seed from each type of greenhouse. Crafting enough to get both Sophie and Plachta up to 99 Alchemy level was also pretty tedious.All in all, it was a great time. I think it would be fun, in future games, to see what happened to the various supporting characters after the end of this game, especially since they officially came from all times and places. Hearing the commentary from the voice actors (game completion bonus), from the point of having finished recording, but not yet being able to play it themselves, was also fun.I can see myself playing it again at some point, though next I'll either finish off Ryza (~85% done), or restart Sophie 1 (50% done).

_childDocuments_.review: I played Atelier Ryza 2 along with this game and can confidently say this is by far the better game.There are obvious comparisons between the two, most of the icons are the same, the art style is the same.The exploration I felt was better in Ryza 2, you could pretty much go anywhere, could crawl (ohhhh yeah) and had a mount for moving around faster. In Sophie 2 there are invisible walls everywhere and a moronic weather system that brings nothing to the game other than annoyance.The alchemy is superior in this game, rather than relying just on item quality now items have tetris like blocks that you need to put in place to get the most out of any particular item. The depth of this crafting system cannot be understated, you can make a normal item, or an awesome item, or anywhere in between based on the items you use, the quality of the items, and your attention to detail in the tetris grid.They seem to have reduced the number of cutscenes. It's still feels intrusive rather than bringing anything of value to the game (instead of thousands there are still hundreds), but it doesn't feel anywhere near as annoying as in Ryza.The combat in this game is far superior. Rather than a quasi realtime nonsense in Ryza they've opted for a much better turn based system with link attacks. Even though you'd think turn-based might result in slower combat you'd be surprised. Combat in this game is much quicker and smoother. You're not sitting around waiting for a "it's your go" gauge to fill like in Ryza.In summary the game still has some issues, they could easily reduce the number of cutscenes to 5% of what they are now and nothing of value would be lost. After the 10 hour mark I literally skipped every single cutscene and still knew exactly what was going on just from the TLDR mission screen. All in all though I'd recommend as it's pretty good.Hopefully for Ryza/Sophie 3 they're more like this game than the former, and they blend the exploration of Ryza with the crafting/combat of Sophie.

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely one of the best Ateliers maybe the best if you aren't into some of the changes the Ryza games introduced. It combines the more 'modern' feel of the Ryza games with some of elements of the more traditional Atelier games. Gameplay -- This one doesn't have real time battles as it returns to the older turn based system before the Ryza games. The big new mechanic that they added is the aura system in battles. Essentially you have to use certain types of attacks or items to break the enemy's aura faster and if you don't break it, you don't do any damage. It works well and is balanced well for higher difficulties and bosses. You have to manage the whole party's items more. You also have to think about the the positioning of the characters, whether you want them in combat or in support. I think the aura system is a better implementation of a 'weakness' effect in these games. Specifically, I'm talking about Persona and Octopath, where the weakness system in those game take center stage and it almost becomes a chore to manage because you are not playing the 'right' way if you are not exploiting weaknesses. However, the auras do have a downside and its that they don't just apply to bosses, random enemies also have this mechanic which just wastes your time to be honest. This actually creates a bad gameplay loop because you need to waste more items/mp in combat when you are just farming, and then you also need to farm for more currency as well because you need to replenesh the items you just used.Story -- Like Ryza 1 & 2 or even Lydie really, there is an actual plot and plot progression. The older Ateliers (before Lydie) don't really have a cohesive plot, and stuff just kind of happens and you go along with the ride, which is fine, but there is just more of a story this time around where you can follow along. You don't need to have played the other mysterious games to enjoy this, but you will be more appreciative of the older games, mainly Sophie 1,  if you have played them before this one. If you've ever played the Tales games, its like Berseria making Zestiria better because you are able to put certain plot elements that seem unimportant in context.

_childDocuments_.review: An overall successful sequel to what is one of the best Atelier games ever made. Not as good as the original, but in the same ball park. Here are what I thought some of the pros and cons were:Pros:Combat was very fun in this game. I'm usually not a huge fan of turn based combat but the addition of barriers and the variety of skills this game offers among characters and their combos really made it engaging.The addition of changing the weather to environments was also really cool. it helped in combat like in Atelier Lydie and Suelle, but also exploration was impacted as well on maps. This does have a slight downside that I'll get to in the ConsSide characters are as charming as ever, and I really enjoy doing their side quests and getting to know them.Graphics in this game are very good for an atelier game, and the sound track is one of the best.Main story was actually really good unlike Ryza 2. The ending struck me in the feels which I did not expect, even more than Lydie and Suelle. It was coherent and progressed wellThe variety and how upgradable the catalysts for the cauldron are makes for convenient synthesis and more thought into which catalyst you should use.Cons:Though the addition of weather is cool, it does make exploring some maps tedious. These maps are big, and there tend to be 3 - 4 subsections in each map.They tried to use more dramatic shots for cut scenes, but it was like a child with a brand new toy. It was a bit much to see a zoom in to someone's grin for dramatic effect every time, or to the fireplace.I know it's an atelier game but the friendship is magic and believing in each other dialogue was reeeeeeally over the top in this game. just made some of the key cutscenes a little less interesting to watch.Having to level up the Alchemy level of both Sophie and Plachta was a bit tedious.I wish it scaled in difficulty like in the original Mysterious trilogy. The only difficulty spike was somewhat 3/4th the way through the game and other than that you really didn't have to worry about losing a fight.Items didn't feel as engaging in this game, though still useful. You could really get by with just skills alone in this game.Overall solid game, definitely worthy of being a sequel to Sophie. The ending was just spectacular, and you get so much gameplay in the main story alone.

_childDocuments_.review: Yet another wonderful experience from the Atelier series. I've left reviews on a couple others, but I may as well restate what I said in those reviews here.First and foremost, Atelier is a different breed of JRPG. Most JRPGs center around chosen heroes fighting to save the world, but Atelier is a bit more humble. Ultimately, Atelier games are meant to relax, stow away your worries, and spend dozens of hours gathering materials and making gear and items with an exceptional crafting system. Though combat can be fun, most of your strength will be gained by creating powerful equipment so you can bash through whatever challenges are in your way.Atelier Sophie 2 is a prime example of an Atelier game. Each party member has their own dream, and they bond together as friends as they work together to achieve those. Combat and crafting are interspersed with many scenes to get to know the characters, and the story is as heartfelt as ever from this series. The previous entries of Atelier Ryza and Atelier Ryza 2 were a bit experimental, but Atelier Sophie 2 feels like a return to form for this long-running series (it's almost as old as me, if you count Japan-exclusive entries that never got localized).If you like pretty aesthetics, relaxation, and a crafting system you'll spend more time in than the rest of the game combined, you'll like any Atelier title, and Atelier Sophie 2 shines as a perfect example of the little things that have made the series one of my favorites, ever since I first picked up Atelier Escha and Logy many years ago.

_childDocuments_.review: Ryza was my first Atelier game and while I thought the alchemy and world were really (really) well done, I just never really got attached to Ryza. She is the driving force of this game and I am immediately going to go play the original Sophie game, and probably Lydie & Suelle because I hear Sophie is playable there too. I can see why she won the popularity poll in Japan that got this sequel made. She's just a joy to be around. Without her character being as strong as it is my interest in the game might have slipped a bit. I felt the alchemy was a bit simplistic compared to Ryza, but it was plenty of fun to craft anyway. _childDocuments_.review: Picking up Atelier Sophie 2 I anticipated a focused, plot driven, signposted experience (in line with how Atelier has been evolving since Lulua). Guilty on all three counts the result is perhaps the most approachable entry in the series yet - one that will not disorient regular JRPG players, and will delight if you're after a bright and cheerful, yet solid experience. Bright and cheer aside Atelier Sophie (first entry) was none of the above; more chill, less predictable, more lived-in, it did a ton with so much less; and like many other Atelier games, succeeded at creating a sense of freedom and serendipity that seems to be disappearing in the process of going bigger, and going mainstream.Isekai-wise Sophie 2 offers a meek rendition which frankly does no justice to the theme; this coming from the maker of Blue Reflection 2, clearly is a choice (but why???); world kinda big but shallow - no lore, barely anybody to talk to outside Roytale.Unsure about future direction, but for now I still recommend this game; the crafting is truly awesome, and the battle system is everything a modern TBRPG should be (raise difficulty whenever you stop feelin it).

_childDocuments_.review: My goodness... I have played many many games here on steam. I have hundreds of hours in games like Rimworld, Oxygen not Included, Skyrim, ect. And I have to say... This game has drawn me in like no game has for a long long time. The alchemy system is easily my favorite part. You can go out and collect all sorts of material, and each material - including duplicates - are very often completely different. The game is super clever with the game progress of such materials as well. You often have to make one item in order to craft another. And there are qualities and traits that can transfer through the crafting trees, leading to endless combinations of traits, and stats for equipment and items. Combat is super satisfying as well. Brings me back to the FFX days. Getting to try out a newly crafted OP item and seeing it wipe the floor with the enemies is quite satisfying.On that note, this game WILL give back in difficulty what you put into it. I finished the game on Very Hard on my first play through ---- without losing a single battle. But I am a puzzle nut, and I put a lot of time into upgrading equipment and crafting items. There is a difficulty beyond hard, but I have yet to try it as of this review. Long story short, the game can be as hard as you want it to be- depending on just how much alchemy you want to do.I don't know how this compares to the other games in the Universe as this was my first one, but as other have said, I could see this easily being the best. If you love exploration, puzzles, and Turn-Based Combat, this is a MUST.

_childDocuments_.review: I would like to touch upon three big topics that I feel cover the majority of this game and will give both new and veterans a quick glance and what Sophie two has to offer. Story, Crafting, Combat. In that order of what I feel is prioritized by the game to you as you play. The story and how it supports the other aspects of the game, Crafting changes and how it elongates without essentially changing anything, and the changes to combat from Sophie 1. As a more direct Sequel compared to Finris what will you get with Sophie 2? Well if you enjoyed Platcha and Sophie before this is wonderfully more of that. The teacher student dynamic between the two get swapped in a bizarre way which leads to a new lens to view them thru. We get to learn more about Sophie's Grandmother and her roll which is wonderfully sweet. The cast as usual is lovable even the two I thought at the start "OMG Snow and Edgy the hedgy dear god no." Yet by the end I was crafting not for stats for myself to continue on, but I was gonna make a sword that could cleave the planet for my friend to help him achieve his dream. Speaking of dreams. It would be poor of me to not address the lazy way the get the story going. The over arcing setup honestly was just an excuse to get these chars to this situation so you can explore their lives in this new setting. I forgot about it till I read my notes, but at the start and end it does hit the immersion. However, since it does bring some really touching Sophie and family moments that can melt your heart I do forgive it. So the Crafting then the main gameplay loop you will be sucked into and spending most of your time doing! How has it changed from Sophie 1. Well.... it's gotten longer. Not necessarily more complex or even harder. The materials you gather now will have a variety of shapes, colours, amount of components up to four which can also vary in colour, traits, and specific link parts in the shapes to connect. You also get the same cauldrons just in different forms. What this all equals too is it will most likely take you longer to gather specific parts with the specific shapes, colours, amount of links, and traits you want and need to pass on. See it isn't harder, but it will take longer if you aim for specific things on specific items. It also means a lot more materials you will have around and have to shuffle thru to find the ones you want. The filter/sort system is decent, but lacks sort by links which was the one I wanted the most almost 99% of the time. You do make this up somewhat by gathering a LOT more boasting a massive basket and I honestly never cleaned my garbage. (Except when I failed a mini game particularly poorly then they hit the ground.) So in the end Crafting is longer, but if you could do it in Sophie 1 then nothing here is gonna give you grief. Combat this part hurts me, but I personally feel they downgraded the combat. I was really hoping they would have taken the previous turn system in Sophie one and really worked being able to move around the turns based on attacks to make chaining easier. They instead just made a link attack gauge that lets you choose when to do so. This means now the turn order is just listed with no blanks. Seems like an odd thing to draw attention to, but I honestly thought the haste/speed up didn't work in this game for around 40 hours. See if you use a speed/low wait move, but it doesn't do enough to over take another person on the turn order it will seem like nothing happens. On top of the huge amount of buffs Debuffs tossed around constantly it can be hard planning out turns on a stunned enemy much less understand the skill is working. That being said you will never need that level of precision. I played on Very hard and ... this game's combat is kind of a joke. I've never wiped and only had two deaths. 80 hours in I had tier one gear and tier 2 bombs. I was waiting for a reason to craft some new gear, but even on Very hard nothing till post game hit me for enough to make me feel the need to craft the next item. Just raw stats and HP on my gear no dragon blessings no demon bombs. Just the tier 2 bombs and Stew to heal. This is particularly disappointing as the crafting allows for some amazing mixes and ideas. I just want a reason to actually do so. Thankfully the characters were so likable I did find myself doing so in the end over the silly things. Olias got a elbow scratch on a job. I made him Dragon god armor and a F-off cannon with auto heals so I knew he was safe. Edgy the hedgy is after a dragon. I lost 3 hours failing at swords to get one I felt was worth it. I bring it up cause it is a positive point in the games favour that it has characters to drive you to do so. Just the combat itself does not till post where it just nonsense anyways. TLDR; Sophie 2 gives you more slice of life scenario with Sophie Platcha and a cast of new friends. The crafting may be longer, but all the good bits are there and it does feel good to just nail everything perfectly and it all comes together. Many unique ways to deliver devastation though the combat even on Very hard will not ask that level of you till post game. -1 points for removing the Jump voice line. You know the one. Sophie 2 is an easy recommendation for those who are still new to the Atelier Series and want more Sophie! No time limits just lovely fun. When you are done Give Finris a Try and tell her Fayt said hi!

_childDocuments_.review: The game is brimming with potential. I love how laid back, simple, and stress-free it is--yet, at its core it offers so much. The alchemy is by far the most addictive part and the depth you can get into is is awesome. It's not just "adding ingredients", you can specify which traits of said ingredients you want focused on during the mixing. It's so fun to improve quality/level of gear, the series does great on that.I actually really liked the free-flow of combat from Ryza 2 (played on Playstation), but going back to the turn base hasn't been a hindrance whatsoever. The combat is a blast and the combos feel amazing. I'm still working on itemization for each character, but the gest of comboing attacks, both in offense and defense and in element weakness/strengths feels so good to watch unfold.The game is centric upon relationships between the world and its characters and Sophie. If you can get over or into the anime-style art, I highly recommend if you're like me and enjoy a game that you really can just chill through. The progression is just enough to where you're unlocking new stuff throughout the game. I have really come to appreciate the Atelier series, even if my first entry was Ryza 2 and now Sophie 2. I feel like the mechanics behind this game have absolutely so much potential and man alive I'd love to see them expand into creature collecting late/end game. Just like gathering enough new materials unlocks more alchemy, to have it where fighting enough of a creature allows you to capture and farm its resource and that eventually lead into taming/assigning fetch quests (similar to Ryza 2) with intent on eventually becoming an alchemy monster collector xD #dreams

_childDocuments_.review: I'm really enjoying this game. I'm a huge Atelier fan and this has been quite fun. I really like the Atelier games that have brought back old story lines and characters. If you haven't drained yourself of the series and played the first Sophie game, I do highly recommend. The art style is absolutely amazing, best graphics so far. Great turn-based combat, with lots of fun combos. Synthesising is refreshing but a lot easier to forge good items, and it's simple to understand. I really do hope to see some major character/enemy design updates in the future though. I have been playing these games since Rorona and if I see one more horned rabbit I'm going to lose it! I get it too, things like Puni are a staple but please give us some more monster variety! They are all the same! Every game!

_childDocuments_.review: I do have to say that I'm glad i got to play this. Gust did a superb job with a lot of the refined aspects of this game compared to previous titles. Wasn't entirely the best in some ways, however the best parts more than outshone the negatives. I think that the worst that I could say about the game is that the alchemy puzzles were getting to the point of way too complex for me, it was a pain in the ass to grind out requirements for certain recipes, and it started sliding towards grindy in the last quarter of the game in that regard, without a lot of things to drive you forward to filling out the recipe book.All in all, I wanted more Atelier Sophie gameplay, and I got it in spades. _childDocuments_.review: This game is both a great follow-up to the first game, and an awesome modern Atelier.  Hell, it's probably one of the best of the series, period.  The game looks incredible (the character models especially).  The only complaint I'd have in this department is that I feel there is less Event Art than in Sophie, and previous Atelier games I've played.  I wish there was more.The world this game takes place in was really cool.  It was both a smart idea, using it to make the game fit nearly in the timeline of the Mysterious saga (Probably, I haven't played Fyris or Lydie/Suelle yet).  The weather system is really creative, and part of me wishes it would be possible in future titles.  The interconnected world is fun to explore and complete objectives in.  ...Mostly.  Near the end of the game, I got tired of trying to remember what way to traverse the map in order to get to a specific spot, since changing the weather can change what paths are open and closed.  Alchemy is the most fun as it's ever been.  The puzzle alchemy is so much fun to try and make happen.  I've spent hours just tetris-ing the best configurations of some items to get certain traits.  It's so much fun.  This game probably contains my favorite Atelier battle system, too.  I love the ability to include your entire party in battles directly, it's a really smart system.  And I love when these games allow you to use items with non-alchemist party members, too.And the story...  Kind of one the weaker side as far as Atelier games go.  This world's logic is kind of wishy-washy sometimes, and the ability to magically solve an issue with alchemy kind of goes beyond the realm of believability sometimes.  I'm not a huge fan of the main antagonist, either.  They are pretty infuriating at times.Gripes aside, I'd like to once again reiterate this is one of the best Atelier games made to date.  You could probably play it without having played Sophie 1 (though it is probably way more rewarding to do so), but if you don't, there's a catchup option on the main menu.  Not that there's a lot to catch up on, since the first game's story is so basic.  Anyway, if you're interested, definitely check this game out!

_childDocuments_.review: Atelier Sophie 2 tries a lot of new things for the Atelier franchise and it does it well! The game takes place between Atelier Sophie 1 and Atelier Firis (both parts of the original Atelier Mystery Trilogy). You don't need to have played Atelier Sophie 1 to play this sequel as you get a TLDR of the first game. I would still recommend playing Sophie 1 to appreciate the references in character conversations and just the fact it's a great game as well. Gust and Koei Tecmo try a lot of new things that take aspects of the original Mystery trilogy and combine them with aspects from the Atelier Ryza duology that had good feedback from the community. There are new aspects of exploring the different regions of this game's dream world by having different control methods for the environment as well has harvesting methods with implemented mini games. Most of it is really clever and fun! The battle system is by far in my opinion the biggest upgrade for the franchise. Taking aspects of Lydie and Suelle and the Ryza games made the combat so smooth and easy to go back and forth on. It's super satisfying to rack up a good rotation of characters, abilities, and items to do some great setups of attacks and damage. Of course we can't talk about an Atelier game without mentioning the Alchemy synthesizing system. The boards feel familiar yet have a few changes with implementing components that works really well. At first it may seem convoluted or tedious to some, but after awhile you get used to the different catalysts and methods of using the board and super success rate to make some great items. There were times were I got so wrapped up in making items, time would pass by in an instant which made it both relaxing and enjoyable to do (especially when thinking about the great stats / abilities / damage that certain items would do).The game gets a solid 9/10 for me because of how much I ended up enjoying the experience. I must preface that the original Mystery trilogy series is my favorite in the Atelier Franchise, and so I had a lot of motivation to 100% (achievements) the game. It took me about 80 hours (in game time), but it didn't really feel drawn out until the very end (trying to max out alchemy levels). Had I just played the game casually, I believe most ppl can expect a solid 40 - 50 hour journey. My only real issue was a few hiccups in performance for the PC version. Some areas would have dropped frame rate or some stuttering while transitioning between connected gateways. The other thing I have to mention is the mini games involved for harvesting via certain tools. Most of the mini games are clever and nice to have, but there's a couple (like the fishing rod) that were nonsensical at best. I appreciate the effort in trying new things, but that specific mini game wasn't the greatest.The story was quite enjoyable and had many moments where I couldn't help but smile, laugh, or even get teary eyed from various aspects of the character's stories (especially Sophie's story two key characters). It's nice to have a straight forward and digestable story where you can follow through and still take time on the side to explore and get to know characters and make a lot of items. By the time I finished the game, I had feeling of joy for a great experience, but also sadness that this alchemy journey would be over.Overall I would highly recommend this game!TLDR: 9 / 10 Great game, well worth playing for fans of the franchise and fun enough for me to 100% the game!Positive - Fluid battle system, enjoyable characters, straight-forward story that made me both smile and get teary eyed, catchy soundtrack, amazing voice acting as always, and intricate systems like weather and mini games to spice up harvesting materials,Negative - A few performance issues for the PC version including some stuttering and frame drop on some maps. Certain harvesting mini games are probably best left out for the next Atelier game, but I appreciate the effort

_childDocuments_.review: As usual with the Atelier games, it's more about the gathering than the combat. This is a level up from the first game for Sophie. _childDocuments_.review: A 7/10 game, but a 9.5/10 Atelier game. Highly recommended for fans of the series, otherwise might wait for a sale.Art direction and game performance were much improved from Ryza 2, A more expansive world, beautiful lighting, improved in-game cinematics, overall stable FPS (albeit there are some minor FPS drops in certain menus), and much less GPU-consuming. Ryza 2's outdoor lighting turned my 3080 into a helicopter but Sophie 2 is really optimized. Regarding visuals, GUST has managed to strike a perfect spot between fanservice and wholesomeness. This could be the benchmark for future Atelier or even other GUST games.Much of the game's core mechanics including synthesis and material gathering were swapped to the original Sophie. I can't really decide if it improved the quality of life or the overall playing experience, it's simply changed rather than improved. Players more familiar with Sophie would find it better, while those more familiar with Ryza might not. As with previous Atelier games, Post-Game is present and offers higher difficulties, a set of swimsuit skins that looks the same for all characters, and a new difficult boss.Story is much more substantial than previous Atelier games. There were some false climaxes which makes the story feel a bit dragging, but the ending was really emotionally moving and provides a sense of satisfaction rarely felt in the series. The story, as with tradition, is gated with a series of quests. Some of the quests feel tedious and sometimes break the momentum generated by key plot points. This results in a poor story pacing, unfortunate for the beautiful story it tries to tell. This is unpleasantly common for GUST titles so fans of the series would probably be familiar with the pacing.The game also suffers from HORRIBLE balancing. Previous titles, even spin-off titles like Nelke, were always on point in balancing enemy levels with player progress. In Sophie 2, you can smoke regular enemies in one turn, and get absolutely wiped in a boss fight without the latest equipment. I tried not to synthesize too much equipment because the regular monsters feel really too easy to take on and I was afraid being too powerful would ruin the immersion for me, only to get crushed by the chapter boss. In most parts of the main story, you fight bosses in unexpected places and circumstances, often leaving you unprepared. You need to be massively overpowered all the time to make sure your equips are adequate against a surprise boss fight. However, this could be a good thing if you consider battles against regular enemies as just a different form of material gathering, removing extra stress and tediousness, so you can just breeze through small monsters and focus on stage bosses.Regarding the combat, Sophie 2 abandons the real-time turn-based system of Ryza and introduced a fresh take of a pure turn-based system, more streamlined than previous titles but more satisfying. The introduction of Twin Actions and Dual Trigger made sure every character in your party is usable and useful. No more leaving out half of your party in a battle again, everyone has a chance to contribute now. This should be the standard of not just future Atelier games, but also party-based JRPG games in general.Conclusion: Beautiful visuals, good performance (for a Koei Tecmo port), superb story, poor pacing and balancing, a revolutionary combat system, and a great soundtrack, all packed in what can be described as a definitive Atelier experience.

_childDocuments_.review: 117,75hrs spent on my first playthrough. This is by far the most emotional title in the whole Atelier series that I've played, and I've actually played more or less every title from Marie, Elie, Iris, etc. onwards (this means through Mana Khemia, Ar-Tonelico [even though this isn't really part of Atelier series, but it IS by GUST and it DOES have the "alchemy" system], and every more-recent title [those available on STEAM now], oh even Nelke).I've actually followed the Japanese sneak peeks and news before the release of this title so I already knew some stuff and what I could expect before buying and playing the game for the first time. For those of you who don't know on the other hand:- The synthesis system follows the good ol' Mysterious trilogy style, but is much much more Alchemist-friendly and simplified.- Navigation, map touring, etc follows their latest engine, so it feels like Ryza, Lulua and Ryza 2.- Transition between combat and adventure is seamless and immediate without loading / long transition times. Combat is turn-based like older Atelier titles so you don't have to deal with frantic button presses like in Ryza and Ryza 2, which to me was a pain in the a... err.... thumb.- The story ties up TONS of loose ends and fills in the blanks for a lot of stuff that happened throughout the Mysterious series like why Sophie is such a cheat in Firis and Lydie & Suelle, and explains how tons of stuff that happened back in Sophie 1 came to be. I won't fill in the details here, just play the game to find out.- You do  to have played through Sophie 1 in order to play Sophie 2. If you've NOT played Sophie 1 before but wish to jump straight into Sophie 2, just do it. There's a short synopsis available in the main menu of the game. Just select "Story So Far".- For those who might ask, No, you won't get to see Firis, Lydie, Suelle or other characters because this happens RIGHT BEFORE Firis.For fans of Atelier series, this is definitely a must have. The story and game mechanics are just excellent. Although it may feel that the whole story might be a bit short (just like in many other Atelier titles), it had taken me almost 120hours of gameplay to go through the game at a casual pace and this is no mean feat as I tend to finish any first playthrough of any Atelier series game in around 90hours.As at time of writing, there are still a few problems with the game though:- A pretty nasty fail graphic screen ghosting can happen sometimes.- The game had CTODed on me a few times  this only happens after long hours of continuous gameplay and FORTUNATELY the game autosaves VERY OFTEN so I didn't lose any progress at all.- The game will jitter if it doesn't detect a controller. If you have one but don't really enjoy using a controller, just connect it and play on mouse/keyboard anyway, it's no biggie.All in all, I'd highly recommend the game if you're into this sort of game, especially if you're a fan of the series.

_childDocuments_.review: My initial expectation was something along the lines of A20/Lulua, where the effort, budget, and creative energy felt very scaled back from the more traditional mainline releases like the Mysterious trilogy games. I'm not very far in yet but I have done my research and been in this business for over a decade now. Music is definitely scaled back, with a return to VSTs from the mostly live instruments of Ryza 2, and with the entire tracklist being loaded onto two familiar series regulars (except one track by the ACRYLICSTAB guy and the opening vocal song by our beloved Yano). However, it's perfectly fine as comfort food and Yanagawa is such a monster he still has lots of pleasant surprises spread throughout.By virtue of being so much more recent than earlier games like the original Sophie, most of the graphics look super good. I can't get over how good Sophie looks now in 2022. However, I don't think I can get anti-aliasing to work with this game. The borders of character models look extremely rough except from a comfortable distance (then they get a warm glow and the issue vanishes). I'm extremely used to this after so many games, if anyone has a magic solution to it that'd be neat though. The movies drag REALLY hard for me, will check a few settings but for now I am just overlooking the issue since I can view them outside of the game anyway and they're mostly extraneous flavour. The grid alchemy from the rest of the Mysterious trilogy makes a return. Personally, I'm a HUGE fan of it. Ryza's node system felt a little too straightforward particularly in the lategame while earlier series didn't have much room for "active alchemy", mostly relying on just tossing traits back and forth in long strings. The little grid puzzles are fun in seeing what you can squeeze out with some obscure materials. I liked the combat in A19 so much and I have yet to delve into it enough to make much judgment on how the lategame parties shape up, but I am optimistic. Very solid release so far, just recognize it's not the same scale of product as Ryza 2 or Lydie & Suelle. I'll take it over a Ryza 1 for sure...

_childDocuments_.review:
A mysterious story of a mysterious dream...
One of the stories experienced throughout the Alchemist Sophie’s many adventures, as she continued her travels after leaving her hometown of Kirchen Bell.
This is Sophie’s adventure as she searches for her friend Plachta in the dream world Erde Wiege, where they become separated, and shows the bonds she forms with the people she meets and passing of hearts.

■Evolved turn-based battles & seamless transitions!
In the 6 member party turn-based battles, the 3 members in the front and 3 in the back form 2 teams cooperating “multi-linked turn battles”, and transitions from exploration to battles without loading times in “seamless battles”, the entire game can be enjoyed at a great pace.

■2 types of panels for everyone to enjoy synthesis!
This game uses panel synthesis, the synthesis system of the Mysterious series, where materials are placed in the panel slots to create new items in this puzzle-like feature. By placing the certain materials in the slots, various effects can be produced.
There are 2 types of panels in this game that players can select from : a regular panel and a restricted panel that has a higher synthesis difficulty level.
The board of the restricted panel is fairly complex, but when materials are placed just right, items with high effects can be synthesized, which can't be generated from the regular panel.

name: Core Keeper
detailed_description: Roadmap More Great Games! About the Game Awaken as an explorer in a long-forgotten cavern teeming with untold secrets. In this award-winning, 1-8 player mining sandbox adventure, your choices shape an epic journey. Harvest relics and resources, craft advanced tools, build your base, and explore a dynamically evolving world waiting to be unearthed. Level up your skills, defeat legendary Titans, and unveil the power of the Core. Grow your garden, fish in mysterious waters, master a vast array of recipes, raise and care for animals, encounter the Cavelings, and carve out your own unique world in an enchanting underground adventure. MINE RESOURCES Delve deep to harvest precious resources and unearth hidden gems. Craft tools to help you survive, from pickaxes, fishing rods, and shovels to traps, bombs, and mortars. Upgrade your arsenal and equipment with advanced tools like the mighty Obliteration Ray, and automated machinery to streamline mining, smelting, storage, and more. Level up your skills and unlock powerful weapons to conquer the depths. DISCOVER AN ANCIENT WORLD Explore diverse biomes with unique ecosystems and long-forgotten lore. From the living walls of the Clay Caves to the crystal caverns of the Shimmering Frontier, discover more about this mysterious world as you uncover the secrets of the Cavelings. Build a boat to set sail across the Sunken Sea, race across the Desert of Beginnings, and encounter the remnants of ancient civilizations. BUILD, CRAFT & GET CREATIVE Create a totally unique base using a variety of different materials and customisations. From the ultimate adventurer’s lair to a cozy underground cottage, shape the underground your way. Customize your character’s appearance and choose from an array of powerful armor and unique outfits to suit the moment. BATTLE TITANS Face legendary Titans that hold the secret to this long-forgotten world. Sharpen your combat skills against a variety of monsters and mini-bosses, spend talent points to level up your abilities, and plan your strategy to conquer these colossal creatures of the underground. Discover rare and powerful loot to help you on your journey and power up the Core. EXPLORE WITH FRIENDS Enjoy the adventure solo or team up in 2-8 player drop-in/drop-out online co-op. Play your way and explore at your own pace — celebrate the seasons, trade with merchants, hatch your new best friends, design the ultimate base, automate resource gathering, host your own dedicated server, create music on playable instruments and discover an unforgettable sandbox adventure.

Play your way and explore at your own pace — celebrate the seasons, trade with merchants, hatch your new best friends, design the ultimate base, automate resource gathering, host your own dedicated server, create music on playable instruments and discover an unforgettable sandbox adventure.
short_description: Explore a vast cavern of creatures, relics and resources in a mining sandbox adventure for 1-8 players. Mine, build, fight, craft and farm to unravel the mystery of the ancient Core.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay, you are reading through the reviews to determine if this game is worth buying, and for you. I'll try to be very brief (LOL) and address what you will see in both the recommend and not recommend comment sections.A lot of people compare Core Keeper to Stardew Valley, which if a fair comparison because Core Keeper does have a very similar farming process, but is a much smaller aspect of the game, and not the central game loop like Stardew Valley was. The crops can be sold for in-game currency (not much) but this isn't their primary purpose in Core Keeper. The different crops (which there are quite a few) can be cooked in different ways to create food that gives a large assortment of status buffs (in the late game all your buffs look like a World of Warcraft buff list for a raid boss).A lot of people will also make the comparison to Terraria, which is a much closer comparison to Core Keeper's central game loop. You explore a randomly generated map (which is massive) with many different biomes, and slowly discover new materials --> upgrade equipment with new materials --> fight new Boss and repeat. However, I enjoyed Core Keeper much more than I did Terraia, and I suspect it has to do with Core Keeper being designed in a angled top-down perspective VS. Terraria's Side-scroller perspective. I just think the game play works better and is overall more enjoyable. The crafting system in Core Keeper is pretty "standard fare" to other games like it. However, I did enjoy and find the Automation systems, in particular the electrical circuit stuff to be rewarding. The game doesn't force you to dive very deep into this aspect if that isn't your thing. However, I think this is the one aspect of Core Keeper that allows the most creativity and a little problem solving when trying to conceive mechanical belt/robot arms/smelting systems etc. It is slightly similar in a sense to Factorio except it is more of a "Factorio Lite" version (which is a good thing in my opinion). MAJOR ISSUE: one thing you need to consider prior to buying the game is how much story element is important in your gaming experience. I know Core Keeper bills itself as a sandbox game and not an RPG. However, I was really shocked by the absence of any kind of narrative at all.... I mean there is not any "meat on the bone". You are presented with 2 or so sentences at the start of the game. Maybe another 2 simple sentences around mid-game and that is it. Don't misunderstand me either, there is no passive environmental narrative going on either. The few NPC don't give a single sentence of flavor text; which would be so simple to put in the game, and go a long way for overall user experience.I think if you are playing with someone else or better yet, a group of people, you will not notice or take much issue with the absence of any kind of story. However, if you are playing solo (like I did) then you really need to consider this prior to purchasing the game. EARLY ACCESS: The DEV team seems to steadily be pumping out new content (biomes/bosses/machines/quality of life) every 4 or so months. They appear to be socially active and taking community feedback and actually adding things in. All great signs for any early access game.
