_childDocuments_.review: This is a game about using literal storytelling logic to reach certain outcomes - you arrange the scenes in order, add the characters, and see how changes to the flow of events affect things later in the sequence, like changing variables in an equation. Scenes can change a character's emotional state, affect what they know, equip them with an item, or even kill them - and the characters themselves have different personalities that affect their reactions to events. It's a clever idea and it's executed well; the characters are rendered in a charming storybook style and there's care taken to convey information clearly so you're never confused about things like what a character knows or how they're feeling. The game's only flaw is how short it is--there are a universe of possibilities here, and the puzzles we get only scratch the surface.  I'm hopeful expansions are planned. Until then, this game is like a tiny box of fancy chocolates: exquisite, but over far too soon.
_childDocuments_.name: Storyteller

_childDocuments_.review: This game is amazing! I'm still only about half through it, but want to recommend it to others. The animations for the "wrong" pictures are super funny, and so far I haven't seen anything illogical. Everything runs smoothly, the narrator isn't intrusive, the puzzles are sometimes challenging to the point I wonder whether there's a bug... But no, I just needed to find a better solution. _childDocuments_.name: Storyteller

_childDocuments_.review: You're presented with a number of scenes and characters and have to suss out the correct scenes in the correct order with the correct participants. To beat a level, the title of the level must match the resulting multi-paneled story you created. Coming up with wrong solution can also be funny as each scene and character react according to a set of rules you discover as you play. For example, in the graveyard scene a person observes a tombstone where another person is buried. This changes the second person's status to dead. Also if the first person liked the second person, the first person would be changed to heartbroken. Heartbroken characters can then meet someone new and remarry, or if presented with poison will chug it and die. Dead characters show as a ghost who will frighten most people, unless they were murdered, in which case they tell their tale. There's some replayability, in that levels can have alternate titles to solve, and after you beat all the levels you're presented with more alternate titles involving a new character who is literally the devil. If this sounds interesting to you, you will squeeze out a few fun hours from this game. Not a lot of play time, but I like stuff like this.

_childDocuments_.review: Storyteller is a really unique and clever puzzle game, expertly polished with wonderful art, music and sound design. There's a brilliant air of wit and humor about it, and I smiled at many of the story outcomes. If you're looking for a charming puzzler unlike anything else out there, you're going to find that here. If you're looking for a challenge, I also personally felt that the difficulty ramps up nicely. A bunch of the later objectives (especially the bonus and achievement objectives) were genuinely challenging and took me a while to figure out. Only on the very last achievement did I finally cave and look up a hint on the forums, discovering that I'd been trying to get it in the wrong level - which feels fair to admit as being my fault. What I want to express with that anecdote is that I think the game does an absolutely excellent job of communicating with you and subtly nudging you towards the solution, mainly through the wonderfully illustrated reactions of characters in various situations. It never felt like I came across a solution that didn't make sense to me. Considering the complexity of the systems at play, I think that's an impressive feat. I've seen Steam reviews complaining about the length - I got around 4 hours out of the game. Did those players skip the bonus objectives and achievements, or am I just slow? Regardless, the game costs less than an average graphic novel (a comparison I base on the fact the game is basically a set of interactive comic strips), and took me longer to get through. I hardly feel like the length is a genuine reason to not recommend the game, especially if you enjoyed it in general. That said, if there's gonna be DLC with more content, count me in, because I definitely would be excited for more of Storyteller!
_childDocuments_.name: Storyteller

_childDocuments_.review: This game has so much potential, but it only feels like it gets interesting with the final few pages of the story. It also has a strange combination of over-tutorializing some elements but under-utilizing and/or under-tutorializing others. To give an example I don't feel bad for spoiling: A relative spying on an affair between their relative and someone else will love it and love that pairing. Most mechanics are understandable as references to stories, but it took a good portion of my playtime to figure this one interaction out. It is also only used once and only in the simplest way possible. On the other hand, it feels that there are way too many pages just introducing the murderous nature of the butler where the puzzle is solved by giving him the gun.This game would be great if there was a way for the community to make their own pages, or a fair-priced DLC that continued on from where the main game ended difficulty-wise. For those that love these types of games, a good example of this is The Case of the Golden Idol, where the DLC gave the game the complex puzzles that the mechanics screamed for. The devil update was a step in the right direction certainly, but the devil himself has rather odd interactions at times. I won't complain about more content for a game that would be fantastic if there was more of it however.I'll say that it's a game that certainly left me wanting more, but at the current price it's a bit steep, and the 2-hour playtime achievement feels a bit off with that in mind.

_childDocuments_.review: Storyteller is a creative logic puzzle game, with unique humour and mindful twists. The game requires players to arrange characters and scenarios to fit into a certain narrative. There are 60 normal stages and 10 twists at the end of the game, which can be finished within 2 hours. Many of those stages can be solved in several different ways allowing some degree of player self-expression. Quite a lot of stages also have references in classic literature, discovering them during the play through creates particular memorable experience. However, the game is too simple and too short. It has many good elements and ideas for creating complexity in narratives but ultimately failed in doing so. It throws out many good ideas without further explorations. Overall, I think it is a good game with some minor flaws, which is 7/10 by my standard.

_childDocuments_.review: Yes it's a short game, but it's one of the better indie puzzlers I've come across. Its art style is charming and fits well with the game's concept. I didn't encounter much difficulty except during a couple of levels. One bummer is that the jester levels from the demo are gone, which is a shame. Hopefully they'll add it in as a free DLC. As it currently is, the game might be overpriced for some. If so, wait for a sale. It's well worth it for me so I'm still giving it a solid recommendation. _childDocuments_.review: I'm going to be completely honest, I've been following this game for a while. I'm incredibly upset to give it a thumbs down, but I was severely disappointed to find the lack of content, especially considering the amount of time put into the game. There were only around 50 levels (52 if I'm correct), and the creators had been working on this game for nearly 15 years prior to the release according to gamerant. I also noticed one of my favorite parts of the demo almost completely disappeared. For those who haven't played, at the end of the demo, you unlock a jester hat that gives you a new challenge for each level that changes the story slightly, while providing double the gameplay. In the full release, I've found that only a few levels actually include the extra challenge mechanic, which ends up being unlocked instantaneously.I'm not saying this game is without it's merits, for example the art and puzzles in the game are incredibly fun and beautiful. I love the hand drawn feel and the different characters, and I found it a really fun game. To be completely honest, I think this would be one of my favorite games if they had included more. One way I would've kept this and even given it a better review would be if they had given us a sandbox mode after earning the Storyteller rank. They could've also given us more gameplay with extra levels, or even a character creator or something akin to that. I would love to get this game again later on, if they can provide us with extra mechanics, or extra levels of some sort, like another book or any other ideas I've mentioned. But for now, I'm trying to get a refund sadly.Creators, please add more, I enjoyed the time I had playing your game, but I need more to keep it in my favorites.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this game! It's a quick 2-3 hours or so of play time. On the challenging prompts, it's really satisfying to come up with a solution and see new little ways that the characters can interact. I did all the achievements and treated them like the bonus puzzles: I gave myself the prompt (the achievement title) and checked a guide to see the location (what chapter and puzzle it could be completed in), just because when I tried without knowing the location I just kept second-guessing whether the prompt was possible where I was, then I'd wind up flipping through the annoying book and trying to remember which puzzles had which characters and which scenes and and and... that just wasn't fun for me, and I feel like doing the achievements the way I did /was/ fun! I don't mind that some people would say I cheated, cause they wouldn't entirely be wrong, but I had fun. All that's not to say I didn't have a few complaints. First was that I felt like the majority of the puzzles were teaching you how certain pieces worked, like what characters' motivations were or what a set piece did. Those ones often felt like a chore once you got past the beginning, because by the middle of the game you don't necessarily need to be taught how it'll work because you understand how the game as a whole works, and if you were going to figure out a particular scene, for example, you could do it in the context of a larger, more challenging puzzle. There were usually just one or maybe two really challenging ones per chapter. Second, it does sometimes fall into the puzzle game trap of 'you've solved the prompt but not in the exact way we had in mind so we're not letting you progress yet.' However, when that happened, usually it was just a little finagling to see what you hadn't fulfilled properly.
_childDocuments_.name: Storyteller

_childDocuments_.review: It's a fun brain exercise.  As well, if they continue to update it with new puzzles down the line, it will be more and more worth it.  The music, while neutral, always fits the storytelling vibe.  The narrator does as well.  Completing it entirely, achievements included, will not take you all that long, especially if you use guides when you can't get something, though I try to avoid that as it makes it last longer and I feel more accomplished doing so.  That being said, it was a low price and fun, so I'd say it was well worth it.  My only real complaint (and it's honestly only if I'm being SUPER nitpicky) was on a few of the stamps.  Whilst you *really* need to think outside the box for some stories, moreso for the stamps, a few stamps weren't really....correct.  By that I mean.....well, look at it like a steam achievement.  What if the achievement was labeled "Eat 8 oranges" but to activate it you needed to eat 5 oranges, a starfruit and 2 papayas?  Or if you had to eat the peels afterwards?  I mean, that's similar but not the same.  Like I said though, great game, good value, and the only complaint I could file would be a nitpicky one, so nothing to worry about.

_childDocuments_.review: I hate to give it a down-vote, considering the concept is great and I had been really looking forward to the game. Bought it as soon as I could. I miss the jester challenges (They're still kind of there, alternate endings, but it removes your original story which I don't much like) and I wish there was some kind of free play/sandbox story mode to play around with. But even then... there just isn't enough for the asking price. I got it on sale but for £10 it only gave me about an hour of content. Only one puzzle really stumped me. It's a cute game, really pretty, but it feels like it's still in demo. Also I hate the 'ending'. Just telling me to go write my own stories... Mate, I am a writer, if I wanted to be doing that I would. All saying this does is make me feel like you've baked a cake, given me a sliver of a slice, then thrown the rest in the bin and told me to make my own now. I appreciate what you were trying to do, but you didn't achieve it, not after barely an hour or so of game time. It's just a shame, because there is so much potential. If there is an update, that releases more, I'd be happy to consider changing my review. Until then... It just isn't worth the price.

_childDocuments_.review: For those interested in puzzle games, this is a nice three hour experience, though it might not take quite that long if you're more experienced with that stuff. That was just my time. It gets a little more challenging when trying to break it for those extra couple of achievements, but it's overall a rather easy game.If you're here for the story(pun fully intended), then this is a wonderful little game. As an aspiring storyteller myself this was so much fun to go through in an evening. Brilliant set-up, interesting prompts, lively and distinct characters, and all while giving you full freedom to experiment with the stories you create. My favourite part has to be how each story can play out slightly differently with the same result. Early on there are even plenty of blank panels not necessary for completing the main puzzle allowing you to customise your story a little with an extra panel, as long as it doesn't effect the outcome. This freedom and the extra goals for several levels are ideas I absolutely love.This game captures the heart of storytelling so well. You know what needs to happen, but you have no idea what has to happen for it to get there. Maybe you'll even be left with some space to fill with extra details, just because you like it. Genius concept, small game, brilliant execution. Probably not for the hardcore gamers out there, but if you're considering this game, then that's probably not what you were after in the first place.

_childDocuments_.review: I honestly hate writing bad reviews for indie games - especially ones that have such a great starting concept! But Annapurna published this one, so they will have had a meaningful budget, and big opportunity to do better. Lots of people have said it's too short for the price tag... But that's not the real issue. Short games can be good, and devs work extremely hard even to create short experiences.For me the real issue is the lack of inventiveness. The game forces you to play out the same scenarios again and again, with the same characters - with very little variation. As such, the game gets boring and predictable within 15 minutes. The sad thing is that there are so many easy wins they could have taken to add variety and intrigue. From changing up the character sprites from time to time, to basing each chapter on a different story concept, to adding a sense of meta-progression. Without these basic features, every level feels like you're stuck a time warp. To make matters worse, the system feels very very rigid. Often it seems like there is only one answer, and sometimes those answers don't even feel logical. As a result, the game doesn't offer any opportunities to be creative as a player - which adds to ultimate sense of staleness.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to start by saying I enjoyed what I played, just like I did the demo. The visuals are adorable and the animations are pretty smooth. The puzzle aspect was nice. I liked getting to make different situations and solutions. I enjoyed the concept which was why I was so excited for the game.I suppose that's why I was so disappointed when I got an hour and 30 mins in and realised that was it. The whole game. I understand that some games are short and are designed to be and ultimately that is the decision of the creator. My problem was that it felt so jarring, almost leaving me with a feeling that there was no conclusion, that there was no end. In confusion, I watched the credits role, hoping there was something else, only to see them repeat. Again and again. I went back and completed any extra objectives or achievements (making this one of the only games I 100%ed) in the hopes that there was something more - like in the demo - only to be left feeling disappointed. I fully completed this game in under 2 hours and I didn't feel happy, I didn't feel sad it was over. I just felt confusion and then annoyance and then nothing. Except maybe a bit down as I had been looking forwards to this game for ages only to feel like I had played another version of the demo. A more detailed demo from later down the line, but still a demo.If the game were ever expanded, I would probably play it. But in it's current state, It just felt a bit of a let down.The game is cute and if you looking for cute puzzle game that doesn't take to long, go ahead. I did enjoy it for what it was worth. I just can't really recommenced it beyond that. Even the price felt a bit much for what it was. I've played other puzzle games that were just as cute and wholesome and much longer for free. So if you do want to pick it up, maybe wait for it to go on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: This is an inventive logic puzzle game, but instead of math or cryptograms, the goal is to use narrative storytelling techniques to solve the puzzles. Plot, character motivation, and continuity are all central to solving the various puzzles, and character archtypes and familiar scenarios make it accessible for anyone who likes a good story. I recommend it to anyone looking for a different sort of logic puzzle game, and especially for anyone who likes playing with narrative techniques.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're read a couple reviews, you've seen it's a short game. If that's a deal-breaker and you want a game with high replayability, you might want to pass on Storyteller.If you're still reading however, I can recommend it as a pretty novel puzzle game with a charming setting and innovative gameplay. It'd the kind of single sitting experience that gives a breath of fresh game design air, and might leave you thinking about possibilities for future game mechanics along this line.Truth be told, I didn't find it to be _the_ storytelling masterpiece I was hinted at in gamedev circles, and my partner who I played it with got bored midway through (but she's not a big fan of narrative games in the first place). The first chapters of the game are very easy and might not show the full potential of the mechanic. Later chapters get more interesting and provide some interesting challenge.I think I would have liked one or two more scenarios in some chapters to explore the setting further. But I'm also happy with the experience as it is overall.So in short, I had a good evening, it's not my GOTY in the genre (do check out The Case of the Golden Idol if you're itching for more story reconstruction puzzle mechanics), but I'll gladly follow what the devs have in store for future games or DLCs... The credits do say "Book One" ;)

_childDocuments_.review: I was mixed on this review for a while, because I wish I could say I recommend this game. It's got wonderfully stylized graphics, simple components with multiple unique interactions, and an exceptionally interesting premise. The narrator and characters all have a great deal of personality, and the sound effects add a lot of charm. This game is extremely well-polished, and it feels like a great choice for those who are easily intimidated by puzzle games. Unfortunately, this game struggles in terms of length and depth. It is painfully short, I found the puzzles overall too easy, and it lacks any real replayability. Most of my time in-game was listening to the soundtrack and narrator. I believe this game can easily be 100% completed within two or three hours for an average player, and I can't justify spending $15 for it when there are many other fantastic puzzle games at a similar pricepoint that offer more. I look forward to future updates, because I know this game has a lot of room for new ideas, mechanics, characters, and stories.Ultimately, I decided not to recommend this game because no matter how enjoyable the experience was, I can't say it was worth the price I paid for it. I think the experience is novel and certainly worth the time investment, but if possible, I'd pick it up at a discount.

_childDocuments_.review: is an excellently cute and charming logic puzzle game where you use a combination of scenes and characters to create a scenario based on a title prompt. Not only is it very clever, but it feels totally intuitive and has endless moments where I feel totally on the same wavelength as the creators, smiling and laughing practically the whole way through. The kind of game you can easily recommend to your parents, or friends who don't even play games that regularly, as all the logic in the puzzles use emotive proxies in signifiers from fables, each with their own intuitive quirks, that resolve much of the inaccessibility in harsh videogame-y logic puzzles. It has easily become a new favourite of mine and will be a go-to recommendation for a casual fun experience.If you liked this game and want more short and sweet charming games filled with love that you can also recommend to similar demographic, I'd recommend , the soothing puzzle home decorating game where you gain insights into your character's life through unpacking their moving boxes.If you liked the storybook style and the aesthetic of the imagery used but want more of a dense story that you can loosely influence in more typical interactive fiction style, I would recommend , the gorgeously illustrated world where you solve murders and scandals in 16th century Europe.

_childDocuments_.review: Storyteller is a rather simple game. You're given a prompt and, using what characters, or objects/settings, are provided, to solve what you need to. The premise is rather simple, but I found it charming enough on it's own. A couple of the extra missions made me stop and think, but overall, I found the difficulty to be on the easier side. The exception to this is that some of the solutions might be a bit obtuse and I found it was a bit of a stretch.Briefly to touch on, visuals and audio. The sound is rather simple and in the background; pleasant enough and not a huge distraction. The visual style I'm a bit torn on, however. I find the background visuals and the settings to be cute and gives me that storybook vibe. However, the character models were a bit off for me, but not taking away from the experience.Overall, the game is quite a pleasant time. I would say, for the asking price, I would think about waiting for a sale to come up. As is, it is a little much, in my opinion, but perfect if it was on sale for a dash less. With that said, if you're curious, I'd recommend picking it up and giving it a play through. It's rather short, but I found myself quite happy from beginning to end.

_childDocuments_.review: Storyteller is a very cute, funny and enjoyable puzzle game with a original and unique concept. Some good chill music, lots of cute art style and fantastic animations! This game make me laugh and smile more than I actually excepted and I was very excited to play the game! Getting the good or bad ending was cool and doing random stupid things or situation with the characters is interesting and nice!But.. I am disappointed. Why? Because I played the demo before and to be honest, I excepted more stories, more characters and more pages ( mostly when the demo say "The full version is coming soon with more characters, settings and surprises!" ). I feel like the game is not done yet, have less than the demo and is WAY too short for the price it have. I completed the game in 1/2 hours and I think it's pretty sad they delete content from the demo (with Adam/Eve) and they didn't make the game last much longer. The puzzles aren't also really hard and getting the achievement is pretty easy so I got a bit more unhappy but I guess I just wanted to have more of that game I was so excited about..The concept of the game is amazing but we clearly need more.. And just to be clear, I don't regret buying the game, I'm just sad and disappointed it didn't last longer. So I'm feeling weird to put Yes as recommendation, even if I liked it. I just don't know if the game deserved it or not.. but I don't want the game to have another negative reviews because it is very wonderful and unique game, just too short. I really hope the devs will really add more stories, more characters, more settings and content later !If you love simple short adorable game, I recommended Storyteller but maybe wait for a promotion since the price is a bit too much for the content we have right now.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR Fun Game, but make your own judgement on if the price is worth it.Storyteller is a puzzle game where you organize comic panels to tell a particular story. The game takes an hour to an hour 1/2 to complete fully. Most of the puzzles are very easy with the exception of the last two so you'll likely blow though the game fairly quickly. I would recommend this game if you're into light puzzles. The art style is beautiful and the concept is unique though the scaling on the difficulty is non-existent. Most of the puzzles are easy or very difficult with no real in-between or transition. The game doesn't really have much replay-ability, either. Only a handful of puzzles have multiple solutions. Whether $15 is worth an hour of relatively simple puzzles is up to you. I personally felt a little disappointed with the difficulty scale and replay-ability for what I paid but this game has a special charm to it and it could of very well just not have been the one for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Storyteller

_childDocuments_.review: I came into this cold with no prior knowledge, fairly happy to try it out at a discounted price. However, the game is shockingly short and lacking in content. I'm not sure I've seen worse value, in basic terms, anywhere on the Steam store.The idea of a puzzler centred on narrative structure is neat and well-executed; some of the levels, in addition to the art and sound design, were pleasing. But Storyteller's replay value is scarce and I'd comfortably seen everything the game had to offer in under two hours. A critical side effect of this is that the potential complexity of the game's systems is never remotely exploited, with only one or two puzzles towards the end requiring significant thought.I've requested a refund, and would suggest the store price is at minimum halved to avoid giving potential players the wrong impression about what this game offers. It would be good to see its ideas fleshed out and deepened in a future release or substantial update - though I'd need some assurances before trying again.

_childDocuments_.review: storyteller is a fun little game that i did enjoy my time with! but depending on how good you are at the puzzles/how much you get stuck, and if you want to get all the achievements or you're fine just beating all the levels once, expect it to take somewhere between 30 min and 2½ hours to fully complete. it's a short, cohesive experience that knows what it's going for and does it well, not outstaying its welcome. this may be a great thing if you're short on time/prefer short games and it does mean that what is here is really polished, but there's only 52 levels and they're mostly pretty short. when i played it, it was just as i was getting into it and really understanding how the puzzles work when it abruptly ended.the first 2 chapters feel like the tutorial, and the last 4 are longer and slightly more difficult, so it's more like 8 tutorial levels, 40 main levels and 4 final challenge levels. there's a handful of levels that have a secondary goal appear after you finished it as a bonus challenge, but if you already did it that way the first time, as i sometimes did, you end up not even getting the extra challenge level to play. and there's already very few of them.the achievements are all easy to get and there aren't many. if that's a pro or a con depends on the player.if this goes on sale for a decent percentage off or they add more levels in the future i would recommend it because i do like the game! but with so little substance i can't say its worth the price tag for everyone. if you're the kind of person that's ok paying more than the average price of a short game to help support small indie developers, then it might be a non-issue for you. but for those with smaller budgets it's a hard sell at full cost. picking it up on sale or if more levels are added on the future is the way to go for those kinds of people in my opinion. this short runtime is going to be especially disappointing for anyone who's been waiting for it for a long time - it's spent a decade in development and while what is here is great, 10 years waiting for a >3 hour game with little replay value at a £12.49 price tag might be a bit of a sting.in short, the game is good! and that's why i wish there was more here.the levels all feel logical. even if you get stuck there's nothing that made me feel that 'how was i supposed to know to do that? it doesn't make any sense' that some puzzle games can fall into. the only one i tripped up on wasn't even a solution to a puzzle, it was getting the martini achievement. but looking at the animation of the relevant character when you see it, i got what they were going for and it made sense. i'm sure depending on the way you think, most people might run in to one or two moments where you just didn't think of something but it makes sense when you know the answer.some levels have multiple solutions, and you're often free to pick from a few characters for the same role so there will be variance but this is a puzzle game and not an interactive storyteller so don't expect to actually tell your own story.music is nice, mostly covers of iconic classical pieces, but that means its not exactly very memorable or exciting. it's the kind of soundtrack that fades into the background and you don't pay attention to. i wouldn't buy the ost myself but it's not bad by any measure. the art of the game is really nice, it knows what it's going for style wise, fitting perfectly with the game and just generally looking really good. there's little animations for every possibility in the stories which does add a lot of charm and help it to feel polished.while i strongly believe that a game shouldn't rely on fan-created content like mods to 'fix' or pad out their game, and the game should be complete and worth the price just for the available official content, having some kind of level editor available so people can create and share levels, either in game or through the steam workshop, would go a long way towards the feeling of it ending too soon. i just kinda think it would be a good idea, regardless of how it's priced or how much is in the game - it just seems like a natural fit for this style of game!

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: A game with great marred by a lack of content. At the time of this review I have 119 minutes of playtime (Below required steam playtime for refund) 100% completion (except some achievements) and I had more than half an hour AFK. Thankfully there is a custom levels mod, you can find information about it here: Foreword: I had initially intended to write this review on September 27th 2023, one day after the "Devilsh First Update" because I played it start to finish then, but life happened as it often does. All of my comments are from that play period because I really wanted to keep the 119 minutes for the review.Storyteller is a rather unique puzzle game, the gameplay regarding around the panels and the timeline they construct. In each level you try to finish the goal set by the level (And some additional ones that come into play later), creating different stories with the provided actors and stages to meet the goal. The game is rather short, currently featuring about 13 Chapters, all of which can be completed in less than an hour and a half, even with the optional objectives and some levels having a "devil mode" in it adding the devil as a character and changing the level goal.One thing I'll like to mention is that the game has no sandbox mode. I'm not the first one to say that a sandbox mode would fit this game extremely well, and I certainly won't be the last. The thing with the game being that across the 13 Chapters we see a variety of characters and scenarios, but they are all self contained, for the most part with interaction between chapters being very rare. Which is a shame because the potential is there, what would Edgar say to the the magic mirror? What would the witch do if she and Snow White were family? Can a gun kill Dracula? Seeing these interactions play out would be certainly fun but it would also take a lot of development time too. One thing that people may not know about Storyteller is that the game has been in development for a long time, like a LONG TIME. Here is early gameplay footage from a literal decade ago: . So this game has been in development for at least 10 years before release, changing wildly from then to now. So I have to assume that there are technical limitations at play that limit development. So a sandbox mode may be out of the questions but thankfully there is a custom level mod that adds some replayability (The game has close to no replayability right now). You can find more information about it here: I think this game would benefit from any kind of content, if they still exists somewhere the old gameplay versions would be fun extra content, it would allow us to see how the "Story of Storyteller" developed and we can see bonus content. Of course this is a pipe dream but it would help with the lack of content if it did happen. For future updates if we are going to get more expansions like the one for the Garden of Eden that we got in the Devilish update, I'd like to see more interplay between existing chapters, also the "Monsters" chapter desperately needs to be expanded. It adds a lot of cool little features that would be great for future levels, but they each last for 1-3 levels, for example the Dracula level alone adding multiple new mechanics let being a single level is such a waste as there is incredible potential in both that level and the whole chapter.To finish, I believe that Storyteller is a one of a kind game, and I'm sorry that I feel conflicted in recommending it. While I love what it does and believe that it is full of potential, the length of the game with high price tag makes it really hard for me to do so. Yet I ultimately still do, I believe in the potential of the game and in the dev to expand on it further in the future, especially considering that he worked on this game for over a decade. The price tag is a bit too steep to buy out of discount for the content present, but if you have some spare money (or a lot, depending on the region) and want to play a one of a kind puzzle game I would thoroughly recommend it. But be aware of the amount of content, you will likely finish the game in a few short hours (3 at most) so make your purchase accordingly.

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't played a game this fun with so much humor in my lifeStoryteller is a narrative puzzle game. You get a number of frames, some situations, some characters and a general sentence. Your task is to use the characters and the situations in such a way in order to fit to the narrative sentence, in short to tell the story you have to tell. The puzzles won't puzzle you much BUT the game includes specific clauses sometimes that turn the challenge up. While the game is called "Storyteller" the puzzles are all about programming logic in a sense "if that and if that happens or that doesn't happen then there is this outcome". Which is another way to interpret narrative tasks. But the greatest thing and 100% of its charm is the presentation and the humor. The game winks in several literature genres, writers, and cliches by subverting them or by making fun of them. I won't spoil it, but the point that Friedrich Nietzsche makes a cameo appearance had me laughing out loud for a couple of minutes.One of the wittiest and funnest games I have played in my life. Congratulations to the developing team!

_childDocuments_.review: A nice little pick up and play puzzle game, where you rearrange scenes and actors into some limited slots, until you fulfill the "chapter heading" criteria that describes a story. _childDocuments_.review: Not only is it short, it's pretty repetitive too.Lets go over some positives first.Good art and animations. The characters are lively, and have a reaction to almost everything. Very nice. No background colours, which is kind of a shame, but its faded backgrounds work fine.Visual storytelling. Few puzzles involve words being exchanged. Makes stories a lot more dynamic and interesting. And it makes the game work just as well in any language, which is great!The puzzles are fun to solve. Plain and simple. New things are introduced and gradually built upon. A good standard.But the best parts of this game are the side-objectives, which make you play through a level with a twist. These were genuinely great, having you take what you just did and flipping it around until the story is different, but the narrative is the same. But they appear only every few levels. Not for all of them. Which is majorly disappointing.Now... the negatives.Waaaaaaay too short. Overall, the main game + side-objectives took an hour and six minutes to beat. The save file indicates that was 100% of the game. What?! So I went and did the achievements that I hadn't already gotten by accident. Took about 30 minutes. So I have literally seen everything that this $20 game has to offer in an hour and a half.Repetition. The puzzles are all very similar, even from chapter to chapter. The game will build upon a puzzle, giving you all the pieces, then DROP EVERYTHING and on to the next chapter. BUT! You come back to previous themes later on. By that I mean, the themes will just repeat for some chapters, but with a very slightly lengthier solution. The last chapter is fine tho, it's got the longest puzzles with mechanics you are already familiar with. They should add at least 7 more of these chapters.No overarching story. The 'stories' in this game are just each individual level. Chapters don't have a running story, just a theme. The book has no story, just the chapters. Bit of a shame, but I can understand why.The ending. Not much of a spoiler cuz there's barely an ending anyway. Your reward for completing every 'story' in this book? A nicely written "you did it" as the credits roll. No final puzzle, you just did 4 mini final puzzles that didn't even have all the elements, but at least now there's a shadow of a crown in your face.This game, plain and simply, is not worth $20. $10 at the most, tho I'd shoot for $8. This game was meant for iPads. a $3.99 IOS game to get a kid to stay quiet on a two hour car ride.Play FRAMED instead. It's half the price and double the length.

_childDocuments_.review: NB: The positive rating is there because I did mostly like the game, but please note the total playtime, so I would consider waiting for a sale.Storyteller is a very simple and relaxing puzzle game, where the one and only puzzle is figuring out how to make a story based on a vague prompt using a small set of "stages" and "characters" (unique for each particular story prompt). Each stage has a limited number of positions for the characters in it, and usually these positions mean something, i.e. placing a character in the bushes while the other two are in the open in the "Affair" stage means that the first character hides and watches the other two kissing (despite the sheer amount of murder and affairs, the game is very innocently cartoonish in its presentation).That's pretty much it. I only had troubles with one level (because it was not obvious that a particular stage with a particular configuration of actors could have a particular effect on a later stage).The newly added Devilish mode, where you need to twist some of the previous stories with the addition of The Devil character, is fun, but rather short. The "stamps" (i.e. hidden achievements) are, unfortunately, somewhat annoying to get, because you need to guess both the story where you can get them at, and the actual prompt, which can be somewhat non-obvious.

_childDocuments_.review: Rating 4/10Pros: The idea of a puzzle game in which you're a storyteller who can change the outcome of a story sounds cool. The demo was enjoyable and made me somewhat excited for the full release of the game.Neutral: Sadly, the main game is disappointing due to its lackluster execution. Its biggest problem is just that it's too short for the price. It only took me 2.4 hours to beat the game and that's while going for achievements and trying to 100% the game. The puzzles are also quite easy. It introduces new scenarios at a breakneck pace but that means that it never has time to evolve on those concepts and get to a challenging level. The final few levels in the game weren't challenging at all and it made it feel unrewarding. The new update did alleviate this problem a little bit but not enough. They did add a lot of stamps which definitely helped the most. Even then I couldn't be bothered to 100% the game as I just wasn't interested enough in its mechanics to experiment more.Cons: There was a content update on September 26th, but this is content that should've been in the original release. The game wasn't in early access or anything so this lack of content is inexcusable. I particularly dislike this sell now, finish later approach that modern games fall victim to. This doesn't happen often with indie games, but this is one of the exceptions. I would recommend that anyone play any other puzzle game than this one as there are many that are much better.

_childDocuments_.review: Unleash Your Creative Storytelling Skills with "Storyteller"Rating: ★★★★☆ (4/5)I like this game and I recommend it, it's a unique puzzle game that require selecting panels to align to the chapter. "Storyteller" is a refreshingly innovative puzzle game that offers a unique twist on interactive storytelling. If you're someone who enjoys flexing their creative muscles and thinking outside the box, this game could be a hidden gem in your collection; it can be challenging too. Unlike traditional narrative-driven games, "Storyteller" challenges players to craft stories using a visual language. The objective in each level is to construct a narrative that aligns with a given title by strategically placing settings and characters that react to each other, forming dynamic relationships that drive the story forward. It's a game of trial and error, where your creative choices shape the outcome. Some choices are obvious while others take a little more thought (or a lot of thought)The game's comic-panel design and charming animations provide a canvas for experimentation. You'll find yourself dragging and dropping characters, settings, and objects to see how they influence the unfolding story. This gameplay mechanic encourages you to think critically and calculate the order of images to complete each chapter successfully."Storyteller" covers a wide range of story genres, from love and intrigue to crime, monsters, betrayal, and more. This diversity ensures that you're constantly presented with fresh challenges and engaging scenarios, keeping the gameplay experience exciting and dynamic.While "Storyteller" is undoubtedly a creative and entertaining game, it may not appeal to everyone as some of the puzzles can be extremely challenging.  Some players might find the trial-and-error aspect frustrating, especially when attempting to decipher the optimal sequence of events for a successful story. Additionally, the learning curve can be steep for those new to this type of gameplay."Storyteller" is a thought-provoking and inventive puzzle game that taps into your storytelling prowess. Its unique approach challenges players to think creatively, experiment with narratives, and craft stories in a visually engaging way. If you enjoy puzzles that require a dash of creativity and don't mind a bit of trial and error, "Storyteller" is worth a try. It's a game that offers a fresh perspective on interactive storytelling, offering hours of imaginative gameplay for those willing to embrace its unique concept.

_childDocuments_.review: A lot of reviews of Storyteller focus on how short it is. My review is a response to those.Please, unlink those synapses saying that $1 = x amount of gameplay time. This game is worth WAY more than 15 bucks, or 3 lattes (for those who probably write their reviews on Starbucks).If you're a hardcore puzzle gamer this game is probably not for you, which should be fine. Instead, try playing it with someone less hardcore, like a partner, kid or a friend you want to introduce to puzzle games. I played it with my partner and they loved it, and I loved it more because of that. It is not often that we can play a game together that has them hooked up like this one. So keep that in mind.Besides that, come on, this game is beautiful, runs without bugs (to my knowledge), and it's just unlike anything else. So if you want to spend 15+ in playing the same games over and over, sure, refund this, otherwise, pay the $14.99, and enjoy a short but very unique experience with someone you care about.Thanks Daniel & Jeremias for bringing such a nice experience into this world.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm torn. Like, genuinely torn. On one hand, this game is an absolute treat; gorgeous graphics, unique vibe, a fun take on puzzling, and a unique way to work in literary references without being "like that". I've been hype for Storyteller since I played it's demo during last year's indie jam and, both stylistically and through it's gameplay, it more than meets my expectations...however...On the other hand...you can knock this game out in an hour. An hour of gameplay...for $15 bucks. Is tough to swallow. The only reason that (as of this review) I have 4.5 in playtime is because after my initial save I did a second pass to 100%, and then after a friend and I did some puzzles together over stream.I am leaving a positive review because it's a beautiful little indie project and I am hoping (HOPING) that there will be future updates with more content. Especially since there were puzzles/narratives in the demo that are NOT in the main game at launch and they could find a way to patch those back in and/or use other classic novels as inspiration for new puzzles! So, yeah, love it, it's an hour of gameplay (maybe an hour and a half if you have a guide up to 100% the achievements first pass), thats a drag, get it when it's cheaper than $15, or not, it's pretty cheap and I'm not your mom. Do what you will with your money.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT AFTER FIRST UPDATE OCTOBER 2023: My hope in the review below was fulfilled: the developer added a free content patch which added a very significant amount of extra puzzles while also improving on the achievement mechanic! I would definitely double recommend this game now, even at full price. My original review follows below.Here's the short of it: this game is great, beautiful art, high polish, fun puzzles with a unique narrative puzzle mechanic you've never seen before. But the game is also about as short as this two-sentence tl;dr review.At the moment, you should buy it, but if you buy it at full price you should see 50% of that as the cost of the actual game and 50% of that as a donation to support a creative indie developer.The game is NOT over-priced, imho, because you can see and feel where the money went, because artists have to eat. But artists also make unprofitable decisions like spending their time and effort on unique and beautiful puzzle games which, due to the nature of the puzzle genre, have little replayability as opposed to another dime-a-dozen roguelike that has barely half the style and polish of this game but milks the content its got for every minute of playtime it can.As a puzzle game, half the fun here is how beautiful and funny the art is. It's always enjoyable to see the characters' facial expressions and getting to know their personality by that and by how they react to different scenes and scenario's. Who will commit suicide upon a broken heart? Who will commit murder? Narrative suffuses every level of this puzzle game, making it a holistic experience as opposed to just a gimmick.As it stands, not having played the demo will increase your enjoyment, as otherwise you're likely to rush through quite a few of the early puzzles. But even having played the demo quite a bit the full game still threw a few head-scratchers my way that let to great "Ooooo, that's how!" moments.I never was stuck long enough to be frustrated. On the one hand that means that overall most puzzles weren't that hard, on the other hand, getting frustrated isn't that much fun so it's a compliment to the intuitive game design that no puzzle out-stays its welcome.My hope is that in the future, the developer will expand with free content patches and (dare I dream?) a sandbox mode. There were some puzzles in the demo that never made it to the full game, so that's a good sign there's more content in the pipeline! But even if that doesn't happen, I feel this beautiful game is worth sacrificing one or two pizza's or happy meals.There are some games you buy because you'll play them forever, and then there are some games you buy because you'll remember them forever. This is the latter type, and well worth it on that account!10/10 Would get all my characters killed twice again.

_childDocuments_.review: At first, I thought it's yet another game published by Annapurna that seems to cater to people who like the "indie" in "indie games", but not the "games". The aesthetic of artistic, independent design - but it has to look good so I can show it to my friends! It's not like I'm going to play much of it anyway...Well, no. This is the real deal. It's a puzzle game, asking you to create a specific situation with predefined pieces. It's not a crappy comic book generator, there's actually quite a bit of game in here.The main problem you'll be tackling is the fact that the pieces all have specific rules that they will abide by default. Rules of the world, so to speak. To choose a random example, let's say we take Undyne, Alphys, and Asgore from UNDERTALE. Let's put each of them next to a pile of anime. Alphys would be overjoyed, Asgore would be perplexed, and Undyne would say "what is this dorky crap?" and throw it into the trash. Right?In the context of the game - say you want the Knight to kill the Queen. You have a cliff scene. Simple, right? Make the Knight stand behind the Queen, he will push her, right? But no. The Knight not only is loyal to the Queen, he's also in love with her. You have to create a motive for him to do it; but how? Well, the Knight is also very righteous, and values justice highly... higher than his loyalty to the queen. Maybe he'd change his tune if you were to show him a wicked deed that the Queen committed?Or sometimes the problem is the other way around: there is no visible means for a person to do something. Let's say the cliff isn't there, but the Knight already is convinced that the Queen is wicked. Oh, but there's the execution chamber. The problem is, only someone who's been crowned a monarch can order an execution. So we'd need to have the Knight somehow usurp the throne first...The stories you'll create to achieve these goals are often bizarre, macabre, ridiculous - . That's what this game is. It's just fun. You'll probably chuckle while playing it. "Oh god, I have an idea how to make this happen..." and then you do, and it's a glorious mess. There's even a collection of hidden stamps - little achievements that you get for creating unique interactions and outcomes.My favourite is having Nietzsche shoot God dead, and then have dead God's spirit cower in fear in front of Nietzsche, who's menacingly spinning the gun. "I finally killed you, you bastard! God is dead, and I have killed him!" "Yes bro, you win, now put that away, man!"Do I have complaints, though? Yeah. I wish there was more. I can't believe I'm saying this, I'm always complaining that the games are too long and don't know when to stop, but here everything is so lovely, you can't help but want to keep playing with the little pieces. Especially considering that many pieces are woefully underutilised. Dracula appears... once, I think. So does Nietzsche. Give Vlad VS Fred epic battle for the heart of the Queen from Snow White. I guess I'll try getting more stamps. And you should probably try playing this.

_childDocuments_.review: The game's hand-drawn graphics style, animations, and sound create a charming experience. Each character possesses a distinct set of desires and behaviors, creating a dynamic playground for storytelling. It is up to the player to acknowledge these motives in order to orchestrate interactions that lead to clever outcomes and unexpected twists. While the characters seem integrated into the game world, I feel like their story arcs lack resolution. I wish there was a "Story" in Storyteller. An overarching narrative linking these chapters would have provided a more cohesive and satisfying conclusion to the overall experience. Then again, perhaps that's not the point of Storyteller. The point is to have fun with self-contained thematic story chapters (and prove that Baron did nothing wrong).

_childDocuments_.review: A short, but delightful experience. I don't like puzzle games, but I like Storyteller. I found myself laughing out loud at some of the solutions, and even when I didn't get the right answers, the characters are so full of personality that I didn't mind experimenting until I got the story right. Most of the puzzles make sense, with excellent iconography for hints. Most of the fun is figuring out how characters will respond to each other within various scenes, and manipulating them until their behavior matches their chapter title.Unfortunately, the menu navigation is awful. Eventually you'll be trying to unlock badges with very specific characters and scenes. With several dozen chapters to scroll through and no listing of their characters and scenes, it gets tedious hunting for the exact combination you'll need. When you've finally achieved 100%, there's no fanfare, no capstone celebration screen--you just go to the menu page and quit.Overall, I love the presentation and humor, but the UI and anticlimactic ending dampened the experience just enough to stop a good game from being great.

_childDocuments_.review: is an enjoyable puzzle game with a unique concept and a solid timeline mechanic. The premise of each level is to build a story using the characters and the settings given to you by mixing and matching them into picture frames, which are then ordered to form a sequence of events. By dragging one or two of the available characters into one of the available environments, you animate them and make them act according to the chosen environment and the story has built so far. Changing something in a previous frame will modify all the subsequent ones to reflect these changes. For example, when a certain character dies, they will appear as a ghost in all frames after the current one, making the other characters interact with them differently than when they were alive.The title of the story will tell you exactly what’s expected of you, and part of the fun is discovering ways to make your characters perform a particular action. Some puzzles are very trivial and can be solved in mere seconds, while others are quite complex and will require you to place the characters in various circumstances so that they end up liking or hating each other, giving them motives to perform the actions suggested by the story’s title. For example, a character placed in a setting containing a gun will pick it up only if they have a motive to do so and will further use that gun to kill another character only if a previous frame made them hate each other.In a way,  is a “find the developer’s solution” kind of game, considering that the levels usually have unique solutions. Some titles are intentionally left vague, though, allowing you to solve a level in two different ways, but even so, the solutions are predetermined and as soon as one of them is reached, the title changes to reflect the flow of the story you chose to create. is a game that will appeal primarily to visual people or those who enjoy from visualizing a story in their minds based on a sequence of pictures, similar to a comic book. While it could look suitable for younger audiences too due to its cute graphics and its unique way of stimulating one’s creativity, I’d say that the logical process required to reach a solution for most of the levels is rather complex, often making one think in terms of intrigue, court affairs, vengeance, jealousy etc.While the gameplay is amusing and entertaining, and the mechanics are well implemented, the game gathers a lot of negativity due to it being overpriced.  can be finished in less than three hours without checking a guide. For that amount of content the asking price of $14.99 is very high, especially since the game doesn’t offer any replayability. Annapurna Interactive is known to deliver quality products (they’re one of my favorite publishers on Steam). Even though  is up to those standards, it’s simply not enough to justify the price, not even at the 50% off discount that the game will likely reach in the next two years.

_childDocuments_.review: Story teller is a very charming game that can really get the brain working. It's simple, the game gives you a prompt you fulfill it, well maybe not so simple at times but that's just game progression for you. The comic panels updating in real time also helps with experimenting and teaching the player how one panel can affect another. It can be really rewarding to find alternate ways to fill in the prompts of each level and even messing around with character interactions. However there is one big flaw. The secret stamp collection. I finished this game 100% and the secret stamp collection was very much my least favorite part of the game. I feel if there was some sort of clue or hint on where to fulfill the conditions of each stamp it would be less of a hassle. I can understand what they were trying to do, making a scavenger hunt of sorts. However it quickly becomes annoying if you plan to 100% the game. Searching each chapter for the characters and setting you need. One of the stamps is also mislabeled. I looked it up and it's because the stamp was in the last version, however it was different in the way you got it. Despite being reused in this version they did not update the description, I had to look up a guide to complete this one, it really ruined my experience by the end, and I felt robbed of a clean 100%. Still I would highly recommend playing this game casually without spoilers, if you plan to get the stamps, maybe look up where each one is located and figure out the solution from there. Final Score 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: An innovative game that features game mechanics that I have not seen before.You place scenes and characters in a fixed number of panels and they interact with each other in sequence. Your task is now to create an interaction that matches a prompt like "Everybody dies". Each character can have different personalities and motivations, but you can manipulate them with your story.What I really love about Storyteller are the small interactions that tell you the current state of a relationship in the panel. The queen will not execute the maid, and will give a thumbs up and put on a royal smirk, while the to be executed maid looks hopeful and won't be executed in this panel. And there are loads of little interactions like this!The game seems to run on some kind of inference engine, in which you input new information with each panel to get a certain output. There is no hard-coding of solutions like you would expect from some low-quality game, but you can - quite surprisingly - achieve the prompt in different ways.EDIT:The recent updates really elevate the already excellent game. The dev did a fantastic job to polish it even more and to add free new content. I am having fun going for 100% completion even though I finished the old base game half a year ago.

_childDocuments_.review: While Storyteller is undoubtedly a short game, at around 2-3 hours for 100%, it is one of the most unique experiences I have ever had playing any video game. Its premise of building a story based on the title to solve puzzles is one that I knew couldn't have been easy to make, and I'm glad to experience a one-of-a-kind indie game.If you want more Storyteller content, I recommend you to either wait for more updates, or check out the Custom Levels Mod. I have made 20 levels myself with it, and plan to make more!

_childDocuments_.review: This game was extremely well-produced. The art is great and the concept is great. But it fails to build its mechanics to an interesting complexity. And how could it, with a puzzle count of ≈50 and a runtime of <2hr? Note that I don't mind the runtime or price of the game per se. If it were an expensive short great game I would be elated with it. But as it is, the game feels like the mere introductory portion of what it should be.     It's something of a question if that means I should 👍 on this review because I want there to be more games like this, or 👎 because I don't think this is there yet. In the end, my choice is determined by the fact that steam says these reviews are Recent Reviews: Very Positive (81) / All Reviews: Mostly Positive (1,805). So, I don't think I'm in any danger of dooming this game to be unpopular and unprofitable by writing this review. I might as well express my measured criticism full-throatedly, with a 👎. Because I would not, generally, recommend this game to other players. Even though some other aspects of this game are very good and I wish success for the developer.     I played the demo of this game last year, and am surprised that this version of the game hasn't evolved much from that, puzzle-wise. I think there are like 5 interestingly new puzzles. Again, I don't care per se that the final version of the game wasn't longer than the demo. I still think highly of Superhot the game, even though it's approximately as long as Superhot the demo. But Superhot the demo was significant enough on its own that I would have bought it as a real indie game with no other improvements. But the final version of Storyteller does, in an important way, still feel like a demo.     I did not do any of the steam achievements on this copy of the game, because I did them all in the demo, and they seem to be largely the same. If you haven't done them though, and you're playing the game, you should; they're basically like 10 extra, good puzzles; they're a title that requires you to create a situation, like every other puzzle in the game. Doing them is like 20% more game, right there.     I will probably now return this game to Steam, and get a refund. Since I finished it before the refund window closed, and feel dissatisfied with it, I don't think they'll deny me. (This may eliminate my ability to edit this review; I don't know.)     I mean this in complete sincerity and with no disrespect: if you are a child or otherwise have not played many puzzle games, you will probably enjoy Storyteller immensely.     Here's looking forward to Storyteller 2!

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a gem. The premise is clever, but what really stands out is the witty and careful execution. All the characters react in a logical way to the variety of situations you can put them through, which makes the puzzles feel fair and clever. Not to mention the adorable facial/body expressions that accompany each reaction. In fact, the whole presentation is beautiful.There are a some issues, of course. The puzzles are often too easy, especially when introducing a new mechanic or character. This does work well as a tutorial, but the number of puzzles the use each mechanic is small, so the tutorial ends up being 1/4 or 1/3 of its instances. It feels like the game struggles a bit between giving the player more freedom (which fleshes out the game's clever systems, but makes it easier to "cheese" the puzzles) and limiting their options (which makes the game slightly harder, but put the solutions on rails). This rarely affected the fun I was having with the game, but I did come out with a taste of wasted potential, due to the incredibly well-crafted systems under the hood. It would be amazing if, in the future, this game gets a level editor (like Baba Is You).I highly recommend Storyteller to everyone who likes puzzle games. Keep in mind that if you have a Netflix account you can play it for free on your phone/tablet.
_childDocuments_.name: Storyteller

_childDocuments_.review: As many have written before I, the game lacks content. It is however an amazing concept of pure creativity. If I was the developer, I would pursue the creation of a tool to easily construct new tales. This is to more easily create more content myself, but also have a chance of creating modding support. This game would thrive on custom stories from the community.Now I understand that it is difficult goal, maybe even unachievable, but a game where a user can share their absurd story by only giving out clues is intriguing to me.

_childDocuments_.review: "Simple" is the best word that comes to mind to describe this game, The art style is simple. The graphics are simple. The game play is simple. The puzzles are incredibly simple. There is nothing complicated about this game. Which is the problem with the game. Sitting straight through, no distractions, it would be easy to finish this game in an hour or two. Either the puzzles are very obvious, or they are totally random: sometimes it's like throwing a bunch of things at a wall and seeing what sticks.The decision to give this game a positive rating just came down to fun. _childDocuments_.review: This is a brilliant puzzle game. It manages to combine stories and puzzles very intimately and naturally. I've completed all the main puzzles, and can say that each and every one felt fair. There were no obtuse puzzles, even for the stories that ended up with contrived plots.The game still feels a bit short, despite the recent update. I think part of it is because some of the chapters felt a bit too easy, so their 4-5 stories went by in a flash. There were some meaty chapters that needed decent think time, namely the chapters featuring the Queen, but even the "medium" difficulty chapters didn't take too long to figure out. Difficulty varies a bit, some of the late game chapters were much easier than chapters before them.I haven't done much with the recently added stamps, since its kind of annoying to go back and forth between the stamps and the puzzles to figure out what you need to do, and they give off a feel of being optional side content.I strongly recommend the game to anyone who likes puzzle games, with the caveat of the short length of the game. Paid $10 for this during a sale, and although I don't regret it, it does feel steep for the amount of content in the game. It needs a few more difficult chapters.

_childDocuments_.review: Update: Since the update I say I can recommend this game when it's on sale, it seems to have gone up in price since I purchased it but there is more content now, however there is still little replay-ability once you get the achievements most of which were for seemingly no reason moved into the game instead of being steam achievements which removed all the achievements I had from my steam profile... oh well.All in all most of the same problems exist but with the extra content I can recommend this game at like 10-15 CAD now.Original Review:Really this game is a good concept but it's over 17 CAD for a game that might just push you over 2 hours to 100%, there is little replay value and there should be multiple books to finish at that price, the mechanic aren't overly complicated and I can't imagine it's too hard to create new story goals, they could really overlap more of the mechanics they introduce and make more stories. _childDocuments_.review: Cute, but fails to deliver an actually fun experience. Beat the game in just under 3 hours. Puzzle complexity is all over the place, ranging from obnoxiously trivial to arbitrary pedantic. Over half the puzzles were so obvious, they could be completed in under a minute. (Several times, I accidentally solved a puzzle just by switching around frames while trying to do something *else). A couple puzzles literally reuse the material from past puzzles; the solutions are 95% the same. A handful - less than 6 - were both challenging and satisfying to solve. The "harder" puzzles often have one very specific way to solve them; though you may satisfy the conditions for a solution, if it's not *the* solution, you don't get a pass. You're not creating a unique story that fits the description; you're playing a guessing game until you do what the game wants. Puzzles are all themed, which is cute, but they borrow from common tropes and fairy tales. While this helped me familiarize myself with the premise, it also meant the puzzles themselves were not foreign to me; they just rehashed existing dramas from mythical stories. That's not as interesting, IMO. I'd return it, but I took 0.9 extra hours to complete the entire game. Not worth the money/time.

_childDocuments_.review: Eventhough the game gains mixed reviews, I think I like it. _childDocuments_.review: A cute, and comically morbid puzzle game about recreating and subverting the tropes and trends of old tales. Brief but satisfying.The puzzles ramp up nicely. You learn how frames affect each other before being tasked with orchestrating scenarios that at first examination seem undoable. Fiddling with the scenario to “cheat” the character or scene’s logic to achieve seemingly impossible outcomes hits like manipulating the logic of “Baba is You”, though this game asks, thankfully, much less of me. A recent update added new challenges, including the quite tricky devil remixes which were great fun. I don’t know that I like the bonus stamps, which ask you to create literary references amongst a large pool of possible stories. I’d rather work with the game’s logic than tab out to search old english literature, but achieving some through happenstance was a devious joy. Eat your heart out, Goethe. For me, $15 is a hair much for this game, but I respect what the developers are charging for their excellent work.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really cute game for those who like storytelling, creativity, and chaos. I did the entire base game in about an hour without any assistance. I have to go back in for the final few achievements, but this is probably a 2 to 3 hour game. I'd recommend picking it up on sale if you love committing cozy crime, casual intrigue, monsters, and all other beloved fairy tale components in a twisty narrative (partially of your own making!). Some puzzles are harder than others, and some genuinely had me smiling at the shenanigans alongside the narrators.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't think I've ever loved a game so much and yet can't recommend it. As a puzzler, it is cute. There's little replayability and there's nothing unlocked.  And yet.. the premise is so strong and the delivery of what it gives you is so well done that you are left wanting so so much more while being so so disappointed at the price you paid. If there was more content coming for already paid customers, if there was Workshop support, if there was a sandbox, if there was anything more I would give it a thumbs up. Since none of that is there, this brilliant niche puzzler will sit with a 'Mostly Negative' because of the amount of content is remarkably short for the price.

_childDocuments_.review: Personally, I actually really liked Storyteller, but it feels too short to justify the price tag.The concept is great, the core gameplay (experimenting with the interactions between characters in different scenarios) is fun, and the way the game introduces new characters and scenes gradually makes for a nice build-up of depth... and then, right as the puzzles get complex enough to be challenging, the game ends. It's not like it ran out of ways to use its mechanics, either--a lot of the interactions are only used once or twice (the witch being able to transform, for example), so there's clearly plenty of design space left unexplored here.Ultimately, I can't recommend buying the game in its current state--which is a shame, really. The concept clearly has a lot of potential, and the content that's there is good; there just isn't enough content! If the price was lower ($5 or so?) or there were a lot more puzzles, I'd be leaving a much more positive review. As is, though, I don't think Storyteller is worth the price of admission (unless there's a big sale on).

_childDocuments_.review: Does length define worth/value/enjoyment? Not necessarily. There are other choose your adventures/point and clicks that last only a few hours but were utterly stellar. _childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: worth playing it if cheap.I'd give a mixed review if possible, but I think the game overall is "good". The art is nice, the concept is fun (although not really original) and the gameplay feels fine. There's nothing groundbreaking about the game concept, it's just a puzzle game about placing characters and situations in order to match the level's objective. If you've played any puzzle game themed around temporal paradoxes you'll probably crack this game very easily.The game is indeed extremely short, I 100%ed it in little over 2 hours, and that included a 20 minutes lunch break where the game was just idle. With zero replayability, the main issue I have with this game is the price. If you pay over 5 dollars for this game, you'll probably be disappointed in the end. If you catch it on sale and want a little, easy, puzzle game, it's worth considering picking up, but only if you can spare the money and don't mind it being a one time thing.PS: this game has an achievement for playing over 2 hours, clearly intended for you not to be able to return the game if you want to 100% it. Personally, I just find it sad that the developers felt the need to include that because the gaming community has such a hard time accepting some games are simply short. Having said that, I do understand some people being genuinely angry about paying full price for such a tame experience. Again, consider buying it if you won't be offended by how short it is.

_childDocuments_.review: Storyteller is a neat, short, focused and polished gameplay experience based on a really clever and unique game mechanic.I was particularly impressed with the game's resuse of characters and scenes to create new stories from a small number of building blocks. Different characters (e.g. Queen vs. Baron) react differently to scenes and other characters, and understanding these different behaviors is required for solving many levels.I had three minor misgivings: Lack of undo is annoying, as is an inability to save multiple solutions for puzzles. The latter is doubly annoying because the game saves separate solutions in *some* circumstances, but not usually. Finally, in the bonus content, there are optional stamps you can collect. But they're only unlocked after finishing the game, and the in-game hints are way too cryptic. Fortunately there was a spoiler-free guide which explained in which levels to pursue which stamps.Ultimately I enjoyed this game and appreciated its short length.
