The concept is easy enough. You have a limited amount of scenes and characters. You then get a story prompt and have to arrange the scenes and characters in a way that the prompt is fulfilled. Alternatively, you get an extra detail that makes you think out of the box to fulfil that prompt. As someone who enjoys writing stories, this was a great exercise for me to think out of the box. I also feel like this concept spoke to me because as a child I loved to reimagine my favourite stories.+ 1 for unique and easy game concept(+ 1 because the game is truly unique and I can’t think of a single game with a similar concept)(+ 1 because of personal bias)+ Charming The game is designed as a fairytale book. The scenes and characters seem hand drawn and once you put them in a scene, they have a cute animation. It fits the theme of the game perfectly and the art style is very adorable.+ 1 for charming graphics+ Theme fitting I personally love the game soundtrack and sounds; they remind me of my childhood when I went to a professional storyteller with my school class and they made all these magical sounds and had a nice tune in the background. The sounds get played once a character is in a scene, which is a nice detail. You can also disable the soundtrack, if you prefer to play the game quietly. You can also buy a soundtrack DLC if you want to hear the soundtrack outside of the game.+ 1 for magical sounds and soundtracks+ Talented While the characters themselves aren’t voiced, there is the option to enable the voice of a storyteller who reads the story prompts out loud. He pretty much has the voice you expect, when you think of a storyteller, so I’d say they did an amazing job at casting this talented voice actor!+ 1 for the storyteller voice actor+ Interesting The given story prompts are really fun in my opinion, on one hand you have classic stories like Dracula and Adam & Eve and on the other hand you have fun reinterpretations such as Nietzsche within the Adam & Eve story. The characters themselves are also very fun, some of them have preferences and personality quirks. While some characters prefer male counterparts’ others can also fall in love with a character of the same gender. Also, the further you play you encounter the same character again and may find out some interesting details about them. Such as one of them is actually a werewolf! +1 for fun story prompts+1 for characters who have a tiny bit of lore+ An I personally feel like the game has easy and a bit harder prompt. While most of the puzzles are very easy there were also a few ones that I had a bit of a hard time trying to figure out. However, once you finish the game there is a secret game mode that will be unlocked and you can also try to figure out fun little details or try to tell other classic storys through the stamp collect that pretty much work like achievements within the game.+ 1 for reasonable (easy) difficulty(+ 1 for a secret game mode)(+1 for achievements within the game)+  Stable storytelling While playing the game it ran smoothly and I didn’t encounter any bugs.+ 1 for no bugs or performance issueso a few While there are already in game achievements, this game also has 5 steam achievements. I think it is a nice addition, although the achievements are pretty easy to get. For some this might be good for others this might be boring.+ 0.5 for Steam achievementso It’s rather  for a storytelling game BUT!While I did manage to play this game through in a relatively short time, I do appreciate the free update with the secret mode and in game achievements. I still feel like it is a tad too short for the price. I think this could be fixed with a creative mode (see: “What I wish the game had”)+ 0.5 for short game play that has been tried to extendedo An awesome one time experience for an While I did greatly enjoy the game and do appreciate all the work that went into it, I feel like the price is just okay. I did replay the game thank to the in-game achievements and the secret mode. Yet there is only so much to do. I ended up playing the game for roughly 4 hours and am already finished. I didn’t rush playing the game either. So, it feels like the price is for me personally a tiny bit hefty for just 4 hours. Others might think differently, so this is extremely subjective on my part.+ 0 for the price that might be a bit much for just a few hours of gameplay.o Three times the charm, yet no true I feel like the first game playthrough is pretty easy and manageable within one or two hours. The secret mode and in game achievements are highly appreciated, however also rather short lived in my opinion. After 3 playthroughs there is not much to do which is a bit sad, considering the price and the potential for a creative mode. (see: “What I wish the game had”)+ 0 because the developers did try to make this playable more than once and for others that might be enough (for me it is still a bit short lived)nothing major :)see “Sort of good, sort of bad” for potential bad points.* I wish there was a  where you could do your own storiesI feel like the sort of negative critique I have for this game could be fixed if this game had a creative mode. The characters and scenes are so fun! It would be great if other players could plan story prompts and share it with others. Or if you could make your own stories where all scenes and characters are available and to choose from. This could improve the games replayability and length by a great shot in my opinion.Out of possible 12 points this game reached:  +  (due to bonus points)This means I absolutely would recommend this game!! I had a lot of fun playing it, because of its unique game concept and adorable characters that make the experience even more fun. Thanks to the secret game mode and in-game achievements, it is possible to play the game a few times. However the game playthroughs are rather short lived, so I suggest getting the game when it is on sale :)

_childDocuments_.review: I had been looking forward to this game for quite a while. The other reviews give good reasons why you might not want to play the game, but I feel that the demo did a great job conveying what you're paying for. It's a game with nice art, cute characters, some puzzles, and some freedom for creativity.It does seem like a bit of a short game, but my favorite part is playing around with the outcomes. There were times I wish I had extra panels, not to solve the puzzle, but to make the most interesting/funny outcome that still told a similar story. What would really take this game from "short, fun, game" to something more exciting is the option to make our own stories and to create and share our own levels. If you watched people play it and/or tried the demo, it's exactly what you expect. I personally had plenty of fun. I just truly wish for a sandbox & level maker option. The materials are all there, so I have fingers crossed it will be available at some point. PS: about the art, I was excited to see each character having their own personality and react differently to the same scenario (all characters have a wide range of emotion/action sprites, and each character has their own slightly different version of the animation. It's not a main point, but I was a really nice touch.

_childDocuments_.review: I have a box of Myrioramas, which are illustrated cards that each contains a piece of an element, a focal subject that when placed next to each other, forms a complete picture. The box I have is called The Hollow Woods, it has a dragon, a dark forest, a knight, werewolves, a horse, a hut sitting coldly at the end of a path. The back of the cards is, just as lovely drawn as the illustration themselves, thorn, and they also cleverly form a coherent wall of thorns like a usual roadblock you often find in fantasy games. It has its own rules like other card games, but you can treat it as a modular storytelling machine by placing cards in an order that resembles a setup - payoff motif.But the thing is because of the modular nature, these cards don't "complete" each other in a fully satisfying sense despite having lots of combinations, they leave enough gap between important events and become the backbone of the story rather than the entire body. It is flexible because it has leftover emptiness like that, so players can fill those holes on their own and the story fully becomes theirs.Which is a funny revelation, because I didn't buy this box of cards on a whim. I looked for them after reading Philip Pullman's The Secret Commonwealth, the second book in The Book of Dust series which are prequels and sequels from the spiral multiverse anti-religious fantasy trilogy His Dark Materials. A big theme of His Dark Materials is truth, the validity of truth, and how far humans would go to preserve, protect and dominate truth. The protagonist Lyra Silvertongue has a pocket compass called Alethiometer that tells her the truth behind everything through cryptic symbols. It's a fun character-building deus ex machina as Lyra herself is quick-witted and isn't above lying to her teeth to get what she wants (hence the nickname), but also a culmination of her devotion towards righteous truth, the kind of truth that Alethiometer tells her but never the method of finding it out. Believing your destiny is one thing, knowing it in the palm of your hands but dreading the process of reaching it and thus getting heartbroken over the inevitable is the kind of tragedy that very few can bear.In The Secret Commonwealth, Lyra meets an old man fluent in French on a train, who introduced the pack of cards he used to entertain a sick child. The illustrations on those cards are separately concrete, portraits of life, but when grouped together, they seamlessly tell a story and bring a landscape to life. But unlike the Alethiometer, Myrioramas are real, played by 19th-century children in Europe even. It is far from a visual spin of chatGPT, but what it offers is a kickstart of imagination in motion, a soul bridge for the mind. Where did the dragon come from? Is it fighting the knight? Is the werewolf an ally of the knight? Is the story about humans versus monsters, or a post-legend story where creatures were eradicated and the woods are more psychologically threatening? The idea isn't about the beginning or the end, but rather the meaty part that is built upon the backbone.Storyteller is far from a card game, but the idea is close. Background elements serve as context, characters are dragged and dropped. Scenarios are divided into levels, levels are presented as chapters in a book. Levels have an objective as the climax, and some often have "side quest" as a what-if question. It can be easily mistaken as a puzzle game, but I think this is where it gets interesting because writing stories is akin to solving puzzles. You can't have a good story without foundation, problems, and solutions. Storyteller let you become the architect of all of those with the only limitation being the number of panels you can tell the story in. "Tell me a story about a healed heartbreak", does it include death, reborn, a difficult path to gain comfort, and unrequited attachment? Dealing with dilemmas is immensely more interesting in this game, because in some ways you are the person who created it in the first place.Of course, simplicity can occasionally be a double-edged sword. A short story can be impactful if it's concise and straight to the point, but sadly Storyteller is fragmented and more interested in visualizing various classic literary themes. It is a game that evokes a lot of great memories in me and a fantastic inspirational experience at the cost of breaking ground and hitting the audience where it's hardest. The truth is Storyteller's value doesn't lie within its replayability or its contest against video games' standards. It's merely a nice novelty that showcases the potential of this medium, speaks to some people, and hopefully inspires game-loving storytellers that one day will dare to tell the truth, not the type of truth that objects to lies and injustice, but rather the truth deep within us, waiting for the right time to sings out loud, fully form and ready to connect to the same souls that simply hold a particular love for stories.

_childDocuments_.review: An extremely fresh concept for a puzzle game. I could try to explain this game but its quite hard to do with text. Its best just to watch the first level on youtube to get the concept. If I had to explain: its a game where you get a prompt and you have to use your assets to recreate the prompt.That being said there is a lot going on trying to make those prompts. You can follow the prompts or make completely different story lines if you want to, those weird situations that you yourself create are incredibly interesting and fun. And beating some of the harder levels is also extremely satisfying. Its a really original and interesting concept and that alone would make me recommend this game. All of this is backed up with a fantastic art style and extremely clear UI design. Animations flow freely and its clear what is going on even if you make a couple of big changes to your story lineup. All in all its incredible.There are 2 problems however. The prompts aren't always extremely clear, there were a couple of times where I genuinely didn't understand what the game was asking of me. A big majority of the prompts are clear and interesting, but those like 3 or so confusing levels are quite frustrating. The reason they are so frustrating is because of the 2nd problem. The games length, all in all you can finish it in around 1 to 2 hours (Maybe 3 with achievements) without any real replay value or bonus challenges. In that length of time everything basically has to be perfect so those couple of bad levels really pop out when the game is this short. A workshop mode where players can create levels for the community would have been really appreciated, or even reusing the same levels and making more interesting prompts like they did for the achievements would also have been fantastic.If you can handle a games shortness then this is a really fun experience, if its worth 13 bucks is up to you. For me it was more then worth it. I enjoyed this more then I enjoyed some games that are 10 + hours long. The older I get the more I appreciate these kinds of original and quick fire games. If you go into it knowing that its short then I guarantee you will have a really enjoyable experience. Now to hope they release DLC or some free updates to expand even more on this incredible concept.

_childDocuments_.review: Such a cute and fun puzzle game! The art is adorable and the stories are actually very interesting. The game is played by going through various 'titles' of stories. It is then up to you to place characters and scenes into various positions to create relationships and various scenarios that prompt the story to play out based on the title. Each of the characters interact differently or have traits that affect how they will behave and you can then further influence their decisions in the panels by creating history with others or establishing events.It's challenging to explain but this game will be loved by people who like to think through puzzles to create a desired outcome. Game overall took about 2 hours to play and 4 hours for all the achievements. Regardless it was totally worth the price and I'd buy it again! Highly recommend!

Indie developers have different financial constraints than big powerhouse studios, and they can't be so aggressive on the pricing. I get it. But here, it's just asking for way too much money relative to its content.Honestly, you need to wait for a steam sale or a  price drop before getting this game. But right now, the price is almost double this threshold that, IMHO, would make the price palatable. I don't recall paying an hour of digital entertainment so much in almost 20 years. And that's definitely not good for this game.I really wish I could recommend Storyteller without reserve, but in an era of games that you can play hundreds of hours for free or for 10 bucks, paying near 15, for barely more than an hour of fun, stings a little bit too much in terms of value. _childDocuments_.review: is a short puzzle game with an emphasis on the player to craft stories, some romantic, some complex but overall charming. This is a game where you piece together puzzle elements to create the story. The game takes the form of a book in which you create the story panel by panel, much like a comic book. For each puzzle you're given a set of characters and are supposed to arrange them to fit a story of the title you're given. So there is no one story in this game but a variety of mini stories to tell divided up into chapters. The joy of this game is to play around with the characters by placing them in various panels to see what happens. Trial and error can be rewarding and entertaining. Some of the tales will be familiar to many. Love, betrayal and jealousy fuel many of the stories. Some are your classic fairy tales to stories of a Shakespearean nature such as Romeo & Juliet. The settings in this game are pretty straight forward and basic. You have audio level, language, fullscreen or windowed, quality and the ability to turn the narrator on or off. The pages of the book are yellowed and look washed out in contrast to the characters (who look like decals or stickers) and have more colouring to them. Once you drop the characters into a scene they will play an animation and those animations will vary depending on their placement in the story. The soundtrack sounds like something you would hear in a story about royalty and the narrator's voice is so well done. I kept the narrator on as I personally enjoyed his humour. * After completing the main levels go back through the chapters to play the Devil levels (the chapter level marked with a pentagram)* There are 31 bonus stamps to collect (for where to find these I suggest looking at one of many great community guides)* I played the whole game with a mouse but the game does support a controller. * To get the achievement for playing over two hours close the game and re-open it after the two hour mark for it to activate. I enjoyed this game. It is quite short so I suggest getting it on sale. But the animations and stories can be pretty funny and entertaining. It is a really different type of game and really can not compare it to anything else I have played. So the uniqueness was very refreshing. There are not a lot of achievements but they are obtainable without too much stress. The only one I don’t like is having to play for over two hours. It is obvious to me why that one is thrown in there for such a short game. Still it did take me close to two hours to actually finish the game (maybe a tad shy). So take that for what it is. Overall a fun game that brings something different to the table. 📖

_childDocuments_.review: I've been waiting for this game for about 10 years. It is fun, but frankly I'm a bit disappointed. Some of this comes from features that were in previous publicly shown versions of the game which is a bit unfair, but it mostly comes from the size of the game. You can finish the entire game in well under two hours, and besides a few achievements, which you have to slowly navigate to a level they're even possible in, that's it.That, paired with a very slow to navigate UI for selecting levels which saps my desire to go back to them (Something like a "Table of contents" that lists chapters is needed so players can jump to the one they want without clicking through them sequentially), is the reasoning behind this review.I'll probably go back and play though the entire game again in some time, because it is a lot of fun and it's interesting to fiddle with it, but I can't recommend it for someone else to spend their money on.Update 1: Original review had 80 minuets at time of review as reference for the opinions stated above.I was going to change my review to positive after the devil update, I believe it added enough to the game with an enjoyable twist that kept things interesting for it to be a worth-while purchase (and re-added previous content as I complained about in my original review.) The other complaints I had at time of review still stand; I find the user experience very poor. Adding more achievements that are now in-game is nice (the reward is mainly seeing unique animations/screens), but does not change how annoying it is to navigate to where those achievements can be earned. The addition of the "Worth it" achievement is what stopped me from ever changing this review. The achievement is only for playing the game for 2 hours, the steam no-questions refund cutoff. This achievement both directly mocks the sentiment I stated in my original review (that the game lacked too much content and was too short to be "worth it", i.e. recommending others to pay money for), and is poorly implemented. At time of writing, I have over 2 hours of playtime but lack the achievement. Forcing any user who did enjoy and complete the game (and the update for some time after its release) to idle for two hours is poor by any metric. If the developer wants his game to be seen as worth buying and keeping by consumers, he must craft it into a state where they see it that way. Obviously some people will game the system, and I'm not endorsing that, but responding this way is not building goodwill.

_childDocuments_.review: The kingdom is looking for a new Grand Storyteller, and you are just the person for that crown. With your trusty storybook, piece together over 50 pages of tales told in comic panel style. With only the ending in mind, put together your people, places and things into the correct order and become known as the greatest story teller this side of the kingdom.In Storyteller, you attempt to tell stories [shocking, yes] in a Jeopardy-style manner: each level has a short sentence of what happens and its your job to make it happen. Move around your settings and your characters to get the desired result. Often times, as you move unrelated things around, you'll discover some funny interactions maybe you hadn't intended, like an accidental death or romance. Sometimes these aren't helpful towards your goal, but they are amusing to discover as you test various what-ifs (and maybe unlock a secret sticker).To make things more fun, some levels have further objectives. For example, one level might be "Everyone is heartbroken". Once you accomplish that, a further one unlocks saying "...and then everyone died." After your first run through, you get one more tool to further change some previous levels with yet more new goals, although I won't spoil who or what it is.Overall, it is just a really fun and unique game. The story book layout is cozy and the actual gameplay is intuitive and easy to use, especially helpful when you have a general idea of the timeline for a level but are just missing one or two aspects to finish it. The music and narrator are great, carrying the fairy tale throughout the game. Although I might have liked a bit more narrator for each chapter, perhaps with a short blurb when you unlock the chapter for the first time. There is a cute part at the beginning where you can cut off the narrator as he is reading the first page to you and cause him to humph, but otherwise he had a comforting voice through your page turnings.The only minor gripe I had were the secret stamps. I am pretty sure they only unlock once you've beaten the main game, meaning you can't unlock them in your initial playthrough, when your doing the bulk of your interaction testing. Luckily, while they didn't straight up tell you which level each is on, they all had little taglines to help you identify where you might start. For example, one might call for John to marry Jim's ex. By the end of the game, you should have a pretty good grasp of the Putting together what aspects are needed (John, Jim, Third character, Marriage, Death/Divorce), it helps drastically lower the possible number of levels.Great game and price for a clever and tittilating experience. Easily 2-4 hour play time depending on your skill/completionist tendencies.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been following Daniel Benmergui's work since I first played I Wish I Were the Moon and Today I Die when I was in middle school. It has been about 16 years since then, and the impact that those 2 games left on me had me hyped to this day for the release of Storyteller. Now that I've played it I can say, I tried to like it, I really did, but at the end the game fell flat in delivering any meaningful experience. Even in a vacuum assuming I hadn't played the two aforementioned games before, Storyteller is at best a mediocre puzzle game. The main mechanic is interesting in concept. The game gives you a storyboard with a predetermined number of panels and it asks you to give each panel a setting and characters. All in order to fulfill a different objective with different panel types and characters per level. Each panel type, each character and even each order of actions creates a different "story"The issue arises with the fact that while the game purports itself to be about telling stories creatively, each level feels as if it can only be solved with a very limited number of configurations. And even worse, many levels wind up feeling like retreads of concepts you saw in previous levels. While game length is not an issue for me personally, I do feel that having a game this short feeling repetitive is fairly troubling.As I said before I had high hopes for this game. But at the end of the day, this is not a thought-provoking project, a vehicle for creativity, nor even a good puzzle game. Storyteller is the logical end result of forcing your way through the sunk-cost-fallacy on a project that only sounded good as a concept, yet clearly didn't work in execution.

_childDocuments_.review: First review, cause this game feels very special. I finished the actual game in about 2 hours, with an additional hour to get the stamps, using a guide for which levels to use. The short time might be a turn-off for some, but I don't regret the purchase at all. The art style is distinct and charming, and it's a really unique puzzler. It was enjoyable to learn the pre-existing relationships between characters, their personalities, and how they interact with scenes, using all of this information to build the steps towards the goal.My only complaint stems from the UI, specifically navigating between chapters. There are tabs on the book to go between the chapters and the menus at the end; I was surprised that chapter tabs were not added as well. This isn't an issue going through the puzzles in order, but when you're paging through the chapters looking for the characters you need for a stamp, waiting for the page flip animation going through each of the ~15 chapters feels very slow. This is ultimately why I ended up using a guide to find which chapters could be used for which stamps. Another potential improvement would be an index at the end of the book, allowing you to quickly navigate to a story that contains a specific character or scene.That complaint aside, I really enjoyed this, and if a sequel or expansion were added, I would certainly buy it. Like any good puzzler, it leaves you craving more of the problems it was asking you to solve.

_childDocuments_.review: Recommended ONLY on sale. I beat it, with the few additional challenges, in 79 minutes as calculated by steam. Requesting a refund. Don't get me wrong, it's cute, it's fun, it CAN make you scratch your head and think, but its Over priced at $15. It desperately needs a way to allow you to create your own levels and more to make it worth this price. Maybe worth $5 at this current state.Keep in mind, this is reviewed before the free DLC comes out, which adds 4 stages, adds a devil mechanic to some previous levels, in game challenges, and probably something else not listed yet. This is the game at launch I'm reviewing.To start, Pros:Cute artSFX are entertainingthe drama you make CAN be funIt does make it super clear when something doesn't align as you need for the specific ending so you're never stuck for long.Funny logic puzzles are funny.Mixed- Little room for creativity in the later stages. While the first few allow you to mix and match things, future puzzles GENERALLY have one path that works. Go into this knowing there will be specific routes for most stages, you cannot go willy nilly with making the butler romance the Duchess to then kill the duke. Trust me, I tried. :(Cons-Play time. Play time play time play time...While I did want to get creative with it, sometimes the answers can be reached in levels before expected. That's fine, except when it doesn't *think* you've achieved your goal.Minor spoiler, Ex. In the Reunited in the Afterlife bonus, I got them together after having them get married. But it didn't register this despite them being together in death. I had to revive one and kill them again for some reason to 'finish' the puzzle. Super odd, but basically, sometimes you need to think in a 'show your work' way.It was fun, but not worth the money. _childDocuments_.review: I don't want to say that this game is too short- that's too reductive. There are plenty of very fun games that explore their concept, offer a fun time, and then finish in relatively short order, no fat along the way.The problem with Storyteller is it doesn't reach its' potential by a long shot. There are several ideas absolutely aching to be explored- the vampirism, seances, the witch and frog- and yet each is over after they've scraped the surface. It demonstrates remarkable detail in terms of putting together 'wrong answers' to get interesting scenarios, which shows that they even already have some of these ideas implemented!I don't quite understand why this was released with so few stories. There is so much here already without even needing to add any new characters, actions, or combinations- and it's disappointing that this was released as threadbare as it is.

_childDocuments_.review: Storyteller is a charming, witty, but oft frustrating game that ends just as it's getting good. Even with the recent (Sept. 2023) update it's still just too short for the price of the game--even on sale.Pros: The art style and narration is perfect and was clearly made with a lot of though and care. I love how the character models change in response to the scene, such as old Edgar or sleeping Lenora. The game controls work well and are very responsive. It feels great when a puzzle is a literary references and you already know the solution. The extra challenges on some level are what I found most fun and I would have enjoyed more of these.Cons: Game length is huge issue. If it hadn't been for my completionist tendencies and the fact that the stamps don't seem to activate until you get the Crown, I probably could have 100% this game within the Steam return window.The devil content update I think would have been better as it's own chapter with more introduction to the content that one lone tutorial level. Backtracking to find the stages was irritating especially as I jumped around revisiting levels and I was stumped because I didn't fully understand the devil mechanics. I think just a little more structure could have really helped both these issues. I'm not sure if this was a bug or as intended, but Stamps didn't activate for me until after I got the Crown, which meant a lot of backtracking to find levels where I KNOW I completed certain challenges, which would activate as soon as I opened the level. This is especially frustrating since the game doesn't tell you what level can solve each stamp, requiring you to go back through every level manually and guess if I can complete the stamp.Some additional feedback, I think a Hint function could go a long way, even one with limited uses powered by how many levels you've completed. There were often times I needed a small nudge or had one wrong scene and would turn to a third-party guide out of frustration. Implementing a Hint function would allow players who want/need the help to get it without hindering players who are fine without.Ultimately, I feel that Storyteller is 70% of the way to the finish-line of making a really good game. I think that in a year's time, after additional content updates it will feel like a complete experience. But in it's current state I don't recommend unless HEAVILY on sale.

name: The Plucky Squire
detailed_description: The Plucky Squire follows the magical adventures of Jot and his friends - storybook characters who discover a three-dimensional world outside the pages of their book. When the malevolent Humgrump realizes he's the villain of the book - destined to lose his battle against the forces of good for all eternity - he kicks the heroic Jot out of its pages and changes the story forever. Jot must face challenges, unlike anything he's ever seen if he is to save his friends from Humgrump's dark forces and restore the book's happy ending. Jump between 2D and 3D worlds in this charming action-adventure - solving puzzles, boxing badgers, flying with a jetpack, and enjoying many more delightful and surprising mini-challenges as you become the hero of a living storybook.

_childDocuments_.review: Everything The Plucky Squire tries, it tries successfully. Whether in or out of the storybook, every moment of this game is a delight.Inside the book is a top down 2-d Zelda clone with the gimmicks of changing nouns and adjectives to shape objects, as well as tilting and stamping the book itself to solve puzzles. It all comes together wonderfully and the controls feel really good.Outside the book the game adds a little more (but admittedly not as much as I thought) platforming into the mix, and takes a page from Mario odyssey and A Link Between worlds, wall mechanics to meld into the pages of anything hand drawn to progress. I genuinely loved when the game told me I needed to leave the book and find an item, because whatever shape the desk you explore took was exciting. Jetpacking in a space themed desk or scaling a dinosaurs tail in a Jurassic one, really it’s tough to decide which form of gameplay is the best.Between both sections there’s also a lot of gameplay diversity in some fun mini games. Punch out, puzzle bobble and even rhythm heaven, these moments are really great and none really stink (though I had a controller issue with one or two)All of this is packaged in one of the most appealing art styles I’ve played through in a long while. The storybook just looks so freaking good. Outside the book doesn’t slouch either, with life size objects reminding me of finding objects in Pikmin. Style can go a long way to boosting a games quality and Plucky Squire doesn’t let you down…where it DOES let me down is the length. This game took me 6 hours and at a $30 price tag, I’m prepared to say that feels a bit steep. The game is mostly a straight shot of linear game design (also very easy I should mention) with the only bonus objective being finding concept art and glitch birds. Miss any and you gotta use chapter select to go back and look. Even with this though, I feel like there should be more game here. One could make the argument that if that happened, the game could end up feeling bloated as a result but considering things stay the same level of quality throughout, I think a few more hours could have worked.After all, of the games 9 chapters, only 5 of them feel like full length levels. The other 4 are actual minutes each which can lead to some really weird pacing problems. If every chapter was an equal length I’d think to call the experience complete.Of course if the only argument I have for the game is in its length (and admittedly a few bugs and lag spikes) then clearly the journey with Jot and friends is worth taking. A wholesome family friendly experience that succeeds at what it set out to do. Current game of the year (but UFO 50 drops tomorrow and Zelda Echoes of Wisdom next week so…we’ll see how long that lasts)(This review is a copy of my review from

_childDocuments_.review: I really wish I could recommend this game. It has an awesome concept, and some very fun core mechanics. The idea of mixing 2D and 3D gameplay is genius, and the storybook aesthetic is extremely charming.Actually, to focus on the positives, the graphics really are beautiful, especially inside the storybook. All the art is really well-made, and the tiny effects that make it seem like this is really all a book on a table, including a little crease in the middle of the book, really bring it all to life.The problems however, start when you actually play the game, and it is insanely handholdy. Anytime anything happens, the game stops you out of nowhere so some character can say a one-liner or blatantly over-explain something you already figured out. Even opening doors gets tiring when each and every time, the game takes away control to show you a painfully show (but very pretty) animation of the door sliding open, and when this happens for everything, you get tired of playing very quickly. I was really hoping this game would be good, but unfortunately it seems it's too afraid to trust its players. Would probably be great for kids though.

_childDocuments_.review: The game has a nice art style and design with the 2d/3d idea however the gameplay is just too basic and easy like it's aimed at little children which is fine if that's who the developers are targeting for their audience, the narrator/npcs constantly interrupting gameplay ruins the flow. The game also just throws the answers to all the puzzles at you even on Adventure mode which is meant to be harder? There should be an option to turn this off or it shouldn't be a thing in adventure mode.The amount of soft locking due to bugs I've experienced in this game is actually insane making me replay parts of the game which is infuriating especially when I was revisiting chapters to collect things I've missed as there is no auto save (weird design choice) so you essentially have to keep replaying the same chapter over and over in the hopes that you don't run into a bug that soft locks the game.I would avoid buying this game until at least the bugs have been fixed.
_childDocuments_.name: The Plucky Squire

_childDocuments_.review: I’d been looking forward to this game for a while, and when I finally got to play it, the first impression was just as amazing as the trailers promised. The vibrant storybook visuals and fairytale-like narration are really attractive, and the puzzle mechanics were fun and engaging. The way the game is presented is also genuinely amusing. But when it came to jumping into the 3D world, I was hoping for something a lot more exciting. Instead, the limited interactions, weird camera angles, and clunky controls made exploring feel less fun. Some of the puzzles were super interesting, and I wanted more of that, but they kind of just ended too soon. The combat is smooth enough, but it also lacks that satisfying depth. Overall, it’s a decent experience, but it could have been something truly great with a bit more polish
_childDocuments_.name: The Plucky Squire

_childDocuments_.review: I want to preface by saying that this game is incredibly charming. You can feel every ounce of effort given by the devs and I really hope it finds commercial success (especially with younger audiences). With that being said, this game ended up being a pretty underwhelming experience for me. Its hard to describe exactly why but I guess I was just expecting a bit more. In hindsight this sounds pretty silly, but I never considered the possibility that this was supposed to be a simple puzzle game aimed at a younger demo. I was super drawn in by the style, the mini games , and the cool looking puzzle mechanics that I figured this would be a more engaging experience. But the mini games ended up being a bit too easy for me to have to engage in any meaningful way. The puzzles were cute and sometimes would get close to being clever, but they never required much thought and largely felt very restrained (which is the exact opposite experience I was expecting). And the story had some very touching themes but more often than not only served to slow down what was already a bit of a tedious experience. It probably sounds like I hate this game, but I really do see the value in it and I hope that this team continues to create from this foundation in the future. It really seems to have the bones of an amazing game and will probably be enjoyed by many people. And because of that I don't feel as guilty not recommending this one. Ultimately I think you should give it a shot if you think it looks cool and want an above average 8 hour experience. Even better if you can enjoy this with your kid or younger family member. But if you happen to be someone like me who was  expecting something else, I would consider holding off for a sale.
_childDocuments_.name: The Plucky Squire

_childDocuments_.review: Nothing makes me more sad then to rain on someone else's parade, especially when so much heart has been put into it. While the game's art and sound design is brilliant the actual game play is a total chore. Not only is the combat clunky and the platforming awkward but there is no trust in the player at all for the entire game. From the puzzles to the exploration. Everything is hamstrung by a lack of belief that the player can figure out anything for themselves. I get that this game is aimed at a younger generation, however I believe even they would benefit from discovering mechanics and ideas for themselves. The story itself and dialogue are simple and passable with some creative flourishes here and there. Now I will say, the way the light and texture of the 2D Pages is rendered is nothing short of spectacular. The crease in the middle of the page, the effects popping up, and even the pages flipping. The 3D sections are cool as you hop back and forth between the book and the room. Yet no matter how nice it looks it never feels like a connected experience.Unfortunately Jonathan Biddle did not learn from his mistakes in Momo's Curse and seems doomed to repeat the same mistakes of unsatisfying game play ruining an otherwise stylish experience.
_childDocuments_.name: The Plucky Squire

_childDocuments_.review: Very solid puzzle adventure game with creative art integration of 2D and 3D. Recommend for all ages.Overall, solid story for children book but i believe story could potentially become more ambitious than currently is. And also overall game design could become more challenging in compelling way.If developer read this review, i hope that next game they could elevate more on story and game design but nonetheless i still happy with final result.
_childDocuments_.name: The Plucky Squire

_childDocuments_.review: Have you ever pondered the profound influence of the stories you read as a child? The heroes you admired, their teachings, the courage they displayed in perilous situations, and their sense of justice. These characters and their choices have shaped us, influencing our career paths, friendships, and, ultimately, our identities. But what if these stories had never existed? And what if brave squire Jot, a character from 'The Plucky Squire" was erased from the life of a young aspiring writer, Sam?That's what The Plucky Squire is about. It is a brilliant tale about the importance of stories and the courage they instill in us.Jot is an unblemished hero, a knight who fights against the evil Humgrump with the help of his friends: Violet, the sorceress, the troll, and Moonbeard, the sorcerer who is fond of disco music. But Jot is not only a brave and loyal warrior but also an excellent writer. It is not that he likes fighting all that much; it is by writing that he delights his fellow citizens with bestsellers that make clear his heart and great imagination. This is paradoxical since Jot, Violet, Humgrump, and all the others are characters in a children's picture book, The Plucky Squire.The work is the favorite story of little Sam, who has an absolute mania for Jot. So much is his love for this character, and so much gratitude for the joy this book is giving him in his formative years, that thanks to some magic (we are still in a fairy tale), we get a peek into his future: Sam will become a children's book writer, and his stories, like a kind balm, will touch the lives of so many other kids, inspiring them. Teaching them that evil never pays. In The Plucky Squire, no matter how ruthless and Machiavellian Humgrump's plan is, Jot always manages to prevent it. This aspect of the book not only entertains but also educates, instilling important values in young readers and inspiring them to become storytellers themselves.What happens if Humgrump, after becoming aware that he is just the character—moreover, the villain—of a children's book, manages to find a way to eliminate Jot from the story? In this terrible scenario, Jot will have to fight to return to his home world and prevent Sam's future from changing irrevocably, and thus that of millions of other boys.That of The Plucky Squire is a simple story, but one capable of touching deep chords. You could imagine it as a kind of Toy Story meets Harry Potter, The Little Prince, or whatever your favorite book from when you were a child. Its strength lies in realizing how these works touched our hearts and how manipulating their direction, even slightly, could have made a big difference in our lives. The genius of The Plucky Squire is that this "manipulation" doesn't stop at the theoretical level but comes in the form of dozens of gameplay ideas that leave the player continually dumbfounded.In its first moments, The Plucky Squire is a Zelda on paper. Printed on the glossy pages of our beautiful little book, Jot moves between the boards, as if in a magical flip book. Trees and florid vegetation, fantasy characters, and colors so vibrant they seem to pop off the page. We are already in a world that is inside another world. Like a window overlooking a universe we are privileged to see, the edge of the book acts as a frame, hinting that something else exists outside that story—a tangible universe made of scissors, sharpeners, and paper clips.The book is also not just a book; it is instead one of those astonishing graphic projects in which, every time you turn the page, you are left speechless at the author's visual inventions: pages that read from top to bottom as our hero descends deep into a cave, others dark (so black that you can see the texture of the print) that color as Jot goes through them. It is a display of styles and ideas that make for unique navigation.The Plucky Squire is the book of a warrior writer who is so ingenious that he can change his universe. In fact, one of the first ideas introduced in the video game is the ability to change illustrations through writing. Many environmental puzzles are solved through a system similar to that seen in "Baba, Is You?" We will find small sentences on the page describing the environment, with some keywords that you can substitute to alter the situation. For instance, a parched riverbed can become utterly full of water, and a giant road-blocking bug can be transformed into a tiny road-blocking bug. This process of looking for words within the page often involves us in layered puzzles involving classic levers and locked doors. When our Jot becomes capable of traveling between dimensions, things change quite a bit.When Humgrump succeeds in expelling Jot from the story and, literally, from the book, our hero finds himself in another dimension: the one outside, the three-dimensional one, which responds to totally different physical rules. At these junctures, The Plucky Squire loses its 2D identity and becomes a three-dimensional adventure, where the colorful fantasy settings are replaced by a world of giant tools, toys, and furniture reminiscent of Andy's bedroom in Toy Story and the home levels of Pikmin. In this new setting, Jot as much as the player must change the way they approach environmental puzzles and navigation: everything becomes tied to more precise jumps or physics, with objects to be moved or dropped to use as trampolines. This transition from 2D to 3D gameplay adds a new layer of complexity and excitement to the game, challenging the player to adapt to a different set of rules and strategies.The creative apotheosis comes at the moment when one acquires the ability to enter and exit these two dimensions through special green portals that allow one to transform Jot from time to time from the hero of the book into a kind of animated action figure and to make the two realities interact in every possible way.It is a gimmick that we have already seen and loved in The Legend of Zelda: A Link Between Worlds, and which, in some ways, especially in its ability to play with the two-dimensional nature of paper, also reminded us of the Paper Mario series. The most exciting aspect is that often, to solve puzzles in the book, you have to go out, look for an object in the "real" world, and bring it into the story. Similarly, in the three-dimensional world, some obstacles can be overcome only by the characteristics of the paper, taking advantage of gimmicks such as the folds in books and the verticality of posters. It is a continuous dialogue between two dimensions that talk to each other, intersect, and play with a physics that is there and then is no longer there. It is almost as if two different games continuously meet in a continuous exchange, enriching each other."The Plucky Squire" is a fun approach that, in each session, manages to shake up the formula, offering new mechanics and callbacks to genres seemingly light years away, especially in boss fights. The first one, for example, is an homage to Punch-Out!!!, but there are also situations where you face a JRPG-like fight against what is blatantly a card from Magic: The Gathering or disputes that seem like something out of good old Nintendo's "Rhythm Paradise".At these junctures, the Plucky Squire's most glaring flaw comes out: its excessive ease. There was no challenging moment in the game. Although the puzzles are fun and well thought out, they never prove complex."The Plucky Squire" is a Toy Story that meets your favorite book from childhood. It does so with all the love and gratitude possible for those stories that inspired us as children to become who we are today, thanks to their heroes' bravery, ingenuity, and ability to speak directly to our hearts. But it is also a fantastic video game, chock-full of ideas, aesthetic inventions, and gameplay. It knows how to make two worlds communicate excellently, merging them into one unforgettable adventure.
_childDocuments_.name: The Plucky Squire

_childDocuments_.review: I just now completed this game. I enjoyed the multiple art styles and the way each "boss battle" offered different gameplay styles like Punch-out and Bust-a-move. The main game plays similar to top-down adventure games. All very niche to popular games from the 80s/90s.Unfortunately this game is a jack-of-all-trades and master of none. It is more like a visual novel type children's book and felt like the entire game was a tutorial with how often the action was interrupted by narrative. The controls are clunky, there is lag when swapping from 2D (book) to 3D (desk), and book manipulation and some mini-games have issues with controller responsiveness. There were even times when my attacks weren't registering in 2D and 3D arenas. There is A LOT of story and it lives up to its "plucky" title, but this is not worth $30. If you can get it for sub $20 then I'd say go for it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Plucky Squire

_childDocuments_.review: The good+ Transferring between 2D and 3D is an incredibly fun mechanic+ Some creative puzzles involving words and turning pages+ Beautiful, adorable visual style+ Interesting story with a lot of meta elements+ Cool mini games including rhythm stealthThe mediocre~ 3D world is a bit bland~ In the 3D world, jumping into other books / objects was underused. What was there was enjoyable, but I expected more. As is, it was mainly used as means of simple traversal. Wish there was more of other books with different graphical styles or comic books or weird art pieces.~ Game is really easy. Depends what you like.The bad:- Controls for tilting the book and flipping pages are annoying. I constantly had to think about what did what.Overall:Plucky Squire is a solid title. I enjoyed it for what it was and can recommend playing it just for the visual style and fun mechanics. However, it did leave me a bit disappointed. From marketing, I expected way more exploration of various stories. Maybe we will get that in a sequel?
_childDocuments_.name: The Plucky Squire

_childDocuments_.review: The Plucky Squire blows me away. I expected a fun game, as the idea was already great, but I wasn't ready for how well the game mechanics were implemented and how much attention to detail there was. It has some missable achievements, completion takes around 10 hours.  Around 10 hours 4/10 1 Yes, I used the collectible guide mentioned in  No Yes, play on the "adventure" difficulty and maybe follow a collectible guide No No No No No Yes, you have to play on the "adventure" difficulty NoWhat an amazing game and amazing story! You play as the Plucky Squire, who is helping out the local wizard on a small task... but then there are some strange things happening and the world might be in danger! So off you go to explore what is going on... and this will be the adventure you won't expect with game mechanics that will blow you away! I love the different mini-games and just the story in general. It felt so unique and so well done. And did I already mention the details? I saw so many small details, like how the world looks but also for example the price of the book and how it changed with the story. At first, the narration felt a bit childish. I wasn't sure if I would be the targeted audience. I'm so glad I stuck with the game as this changed. and the narrator does such a good job of telling the story interestingly and encouragingly. The change of tone later on after a huge event was also amazing. That I love this game shouldn't come as a surprise, as I'm such a fan of the games Devovler publishes. I don't know where they find all those gems but man they do a great job finding/publishing crazy, unique, wonderful, and beautiful games. The Plucky Squire has a lot of collectibles. 50 Scrolls, most of them can be found in the wild but always keep money on hand to buy the one from the shop. As it will be a different one in every new shop you encounter. You can also find a Glitchbird in each chapter. And you will need a lot of bulbs (coins) for all the combat skills. So I highly recommend destroying every bush and hit every tree just to find enough money. However, the screen with the mouse and the big block of cheese is a nice scene to grind out money to make sure you will have enough money for sure, as you can find quite a bit of money close to the beginning of that area and then get killed instantly by that mouse to do it all over again. I believe you find this scene in chapter 6. I followed a collectible guide to not miss out on any of the collectibles as different guides mention different things about missables. It might be that with one of the later updates they aren't missable anymore but I didn't want to try that out and find out it would still be missable. The guide by PowerPyx will also mention the areas for some achievements and what to do, so you don't have to replay those areas to get back to that point, while it doesn't tell you how to solve everything or where to go. With just checking the next collectible in that guide, so you can keep it in mind you can still explore and enjoy the game without reading too many spoilers.  I give The Plucky Squire 4.5 out of 5 stars, and I'm looking forward to what All Possible Futures (The developer behind The Plucky Squire) will be cooking up next, as I hope they will continue making games!
_childDocuments_.name: The Plucky Squire

_childDocuments_.review: The Zelda equivalent of bowling with bumpers. Gosh, I was so excited for this one. The storybook art direction is wonderfully whimsical and you can feel the passion that went into making this game. I think it'd be more enjoyable as a literal storybook or an animated feature. Unfortunately, it's just...not fun. I expected something a bit more "all-ages," but instead it feels infantile. I absolutely love cute characters and stories, so it's not that I wanted something mature and edgy here. It Baby's First Zelda—as if Fi from Skyward Sword is hovering over you, asking repeatedly if you need help or if you understand what you're doing when all you've been asked to do is walk up to a sign and press Y to read it. There are two separate characters that exist specifically to give hints, some of which are forced upon you before you even attempt to proceed. The game doesn't seem to trust the player to simply digest it at their own pace. It takes no time at all for it to start feeling like a chore to complete.I don't intend to refund this because I want to support the idea behind it. The creativity on display in the game's visual presentation is notably absent in its level, combat, and puzzle design. The writing is tougher to deem objectively bad; it's simply twee. I found it hard to endure, personally.It's a shame that actually playing The Plucky Squire is much less exciting than imagining the adventure it could've been.
_childDocuments_.name: The Plucky Squire

_childDocuments_.review: I could nitpick a couple things here and there (game holds your hand too much at times, 3d sections for the most part aren’t as interesting as 2d, etc.) However this didn’t bother me at all really. This game is so creative, charming and fun from start to finish. A breath of fresh air and an easy recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: The Plucky Squire

_childDocuments_.review: Ok, let's start with the good stuff.The game is gorgeous. Both the 2d and 3d phases are really immersive, you really get the feeling that you're in a book version of The Legend of Zelda ambient-wise, and Sam's desk really holds so much soul it's impressive. Big shoutout to the artists, their work on this is amazing. The concept of going from 2D to 3D is really well exploited on this side, and the visuals live up to the expectations.I found the mage quite funny as well ; he looks like he's out of this world, his contrast with the world he lives in is well done and expressed (shoutout to his music taste!)Now with that being said, I have a lot of problems with this game. I had been expecting it for quite some time. I had been sold a mind blowing adventure playing between different mediums and supports, with a large variety of gameplay, some kind of It Takes Two experience.First off, the gameplay isn't very new ; as we say in French, it doesn't break the 3 legs of a duck. What I mean is for the approximately 2 hours I played, I didn't experience anything different from any other top-down adventure game. The infiltration during the 3D phase was clunky in my opinion ; I restarted 10 times the sequence where you have to walk over a bridge above the beetles, just because I couldn't see where I would land at the end of it ; in the worst case scenario the challenges aren't difficult, just annoying. The bug boss for instance wasn't hard ; the bow gameplay is the same as in the sequence from 5 minutes ago, it's as boring as before, to the exception that the whole body of the bug isn't where you must aim : you have to reach SPECIFICALLY for the eyes. I might have missed the memo ; but I had to die once with the frustration of aiming on the boss and not touching him or dealing any damage, before I understood that I had to go for the eyes. The mosquitoes that he throws are too fast and too close to each other for you to snipe them when the boss throws them ; your target has to go back and forth from the boss to your character, to try and get them before they get you (which they often did). You are encouraged to aim for the longest possible time so that you deal optimal damage, but nothing actually tells you that hey, you don't need to do that for the trash mob, any 0.1 second charged arrow will do.It's not the case for all of the challenges, thanks god, but when they aren't annoying they are just very easy.The puzzles as well are not very challenging ; the only time I got stuck was when there was a whole mechanic I did not know existed ("oooooooh so I can do that ??? but how would've I known ?"). The game is awfully linear, and it's a shame in my opinion the 2D-to-3D twist wasn't exploited for more than "go get this 2 pages ago and get it 2 pages forward"; there is no room for any type of creativity for the puzzles. I almost always immediately understood what the game wanted from me, and all I had left to do was the execution (the only exception being the broken bridge with the frogs sleeping at night ; this one got me stuck for 2 minutes. It was quite good, but imo it should be the low/standard challenge for the puzzles, instead of being the hardest one I encountered). The use of words to impact gameplay could've left so much room for creativity as well ; you could have a dozen of different words, each of which impact the game in some way, and up to you to figure out how to solve the puzzle ; but most of the time there are 2 to 3 words you can move, the solution is to intervert them, and tadaaaaa - moving on to the next page ; the average use of the words being "switch a door from Closed to Open".The narrative rythm is quite slow, which isn't in itself an issue, it's nice sometimes to take your time and enjoy a story being delivered slowly instead of just skipping through every dialogue ; but I perceived every interaction with any NPC as a waste of time. Here it's not "Show don't tell", it's Show AND Tell. "Oh you need a long range weapon" *the camera moves to show a playing card with an archer on it* > ok, I get it, I must reach the archer. I understood : it's a pretty common structure, I'm being shown the point I must reach, so obviously I'll go there. But just to be sure, let's have the worm interrupt me to tell me "Hey, you should get that bow and arrow over there, shouldn't you ?" I didn't find the dialogues to be very well written as well ; they state a lot of obvious things that were already implied (like the example just before), and use the same cliché lines you've already heard thousands of times. I found the two sidekicks to be useless as hell, they don't help, I didn't find them funny ; they just follow you around, interrupt you from times to times and desperately try to catch a smile from you.To conclude : I'd say the game is overall more of an aesthetic experience. Play it for the immersion, for the -once again- STUNNING visuals, but don't play it for the gameplay as such ; it's really been disappointing for me. In the end I think there was a lot of passion and hard work behind this project nevertheless ; making videogames is hard, especially today, and nothing comes easy ; it's also always easier to criticize than to make, and I would be far from achieving anything as impressive as this (even gameplay-wise). *I also figured out that I probably wasn't the target audience* ; I really wanted to love this game, but I think it's just not a game for me. If you have kids and want to play a relaxing, fun, immersive experience with them - go for it ! This is in any case and regardless of what I've been saying above better than a lot of kids-targeted games.I won't put a thumbs down, because I want to acknowledge the work of the devs and artists, and a lot of people seem to love the game ; good for them, good for the team !I just want to warn potential players, so that you don't get caught by marketing and overhype as I've been : this isn't the game of the decade, don't play it for some revolutionary gameplay ; but it's an above average fun little story.
_childDocuments_.name: The Plucky Squire

_childDocuments_.review: Wonderful mix of 2d top-down action-adventure, like Zelda: A Link to the Past, and 3d action-adventure. There's a good variety of fun mini-games, perhaps a dozen types, that don't overstay their welcome as most aren't repeated until the end. Can also be skipped. Environments in 3d are limited to the desk of the kid because of the game's concept, but the designers made the most out of it as the objects on it change with time creating drastically different environments. The 2d art style is simple but charming. The creature models in 3d are nice but very basic. The 3d environments and objects look very good. Combat is not as elaborate or varied as a Zelda game, but it does the job. The puzzles are fair, clever and use the 2d/3d transition mechanic very well. It's a delightful whimsical game worth playing. Not just for kids despite what you might think of the esthetics.
_childDocuments_.name: The Plucky Squire

_childDocuments_.review: These kind of games really piss me off. It makes me feel this rollercoaster of elation to anger. It's so exciting because of its combined concepts of art and mechanics. But then I start to feel frustrated that gamers have put up with such slop like the garbage dumped out of Activision, EA, and Ubisoft for so long. Where was more of stuff like TPS before? And I know this game won't do as well as it deserves because gamers will keep glazing games like CoD.Truthfully, the gameplay is a little simple and the time spent may not be as high for the price as people would like to see, but the way the devs chose to present this art as a story game is really delightful. I personally feel like this is something I am fine paying $30 for the unique experience that sets it apart for other great games in the genre.
_childDocuments_.name: The Plucky Squire

_childDocuments_.review: (Steam stats are wrong for me due to playing in offline on my Steam Deck; actual time is closer to 10 hours played)Most disappointing game I've played in a while. The aesthetic is cool, but it can't save the gameplay. There's no depth to the game at all, and you're constantly interrupted for obligatory comments from your allies to hold your hand, even when you've just completed something that would imply you have the observational skill to not need a 5 second camera pan combined with 5 text boxes from a friend to tell you "Woah maybe you should look for a green portal and use your special ability!" Everything in the game is really just super half-baked. The combat is incredibly simple, all the skills you can buy are pointless, buying stuff from the shop basically just mandates you to have cut down every bush you see to have money, and your minimal range of special powers rarely get combined in a meaningful way. The only mercies offered to you are that you can skip the very simplistic minigames (with no punishment), the game is short, and that they clearly realized at some point in development how obnoxiously tedious the more "clever"/involved puzzles were and slowed down on implementing them, with how solving them isn't really hard but just tedious because even once you know how to solve them, you still will often have to go through a minute or two of rote gameplay where you already know what to do but to execute it you have to run across a room to a portal, use a special power, hop in a portal, run to a thing, etc. which makes it even more painful when the game extends the process even further with its insistence on obligatory unskippable text boxes to tell you what to do, despite having a little guy in most rooms with puzzles who will give you hints who you can talk to if you actually need help. It's just... bad. The game has a promising start with some of these puzzles being a bit interesting but annoying to execute the solution to, but it never goes deeper and the interruptions just wear on and on (and honestly get worse) and you realize that that's just the game.Some will probably still enjoy the game overall because it does have some charm, and it's short enough that they'll be willing to put up with annoyances, but even the biggest Adventure Time fans  children are likely to end up frustrated to an extent by how obnoxious the hand-holding interruptions are, and the gameplay past those interruptions still fails to actually be fun at any point. I've never played a better example of "style over substance" in my life. Even other crowning offenders of excessive hand-holding that I've experienced like Legend of Zelda: Skyward Sword at least have some engaging/clever gameplay to make you want to continue playing in spite of constant interruptions. The only thing that kept me playing this to the end was that I realized it was already almost over (and it still didn't end fast enough).
_childDocuments_.name: The Plucky Squire

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fantastic and does what it aims to very well.1. Unique artwork and style2. The mix of 2D and 3D gaming inside and outside of the book3. Classic collectables4. Throw backs to retro games in the mini game eventsIt is fun, funny, and well worth your time if you love this style of game.6-10 hours of gameplay, and it is not difficult. The game will hold your hand the entire time, so also perfect for those with kids who want to play but may not get all the references.As an adult, it is the perfect game to just switch off for a bit and enjoy the whimsical theme and story.
_childDocuments_.name: The Plucky Squire

_childDocuments_.review: I wish I could recommend the game. There is a lot to like about it. I really only have 2 problems with it. 1) The game will not shut up. Ever. There is so much dialogue, and it's always something that you could figure out yourself. It's just too much when the game gets interrupted constantly. You are always spoon fed information, and it gets in the way of exploring, it breaks the flow of the game, and ruins any sense of discovery for yourself. I get that it's meant for kids, but even kids will get bored of just being told what to do all the time. It's a puzzle based game, you should have to actually problem solve for yourself at some point. And you should be able to explore the world in peace, especially since it's not like it's a massive open world to get lost in. 2) There are several times (especially in chapter 6) where portals simply do not appear, or do not work when they do appear, forcing you to reset the game. Sometimes controls do not pop up, like when you need to turn the page to the book, but the game only lets you tilt the book, not turn the page entirely. I have reset the game 5 times in chapter 6 alone, and it's getting very frustrating. I think this can be fixed with an update, and I really hope they do. If they fix the game breaking bugs, and let users opt out of puzzle hints then the game is an easy recommend. The graphics and soundtrack are excellent, it's a unique twist on the old Zelda formula. It's so good that, these two issues aside, it truly could be on par with Nintendo's IPs. But as is, it needs some polish. Please, PLEASE update the game asap.
_childDocuments_.name: The Plucky Squire

_childDocuments_.review: Although this is labeled a negative review, that doesn't mean I think the game is bad. It's charming, has a good visual style and a nice soundtrack. However, I just can't recommend it for a two main reasons; the game holds your hand too much and constantly interrupts you, and this is all the way through the game. I would understand if this was only during the prologue, but it isn't. It doesn't respect your time or intelligence. Good for a younger audience maybe, but if you've played any Zelda game, this will feel too easy by comparison. If they added a no-dialogue feature, this game would be a recommend for me, but as it stands now, it's a drag to play.
_childDocuments_.name: The Plucky Squire

_childDocuments_.review: I've never been so torn when reviewing something. I hit credits so I must have enjoyed it but It's strangely a game of high highs and low lows. Some bits feel like they drag on a bit too long and not all mini games hit but some mini games and parts of the story were great. The 2D/3D nature of the game is awesome and unique and the devs clearly put alot of effort into making it seamless. It had a good enough story and it does make you want to get to the end to see how it plays out. For me this is a firm 7/10 I'd recommend it to others but it's not a run out and buy tomorrow kind of game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Plucky Squire

_childDocuments_.review: Like a lot of people, the game really got my attention with its art style (which is absolutely delightful), but I didn't expect it to be the only thing it would have going for it.The gameplay is simple (if not primitive) to the point of dullness, the few interesting puzzles and gameplay sections that are there are often immediately spoiled by your companions, the mini-games are fun but have bizarre difficulty spikes while the rest of the game is piss-easy, there's barely any flow or pacing as the game CONSTANTLY interrupts you to explain something, and it has no respect for your time as everything takes waaay too long (the animations, the unskippable dialog and cutscenes). About a third of the way through I was so bored, I could barely bring myself to finish it, but it was too late to request a refund.Not to mention the game's awful technical state — nearly every session I ran into some kind of progression-blocking bug or glitch, where I had to either reload an earlier save or replay an entire section because an important object wouldn't spawn or I'd run into an invisible wall.This all sounds pretty harsh, but I wouldn't say the game is necessarily bad, just really really disappointing. While the visuals are undeniably charming and beautiful, the rest has barely any depth or substance to it.If you're looking for something simple you could play with a small kid, then by all means give it a shot (after another patch or two), but if a more substantial Zelda-like adventure is what you're after, then you're gonna have to look elsewhere.
_childDocuments_.name: The Plucky Squire

_childDocuments_.review: I was really looking forward to this game.It looks great with really cool concepts but unfortunately, it's far too simple with a ton of hand holding. It's so easy that it feels like it was made for 7 year olds.  The gameplay stops you constantly to show more text and tedious story narrative.The constant page flips & slow animations make the pace of the game feel like molasses.I just wanted to play a fun action/puzzle game like Mario or Zelda.You won't find that here.They didn't explore each of the fun mini games enough. They should have been much longer and more challenging.  There was a nod to Punch Out for a few seconds, and then it was gone. There's no exploring either. The levels are extremely small and linear. This game could have been fun with a co-op mode also, but they opted out. I have more game time off of steam.It's unfortunate as I know this game was being made for many years, but they made it far too simple and slow.

_childDocuments_.review: Not sure if the people saying this is for 4 year olds were playing in Story Mode or what, but like any good book, I simply could not put it down. I, personally, wholeheartedly enjoyed and loved every minute of this game. The art style and animation are superb. The jokes and easter eggs are great. I've played games that have been in development much longer than this that do not hold a candle to this one.Don't expect a super hard, super long, impossible to figure out game. Do expect a super cute, super funny and very very fun experience with The Plucky Squire. Definitely would recommend to anyone not looking for the longest and most difficult game to play. If you're a Zelda fan, this gives major Link Between Worlds/Links Awakening/Link to the Past vibes and being that that franchise was my favorite growing up, it sat very well with me.Literally 2 of my favorite things ... Books and Video Games ... all rolled in to one.Great job to the team. Kudos.

_childDocuments_.review: A first look:Honestly, from the moment the "dust-up" scene came to play, I just knew this game would rock socks throughout, and so far, it's been a joy. A little bit of hack and slash, a little bit of puzzling, some stealthy moves. _childDocuments_.review: To start this review I would like to point out that the game is very charming and kind of cozy. The overall art design is cute, colorful and unique, the music is pretty good and I appreciate the idea to basically bring a children‘s book to life, to adventure in its cute little world and to switch between 2D and 3D. (Also I didn’t have any technical issues, one small bug in 9 hours)But I do have some problems with the game. First of all I had different expectations for what the game would have to offer based on trailer footage and some preview videos. For the story I won’t go into any spoilers. I will just say that the story itself is pretty basic, which is not bad but simply not what I was hoping for in advance. Same goes for characters and dialogue. A bit more interesting and thought-out characters as well as a hint of a deeper, more complex story would really benefit the game in my opinion. The humorous moments are fine, but while playing I thought that there could have been more smart or witty jokes that would still fit in a videogame for a younger audience. I also wished for more diversified mini games. The mini games are fun, the puzzles get kind of repetitive, but they‘re short and keep up a good pacing which is why the game doesn’t get boring.One more small thing is that you should be able to change language in the menu. It’s a standard nowadays. I couldn’t find a way to change it.A thumbs down here on steam doesn’t mean that this game is by any means bad. But before I played the game I had hoped for more with regard to the story, characters and gameplay. Nonetheless I genuinely hope that this game will succeed economically and resonate with a younger audience, families and people who can appreciate it a little more than I do.

_childDocuments_.review: I must give this game a positive review because I do think overall it is very charming, cute, enjoyable, interesting, and unique. However, I think the expectations I and many had for this game were too high. While it does explore the idea of interacting between a 2D and 3D world, I found the 3D art style to be more "generic" than it's incredibly stylish 2D counterpart and so is true with the gameplay. The puzzles between worlds were certainly unique but also barely scratched the surface of the possibility space before the game came to a close. Overall I still recommend this game as I think it is very good, but for me it came up a little short of my expectations.
