_childDocuments_.review: This game is truly a delight to play and it’s genuinely shocking how a relatively unknown studio has produced a title that is of such high-quality that puts AAA developers to shame. Superb gameplay, incredible worldbuilding, excellent pacing, unique bosses, beautiful graphics, and a flawless PC port; here’s why Lies of P has become my surprise Game of the Year. This review contains some minor spoilers. You are P: a puppet awakened during a crisis who can do the one thing other puppets cannot: Lie. Telling lies is a central theme to both the gameplay and story as the more lies you tell, the more humanity you will gain which has ramifications later on. Without any specific details, the story of the game is fairly straightforward and easy to follow; rather than being annoyingly obtuse, it’s instead told well through cutscenes, dialogue, and lore books, along with clear goals and pacing that feels just right. Whilst this also means there is less ambiguity and means for interpretation, it does result in a complete package that does exactly what you want it to. The game is clearly gothic-themed, inspired by European architecture, and the tone of the story reflects this dark theme with setup for future content. As expected from a game like this, there is not just the main story, but also side content in the form of character quests. These can provide opportunities to lie, unique items, or further lore on the well-developed main characters. Whilst there are no fake walls here, there are some secrets and hidden areas that are rewards from exploration. Something very player-friendly the game does is show a simple icon on the Stargazer screen when you teleport to indicate there is a quest update – much nicer than having to rely on a wiki. Just as a random point: Sophia – your level-up maiden – doesn’t really fit the theme of the game at all, but the devs knew what they were doing. The top Nexus Mods for Lies of P are  what you’d expect them to be.From gothic streets to godly castles, Lies of P has huge environmental variety that despite all feeling different, each area fits perfectly in the game world. Locations are believable with added clutter to build on the game’s themes and tell environmental stories. Everywhere is dark and depressing, but that tone is consistent makes sense for what is happening. You can feel the hope these areas might have once radiated with, but for the player, the abbey, opera house, arcade – all are places of despair. There is one area at the end of the game that feels completely different with a magical look – felt very inspired by Elden Ring’s “Consecrated Snowfield” with a giant fortress at the end.Inside of all these locations are main bosses and mini-bosses. For almost all main bosses you can summon a spectre to help you fight though you’ll get greater satisfaction by not doing so even if the spectre is fairly useless. I did my whole first playthrough without any summons and felt the game was well balanced in almost all cases with bosses equating to a fair challenge. NG+ however, despite carrying over your items, became much harder as the boss health feels like it doubles so fights increasingly demand perfection as you simply cannot afford to take damage to last the whole duration – especially on bosses that have multiple phases. All bosses are well designed and unique, though some definitely stand out more than others. A mid-game boss  felt very overtuned on the second phase, whilst a late-game boss  was ridiculously easy outside of his larger health pool in NG+. The only gimmick fight which I have to mention is the Black Rabbit Brotherhood who you have to fight twice and both fights are quite annoying – the second time you face them you practically need to fight them in the order the game presents or you’ll have a bad time.There is a lot of depth to combat and it feels great to engage in: there is weight to attacks, seemingly flawless hitboxes, an impeccable parry system, reasonable i-frames from dodging, utility items to change the flow of combat, summons, different weapon types, and so much more! All of these aspects culminate in an experience that is varied and engaging with no set way to approach any scenario.There is the traditional health restoration item for when you do get hit, but for not getting hit, the game promotes parrying more than dodging. You can indeed dodge – and will need to at times – but instead the parry system promotes perfection. You can just hold down the block button to block standard attacks, but this will incur a type of health damage that you can only regain by attacking – encouraging aggression in combat as if you don’t regain it fast enough it will start to drain. Alternatively, by having a perfect parry you take no health damage, and it feels amazing when you pull off perfect parries on a chain of boss attacks. I was more amazed than annoyed at hitboxes as there were times when attacks just managed to miss  though you’re more likely to get frustrated when your own weapons don’t hit due to reach as you really do need to get close to who you’re fighting.Weapons wise, there are lots of different types – standard and boss weapons too – and you can buff them with status effects or use other items to help in combat. Weapons have special moves that are unique to each type, and there are other combat options like your Legion Arm which can be modified with different effects – not to mention other elements like P-Organs. Lots of depth available here and a smooth progression system meant you could always experiment when you felt like it.There is no question that Lies of P is the best PC port I have played all year, but arguably one of the best ports I have ever played. In a year filled with broken and buggy releases where even an RTX 4090 might struggle, it’s so refreshing to have a title not just work, but be complete. With my i7-13700K and RTX 4080, I played with ultra settings at 4k native quality (no DLSS) and generally maintained my 140 fps lock – there were only a few instances where it dropped to about 110 fps in heavy vegetation scenes but it still felt so smooth. There were zero crashes, zero stutters (on a UE4 game that is rare), UI and textures scale to 4k, mouse + keyboard or controller is completely viable, and everything just works. It runs great, looks great, and it’s just so nice to be able to say that about a game – especially this year. Really the only areas it could improve would be by expanding supported options: adding Frame Generation (though it does run well so it’s not strictly required and there is a mod available for it), adding support for XeSS (it does also support FSR so might as well have parity), and then also supporting ray tracing technologies – though the image quality using rasterised techniques looks more than fine.Future content is teased in a post-credits scene and I very pleased that is the case. Lies of P was a game I had lightly heard of over the years but didn’t expect it to have such an impact. I’d say it’s definitely underrated at the moment and honestly can’t think why it didn’t score higher than the low 80s Metacritic it did get. This is the best non-FromSoftware Soulslike game out there, and even I have to admit it does some things better than those who made the genre - getting all achievements felt great here too.Lies of P is a must-play if you’re a fan of these games and should be on the list for GOTY contender. For me, this has my vote for GOTY and I will be instantly jumping into whatever new content is released – DLC or sequel.

_childDocuments_.review: I beat this game after 33 hours and excited to dive back into new game plus. The game was excellent. As others have said, it fills the Bloodbourne PC itch we all have. The setting is fantastic, the story telling was well done and had me hooked. Some have complained about the skill tree (p-organ) locking some basic things like roll recovery when knocked down or a wider dodge behind an upgrade path but I love it. I found the game to be hard during the first few hours, but once I got some of the basics unlocked - it became smoother and smoother. I like having to work for things in games, but some may find these basics being locked at first annoying. It does contribute to stiffer game play but stick with it, it becomes much smoother. Another big plus for me is performance, the game was rock solid and looks great. So many games this year have had crap performance at launch, so it was worth a call out. I'm on a 4090 + 7800x3d and was getting random UE4 crashes every hour or so, I couldn't figure out why but I updated the steam launch command to -dx11 and that fixed all my issues. I think I'm a one off and its most likely just something software related on my side with drivers or maybe even hardware, but fyi. I've played FF XVI, Jedi Survivor, BG3, Diablo 4, and Zelda and this is in my top two for game of the year. 10/10 recommend!

_childDocuments_.review: This might be one of the best soulslikes ever made, period.Sekiro was so good that it ruined many other games for me, that is, until Lies of P came around. Lies of P recaptured that 'Sekiro/Bloodborne' magic that I'd been missing for so long. The combat in this game is absolutely sublime, but only if you're willing to meet it on its own terms.Don't be surprised if you spend 1-2 hours on a boss fight. A lot of the enjoyment in this game comes from trusting the designers: It's really easy to get beaten down a few times and assume "this boss is unfair". Instead, I recommend that you trust the design, learn when to parry, when to dodge, and when to run away, and you'll find that every challenge in this game is actually very approachable.Every boss is fun in its own way. Every level has tons of interconnected paths, with only a handful of checkpoints per chapter that get re-used a ton. There aren't many secrets, and outside of the many shortcuts, the levels are mostly linear. This is okay to me: The combat is the real focus of this game.Every aspect of this game's design is yelling "don't give up".  You can always rally back some health if you mistime a parry. You can always recharge 1 health flask if you're out of charges, meaning you can always make a comeback. Boss attacks are consistently telegraphed so you can always learn the mechanics of a fight if you're willing to put in the time. As a result, this game is much more forgiving than you'd expect.I don't want to hyper-fixate on the insanely high-but-satisfying difficulty though: This game is also absurdly polished. The music, the visuals, the performance, the controls, everything is executed amazingly well. Soulslikes often die by their least-polished or most-clunky aspect, so to have a non-FromSoft soulslike execute everything so well is really something special.In the end, I think non-FromSoft soulslikes are, ironically, often held to a higher standard than their FromSoft counterparts. Think about all the nonsense you've excused in games like Elden Ring or Dark Souls 2 and ask yourself: are you willing to give Lies of P the same clemency? To that end, I think Lies of P is an excellent game that gets nitpicked to shreds by soulslike fans who've forgotten how tough a soulslike is supposed to be. After years of playing souls games, I think we've all gotten a little too comfortable. Lies of P is a great wake-up call.Remember how hard Bloodborne and Sekiro felt when you first played them? Lies of P is tough, but if you accept that it's NOT dark souls, and learn the correct way to play, I really think this game will recapture that magical feeling you've probably been missing since you first started playing soulslikes.

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoy how easily this game lets you switch and swap different weapons that you might like into your build, with how the scaling is tied to the handle along with the move set, then the damage coming from the blade. You can also switch out how each weapon scales (to a point, only moving a letter at a time, B->C or  B->A) for the 3 different attributes that scale your weapon damage, allowing for pretty much any weapon you want to use, with pretty much any build and keep it working and doing damage. This seamless process is also not difficult to understand and is introduced to the player very well. Gone are the days of sticking to one build for the entire game, now you can do whatever you want, whenever you want in the game, as long as you have the materials to change your weapon scaling and then to upgrade it. my only complaint is that you can hear an NPC coughing relentlessly from one of the Stargazers "Bonfires/Grace" and I sometimes like to just sit at the rest spots and chill, this was not one of those locations.This game also runs very well on my laptop, versus world of warcraft which CHUGGS the ♥♥♥♥ out of my laptop for seemingly no reason.

_childDocuments_.review: Perfect guarding is so much fun, and I love a lot of the mechanics that this game has that make it different from other souls games. Guard regain is like Bloodborne's Rally mechanic that lets you regain health, but it's not as simple as take a hit and then hit them back. Fable is basically what replaces a mana bar, and it lets you do really awesome attacks or give yourself buffs, depending on the weapon you are using. Legion arms are kinda like a second mana bar that you use for even more unique attacks, from shooting flames to firing a grappling hook at enemies to throwing a small puddle of acid on the ground that does literally nothing because that one arm sucks. I also really love that your "armor" in this game doesn't change your appearance and lets you customize purely for cosmetic reasons, it's just a shame that this is used in a game that has very limited cosmetics and no character creator. However, the narrative and art design of this game is so amazing that it makes up for that pretty quickly. Also there is a kitty at the hotel that you get to be friends with :)

_childDocuments_.review: Game is good if you like hard games. So if you like games that most quit because you like a challenge or like to brag about beating them to stroke your ego then this probably for you. For me it has not really been fun. I mean love the world, the music pieces you can find and anything else that enthralls you into the story. How ever i have not really been having fun. The combat is not making my heart pump with excitement nor did finally defeating a difficult boss give me that huge boost of excitement that the whole souls-like community swears by. When i died in combat it just felt like a cheap death and same thought would come into my mind  "i know i pressed the dodge button but i guess i messed the timing again..". To me it feels more like boring memorization than an blood pumping endeavor. For example with archbishop Andreus, which to me was my big first road block and i spent over five hours on, i never really felt like i was having fun it just felt like oh he is doing this move so i need to do this. Oh look your stamina is low so get some space and wait for it to refill... and any little mistake would spell death. Could it be that rolled a die to choose my combat type and it landed on technique so i went full stamina and technique build without putting any points on health? maybe. Still for me this game plays very slow and formulaic. Deviate anything from the script and you will die. Areas leading to the boss fights feel artificially difficult. It feels like enemies are just given lot of health and are not really challenging just annoying. They all seem to follow the same formula. Either you attack them first and stun lock them or wait for them to attack so you can stun lock them. For larger enemies you can attack once or twice depending on the move and then dodge immediately. Rinse and repeat many, many times until they die which just feel like a slog fest. Talking about dodging and parrying  don't feel good. Like dodging feels like you are stuck in place while parrying is very tight to pull off. All these things combine together lead to repeating the same thing over and over again. Replaying the same area or boss fight is not really fun and I am at a cross roads. I am currently stuck on the puppet king. Do i find him impossible to beat? not really i have made it to his second form fire scythe mode but i am not enjoying the game. It is feeling more like a chore than a thrill. I will take a break and see if i want to come back to this game. Who knows, maybe after a break i will find it more fulfilling. On a final note i know the game is loved by many and do not wish to insult those who do, it might just be that it is not for me.

_childDocuments_.review: This game ranks among the best that Fromsoftware has put on the market. The visuals, music, build variety, and combat are simply top notch. In a world where the "Souls-like" genre is a swamp filled with the nastiest sewage imaginable this game truly rises above and I will happily recommend it alongside any Fromsoft game. This game does have some issues, a few bosses have annoying mechanics that force you to guess when an attack is coming, bog you done with the worst status effect in the game, or the boss will use spells to keep you running away from them to artificially prolong the battle. However in a game with 25+ bosses having three or four that are somewhat annoying really does not damage what I would consider to be a pristine and successful entrance into the souls genre. For anyone who is on the fence about purchasing this game let me tell you first hand the entire 30 hour experience I had was worth it for the last three bosses alone. There is so much to say about what this game offers but the last three bosses will certainly stick with me as some of the most well designed bosses I have ever come up against.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly one of the best games I have ever played. 120hrs, max level 561 at NG+7, because I didn't want to farm for Ergo so I just decided to play through it 7 times. There in no confusion to where you need to go, you are guided throughout the story. Side quests aren't as direct but they are side quests for a reason. Also, main NPCs in Krat Hotel also have character side stories as well. Lastly, there are 3 total endings in the game, so while you don't have to do all 3, to get the most out of the game I would recommend getting the endings, especially the True Ending. All in all, it's a beautiful game. It is quite challenging but for those that have played Sekiro, you may find the guard system to be very familiar and the overall difficulty to be similar in comparison as well.I would highly recommend the game. Enjoy the story, be patient and yeah, enjoy!

_childDocuments_.review: Still at the top of my list of soulslike games not made by FROM. Neowiz really nailed it and kudos to the team for an almost flawless buttery smooth 1.0 release that performed without any stuttering and perfomance issues. The game was hard at first and I was initially thrown off by how tight that parry(pefect guard) window was compared to Sekiro, but once you get the feel for it, it's very satisfying and unlike Sekiro, you don't actually need to execute it to win the battles as the game's combat is open ended enough for different approaches. I love the weapon handle/blade dismantlement system. It essentially allows you to create a lot of unique weapons with different movement styles. The rally system from Bloodborne encourages aggression, but you don't have to play this way and the health flask reward system for barely surviving is really cool. There's also something to be said for the more direct and less obtuse story-telling here than the trend of deliberate crypticness of the narrative in the souls games. There's a lot of heart in the story and you really feel for every NPC and enemy you meet, even the final boss. Way opposite tone from Lords Of The Fallen, but I enjoyed both.

_childDocuments_.review: Lies of P is an amazing souls like game with amazing graphics and a very interesting theme. During my first few hours of this game it reminded me lots of Bloodborne and Sekiro: Shadows die twice because of the character movement and setting of the game. If you liked Bloodborne and Sekiro, get this game right now and play-through it because i guarantee you will love it. So far i only have about 6 hours on game as of now and have only touched on all the bare basics. Here are a few of the mechanics in the game: Upgrading with "ergo" is very reminiscent of previous souls games in which you collect ergo by killing enemies or finding ergo crystals which you can use to level up. This can be used to level up your vitality, (health) vigour, (stamina), motivity (strength), capacity, (carry load/prosthetic arm) technique, (dexterity) and advance; Secondly this game also has a blacksmith character which levels up your weapons and weapon handles which buffs its damage and scales with your stats; There are various weapon arts in the game depending on what weapon you use which do a special attack. The handles also have a similar system where they can buff your damage; There is also a passive ability levelling system which uses quartz to gain the levels. These do things such as adding to your health flasks and making the enemy stun cooldown longer etc.The setting of this game is dark but beautiful at the same time. As someone who has always appreciated old architecture, seeing in its prime is really cool. Where it takes place is called "Krat" and its a 19th century, Victorian esque city, swarmed with puppets which have gone mad because of "the frenzy" which is a name dedicated to the puppets becoming rogue and killing the people. Any thoughts or concerns before buying this game? Message me in the comments and i will try to help.

_childDocuments_.review: I rarely review but this game deserves it. Besides growing up in the SNES era of hard games, this is my first souls like, if you do not count Tunic and Death Doors.No, it is not a perfect game. It definitely needs balancing, especially for the beginning, when dodge is gimped (they are now fixing this by giving you early access to some abilities which you unlock later) and you cannot respec. Those parts can be VERY frustrating.Still, if you can get past the rough beginning and some unfair moments, once you understand how to spec (vitality, stamina and capacity are the most important things to upgrade) and how to play, there are only a couple of rock hard bosses, the rest is more than doable and discovering how to beat the bosses becomes a pleasure.Flexibility is key, knowing when to parry and when to block, taking advantage of elemental weaknesses and so on. The story is interesting and so are the characters, you can really see how much passion went into this project and it is a feat for such a small team to have pulled off something like this.It is one of those games that is hard to put down and that you keep coming back to.I would say that just for that this game deserves a play, despite the growing pains which I hope will be smoothed out with the next patch and in the dlc and sequel.Recommended!

_childDocuments_.review: Lies of P is an amazing game, developed by Korean Developers NEOWIZ, which blends aspects of Sekiro, Bloodborne, and Dark Souls. Had a great time playing through it and finishing my first run. I would rate it an 8.5/10.Pros:- Combat Parrying takes a bit to get used to as it is a much tighter window then Sekiro and does not stop enemy attacks. Fable arts are amazing and diversify the way you fight bosses, for example some may grant an attack buff, while others offer perfect guard.- Weapons There are a lot of weapons to make builds with and you can mix and match different hilts and blades to make strong combos. Hilts offering different movesets and scalings, while the blades offer damage. You will spend some time in the hotel testing out combos, fable arts, and weapons on the training dummy fairly often.- Bosses The bosses are amazing, they have the right amount of difficulty, not too hard, but not extremely easy, the way you approach a boss can differ depending on build, weapon, even the puppet arm can help.)- Story The story is pretty good, you definitely feel more involved in comparison to other souls-borne games, with loads of books and notes scattered throughout the game, you slowly figure out what is going on.- Music The OST and songs are very nice to listen to when in the hotel, especially 'Feel' which is the first one you get. You receive music discs from quests from NPCs.- Decision Making I like the Lie or Truth aspect of dealing with NPCs as depending on your answers, the outcome of the story may change, although it is stressful at some points as there is a timer to select an option.- LevellingThe levelling in this game is very proportional to where you are in the story, it is not grindy at all, and you will never feel the need to over level to defeat bosses.Cons:- NPC QuestlinesFor the most part there were no problems with questlines, however there are a couple exceptions. Some questlines have really dumb decisions put into them by the developers leaving the player feel cheated out of it. for example and I say this without spoilers as a warning to future players, most NPCs in the game have distinct looks and are unable to be hit by players, in chapter 9 there is an NPC in a train car that looks like a zombie, do NOT hit him, the dialogue starts way too late and he only starts talking when you are in the middle of your swing. Also there are certain quests where if you do things in the wrong order it screws it up. For Eugene, there will come a point in the game where you receive a cryptic vessel after slaying a certain character, take that cryptic vessel straight to Venigni and do NOT talk to Eugene first, I cannot stress this enough. Also one of the boss soul weapons are needed for a side quest, which honestly baffled my mind as I chose to receive the amulet instead, Just know that if you get a boss soul that gives you an ice great sword take the great sword not the amulet.- CubeThe cube is a heavily underutilised system that could have been something akin to magic scaling off advance with different spells of different elements, instead it is a tool used to buff the specters, summons you can use for boss fights, making these items pretty much useless to most players including myself, who choose not to use summons. It doesn't help that the cube itself has such a slow cast speed that it is borderline worthless in practicality. I do believe if the devs can rework it into an advance scaling magic system it could be salvaged.To conclude, I believe if you are thinking of getting this game, do not hesitate it is extremely good, like it could be an actual FromSoftware game type of good, and I am excited for the alleged DLC and future games NEOWIZ may make in the future. To whoever read all this, sorry for all the Yappanese and have fun :D

_childDocuments_.review: I've been a longtime fan of soulsborne games, having started with Dark Souls 1 back in 2011, with my favourite game being Bloodborne. So when I first caught wind of this game, I was instantly interested, considering how much the developers have clearly taken inspiration from those games (especially Bloodborne). After playing the demo, I knew I was instantly going to love this game, and having now completed the full release (it took me about 30 hours for me to reach the ending), I can safely say this is one of the best soulslikes ever made. The amount of love and polish poured into this shows right from the beginning until the end. When compared to something like Code Vein, which I still considering a 'decent' game, it's very obvious the developers of Lies of P understood exactly what makes Souls fun, and were able to replicate the feel of those games to the absolute best of their ability. I want to list some of the pros and cons I have with this game so it may help you decide if this is something you want to pick up. :1} Combat and Movement: This is the closest I've felt any soulslike has come to actually feeling like an official game made by Fromsoftware. Movement and combat is on point, your character has weight to them, attacks feel visceral and flashy, there's no floaty movement and when you hit an enemy, there's some real meat to each attack. 2) Game Performance: Runs like a dream. It's sad that I have to list this as a pro, but in an age where developers seem to snub actually optimising games for PC, I have to give it to the developers for making a game that looks gorgeous and runs smoother. 60fps constantly, very few (and I mean almost virtually zero) frame pacing or stuttering issues. Compare this to Jedi Survivors Fallen Order? It's like night and day. 3) The Story: Most souls games have decent story... if you know where to look. Some people hate the ambiguous nature of them, and I get that. Lies of P though? The story is very in your face, and it should be. You grow attached to the characters, to the world, and even to the main character, despite him being voiceless. No spoilers, but considering the ending of the game, I'm very excited in the direction they take this next. 4) Level Design: Loved almost every level in this game, even the so called 'swamp', each were visually appealing, fun to explore, and don't overstay their welcome. Standouts for me, without spoiling too much, were Rosa Isabelle Street and the Grand Exhibition. 5) Upgrade Systems: The game throws multiple different things at you to use to enhance your own power and make the game easier. There are some stuff that are staples of any soulslike, live levelling your characters stats, or upgrading weapons, but then there are really unique things like the P-organ system, that allow you to cater how you play by the upgrades you choose. There's also the legion arms, a mechanical arm that you can change to do different functions, like act as a shield, or flamethrower, with upgrades that make it actually change and evolve. Finally, there's the golden tree and the wishcube, mainly used to buff up your Spectre (An NPC summon you can use for boss fights). Whilst these systems seem overwhelming at first, I found myself excited every time I could interact and use them to become stronger, making me feel like I was actually getting better equipped as I went further into the game. 6) Enemy Variety: Actually was surprised at the amount of enemies there were. I initially thought it'd be just different puppets, which there are, but they throw in a lot of surprises into the mix. Some are annoying, for sure, but hey, that's part of the souls experience. 7) Bosses: Super memorable bosses, enough said. Final boss in particular is one that I will never forget, the Melania or Orphan of Kos of Lies of P, so to speak. 1) Parry System and Dodging: Alright, let's get the biggest point of contention amongst Lies of P players out of the way. The parry system is far too strict, the window for parrying is insanely small. As I played, I did get better with it, and I'd say by the final boss I'd gotten to a competent enough level to feel like I could reliably parry even the fury attacks. So what's my problem? Well I consider myself a souls vet, I've played these games for hundreds of hours. And if someone like me found it tedious and difficult, what would an average player think? Or a new one? Some would say 'git gud', which... it's true, sure, but with a system as strict with this, most will give up on it, and thus rely on dodging. Dodging, in the demo, was so awful that the developers changed it for the full release. It's better, but still not great, and part of that is because two of essential upgrades for dodging are stuck in the P-organ upgrade system. I just praised this system, but chief? This ain't it. Locking essential upgrades for the dodge in there was a bad move, it forces you to choose them, limiting build variety and also punishing you early in the game for simply not having them. If the parry system was better, this would be a none issue, but as it stands, you are stuck with either a system that is unfairly punishing, or one that you are forced to invest into the make it passable in a game that should be about player choice and freedom. 2) Delayed Attacks: The bane of Elden Ring comes to haunt us once again. It's funny how the cons are so entwined together since this issue would not be nearly as bad if it wasn't for the previous one, and vice versa. Good parry system and dodging? Then delayed attacks become much easier to deal with. No delayed attacks? Then a lacklustre dodge isn't as bad. This wouldn't be a problem if every single boss and mini boss type enemy didn't behave this way. This isn't difficulty, this is just annoying. 3) Overabundance of Miniboss Enemies: Towards the end of the game, they decide to throw every annoying enemy they can at you, over and over again. Some don't respawn, which is good, but others do, and it becomes a chore to deal with them. Never should you find yourself thinking if you should just run past an enemy instead of fighting it in a game designed around combat. In conclusion, as you can see, my main gripes with the game were to deal with some of the combat mechanics and how the developers abused certain types of enemies and attack patterns. I wanna make it clear these are minor gripes, and became more of an issue towards the end of the game. These are also issues the developers could either fix in patches, dlc, or (and here's hoping/praying) a sequel! Whilst they did detract from my enjoyment of the game, they did not cause a big enough impact for me to be upset and lower my final. The pros, undoubtedly, outweigh the cons, to such an extreme degree that the cons became something of an afterthought.  If you enjoy souls games, particular Bloodborne, this is for you. I've seen the meme about this being 'Bloodborne on PC' or 'Bloodborne at home', and whilst the devs clearly took inspiration and would probably be flattered, I think it's a disservice to say that. Lies of P stands on it's own, of what a soulslike should be, without being just another copy. It's a game the developers put a lot of love and thought into, and I hope you will give it a chance.

_childDocuments_.review: Elden Ring made me question if I even enjoyed the soulslike genre. I saw lies of P later, saw some reviews panning it as often cheap and unfair, and decided to steer clear. Fast forward a year, and my partner recommended it to me, and she not only has crushingly high standards but also soulslikes aren't usually her jam, so I decided to check it out. This game pleasantly suprised me. Then it kept those suprises coming. Then, most of all, it made me remember why I *LOVE* soulslikes, and this is the best one I've played (I don't really consider sekiro one, it's sort of its own thing).To summarize Lies of P, it's a game that understands the main strengths of the souls series and its biggest weaknesses and addresses both. Love the RPG elements of the souls series, collecting new upgrades, experimenting with new builds and working towards a favorite weapon? Lies has a smaller but more potent weapon collection with every single weapon having a unique moveset, then adds in a frankly fantastic weapon customization system where you can mix and match weapon parts to, say, keep the moveset and stat scaling of a curved sword with the heft, power, and reach of a giant saw cleaver (my weapon of choice became the starting saber blade mounted to a rocket-powered glaive). It also adds in a really enticing upgrade system on top of stat leveling where you can pick all manner of passive upgrades to lock into your preferred playstyle.Love intense boss fights where you have to carefully study their moveset and learn their patterns, dying over and over again and getting closer every time? This game's boss roster is incredible, with only one boss I actively hate. The later game bosses seemed overwhelmingly, even impossibly difficult at times, but when I beat them it felt as if I cracked their moveset like a safe. This game also features a very intuitive perfect guarding system on top of a dodge roll, allowing bosses to be a lot faster and more engaging (the timing is a bit tighter than sekiro but still very doable), and a rewarding stagger system where enough heavy attacks or perfect guards will open up a devestating counterattack opportunity. There's also an incredible addition where if you're completely out of healing flasks you can recharge one by dealing enough damage, encouraging fighting to your last breath to overcome running out of resources. The bosses start out great and get even better towards the second half of the game.Overall though, the biggest thing lies solves is the biggest flaw with the souls series: Quality control. Let's be real, every souls game has high highs and CRUSHING lows. A lot of them. If you disagree, and think that Elden Ring's bosses are all of high quality... If you can look me in the eye and say that the 70+ bosses in elden ring that are a crappy refight or a basic enemy with a boss health bar are as good as Godrick the Grafted, I'm gonna question your standards of boss design. This game keeps its head held high through almost the entire experience. I just found myself having a good time throughout, even the poison swamp area is shockingly good. When I found myself frustrated, I realized how rarely that was happening. This game is just an absolute blast of a soulslike and rekindled my love for the genre.Lies of P is *exceptional* and I'd recommend it to any lovers of souls games and anyone disillusioned by where the series has gone. 9/10, ignore the haters.

_childDocuments_.review: I saw the trailer, got a good feeling about the gameplay and the visual looks nice so I walked into this world expecting the gameplay to captivate me. There are quite a few collectibles to find in the world and the rewards for finding those are very satisfying. Even the visual reminds me of DS, ER and BB, it's nothing cutting edge but it's very well done. The voice acting is good and the character designs look fantastic ( I mean it's a Korean game). The only downsides I can think of about the gameplay is that some bosses are very lackluster in the design. All of the "big" boss only has 2 phases. The game is relatively short if you're decent at souls like game, around 30 hours, could be a lot longer if you really suck. But with all of that I don't think this game should worth 60 dollars, it's a very good game with a delusional price tag, with the amount of playtime and the quality this game should be at max 50 dollars. _childDocuments_.review: Lies of P is the most faithful soulslike game to release yet. Although it holds hands with the fromsoft games, it combines the best elements of each release into an incredibly satisfying gameplay loop. The game is linear, but any fromsoft vet will be pleased to comb through each area to discover useful gear to unlock truly useful abilities. One of the most consistently fun soulslike experiences, all while being backed by a truly beautiful soundtrack. This game is truly underrated and underappreciated, and I am ecstatic to see what these brilliant minds will deliver with their next project.

_childDocuments_.review: The best souls-like I have played that's not made directly by From Soft. Only a couple bosses and moves I think need tweaking () There are some minor gameplay annoyances and bugs like stamina regen being a bit slow, and some status effects applying affects before they're even fully applied (shock reducing stamina regen , as well as break applying healing reduction), though these could be design choices but they seem like bugs to me, as usually in souls-like games the bar needs to fill before you are actually afflicted with any negative affects. The one major thing I think is a problem for the game is the general spongy-ness of enemies later in the game. In my opinion Elden Ring also had this issue to an extent, the amount of damage you can take is far less than even minor enemies who seem like they should be on even footing with you, and it can feel like a slog especially in NG+ to fight bosses with ridiculously inflated health bars, I am one who enjoys spending extra time doing NG+ cycles for new gear and trying new weapons/builds, but in this game I am a bit unmotivated because of the amount of time each fight takes. For right now I rate this game an 8.5/10, if they fix the spongy-ness and the other things mentioned I think this game enters GOTY territory. Great stuff looking forward to DLC if there is any.

_childDocuments_.review: SIGHTS (GRAPHICS): While it's basically up-to-par with Bloodborne and other gorgeous PS4 titles, it didn't really feature any visuals that made my jaw drop. The design aesthetics were very cool, especially with its choice of setting: like a mish-mash of Bioshock, Bioshock Infinite, and (obviously) Bloodborne. They clearly put a lot of work into this part, and it was easy to get immersed in the world they created. It was consistently moody, and I liked it. = 3/5SOUNDS (MUSIC/EFFECTS): This is what really sold me on the game. They knew what they were doing when they chose the song "Feel" to be featured in the trailer, because that ♥♥♥♥ was magical. I was even considering getting a vinyl player and picking up some jazz records from the 20s-30s because the music was so evocative. That quality was pretty consistent throughout the game, both in their music and their atmosphere. The only downside was that nothing really topped "Feel", though asking for that is probably asking too much. = 5/5SYSTEMS (COMBAT/LEVELING): Even though most of the game was clearly based on Bloodborne, the combat actually felt more like Sekiro to me, with it's emphasis on perfecting the rhythm of blocking and dodging. The company behind this game "NEOWIZ" actually made their start on game design with their music rhythm game DJMAX, so it's cool to see them continuing with a somewhat rhythm-based combat system. I had no complaints about the RPG mechanics, because it's just Bloodborne/Sekiro again. The game felt fair and approachable from any combat style until the final boss showed up and properly stuffed my ♥♥♥♥ in. I eventually broke down and had to start memorizing the block patterns. Even then, the game felt much more forgiving than the standard Soulslike, where it would leave your souls OUTSIDE the boss door, and wouldn't take away ALL of your souls if you died trying to retrieve them. Much less stressful than DS. = 4/5STORY (CHARACTERS/WRITING): I have to wonder how they convinced the shareholders to approved the concept of "Pinocchio but Bloodborne", but they still went all in on it and I can't help but respect the commitment. MANY of the staples from the Disney cartoon are here, from Lampwick showing up as an enemy wearing a donkey mask, to Jiminy being your ever-present AI conscience. It felt absurd at times, but the game is so INTO it that it never became distracting. The story wasn't innovative, the characters didn't stand out much, but it was still compelling because it was clear that SOMEONE was all in on this. = 3/5SUCKINESS (BUGS/GLITCHES): I only ran into a few technical issues, so in terms of raw playability, this game gets top marks from me. Considering how studios today usually ship what feels like an unfinished product, having this come out with little-to-no glitches meant I could get wrapped up in the story. The sound became delayed a couple times in my 50+ hours, but a restart fixed it easily. I also fell THROUGH an elevator once because I was half-on and half-off a landing platform, but that was the worst of it. Everything was mostly stable, and seemed to behave as it was intended. = 5/5SUMMARY (OTHER THOUGHTS): The game included some nice quality-of-life improvements that I will miss when I go back to other Soulslikes, like not perma-losing all of your collected souls if you die twice in a row,  There were some welcome new ideas, like how stat scaling and moveset customization worked, so that was a nice change. There were a few ideas that didn't land for me at all, like a separate fruit currency that grew on an IRL timer, or some of the passive enhancements feeling WAY too specific ("less weapon durability loss when health is low"), but overall it felt very polished. So even though it was copying Bloodborne and Sekiro, those two are still VERY good games, and this game does enough with its setting to make the formula feel fresh again. FINAL SCORE = 4/5

_childDocuments_.review: I have just finished my first play-through with almost 60 hours, trying to do everything possible (without searching anything up) and getting the true ending on my first try. I am no "souls-vet", I've only played Elden RIng and DS3.Do not listen to anyone that says that dodges and parrys need fixing, they do not, they work as intended, ppl complainig have a problem called "skill issue". At most, I would say add a single frame more to the perfect block, and the first dodge upgrade should be a starting mechanic. But the way it all works now, it is fine.From the first boss I was already trying to perfect block, and by the fourth boss I was already very good with it, by the end of the game I felt I could parry anything God threw at me.Combat in this game is reaally, REALLY fun and rewarding, in so many different ways- Mixing and matching weapon hilts and blades so that you can change your play style without changing your build- Doing the same mixing of weapons to get some crazy looking weapons with crazy abilities- Parrying full combos and strings once u get the parry window down to muscle memory- Dodging full combos and strings once u get the dodge window down to muscle- The fact that u can parry AND dodge and don't have to rely on a single form of defense, and u can add a legion arm to the mix if you want as well- YOU CAN RECOVER HEALING IF U ARE OUT. This alone adds so much, you have so many come back moments with this- The animations and telegraphing in this game ARE SO GOOD. A lot of bosses I could parry first try because I could just tell when the attack was coming. And it doesn't make the game easier, goes to show you don't need BS to make a game hard and challengingI like the old souls formula of dodging and clicking but this game adds so much to the combat. with so many options, it's gonna be really hard getting back to that. It's crazy they pulled this off for their first attempt at this genre.If you like souls-likes or any game that focuses on melee combat, .Delayed Attacks: First of all, although it is present in the game, the game's very well designed animations and mechanics make this type of attack less annoying than Elden Ring for example, and the story and enemies kinda make sense for them to exist. But still, for the love of God, anything beyond 3 seconds is just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥P-Organ: I was expecting it to be a game changing mechanic, and it is, but more in the way of upgrades that you NEED, rather than upgrades that can add MORE FUN. Also, the upgrades that are not needed, really don't catch the eye for me. I wish they went a bit more crazy with the upgrades. Luckily the Legion Arms do exactly what I wanted from the P Organ, they add to the fun factor, with different ways of approaching combat.Groggy: Now this was making me REALLY PISSED at the start of the game, where in all honesty, it doesn't just feel like bait, IT IS JUST BAIT. That is until you get the upgrades that increase the enemies groggy window. You see, in the start of the game, the groggy window is so so small, that you feel really pressured to just try to get a strong attack in. You can't wait for a good gap in the enemies attack bc then he will just not be groggy anymore. With the upgrades this changes, YOU CAN WAIT NOW, and it really adds to the combat, where you have to really time your attack and learn the boss to be able to hit these groggy states and punish the boss. Too Linear: The game's level design is very very linear, it has it's moments, in the last level for example, but most of the game you're just going through pseudo-corridors. It's not all bad but they should try to make more complex level design in the future.Unresponsive Healing(sometimes): I had a problem that really got in my nerves, YOU CANT DODGE AND IMMEDIATELY HEAL. It's so so frustrating, to have to dodge and then press to heal ♥♥♥♥ 3 times to actually heal. It surely has to be a bug, bc in every other aspect and moment of the game this is not a problem. I can attack and heal right after if I queue those buttons, I can attack and block/perfect guard one after another. But for some reason, A LOT of times I just watched as P died when I told him to heal and he just ♥♥♥♥♥ didn't. This problem is within every souls like but here it was just too much. I'm 100% sure it has to do with the dodging + healing but there might be other moments that this happens as well

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished my first playthrough (Clocked in at about 45 hours for a first run; based on what I've seen so far, subsequent NG or NG+ runs will go much quicker) and it's Puppet souls-- what more can be said? Okay, maybe a lot can be said.Probably the best non-From souls-like game mechanically and aesthetically, even with what is going to sound like a lot of complaints-- but want folks to know what they're getting into. For the sake of comparison and a bit of a tl;dr: big Bloodborne vibes environmentally, similar story combat wise, but with a strong emphasis on parrying like in Sekiro. Combat felt mostly fair with several encounters requiring trial and error prior to mastering them, but there are a few pain points. Trash mobs are mostly insignificant as they should be, the mini-bosses range from being pushovers to being tougher than some of the early game bosses... but a few of the late-game bosses are absolutely punishing damage sponges. One boss in particular (the "last" boss outside of an optional boss fight afterward) was particularly frustrating to manage due to how their AoE/ranged attacks and physical attacks could be chained together with virtually no down-time in between them. This may sound nitpicky, but easily the boss that took me the longest to beat based on having to dodge multiple simultaneous ranged/AoE attacks and wide-sweeping blows all at once. I barely managed to scrape my way to victory on my final attempt by spamming upwards of a dozen throwable items at the end.Parrying (called "perfect guarding") for all the emphasis it is given can also feel a bit inconsistent since many enemies can and will mix-up their attack combos and timing... make sure to leverage blocking and dodging as well; all of these mechanics are essential to making it through to the end with different enemies forcing you to approach each situation differently.Level design overall is fairly linear with decent environment variations throughout. There are some fun nooks and crannies to explore, but would not have minded more involved side-quests (almost all consist of stumbling upon random mementos and suddenly having NPCs jibber-jabber at you, sometimes without you realizing why) and meandering side-locations. Gravity is also not your friend either and this recurring boss will frequently rear its head throughout the game with hidden enemies knocking you to your death on many occasions. Additionally, there are certain arenas that could have benefited from fewer items to clip on; it is disarmingly easy to end up stuck on an environmental asset only to get gutter-stomped by a boss or horde of enemies. There are a few novel mechanics mixed in here as well with the two best being the legion arms and weapon assembly systems and the least useful being the fable arts system. Legion arms allow you to swap out the playable character's mechanical arm for one of a different flavor, including ones with elemental effects, ranged/mobility attacks, or defensive properties. These can be an absolute lifesaver mid-encounter and your experience will vary dramatically depending on how you do (or don't) utilize them. These are balanced out via either a charge-up time or recharge period and by utilizing a charge system that is not easily replenished without reaching a stargazer. More impressive, in my opinion, is the weapon assembly system which allows you to swap out blades and hilts of any non-boss weapon in the game to change up weapon animations and special weapon properties. If you want to use a certain weapon, but it either doesn't scale well with your build or perhaps you just hate the move set-- you can change out parts on a whim to remedy that! My only gripe is that the game does not explain or really call out specific qualities that may limit the effectiveness of certain weapon combinations.The final more novel system in the game are Fable Arts... I don't have much to say on these as my playthrough did not incorporate them often. These must rely on having both a favorable build and weapon combination to take full advantage of and in my playthrough they felt more like a free hit option when you're low on stamina than anything else. It felt like there were relatively few options to utilize these as shown in many of the trailers. If anything were to be patched (other than a slightly wider parry window and some sort of rebalancing for the aforementioned boss), it would be to either expand options in this system or at least explain the hidden mechanic that governs their effectiveness because it apparently eluded me for the entirety of my time in-game.Imperfect as it is and brutally difficult at times, this is not for the faint of heart (even if you've enjoyed other games in the genre) but utterly worth it at full price if you have the willpower to dig into the deep in-game mechanics and keep pushing when you hit a wall.

_childDocuments_.review: After first coming across NEOWIZ when they made a little-known rogue like called Metal Unit, I knew there were some exciting prospects yet to come from this Korean-based developer. Seeing how much they managed to deliver with Lies of P has honestly left me astonished at times.From the innovative interwoven mechanics that play like an orchestral symphony when mastered to the elegance of the art direction and sound design that feel like you are stepping into a Tim Burton-esque, gothic tale of Pinocchio with a healthy dose of Bloodborne.The staggering amount of work that has gone into creating this beautiful, fully-realised world is incredible. It is oozing with inspiration not only from FROMSOFT's aforementioned "Bloodborne" but also from many other Souls-Like games. It's important to note that while the inspiration is evident, it is never used to simply copy what has come before, only to build upon what created this magnificent genre, making it its own masterpiece in the process.During your roughly 25-hour playthrough, you will be, of course, levelling your character as you would in other Souls titles. However, they have also integrated a deeper skill system, which helps you have even more control over how you want your character to be specked out, which I thought was a fantastic addition. On top of this, you will also have a healthy dose of weaponry to choose from and build yourself. Yes, I indeed said build. I had a lot of enjoyment in breaking down some of my swords to create an unholy union of a fancy long-sword attached to an electric coil stick (hey no judging!). As with many Souls-Like games, you have a home base filled with an interesting assortment of characters that will help you progress throughout the world, upgrade your weaponry, and refine your latent skill abilities, which become more important the further you get in the game.I have found that many Souls-Like games are not particularly renowned for their musical scores, but Lies of P manages to carve out its own niche. Not only does it deliver exceptional tracks during epic boss encounters, but it also introduces a delightful twist with collectable vinyl records that can be played on a vintage jukebox back at your home base. The quality of some of these tunes is nothing short of extraordinary and made it an absolute treat to start a record in the background whilst upgrading and forging new weapons at home base.Also, what has got to be one of the greatest systems I have had the joy to experience is the legion arms. This is an ability that you gain from the very start of the game. What makes it so special is all in the variety of Legion arms you gain throughout the course of the game. You will start your journey blasting people from a distance like Iron Man to my personal favourite, pulling people to you with a dagger attached puppet string, ala Scorpion style.This also can be tinkered with, upgraded, and even created just like with weapons. I grew far too fond of the puppet string and once I upgraded it and changed it up, I eventually found myself using it to grapple from one enemy to the next, which elevated the gameplay for me tremendously.Lies of P also integrates a durability function as well, and I can already hear the groans emanating from my screen as I type that, especially as I am not always a fan of weapon durability, especially in a Souls-like game. However, the way the durability has been integrated is more of a feature that I never even knew I needed in my life. Every weapon has a set durability meter, and you are allowed to repair your weapon on the fly, even while walking. It only takes a few seconds, and can be done an infinite amount of times. However, if you were not paying attention and find yourself at the closing strike of a boss fight as I once did, only to find your weapon to break and have the misfortune of the boss landing that final strike on you, then you quickly realise the importance of maintaining the durability on your weapon. Once you progress further into the game, you will gain the ability to engrave a status during a durability repair, which could embed your weapon with fire, electric, and other type effects, which is something that I absolutely loved having in my arsenal for that elite enemy that could be waiting for you around any corner.All in all, this game will forever mark one of the greatest Souls-Like games I have ever had the pleasure to experience. I could go on for a significant amount of time discussing how fantastic the enemy and boss design has been perfected here. It is a challenging game, there is no getting around that. I had to walk away more than once and come back finding myself beating that boss I had been stuck on for hours in one go. With that being said, Lies of P truly delivered in some memorable and absolutely unforgettable boss fights. The amount of work that went into designing these encounters was truly incredible, and even if I was being subjected to multiple beatings before I was able to overcome it, it was always an absolute spectacle to behold.As with all games in this genre, practice makes perfect, and if you have the dedication to keep pursuing it, the rewards will be bountiful. Be warned, actions have consequences, so it's important to pay attention to what is asked of you as there are multiple different endings, but that's always a fantastic excuse to revisit and experience another playthrough of an already beautifully crafted game.Apart from a couple minor bugs at the start of my 25 hours of playtime, I was very happy to see that I did not have almost any major issues playing this title at a comfortable 120 FPS in 4k. In fact, this game ran so well for me that many AAA game developers should take a note out of NEOWIZ's book on how to release a game in such a polished state.It is a challenging game, and there is no getting around that fact. However, isn't that one of the major appeals of the genre from the get-go? If you could just steamroll your way through everything without any challenge at all on a hypothetical "very easy" mode, would it still give you that same satisfaction that you had when you finally beat that boss or any other challenging segment? Food for thought, especially for fans of the genre itself.PROS:* The narrative is truly immersive, featuring captivating characters with undeniable charisma.* Memorable Boss Fights and enemy design.* A dark and enigmatic world that offers immense satisfaction through exploration and replay value.* The soundtrack is exceptionally stunning from beginning to end.* The weapon system's incredible capacity for creativity and adaptability is truly amazing.* The combat system is intricately designed with numerous well-coordinated components that synergize seamlessly.* One of the best games in its genre you are likely to ever experience.CONS:* Very minor bugs encountered during the start of my playthrough that seem to already be addressed by the developer.The way 'Lies of P' borrows the elements of what worked so well in multiple FROMSOFT titles and delicately interweaves their own system of weapon crafting, branching skill trees, and latent abilities, all enclosed in a visually surreal and gorgeous world with a beautiful soundtrack, is truly incredible.'Lies of P' was not just one of the best Souls-like games I have ever played; it was one of the best games I have ever played, period. What the developers over at NEOWIZ have managed to accomplish is nothing short of extraordinary, and if the rumours of a Wizard of Oz sequel in a shared universe are true, we are in for a very bountiful season indeed.Rating: 9.7/10

_childDocuments_.review: Lies of P – 8/10World-Building and Atmosphere (8.5/10)Strength: Lies of P leans heavily into the gothic, industrial aesthetic, drawing clear inspiration from Bloodborne and Sekiro, while also nodding to its Pinocchio roots. The world of Krat feels eerie and mysterious, with its dark streets, twisted machinery, and haunting atmosphere. There’s an impressive amount of detail in the environment that sets the tone for the game.Critique: However, while the world is beautifully designed, it doesn’t have the same interconnectedness that makes Miyazaki’s worlds feel so alive. In Dark Souls or Bloodborne, every area feels organically woven into the next, creating a sense of discovery and cohesion. Lies of P feels more disjointed, with areas that, while visually stunning, don’t always feel like they belong to a larger, connected world. The level design lacks the tight-knit, maze-like brilliance that we’ve come to expect from FromSoftware titles.Combat and Mechanics (8/10)Strength: Combat in Lies of P is sharp, visceral, and undeniably influenced by the Soulsborne series. The parry system and the emphasis on timing is directly comparable to Sekiro and Bloodborne. It requires precision, forcing players to learn enemy patterns and strike when the moment is right. The weapon customization system is a neat touch, allowing players to experiment with different combinations to suit their playstyle.Critique: While the combat is engaging, it often feels like a watered-down version of Miyazaki’s best work. The parrying mechanics feel a bit clunky compared to the tight, responsive system in Sekiro. The combat, while challenging, sometimes feels like it’s trying too hard to emulate Soulsborne titles without truly innovating. The enemy variety is limited, with many encounters feeling repetitive after a while. Miyazaki’s games always manage to keep combat fresh by introducing new mechanics or enemies at the right time, whereas Lies of P struggles to maintain that balance.Boss Fights (7.5/10)Strength: The bosses in Lies of P are impressive in terms of design. Their grotesque, mechanical designs fit the game’s dark, twisted world perfectly. Some boss fights, like the King of Puppets, are visually stunning and serve as memorable, tense challenges.Critique: However, the boss fights lack the variety and depth seen in FromSoftware titles. Many of the fights boil down to memorizing patterns and perfecting parries, but without the intricate lore or emotional weight behind the battles that Miyazaki often excels at. In Dark Souls or Bloodborne, bosses often feel like living parts of the world’s lore, with their defeat carrying narrative weight. In Lies of P, while they’re visually striking, the bosses can feel soulless, as if they exist purely as gameplay challenges rather than integral parts of the story. They also fall into predictable attack patterns, which diminishes the tension after a few attempts.Story and Narrative (7/10)Strength: Lies of P introduces an interesting twist on the Pinocchio story, with a darker, more dystopian take on the classic tale. The idea of lying as a mechanic that influences the world and the character’s growth is unique and intriguing.Critique: While the story has potential, it doesn’t hit the narrative depth we’ve come to expect from Soulsborne games. In Bloodborne or Dark Souls, the lore is rich, layered, and often hidden beneath cryptic dialogue and environmental storytelling, leaving players to piece it together. Lies of P tries to replicate this, but its lore feels shallow in comparison. There’s a lack of emotional engagement with the characters, and the narrative doesn’t feel as mysterious or captivating as it could be. It’s a game that’s trying to be deep, but it ends up being surface-level in its storytelling.Innovation (7/10)Strength: The lying system is a novel mechanic that adds an interesting twist to the decision-making process. It adds layers to the protagonist’s morality and offers some variation in how the story unfolds, even if it’s somewhat underutilized. The weapon crafting system is another nice touch, offering players some customization in combat.Critique: But outside of these small innovations, Lies of P doesn’t do much to stand out from the shadow of Miyazaki’s influence. It feels like a follower rather than a game that’s breaking new ground. Where Miyazaki constantly pushes boundaries—whether it’s with the Posture system in Sekiro or the seamless open world of Elden Ring—Lies of P feels like it’s playing it safe. It mimics the surface-level elements of a Soulsborne game without truly understanding what makes those games great on a deeper level.Pacing and Progression (7.5/10)Strength: The game does a decent job of keeping players engaged with a steady flow of upgrades and new abilities. The difficulty curve, while steep, feels fair, and players are rewarded for their perseverance.Critique: However, the pacing can feel uneven at times. The game tends to drag in certain areas, with long stretches of enemy gauntlets that don’t add much to the overall experience. Where Miyazaki’s games excel at keeping the player hooked with carefully curated moments of tension and release, Lies of P lacks that ebb and flow, leading to moments of frustration rather than satisfaction. The progression feels more grindy than rewarding, with certain parts of the game dragging on longer than necessary without meaningful progression in the story or combat systems.Replayability (8/10)Strength: With multiple endings and the option to explore different choices through the lying system, there’s definitely incentive for multiple playthroughs. The various builds and weapon combinations also offer some variety in gameplay, giving players reason to experiment.Critique: Despite these options, Lies of P doesn’t have the same replayability appeal as Soulsborne games. The lack of meaningful build diversity and limited enemy variety means that, once you’ve beaten the game, there’s less incentive to dive back in for another round. In contrast, Dark Souls or Elden Ring offer near infinite replayability thanks to their rich build systems, intricate world designs, and ever-changing metas.Final Verdict: 8/10Lies of P is a solid Soulslike that offers a unique twist on the genre with its Pinocchio-inspired world and the lying mechanic, but it’s clear that the game is heavily influenced by the works of Hidetaka Miyazaki. While it captures some of the magic of Soulsborne titles, it falls short in key areas like boss variety, narrative depth, and combat precision. It’s a game that wears its influences proudly but struggles to forge its own identity.For fans of the genre, Lies of P will scratch that challenging, gothic action itch, but it never quite reaches the brilliance of its inspirations. If you’re looking for a true evolution of the Soulslike formula, you might walk away feeling like Lies of P is more of an imitation than a revolution. That said, for what it offers—a gritty, mechanically challenging experience—it’s still a fun and rewarding journey, just not a game that redefines the genre the way Miyazaki has done so many times before.

_childDocuments_.review: Lies of P is an excellent Soulslike game, but it has its faults. 8.5/10 would be fair.For brevity, I'll only go over the cons.I enjoy a challenge as evidenced by the games I've beaten, but some of the bosses in Lies of P are just too hard and not enjoyable to beat. I had to respec for Walker of Illusions because my motivity (strength) build just wasn't working. I ended up beating Walker with a technique (dexterity) build after the second attempt. Laxasia is just ridiculous - she performs a 12-hit combo and then barely pauses before starting another flurry of attacks. Laxasia should have similar stamina limitations as the player. Nameless Puppet's second phase is just completely unfair. Beating Nameless didn't feel good at all. By the end of the game I was just happy it was over.A great Soulslike is hard, but if a player has a reasonable amount of skill and learns to counter most of the attacks, they can be beaten. Lies of P wasn't like that for me - I had to completely respec my character to progress, which feels lame.Keeping my weight under "slightly heavy", for vigor (stamina) purposes, was a slog. I ended up with a capacity of 41/99, and still had to wear an amulet to increase my capacity because I had to carry two weapons for the final boss fight (only!) due to durability concerns.I'll never understand why so many Soulslikes don't allow the player to pause, but there really isn't a good excuse for this. It's like a cupholder in a car - it's NOT OPTIONAL. A phone call, a knock at the door, a child screaming - these are normal occurrences that a pause feature addresses.Overall I think Lies of P is a shockingly good entry from a newcomer developer in the Soulslike genre. It isn't perfect, and some of the time it's totally unfair, but overall I would recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful graphics and environments tarnished by terrible combatI finished Lies of P and immediately uninstalled the game without any interest of ever going back and playing it again. Overall, the environments, characters and bosses all look visually very appealing, some of the best graphics I've seen in a souls-like game. Sound effects and music, especially in boss fights, is all top-notch.But...The combat is just horrible. Literally the worst souls-like combat I've seen to date. I really love games like Elden Ring, the Dark Souls games (yes even 2), and Bloodborne, and coming from those games to a game that tries to emulate the combat but fails is just sad. My biggest gripes are that P (Pinocchio) has no "poise", or what the other souls games call poise. Essentially, in those games, if a smaller enemy like a human or dog hits you with a light attack, or even a heavy attack but a light weapon like a dagger, you could "poise through" and trade attacks with the enemy. You'd still get hurt, but at least you'd do something to the enemy. Also, same goes for the giant weapons and hyper-armor, doesn't exist in Lies of P at all. It's as if P is made of paper, and even if a flea bites him, he flinches. This leads to the most frustrating encounters with any kind of enemy, whether it be a low-level zombie or a giant boss swinging a mallet, any attack that connects immediately knocks P out of his own attack animation. It becomes downright nonsensical at times, when P is swinging a giant saw blade and just as the attack is about to connect, a little baby-looking puppet crawling on the ground touches P's foot and P flinches. I really don't understand how they could **** up poise and hyper-armor this badly.But wait! It gets worse!! The enemies do have some kind of flinching build up, usually after 2 attacks, but even knowing this it is very difficult to get 2 attacks in (in most cases) to cause a flinch. So many enemies can just poise through whatever the hell you just did, even hitting them with a giant greatsword R2 heavy attack. They essentially see you attacking, their AI suddenly starts an attack while you're mid swing, they get hit and there is no time (really 0 seconds) to either dodge or to block their incoming attack. Which reminds me...all of your attacks are 100% committed attacks. The moment you press R1, R2 or L2 (to use your arm), P can no longer back-step or roll out of the animation. It's like he has a single track mind "P gonna smash enemy with club P gonna!!!"...It made me so furious when you want to recover before getting hit or simply switch from the attack to a dodge or block and P just doesn't...why!?Finally, let's talk about the ludicrous AI targeting and tracking. Literally in every souls game besides this one, when an enemy commits to its attack, they target the player, and the tracking is that X/Y/Z coordinate. Unless they have a long wind up to "roll catch" you, it makes no sense to see every single enemy, EVERY ONE, have tracking on their committed attacks. So many times I felt that this was just way too unfair and punishing, you see a low level enemy like these guys with clubs or street-signs start to wind up an attack, you run to the left or right of them to avoid and maybe get a backstab, and its like by magic they just reface themselves perfectly to where P is and smack him. I hate this kind of **** because P doesn't have 100% accuracy, but the weakest enemies do!? Wtf?Btw, if you want to cheese 90% of this game, just always carry grenades and summon the Specter for each boss fight. For some reason, I noticed that almost every boss can be burned or acided or both, so might as well let them be "poisoned" while you chip away as best you can while avoiding their attacks...
