_childDocuments_.review: A mechanically perfect pretender to Fromsoft's throne. Maybe there's some metaphor there about it's puppet theming and them being mechanically perfect clones of humans, but literary pretensions aside, studio round8 definitely deserves the praise for finally being able to crack the Soulsclone code with this level of perfection on its first try. Controls, animations, effects, pacing of exploration are definitely on par with Fromsoft's creations. They do lean into the git gud meme super hard and the Fromsoft postgame skillcreep goes through the roof, with each boss progressively aiming for "break the internet" tier difficulty infamy one after the other. Some people might not like this design ethos, as literally every enemy in this game is designed to be full of unintuitive gotchas, and depend on knowledge and muscle memory more than twitch reactions, but it's a fun route to figure out as a post-fromsoft kinda journey, as there is no "universal solution" between dodge or parry for each attack pattern. While levels are linear, the levels themselves are well done and the 'exploration logic' is solid. The design is almost too lenient, as the proximity to a bonfire or shortcut kind of becomes transparent as you go through them, with no subversions or inversions throughout. There's a small problem of filling the levels with near identical-feeling sections, and you tend to remember the level only in terms of left and right turns instead of distinct sections and chunks, kind of hampering the thrill of exploration (It's head and shoulders above 99% of games out there, just unfairly comparing them to the masters of the genre here). The story is kinda schmaltzy and lacks the Fromsoft "upscale-ness" despite the High Society Arts Beaux aesthetic and is not helped by somewhat questionable english translations (kind of a mystery as the English VAs themselves are very good) but is still completely serviceable and the lore is easy to deduce. The new mechanics introduced like swapping weapon parts is great, and qol changes like last estus recharging with enough hits, soul dropping outside the boss gate, and infinite one-time elemental buffs are something even Souls games themselves could copy. I particularly love the Mortal Kombat Scorpion spear that turns the 'prank ambush in tight corners' and 'annoying sniper on another platform' level design on its head, but still tied to a manageable resource as a mechanic. There's still a huge selection of playstyles I'm yet to explore after the first playthough, but I rest assured as this game has definitely earned my trust as a labor of love.

_childDocuments_.review: Do not miss out on this game. It is a Souls game through and through, and one might argue it has the most polished and satisfying Souls combat of them all. Taking the best parts of Sekiro, Bloodborne and Dark Souls combat, and *actually* managing to surpass them - it's an incredible achievement by the developers.Souls comparisons aside, this game also has a beautiful melancholic atmosphere. The story is extremely dark, depicting a disaster where puppets and zombies rampage through what used to be a thriving human city on Earth. But the arts, the music, the architecture of this once-beautiful place still shine through thanks to the level and audio design.

_childDocuments_.review: NEOWIZ takes the soulslike formula, and runs with it. While Lies of P takes a lot of detailed notes from the original Souls games, it easily stands on its own with its unique and creative takes on exhilarating combat, metroidvania level design, and extensive character optimization.If you're familiar with the games that inspired Lies of P you'll be familiar with the environmental storytelling set in a post-apocalyptic universe. Lies of P has a bit more direct narrative than those games however, thanks to a very strong cast of charismatic and memorable characters. The plot isn't nearly as mysterious as FromSoft games are, and items will directly tell you what they do- for better or for worse. The protagonist is accompanied by a talking partner who does most of the talking, sometimes even too much (the game is self-aware that he can get annoying, and plays off this very well in my opinion). The uneasiness and distrust between all the survivors of the prologue of game is some of the most tragic and unforgiving storytelling I've experienced, as well as introduces very formidable antagonists.Each standard weapon can be separated by blade and handle. The blade controls the base damage while the handle controls the moveset and stat scaling. You can freely (quite literally costs nothing) switch between blades and handles to mix and match to your liking. There are some really fun and interesting combinations you can make with this. The only exception is that boss weapons cannot be separated, and that you can't change it on the fly so you must return to the hub or a resting point. Impressively, almost every weapon/handle has a unique moveset which makes Lies of P's gameplay customizability top of the line. I will not spoil anything about boss weapons other than they're the coolest, most badass weapons in the game.Lies of P features some of the most challenging yet fair enemy designs in any soulslike, even surpassing some of FromSoft's titles. None of the bosses feel like they have any moves that are straight up BS, everything is telegraphed and adaptable. Lies of P has a combination of Sekiro parries, Bloodborne dodges and Souls rolls that are meant to be woven together to give you great freedom in choosing your defensive options. The game also features classic Miyazaki traps, ambushes, and swamps, all your typical soulslike shenanigans that reward awareness and clever maneuvering.Do yourself a favor and play Lies of P.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the best non-FromSoft game to enter the soulslike field imo. It took me a good deal of time to 100% this game over multiple playthroughs - luckily, LoP rewards you with further character progression unique to NG+ that keeps the game feeling fresh and significantly alters how you may approach boss fights. It's definitely difficult, but you don't have to be a parry god to beat this game. I highly recommend this to people who like FromSoft games. Also the soundtrack is killer.

_childDocuments_.review: This review comes from a person familiar with the Soulsborne formula. I'll be listing a few notable points that caught my eye through the playthrough, for any player feeling skeptical about giving this a try (spoiler free):Starting from the Boss Fights, I found myself averaging from 1-4 attempts across battles (Main & Optional). They often provide an NPC summon for assistance, which is entirely optional. Aside that, I find it concerning that I could brute force every encounter, without the need of carefully observing patterns.The titles main issue lies in the animations. They feel half-baked. You can observe the clear Sekiro and Bloodborne influences, attempting multiple mechanics from both titles. Parrying is a core mechanic that unlike Sekiro requires you to hold down the block action instead of tapping the queues. This may not seem like an issue, yet I continuously stumbled upon combos feeling awkward and unrecoverable if you missed the first hit of a chain attack. The dodge roll or quick step animations are not very consistent. Consider 'running' your best friend instead. Most of the enemy attacks try to follow asynchronous patterns, mimicking a puppets behavior. The patterns could be better polished to feel more identifiable, allowing more room to engage in combat.The upgraded double roll functions as: one roll (on tap), followed by another faster roll (on the second tap). It feels like it's cutting through / interrupting the previous roll, even though that's not the case. The biggest instances of you taking damage are due to battling with controls.The characters and the story are decently written, the music is properly written yet not so ingeniously placed, the level design was not very impressive pinpointing nearly one or two sectors that felt creatively connected. The majority of the boss designs are well made. Even though the art style can stand on it's own two feet, it sometimes needs a crutch. The weapon designs are a hit or miss, narrowing the interest or need to switch between loadouts. Good voice acting on most of the dialogue.The areas felt a bit disappointing to explore. Linear progression is never an issue, but it felt like they played it a bit too safe, hastily trying to keep the players attention by narrowing the routes to each Boss Room. On top of that, the majority of the areas were a hit or miss as well, remembering them through a foggy cloud, they lack identity. The majority of my playthrough I was above weight limit and using heavy weaponry. Still, the character feels like a feather. There's an evident disconnect that keeps me from enjoying the movement, either by the awkward walking animations or the weapon grinding animation clipping through the character. There is a certain weight missing in both movement and combat, better found even in the original Dark Souls.If you have previously played any FromSoftware title, give this game a try for the comparison. The reference points I introduce are better experienced hands on. I am unsure if I would recommend it to someone who hasn't played any games of the genre as there are better candidates to invest your time in.

_childDocuments_.review: Preface: If you like souls-like games you will like this game.I got this game because I have wanted to like a souls-like game and have yet to find one I can bear to play the whole way through. This game got the closest, and fought against a lot of the shortfalls that I found in other games in this genre. Even so, there are SO MANY FUNDAMENTALLY WRONG THINGS ABOUT THE GAME. It makes me want to rip my hair out. The core spirit and quality of the game are incredible but they are shrouded by awful game design that I could go on and on about. Minor spoilers ahead:- The story is convoluted and either told through cut scenes with almost no dialogue or on-screen text with way too much dialogue.  Some of the characters that you are supposed to care greatly about have very little personality, screen time, or motive. This makes the finale that I can tell was supposed to be riveting fall flat.- The stage design is toxic. At least 50% of the design is to have an enemy hidden around a corner, on the ceiling, behind a wall they will break, etc. which yeah I learned over time but it makes the game so slow and monotonous to carefully 3rd person peek every comer when the game could have just given me honest fun fights and not be a troll.- The stage design is toxic pt 2. There are sections that are semi-platformers. This should not exist in a game that has a short and uncooperative jump ONLY WHEN SPRINTING. And even if there was a solid jump, I also cannot jump whenever there was no hole but rather a bridge that didn't break when an enemy walked across it but will when my character does. Now whenever I see any bridge, especially those that appear even more perilous, I jump over them automatically like a Pavlovian dog.- The stage design is toxic pt 3. There are multiple sections where you have to walk your character across beams that are literally smaller than your character's width. you do this while enemies fire at you from across the chasm or poison swamp. Blocking may still knock you back, and dodging must be done perfectly. It's just tedious, I just want more basic fun combat.- Most of the enemies are bad. There are some great enemies, and I will no doubt praise the combat when it is in its best form, but this is infrequent. There are enemies with one health that spam powerful attacks if left alive for one second, often in groups or paired with unstoppable tanks that allow these attacks to kill. There are enemies that ARE LITERALLY JUST TORSOS AND I HATE THEM. There are enemies just designed to grab you and shred health. There are enemies that make the enemies around them nearly invincible, but also stay back and are nearly impossible to kill first because y'know it's a sword game. There are enemies that just explode to damage you. No engaging combat, give or take, challenge and reward, just exploding instantly. There are pitchfork puppets (trust me they suck). There are canons that shoot from across the map while you fight other enemies. These canons can be destroyed, but honestly it would be easy to miss that fact. There are mini-bosses that are the size of buildings and are slow but will kill you with ease. There are enemies with riot-shields that force you to just stand in place and wait. There are enemies that spawn from traps that also explode when they die. - The status effects suck. There are six of them:> You take damage over time. Okay fair enough.> You take damage and your weapon decays. Inconvenient and dumb, especially when an enemy's only design is to inflict you with this constantly.> Your fable (ability energy) drains. Okay but unengaging.> You heal less. Okay but also healing is already scarce this isn't over watch you can just keep damaging me> You regenerate stamina more slowly. Only massive troll enemies use this to make you play the game less.> You instantly die. WHO'S MAKING THESE IDEAS UP JUST ATTACK ME NORMALLYThese can be resisted or cleansed using items that are consumable, so I am constantly trying to preserve them and being punished for it. There should be a consistent way to cleanse them if they are going to be applied to me consistently. Every time I see any enemy inflict a status effect I know it's gonna be dumb.- The item design is bad. All items look the same on the ground, so I will find myself taking damage, dying, or spending resources at a net-negative because the reward was a lore-bit/gear/nail/grenade/rock/magazine/etc. which I never use because they are more trouble than they are worth to equip, cycle through to use, decide when to use, spend time to play animation to use, to get .000001 of my arm or something back. - Run-backs are dumb. period. If I want to fight a boss then spawn me at the boss not a minute's walk from the boss where I have to fight enemies or hope they don't hit me.- The difficulty is dumb. I don't mind a challenge, but it had better be a fair one. All the stuff above makes the game hard, but not fun, challenging hard, but stupid, bash your head against the wall in frustration. One of the solutions to this is to allow an assistant into boss fights to help you in combat. This does mostly make the boss easier, but 1. The game is forcing me to admit that I am a baby, 2. The game is going to give me a different experience, since the boss focusing on two opponents makes the game fundamentally different (and sometimes unfair/finicky), and 3. Will force me to use a consumable item, that if I run out of, will force me back into difficulty or to wait to buy more of the consumables.- Some of the bosses are dumb. Some are good, and most are fine barring their infliction of status effects, but some are not fun. Bosses should consistently either have two full health bars for two phases, or always switch phases halfway through the first health bar. Obscuring the end of the fight is not "a challenging surprise" it's just demoralizing.- There is no reason that the game would allow you to level up at a checkpoint at the start AND end of the game but at no other time.- Weapon upgrading is tough. Weapons deal more damage depending on your character's stats and their level, and in a difficult game with scarce resources, I'm surely going to put all my eggs in one basket (police baton + motivity for life). This on top of mastering an early game weapon makes it difficult to change play styles, as the change will come with being noticeably less powerful, which can only be changed by respec-ing your skill points at the golden tree.- The side quests are really obscured. The game gets a plus one for showing icons on the fast-travel menu for some things, but this is a far cry from the basic good design of a quest list, reminders, or something more especially when these quests can give vital upgrades and also be missable.- The "choose your fate" system is bad. There are times when the game gives flavor texts implying that your decision is going to have an impact (telephone calls) but does not. There are times where the options given are not clearly corresponding to the different fates you can choose. I didn't feel like I was choosing my fate because I believed it to be true or wanted to pursue it, but because the game is called Lies of P and everyone wants me to lie so whoop-dee-doo I guess I will- The game, besides having missable content is side quests and such, also has A MISSABLE FINAL BOSS. LIKE THE WHOLE REASON FOR ME TO TRUDGE THROUGH THE WHOLE GAME WAS TO HAVE THE SATISFACTION OF EARNING VICTORY OVER THE FINAL BOSS AND A DIGITAL PAT ON THE BACK AND NOW I CAN'T. THE CHOICES I MADE THAT CAUSED ME TO MISS THE BOSS WEREN'T EVEN ONES I WERE PASSIONATE ABOUT. So the only way to fight the boss now is either to replay the entire game (either speedrun and have a weak kit at the end or grind all over again) or play “new game +” which turns the final boss from a hard final challenge to an impossible masochist festival. I'll pass.Overall, the game could have been great and I'm just really sad it wasn't.

_childDocuments_.review: Right up there with FromSoft's games, but not as good as a FromSoft game.- Combat in general feels amazing- Enemy variety is high (visually and their movesets)- Bosses are awesome (visually and their movesets) and there are like 15 of them- Story is mysterious and intriguing and the broad strokes of it are pretty interesting- Runs perfectly (this one makes it way better than From games outside of Elden Ring)- Upgrades are very meaningful (especially via the Quartz system). You get upgrades like "can now dodge from grounded state".- Builds aren't really that diverse. Motivity, Technique and Advance determine which weapon handles you can use. And weapon handles determine movesets. But there are very few movesets that are entirely unique to one of those stats. Maybe 1 or 2.- Characters aren't very well developed. Pretty bad voice work. Pretty inconsequential dialogue that usually goes on for too long. Gemini talks way too much and usually says stuff that doesn't quite follow the events that took place prior.- "The Truth" in this game pales by contrast with The Truths revealed in Bloodborne, Dark Souls and Elden Ring. Actually sort of amounts to a schlocky SyFy/horror plot, once you learn what's going on.- Level design is very linear, and shortcuts aren't very impressive outside of one great one. _childDocuments_.review: As a standalone title, Lies of P is a well thought-out and implemented game that has some quirks that hold it back from being an amazing game. I would personally rate this a 7/10 as a standalone game.BUT.....The combat is fun for the first few bosses but quickly becomes annoying with some bosses having moves that stun lock you for making a single mistake during a combo. Some bosses heavily rely on dodging attacks while others rely exclusively on parrying due to their aggressive nature and as such you often find yourself fighting a boss a few times just to see what type of boss they wanted it to be and you can destroy it from there on if you get a feel for the timings quickly. This results in a very shallow experience to the game.The level design is interesting for your first run but quickly becomes mundane on a subsequent run through of an area. Most levels are very linear with shortcuts opening up as you progress until you ultimately find a magical one that happens to be near the start of the level and leads directly to the boss (if only some grunt would have left that damn door open or ladder down this whole time!). Coincidentally, weapon upgrades are also very linear leading to frustrations if you want to try a new weapon. Your new weapon will be a lower upgrade level than your main one because you haven't passed a specific boss you may be stuck on that gates more upgrade materials or the supply crate to unlock the material you need for purchase. On top of this, weapon scaling is an incredibly simplified version of the souls counterparts of weapon scaling. If a weapon handle has "B" scaling, all blades attached to it will scale the same. This can lead to feeling overwhelmed with choices and fear of commitment to a specific blade as you cannot upgrade more than one before certain milestones.The bosses are also not very unique after the first part of the game . This again leads to a shallow feeling experience.If compared against similar titles it obviously takes inspiration from (bloodborne, sekiro, and the dark souls series) this game falls apart in terms of quality and struggles to beat even dark souls II in my eyes, the "worst" game in the souls series (objectively, dark souls 2 is a good game it just falls short compared to the other games just like this one LOL). In this context, the game is a 5.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: This is a review originally written for . The full article can be found . Feel free to take a look at the Opium Pulse Steam Curation page  as well.Lies of P is a beautiful, story-rich Souls-Like RPG brought to life by Neowiz Games with Choi Ji-won at the helm as lead director. Taking place in the city of Krat, you play as P, the “son” of Geppetto. Awakened by a soft, mysterious voice, beckoning you to Hotel Krat- you arm yourself, (find a friend) and depart the train station. Much is still shrouded in mystery as you make your way through hoards of puppets, suddenly in violation of The Grand Covenant- a set of rules inscribed on each puppet upon creation that they are bound to.First Law: All puppets must obey their creator’s commands.Second Law: A puppet may not harm a human.Third law: A puppet must protect and serve Krat.Fourth Law: A puppet cannot lie.Amidst the Puppet Frenzy, find your way, find the truth behind who started this revolt, and why. The city of Krat is a beautiful, eerie and mysterious place. There is much to do, and plenty to uncover. When it comes to game play, Lies of P is what you would come to expect from a AAA Souls-Like title. The controls are tight, well defined and responsive- what I could call an industry standard from a game of this nature. As one might guess, you will become very well acquainted with dodging, blocking, and, as one may surmise, dying. Players new to Souls-Like may find this game very punishing in more ways than one- possibly missing access to maps and quest markers, as well as the ease with which you can suddenly meet you end. However, while boasting beautifully detailed maps, Lies of P is actually quite linear- you may take a wrong path, but you can only go so far (and you will usually be rewarded, in the process) before needing to turn back to the more obvious way forward. This leaves little room for the need of any maps, as you can fast travel by way of Stargazers. Conveniently, any side quests you may pick up along the way, and are able to complete, will be marked in the fast travel menu so you have a general idea of where you need to go. Another aspect new players may be unfamiliar with, is that upon using a Stargazer, nearly all enemies (with select few exceptions) are revived. While some may find this frustrating, this is common place to the genre, and will likely be dismissed over time. As you get stronger, traversing old stomping grounds is a breeze- a simple way to gain additional ergo and grow stronger. Enemies have beautifully haunting design, most bosses boasting a depth of backstory, as well. From Train station workers, to factory workers, to water-logged corruption spitting tricksters, you will find puppets in all shapes and sizes. Some move quickly, others slowly- but all have an arsenal at their disposal, and absolutely all are more than willing to kill you, given the chance. While simply dodging may seem to be the easiest path to survival against such enemies, to truly master combat, you will absolutely need to learn how to block. Smaller puppets can easily be disposed of, requiring very little effort. Large enemies, however, will require skill- especially bosses. Graciously, the developers have given players an option to use a Star Fragment outside boss locations, allowing you to summon a Spectre into battle to fight along side you. While it won’t carry you all the way through- it will make life remarkably easier.What can help carry you through the dangers of your journey, is a set of reliable weapons, and gear. While there are basic equipment slots for augmentations, you have multiple other options. Customize your frame, converters, cartridges, as well as swap out amulets, and change out your Legion arm. Not only are there a slew of options available to you on your quest to separate the Truth from the Lies, but your weapons are able to be customized as well. Nearly every weapon is able to be split into a blade and handle- with some exceptions. Both the blade and handle have unique Fable Arts- specialty moves unique to each piece that will give you the upper hand in battle. Mix and match them to suit your needs, as well as play-style, which will be more clearly defined based on how you choose to level up your character. The city of Krat is beautiful, but dark and forlorn- carnage rampant throughout the once glistening city. Players can easily get lost marveling at the Glory of What Once Was, as it ends up telling a story on its own. Beyond this, the musical score that backs Lies of P is insanely beautiful. Collect vinyl to play at your HUB, Hotel Krat. Rife with amazingly raw emotion, I often found myself immediately setting a new record on the phonograph as soon as I entered. Neowiz and Round 8 have mastered storytelling through every medium available to them, if you are willing to look. Stories are told in the desolate streets, what appear to be inconsequential side quests, music, character interaction, notes, posters and superior overall design. If you love depth and lore with heavy, dark undertones, paired with moral gray, you will find it here, in abundance. While games of this type are simply not for everyone, it seems the brilliant teams behind Lies of P has done it’s best to provide as much balance as possible. Many tools and assets have been made available to give players with varying degrees of skill and experience with Souls-Like games a fighting chance. Specters in boss fights, as well as very convenient, comfortable and “safe” Stargazer are two of the biggest notable graces.  Ultimately, this is a brilliant game with vast world building, gorgeous graphics, finely tuned controls and an enchanting musical score. With DLC slated for the second half of 2024 (likely around it’s one-year anniversary), you can easily expect there to be more high-quality craftsmanship and passion behind it. I can’t wait to see what’s in store for us as the next chapter of Lies of P unfolds.

_childDocuments_.review: Lies of P  – The Almost Souls Game (Or How Pinocchio Learned to Parry)Alright, buckle up, because we’re talking about Lies of P—the Souls-like that somehow took Pinocchio and made it dark, gritty, and weirdly intense. Think of it as the love child of Bloodborne and Disney, with an extra dash of puppet existentialism. It’s packed with good stuff, but there’s enough questionable design here to make you wonder if Geppetto put a little too much wood glue into this one.The Good: Combat, Atmosphere, and That Almost Perfect Souls FormulaLet’s get into what Lies of P absolutely nails. Combat? Chef’s kiss. Hits feel weighty, and perfect guarding—a high-stakes parry move—is almost addictive… when you get the timing down. It’s like hitting a three-pointer in a Space Jam game—difficult, risky, but oh-so-satisfying when you pull it off.The vibe? Spot on. The whole “dark puppet apocalypse” setting is visually incredible, and each level is a twisted mix of moody and imaginative. You get that deep, eerie lore that every Souls fan loves, but without so much story that it derails the main experience. It’s like Elden Ring’s lore met Pinocchio, but way more gothic fairy tale.The Bad: Weapon Babysitting and Perfect Guard ObsessionBut Lies of P has some issues that go from “quirky” to straight-up frustrating. First up, weapon durability. Your sword’s going dull every 10 minutes, and you’re left sharpening it mid-battle like you’re prepping for Gordon Ramsay’s Kitchen Nightmares. Meanwhile, enemies are out here with blades that apparently don’t even chip. It doesn’t add combat strategy so much as it turns durability into a “you” problem—one that interrupts fights and feels more like an extra chore than meaningful gameplay.And that brings us to the perfect guard. This is where Lies of P goes a bit “too hardcore Souls” for its own good. Perfect guarding is the game’s version of a high-risk parry, but by the time you’re in the late game, it’s practically required. Get it right, and you don’t take damage or even lose stamina; miss, and your guard breaks faster than my patience in an Overwatch solo queue. It’s cool as a concept, but in practice, you’re stuck perfect guarding just to stay alive because normal guarding drains health like a TikTok trend that’s already outdated by next week.Late-Game Bosses and the Quest for SurvivalNow, about those late-game bosses. Look, we’ve all faced aggressive bosses, but in Lies of P, it’s like they know when you’re struggling and immediately come in with the “Big Bad Wolf” energy. Trying to heal? The boss has already closed the gap. Want to sharpen your weapon? Prepare to get smacked back into the loading screen. There’s this hyper-reactive AI that feels less like smart design and more like it’s reading your inputs, making it insanely hard to catch a break.And just when you think you’re about to make it out of this puppet hellscape, you hit the final bosses and… yeah. These guys make it feel like you’re playing Dark Souls on Legendary difficulty. You’re expected to rely entirely on perfect guards, and when you finally get to the Unnamed Puppet, he’s an absolute beast—great design, but tuned to eleven. By this point, the game isn’t testing your skills as much as your sanity, and trust me, you’ll feel every one of those 40 hours.Side Bar -The Redemption Arc: The Aegis ArmNow, there is a hero in all this chaos—the Aegis Arm. This shield can stun enemies and finally give you some room to breathe, but the catch? You probably didn't think to use it until the very end, and upgrading it costs a small fortune. It’s like being handed Captain America’s shield right before the final battle and then being told, “Oh, but you’ll need to pay for those upgrades.” The shield’s a game-changer, but only if you max it out first to save your sanity later.And the Story? A Dark Puppet Fairy Tale Worth a Second LookStory-wise, Lies of P does its best to give that classic Souls-style cryptic lore while pulling from Pinocchio in a way that’s both unique and oddly gripping. There are enough layers here to keep lore-hunters engaged, but if you’re just here for the action, you can totally ignore it and still have a good time. Let’s just say that by the end, the story leaves you with more questions than answers, and if you got one of the secret endings, get ready to be hit with that classic, FromSoft-esque “Huh?” moment. There’s clearly a setup for a sequel, but getting there might cost you some controller life.The Final Verdict: A REALLY strong 7.5/10Lies of P has the makings of a great Souls-like and does a lot right for a first attempt. It captures the look, the feel, and that classic “soulsborne” vibe, but the relentless focus on perfect guarding, aggressive bosses, and the annoying durability mechanic will test your patience. You know it’s tough love when a game makes you go from “I’m loving this” to “I just want this to be over.”So, is Lies of P worth it? For Souls fans, absolutely—it’s a solid 7.5 out of 10 and scratches that itch pretty well. But if you’re looking for a smoother ride or expecting Elden Ring levels of polish, be prepared for some wear-and-tear on your patience, just like on your puppet sword. It’s one of the best non-FromSoft attempts at the genre, but those final levels are basically a gauntlet to see how much mental stamina you have left.Lies of P—it’s a beautifully flawed gem that’s one patch away from greatness.

_childDocuments_.review: To cook a good Lies of P, take Dark Souls as a base and:-Remove the maze like structure of the world(there are still shortcuts to unlock but the progression is linear)-Make the world way more interesting(Sorry Fromsoft but you've been schooled there)-Make the crafting more interesting(You can pair a blade with a handle of a lot of weapons which will vary its range, speed, effects and specials)-Your left hand can be a fire thrower or electrocute enemies or even become a missile launcher.-Lower the difficulty. This game is clearly easier than most souls like, which maybe be a pro or a con depending on your experience. The gameplay is faster which makes it easier to perform a perfect parry and the game is generous with your healing pots too. In addition you don't lose all your Ergo(the souls of the franchise) when you die before reaching your death points again, only a portion of it(which can be reduced even more with pots). Overall after 12 hours I've not yet finished the game(I'd say I'm not even half way, looking at the progression systems) but I can already tell it'll be one of, if not, my favourite souls-like.

_childDocuments_.review: Really enjoyed this, for about 90% of the playthrough. Will give you the highs and lows quickly.Fantastic and why Lies of P was more enjoyable than Elden Ring:- NO INPUT READING. Dark Souls and Elden Ring essentially cheat by reading your keypresses and responding instantaneously. Frankly, its garbage, and an idiotic mechanic that should never have been implemented. You're basically fighting yourself, or finding ways to 'cheese' the boss, which takes away all the fun and skill of the fight because the AI is straight up cheating. LoP doesn't input read therefore each fight feels organic and rewarding. - IT LETS *YOU* STAGGER THE ENEMY! God, how many times in Elden Ring did I take entirely unncessary damage because of basic hits staggering me. Then you'd fall down, get hit more on standing up or at the end of a roll. Meanwhile, yes you can guard counter, but you can't stagger and you can't hit them when they're down (but they can hit you!). LoP gives this power back to you, and puts you on equal footing with the AI. They can stagger but so can you. Its actually fair and I can't believe I even had to type that.Pros:- Beautiful, stunning game on the Unreal Engine. Looks fantastic, ran at constant 120 capped on a 3070 super on ultra. A++- The characters are all voiced well, interesting, and their individual stories intermingle and flow together. I, for the most part, found them quite interesting, notably the King of Riddles.- Combat is challenging, but not busted. There are one or two fights in the game you will likely struggle hard with, but for the most part this is far more palatable than ER or DS. And for that, I'm appreciative. I enjoy 'hard' games, I don't enjoy overly punishing and brutal boss fights that require dozen upon dozens or more attempts or even full character ability/build respecs just to get past. - The overall story, while somewhat confusing, was a very cool spin on the classic Pinnochio tale. The devs really did their homework and wove in some very unique color that you might not even know about. For example, one of the groups in the game are the 'Alchemists'. A weapon you can find later in the game is called the 'Uroboros Wheel'. The 'Oroboros' is, in fact, the sigil of the actual Alchemist guild from about 400 CE and represents the duality of man (ring any bells?). Cons:- Like seemingly every Korean game, some of the translations and phrasings feel weird in English. I can't quit put my finger on it but it just feels off. Many people are quick to point out that Pinnochio's heart and the skill tree in the game is called 'P Organ'. Im as juvenile as the next guy but this just feels too obvious...- This game, like seemingly every other soulsborne on the planet, suffers what I consider to be the cardinal sin of boss fights in gaming. They give you an incredibly challenging boss with limited resources that, once dead, you guessed it....turns into something else and surprise...phase 2. Now you have no health, you've burned your resources and hes even harder than phase 1. Can we collectively agree to stop doing this in video games? Im so !@#$ing done with it. Just give me the boss and let me move on. Phase 1, phase 2, phase 3, 'bonus boss' is just straight cancer.- Lastly, I gotta echo what others have said and say that the final chapter of the game dragged on WAY past what was enjoyable. It was a brutal, painful, monotonous slog. On top of this, I clocked in at about 25 hours to complete this. I would say that act 10 alone was about 6 or 7 of those hours. They basically wrap up the story, ship you off to boss island, build you up for the 'Ok this is it!' moment. And that moment doesnt come until about 7 hours later, and that was playing quickly. And JUST WHEN YOU THINK ITS OVER...SURPRISE...IT ISNT. (I did enjoy the story element of this but I did not appreciate being dragged along for this seemingly endless ending). Its like that movie thats 3 hours long but could easily have been 90 minutes and you just get exhausted and want to leave the theater half way through. The game, up until this point, was fantastic, gorgeous and flowed beautifully across the different zones. Then it all came to an abrupt halt that absolutely sucked my energy out to keep going, it truly was a marathon I did not want to finish (but did).Looking forward to our, ahem, red-heeled heroine next, Neowiz. Nice job.

_childDocuments_.review: Combines everything I like about Bloodborne and everything I like about Sekiro and wraps it up into one neat package. I also feel a little bit of Resident Evil in there too. I was anticipating it to feel like a cheap knockoff at some points, but they even nailed the horrible "Poison Swamp x Dingy Wooden Scaffolding" area in every FromSoft game since Demon's Souls. While the first 3/4ths of the game are really enjoyable, my enjoyment takes a total nose-dive in the last few hours. Some annoying and generally disappointing bosses at the tail end of the game is what makes classics like the original Dark Souls not so fun to revisit, but none of them are truly egregious, save for one. Not too long, and not too difficult either. If you're itching for more From Software but you've played it all, I'd look here first. No masterpiece, but it's damn close, and sets a high bar for other "souls-likes" in the future. Solid 8.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: Holy moly I loved this game.  I got turned on to Lies of P from a video by Joseph Anderson and decided from that critique that this game was worth a try. And NEOWIZ decided an exemplary combat system was not enough- Lies of P story is nothing to ignore either.  Originally I thought "dark Pinocchio, really?" but holy dang I LOVE IT.  Some characters are hit and miss with people, but overall I cared about these characters and I needed to see what happened to them... and the treat is that finding out what happens, see more of the game world, is all executed through that excellent combat system.Have you enjoyed From Software's recent games?  Then this is an easy recommendation for an experience you are probably going to thoroughly enjoy!  Heck, even if you're new to this style of game, I still recommend it as a fun and challenging game on its own right.The best part?  They announced a sequel and a DLC expansion! _childDocuments_.review: Bloodborne Aesthetics, Sekiro Combat. You've probably heard this a lot about the game. Well, it's true. Maybe I've gotten better at parry mechanics, maybe the games have a deeper difference I'm unaware of, but it certainly isn't because Lies is "easier". Those looking for a challenge have found a good game.The pure graphics are passable, the art direction is excellent and extends upon what made Bloodborne great without simply copying it. _childDocuments_.review: Lies of P is my first souls-like and it has awoken something in my brain. It's that feeling you get when you discover a new genre and you just want more. I rarely replay games just after seeing the credits, but I immediately booted up NG+ as I was dying for more boss fights.My favorite aspect of this game is the guard system. The sound you get from getting a perfect guard is immaculate and left me wanting more blocks even if it made me play worse. Combining it with the stagger system creates an engaging system where I played passively getting perfect blocks and was rewarded with great damage. All of the bosses felt great utilizing this strategy, except for  as the black sheep in otherwise fantastic boss move set and design.If you're scared of souls-likes because everyone on the internet raves about how hard these games are, I urge you to just try one and see if you like it. I was scared for a while until I found this game on gamepass and after an hour was sold on the combat. It was frustrating a few times spending four hours on a single boss but that only made victory sweeter when I conquered him. Excited to play more of the genre and thank you Round 8 Studio for making this remarkable game!

_childDocuments_.review: A really good game overall being hardcarried by Fromsoft's previous work.This game was from the core a soulslike game. You have the Rally and Dash system from BB, the deflect system from Sekiro, and everything else from ds and er. This makes the gameplay absolutely amazing, with deflects being very satisfying to pull off, and just a combination of Sekiro and Dark Souls. However, there is just no real quirk to this game why don't I just play some From games?Every single area feels really inspired by From, down to the poison swamps and oneshotting status enemies. What sets LOP areas apart are its minibosses, which are much more reacurring then from's "minibosses" (ex silver knights at the start of ds1). However, personally I felt a huge lategame decline in area quality.Bosses:I'm gonna break down what makes bosses good for meMemorability- Gale shoots a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ machine gun while jumping in the air swinging with his greatsword and cape releasing dark souls, Melenia's Waterfowl Dance/Big Flower Moveset- how telegraphed, fun to fight.For LOP bosses, i just didnt find most of them fun to fight, and the only memorable bosses are nameless puppet and Laxasia. However, this game overuses delays on attacks, so a charged attack can take 3 sec to charge, which honestly is just not very fun to fight against and also slows the fight down. There are also some random instant attacks that do half of your health bar like wtf its like dancer for every single boss (dancer was a good boss because her gig was that she had weird timings, and other bosses doesnt). The parry window is also to tight so this + weird timings + red attacks = painful bossesMusic is amazing, don't have much to sayGraphically it is one of the most stable games I've played. It has its own Pinocchio puppety Art style. However the areas are not very distict. I can name a total of like 3 different areas from this game (alchemist place, really annoying Disruption Krat, Opera House), but can name everything from ER and DS3 (Cathedral of the deep, Ringed City, Raya Lucaria, Faram Azula)I've been pretty harsh on this game but I really like it. I think it surpasses many AAA games like Starfield and has huge potential. However it just doesnt have a distinct identity from From games. For ex. Hollow Knight is DS but 2D, etc. Amazing game for the 2nd game of a game studio.8/10

_childDocuments_.review: is the best description and praise I can give to this game. Finally somebody who actually understand what a souls game is, most souls-like only get one or two things right and completely missing on other aspects. I can't believe this is their first attempt at making a souls-like. It's one of the best game I've ever played not just in term of Souls-like, it's a very well made game and probably harder than most without needing to use cheap trick like Melania's Waterfolw dance to make the game "hard".The game is truly awesome in every aspect. It runs well on my low-end PC without needing DLSS, looks great without raytracing, art direction is peak design, phenomenal soundtrack, great sound design, a story that is easy to follow, good combat, top notch enemy and boss designs, enemy placements and traps are done just right with enough gotcha moments and never being swarmed, a unique weapon system that I can't believe no game has ever done it, amazing level designs despite being quite linear with some paths lead to dead end or loop back to a stargaze (bonfire) or a shortcut.As for replayability, I don't feel like making new save file to try different builds and I made like 15 characters for Elden Ring and still have more builds try before the DLC even come out, going to NG+ make more sense since you unlock more P-organ phases in NG+ and NG++, phase 7 and is the final phase has the most important upgrade that will make the same much easier.Boss designs in this game is peak, there's only one fight in this game where I feel the boss moveset is completely BS. There are 2 gank fights in this game and both are pretty good, bosses don't attacks at the same time, the pacing is really nice, you have breathing room for healing and attacks.Puppet bosses are the best fights in the game, their attacks are well telegraphed, no BS attacks, easy to learn timing, it's a shame there are only 4 of them. As for why I don't like carcasses bosses, read the rants.Human mini bosses are just alright, you can just circling around most of them and backstab, any weapons can stagger them easily as long as they are not in attack animation because then they'll have hyperarmor.I'm gonna be honest, the combat didn't really click with me until  fight in NG+, before that I didn't feel like I've earned the win. I used Motivity build majority of the time, big blade with medium-large handle, high guard damage reduction, charge attack stagger build. I didn't really learn much about the combat the entire NG, mostly win by a crutch, no summon. Once you learnt that the game suddenly became way more fun, boss fights starting to become a dance. _childDocuments_.review: The game started off promising. Although it is extremely derivative of Fromsoft games (to a comical degree), I was having fun for the first few acts. The story is completely nonsensical but the aesthetic is cool and the first few bosses were great. I like how you can customize your weapon by mix-and-matching parts. As I progressed further into the game I started noticing some glaring problems that eventually led me to quit before finishing it.1. Boss health pools are absurdly large. Every mid-late game fight felt like soloing an MMO Raid Boss with 2 phases. I had a fully upgraded weapon and even if I used a summon to tank and just wailed on the boss freely I was doing pathetically low damage.2. The perfect parry mechanic is horrendously designed. The window for a successful parry is extremely small compared to Sekiro, but at the same time the reward is much lower. Executing a successful chain of parries usually just means you get to hit them with 1 or 2 attacks after, dealing 1/500th of their HP. There is a posture system, but breaking their posture just puts them into a "vulnerable" state, where you are given a very brief window to land a fully charged attack, which is frequently impossible due to the enemy running away or beginning an attack you must dodge. If you manage to do all that your reward is 1 backstab. Amazing. Despite all this, the bosses are designed so you are required to parry them many times to win.3. Big slow weapons are completely unviable. Your character has no poise and a slight breeze will interrupt his animations. Enemies also attack quickly and in rapid succession so finding a window to swing is close to impossible.4. Pointless time waste. All the upgrade vendors are like a 45 second walk away from each other for some reason. You have to return to the hub town to level rather than being able to do it at the bonfire. Excessive runbacks to bosses. There is a time-gated currency in the game that you only get 1 of every 10 minutes and the timer does not work while the game is closed.5. All the prosthetic arms felt pretty much useless. The shield one for example does an explosion when you block with it. It has a pretty hefty cooldown and was doing about 1/4 the damage of my light attack. 6. Obnoxious level designs reminiscent of Dark Souls 2. Stuff like walking on rafters while ranged enemies shoot at you and if you get hit once you fall off and die.

With all this in mind, I still highly recommend the game, as the atmosphere enough is steller

_childDocuments_.review: Lies of P is by far the best souls like game to date, grab it on sale no debate because it's worth the full price.This hybrid of Sekiro / Bloodborne is executed flawlessly, honestly feels as if Miyazki was in the room with NEOWIZ telling the story of Pinocchio. The devs stepped out into the souls genre and it was the greatest thing they've ever done. Do yourself a favor and just look at their previous releases and be amazed at the gem they have blessed us with. NEOWIZ thank you again for taking the leap into this genre. The story of Pinocchio in a beautiful elegant setting was very refreshing to this genre but still brought the dark grunge that makes a souls game. The customization and character designs are incredible, the story is Pinocchio's Adventure and offers choices in main quests and side ones too which gives you the ability to be a puppet playing with mortality. You are Pinocchio after all.The bosses and enemies provide a challenge that souls vets will find satisfying and extremely challenging. The games replay-ability is 10/10 and allows for some build freedom as well. There are 40 common weapons that can be altered through this blade - hilt system allowing you to create a whole new weapon with new move set and stats. Lies of P included the Legion arm which is a great variation of the Shinobi arm from Sekiro, you also receive a Grinder to sharpen your weapons throughout battle and doubles as a enchanter. There's a lot more but you'll figure it out.TLDR: Ultimately the game is worth the full cost and is the best souls like game to date with all the QOL improvements we wish we could add to our favorite Fromsoft game.CAN NOT WAIT FOR THE DLC!

_childDocuments_.review: After playing this game extensively I can finally write a well thought out and composed review of this souls-like title. I will split my review into sections that I find will highlight some of my favorite parts of the game and some things that others may find aggravating. Story Length: 7/10 The reason I have this one lower is because is because my first run through of the game took 27.3 hours to get through and my last run took me little under 2 hours. The reason I have the story length lower is due to the fact that the game is as extensive as one wants it to be and as explorable but you have to have the souls instinct to know to go out of your way. However the companion guide in-game makes finding these quests and completing them much easier should you choose to turn it on. Story Writing: 10/10 It's very rare for me to give a game a 10/10 story, the last time I did so was for Dark Souls 2 and Bloodborne. This games character story lines, overarching villain and musical composition story telling really suck you in from the get go. Through the letters you find, the heart breaking tale of Sophia and the other clues and things you pick up on from the world around you its hard not to really get immersed in the city of Krat and to keep slashing your way toward answers to the worlds mysteries and the secrets of Ergo. Musical Score: 10/10 To say that the musical score for this game is anything short of a masterpiece would to put it at a dis-service. The use of records in game to tell the story of a sad loss or the boss score line for the swamp monster. This game spent most its budget making sure that it's music is just as immersive and telling as every other aspect of the story. To not listen to the records, to not listen to the slight fluctuations of a cord that may give way to a certain attack pattern you'd be cutting off a whole extra sense through the soundtrack this game so wonderfully provides. Game Mechanics: 8/10Overall if you are a dark souls 2 lover and Bloodborne fan this game will immediately tickle your fancy. The variety of combat options through the use of weapon assembly (mix matching handles and tips of a variety of weaponry) and the Legion Arms, This game adds a new spin with its combat that I found as a pleasant surprise introducing new blocking mechanics and movement abilities I was not privy and spoiled to in other Souls titles from FromSoftware. Overall you can see the games influence and inspiration there is no doubting that, But I think that it has enough combat mechanics they either tweaked or added to make itself a unique standalone/definitive experience anyone could enjoy. That's that! Hopefully you find this to be helpful and remember everyone... The secret to Ergo is a key found within!

_childDocuments_.review: Lies of P might be the only game I know of that has the balls to directly compare itself to a Fromsoft game and actually pull it off to deliver similar quality. It is without a doubt one of the most remarkable games released last year.To me the soulsbornes are very much a circus ride and have always been; you don't really go in expecting a particularly well designed game. You expect the same, dated formula with new gimmicks and new cinematic encounters. Out of all games in the series the main driving force for me has always been just what a grand adventure they all convey - even if the notorious difficulty the game achieves feels cheap and unearned. Lies of P does not innovate much; if anything it takes a slight permutation of their favorite entries. As such it is not a game I consider anywhere near a masterpiece like some people do: reading arbitrary animation frames to then "parry" during the few active frames is a crude, ill-defined and, in my personal opinion, thoroughly unrewarding experience.Those that do see the appeal in it will enjoy Lies of P. Parrying allows players to take some control of the pace even when hopelessly overwhelmed; allowing you to break the enemy's stance for a powerful follow up or, in specific situations, even break their weapon to reduce their damage output (which is a very strange reward considering this will usually be the reward for reading an opponent perfectly - implying you aren't getting hit to begin with).Quality control is extraordinary. I would not say it can tip any recent Fromsoft game in terms of scale, but despite its comparatively limited scope I was thoroughly impressed from start to end. Beautiful animation work. Beautiful environmental design. A passable story (mostly held back by the generic characters) and great sound design across the board. Lies of P is quite special, even if it doesn't feel like it most of the time.

_childDocuments_.review: Lies of P is a fun challenge. That last word is important: If you don't enjoy a challenge - and especially if you're not a fan of getting comfortable with some wonky mechanics and overlong levels - you will likely not have the fun the developers intended here.Lies of P gets a lot right. Art design? Awe striking. Story? Pulls right in (with a lot of obvious and not-so-obvious references to the original Pinocchio story). Sound design? There's an opera house level that was made for headphones.Lies of P also gets a lot ... OK. Not great, but certainly not bad. Right down the middle. Level design in Lies of P is highly linear, which would be fine except that there are stretches, especially near the end, where you're asked to navigate long paths of extremely finicky terrain with the worst one-shot enemies planted right before the next checkpoint. Basically, the only way through is straight through: there are no rewards or opportunities for figuring another way out of boss-rush hallways. There's also the issue of mechanics. I LOVE the weapon crafting aspect of Lies of P, which far outstrips the weapon customization of even recent Souls games like Elden Ring. I slapped a wrench head on an electric baton the first chance I got. This game celebrates all that damage you want to inflict. But all that damage coming AT you can only be parried in a mechanic that has the same sluggishness in comparison to a Dark Souls that Super Mario's jump feels after you've played a platformer as tight as Super Meat Boy. There's no reason for defense timing to be this unforgiving.That said, these are not impossible mechanics to figure out. They're tough. I think in several cases they're unbalanced (which does not mean "are easy for speedrunners" - classic fallacy). But they can be overcome, and more importantly, for all enemies and bosses, there is a way to approach them that has enough challenge and generosity to feel "fair". For example, there's a four-on-one boss fight near the end that will feel like the developers dunking on you, but which I promise has a design that rewards attention and proper targeting.So like I said. Looking for a fun challenge? You'll get it and more in Lies of P.

_childDocuments_.review: Version:- 1.1.2.0Positives:- The game is well-optimized and I did not experience performance issues or frame-time problems during my 25-odd hours.- Shader pre-compilation on game launch.- Short loading times between warps.- The game's setting is intruiging and there are several sidequests with recurring characters worth doing.- Interesting and unique story.- Exploration and being inquisitive is usually being rewarded, thus making even dead ends worthwile.- Various small quality of life features like stamina automatically refilling when passing through a fog gate or quest indicators on the quick-travel list are highly appreciated.- Decent amount of map variety with enough unique locales to keep the game fresh throughout.- Main hub vendors inventories can be expanded.- The game is beautifully scored, the music heightens every moment.- The changing weather is a really nice visual touch.- Interesting roster of bosses, including (but not limited to): Beast-like robots, gank squads, Mr. X, cut content from Nier Automata, Nightmare on Sesame Street, Konrad the Traitor, and much more!- Mr. Venigni's dialogue is awesome from beginning to end.Negatives:- The story is being pushed onto you with the subtlety of a sledgehammer.- No option to switch between Xbox and Playstation button prompts for us Steam Input users.- The roll feels bad and off, because it is artifically gimped for the game's skill tree. Until you pump skill points into the respective perks, you are effectively being punished Dark Souls II-style just for the audacity of playing the game.- Enemy chain attacks - even when blocked [normally] - chip off a considerable amount of health.- There is no telegraph as to how many of these chain attacks are being chained together, it is random. Fuoco spinning five times in a row isn't challenging - it is just annoying.- The timing of certain enemy attacks feels "off", making it incredibly hard to judge when to time blocks. Not sure if this is an animation issue or whatnot.- The player has no poise, while enemies seemingly do. This makes trying to use heavy attacks for staggering enemies or trying to seize the stagger state a complete chore because you will be interrupted during these precious few seconds.- Player movement speed feels anemic compared to the enemies.- Enemies attack faster than the player can recover. Again, this is something that can partially be mitigated through the skill tree later on, but why is this an issue to begin with?- Perfect guard is just a split second, the window to execute is way too small.- Backstabbing is unreliable (does not work despite prompt or does work despite having no prompt) and seemingly vanishes completely in the later half of the game.- Game suffers from having Bleak Faith's long ladder fetish.Final thoughts:If only Neowiz hadn't tried to innovate on Bloodborne's combat system by introducing some of Sekiro's ideas into the game, we would've ended up with a good Soulsborne game. What we are being left with instead is an overtuned game that was made artifically harder by gimping the player and favouring the enemies to force the use of blocks over dodges and strongarms you into its own flavour of combat flow. Unfortunately, this isn't what I wanted from the game and therefore it is not enjoyable for me.So note: If you want Bloodborne-like combat, this ain't it - despite appearances suggesting otherwise.

_childDocuments_.review: I just want to give some appreciation to some of the subtler aspects of the game design. Everyone's saying they know exactly what makes a soulslike good, but what does that actually For starters, the performance is smooth. I've experienced no stutters or framerate issues, something that can easily make a soulslike feel horrendous to play. Animations feel fluid, and telegraph attacks well while still demanding a level of memorization, and the hitboxes feel accurate and representative of the attacks they're attached to. The fundamentals are 100% there.Lies of P takes a really creative approach in addressing many of the criticisms people have had with the various fromsoft titles, adapting them instead of simply removing them. Case in point, the poison swamp. A classic in the souslike, something we've all gotten used to but hate nonetheless. Lies of P addresses this by never outright forcing you to get poisoned. This is achieved by ensuring there is always an island or river embankment within the player's reach, forcing them to approach the situation swiftly but cautiously, ensuring no enemies are in the way. It rewards both patience and aggression when the times are right, something you'll come to find is a recurring theme. In addition, a decent portion of the poison areas are actually just simply drained at the end of the level by dropping a giant torch on them, burning all the poison away. It's an incredibly satisfying reward for reaching the end that allows you to reapproach the area with more free exploration, with things often hidden beneath the poison.In a less-subtle tweak, we have the weapon system. In Lies, weapons come in two pieces, the blade and handle. The handle determines the scaling and basic moveset of the weapon, with the blade determining damage output, damage type, and the weight class of the weapon. You can put a greatsword blade on a curved sword handle to make a heavy curved sword. You can put that same greatsword blade on a spear handle to make an incredibly long-ranged greatspear. You can put an elemental blade on a dex-scaling handle, simply bypassing the special stat requirement you often see. In addition, both pieces contribute their own special move, one that expends a special bar seen beneath your stamina, known at fable. The blade is often a strong attack or buff, with the handle often contributing a defense buff or special parry. The system doesn't just encourage experimentation, it facilitates it. If you want to try a new blade, just put it on your handle. If you want to try a handle with different scaling, there's a training area in the game's hub area that'll let you test its moveset and decide on a respec. It's so much fun, there's no other way to put it. You're no longer just building for a single weapon or loadout, you're building for a playstyle.I feel like i could go on and on about stuff like this, but at that point I'd just be explaining the whole game and not much more. I didn't even touch on boss design since I feel like they're all great and need to just be experienced. The positives of this game are self-explanatory and evident from the start, and that's the best part of it all. All in all, while I don't feel like Lies manages to hit some of the explosive highs of the fromsoft games, never once did I ever feel like something in the game was mediocre or bad. There is no Bed of Chaos or Capra Demon, no Curse-Rotted Greatwood or Farron Keep-type area. Everything this game has to offer is at least good, and that's an incredible achievement.

_childDocuments_.review: I just finished my first playthrough. It's so good. It's everything you want it to be. It feels extremely tight and refined, and truly feels like a true to form souls-like. Honestly, probably better than bloodborne, and I put hundreds of hours into that. It's also ******* HARD. As a seasoned vet of the genre I can corroborate everyone else's feelings. The combat feels akin to Sekiro x Bloodborne in many ways - you will find quite a few bosses that require long strings of quick attacks to be perfectly parried. The weapon variety is... it's endless. There are dozens (I found 37 on my first playthrough) of extremely interesting and unique weapons, ALL OF WHICH (barring boss soul weapons) can be disassembled and mix-n-matched into wild wacky combos. Want an ultra greatsword with a rapier moveset? Just put an ultra greatsword blade on a rapier handle. It's that easy. Want a giant ripper-saw? Well you can give it a spear or hammer moveset!The story is awesome and intriguing. The story unfolds at a nice pace for a souls game, and has few but crucial plot twists. The world is alive, and the environmental storytelling that comes hand-in-hand with the genre was evident throughout the varied locales. One of my first impressions was that they took all of the mechanics that Fromsoft learned over 10 years of souls games and said "we want that". There is one exception... boss soul upgrade mats are capped per run. ALL OF 'EM, not just +5 mats. I just got the final boss weapon and can't upgrade it at all because I used my mats on earlier ones. Don't be like me and upgrade all of your boss weapons to +2 on a whim... A slight oversight that could easily be fixed later on.Almost forgot this, but it's important in 2023's climate. The PC performance is great. No need to worry about that here. I have an RTX3070 playing on 4K medium, and running at 144fps. RARELY it drops to 120, but that's the worst it gets. Did have to restart after a weird glitch locked me at 40, but wcyd.This is one of the good ones!

They understand  Souls games are fun beyond the surface level, and it shows here. is honestly a pretty even mix between Souls, Bloodborne and Sekiro. This game borrows certain elements from each, but combines and remixes them in a way that feels fresh. I was never bored, even after two runs back to back. are all S-Tier. No complaints. However, some of these bosses are . The difficulty of the bosses in this game spikes dramatically at around the halfway mark and doesn't really let up until the end. Across FromSoft's catalogue, if we're talking mainline bosses only (so, not Malenia), this is the game that gave me the most trouble - There were a few bosses that humbled me for literal hours, which was an honour previously only reserved for Sekiro's final boss (again, mainline only).Most Souls veterans will embrace this and love the game all the more for it, but genre tourists are in for a bumpy ride.While it's pretty linear, the  is excellent, wrapping on itself over and over with shortcuts. _childDocuments_.review: I'm an extremely casual souls-like player. This was only my 3rd souls-like after Remnant 2 and Elden Ring, so this review is from the perspective of someone who is definitely not a souls veteran. This was easily the hardest game I've ever played. It is significantly harder than Elden Ring. But it's also an amazing game. This studio really knocked it out of the park with their first souls-like attempt.The game isn't perfect. The devs made some decisions that I disagree with. Probably the biggest being I don't think you should be able to get staggered when making a successful perfect guard. It's ridiculous this happens during boss fights and it feels like you are being punished for doing a successful and precise combat move. There is also no poise for you in this game. I don't think the lack of poise totally ruins heavy weapons, as some people have said, but it definitely makes them useless in fights with more aggressive bosses. That being said you can always put a heavy weapon blade on a handle that has a faster move set.This game has so much good to talk about. The graphics and art direction are reeaaalllly good. The game looked great on my ultrawide OLED with HDR enabled. The story of this game is very cool. It takes the naive morale of the original Pinocchio story of lying makes you bad and has consequences and reverses it to illustrate how to lie is to be human. Nearly all of the lying in the game is humane in the sense you are protecting people from truths that would cause them pain. So lying is a way to be a better person and makes you more human.The combat and weapon mechanics in this game are fantastic. experimenting with building your own weapons is a really cool addition that sets this game apart from other souls-likes. I also love how you can change the scaling of your weapon handles so you can mostly use the weapon you want to, even if it doesn't initially match your build. Combat feels good and while perfect guarding is difficult at first, once it clicks it feels really good.The bosses are insane in this game. They are all very cool and well animated. I think the hit boxes could maybe use a little tweaking, but they aren't terrible. The bosses, unsurprisingly, are extremely hard. The game does give you some help with a npc summons in some fights and you can use throwables to make your life easier, but you don't want to lean on these too much. The final, and hardest, boss in the game has no summons and attacks too fast for throwables to be useful, so you're better off just fighting bosses without these and getting good at perfect guarding their telegraphed attacks, although in this game I think you need to do what ever you need to to get through the bosses.Elden Ring is still my favorite souls game, but this one definitely felt more gratifying to beat. A cut scene at the end of the credits suggest we might be getting some sort of sequel from this studio. I sure hope that's the case, because I can't wait to see what they come up with next.

_childDocuments_.review: This game captures the essence of what a Dark Souls game for casuals should be like. The difficulty as a main focus point is not terribly nuanced, but let's talk about why that's even as a con, I would still consider that a pro.: Lies of P offers something that we saw a little bit of beginning in Elden Ring, and I'd really like to see developers expand on with future souls like games: weapon and tool combinations. Lies of P has a robust weapon combination system that drastically changes the way your skills affect your weapons. If this weren't enough, you can also imbue them with specific abilities, and you can then further customize those with grindstones. They took it even one step further by letting you do the same thing with your gauntlet, which is a bit like the sekiro tools with more flexibility in their use. : The music sort of lurks in the background, and it is definitely Sakuraba quality, if not better due to a classical element that lurks within it. The music hangs out in the background, almost as a pleasant white noise until the moment when it needs to crescendo, and oh boy does it do that well. I think the addition of the record player system also adds a unique element- restoring "humanity" is done through a mechanic focused on specifically music.: The combat is smooth and intuitive. While not as complex or quick as games like Sekiro, the combat definitely feels fun and enjoyable. The weight of weapons feels immaculate overall, until you run up against the big bad bosses who just sort of shrug it off because well- an ant won't make a bird stagger often. The weapon skills are all definitely unique and combo really well with the basic attack combos.: I thought I had an idea of what I was getting into: Pinocchio, robots overrunning the city, chasing after a wish or something. Let me tell you, the name of the game only scratches the surface. The story is so much deeper and so much more well told than I anticipated. I do feel that the level of lore is somewhat shallow, but overall the storytelling and the quality of existing lore is definitely a solid 9/10.: I think if I had to have one complaint about this game is it feels a bit rushed/short. The zones immerse you just in time for the boss room and the end of the zone. I think that with a bit more content, this game would definitely feel as expansive as a True Dark Souls game.

_childDocuments_.review: I've beaten all the Darksouls trilogy all dlc and all bosses, Bloodborne and all DLC, all endings in Sekiro, and every boss in Elden Ring and I slammed my head against the King of Puppets for two days and cant get past the 50% mark on the second phase. This game is beautiful and the music and sound design are awesome but I can't recommend this game even to a souls veteran without the warning that this game is balls to the wall difficult. It almost felt like a joke it was so hard until I didn't have the patience to keep going. This game is flawed in an infuriating way. All enemies seem to have purposefully been given a jerky random move-set that makes it very hard to naturally predict the parry timing. And I see the 'They're crazy puppets of course they move like that!' but it doesn't sway me because some puppets have reasonable arcs to their swings and others will jump in the air then float for half a second to through off your timing. It requires parrying entire combos to get a critical off that barely does more damage than a charged R2. You can't parry out of attacks to make the combat feel fluid and the parry timing is different depending on the weapon so changing your weapon results in having to relearn the timing of the parry on whatever boss you're stuck on. Accidentally hitting the use item button when you're out of items results in the puppet staring at his hand for a full three seconds resulting in getting hit. The ability to dodge from a grounded state is locked behind the P-organ system. The dodge is basically useless against the bosses because they follow up in the window when you're vulnerable. Stat reallocation is gate kept until 65% through the game so if you start with a motivity build and want to try a technique or advance build to see if that helps against the current roadblock you're out of luck until you get to that point. This game is just an exhausting trial of learning random patterns to parry just to get 10% damage in on the first phase of yet another two phase boss battle. I have limited free time and I cant spend it frustrated all day because after an hour of okay souls-like gameplay I have another 30 attempt boss to struggle against.

_childDocuments_.review: Great setting and great combat/gameplay along with some great concepts like being able to  switch weapon parts freely. So be ready to have to run a while to get back to bosses. In general it can be sumed up as ds1 meets sekiro.

_childDocuments_.review: A perfect soulslike. Genuinely on par with Fromsoft soulslikes, this game has some of the best bosses in any game I have ever played. The game balances dodging and parrying (called perfect guard in this game) extremely well and switching between both in combat feels very rewarding. The parry system is somewhat akin to that of Sekiro, but unlike Sekiro you are encouraged to mix parrying and dodging a lot and weave between them, with some bosses being easy parry targets and others being much easier to dodge roll - but with no boss feeling like you are better off only parrying or dodging.For me the (first) playthrough took 35 hours, which I think is perfect for a game like this, provided it can stay interesting - which Lies of P very much could!Cannot recommend this game enough.

_childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately, I think this game is a disappointing slog. I am definitely a souls fan and I think I'm fairly good at them, but this game just feels frustrating most of the time. It feels like it's so close to being great but every aspect just falls very slightly short of the finish line. There is fun to be found but it always comes with a lot of downsides. No part I have experienced yet hasn't annoyed me at least a little bit. A few thoughts on the game:-The game feels overstuffed with needless mechanics instead of fleshing out just a select few.-The boss design is just straight up terrible for the most part. Most bosses in the first half are just easy and forgettable while pretty much every boss in the second half is extremely flawed with half of each fight being a good boss and the other half being annoying or straight up awful. One boss, which is a rematch of what was already the worst boss in the game, might genuinely be the worst boss I’ve ever had the misfortune of facing. Don't get me started on how ever fight in the later end is an extreme test of endurance with WAY too many bosses having a second phase that just ruins them. I would have really enjoyed the king of puppets second phase if it wasn't attached to such a terrible first phase. Similarly with Laxasia, the second phase is just obnoxious and unnecessary. None of the duel health bar fights even build upon the last phases moveset, opting for a brand new one. That's all fine in moderation but this game takes it to the extreme.-The game also is trying way too hard to be like a fromsoft game, cobbling so much from those games together(including their flaws like the terrible jumping controls), creating just a blob of past ideas with a new coat of paint. It doesn’t try enough to be its own unique thing. It also tries way too hard to be difficult. I’m fairly good at souls games but this game is just frustrating in its arbitrary difficulty. It feels like it just tries its hardest to be as difficult as it can just so people can compare it to Fromsoft. It prioritizes boss difficulty over enjoyability and engagement, making me dread every boss encounter because I know it’ll just be annoying.I haven’t fully finished the game yet with about two bosses left but I don’t think I will. It’s just become a chore that I’m having 0 fun with which is severely disappointing. The studio shows promise though so I hope they learn from the mistakes they made here and create something great some day.
