_childDocuments_.review: The gameplay itself is easy--- using your mouse to color in paintings and do sketches with very little mechanical precision required, and finding obvious clues around the apartment. It's meant to accompany the story and the charming, leisurely feel of a day in the life of an artist. You would especially resonate with it if your idea of a good time is waking up with no plans for the day except to indulge in a creative pursuit while sipping the simple pleasures of life, all in a cozy, rustic apartment with a big window. However, if you'd like a little bit more action then you'd probably prefer this game less. Storywise, there's no denying it's a romantic boy-meets-girl cliche, ostensibly drawn from similar stories in the Studio Ghibli movies that the creators cite as their primary inspiration. You can even say it has some similarities to 5cm Per Second. And yet, I found myself liking this execution of the cliche a lot more than the sources of inspiration, which I'm lukewarm about. Perhaps it's the fact that the video game medium naturally allows the player to be more directly immersed in the lives of the lovers, especially since the game is told from a first person POV. In addition, I think the art theme greatly enhanced the story in several ways. First, the more stylized paintings in the game compared to regular animation backgrounds allowed for a more poignant expression of the character's experiences. Secondly, it enhanced the romance by having the characters connect through their shared love of art, as opposed to just nice girl meets nice guy. At least, I personally found it be more relatable. Third, without getting into spoilers, they used the art theme to great effect by demonstrating what a work can mean to an individual artist and the power of art to preserve and communicate a precious memory. It's a short game with moderately enjoyable gameplay, but it left me with a pleasant aftertaste that I can continue to savor long after I've played it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game; wow! Absolutely beautiful graphics with a wonderful storyline that tugs at your heartstrings and pulls you in if you're a sensitive, empathetic person like me. _childDocuments_.review: Behind the Frame: The Finest Scenery is a story rich puzzle game. where you'll be involved in solving puzzles to continue the story. usually involving adding something that's missing to a painting on the wall. There are also puzzles involving using clues to press specific buttons on an item.In Behind the Frame the player takes the role of a young woman who spends her days painting by her window. Across the alley from her is and old man who is also a painter, as well as his rather chunky cat, and she greets him everyday but he never responds to her greetings. As she sits down to color her latest work, she realizes that she has lost her tubes of paint and must search her apartment in order to find them. What follows is a slightly fantastical journey through memory lane, and a peek into the woman's goals and aspirations.The game is simple and incredible short experience, however Behind the Frames makes up for its lack of length with its gorgeous art and animation. Pair that with relaxing in game sounds and a touching story it makes the game a memorable experience. Rating: 9/10

_childDocuments_.review: Keeping things wholesome, we have Behind the Frame: The Finest Scenery. This one’s a point and click adventure with a strong focus on narrative, and seems heavily inspired by Studio Ghibli and the work of Myazaki, with its gorgeous hand-drawn artstyle.  Developed by Akupara Games, Behind the Frame tells the tale from the perspective of a painter working on her final piece of art for her new exhibition. Events primarily take place in the artisit’s apartment. The walls are adorned with paintings of two lovers, and these become central to the narrative – which is fragmentary, and not always chronological, making the story a puzzle in itself.  To complete your masterpiece, you need a full palette of colours, and only yellow is available at the start. As you work through the chapters and solve puzzles, more colours become available.  Gameplay involves typical point and click mechanics, with the player moving a cursor around the apartment investigating objects and searching for clues. Many of the puzzles include adding specific colours to sections of paintings based on notes you’ve made in your journal. It won’t take long to complete Behind the Frame; it’s another game that can be completed in a single sitting. But it is one of the most memorable games I’ve played this year, with the story building to a wonderful denouement, and reveal at the end.  It’s an indie work of art, about art, and one that is an experience not to be missed.

_childDocuments_.review: Art sits alone in its creative outpouring of expression.  Mediums from centuries past tell tales to this day of men and women lost to the passage of time.  Many mediums can bring that sense of life to not only the eyes of society, but their ears and hearts as well.  Poetry, music, film, drawings, paintings: all subject themselves to the emotions of the creator, to express feelings felt within in the hopes the few who view it can share those same emotions whether in person or across the world.For this aspiring artist, she guides her emotions through paint and canvas.  Scattered pieces of personal memories to award winning details hold steady across the walls of her studio apartment.  For now, colors of green and yellow and red comfort each other closely as they reveal the scenery of a vivid town’s summer day.  Often taking a break for coffee and toast, she’ll pique her curiosity for her older neighbor, an artist himself, and his like-age cat.  Taking refuge in her notebook and sketches of a life she’s curiously watched over, she reminisces about the past, the mysteries of the present next door, and the curiosity of her future as the emptiness of her canvas becomes enveloped with each selected color.Gently mixing together Point & Click with Hidden Object and Puzzle-Mystery combines the foundation for Behind the Frame: The Finest Scenery.  Detailing small tasks like making breakfast and typing out requests for inclusions to art exhibits carry over to putting final touches on past paintings to unlock various memories that have since been forgotten.  With each painting finished and memory re-awakened, more paints become available to finish her current project alongside little happenings to fill the days.While her current painting leans more towards impressionism, Behind the Frame’s art direction plants itself firmly in the magical.  Rivaling some AAA animated titles of recent years, scenery is packed with love and care as the studio apartment is lifelike yet cluttered, messy yet organized: where someone with fleeting ideas and sky high fixations would most certainly settle.  Cutscenes are short but sweet, each one striking and vivid in its color design and direction and just begs for a short film to be made alongside this game because, I mean.  Wow.  I can’t say enough about it.The musical score pulls its weight just as well.  Cassette tapes of soft jazz and tight upbeat piano fill the room with delight and creativity, while the somber bass tones amidst rainstorms and fuller orchestral pieces imbue each emotional checkpoint with a kind of grace and comfort that really shows the developers took every angle to pack as much volume into each scene.There’s not much that hasn’t been meticulously fine tuned and crafted masterfully to draw a perfect circle around this 75 minute experience.  The puzzles are not easy enough to insult the player, but intriguing enough to elicit a pleasant response to completing.  While the game may feel short, Behind the Frame doesn’t waste any time nor does it overstay its welcome.  The only issue I had was the camera pans in the room in a way that really triggered a bit of motion sickness that caused me to take a break about 45 minutes in, but this could be solely on me and shouldn’t deter anyone from trying the game.With the past year or two being a somber reminder of how fragile the world can be, it begs the mind to recollect, reflect, and rejoice the memories of good times that were had and the better times that could lay ahead.  Behind the Frame takes these emotions and paints a commandingly emotional yet poignantly human tale of what was, what now is, and what we do with what could be.

_childDocuments_.review: "Behind The Frame'' is a story of two lives. Two human beings so near yet so far away...a love born from coincidence, immortalised in memory and in art forever. During my first play-through I was initially confused: it started as a cosy art story, then it started hinting at a tragedy and the ending was somehow haunting at first. When the story resolves itself everything becomes clear and the only things I could feel were love, sorrow and gratitude.I think I should stop talking about the story now though, the game is really short but intense and any more writing could give away the feelings that the game wants to transmit at the end of the player's journey. Let's move to the technical aspect instead.Graphics are gorgeous, the game is an interactive anime with a great direction and such a great art style that for a moment I forgot I was playing entirely. Every character is well designed, places feel true and genuine and the choice of colours, camera angles and "acting" is simply spot on. This is one of the games which proves that art doesn't need realism to feel authentic and give an experience to its consumers.Music is simple, original, outstanding and really broke some tears in the end. I am a musical person, I play instruments and I always love exploring games music and even buy the soundtrack when I feel it; this game gave me excitement, worry, sadness, loss, healing, memories, happiness...all thanks to its music. It truly is a work of art, I would love to buy the vinyl as soon as I can, but at the moment it is only available from iam8bit-US, so it is a bit pricey to get plus the risk it gets damaged during shipping, I just hope some stock in Europe will be available again because it is that worth it.In conclusion, I opened my mind, ears and heart for two hours and I came back with a sad smile on my face, grateful to have experienced someone's love, someone's loss and someone's craft. I will always cherish this experience and it might be that is because I'm getting older but these little gems are really starting to leave a trace that I thought it was only possible with music and reading but I never thought it was possible to feel like that after a game. I just wanna say thank you to the devs, you just made my Christmas 2023 more special. <3

_childDocuments_.review: "Behind The Frame: The Finest Scenery" is a great point-and-click game, but very short game, and although it's a story-rich adventure, its ending is how you interpret it... It's not emotional by any means, but I'd say it's very wholesome.You take on the role of Amber, a painter, who at first seems to be absorbing inspiration from the old man living next door by peeking at him through a window. He is also a painter... The thing is, the more she does, the more she grows attached to the old man, and she can't shake the feeling that she knows him from somewhere. A few chapters in and Amber realises that she is just the MEMORY of the old man, that has become sentient in order for it to recount her story with Jack. Jack and Amber have been lovers, friends and best friends and the story depicts how some men act and react to certain things... Although Amber has moved on, and made Jack into this "penpal" after she had left for New York to pursue a career in painting, Jack, who is by far the BETTER painter, could not move on; Amber was his muse, his source of inspiration, and her leaving made him think that maybe he's not cut out to be a painter, and maybe his skills were not enoug (Talk about toxic femininity, right? lol). Anyways, dozens of years past and Amber hears of Jack's death, and honors him by opening a museum in his name where she showcased all the paintings he inspired her to do... Of course, she is married and has two kids, while he lived his entire life waiting for her occasional letters... I do not want to delve deeper into men's psychology but this game seems to have no problem proving that while some have the common sense to move on, others are super clingy and will live an entire imagined life with a partner they never had and never will have. Jack's paintings seem to build on that, painting him and amber in cafés, in landscapes... some of it did happen at some point, some of it was pure fiction. Even the memory of Amber seems to have forgotten Jack, but Jack, being the teenage 70 year old that he was before his death, seems to continue to live a fictional life, until his very last breath.Other than that, the game gets , what I loved most about it is the art... Whoever drew these sprites should probably get a salary raise lol

_childDocuments_.review: I went in this game totally blind. I just saw few screenshots of the game and instantly fell in love with the artstyle, so I think that is the thing I should talk about first.This games artstyle is heavily, and when I say that I mean HEAVILY inspired by the works of Studio Ghibli. I personally love the artstyle, as I've grown up with movies like Spirited Away, My Neighbor Totoro and Laputa. Those movies have been a big part of my childhood, and seeing their artstyle being adapted into a game is wonderful. The art during the gameplay is beautiful, and the art in the cutscenes feel like something straight from a Ghibli movie.I am not sure if there is multiple endings available, as of right now I've only played the game once. The gameplay is typical Point & Click adventure, with quite interesting gameplay mechanics, which I haven't at least seen in a game before. The gameplay mechanics are interesting, even though they sometimes guide the hand of the player a bit too much.The story is surprisingly rich, I love how the developers managed to put in such a deep and interesting story into a fairly short game (just about the length of a short film).Then, let's talk about the music, which is absolutely beautiful. The OST is such a nice cherry on top of a beautiful story and a beautiful visual presentation.This game is less of a game, and more of a movie, with beautiful visuals, beautiful music and a nice story. And I feel like thinking of Behind the Frame as a movie/cinematic experience, instead of viewing it as a game, is the right way to view it.Overall, a beautifully crafted, beautifully written story. Even though the game is fairly short, it's still easily worth the price tag.

_childDocuments_.review: The visuals are truly beautiful, but the lack of customization is disappointing. This experience feels more like a short movie than a game.As someone who enjoys art, sketching, and drawing, the way sketching is implemented in this game doesn't resonate with me. In the game, you simply drag the cursor across the screen, and a fully sketched version is automatically revealed where you have touched. However, in real-life sketching, you start by forming the general shape and then gradually add details. Initially, the game only provides yellow paint, followed by green paint. I wanted to mix yellow and green to create a different color, like lime green, but it's impossible to do so. Considering that paint is central to the story and the two main characters are painters, it's baffling that you can't even mix colors. Moreover, you're restricted from choosing colors in different areas when you paint , as you're forced to use the exact color dictated by the game.This lack of customization extends to other parts of the game as well. For instance, when making breakfast, I waited a long time for the egg to fry and earned an achievement for not liking over-easy eggs. However, even after waiting longer, the egg never overcooked. When I finally put toast and egg on the plate, it inexplicably turned into an egg and grilled cheese sandwich. I couldn’t add the egg between the toast slices to make a sandwich. It’s also frustrating you are always cooking the same dish.Although the art is stunning, the game lacks soul. You're forced to follow each step precisely, clicking for puzzle-solving and dragging the mouse for painting. Everything is pre-defined, leaving no room for creativity. I'll probably just watch the storyline play out through others, rather than waste my time playing it myself.Update after watching the entire gameplay: The storyline moved me to tears, and I was captivated by the breathtaking scenery, but I still believe there's significant room for improvement in this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Amber, an aspiring artist, is preparing her art piece for a gallery exhibition. Right across the street lives yet another artist, an old man with an old cat, and every morning she watches him working on his canvas. The daily routine of her life gets twisted and old memories becomes to resurface. The truth is hidden deep below the dried paint.I think I am slightly torn apart on this one, but gosh, I simply LOVE the visuals! It's like playing through some of  movies! The music is beautiful and creates a fitting atmosphere. I also liked the gameplay, you are not being rushed anywhere and can just enjoy your surroundings, but you are just a passive watcher and you can't influence a thing in the story (which is a little bit disappointing). Painting and sketching are done in a simple way, but it's fun. Puzzles are nice, varied and some even challenging.The story is bittersweet, with DLC's story being more bitter than sweet. If I understand it right, the game is inspired by the lives of two real artists… which sadly doesn't make the whole story any less sad (for me). is a relaxing and visually beautiful game. The message of the story missed its point with me, but that's just because I value and search for different things in my life... I have still enjoyed my time with it. Also, in one chapter I had the feeling I am playing  , but don't worry it doesn't turn so . ;)
_childDocuments_.name: Behind the Frame: The Finest Scenery

_childDocuments_.review: It's a fantastic game, a very deep and mature story inferred from the hints provided at every step of the game. There's enough time to sink in what each means with the puzzles to break up the pacing. Did this game win any awards the year it was released? I'm not sure, but I feel it definitely deserved one for the story-telling.Spoiler warning for those who haven't played the game below:I can't begin to explain how this game makes me feel.On one hand, you have Amber, brought up in a not-so-perfect family, seeing her role models find happiness only after parting ways. She becomes inspired by them, she takes after them and seeks her own happiness without the interruption of others, a desirable solitude that's seen too often how relationships sour. She sought to maximise her own pleasure, and lives as a free spirit, unbound and untethered to anything, and that's why even at her age she understood how to use a laptop while Jack still relied on letters (but even his revised correspondent letters show hesitation like he's holding back some terrible secret - that he loves her). Eventually, her age catches up to her. She didn't remember that the paints she put in each painting were precious reminders / memories of the time she spent with Jack, until they've all been used up in her artworks. Even then, to Amber the paints were more meaningful on the canvas than they were bottled within their tubes. When her senile dementia goes in full force, her memories were to the happiest times in her life, that being the finest scenery, the time where she painted and pursued art with Jack in the purest form without the turmoils of favouritism, office politics and messy human affairs. Or perhaps, to admire each other as muses from afar is her own idea of love.On the other hand, you have Jack, the hopeless romantic who's already had commitments. He has cats to care for, bills to pay, too much baggage to let go and pursue a life with Amber. He admires her, thinks of her fondly to the extent that he remembers Amber's face, in her prime, perhaps to immortalise the version of her he cherishes the most, the version as his companion in drawing. To choose between the cats or the free-spirited Amber, he chose to minimise the pain he would cause by caring for the cats - even if he were to live in poverty, the cats must luxuriate on delicious canned food. Deep down, Jack yearns for a shared life, a family, a deeper connection with Amber, a life that was not to be, for none can tame the wind. In doing so, however, he bottles up his feelings and deprioritises his own humanity, putting himself in pain, preserving the paint in his tubes and going without bringing his palette when drawing the snowy scene. For if you truly love something, you would set it free... yet all too common we forget the survivorship bias behind the quote. Too easily do we overlook the pain of loneliness that, though imagined, is just as powerful as real pain. At least Biscuit's with him, and at the very least he can put down that baggage and finally face art honestly by Amber's side by the end of the story like a cathartic graduation from pain and trauma.Artworks are often burdened with untold pain, untold stories too difficult to capture in words. Amber sought to maximise pleasure, Jack sought to minimise pain, and though their paths crossed for a while it's not likely they'll meet ever again. It's a shame because I think they could have developed as pretty decent lovers, with them sharing a kiss in Fluge and all.One can only hope for a happier fate, one in which their love for each other becomes realised, an alternate reality where they can find joy and inspiration springing from each other on a daily basis.I guess it's time for me to hope for Taiwanese fan-fiction coupling the two of them together.

_childDocuments_.review: Behind The Frame The Finest Scenery is a short point-and-click puzzle adventure with painting elements. It’s sweet, beautiful and original, but is it a masterpiece?When the game starts you’ll immediately be painting a few strokes on your canvas with the help of your mouse. Except you only have the color yellow at your disposal at the moment; the rest of the needed colors are, somehow, lost at the moment. So time to look around your apartment where pretty much the entire games also takes place.In your apartment there are lots of items; some that can be clicked on for a little background story and others that can be interacted with for some seemingly casual fun at first, but these usually turn out to be part of a puzzle later on. The rest is basically just decoration. The apartment can be looked through in 360 degrees by using your mouse.There are six more colors you need to find in order to finish your painting - purple being the most wanted and needed color - and these are usually related to solving puzzles. Easy in the beginning, and they can get mildly difficult later on, but never truly difficult. The solutions are usually only a few feet away since it almost all takes place in the apartment anyhow, or you can find help and solutions in your notebook/sketchbook that automatically keeps track of everything you see and do. This includes your neighbor and cat from a different apartment building next door that will tie in to the story in unexpected ways. But usually the puzzles consist of finding notes (or similar items) and finishing paintings hanging around in your apartment.Solving puzzles and doing simple tasks is sometimes rewarded with a nice and simple, but beautifully animated cutscene. These feel cozy, even if they’re not always there to advance the story. Think of something like drinking a cup of coffee and looking out of the window after you’ve just made one. It’s such a simple thing, but little touches like this give the game its own personality. It would’ve stood out way less without them; it just would’ve been another puzzle game to many of us. Including me. Even though painting is the most important aspect of the game here; it’s a fun mechanic. The puzzles are just there for entertainment and for the story.You’ve probably noticed by now that I haven’t really talked about the story and that’s intentional. This is yet another one of those short games where the less is said about it the better. If you ever decide to give this a try I’m sure you’ll agree with me. Some of the last few minutes are absolutely gorgeous and beautiful.The game has six chapters in total, lasting about 60-90 minutes.Visually the game is gorgeous with lots of colors while still making it feel like a natural environment. It feels a bit like something taken out of an anime scene. So lots of detailed objects and all in 2D (or made to look like 2D).With the exception of a few simple catchphrases there’s no voice acting. Everything is told with subtitles and by reading from your notebook/sketchbook. The sound effects are limited and the music is relaxing with every day having a new instrumental song (I think?). The end credits contain a song with vocals. It's quite nice.I had one game breaking issue happen to me twice where I couldn’t move the mouse when looking from SPOILER! the inside-the-painting perspective, locking the ability to progress. Opening up the menu by pressing Escape and then returning fixed the issue.In the end I think Behind The Frame The Finest Scenery is a mighty fine game with an original way to tell a story. To be honest I haven't really seen anything like it before. At least, not in this way. I wouldn't go as far as to call it a Mona Lisa, but it comes close. It’s definitely one of the higher quality paintings out there, metaphorically speaking of course, and that’s absolutely nothing to be ashamed of. Considering the asking price this is an easy recommendation for sure. Beautiful!

_childDocuments_.review: Before anything else I have to say this game is BEAUTIFUL! No matter what I say about this game, good or bad, its absolutely gorgeous. To start, I will list a few things you should know about this game before you buy it.1. It has a start and an end so it's not like you can play it endlessly. It took me about 1-2 hours to complete.2. It's very structured in the sense that you don't just do whatever you want, it gives you hints and clues as to what you're supposed to do.3. You can replay the game but it will be exactly the same every time, so once you play it, that's how it'll go every time you replay it.4. Its not just about painting. It's a mix of painting and using clues to solve a kind of story/mystery.5. If you haven't already, I highly recommend playing the demo (I did) first to give you a feel of how the game is going to be. However, keep in mind that the demo is only chapter 1 so it has more painting and less clues/mystery than the later chapters.6. Lastly, as I'm writing this the game is $12.99 USD( plus 82 cents tax for me) and there are 6 chapters which means each chapter ends up being about $2.30 each, so make sure it's worth it to you.On to what I like about this game.1. The story. not only is it beautifully illustrated but it has some twists and surprises towards the end that leave you, in a way, trying to figure out what just happened. I think I understand the ending but I could be totally wrong.2. The "mystery". I say "mystery" because I'm not quite sure how to describe it but it was fun deciphering each clue and having it lead you to the next one.3. The music. The music is generally enjoyable with a mix of classical and elevator jazz, not distracting yet nice to fill the silence.Here's what I didn't really like about it.1. Choice is very limited. Throughout the entire game you have to just do what it's hinting at which I didn't love but I suppose that's just personal preference.2. The length of the game. I did know going in that it wasn't going to be very long but I do wish that it didn't go by so fast, and it's definitely the kind of game you start and finish in a day. It's quite nice for a cozy day at home. All that being said, I realize that it takes a lot of time and effort to make games and they did a very good job. Finally, I'll end this by saying this game was fun to play and well made, and all things considered I would recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Be Warned: Spoilers Contained Below...This game strikes a unique chord with me when I play it, and as such I have gone back and forth quite a bit when considering my rating.  Were it possible on Steam, I would simply leave a written review without a recommendation one way or another.On the one hand, the game itself plays well.  It is visually striking, and both the art style and the narrative of the piece may resonate with any fans of late-era Studio Ghibli.  Similarly the puzzles, which all seem to be memory based, are well done, even if they are painfully simple.That said, the narrative seems to romanticize what I refer to as "the artist's sacrifice", namely the protagonist's sacrifice of her relationship with the deuteragonist, which, as can be seen in the epilogue/hidden chapter, haunts him for the rest of his life.  Even Amber, towards the end, seems to lament (or at least still be pained by) this decision as she sheds a tear before the portrait of her that Jack painted.  I am not saying that the decision to sacrifice something, even romance, for your art is wrong, but I am hesitant to romanticize such decisions.  A choice such as that carries tremendous weight, and, in my opinion, should be considered carefully.  Romanticizing such a thing can provide a convenient escape for people who do not want to confront such a difficult decision directly.  This avoidance can be particularly problematic, even irresponsible, when the hearts of others are involved.Of course, this is just my interpretation of the piece.  Perhaps the story is not meant to romanticize sacrifice at all.  Perhaps the intention is to draw attention to just how broadly the strokes of one's decisions can impact another person.  Perhaps it is simply a reflection on the nature of life in which every decision leaves unanswered questions, and how we can all be haunted by our own "what-ifs".  Whatever the case, there is no doubt that the story contained within this game is a tragic one, and it succeeds in stirring up heartache and frustration within those with whom the story resonates.  The narrative is incomplete without it's epilogue, so be sure to play both the main game, as well as Jack's chapter once unlocked.Visually striking, emotionally evocative, and heartrending to the core.   is the best game I will never play again.

_childDocuments_.review: A prime definition of "style over substance" that shows that the game designers have the knowledge of portraying emotional imagery through painting but failing at applying game mechanics to truly makes those emotions come through. Clearly inspired by Hayao Miyazaki and traditional East-Asian animation, Behind the Frame tells the tale of a young painter and her life through paintings. It features absolutely gorgeous animated surroundings and interactive animations with a peaceful score in the background. The problem lies in the main theme that also is meant to be the main mechanic: painting. The freedom of painting is constricted to extremely simplified puzzles that doesn't allow for any creativity or experimentation of any kind, but rather merely paint according to instructions (which barely allows you to even paint at all). The puzzles don't exist to widen the theme but merely are obstacles to progress the story. While the individual paintings are nice, the mechanics are so bare-bone that any required interactivity becomes a bore, making the Player endlessly await the next gorgeous cutscene. The game also suffers from exposition overload by including the characters thought-process at the bottom of the scene, taking every emotional moment and overexplaining it and not letting the images flow on their own (the opposite of the styles of Miyazaki for example). In short, it's a beautiful tale hindered by a flawed concept that makes the magic of painting dull.

You are often locked to one view but they use it wisely and you can interact with many things in the scene. It is cool seeing your environment change as you work through it. _childDocuments_.review: I open my eyes. A canvas is in front of me. Sweet, I can draw some stuff.Nope, there is a pre-drawn draft to follow and no matter what you draw, the final painting ends up the same.I stand up, realizing I run out of paints. Should I go get some new paints?Nope, there is a to-do list, and buying new paints is not on that list.I walk around and make myself a breakfast. I want double side eggs.No can do. A single sunny side up is all you get.I put some elevator music tape in some old ass cassette player. It starts playing and becomes annoying real fast. Please stop.No, no no no. You don't get it. Once the music is on, it stays ON.I look down. I have this seemingly highly important resume to finish. Let's work on...NO. ON. NOON. Forget about it. It's not your concern anyway.------------------So. In a mere 10 minute time span, I have been constantly reminded that this is not my embodiment, not my home, and not my story to be in. I better head out, and I did.------------------Point & click games can easily be a hit or miss experience. I think what makes the genre popular back in the days is making clicking on the screen a genuinely enjoyable experience. Think  series, where every object on the screen is interactable and every scene fun to watch. Or what keeps the genre still alive today, the dialogues, monologues or even puzzles should be thought provoking for a mind to dwell with, while clicking from one object to the next. The in between such as this game leaves too much to be desired for me to care about the story behind the scene. It is to the point that I have to raise this question: What story telling purposes does making a player make breakfast and coffee in a game serve, other than training them to click on shiny objects on the screen?

_childDocuments_.review: I installed this game expecting relaxing gameplay and I was not disappointed; rather, it exceeded my expectations in this short interactive point-and-click story. Behind the Frame: The Finest Scenery tells a beautiful and compelling story despite taking less than two hours to fully complete the game with all the achievements. You take upon the role of a young lady who is an aspiring artist, aiming to have her piece shown in an exhibition. The game tells her story, along with her interest in the skilful painter in the building opposite her split into multiple short chapters. The game includes an added DLC, which will show up in the main menu underneath the title upon completion of the base game. The base game came to a bittersweet conclusion which I enjoyed greatly, and in combination with the ending of the DLC it brought me to a feeling of wholesomeness, and contentment. For a game with less than 2 hours of content, there was nothing more I could ask for. The story did not seem forced, it did not appear to be abruptly brought to an end, and it was not dragged out. It was phenomenal, and enjoyable the whole way through before coming to a touching close.  Being a mobile game ported to PC, the controls were very simple and easy to get a hold of. This made it very accessible and relaxing. Having not really had any prior knowledge about the game (I hadn't read the synopsis or the tags, I simply just saw the title and quickly clicked through the images on the store page), I found out that it was a puzzle game.  The puzzles are quite simple, not requiring too much thought into it, and is quite instinctive.  I did struggle at one point to figure out what to do next in one point, and could not find the answer to one puzzle, so I ended up brute forcing it, so it may lack some clarity at times (or it could just be at the fault of the player). One thing though, is that I would have liked to have been able to access the settings of the game while in a chapter, rather than only in the main menu. However, overall the gameplay was very calming and pleasant (you can also pet the cat).  Graphically, Behind the Frame: The Finest Scenery is phenomenal. The art is incredible, very reminiscent of Studio Ghibli type art for the cutscenes and it was lovely to look at. While sketching during the game, the artwork was also beautiful and intricate. For the artworks that you paint during the game, it is relatively simple, I would have liked more fleshed out pieces to paint, however, everything else was fantastic.  The soundtrack for this game is remarkable. The music was very soothing and gentle, I loved it. I originally had my own music playing over the game, but once I heard the music kick in, I turned my music off and enjoyed the experience to its fullest. I did not enjoy the voice acting so much, as it seemed minimal and there were only minor comments made by the protagonist. I would rather the voice acting be done throughout the whole game, or not at all. I was, however, very fond of the soundtrack and the sound design of the game.  Due to the game being very linear, with not much freedom with different endings or actions, I don't believe the game to be very replayable, I only did so to attain all of the achievements. Potentially once in a while if you'd like to revisit the experience, however in itself, it does not have much replayability. I loved Behind the Frame: The Finest Scenery. It was a short game, but it had beautiful graphics, accompanied with a delightful soundtrack and sound design. Behind the Frame is a very chill game to play to wind down, with a short yet sweet story, as well as an included DLC from the perspective of a different character to make it all the more interesting. For those interested in a wholesome, casual one to two hour gaming session, I would most definitely recommend this. Make yourself a coffee, sit down and enjoy.

_childDocuments_.review: Bought this little gem on sale a few months ago and only got around to playing it a few days ago. It's a short and bittersweet game, can be easily finished in a few hours even when going at your own pace, about a young woman, a painter, living in her apartment. An old man, also a painter, lives in the apartment across from her but never looks at her. Soon enough the game has you solving puzzles, unlocking new colours for the woman's painting and slowly giving you more and more information about your elderly neighbour. It's a very short game, as mentioned before, but one that is well worth its price. The art-style will melt your heart, everything looks so damn good and the Ghibli-esque animations will capture your heart if the rest of the game's aesthetic has not already. If this game had just been an interactive film with these same animations, I would've still bought it. Some of the scenery in Behind the Frame also heavily reminded of me Howl's Moving Castle.The gameplay is very much point-and-click, but it fits the vibe. The puzzles are really not too hard, some take a few tries to get right but there's enough of a problem-solving element to make it fun and captivating. The game really shines with its lovely, touching story though, which will be sure to at least make you choke up a tiny bit. I know it did that for me.At an extremely reasonable price of £7.19, this game is very much worth buying. Look forward to what else this studio has in store!

_childDocuments_.review: 1.9h (100% achievement, finished the game) 1.5h No. Yes (~13 achievements). No. is an interactive fiction with puzzle elements in it. You'll watch a story, displayed in anime-like visuals while trying to solve puzzles in point-and-click style in between. It has 6+1 chapters in total, all of which can be completed in a short time.- Smooth animation- Clever puzzles that utilize the use of paintings- Story that you experience with emotions rather than dialogues- Unable to speed up the game for the second playthrough- The letter detection system in the last chapter is off- Some parts in the earlier chapter can feel repetitiveIntel Core i5-9300H 2.40GHz, 8GB RAM, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650 makes you feel as if you are watching an anime while playing. Animations look smooth, although in the point-and-click sections, some objects can be differentiated easily from the backgrounds. Not that I'm complaining since I like to see all interactable objects on the screen, which the game doesn't have, though.You'll play as a woman who is trying to figure out someone else's past. This means that the story won't be spoonfed to you; instead, you'll have to figure it out based on pieces of facts that are scattered throughout the chapters. The story becomes open to interpretation, which for me, hits me more emotionally than if it was told in full. I like how the storytelling was done, to be honest. It feels as if you are the main character since you have to deduce what happened on your own, bit by bit. There are some fantasy elements in the story, but I don't really mind with it.  is played similarly to point-and-click games. You'll have to figure out what to do to progress the story, which can be done by interacting with other objects in the area. The puzzles are mostly related to painting and are easy to figure out, although there are also some in the latter part of the story that can be confusing unless you know what to do. Sadly, there is no hint system or whatsoever to help you in case you are stuck.Most of the time, you'll be doing sketches. You'll either have to color your painting or do a sketch with your pencil, all of which require you to drag your mouse around in a select area. I like how easy it is to paint and/or sketch everything, although the one part where you have to draw letters in the last chapter gave me trouble since it hardly detects what I wrote.There is no backtracking. Well, it's kinda understandable given how the game works, but it's still a bummer for achievement hunters. I had to replay a chapter once because I missed some achievements midway and had to restart the chapter from the beginning. Luckily, there is a chapter select, but you can't speed up the cutscenes or the dialogues. I finished the game in 1.5h. I then replayed the last, bonus chapter again to get the missing achievements. Some puzzles can leave you stuck for some minutes, but it's nothing difficult as long as you pay attention to the story.To be honest, there isn't much to say about this game. It's a short, beautiful game that makes you feel as if you are watching an anime. I couldn't stop saying how beautiful it is because that's the fact. The puzzles themselves are easy, and those who like to play games for the emotional aspect will enjoy it more. However, the asking price might be way too much compared to the playtime it offers (less than 2h), so I suggest buying it at a sale instead.

_childDocuments_.review: Behind the Frame is a game with beautiful graphics and a story worthy of an animated film. However, I have mixed feelings about it because I believe that presenting it as a PC game was not the most suitable choice.Graphics and Story:The graphics are stunning, creating a truly visual experience. The story is captivating and could easily be adapted into an animated film. The artistic qualities of the game are undeniable.Gameplay Experience:Unfortunately, Behind the Frame offers a limited gameplay experience. Interactions with objects are minimal, and the puzzles are simplistic. Moreover, the game is extremely short. I was able to complete it in less than 1 hour and 30 minutes. This very short playtime is disappointing.Replayability and Value:In my humble opinion, this game would have been better suited for a mobile platform or could have been transformed into an exciting animated film. As a PC game, it lacks replayability. The absence of additional content or elements that encourage replaying the game is regrettable. The initial price of $11 that I paid for the game felt too high for the limited content it offers, leading me to request a refund.Overall, I give it a negative rating. While the game boasts stunning graphics and a captivating story, it suffers from a lack of content, limited interactivity, and an extremely short playtime. I believe the game would have benefited from a different approach. If you are looking for a game with high replayability and more substantial content, I suggest looking elsewhere.

_childDocuments_.review: As a lover of immersive storytelling and captivating visuals, I recently had the pleasure of experiencing "Behind the Frame," and let me just say, it's an absolute gem in the world of indie gaming.From the moment I delved into the enchanting world crafted by the talented team at Silver Lining Studio, I was spellbound. The game effortlessly weaves together a touching narrative with stunning hand-painted visuals, creating an experience that feels like stepping into a living, breathing work of art.At its core, "Behind the Frame" is a story about creativity, passion, and the beauty of human connection. Through the eyes of a budding artist, players embark on a journey of self-discovery as they navigate the complexities of life, love, and art. Along the way, they'll encounter charming characters, each with their own unique stories to share, adding depth and richness to the world.What truly sets "Behind the Frame" apart is its innovative gameplay mechanics. The clever use of perspective puzzles adds an extra layer of immersion, allowing players to interact with the environment in creative ways that feel both intuitive and satisfying. Whether it's rearranging objects in a cluttered studio or piecing together a forgotten memory, every puzzle feels like a natural extension of the narrative, seamlessly blending gameplay and storytelling into a cohesive whole.Of course, none of this would be possible without the game's breathtaking visuals and enchanting soundtrack. From the vibrant streets of the city to the tranquil solitude of the artist's studio, every scene is rendered with meticulous attention to detail, inviting players to lose themselves in a world of color and imagination. And the hauntingly beautiful score, composed by the talented team at Triodust, serves as the perfect accompaniment to the journey, evoking a wide range of emotions from joy to melancholy.In the end, "Behind the Frame" isn't just a game – it's an experience. It's a reminder that sometimes, the most profound moments in life can be found in the simplest of pleasures: a brushstroke on a canvas, a shared laugh with a friend, or a fleeting moment of inspiration. So if you're looking for a game that will touch your heart, stimulate your mind, and leave you with a newfound appreciation for the beauty of the world around you, look no further than "Behind the Frame." It's a true work of art in every sense of the word.

_childDocuments_.review: The game lasts only two hours, but how much this intense playing time remains in the heart. A touching story about drawing pictures, feelings, the importance of the moment and the importance of a cat. Perhaps due to its compact duration, or maybe due to the skill of the scriptwriters, the game does not out of tune in any of its notes, concentrating on pure emotion. It turns out that for a beautiful ending, you don't need someone to die from an incurable disease, you don't need fanfare and applause, just a quiet look at the paintings and brushes with the name is enough. The gameplay includes interacting with the paintings and solving puzzles (even if there are not so many of them as we would like) with wonderful unforgettable music.The work of the designers is phenomenal, the visual in the game is so juicy that you want to bite off a piece of it, that's it. so smoothly and in detail, it is pleasant to look at what is happening. This is the case when quality is much more important than quantity, and the fantastic journey that this game gives you will be remembered for a very long time.

_childDocuments_.review: Big disappointment :(    (spoilers ahead /!\)I was so excited to play this game due to super positive reviews and the fact that I love indie games of this kind; however the game didn't live up to my expectations. If it was a bad game without any "soul" or talent behind, I would'nt have written this comment. The animation and the drawings are amazing, and it shows that the team was really into this project, and that's why I am upset. They missed an incredible opportunity of creating a short film; there's not really a gameplay and the puzzles are too easy, even a young child can do it. I know, the point is to feel and discover the story, but the clues (to the story not the puzzles) are given so easely I knew what happend since the begining of chapter 2. My point is that it doesn't really feel like a game, more like (as I said) a short film, and the gameplay could have been more interesting with harder puzzlesSpoilers for the story here !!:The saddest thing here is the story: it hint since the begining that the 2 characters knew each other and had some kind of a relationship (confirmed at the end or just in the whole game) and Amber (the protagonist) doesn't remember any of it; the supposed husband is an old man that ignores or doesn't seem to see Amber. All of it can make us come to the conclusion that Amber is dead and her ghost couldn't move past that (or something like that). Furthermore, in the 5th chapter, it looks like the reality around Amber begin to shift and she appears to be in a sort a purgatory to confront what happend with her past/husband/New york exhibition and her (logicaly) death. But no, it just confirms that yeah, her husband is/was/will be (????) the neighbor and she sees her old self in front of her husband exhibition and the credits are rolling. So many questions unanswered : why can't the dude see her? why is she seeing her past/future/present (I don't even know) and hallucinate paintings? Why doesn't she remember anything ?? I know some stories need/can let some things in the vague, and let people think about it, but not the main plot that the game wants us to know ?? I really don't know the story of the game, not because I didn't discovered some secret info, but because the game teased us a story that doesn't really have an end. If I missed some critical notes (it doesn't seem like the case) my bad but the key point of a video game story shouldn't be in a missable note !!! But I will give credit when credit is due: as I said, the drawings are amazing; it seems straight up from a ghibli movie, the colors are vibrant, the environnement is breathtaking and the musique is just so immersive. I loved the passage in the 5th chapter where you go into the frame and stand in the painting; for exemple in the purple field. And that's why I am so disappointed: there is SO MUCH wasted potential; so many good ideas that were not developped, a story that isn't well explained (and sometime it's to much explained as the main character insist on "oh I wonder who put that here" or "oh who is in that painting ?" whereas it's litteraly her) and certain cool gameplay mecanics that appears in the first chapter then dip in the others. In my opinion, this is a problem of platform: this story wasn't really made for a video game; it would have work perfectly in a short animation film, it really would have been a masterpiece. If you wanna buy this game, or you bought it and loved it, there is absolutly no problem, it's just my personnal opinion. Another thing : 1 hour of """""gameplay""""" for 9$ with a story that could have been explained in 5minutes isn't really something that I like. The team did an incredible job (no hate for them of course), just some mistakes that ruined the experience for me; I still liked the game, just think it was really disappointing for every price awarded and the reviews saying this is the most incredible indie game ever made. I hope this review helped in someways !notes => sorry if there is some mistakes, I am not a native english speaker

_childDocuments_.review: Behind the Frame: The Finest Scenary is a visual novel about two people who bond over sharing a love of art. You play as the painter Amber, though there is also a section where you get to play as Jack, and you learn their story of how they met, their friendship and what led them to part ways. You collect colors along the way that you use to complete each painting. While doing so, you are rewarded with more clues as to what happened between the relationship of Amber and Jack. The soundtrack will make you feel very relaxed too and everything is lyrical and poetic about the tone of the game. There will be many puzzles involved where you can take everything at your own pace to figure out where you need to go next. It doesn't feel frustrating because the music that is playing is always calm and will accompany you with a relaxing puzzle-solving experience.The visuals are breathtaking and beautiful and if you are someone who is into that, character narrative and interpersonal relationships between characters and you are also a fan of arts, then this game is definitely one for you ^^

_childDocuments_.review: “Behind the Frame” is a cute and very relaxing art game. You dabble a lot with painting pictures, have to solve some easy puzzles and follow the story of two talented painters with their unfulfilled love-story. This is a good-natured game that left me with an overall feeling of pleasant warmth. The weaker points of “Behind the Frame” are some repetitive game elements in the first chapters (you have to prepare breakfast and coffee three times in exactly the same way) and I feel the price is a bit steep for a game that I could finish twice and get all the achievements within 4,6 hours. So if it is on sale and you like this type of game you should go for it.

_childDocuments_.review: When i picked this game for the fact that it looked chill to play, i was not expecting the amount of quality that was put into this. The game is a simple point and click game, not alot of difficult puzzles since it felt like it just flowed easily into place for the most part. The story tells a tale of a up and coming painter whos looking to get known in the world, painting masterpieces, all the while keeping an eye on her neighbor who has his own story mixed in that the painter will soon come to realise. The animations in the game was breathtaking, i was not expecting it to be so incredible, it was like a mix of anime but also at the same time, one of them old silent film movies where if a person spoke, the screen would go black with the persons message, and i like that as it makes it really unique. The soundtrack was calm and soothing to listen to, and at one point a lil mysterious. While i did only one casual playthough from start to end, i did not earn every achievement *because i'm not into such things, i'm more into stories*, however there are alot of hidden achievements that'll be tricky to find. My only complaint would be its not a long game, but that itself is alright, not all stories needs to be hours upon hours long, sometimes the best stories, like this one, can be short but sweet.While the game can be short, the amazing work that has gone into this game is well worth full price in my opinion, that and with the quality of the animations, i would love to see it be turned into a anime or a movie, i think it has soo much potential. I've played many games this year, but i would have to say that this game, even if it was short but sweet, would have to be my game of the year~

_childDocuments_.review: For artists, visually or musically. Will always have a story behind its piece. You always wonder what goes through an artists mind when you find a particular illustration or song that resonates with you. At times, you find yourself listening to a song or looking at a picture, and all of a sudden, you instantly receive a flashback of a particular time in your life. Whatever emotion that memory holds, it will always be a memory you're fond of. Be it a memory of a past relationship with someone dear, or simpler days where the expectations of the world didn't weigh upon you as much. Though I believe that's the best part, it's cemented for the rest of your life. It may be a famous piece that people will one day browse at an art museum, or a song that many others will listen to online or on the radio. Then, there's always those that will never see the recognition it  truly deserves. Though the game was short, it did bring a tear to my eye. The art style is definitely inspired by works from Studio Ghibli. The puzzles weren't too difficult and weren't that straight forward. Those with photographic memory will prosper aha. I hope to see more completed titles from Silver Lining studio in the future. What would the world be without Art?

_childDocuments_.review: During my play through, another game came to mind. The Graveyard, a game where you play as an old lady walking around a graveyard. It truly was a revolting game, I don't know how you make a game that simple run so badly.So why am I bringing up  a really ♥♥♥♥♥♥ and kind of pretentious game? Well, because it advertised itself as an "explorable painting rather than a game". And that's kinda what Behind the Frame is.  It's an explorable painting with so many tiny details and artistic value put into it.Let us forget the Graveyard and never think about it again. Behind the Frame is a very good game. It's a point and click game where you paint. It's easy, fast, and responsive. I found great joy when my barrage of scribbles just suddenly transformed a very well drawn umbrella. Which I suppose is a plus, you don't really need to draw anything as the game knows what you're doing. The only time it was an issue was near the end of the game where you needed to write some letters. No matter how much I tried it would not register and then I just drew a a black square and the game was like  "ah yes, this is the letter A".There's a lot of puzzles(duh), it's how you advance the story, and I mean, they're kinda easy but maybe that's just me though, since I have a galaxy level gigabrain. It's certainly not a detriment against game, a lot of these puzzles are cleverly laid out, and they're chill. The whole game is chill.So basically, the animation. It's very good. Really good, paired with the cute art style and beautiful background art. II won't speak about the story since it's better to see it first hand, but it was sweet. I'm sure someone will cry because of it. Not me since I'm a manly man who eats bricks. But even a brick eater like me can realize what a heartful tale this is.Behind the Frame: The Finest Landscape, which, by the way,  why the colon. Both titles work fine on their own. My guess is the devs just couldn't decide which one to use. Anyway, it's very good. Short and memorable, and it was worth my money and time.

_childDocuments_.review: We as humans tend to dwell on death and what lies beyond. It's only natural as we simply don't know. Behind the Frame explores this concept with an emotional tug-of-war of a story, but you really need to pay attention, and a lot of the story is more between the lines and not what's really being shown in front of you. There's a lot of assumption that you know what's happening when the main character looks shockingly off in the distance based on the previous scene. It's done fairly well too.Most of Behind the Frame is puzzle solving. It takes a dark twist halfway through and it surprised me. Your goal is to acquire all five missing colors on your paint palette to finish your painting. To do this each color is locked away behind a chapter puzzle. These got rather complex towards the end, but nothing you can't figure out without exploring and finding that key item that gives you that "AHA!" moment. Some puzzles are as simple as matching colors on a painting to memorization. Nothing is overly complex and it does eventually come together. The painting itself is a matter of scribbling enough in the empty space and it will auto-fill. Nothing extraordinary there. There are some other small tasks like making food which is as simple and dragging items around.There isn't a lot of context on the main character's life itself through any reading of notes or anything. It's pretty much learning about her past and her connection with her neighbor. The game has gorgeous anime-Ghibli-inspired art with a few small cut scenes thrown in. I never got tired of looking at the game, but it is confined to mostly her apartment. Every so often you "dive" into a painting, but it's usually just for story context. There were a few panoramic scenes that were breathtaking. I actually felt like I stepped into a painting myself a few times.In the end, the game is over in about 90 minutes or less depending on how long it takes you to solve the more complex puzzles in the final chapters. Without having to solve these this game is over in an hour. The story does unfold quite a bit towards the end and without voice acting it gets a lot of emotions across and I have to give the developers credit for that. Most of these short indie games don't have any meaning behind them. They have some clever gameplay ideas or neat visuals and nothing beyond that. Behind the Frame actually tugged at my heart strings a bit and got me thinking at the end which is more than I can say for 60-hour-long AAA titles. If you want a puzzle-filled emotional evening with great visuals and fun gameplay mechanics then look no further.

_childDocuments_.review: "Behind the Frame: The Finest Scenery" is a mobile app that's been dumped on Steam as if it was a real PC game (it's not)... it's a cash grab from greedy mobile devs.It's a point and click adventure mobile app interspersed with Taiwanese animation (in the Japanese anime style, I guess imitation is the highest form of flattery) and tells a whimsical story about an aspiring artist, her hopes and dreams, in a pleasant slice-of-life style that is a mainstay for a lot of professional animation.Before we get into the defects, which are few but enough to disqualify this as a PC game, it's worth mentioning that the story is good, the animation is top notch... and uh, we can get all of that from watching a YouTube playthrough of the game, so it's not going to factor heavily into the review, especially when gameplay is incredibly shallow and just exists to step you through to the next bit of story.   My gaming rig is not primarily intended for me to watch YouTube on.   YouTube, by the way, is free to watch... this free mobile app, however, will cost you money on PC.  Even though it's free on mobile. From a technical perspective, as a mobile app, this doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.There's no option to change the resolution and no useful graphics tweaks.  There's no way to ensure this is running at the native resolution of your display.  There's no guarantee this game will look right on any PC as a result of this hamfisted design decision.The controls can't be customised because the game has such a dumbed down, simplified interface that it's just iPhone screen tapping stuff.  The fact that the interface is this dumbed down might be seen as a problem in itself, however... this is a fairly shallow experience if you're the kind of gamer that likes to play games with deep, rich control schemes and interaction.  You'll get none of that here.Because this is a mobile app, it carries a number of deliberate design deficiencies.  Compromises were made to cater to the iPhones that the mobile app was designed for.  These are unfortunate handicaps and limitations that PC gamers shouldn't be forced to accept, but it's evident that PC was an afterthought for the iPhone developers who are to blame for this.  The mobile app is deficient as a result of these choices, and would have been so much better without the handicaps that designing games for mobile phones forces upon a game.  Once more, mobile devs have made gaming worse for everyone.  I didn't spend thousands on building a gaming rig just so I could pretend it's an iPhone.These technical defects push this mobile app below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.Once more we see greedy mobile devs trying to scam PC gamers. On Steam, this is $13 USD, on app stores, it's free. Mobile devs must learn PC gamers are not here to be gouged, and can't be expected to pay a premium for a free mobile app just because it's been lazily dumped on Steam.  This is unacceptable disrespect for PC gamers.For comparison, the $13 asking price for this mobile app on PC could get you games like "Project Zomboid", "Dead by Daylight" or "Rust".  That's right... if you want this game, you can go buy Dead By Daylight, .See why I must recommend against paying money for free mobile apps on Steam??Because this can be played free elsewhere, and because of the other defects, it's impossible to recommend.Who do they think we are?

_childDocuments_.review: First I want to say that the idea behind and the artistic style of this game are both very good. So, why cannot I recommend this game? Because in my option this shouldn't have become a game at all. Would the company have created  a 20 minute animated short film out of the story, chances are I would have liked it a lot!However they chose to make this a ~2 hour game, 30 minutes of which I spent trying to figure out why the game repeatedly hangs in the between-chapter cutszenes (see forum entries), which already spoiled most of the pleasure. Then there's about 10 minutes of cutscenes (which are just fine) and the rest is some crude painting and some "EXIT ROOM" style mini games, just so easy and with so many hints there's not a chance you can do them wrong. And no, baking toast and making coffee in a computer game is not exactly "fun" either, and it's mandatory.Besides this I must admit that I had to read some forum thread in order to  understand the story ... and usually I don't have that much trouble understanding short films.The music was very fitting and one of the good aspects of this art piece.Short game short: If you like interactive, twisted stories, like to look at paintings and don't mind waiting and prefer relaxing games over mind-boggingly ones, this can be a good choice. But if you are looking for a challenging fun game, there are many better ones out there, even with equally good story and art style.P.S. I'll never understand why some game makers require you to press a button or click somewhere just to make the main menu appear. As if the start screen is sooo much nicer with a text like "Press here to start" than with the menu itself.P.P.S. If you like paintings and interesting stories, you might want want to have a look at "Eastshade". I very much enjoyed that game and in "Eastshade" you can at least choose yourself (most of the time) what to paint. Also it's much longer and a feast for the eyes as well.

_childDocuments_.review: Behind the Frame is a story-driven point-and-click game with light puzzle elements.The narration is done through texts, stunning visuals, and paintings.You may consider this more of an interactive story that can be completed in one sitting (around 2 hours).The art style and animation are top-notch. It's worth playing for that.The story is quite emotional. The timeline seemed messed up. And it's possible that you may not understand what's going on in the first place since there is no explanation given. So, it relies on the player's imagination and ingenuity.The story reminded me of the movie "La La Land." It felt like the theme was inspired by it (intentionally or not, I don't know). But I expected a different ending (a bit let down by it).The music tracks catch the various moods perfectly. The sound design is also on point.So many of the achievements don't make that much sense. So, you may need a guide to get them. But it's easy to get them through "the chapter select" after completing the game.Also, there is a short DLC that can be played after finishing the game. Nice addition, and quite important to understand the story.I'll recommend getting it at a discounted price if you are looking for an interactive story-like game (Duration: 1 to 2 hours).My verdict: 7/10

_childDocuments_.review: Sound, images, words. This is a game that has been carefully, lovingly crafted in every nook and cranny, so that everything works together to immerse you in the cosy, cluttered apartment of a young artist whose world you inhabit. She stares at a large canvass which you must help her finish, over the course of the days to come. You are quickly enlisted into her daily routine; find a cassette and put on some music; fry an egg for breakfast; make the morning coffee; get a bit further with completing her resume and application for the art exhibition. Then the day’s painting must commence. The way the routine repeats each day until it becomes a familiar ritual creates a peaceful, calming backdrop which, for me, evoked something of the experience of lockdown; the artist, alone in her flat with her daily routine and work to immerse herself in; glimpses through her window of the sad, solitary man who lives in the apartment opposite and who also seems to paint; the sleepy presence of a cat who acts as a bridge between the two in the absence of any spoken contact or communication.Each day you paint a little more, but then the direction of travel starts to veer off in unexpected, mysterious directions. The comfortable routine which has been so carefully established to the point that the player is expertly racing through each item (eggs, check; coffee, check; morning sketches, check) starts to be subverted as fragments of a totally different narrative start to emerge. It is like the process by which layers of paint are painstakingly scraped away from a canvass to reveal a different, startling image, related to the first but representative of the artist’s original intentions. The true image which starts to emerge is one of love, loss, and the recovery of memory. Plenty of space is left for the player to interpret exactly what everything means, but clues and suggestions are littered around both the apartment and the wider scenes and spaces from the past which we start to visit. As you piece together the mystery and reassemble the full picture of events, the puzzles are unlikely to impede you for long; frustration rarely builds, and the pervading atmosphere of cosy calm never really departs. Part game, part interactive narrative-audio story experience, Behind the Frame is a magical and peaceful world to immerse yourself in for the several hours it will take to complete.

_childDocuments_.review: Played a game that felt exactly like watching an anime? Meet Behind the Frame, a wonderfully drawn, animated, and sound tracked game with a very beautiful story. In Behind the Frame, you play a painting student going through the normal routine of every day life, until an event/encounter causes you to discover that not everything is at it seems. It's a journey of happiness, discovery, pain, and nostalgia, rolled into a few hours of gameplay.The game is a puzzle click-through where you have to complete certain tasks in order to unlock and move onto the next scene. Some tasks involve simply clicking things in the right order, others require you to find hidden objects and connect them to certain pieces, some involve a little artistry (you do play a painter!); all of it as a means of going through the story. Behind the Frame has a really beautiful soundtrack to accompany the scenes, done to match the emotions and flow of the story. The artwork is also breathtaking because it is reminiscent of something from Studio Ghibli in some parts, but then shifts to a watercolor-like or painting scenario the next. You can see that a lot of effort was put into each scene and each act in the game, and they put a lot of detail into even the littlest of things.It's hard not to appreciate or love a game that one can feel they can relate to, even if the game can be played in about 1-2 hours only.Pros: Great artwork, story, and soundtrack. Cons: The game is short. Right as you feel you start to feel emotionally invested, it ends. Also, certain parts of the game aren't clear about how to move on or what the next step is. Some click-guessing may be involved. I had to close and restart the game because the game hanged.Still, a great game to try. But best to purchase this on sale since it doesn't take long to complete.

_childDocuments_.review: The visuals are nice and reminiscent of the animation works of Studio Ghibli and are definitely the highlight of the game, the background music is very chill and soothing, the atmosphere is neat. The gameplay was....meh. It was okay for a two hour indie game and i liked that there were more puzzles than i anticipated, but it was nothing too memorable and engaging.However, there were a few things that made me dislike the game.First, it isnt a very long game. So there definitely was room for voice acting. I understand that when a game is very long or has a load of text, you dont want to invest in a voice actor. BUT interestingly, there IS some voice acting. Everytime something happens or you interact with objects, your character will say "Oh", "Aah", "Hmm", "Wow", "Weeell". And it was....so....effing....annoying. It actually made me put down my headphones after ten minutes and play the game without sound. I know i could have disabled the "voice acting" in the options, but it infuriated me enough to just simply dont play with any of it. Like seriously, instead of those redundant interjections the voice actress could have been used to speak meaningful lines.Second, there were lots of text bugs, where not even sometimes, but very often the text just wouldnt disappear. That perse be isnt a major problem, unless of course as long as there is text on the screen the game disallows you from interacting with objects. So you just sit there a whole minute or two, waiting for the text to disappear. Thank god i had a cup of tea to sip on. This nuisance actively discourages you from interacting with the game world.Third, and this is completely nitpicking a design choice and just for the achievement hunters out there. Some of the achievements are just....stupid. Click this painting ten times, walk up those stairs four times. Like, wtf? Ironically i did fulfill some of those requirements, where i would just randomly click on things a few times. But "OH NO!!, you only clicked that specific thing 100 times, not 101 times! Jokes on you!". What was the train of thought behind some of those decisions?Fourth, when you look around your apartment you technically dont stand in a rendered environment, but in a drawn frame. Which is consistent with the rest of the games art style. But it also means the objects and perspectives are all set, which isnt how we humans experience reality. Even the slightest tilt of your head will change how objects are oriented towards your eyes and each other relative to you. This resulted in me feeling some dizziness when looking around the appartment too fast, especially when searching for something on the floor or looking higher up towards the ceiling. However, i didnt see anyone else complain about this in the reviews, so i might be a 1% exception to this.Fifth, the story might be heartfelt and fundamentally a good take on the compromisses of life. And it is in fact executed pretty nicely! But, to my personal taste, it was way too depressing for me. After closing the game i felt some sort of relief that i could go back to my real life problems and not having to think about those fictional characters again, and that is usually not a good sign for the enjoyment of a game, or any story at that. But maybe i am too cynical in that regard.So all in all, Behind the Frame: The Finest Scenery is an okay indie game with all its heart in its art design and a nice concept for a story and gameplay loop. But some of the design choices and the execution of some technical realizations are done really poorly. There were way too many things that resulted in me abhorring this experience.
